Let me first off say, i was just having aconversation with my Girlfriend yesterday about the assassin's creed series being a bunch of rushed projects off the same cloth, given to us as a new game every year, with a bland, forgetful protag, (Minus Earlier renditions, First and Ezio's life and i suppose black flag.) with a bland, over the top "Stealth" mechanic that was more of "Why the hell would i sneak around when i can walk into a fortress and destroy everyone without much hesitiation?" So when i saw this on sale, i was looking to scratch an itch similar to the one you get after you assasinate one or two people. That bland, "It needs to be dead with some style". I expected to scratch it, get through about 30% of the game, and let it sink into my library, much like AC3, and the rest.
Now i'm going to tell you why most of the reviews and my first oppinion, were really, really wrong.
Know this is where assassin's creed SHOULD. have been years ago, There is a lot of decent moves forward for the genre here,"(Albiet forced co-op that can be fun, but mostly hurts your progression and an app thing thats plain blasphemy) Such as being able to scale down, acctually being able to crouch and move stealthfully by your self as oppsed to merrily jaunting "Stealth". and a new fighting mechanic that feels more personal and adds a bit of skill to what was a pretty wompus fighting system at the end.
The Graphics here are wonderful, after you see the intro, compared to the last entry before this one, i belive it was rouge, its a night and day difference, and you know that years down the road that you will be able to draw the line where the xbone and psuck stopped holding the damn series back graphically. The game looks wonderful and it's cities, people and fighting sequences impress, its the first game since AC2 where i could see a major graphic step, and also read faces as they should be read. I no longer feel like im playing "Protag of AC such and such" I'm Playing as Arno Dorian,
On that note, alot of flack coming to and about Arno's character, I have no reason why or how that was ever a thing, but Arno is a fantastic character COMPARED TO THE BLAND PROTAGS OF THE LAST 3 GAMES (excluding addon's and expansions and yaddayadda. but not really, they sucked too.) At least he has SOME semblance of back story, and whats this? He acctually doesn't start off as some whimsicall killing machine that some how skipped years and years of training to become a master assassin? Yeah. looking at you AC:BF. He is introduced to the assassin's in a pretty neat way, and earns his way up to master through the story and how much you apply skills that are common to the AC genre. he's a breath of fresh air, i feel like they borrowed from Ezio a bit, but at the same time i feel he is his own, so i don't regret throwing it out there that i genuinely like Arno's character.
The meat of the game is wonderful, the new system for getting up, down and round with your assass-creed-core running is nice and at least updated, i no longer feel (Most of the time) that i am running with some whimsical string tied around my hip and throwing me throught the air with my feet occasionally hitting a roof or something. It feels nice, i thourghly enjoy the idea that a button keeps me moving forward, down or up in a direction, it's not perfect, i'm not stating it its, but it is a step in the right direction. i appreciate the movement that should have been around a long time ago but, better late then never.
Customization. Theres a word we sometimes get with AC, some colors and some cool armor at the end. Customized. Not this time friends, this time you acctually get to pick what your assassin wears! If that doesn't some how excite you from what you were doing in previous AC games, well then this probablly isn't the game for you to begin with, but if you are still reading know that Arno is by far and large the most customizable assassin you have played yet and hosts a SLEW of ways to make him yours, its a neat thing that, like the rest of the things they added to unity, should have been there before, but better late then never.
TL;DR
Unity is a great step forward for the series, people are ♥♥♥♥♥ing and moaning that the protag is not an Edge-master-9000 or that co-op is lame, and pick apart what we all should be saying is a wonderful step forward for what was a stagnant series. So if you were like me and hesitant to come back to something that was dead, don't be, the sale is on, pick this up, and appreciate that things are being done to help out a dying breed. And you know, enjoy the game.

Wow what an insane game. I was already totally hyped about this one, since I love shmups and played other edelweiss productions already, I knew this will not turn out badly.
So first what makes it different than other shmups, you have a f*** big sword. It was the first shmups I played where you fight close combat.
At the beginning I was a little disoriented because most danmakus/bullet hell you have to evade the bullets, so every new game mechanic which involve you to "absorb" bullets makes the gameplay really interesting.
In addition I dislike the limited continue system in other shmups, these were acceptable in the arcade era but not nowadayws so I prefer the checkpoint system, where you can instant starts over.
And even the story feels great, ok nothing more then the standard cliche anime but who cares, I like the ending, I like the characters (awesome seiyuu) and since it is mostly a highscore/gameplay-driven game it is a nice extra.
What is left to say, actually I only finished this in easy mode (yet) because I struggle on my first try at normal which is great, because at first I did not understand the score/health system and in my opinion shmups have to be difficult. If I could finish a shmups on first try in normal something is definetly wrong. So for people who say it is short and do not have enough content, this is not a game made for them, you have to set you own goal and play it over and over until you beat the next stage, get higher score, no damage etc.
Play this game one or two hour, get better with every run until finally beat the stage and this will be the most satisfying game moment ever, at least for me.

So, when I first played it, it was horribly bugged. Just... Bugged out of proportion. This is quite normal for game nowadays, they fix that in later patches. So I waited, and waited, and waited. Looking for the positive reviews, but they never really show. I thought welp - I own the game, might as well try it. During the first five minutes of play, I encountered two bugs. NPCs walking on top of one another, and trees floating above ground. Gritting my teeth, I played on, thinking I could look past these things. And to my surprise, I could indeed look past it.
In spite of this, I had to uninstall. Just... Give up. Combat is horrible - every guard owns a gun, and every guard is a marksman. They have no problem unloading their guns in a crowd, nor do they miss someone running past them at a distance with people in between. Those are shots really good marksman have a hard time with, with a modern gun, and these guys are shooting ancient crap that has the same precision as say... Boomerangs. Only these ancient boomerang guns seem to be magical. I had no idea ubisoft implemented magical weapons. But there you go. If someone aims at me, I could do nothing about it. Oh yeah, the dodge feature, which instantly allows you to become a target for meleers while the marksman (perhaps) misses. Great, dodge the bullet, stabbed with the sword.
Fine, fine... I thought. Perhaps I'm just bad at this. And after all, I am an assassin, not a knight or a samurai. I should be competent in melee, but not a superhero. I'll kill them in stealth instead. Only I can't because many enemies are also clairvoyant. It's my fault really, if they have magical guns then chances should be good that they're also wizards, who can instantly tell that their friends die even though their backs are turned and their friends make no sound as they die. Even around corners, if they're a pair walking down the street. So, stabbing is out of the question unless you stab all your enemies in the same moment.
Again I thought; fine... Fine... Assassins are not mass killers. They don't take out several people. They're pinpoint killers, focusing on the one target they're supposed to hit then running for it. But again - running for it only works if your enemies doesn't have the time to draw their magical guns and firing through masses of people, hitting the one person who's running. Which they often do.
I mean, I am not bad at these sort of games. I've played almost all other assassin creed games. From Altair, to Ezio, to Connor and Kenway. I never had any problems in any sort of combat, and I liked them all in varying degrees. But this game... Can't do it. Combat is out, stealth is out. What am I supposed to do? Petition a ban against magical guns? I know I haven't played the game that much, but that's not really a feature is it?
In either case. Buy this if you're a huge fan, or if you just like wonky gameplay. Otherwise, don't bother.

Nicely done enjoyable game. Things of note:
Pros:
- Nice 2D/3D blend. View  aestetic aside, there are enemies/attacks that come from far away and have to be dealt with using lock-on. This offers both additional gameplay depth and immersion.
- Graphics/Aesthetic: great particle effects, in a sense that they look modern and flashy, still preserve expected animesque visual style as well as keep gameplay reasonably clean. Also, good visual consistency between attacks and their effects. You always have a very clear idea on how to deal with any type of projectile coming your way.
- Special notice in my book: an actual tutorial which explains every single game mechanic there is, complete with demonstration. It's really different mechanically from "classic" bhells, so props for recognizing that.
Cons:
- Obviously console-oriented controls. Like, "back" in the menus when you launch it up, is on Shift. That was a big WTF moment for me. Also, keybindings... ugh. How the hell do I know what is "Button0"? It's not anywhere on my keyboard.
- A few minor polish/stability issues (like the ability to push the game to higher resolutions than your monitor supports resulting in a crash)

Blockade 3D is a FPS block style game stylized after MineCraft, Ace of Spades, and other block style games, but this one is one of the free ones so don't expect a perfectly pollished game.
For those of you who think it is a p2W or stinks of it, well you are partialy right but from what ive seen so far you don't have to buy guns to be good, and besides when you level up sometimes you get a weapon. Since i started playing ive leveled up 3 times and have gotten 3 weapons that would have cost me about $2.50 usd total if i decided to buy them. The only thing is that i dont know if you could unlock the Really good guns like the "1 shot even with a helmet" sniper rifle, or the helpful items like armor/ a helmet.
As for gameplay i will say that is is indeed a bit laggy like the fact that half the kills i get, the person i kill gets me AFTER they die, which tells me that the bullet damage is a bit laggy as well as sometimes seeing someone lag jump from one spot to another and not being able to get a kill. Another thing I noticed is that there is literally no recoil or negitive influences on your gun, i mean i have gotten mulltple headshots mid air or from the other side of a map before which does make the game easier but lacks a challenging aspect to the game, because it makes it so easy to get a 2.0-4.0 KDR without even trying really.
For gamemodes they have enough to keep you busy for a while, but some of the game modes, Survival and Zombie mode, will glitch up sometimes and not let me join a match no matter how empty it is or how long i spectate, in fact since downloading the game i have only sucessfully played one zombie mode match will the other 20 attempts ended with me mad and no dead zombies :/
For Weapons they do have a good selection but like i said you would have to wait to unlock it, if you can, or buy it. The only drawback to buying a gun is some of the better guns arent available till you level up enough, which as someone already said, may lead to you buying one crappier gun then having to buy a better gun later thus wasting you money.
Atleast most of the guns would be cheaper than buying them in CS:GO, but you cant re-sell/ trade them if you no longer want the weapon you bought.
As for maps the game has plenty of them, the only issue is half the maps are either way too small for the gamemode, or way too big for it, either making you die faster than you should or take a minute or two just to get a couple of kills.
I have also noticed that sometimes servers do not let me join even though there is clearly enough room for 5 or 6 other players, i dont know if this is a server issue or the game itself though. There is also still the issue of hackers, while ive only ran into 1 or 2, it still gets on your nerves sometimes that some gets like 40 headshots in a row and you cant even see the person shooting, but hey its a free game :b.
So that about sums up my experience with the game Bockade 3D, i do indeed recomend the game but not as a game you play all the time, just as something to waste time when your bored or just want to play a differnt game.

I don't care what anyone says, Realm of the Mad God is absolutely amazing. I have logged literally thousands of hours into it over the past 2 and a half years and I don't regret a single second of it. I've gotten several of my friends and family members playing it and they all love it. You can whine about it being "Pay2Win" all day, but the nitty gritty of RotMG is you point the mouse at your target and rip it apart with your shots, and team up with other players to do harder content. Yes, gold, the premium currency, allows you to get more storage space, character slots, equipment, and cosmetic items such as skins and dyes, however all of the content in the game is completely accessable for free to play players. The only disadvantage is that you don't have as much storage space and 1 character slot, and there are ways around that.
Overall, Realm is one of the most unique and fun games that I've come across and I'll likely keep playing it until it gets shut down, which I don't see happening any time in the future. I highly, highly recommend playing it just for the heck of it. Word of warning though, once you're hooked, you're hooked.

Can you trust them? Are they a threat? Is it safer to ignore them? Try to coop? This is something that can suddenly give you emotions during the game.
Just a little example. One of the first players I spotted was a bandit, he didn't spot me but that was enough to scare me and fear for my life. I rushed immediately into my vehicle and stumbled against an obstacle after some meters as I was very inexpert with the roads and all. Then I was almost dead and I tried to ask help just to that bandit that was around...
It's an alpha, has bugs, glitches, needs some balancing to reduce the kill on sights issue probability... but I had a lot of fun with this game so far.

Essentially, this game isn't bad, it's just in a very unstable beta which could be considered to be alpha - and is still in this state 2 years after the intended release date. I am immensely disappointed, I waited for a major update before writing this review, in hopes that a final release might be able to provide some saving grace. However, the quality of the update is that of a generic beta update, despite the amount of time spent to create it.
For me, I would say at this point the game is worth about five dollars. I bought early beta a while ago to support the company, but it would seem I took a chance on a company that can reliably promise nothing but disappointment and false promises.
If you enjoyed terraria and minecraft, stick with them, they are both excellent games, which is unfortunately more than I believe I will be able to say about this game for at least another five updates or so of this size, but of higher quality. At this pace, the game will be at it's proper release state in 2019-2020, which is unreasonable.
All I can say is don't buy this game unless it's on a major sale. It's not worth the money, and it won't ever become what was promised in all probability. As for supporting the company.. well, they made an incredible amount of money and have done nothing to show for it. I guess all I can say is that I wish they'd used some of their excessive earnings to give a refund to all of us who invested in them and trusted them to produce a decent game in a remotely timely fashion.

I'll will simply start by saying that this game is amazing. It's got everything you could ask for in a singleplayer game; art, music, gameplay, story, and exploration are all the best of the best in this game.
If you still need more info, keep reading.
Pros:
-Incredibly fun and surpsisingly deep gameplay.
-Very well thought out story that takes inspiration from all kinds of japanese folklore
-Open world that only gets bigger as the game goes on. There will always be places to explore and rewards for exploring.
-Combat is fun and easily understood
-Puzzles are perfectly difficult (although this is subject to taste)
-The Celestial Brush mechanic is a very unique one, and significantly contributes to the game's overall level of fun.
-Absolutely incredible art style, inspired by classic japanese paintings and legends.
-A very long game for the price, with the average playthrough being over 40 hours long.
Cons
-The controls can be a bit strange (as it was originally designed for a controler) and could do with more customization options
-There seems to be some errors with the options, namely they tend to reset when you launch the game, but this may be fixed in the future. Nothing unusual for a new port.
-The game is LONG and requires a lot of time to be dedicated to beating it.
All in all, this game is a 10/10 and this port is a 9.5/10

This is my first Fallout game, so I can't compare it to the others.  The only thing I've played recently that compares is the Witcher 3.  Some might say that's apples and oranges, true, but if this game is an apple, oranges taste better and cost less.  But you can't live on oranges alone and this game has a lot going for it too.
The Good:
Fallout has really good graphics, not the best, but they're up there with the best.  I found the soundtrack to be wonderful, and character creation, both looks and stats is great.  There's plenty of well done friends, factions, creatures and enemies you will love, or love to hate.  The whole sci-fi '50's after a nuclear war makes for an extremely immersive world.  Fallout is it's own thing; this isn't just another sci-fi or fanasy RPG, and that's pretty cool.
The Bad:
The story itself isn't terrible, but there will be times you'll feel as though it was written by a child, or at least someone who has the mind of a child.  Other times you'll be convinced the writer believes you have the mind of a child.  Also, be advised, this game is buggy.  I've had to do things like enter console commands just to complete a quest.  Be prepared to sacrifice a significant amount of time you should be playing this game to managing mods and googling bugs and how to fix them. There are a lot of little things you'd expect in a modern game that just aren't there, like being able to holster your weapon. The biggest knock on this game, and it's legit, is the DLC.  It's actually good content, but there's no way, no freaking way in hell the dlc is worth twice what you paid for the base game.  Shameless cash grab, and you're gonna want the stuff for the DLC.  So be prepared to have a bad taste in your mouth when you overpay for the DLC, and then see they're trying to charge you again for paid mods, when you can get way better work outside thier system by a great community making amazing mods.  Some things are just ridiculous, like enabling mods disables steam achievemnets... why? there's a freaking built in cheat console and for some reason mods disable achievements??? why?  Have no fear though, there is of ccourse a mod for that.
TL;DR:
If you've already played the witcher 3, and haven't invented a mind ray that will let you forget it so you can play it again for the first time, give this one a try if you don't mind overpaying for DLC content.

I ♥♥♥♥ed up the mission, and Eden Phase was caught, taken away, and imprisoned by Offworld Security. Up until that point, she had been the most successful galactic renaissance leader we'd ever seen, ruthlessly hijacking any ship she deemed fit weilding concussion hammers, traveling so quickly no one person ever saw her for a mere second before flying down the corridor, ribs shattered from the impact. Up until the last mission at least. She miscalculated, didn't have enough time. Didn't have the key, or the tools, to get through the door to get to the pilot before they arrived at the station, and was caught.
This is where Pavo Starspelt came in. Eden Phase's father. He heard that his daughter was abducted and threw his life away to hunt down the Offworld Security ship that had Eden, and swore to bring her to safety. He armed himself with anything he could find, including a silenced shotgun, a self-charging visitor, a concussive grenade launcher, a subverter, a long-range extreme capacity key cloner, and a personal shield amoung other things.
He finally hunted down the ship with Eden inside and went to infiltrate. Eight layers of security. He didn't have enough memory on the key cloner to get through quietly. He managed to sneak past the first four layers of security without much hastle, stealing a key from one of the guards while he wasn't looking and getting into the fifth to kill off the pilot. They weren't going anywhere any time soon. He managed to sneak past a group of five guards and hack one of the panels, unlocking level 6. This is where he started to run out of utility.
There were turrets around every other corner at this point, and hordes of police that would swarm him if any of them went off. He had to time his movements perfectly to get past everything without being seen and sneak up behind them, which he managed. He got to level 7 security - and that's where he messed up.
There was a turret on the other side he hadn't seen that immediately went to shoot him. In a split second he managed to pop the security shield that absorbed the rounds and teleport away with the visitor to kill every guard within range of the sound with the silenced shotgun, trying to wipe any form of alert from the ship. But it was too late. He had to fight his way through. He killed everyone that came towards him, coming inches from getting shot on multiple occasions. Always on the move, eventually getting close enough to the turret to subvert it, turning it to his side. He was lucky enough that the guy with the key card turned the corner and was shot by the same turret, grabbed the key card, and sprinted through the security 8 door.
This is the area Eden was in, but he had used almost all of his utility to get to this point, and there were still guards in the first 4 levels of security he had bypassed, so he couldn't go back to his ship, not directly at least. He popped a shield and ran directly for Eden, the single room surrounded by at least 12 guards. At this point, he had no more ammo, and no more grenades. The key cloner was useless, and the visitor would only bring him back to where he was after a second and leave Eden behind if he were carrying her, so he couldn't use it for getaways. That left the two charges he had left on the personal shield.
He managed to make it to Eden, using his shield again to protect her as he ran away. One charge remaining. There were too many guards to make it out the same way he came in, so he had to find another way. The glass. He ran past a corridor with one of the police looking for him. He had a personal shield as well. Running back towards the way he came, careful not to round any corners before the enemy could see him, luring him back to the Security 7 zone, and past the turret he had subverted. The only problem is the round would bounce right off his shield.
He rounded the corner to the hallway the turret protected as it turned to face his direction, the Offworld Security Officer followed, and was nearly instantly barraged with a burst of ammo from the turret. The rounds passed Pavo, inches away, and slammed into the Offworld Security Officer's shield, bouncing back towards him. He threw Eden behind him and popped the last charge of his shield, and the ammo bounced off of him. It went flying straight though the massive observatory window, shattering it and sucking all of them; Officer, Pavo, and Eden, into the depths of space.
Pavo knew he had to exhale in order to get all the air he could out of his lungs. Otherwise, they'd expand inside him and kill him. He looked around for Eden, having been ripped from his Offworld Security ship as the glass broke, thrown out into the vacuum of space. She was floating away from him. He went for the remote control band on his arm and undocked his ship, hurriedly flying it past the wreckage he had just been through and towards Eden, trying desperately to catch her first incase he suffocated there in space, at least knowing she would be safe. He managed to catch her as he was starting to black out, and throttled the ship towards himself as he started to lose his own vision, managing by some sliver of a hair to catch himself in the depths of space before passing out on the floor of his ship, drifting deeper into space.
They eventually woke up and flew back to their home system, where Pavo retired. And rightfully so. He had "Eden's Protection" engraved on the side of the silenced shotgun he had used, and gave it to Eden. He would have used the personal shield, but it had been though so much it wouldn't work any more. Since then, Eden has been the most successful Legend, liberating over 7 star systems single-handedly with the help of her father's shotgun. And she continues to do so to this day.

I am a very -large- fan of the Assassins Creed franchise. I say this upfront because that is the only reason I played this completion.
First, the good! Paris is a character in it's own right. The city is vast, filled with such realistic and charming arcitecture that makes you feel that no matter where you go, you are fully immersed in world with some pretty spectacular graphics and facial animations (even if half the city are cut and paste clones, especially in crowds). Now the bad...
Everything else.
Even after a year since it's release, on a rig that can run The Witcher 3 on ultra with very little hitches, this game chugs until I was dropping the graphics to Low just to finish up the last few chapters when my frustration ran too hot. This is a very poorly optimized port, and whatever progress the patches have made to the fact have done little if anything. I personally experienced very few bugs, but I know they were rampant for some during this games early days. It was this stuttering that ruined any immersion that the game had built up for me when I would be running down a road, freeze, and get suddenly teleport and get my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by some random thugs.
While the political intrigue of Paris during this time was very interesting, that was because the characters themselves were not, the main two characters being given a basic motivation and nothing else in terms of character and the relationship between them leading to an ending I predicted hours ago, and did not care a bit about. The story fails to make you care as you kill your way up the normal hierachy of villians for no other reason than one mans juvinille quest for revenge, conviently leading from one to another like a transperent way to pad out the time as interchangable, and almost visually identical bad guys get the knife.
I wanted to like the game, but after 15 hours in of messing around Paris, I no longer cared. Whatever good traits this game has are drowned in the mediocraty. I won't call this a bad game, but it's forgettable, just like I've already forgotten who the last boss was ten minutes after just finishing it. This adds nothing to the overarching story, and by looking up cutscenes on youtube, you will save yourself alot of time and money

UPDATED FOLLOWING FULL RELEASE (updates marked w/ "UPDATE"):
Brigador is one of about 3 games I've purchased in Early Access and the only one I felt strongly enough about to recommend.  I'm assuming you've watched the trailers and are familiar w/ the basics of the arcade-style shooter genre.
Gamplay:
UPDATE: With the release of the full game, the quantity of vehicles and weapons available to the player in campaign and freeplay mode have increased greatly.  Whereas the EA was working w/ about a dozen vehicles and weapons, there are now 4 or 5 times as many.  This obviously makes for a much more replayable game; figuring out optimal builds for each vehicle and which vehicles suit your playstyle has become a much richer experience b/c of the increased variety. You can choose to play either through the game's 20-mission campaign which follows the story of liberating Solo Nobre as a mercenary, or play one-off missions in the game's freeplay mode.  Any currency gained from either mode carries over to the other and allows the player to purchase intel, vehicles, weapons, lore, and different pilots for use in freeplay. I think this mechanic works well as it doesn't lock the player in to playing strictly the campaign, everything in the game is accessible at all times, provided you've racked up enough currency from completing missions.
EARLY ACCESS:I've been having a ton of fun w/ Brigador; it's relatively simple in gameplay, but w/ depth of difficulty and strategy that emerges the longer you play.  I was up and running w/in a few minutes of booting this game up for the first time, but even after 20 hours or so, I'm still learning about the nuances of each vehicle and weapon available in the game, as well as enemy behavior and countering tactics.
Audio:
UPDATE: Following the full release of the game, music and sound effects have been more fully integrated into the game. Updates include a greater quanitity of vehicle and weapons sounds, as well as the integration of the full OST into campaign maps.  I can't overstress how much the original music adds to the experience of this game; if you're into synthpop, this game is just a joy to run around in.
EARLY ACCESS:The in-game audio pushes Brigador from something that I'd probably otherwise enjoy to a great gaming experience.  The music is a stand-out as contributing a great deal to the atmosphere and enjoyability of playing, but it's not alone.  The weapon and vehicle sound effects, automatic weapons in particular, are rich and obviously got a lot of love from the devs.
Graphics/Misc:
UPDATE: Nothing much to add here over EA; I'll note that I haven't experienced any bugs or crashes.
EARLY ACCESS: I've seen a few pre-release builds since purchasing and all of them show a great deal of attention to detail from level design to animation to UX: I've gotten a great deal of satisfaction out of how smooth the game's animations are.  I get the feeling that the devs took a great deal of time in getting vehicle movement and weapon usage right; I've seen other games that use mechs and tanks end up w/ much clunkier vehicle movement, which can kill the fun quickly. Every vehicle in this game has a realistic sense of movement and presence in the game world, as do environmental destruction and weapon effects.  Graphics options are limited to resolution, V-Sync, and a few other options, but I found that these options are sufficient.

Devs:
Lastly, I always consider it a good sign when the developers of a game have a presence in the Steam forums and these guys are on top of that.  I've asked several questions and have always received quick answers from devs or knowledgable community members.  I always enjoy knowing that I can run to the forums w/ questions or comments and receive something other than a "get gud" response from the community.

In the history of mech games (at least in the U.S.A) have been usually terrible. Mechwarrior(GC) is an example of a good mech game fun and challenging in its own right. Astebreed throws it's hat into the ring and is ambitous if anything. The developers of Astebreed favor the eastern style of mech combat much like Gundam and Eureka 7 type where you move fast in the air obliterating everything in your sight. You will feel like a king on a keyboard killing millions every mission you play.  Story takes a backseat to the action clearly, there are datalogs for the plot if you're that curious but it doesn't help nor hurt you gaming experince. The overall spoiler free summary is "Climb into the pilot's seat of an otherworldly war machine and take down a genocidal alien race bent on eradicating humanity to preserve their own civilization." Thats it. Another thing I should mention is that all dialog is in Japanese but can be skipped at anytime. For those you cringe at a language unfamiliar to your own spoken native tongue you can play with the audio options to mute it. I for one had no issues.
In conclusion, stunning to look at, slick and fluid to play as well as being a satisfying -- but never insurmountable -- challenge, Astebreed is a top-quality game that everyone with even a passing interest in mech games should have in their collection

As much as I used to enjoy this game, I cannot recommend it any longer.  This game has a fantastic variety of ships, which all bring a plethora of different types of weapons and tactics to the game.  What ruins it for me has always been the broken match making and now the slide towards making this a close quarters, smash and grab type game, and the persistent bugs and crashes since the game is still in beta (wink-wink).
Match making has always been terrible.  This is a team-based game, and oftentimes, one person can nullify the efforts of the other four.  You will never see an increase in your MMR if your team loses.  What's that?  You went 14-2 with 10 caps, but you lost because the guy in the Centurion was chasing caps during Gamma III instead of helping the team?  Well, YOU obviously suck and your rating will reflect that.  And so you get kicked to a lower tier, with more mediocre talent or people who are still learning, and you end up feeling like you're climbing a sand dune to get back to where you belong.  I've been in matches at level 40, where the highest ranking of my three team mates was 13.  With the oppposing team similarly stacked, I wandered around in a Pioneer, blasting level 6 players like it was a turkey shoot.  It was shameful, but we lost anyway, again, due to the whole team not being up to speed on the tactics needed to win.  Kills alone will not win you the game.
Which brings us to the gameplay issue.  The developers continue to take steps to make this a high-speed, close quarters type of game, which ends up negating what made this game interesting in the first place.  The game is marketed as and is supposed to be about capital ship warfare.  I don't know about you, but when I hear the words "capital ship warfare", I think of huge, lumbering vessels pounding it out with eachother, not quick, zippy warfare.  The slow speeds which used to exist in this game meant you had to strategize a bit more because you couldn't just hop over and fix something if you overlooked it or if the enemy slid by you, and there WAS room for the enemy to slide by you.  Now, with the shrunken maps and increased speeds, you're almost always in range if not on top of the enemy, so there is less strategy involved and it's just a brawl-fest.  As some have said, COD has gone Intergalactic-Planetary,Planetary-Intergalactic.
And then there are the bugs, crashes, freezes, and more.  This game dings your stats for disconnects, but this thing crashes like a drunken unicycle rider.  But it's ok, right, because it's in beta, ya?  Pfft.  Steam should stop letting developers collect any sort of money, in-game or otherwise, until the game is out of beta and is fully released.  You want the community to help you work the bugs out of your game?  Sure thing, post the game with a free license which needs to be paid for only if/when the game loses the "Beta" tag.  Deal.
350 hours on record.  Uninstalling.

What can be said about this game that hasn't been said already?
I'm writing this review in 2016, eighteen years after this game was released. Having never played a Half-life game, I wanted to jump in with the first in the series, and I was so glad that I did.
Being an older title with dated graphics, gamers today may be quick to overlook this game and head straight for Half-Life 2 and its consecutive episodes. It could be considered a fair decision given how long it was before HL2 came out. It isn't
for you to play this game to enjoy Half-life 2; but I'm here to tell you that despite its age, this game still deserves the right to be rediscovered and enjoyed by newcomers. Half-life 2 gives plenty of references to its origin and they'll go over your head if you don't take a look here first.
The game can feel clunky at times. The shooting mechanics see plenty of improvements from Valve in later titles, the AI is dumb, the graphics are bleak and there are very few voice actors- but these are caveats that can be easily overlooked once you are invested in the plot and having fun figuring out how to progress through the levels. Not only that but once you learn a little about the context in which this game was released, you'll forgive it entirely.
It's 1998 and this game busts on to the scene to become the first narrative-driven shooter. Pioneering for its time and provided a benchmark for the genre. Treat your playthrough of this game as a history lesson, let the game transport you backwards in time and afterward you will be left enriched. Do you enjoy using Steam? Valve make great games right? This was Valve's first project. It all began with this game. Play it. If games were like novels this would be required reading.

This game is incredible. The basic premise is pretty simple - break into spaceships, use your cool gadgets to complete the objective, and get out without dying. Withing that framework, however, there's really no end to what you can do.
Want to teleport around and swap places with guards so they all kill each other with friendly fire? You can do that.
Want to smash windows and throw guards into the icy vacuum of space? You can do that too.
Want to just carry around 8 swords and chain-stab your way through an entire room full of angry people with guns? Go for it.
Want to propel yourself into the airlock from the icy vacuum of space with nothing but a shotgun? You just might have to.
Want to blow everyone up with a grenade launcher that fires 5 grenades at once? That can be arranged.
There are loads more crazy tools that I haven't even mentioned here. If you can think of an insane way to get through an enemy ship, chances are it can be done in Heat Signature. This game is worth every penny. If you enjoy fun, buy it.

Well, this is the game that actually got me into games. I remember my father playing it. I was like OH GOD STEALTHY, DAD WATCH OUT, DAD WHY DONT YOU CHANGE TO THOSE CLOTHES, DAD LOOK THE IDIOT LEFT A MASTER KEY ON THE DOOR. Good times.

The game's hardcore and unforgiving. Depending on the difficulty setting, you're given a number of lives. Resurrecting doesn't make the guards forget about you LOL. In the hardest setting you are given one extra live only in the hardest missions. Be patient and play well. Plan your assasinations, choose well your targets and weapons. "Wake up! Wake up my friend!" :D
Conclusion: This game is a classic, it has its flaws but its enjoyable. I'd recommend buying it on a sale. It's worth it. If you have a config problem just leave me a comment. Maybe I'll be able to help.

I'd start out by saying; If you like Schmups, or anime-related games with a pretty nice story - then buy it. Now.
Astebreed is a Schmup (Shoot 'em up) with an anime styled theme, based on, obviously, a futuristic type warfare.
There's a prologue and a main story. They are both, together, only lasting enough for around an hour of play (if you don't die a bunch of times, which, honestly, shouldn't be too difficult to avoid on Easy, though I havn't tried any other difficulty - That's how long the game is). The story itself plays through as you play the game - which can get a little difficult to follow if you're terrible at multi-tasking, though I liked the idea of the story following what's actually happening in the game itself. The voices are in japanese (with English subtitles). In the main story you play as a character named Roy, who, with his sister, is out to save the sister's twin, and save the Earth from evil.
I honestly don't know much about Scmups at all. I never really played them (nor liked them), and initially brought this because it looked good with the anime styled graphics and I've heard good things about it. I can honestly say; This was the fastest hour I have spent on a game in god knows how long - and this is meant in a good way, as I was really entertained both with the gameplay and the story all the way through.
The gameplay in itself felt smooth, and it worked really well with a gamepad too. I really don't know what to say about the gameplay - As I said, I don't usually play these types of games. I had no problems with it, and I quite liked the variability in the attack forms.

Oh gosh is this game the best. It feels like an old roguelike: there are many ways to grab the key. Run into the room and shotgun everyone? Use your stealth shield and steal it from that guard? Lure them into your trap and teleport them out into space? A combination of the said tactics? Since each ship is randomly generated, the adventure is always different and never gets old. And while you think that your plan is airtight, the shotgun blast misses a few of those guards. so you pause:
you could pull your pistol out, but that would take to long to reload and shoot the other one. That swapper would be useful, but it only has one use left. You're just too far away to use your concussion hammer. But you find a plan: shoot one guard, wait until the other one shoots, and swap with them so they take the hit. And you feel brilliant. Some solutions are simpler. Some are even more complex. Some are downright hilarious. But there's one for almost every situation, and it feels good.

This is a game about making the best of a bad situation, as the game itself put it, and I found that aspect of it to be very enjoyable. Generally speaking, most of the monsters that you fight are tough, but manageable. What makes it difficult is that in addition to that, you're working with four "heroes" to clear the dungeon. This is somewhat like the XCOM games, which is to say that you "order" your soldiers instead of controlling them directly.
Because of that, they will occasionally make a mistake to emulate where players might do the same if they were in that situation. This can be annoying at times, but I feel like it improves the game’s depth and immersion. In my experience, it didn’t become too much of an issue as long as I was doing what I ought to do anyway.
I also liked the idea of making the game’s characters vulnerable to stress, which I was told was the idea that the game was based upon. It's not something I see very often. It can cause things to get bad at times, but it isn’t much of an issue to work with as long as you don’t push them too hard.
Because of both of these characteristics, it’s important to have a backup plan if things do get too bad, but thankfully the game does let you retreat most of the time.
Other than that, I would say that I quite liked the art direction and the narration of the game.

Astebreed is an incredibly fun shoot 'em up that's as gorgeous to watch as it is to play. It runs consistently smooth, and the changes of viewpoint throughout each level keeps things fresh and exciting.
Controls are tight and responsive. The game provides a large number of attack options between wide & focused fire, lock-on variations of both, sword attacks, and ex attacks. It can be initially daunting but once you get a handle on each option's strengths, Astebreed becomes absolutely sublime to play.
The only negative thing about the game is the story. Like most shoot 'em ups it's not particularly memorable. There is a handful of dialogue during levels via subtitles in the corner; but with how much is happening on screen it is troublesome to read while playing.
That aside, Astebreed can put up a moderate challenge. It's not quite bullet hell, but there are times were it will feel close to it. Highly recommended for shoot 'em up fans.
The game has it's good points and it's bad points for sure but even so I still would say it is worthy of a try.

The most stressful shoot 'em up I've played since Ikaruga in the best way possible.
Mechanics are complex (continuing my Ikaruga analogy: instead of polarity, there's A LOT more things to keep track of and worry about, but there's also A LOT more ways to kick butt and win and look like a hardcore shmup player with little effort) but the learning curve isn't too steep, although mastery of the different abilities is key to a low-damage, perfect playthrough. I also appreciated the seamless transitions between chapters (that title card!), and how great the presentation was with regards to the scoring at the end of each chapter. In that respect, it had one of the most elegant UIs I've seen from a shmup.
Visuals are top-notch for the shmup genre, accompanied by a great OST and solid Japanese voice acting (with subtitles), although the VA sampling is a little uneven at times, so be careful with the dialog at high volumes.
Astebreed even comes with a shounen anime-y space opera story. (Campy to point, but appropriately so, and told quite tastefully.) Frankly, it's the most story I've seen out of this genre since the entirety of Touhou. Storytelling is succinct in that the cutscenes don't detract from the fact that this is a shmup.
It is definitely challenging, which is why I opened stating it was my most stressful experience since Ikaruga (and what I've played of Touhou, I guess) but there's a Chapter select and as far as I know you're not limited to any continues, unless you're going for the achievements. The game is brief but due to the challenging nature of having low-damage runs and maximizing your score by mastering the mechanics, it's definitely up there in terms of replayability if you're a shmup fan. I might revisit this a lot more than I revisited Ikaruga, as much of a labor of love that was.
Overall, I'd recommend Astebreed to everyone since I daresay it's one of the most modern evolutions of the shoot 'em up genre I've had the pleasure of playing.

Ever wanted to stomp through your town with a giant robot, flattening people and buildings alike with mad, cackling glee? Neither did I actually, until Brigador showed me how much fun machine-assisted murder can be. Happiness, as they say, is a warm Howitzer.
I've now spent about 6 hours playing Brigador, and I really like what I've seen so far. There's a lot more depth and immersion to it than I'd expected from an isometric shooter—you can interact with any and every object in the map, which generally involves either smashing it or blowing it sky high. Some structures are relatively benign, others will explode and take a big whack of your shields out with them. So you'll want to start thinking at street level even as you take advantage of the top-down perspective to locate enemies and engage them on your own terms.
Brigador is tough. Very tough. Like, approaching roguelike levels of hardness. There's no quicksave—you either complete your run by escaping via the spaceport or you die in the process. This engenders a more methodical pace than you'd expect to see in your typical shooter—cover becomes critical, and all your weapons make noise which serves to attract more enemies. As much fun as it is to Gatling Gun that MiniMart into rubble, letting everyone know where you are will get you swarmed by more enemies than it's humanly possible to fight off, losing you the game in a matter of seconds. So destroy responsibly.
Controls feel unworkably clunky at first—using WASD and mouse for Resident Evil-style tank controls (to be fair, you *are* actually controlling a tank) takes some serious getting used to. Don't expect to feel very fluid with it for the first hour or so. After that you kind of grow into it. No controller support currently, but with the way aiming works I can't see how they'd ever be able to implement it anyway.
I don't regret dropping $20 on Brigador despite it being unfinished at this stage—though if you're on the fence you can wait until it's out of Early Access and judge the complete game then. Devs have said they won't raise the price at launch, so it's not like you have to jump in now. But yeah, good game. Check it out.

There's a lot of great things bout Brigador that have been pointed out by most of the other reviewers here, like the brilliant artstyle and music, fluid gameplay and surprising depth of the game mechanics.
But even with all of that, I doubt I'd have spent as much time in this game as I have - it is in Early Access after all and still lacks quite a bit of content. But thankfully this game is extremely easy to mod. I don't know anything about code, and I never modded any game before, yet in Brigador I was able to make an instagib mod, change all the weapons' attributes and make my own weapons, make enemies tougher, completely revamp the lighting, modify the movement behavior of all player vehicles and change the enemy spawnlists (and thus even get access to unimplemented content that was present in the gamefiles) - and most of those things can be done on-the-fly while in the game. On top of that there's a map editor as well. You could even make your own units, though for that you need experience in either 3D modelling or at least basic spritework - unless you're fine with recombining the existing leg and chassis parts which you can do pretty easily.
In short, pretty much every aspect of the game can be modified either in-game via a really handy and easy to use dev-console, or by basic text file editing in the gamefolder. That alone would already be enough for me to recommend this game, but since it's coupled with an excellent base game as well I really can't stress how much you'll get out of this game if you're even remotely interested in mech and tank games.

I am a new player (at time of review, 5 hours of play), one who has started playing after the dreaded "Phase 3" patch, and I gotta say... I really like this game, and I think people *might* be overreacting a bit (as people tend to do, whenever something new happens).
To explain the implants system that everyone seems to hate so much, let me use League of Legends as an example - Runes and Masteries. Got a pretty good picture in your head? Now, imagine that the game gave you a bunch of runes for free, and continuously does so as you keep playing; they aren't nececarily exactly the ones you want, but they are at least SOMETHING so you aren't left completely in the dust.
Now imagine that they have personalities - not just stat sticks that you equip at the begining of the game, but characters who talk to you throughout the game - a CREW. Who you can further upgrade and make stronger and... Yeah.
TLDR: People are upset that the game has changed in a way that they don't like. What got added is just a better runes and masteries system, and you really don't need to spend a thing on this game to have a great time with it. I have played and re-played this game more times than I care to admit, and I don't foresee there ever being a time where I don't feel like I could happily re-play this game.
It is a game rich with beauty, a light-hearted and hopeful nature, but not without sacrificing its serious points when it comes to character growth. It stays true to its roots, with artwork that is simple, but gorgeous in its simplicity, and with wonderful more detailed examples of the artwork scattered throughout the game.
The gameplay itself is also a joy. Not only does Amaterasu herself feel very fluid and easy to control while fighting or platforming, but using the celestial brush is extremely easy to use and responsive. And with the HD remake, I find that I'm having absolutely no issues at all getting the brushwork to do what I want it to do, which I had little problem with in the original anyways. I personally also enjoyed the way that you use weapons, mixing and matching primary and secondary weapons to change up your fighting style.
I know most people have already played Okami, but if you haven't, you are seriously missing out. It's a beautiful gem of a game, one-of-a-kind in every aspect. It's a game well worth the $20 price tag, even if you're just upgrading to the HD version.

XCOM 2 is the sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It takes notes from Enemy Within, and integrates some of what made that expansion so great.
The story is canon now, that in the first month or so of EU, Earth was overwhelmed by the alien threat, and 20 years have passed since then. The ADVENT coalition is the sole authority of the entire world, and a punished Bradford sets out to set the Commander free. So begins the revival of XCOM as a guerilla front...
XCOM 2 is a mixed bag. For every improvement it makes, there is a similar blunder in that territory as well. List of pros, new stuff that is kind of mixed or no reaction, and cons: (For vanilla XCOM 2)
Positives:
-Reloads only take one action, not a full turn, with the absence of Auto-Loaders
-Customization options are vastly expanded
-Naming guns(albeit only primary weapons, but sure there are mods that fix this), and attaching attachments really make the weapons more versatile, and varied, you can also customize the color and pattern to make it look prettier when you have to recover it from your dead soldiers.
-Mods (Never personally touched any of them in initial playthrough, but some of them look absoultely amazing)
-Cinematic overwatches. A small thing, but I thought they were cool.
-Advanced Warfare Center. Though I only had one person who gained an extra ability from outisde their ability tree, it granted "Guardian" to my Grenadier. Shreddin' armor for days.
-Soldier skills are now varied in their decisions, so you might have to put some thought into picking the skills. You can also retrain skills now in the Advanced Warfare Center if you do not like your choices.
-Shen's Last Gift is likely one of the only DLC you will need for XCOM 2, since it adds an underwhelming, but cool class known as SPARKS (Basically a watered-down version of MECs from EW).
-Psi Operatives are now a force to be reckoned with, as they don't need to go on missions to gain skills, they can literally incubate in the Psionic facility, and you can make 2 or 3 people (depending on how long you want to prolong the game) into PSIONIC GODS. (+5 Points if you get that reference)
-"Heavy Weaponry", such as Flamethrower, Rocket Launcher, and such, can be used by soldiers that are not the Grenadier class, in the prescence of EXO or WAR suits. Though it is still advised that Grenadiers carry the best heavy weapons, when coupled with the "Salvo" ability, for maximum benefit.
-Watching enemies fall to their death after having the ground beneath them be blown away is mildily satisfying, more so for stationary turrets.
Neutral:
-Discretion for explosives in EU/EW was that you could not recover weapon fragments from blown up targets. Now you run the risk of destroying loot on enemies, if you are not careful. Personally, I played it mostly safe, but once you get loot from enemies, feel free to let loose with explosives. Might be a pro or con depending on how you play. Loot is also quite dependant on making your weapons more stronger, as they may drop weapon mods, intel, or Elerium Cores, essential to making anything useful for soldiers.
-Armor. Newly added to XCOM 2, some units will have armor that will reduce the amount of incoming damage to those units. Only the Grenadier's primary weapon (if you invest in that skill), and explosives, can shred the armor of units. Again, might be a kicker for some, if you are not explosive-happy.
-Soundtrack is not quite as epic as EU/EW, but fits the theme that XCOM 2 is trying to go for well.
-Wide variety of aliens, but one wonders how exactly humanity can eat up the fact that a giant sentient ball who can kill humans to become zombies is a good thing. (Little thing though, it's just a videogame, of course)
-Map. The map is kind of a mess. It never quite leaves you alone enough to feel like you are making sound progress on what you want to do, rather than doing an "important" mission so you don't immediately lose the game. Compared to EU/EW, it is a lot more busier. Of course, in the context of XCOM 2, it should work...but too well.
-Continent bonuses are randomized, so no two playthroughs will have all the same continent bonuses as before.
-Timers. The one thing that everyone can agree makes things a lot more hectic in XCOM 2. I personally did not find it to be the worst thing ever (Although I did savescum a little, Alien Hunters.). Avatar Project in the GeoScape is also an end-game solution for the aliens. It makes it the highest priority to get rid of Blacksites and to deter progress on it. It is supposed to be really something, but many will agree that it was just there to make things harder, for the sake of being harder.
-Random environment generators. Great for varying the battlefield, but terrible for if you want to get specific maps memorized.
-Hacking and melee. Hacking turned out to be just another RNG based mess, much akin to the general battles that ensue in XCOM 2. However, the more you hack, the easier it will be for further hacks. Now that melee is more of an option, say goodbye to 100% hits from EW, and hello to 90% hit chance on swords, and 86% chance for melee on SPARKS. This also means that melee-based aliens, like the Berserker or Chrysallid, can miss, with amusing effects.
-In EU/EW, you used an Arc Thrower to neutralize aliens to get to know more about them. That has now been replaced with the wickedly cool "weapon" known as the Skulljack. Forcibly inserted through an ADVENT soldier's cranium, provided the distance is close, a hacking portion will appear, where you can gather Intel from them, and even try for a Blacksite lead, if you are feeling lucky. Of course, with any melee-based equipment, you can miss...but if you do initiate the Skulljack, it will finish the unlucky soldier off instantly, so it might be worth your while to do some jacking in.
Negatives:
-Concealment. The one thing that I believe was quite hyped up, is mostly just a gimmick, but still somewhat of a mechanic. You can regularly take out a good pod with the no aim penalty on amubushes, but after that, you're exposed to every alien scumbag on the map.
-Early game difficulty. This might be a real kicker for some, since you literally encounter a mind-controlling sectoid in the first mission, and mind controlling never became a big thing until the later months in EU/EW. Or they revive a dead mate in the form of a zombie which has more health than regular early soliders, and rarely miss with their melee. Now you run the risk of being annihilated because of the evident superiority of the aliens. Again, works well in context...but too well.
-Alien Hunters. Not only are the initial Rulers themselves buffed up in terms of health, and armor, they get to take an action whenever any solider uses an Action Point, known as a "Ruler Reaction". It's bad enough that the Rulers are superior versions of their respective species (
), but this gimmick they have makes it so that they pretty much take free potshots anytime your soliders do
. You also need the special new weapons, to make the bosses more easier to handle with, but that means you will have to carry them in all your missions. Granted, most of the new stuff improves, like the Axe and Shadowkeeper, but the forced necessity is off-kilter in a sense. The armors afterwards, make it slightly worth your while, but it's too much for me, honestly.
-Action Cam. In EU/EW, Action Cam was this cool cinematic shot of your soliders killing the aliens (or the aliens killing your soldiers). Now Action Cam can initiate when you miss the shot. It kills off the significance and novelty of the Action Cam for me.
It's really a tough pick, but XCOM 2 adds as much depth to the game, just as it also introduces many problems with the changes as well. I personally enjoyed most of the experience, minus Alien Hunters related missions. I find myself humming the battle music as much as I did with EU/EW.

I'll start by saying I have very little negative things to say about Brigador. The visual aesthetic; a  beautiful mash-up between classic 90's PC mech/strategy games, and the 80's neon retro-wave which has been coming back in a big way. Playing this has made me wonder why this pairing hasn't been before, as when combined with the amazing retro-wave soundtrack it makes an incredible overall look, sound, and feel. The HUD also feels pulled straight out of those old games, presented in a minimalistic fashion that fits perfectly.
Now the gameplay is what makes Brigador truly stand out. The isometric view coupled with WASD + mouse will likely be slightly disorienting at first to those first picking it up. An hour or two into the game, there are moments where was still tripping up. Keeping evasive while also keeping on target is very challenging-- at first. Always keeping yourself properly oriented is a challenge-- at first.
Oh, and let's not forget about aiming and shooting. THAT was very hard to get the hang of. I'm still getting better at it, too, which is satisfying in the way that good, challenging games are. However, I DO believe that the "aiming system" can be improved. After the number of hours spent playing-- essentially the amount of time it took me to beat 'The Tears of the Ancestors' mission-- I'm still only 90% sure I'm going to hit a guy AFTER I take my time getting oriented and ranged in. The isomentric view makes some angles very awkward for aiming.
The only suggestion I can think of is to make the path of the projectile more clear by showing the point of impact. I will often overshoot or undershoot distant targets (with things like a basic tank-style cannon) because while I know my direction is correct, the "height" is harder to guage.
Also, that mission was damn hard. DAMN hard. My vast majority of my 4-5 hours played were trying to beat that mission. However, after finally beating it, I felt two things: a disappointment that I didn't get another story mission to beat myself over the head with, and an overwhelming sense of satisfaction that I managed to beat the stage by incorporating all aspects of the game's depth.
I used stealth and evasion, shooting through objects such as trees and buildings to hit enemies that couldn't see me, to take on the overwhelming amount of enemies. It was incredibly satisfying to overcome the mission by playing smart.
That being said, I was still a little bummed out to have not gotten another story mission, but this game is in Early Access for a reason, so I'm not knocking the game or devs for it. Of course more missions/content and balancing will be coming.
Here's a TL;DR to wrap it up.
-The visuals and music are ♥♥♥♥ing incredible.
-Gameplay is complicated and must be learned through practice. Lots of practice.
-Guaging distance (not direction) when aiming your shots is the hardest part about the controls. I believe this can be remedied.
-The game is HARD in a way serious players will really dig into. Not sure about casual players.
-Surprising amount of depth; makes for satisfying gameplay.

Early Access Review:
A solid little title.
Probably best described as a good blend of SCHMUP and Strategy isometric shooter, Brigador is currently sitting in my 'Gem' folder - and it's only in Early Access.
Pumping, pulsing electronic soundtrack; neon lights from environment and gunfire; beautifully rendered sprite environment (which is fully destructable and with multiple stages of damage being detailled just as finely through their beautiful art style).  People have compared it to Syndicate although I never played.  It feels more like a Crusader mixed with Mech Commander to me.
Pilot one of several mechs/tanks/hovercraft with a selection of primary/secondary weapons and a special skill (stealth/assault modifier item) and murder your way through a city for the good of the people!
There are -currently- 4 'zones', of which the first three contain 4 levels.  The final zone being the 'Solo Nobre' of the trailers which has 12 levels within.  There is currently no save feature, so running an assault on Solo Nobre is quite the marathon (if you can make it in and out alive).  Enemies initially are light and sparse but quickly ramp up to heavy and thick in numbers as you progress, creating a tense and exhilerating environment to literally shake to the ground.
At this point in time, it still feels 'bare' in that there is no story, the pre-mission screens are sparse and look like under construction, certain assets appear to be missing, and it's really just 'the game' without bells or whistles at the moment.
The game however plays and feels excellent and is still having things added to it.
If you're a fan of shmups, isometric action/tactics (real time) or cut your teeth on Mechwarrior or Heavy Gear (or the like) as i did as a child, this is definitely something to either get, or watch the price on.

Brigador is the ambitious and exciting debut from independent developer Stellar Jockeys, boasting lavishly rendered isometric spritework whose variety of design styles and nighttime-neon colour palette fit perfectly with an unforgiving, crisp control scheme to remind me of the classics of the 1980's and 1990's (Akira, Mechwarrior, Blade Runner) in both gameplay and looks.
It's important to note that the game is in early access, the way the term was likely intended to be used. The developers are actively following a development roadmap that sees them churning out maps and vehicles as they continue to build the game around the existing skeleton you can play here. Yes, the current experience is rough if you are expecting a paid beta experience: the menus are barebones, most of the sound effects are missing, there's a lot of functionality on the cards such as an unlock system and selectable pilots that we won't see for a while. That's okay, because it means the majority of work has gone into fine-tuning the game's systems to create an enjoyable and frentic experience best likened to a curious mix of
,
,
and the
titles on the Super Famicom which featured similarly isometric views and wanton destruction.
Brigador's difficulty is, once you're familiar with the simple controls and the flow of the game, somewhat self-imposed. You can identify pretty quickly which of the game's vehicles (tanks, mechs and antigravs) gels with your playstyle the most and then which weapons you find the most useful on top of that. Whether you go with the same pair of big, kick♥♥♥♥♥cannons in every run or try to mix it up a little is up to you, and the vehicle mounts available. The longer you stick around, and the more maps you complete, the more difficult the enemies you'll find coming at you. If you're low on shields and ammo and aren't feeling like you can weather another big fight, the option is always there to hit up the spaceport as your next map and fight your way to an escape.
The soundtrack, by New Retro Wave artist Makeup and Vanity Set, is pretty damn good. It's not just playing at the 80's throwback fad half-heartedly, it's lurid and drenched in neon with big, dramatic synth. The only downside is the song selection is another aspect under development: the game just picks from a playlist right now and runs through it. What's there is great, though, and helps make up for the lack of sound effects currently implemented.
The game is by no means perfect, but it's short and sweet and to the point. For something so heavily under development, what's playable is incredibly crisp and very enjoyable. Whenever you die, it usually feels like it was something you did wrong rather than getting caught out by imbalanced mechanics or ♥♥♥♥♥♥ bugs. The onus is on Stellar Jockeys to keep the pace of development up, because the quicker this game's skeleton is built on, the quicker the attention is going to snap to it. If you're scared off by the very minimal trappings of a game under construction then you probably don't want to buy Brigador just yet. On the other hand, if you like the idea of tossing some change to a handful of guys making a very earnest and solid shooter with a bumping soundtrack, go for it. Unlike most of the early-access survival FPS pixel garbage on Steam, this is actually fun and cool.

Alright time for me to put in my two cents on Fractured Space for a review.
At first glance its a space combat game, you pick out your ship, choose your loadouts and crew when possible.   And go fight some bots or player versus player.  The good news is this game won't cost you anything to go try out, the bad news is that is has a rather step learning curve for starting out with no similiar experience.
So now more detailed explaination time.
Fractured space is more then just slugging it out with bots, theres real time stategy and teamwork that needs to be atleast somewhat considered to be "Successfull" in the game.  Further more you do have to consider things like your ships armor and health while you fight as well as positioning yourself to utilize the levels various obstacles as cover.
To complicate things a little, theres upgrades during combat (levels) for your team doing well (or poorly).  As you can imagine that if someone is screwing around a bit, entire team (deserving it or not) suffers because of it.  The bots before and after phase three were and still are nutorious for taking advantage of players derping around and not playing like they should.
It is entirely possible to take on the roles of DPS, Tank, and Healer.  However theres other ships for other roles like the utility craft and stealth ships.  Really the possibilities are numerous, so its really up to the player to specialize in a particular type of ship(s) and get good at that.
So now the grim/dirty sides.  The game has some issues running properly still, and has some rough edges that can be incredibly irritating at times.  Especially when it keeps crashing or disconnecting some random player during match making and you have limited time to do your dailies if you care or to play.
But on the bright side the Developers for this game atleast havent given up on trying to make it better so time shall tell if this can be fixed.
Matches are 5 v 5, ships have some customizability (Skin and loadout), as does your crew.
So.. Yes I can say I would recommend this title to someone who actually enjoys playing space combat games.  However at the same time I would have to warn off anyone who does not like rough edges (at this time) or space combat..
-Edit: nearly forgot to mention, yes this game has an ingame store were you can buy their "platinum" for more unlocks like ships or crew implants or skins.  But if you play and just do dailies at the least, you can get platinum from the daily rewards anyways so its entirely possible to play without paying.

Title : Trove
Developer : Trion Worlds
Publisher : Trion Worlds
Genre : RPG
Trove is a Sandbox massively multiplayer online role-playing game.
Players assume the role of one of multiple classes each with different play styles and abilities. After a brief tutorial players arrive in a central area called the 'Hub' In this area players can access Portals which act as access points to different in-game worlds each one tailored for a specific stage of progression. Each portal requires a minimum level to enter which gets higher per portal, allowing for progression from easier worlds to harder worlds as the player gains in level. Each world gets progressively harder but rewards higher levels of experience and better loot/resources. Each portal is of a specific color which is designed to indicate the quality of the 'loot' which can be most commonly located there, although there is a small chance that loot of a higher quality will be found. The exception to this is the higher level Red portals which predominantly drop Legendary (orange) quality loot but have a higher chance to drop loot of relic (red), resplendent (rainbow) or shadow (dark purple) quality as well. Higher Level Red portals have a better chance for to drop the rarer loot types.

First of all, I would like to point out that many people have already written an excellent review about this game. However, after finishing this one I really felt the urge to let you know how I experienced this wonderful game.
Well, as far as the first impression (~1 hour playtime) is concerned, I have to admit that I was delighted by the “cartoonish” texture and the “emotional depth”. I only expected and heard the best from “Telltale Games” but they somehow managed to surprise me.
So, now let´s talk about the story and the gameplay as such. Throughout the game you are playing as Lee, a convicted murderer. However, it might sound weird but I never felt any sort of hatred since the current problems (epidemic) are obviously far more important. As I already pointed out, you are Lee from now on and every following day might be your last one. The good thing though is that you aren´t alone. You are lucky enough to find Clementine, a girl aged 8 who lost her parents in Savannah. While Lee and Clementine stick together throughout the game some other “friends” you will make get lost or die, it´s all up to you. You don’t really have a final destination that’s why you are going to places where you expect to be safe.
As you might have already figured out that choices are fairly important in the first season of “The Walking Dead”, I would like to spend some time on figuring out whether choices modify your game completely. Well, I guess “Yes” and “No” is probably the most appropriate answer. You can pick one out of four different answers/reactions, which is of course and enormous variety. On the other side it doesn´t really change much. Let me explain myself with the following example: You have to choose what to do. Do you want to save a person XY our will you leave him/her behind? You have two totally different things you can choose from. But the story which follows afterwards will be the same for 100 per cent. You could argue that your decision you made is in some way really emotional and tragic but it doesn’t really change the gameplay. (I hope that was understandable since English isn´t my mother tongue. :/)
The texture used is really unique. It´s just typical for all the “Telltale”- games. You can like it or hate it. (Well I guess that wasn´t really helpful but the graphic standards are really high nowadays which means it´s up to your choice. Look at some screenshots and you will know what I mean.)

Heat Signature is one of those rare gems, that shine with a sense of simplicity and let you discover lot of approaches to the problems it poses in front of you. Sure, you can go in guns blazing, picking up new weapons on the go and rarely use the pause option - or you could take a long hard look at the gadgets you brought or found along the way and come up with fun and surprising ways to get to your objective.
As with other roguelikes, death (or captivity, which boils down to the same - a do over) comes quickly. But once you're in the flow (and use the goddamn pause function), you'll be flinging deadly wrenches left and right, knock out windows to suck your enemies (or yourself and your objective) into space.
There is a lot to discover behind the rather simplistic graphic set.

Well, I couldn't believe my eyes when I've seen this game for sale at one of those magazines that would provide a copy for certain tiles. That's because I'd always read articles about it and I was always dying to give it a try, but of course, the prices were often outrageous. Anyway, after I've got home and installed, I've noticed was that the game wasn't easy at all, so I've failed several times only by trying to learn how to work around my way with the tools of the trade. After finishing almost every single mission, eventually I've got to the penultimate and I've got stuck (there were no FAQs available in my mother's tongue and my english was even worse than now). Ok, so after a whole lot of frustration I've deleted the game and later I found redemption in the series through the following volumes of the franchise (except maybe for Contracts, it was kinda disappointing in my opinion). Now after all these years, Steam released the first game for an interesting price and I was like "what the hell", so I decided to give it a go again. I don't know if my memory is bad or not, but I don't really remember anything about having a checkpoint during the missions. Besides that, for some strange reason, no matter how perfect my aim would be, I'd always end up shooting at the wrong places (such as the arms of the bad guys, who'd end up looking like a bunch of tubemen). Seriously, no matter how many bullets you'd fire there, they'd still have enough strength and control to shoot you down as if your projectiles were mere flea bites. Well, after a few rage quits, I've finally got to that same part which I was stuck in the past and naturally the same thing happened again, only that this time I had the necessary means to get through that situation and finally manage to beat the game. Ok, after all that, what's my conclusion? It was a mix of nostalgia with disappointment, but I'm still giving a thumbs up for the good times I had before (especially with the wistful cheat codes).
