TL;DR: I just beat the game. Again. What I stated below still stands. It's an AC title. It runs well but is unpolished. I had a very meh time finishing it twice. It was fun to run around and stab people, but the actual game just honestly wasn't enjoyable. I ONLY recommend this if it's on sale and you want to beat it so that you can say you've played and beat every AC game. There are far better AC games out there to play...hell...there are much better games in general to spend your money on.
Edit: I re-read and edited some stuff to reflect my most recent opinions after beating it a second time. Once again, get this game if you care a lot about the AC series and want to experience all the games. I realize that that statement sounds dumb, but with all the hate that AC gets, I feel a lot of people are skeptical about this game (or other games) but aren't big fans of the series. So, if you care, get it. Otherwise, skip it.
The Good:
+ Story up until the end
+ Lots of stuff to do
+ Customization
+ The level system. You are better suited for certain missions based on armor level and weapon level.
+ Environments look good.
+ Dedicated sneak mode.
+ Cutscenes looked good.
+ Performance: What was a terrible gaming experience has turned into a very playable one. No performance issues on my part. Specs: i5 4690k (no OC lol) | GTX 970 | 8GB RAM | played on an SSD
The Bad:
+ Terribly frustrating combat mechanics. You can honestly just tank your way through the game with smoke bombs and a decent weapon if you don't feel like stealthing everywhere. Yes, the combat is clunky and annoying. Yes, there are some decently difficult enemies that get thrown at you, but nothing a smoke bomb can't fix. Guns are not fun when you have a sword.
+ Pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ textures (honestly not that important, but still)
+ Microtransactions
+ The ending. I went from really enjoying the story to really hating the story in about 5 seconds.
+ Clunky everything. From movement to combat to entering buildings.
+ Horrendous pop-in.
+ Modern day stuff seemed to be just filler content without any substance
+ I feel like when you loot enemies, you should have at least a 50% chance of getting your phantom blades back if you fired them.
*Extra*
+ I don't understand why throwing knives aren't in every AC game.
+ Why can't we use our fists, or hidden blades as primary weapons? I miss that.
+ Arno and Elise were both very decent characters. They weren't bad enough to take away from the game but they weren't good enough to make the game better.
+ Perk system. I don't know how I feel about it. I am not a huge fan of how it works in this AC game.
It seems that Ubisoft has trouble finding the right formula for an AC game. Each one seems to have something great but huge drawbacks. I haven't played Syndicate so hopefully that one is better, but I'll have to find out myself. Who knows, maybe AC: Origins will be pretty good.
*Unpopular opinion*
AC1 and the Ezio games remain the best of the AC series. Then AC U > Black Flag = Rogue > 3
I have not yet played Syndicate. I stated that AC U > Black Flag simply because Black Flag is a ♥♥♥♥ing pirate game. A game that exists because Ubisoft found out how much everyone loved the ship combat from AC3. Yes, Black Flag is a better game than AC U. But AC U is a better Assassin's Creed game. (obviously IMO)
If you disagree with anything in this review or something I stated was wrong, please let me know and share your opinion below.

This Game is a "Must Have" for everyone who is a fan of the Harvest Moon Games!
It is everything the series was and so much more. I've been waiting long for it's release and still LOVE to play it! I just started playing it again after some time and it didn't lost any of it's magic, on the contrary it just got more amazing with the updates and I just had to finally write a review of my own for Stardew Valley.
It was developed by a single(!) person, which makes it just even more awesome: great pixel art, beautiful music, interesting characters and a world just filled with love.
You can customize your character with many different clothes and hairstyles, just like you can craft and decorate your house with all kind of furniture. The same goes, of course, for the farm itself with it's crops, trees, barns and coops for your animals and even the farm map itself - be it a river with most of the area covered by water, a mining area with ore, geoges and cliffs, your standard map and some others as well.
Like you already figured there are a lot of activities as well. Farming, foraging, fishing, mining, even fighting monsters with the ability to level and skill in those 5 professions for additional perks. But this isn't the end of the line! Astebreed doesn't disappoint. It's a great addition to the genre, with very little negative to say about it.
The gameplay is fast paced, action packed, and chaotic. The game on normal isn't very difficult, the challenge comes from trying to get the highest score possible. Astebreed is a game that's made from the gameplay, and is one of my favorites in the genre.
The story was a bit hard for me to enjoy, because I found myself hardly able to read the subtitles. That being said, if you're playing this for the story, you're doing it wrong. There's also a few drawn still shots which looked alright, and were a nice addition.
The soundtrack is very fitting, and voices sound just like an anime would.
On the negative side, the game is very short. There's plenty of replay value, but if you're the type of person to play the game once and be done with it, I wouldn't pay full price for it. You may only get about 2 hours of entertainment. Also to note, the game runs well, but it randomly crashed near the end, and I had to restart from the beginning.
It's a great game, well worthy of it's current metacritic score. Buy it, so long as you're prepared for a very short campaign. If money is tight, you may want to consider something longer until it goes 75% off or so.

Bullet hells seem to be pretty hit and miss for me. That being said, this is quite frankly one of the best games of the genre I've ever played. The difficulty scaling is perfect, slowly advancing from "this is pretty easy" to "Oh my god how am I not dead yet?". The story was interesting too. You only get very small chunks but it's enough to work on in my opinion without bogging the game down.
Gameplay is what you'd expect from this sort of thing. There are like, infinity enemies that you shoot on the way to the boss. Camera angles change dynamically to make things interesting (but in a logical, controlled manner so it's not like you're going to get killed while you can't see or anything) and the visuals are very pretty.
This game seems like it's accessible to newbies to the bullet hell shooters but it's also challenging enough for veterans. For example, you have regenerating health and bombs. It means that you're not going to get a game over because you accidentally got shot 5 times in one stage but it certainly doesn't mean the game is easy. HP recovers slowly so it's less about "don't get hit, ever" and more about "you are currently in the middle of a rain of bullets and you are probably going to die if you don't do something about it"
There are several options for not dying, such as activating EX attacks (Similar to bombs from other games). You can even destroy certain projectiles, clearing part of the screen.
Even if you don't like bullet hells I'd recommend this game, it's something even someone terrible at the genre as me enjoyed.

Around a year ago I was in two minds when it came to recommending XCOM 2 or not. I enjoyed my first playthrough, but there was something I could not put my finger on that, unlike XCOM:EW, deterred me from repeat playthroughs. That has certainly changed with the introduction of the Long War 2 mod. It turns a solid but somewhat unoriginal sequel into something that I'm enthused by all over again. It makes the game different enough from the preceding game in ways I care about.
Without mods, XCOM 2 felt like a solid refinement, but not enough to sustain the time investment that multiple playthroughs would require. And without multiple playthroughs, it's hard to get a solid feel for how the hidden numbers behind the strategic layer play out. And without a firm understanding of that, it simply becomes a long string of loosely connected tactical missions.
I'd still recommend XCOM: Enemy Within before this. If only because that's bound to be cheaper, and is still an excellent game. After finishing that though, I do feel that the current state of XCOM 2 with the mods that are available makes it worth moving on to once you are done with EW.

The pick and roll never works as the players cannot seem to set a pick to save their lives.  The control mapping to call plays was also unnecessarily complex even for quick plays.  Even the shot timing just felt...off.
Defense
The defense in this game is a joke.  Your AI teammates will stand around while the other team moves around them to the basket.  Playing defense myself, the AI will be stopped before making a jaring motion to the side that your player can't apparently handle regardless of your controller input, leading to an easy basket as your teammates wave them on.  In the myCareer mode with player lock, the arrow indicating who to guard cannot seem to decide who you should be guarding and, as a result, your AI teammates will randomly decide that you are responsible for the guy they were moments ago closely guarding.
Style
The layout of the menus in the game made it difficult to navigate and just looked flat.  The diagonal text for everything wasn't as cool as someone thought it would be.  Are we suppose to be playing the game with our head cocked to the left?  Even the 2k13 Jay Z gaudy layout was better.
Story
I knew it was going to be bad and it met those expectations.  I like the attempt to innovate but this was a horrible overly scripted mess.  People want to feel like they are in control of a player rising into the NBA.  We do not want to be told some over dramatized story that is way to ridiculus to take seriously.
This game felt so horrible that I have to uninstall it and reinstall NBA 2k15 to get the bas taste out of my mouth.  Seriously 2k, stop trying to reinvent the wheel everytime with the gameplay.  Focus on innovating the modes.  The myCareer this year failed but I would have been perfectly fine with it if the gamplay wasn't also this broken.

This game, 'Brigador', brings you to series of vehicular combat in futuristic urban environment.
You are a mercenary pilot of mechs, tanks or anti-grav crafts, and you just engage in subversive activities on the city of a colonized planet.
Being more specific, Objective is eliminating a certain number of garrison, terminating all captain units, or destroying all orbital guns in the sector.
After that, you will escape with your life and reward by getting to a sector gate or a evac-spaceship.
Turret rotation and legs operation are separated (like 'Mechwarrior' or 'WoT').
Operating turret by mouse, steering by [W][A][S][D] keys.
When you drive anti-grav assault guns, chassis rotation is operated by lateral mouse movement, and [A][D] keys are used for strafe exceptionally.
Maneuverability varies by vehicle spec..
The heavier or the more robust the machine is, the lower maneuverability it has.
The player vehicles carry 2 guns and 1 special equipment (smoke/EMP/optical camouflage) .
Mouse Button 1 for firing gun 1, Mouse Button 2 for firing gun 2, and Mouse middle button (wheel click) for activating equipment.
Guns and equipment have various ballistic specification.
aiming might be felt hard cause inertia works slightly, but I like this realism.
You have to manage health, shield, ammo, and cooling/reloading time.
Health is not regenerative during a contract(series of missions), but shield energy can be refilled by enemy drops.
Ammo also can be recharged by enemy drops and ammo stations located in the sector.
Guns and equipment have reload/cooling time. take care of it.
Damage dealt varies by the status of caution (detected by foe or undetected).
Also it varies by hit direction. 100% for front, 140% for side, and 200% for rear.
If you sneak up behind the enemy, you can knock it down easily.
You can make your path and line of fire by smashing shacks, houses, walls, barricades, plants, and etc.
You will see some explosive objects in the sector, e.g. gaspipes and ammo stations. You can utilize them as powerful weapons. In some cases, you may  suddenly kill yourself by ramming into those explosives  as well.
This game is simple but still offers a many choice of tactics.
It may rely on chassis spec, weapons, equipment, resources and situation(enemy position/environment).
I really love those choice and making attempts.

At the time of this writing Hitman: Codename 47 is closing in on being 15 years old.
Hitman: Codename 47 has a great concept. It is the first hitman game I have played and has the series' iconic game mechanic of changing clothes which I found to be very fun. Sadly, that was one of the only things fun about this game.
The game maintains a level of enjoyment throughout except during longer missions where everything goes horrible every possible time for the player.
This game is a stealth game but often times I came to realize that the game doesnt seem to understand what a stealth game should be. Often times Agent 47 is forced into shootouts or situations that cannot be stealthed through. This becomes frustating very fast as the game also has no checkpoints and Agent 47 is relatively fragile compared to most action heroes. This lack of checkpoints makes the game challenging but less fun. Mechanics sometimes further amplify this problem as controls are imprecise and patroling guards sometimes randomly know you are the mysterious man who killed someone 2 blocks away in that back alley that no one saw or heard anything from.  The game does feature a respawn mechanic which allows the player to come back to life at a preset area (usually where you completed your last objective) ; HOWEVER, it does not make you incognito and every guard that was shooting at you before will still be shooting at you now.
The AI is terrible (Its understandable given the game is 15 years old)
Sometimes guards will be overly suspicious for no apparent reason. It is not unusual for a guard to hear a silent takedown and come running around the corner to see you over the body.. but because it was a silent takedown he obviously doesn't know it is you that performed the act. You can easily outsmart the AI but sometimes the game doesn't play by its own rules and someone downstairs three rooms away heard you when the guy right infront of you didn't.
The rules / game mechanics are vague
Even now after beating the game and understanding the game a whole lot more than I did while playing it, I do not understand the rules of some AI or mission objectives. Often times the game throws you into a level with an absurdly vague objective and lets you wander to figure it out. Usually what you are supposed to do has very little to do with the information you were given or objectives are exponentialy more complicated than the brief mission objectives say. Mission objectives do not tell you if you have completed them or not leading to sometimes trying to leave a mission and not knowing why you cannot. Often times I have wandered into an area that gets me killed not knowing it was restricted access or worse guards only sometimes care which leads to situations where you play the exact same way twice with different results.
The difficulty
Overall the game is challenging, but its a stealth game and getting caught is bad and gets you killed. Even ignoring the other flaws in the game the difficulty is still absurd. Missions can sometimes be really short and easy and then immediately you are thrown into a half hour minimum warzone with no idea what to do. Some missions I beat on my first try with no assistance from any walkthroughs and other missions even with walkthroughs it took me 5+ hours to beat a single mission. The first mission was almost impossible despite being incredibly straight forward. The first major assassination that takes place at a seaside restaurant is potentially the hardest. A later mission you are forced to take on a boss battle with Scarface Tony Montana who has an M60 while you have whatever little toy guns you can find lying around AND this is also in the middle of a larger mission where if you die you have to start all over due to no checkpoints.
Final Thoughts
Overall the game isn't the worst experience of my life. Some missions in it may qualify for that title but the game overall is enjoyable. If you had checkpoints and could skip levels that were overly hard and long the game might actually be somewhat recommendable. I think the games age does play a part in why it was so hard but a little extra effort to explain details of what needed to be done would have gone a long way in making this game a much more enjoyable experience.

Although there were definitely many flaws to this game, it was still incredibly fun to play and I was always challenged on every single mission. Probably the worst part of the game was the inability to save your progress in a mission. There was a checkpoint system in place, but if the guards were alerted before you died the first time, they would remain so when you respawned at a checkpoint. Furthermore, the difficulty of this game doesn't really allow for you to alert the guards very much. You pretty much have to be stealthy or very strategic when killing guards because their bullets do massive damage to your health, even on normal difficulty. Some of the missions are incredibly long as well, and many of them include large amounts of running before you can even encountering your objectives. Therefore, if you screwed up, it can cost you about 5 minutes of running around before you can get back to where you were. Other than that, the game is great. The weapons are fun to use, the stealth system is pretty solid, the missions are unique and well thought out. Most missions have multiple approaches of taking out a target, but most are fairly difficult to find. Other than the name and general location of the target, the game really doesn't help you out in terms of hints and clues. If you aren't very good at problem solving like me, you may have to use a guide to give you an idea of what to do in some of the more tricky missions. Overall, though, this game is challenging and entertaining and a good introduction to the Hitman series

This is a prelim review for early access, just to get the word out.  Brigador is an isometric vehicular shooter with fantastic production values and excellent look and feel.  The devs have focused early resources on the core gameplay, which is really quite good.  Even with the small subset of weapons and vehicles now available, the game manages to pull me back every so often just so I can experience that kick♥♥♥♥♥ blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up feeling one more time.
That gameplay features a modest number of player vehicles which fall into three categories: Mechs, Tanks and Anti-gravs.  Mechs have high acceleration and modest speed, but have a powerful stomp attack that is devastating to grounded enemies and the environment.  Tanks can boost for short periods to plow through the same at high speed (although the 'Dragon' actually slows down, it pretty much obliterates anything it touches).  Anti-gravs are unique in that they turn their entire chassis to aim, but they can move in any direction and can float over short obstacles.  They also slam the ground, but typically deal substantially less damage than the mech or tank equivelant.
The weapons available have varying statistics of shield damage, hull damage, environment damage, penetration and rate of fire.  At this point, ammo doesn't appear to be used to balance weapons, but is simply commensurate with the rate of fire.  Each vehicle can mount two weapons.  Usually these are weapons of different size categories, but some vehicles have two of the same mount.  The weapon balance is currently spotty, due to the fact that the unlock system has not yet been implemented and we're likely several balance passes away from 1.0 as it is.  Some weapons are fantastically effective, like the tank cannon (can't remember its actual name), while others are less than spectacular (the 8mm burst-fire, for example).
Brigador features a host of mechanics that really bring the visceral combat to life.  The AI is excellent in that it relies on line of sight, as well as the sound of weapon fire to locate the player.  The enemies start off basically flat-footed, many with their shields unpowered.  If you get the drop on them, you can take down quite a few hit-and-run style.  The moment you join battle though, nearby enemies will start closing in to investigate.  If you hide at this point, it's quite doable to avoid contact or better yet, lead your enemies into a killzone of your choosing.  Attacking enemies from behind is literally twice as effective as shooting their fronts, so it's often better to hit them on your terms than to simply charge into the middle of them.  You can use the environment to your advantage by setting off devastating chain reactions from explosive structures or by attacking the enemy through the very obstacles blocking them from returning fire.  Even the height of individual units is important, with the 'tower-like' enemies being able to spot and return fire over low-obstacles, whilst the tanks and infantry are stuck moving to get a shot.
As other reviewers have said, the price point is high for the content the game currently has, but let's be frank; This is Steam.  The dev needs to set their price point high if the game is going to display value to potential backers, and so that it can still be an equitable return when the inevitable Steam sales roll through.  It also means that they can get additional resources early on and not live in squalor hoping their game will make it big when it leaves early access, which we all know is /far/ from a guarantee; It's a fool's gamble.  For what it's worth, the game in its current state easily convinces me that the dev can fulfill their remaining content goals within the six months they've given themselves.
EDIT: Oh, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the excellent original score.  It's a high-tempo, arcade-style throw-back to 80's action movies that suits the aesthetic and general tone impeccably.

I would like to start off by saying that, as of writing this review, I have played every Hitman game, with the exception of Contracts. This gives me the opportunity to compare the games with each other and how well they (still) hold up.
Unfortunately, “Hitman: Codename 47” does not hold up very much. Time was not very kind to the game and it surely hasn’t aged all too well, making it rather difficult to recommend a playthrough.
There are a number of issues that plaque Codename 47. Being made 2000, it sure looks and plays like a contemporary game of that era. The graphics are okay at best, but like many early 3D games, everything is kind of blocky, which might be the result of IO-Interactive being a very small developer with limited resources back in the day. The gameplay is just plain clunky and overly complicated for no apparent reason. Seriously, different buttons for normal walking speed and running, sidestepping (strafing) and turning around? It took a while and a lot of key rebinding to get used to these controls personally. Anyone who played other or modern FPS/TPS will likely have the same issue.
Regarding the music, it’s good. Jesper Kyd, whom you may know as the composer for other games such as Assassin’s Creed, Borderlands and Kane & Lynch, is doing a fantastic job with very ambient, moody pieces, setting a perfect tone to a gritty game full of wetwork. The sound engineering in general is okay, nothing to complain about.
However, the voice acting is atrocious. Thank god they casted people with their respective dialect to fit the correlating character, but none of them are any good. Especially Agent 47 himself sounds just really silly and it’s hard to take him serious. Then again, a lot of games had this problem and still have, so it’s hard to fault the game just on the VA alone. David Bateson, voice actor for 47, reprised his role in subsequent sequels, doing a lot better in those thankfully.
Now, the biggest problem with “Codename 47” is simple: it just isn’t very good. What first appears to be a game about being sneaky and confronting targets with care and silence quickly just turns into a game that feels like a run-and-gun shooter, a pretty bad one. With the exception of two or three missions, the most part of the game is spent on gunning down the henchmen of your targets, before executing the targets themselves. Normally I don’t have a problem with blasting my way through waves of bad guys, however the problem here is A) we’re supposed to be a silent killer, so what gives? And B) the enemies have an unforgiving pin-point accuracy, leaving you dead before you can even insult the game for the cheap enemy fire.
Things that are supposed to aid you in your quest are meaningless. Taking on disguises of dispatched enemies often times doesn’t work in your favor, simply raising an alarm for the AI, which, in this game means “Everyone knows who you are, even in disguise. Why? Because the game hates you”. The AI WILL see you, disguise or not, from across the map. They will follow you, find you and they will kill you, because apparently everyone absolved with a diploma from the Liam Neeson School Of Premeditated Murder. And did I mention some missions have a failstate? So when the alarm is raised, you’re pretty much out of luck and will have to restart the mission if you’re not quick enough to get to your target. Simply put, the AI is broken beyond belief and leaves a bitter taste on an otherwise promising game.
Although I’ve been very critical about “Codename 47”, I want to address that I’ve had my fair share of fun with it. I loathed it more than enjoying it, but I would be lying if I didn’t enjoy some aspects, like the few missions which feel like actual Hitman games (the missions “The Lee Hong Assassination” and “Traditions of the Trade” come to mind).
“Hitman: Codename 74” sets the foundations for a fantastic and still mostly unique video game franchises. The debut game is sadly overshadowed by subsequent games in every conceivable way. With the second game in the series, “Silent Assassin”, IO-Interactive out-done themselves already.
If you would like to know how the franchise started, give it try. However, if you want to play a game that feels more like a proper Hitman, skip this one and just continue with the second game, Silent Assassin. Otherwise, try “Hitman: Contracts” which is basically an expanding and proper remake of the debut.

Hitman: Codename 47 is a wonderful little piece of beauty, and is a wonderful example of a good third-person action/shooter sandbox mess of fun, which I totally recommend.
The game, while dated graphically and audialy, still holds up in fun shooter/stealth gameplay. It's controls are a tad odd, but once you adapt to them in the game's Training level (or rebind them), the game can become a blast to play, figuring out where your targets are going to be, reading target information and watching target videos, choosing your weapons and ammunition all while hearing the game's badass music, composed by music industry veteran Jesper Kyd and his wonderful assortment of electronic tools and instruments.
The start to an amazing video game series, Hitman: Codename 47 is a great cult classic and, in my opinion, a must play, IF you're planning on getting into the series.

Fantastic and unique core gameplay, expanded on using roguelike elements, but limited by a lack of long-term consequences, variety, and narrative, plus confusing graphics and UI. If you're like me, I'd recommend it on the basis of being interestingly innovative alone, but you'll also get a ~12 hour playthrough if you only play the enjoyable parts. A 100% completion run isn't worth it, though you'll probably keep popping in during lunch break.
I wouldn't ask you to believe me without verification, so let's go over some specific examples (without spoilers):
Real-time-with-pause top-down 2D shooter with one-hit-kills/knockouts. WASD to move, mouse to aim, click to fire, all controls rebindable. Missions rarely last more than five minutes, and you can speed through most in under thirty seconds. However, you have infinite slo-mo (automatically applies while in sight of an enemy, but can also be bound to a key), and can pause, adjust your aim, and fire. Thrown in the mix is a simple stealth system; there's no fog of war on the player's end, but stay in a guard's cone of vision and an alarm sounds, causing a doom timer to start (game time; pausing and slo-mo stop and slow the timer, respectively). Expect to ask yourself "If I pop out of cover, can I shoot everyone in the room before they raise the alarm/shoot back?", and "Can I use a gadget to lure people out of the room, sneak by, or give myself extra time to shoot?" The quick time to kill makes combat visceral, ala twitch shooters, but adjustable pacing prioritizes thinking over reflexes and marksmanship, ala tactical shooters. It's beautiful.
"Soft" permadeath: death wipes your cash and inventory, but campaign progress remains. Also noteworthy: getting hit knocks you out even with weapons that kill everyone else. However, taking hits reduces the likelihood you'll survive next time. The game randomly generates the player characters, mission layouts and objectives, guard positions and equipment, unlock trees, and shop inventories, but tempers this with player choice; get a mission or character you don't like and you can choose another from a small list. There's little overarching story besides "end the war", but there is some short, structures, and surprisingly philosophical and funny conversations to unlock (When is it right to kill? What constitutes a person? What drives corporations? Why does the training machine have a "MORE VIOLENCE" button?).
We've gone over how bullets treat you special. There's stat tracking for kills, knockouts, alarms, and living witnesses, but these oddly don't matter outside the occasional bonus objective. Kill with impunity and guards never think to ditch stun guns. Cause alarms and no one steps up security. Leave witnesses and no one comes after you. It's a fantastic foundation for a reputation system, and nothing's utilized. The absolute worst setback the game throws at you is death, but you only lose your cash and inventory (replaceable with a half hour's play at most, and you'll still progress the campaign during that time). There's never any meaningfully risky missions, which means you're never too worried about consequences, which robs the game of meaningful long-term choices, which limits long-term replay value.
The positions of rooms themselves vary, but you'll recognize room every layout within an hour. You'll have seen most of the gear in six, minus a few rare variants you'll never get to keep anyways. Not helping matters are the defector missions; optional challenges that give you limited but interesting gear restrictions in an effort to make you aware of new playstyles. Unfortunately, this spoils a lot of mechanics while giving no progress whatsoever, thus making the rest of the game a retread. Even the guards follow predictable patterns, never looking for missing comrades or leaving their designated section unprovoked. There's missed opportunities for variety everywhere; every bullet flies the same speed, room layouts never combine into larger rooms, guards use only a handful of available weapons, the game's set in space but never uses aliens, and so on.
Am I the good guy? Who am I working for? What am I working for? Supposedly the region's at war, but who does that affect? What's at stake? There's the extremely well-written conversations that flesh out the faction's beliefs and government, but there's not much payoff besides a few laughs and some interesting ideological discussion. The characters you're talking to never do anything, the factions function mostly the same gameplay-wise (good idea making the police faction use non-lethal weapons, but the illusion was broken when they put missile launchers on their ships). I have very little reason to suspend disbelief, which makes caring about the story or messaging near impossible. I mean, I guess there's some anarchist theming? You're fighting for the region's independence, and that corporate faction's pretty bad, so I guess it's better than those guys. But there's three other factions with roughly the same influence, and there's no obvious ideological reason they can't get along. You got an engineer faction, a police faction, and a nomad faction, with no known history between them. Not exactly Sunnis and Shias. Why are we fighting again? Oh, right, it's a videogame.
This is better served with screenshots. Best of times
, worst of times
. They should speak for themselves.
It's all instrumental tracks and they're typical sci-fi-esque. Mysterious electronic theme while flying through space, neutral electronic theme while at a friendly station, slightly more intense electronic theme while on enemy spaceships, you get the drill. Not that it's phoned in; the beeps and boops have just the right amount of polish to convey the tone. Unfortunately, that tone is too generic to convey anything interesting. I blame the narrative; without anything interesting to say, the composer doesn't have anything to reinforce. Maybe if the factions had individual themes? The mechanic faction could mix in industrial, the corporate faction could mix in pop chords and beats, the police faction could mix in academy-style drums, the nomad faction could mix in classical strings. Right now, the music just...exists.
Buy it, the core gameplay's just that good. Avoid the defector missions that aren't labeled "special". Hunt achievements, they're decent enough excuses to play. I'd love to see some tweaks, and I'd pay money for an expansion, maybe something a little more narrative focused or with long-term consequences. Regardless, it's enjoyable as is. I'll miss real-time-with-pause when move on to other shooters, top-down or otherwise.

I remember this game being very unique for its time. Definitely a classic in my book gaming through the 90's. This game is very in style for Microprose. Another one of theirs that I really liked was the Return of the Phantom, which is not yet on steam. The graphics with Dragonsphere were very good for the time, and a very different style to what Sierra was doing. I think that with Dragonsphere, the vision was very big with the animations, but the technology was limited. This game is also quite difficult as were many point and click adventure games of the time. They alwasy left you wondering on what was next to do, and you would spend hours traveling around and clicking things to find the next step. I have no idea how I did it when i was younger with very little access to hint systems. I replayed this and many other games so many times I could usually start new and from memory go through each of the points in the game and finish it within a few hours, or less than a days time. Its fun to go through these classics for the nostalgia, but I am also surprised at how much I have forgotten and how new feeling it can be too. Even though I probably went through Dragonsphere a several dozen times as a child, I would be totally lost without a walkthrough now.
Some negative reviews have noted about the 'meh' story line. I think the plot is very simple, but the game is filled with all types of content that I have never seen anywhere else. You do have to dig a little deeper than just the introduction and your first venture out of the castle. The story is not going to blow your mind, or get you too emotionally involved with the characters. But it has some interesting things non the less. The voice acting is also a bit 'meh' but for me the nostalgic memory of the time was in awe over the fact there were voices at all. CD-ROM and voice acting in video games were just starting to make an appearance. This was like magic and this game and several others were pioneers to the craft.
I think the price of the game is worth it for what you get. But the game is not going to be for everyone.

I wouldn't know about you, but I've always been a fan of the old school adventure games with rich stories and ridiculously hard puzzles back in the day.
is an old school point & click adventure, originally developed and published by Microprose in 1994, and carries all qualities of its genre from obscure puzzles to incredibly rich narrative.
We take a quick glimpse on the land of Callahach, a medieval realm with high fantasy elements. 20 years ago, the evil sorcerer Sanwe was defeated and sealed into his own tower by the King, young prince Callash and court wizard, Ner-Tom with the usage of the Dragonsphere. 20 years later, the seal begins to wear off and once again, the realm is threatened by Sanwe's probable release. Prophecies of old call - now King Callash, to finish the battle started 20 years ago. After his coronation, our King decides to take the quest of facing the evil sorcerer and see to his demise once and for all.
Here in the land of Callahach, our fair hero is to embark on a journey to collect aid from neighboring nations in hopes of defeating Sanwe. Callach is to solve faerie riddles, deal with cunning shapeshifters, drink and gamble with the Caliph of Soptus, tread the Spirit Realm, wrestle with beasts of deep realms, avoid deadly traps and even prejudice of his own people. In the end though, the deceit comes from our one blind side, of course, with the addition of one major plot twist.
Without revealing further details of this beautiful, yet short story; let's take a look on what
has to offer. The game hails from the day when we used MS-DOS to play games, and it still uses a DOS BOX, which is both nostalgic and cute in my opinion. If you are in favor of realistic and magnificent graphics, this surely is not it. Yet, with the technology of the given era,
doesn't fail to deliver an elegant and beautiful display, accompanied with surprisingly catchy midi music. The movements of characters, background art and interactive animations do seem like art: pretty and elegant. I'm sure that some people made this game with much time and love spared. Voice acting is a bit hoarse and unimaginative, but script itself makes up for its own.
Gameplay menu presents you a list of actions and an inventory, in which you can combine actions with either items or the environment. Combinations are not always logical, but always imaginative. For everything you look at, you are rewarded with detailed narrative descriptions which enrich the setting greatly. Puzzles are really hard, I won't lie. For the first puzzle of the game - the Faerie Maze - you have to go through a logic puzzle, which did take 3 hours for me to figure out! When I finally figured the correct combination out, I was about to shed tears of joy! Aside this one, you will be encountering movement puzzles, language puzzles and lore puzzles, all obscure, yet imaginative and well thought. There is no replay value at all, but one playthrough is challenging enough.
is certainly not for everyone. I'll recommend this game for the nostalgic and the one who'd like a real challenge in brain gymnastics only. Also, I have to inform you that the game is free for you to grab in GOG, so you may prefer not to pay for it here on Steam. I, for myself, was happy to lend some financial provision for Microprose, for the old times’ sake.

Strong action-RPG gameplay with absolutely superb audio and even more superb visuals, and a compelling storyline narrated by a guy with like the most badass deep gravelly voice ever. Combat is varied--different weapons play differently, and their natural strengths and weaknesses against certain enemies or situations make it gently profitable to swap loadouts without forcing you into a particular style. There are secrets and bonus levels to keep you going for 100% completion without feeling padded, and if you like the game enough to keep playing post-story, it lets you start over from the beginning while keeping all your unlocks from your previous playthrough.
Bottom line, it's fun, beautiful, and polished, and I recommend it pretty highly.

This is a prelim review for early access, just to get the word out.  Brigador is an isometric vehicular shooter with fantastic production values and excellent look and feel.  The devs have focused early resources on the core gameplay, which is really quite good.  Even with the small subset of weapons and vehicles now available, the game manages to pull me back every so often just so I can experience that kick♥♥♥♥♥ blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up feeling one more time.
That gameplay features a modest number of player vehicles which fall into three categories: Mechs, Tanks and Anti-gravs.  Mechs have high acceleration and modest speed, but have a powerful stomp attack that is devastating to grounded enemies and the environment.  Tanks can boost for short periods to plow through the same at high speed (although the 'Dragon' actually slows down, it pretty much obliterates anything it touches).  Anti-gravs are unique in that they turn their entire chassis to aim, but they can move in any direction and can float over short obstacles.  They also slam the ground, but typically deal substantially less damage than the mech or tank equivelant.
The weapons available have varying statistics of shield damage, hull damage, environment damage, penetration and rate of fire.  At this point, ammo doesn't appear to be used to balance weapons, but is simply commensurate with the rate of fire.  Each vehicle can mount two weapons.  Usually these are weapons of different size categories, but some vehicles have two of the same mount.  The weapon balance is currently spotty, due to the fact that the unlock system has not yet been implemented and we're likely several balance passes away from 1.0 as it is.  Some weapons are fantastically effective, like the tank cannon (can't remember its actual name), while others are less than spectacular (the 8mm burst-fire, for example).
Brigador features a host of mechanics that really bring the visceral combat to life.  The AI is excellent in that it relies on line of sight, as well as the sound of weapon fire to locate the player.  The enemies start off basically flat-footed, many with their shields unpowered.  If you get the drop on them, you can take down quite a few hit-and-run style.  The moment you join battle though, nearby enemies will start closing in to investigate.  If you hide at this point, it's quite doable to avoid contact or better yet, lead your enemies into a killzone of your choosing.  Attacking enemies from behind is literally twice as effective as shooting their fronts, so it's often better to hit them on your terms than to simply charge into the middle of them.  You can use the environment to your advantage by setting off devastating chain reactions from explosive structures or by attacking the enemy through the very obstacles blocking them from returning fire.  Even the height of individual units is important, with the 'tower-like' enemies being able to spot and return fire over low-obstacles, whilst the tanks and infantry are stuck moving to get a shot.
As other reviewers have said, the price point is high for the content the game currently has, but let's be frank; This is Steam.  The dev needs to set their price point high if the game is going to display value to potential backers, and so that it can still be an equitable return when the inevitable Steam sales roll through.  It also means that they can get additional resources early on and not live in squalor hoping their game will make it big when it leaves early access, which we all know is /far/ from a guarantee; It's a fool's gamble.  For what it's worth, the game in its current state easily convinces me that the dev can fulfill their remaining content goals within the six months they've given themselves.
EDIT: Oh, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the excellent original score.  It's a high-tempo, arcade-style throw-back to 80's action movies that suits the aesthetic and general tone impeccably.

Brigador has just released on Steam Early access and we're taking a quick look at it in its current early stages.
Brigador is a isometric tank shooter with a few different play styles. You can play brigador sneaky deaky like and cloak or if your the Arnold type rush in guns blazing.
Currently there are 9 vehicles to pilot ranging from hover tanks, to mechs, to something that looks straight out of a red necks fantasy... yep an el camino with a giant monster cannon.
Your goal in one of these vehicles is to either sneak or shoot your way into various locations and destroy the glorious leaders cannons, generals, or just massacre a percentage of his army.
The controls are a bit difficult at first to get used to as you must handle your turret, your legs/tank (which rotate separately) while maintaining aim with your guns and their ranges. Meaning 3 things at once which I am rather poor at.
If this hectic gameplay isnt your style there are hover tanks you can use that have locked turrets. Keep in mind the developers have promised 40+ new vehicles coming before Brigador leaves steam early access.
That being said after a few hours with the game the controls get simpler. I found the sniping / sneaking gameplay to be my forte as it let me move slowly and set things up as opposed to the large hectic fights where I ended up slamming into the walls screaming at my keyboard.
Overall I think Brigador is a solid game for being at the early stages of development. I do think the price point is a bit high but once the game is finished it will definitely be worth that cost.
My only real complaint with the game was the controls and thats more my fault at being an old man than the fault of the game.

Hitman is a staple franchise of the IO Interactive company and was distributed by Eidos, the same company that distributed the first two waves of the Tomb Raider franchise. The game centers around a genetically engineered clone who goes by no name other than "47" escapes from an asylum after going through various tests in both combat and weapon skills. A year later 47 was recruited by the ICA(International Contract Agency) a government division that specializes in assassinations, espionage, & terrorism. Agent 47 goes on global missions to assassinated various crime lords, drug dealers, weapon smugglers, thugs, terrorists, etc. Upon his travels, 47 notices that there's a connection between the targets he's executed and is willing to piece the puzzle together to find out who they all work for. The first entry in the series has it's share of clunky controls, occasional glitches, and situations that defy logic. These isssues, I can look past as the game does offer a challenge and fun factor. After the release of this game, Agent 47 would soon be ranked as a favorite anti hero for games. His cross of Vin Diesel and Golgo 13 gives him an iconic look along with situations and moments that will remind you of Terminator, Nikita, Scarface, and Leon the Professional. This was the first game to use a fully composed orchestra, the first to use the rag doll function(whenever you drag a corpse is moves like a doll), and the earliest use of the cloth function on the character's clothing. Keep in mind that the later games do get better, as at times this game can be frustrating with no mid level saving,minimum health meter, and poor functionality of disguises. But again this is only the first game, so give it some mercy. Anyways if you like playing a third person shooter where you have various options to kill a target, choices of prefered weapons to use on the missions, and various disguises to put on will make this game worth your while.

I bought this game for PS2 originally, and when I played it so much that my disc became unplayable, I bought another PS2 copy. This makes this digital version the 3rd copy of this game I have owned.
The game itself is a masterpiece of art, writing and gameplay. It will make you laugh, and cry, and think deeply. All these years later and I am still not over the emotional impact my very first playthrough had on me. It appears to be completely unchanged, which is mostly good with one caveat. The original had a 15 minute long into sequence on a new game with narration that MUST be clicked-through. You can't leave it running while you go get a glass of water and just get the gist. Unfortuantely they left this as a manual click-through in the PC version, rather than trimming down that opening sequence or making it scroll automatically. This is not a big enough reason to opt out on this game, but if you have never played Okami before, just be aware that it exists.
My first playthrough of this game took 60 hours just to do the quests. Since then, I could finish it in around 40 hours if I didn't go for all the collectibles. If you have never played Okami before, it isn't organized by MQ versus Side Quests in quite the same way that most games are. There is optional side content that you can skip, but it isn't organized clearly into one category or the other. It feels cohesive and organic when you play.
(I will add any other comments about the content of the game above, should I find any differences between this and the original).
I am going to focus the rest of this review on the technical aspects of this port.
First of all, it IS a port and the game has not been restructured for PC as far as I can tell. While it is performing very well, and the HD graphics look amazing, I do have a few technical complaints about the port.
1) Aspect Ratio. While it is advertised as being compatible with widescreen and thewidescreen options ARE 16;9, there is no native 1920x1080 option, which is an annoying detail for most monitors. I run the 1280x720 option in full screen and it fits my screen, but no native resolution options are not ideal.
2) Low FPS = Slowed Animations. I started running the game at the highest settings. My FPS was extremely unstable, and when dips happen in Okami HD, the result is the "voices" and animations are all slowed down with the frame rate. This means that a low frame rate isn't "choppy" the way it would be in say, a Bethesda game, but it is still very undesireable.
3) Capped FPS. As discussed and announced before release, the FPS is capped at 30 by the game. The upside is that my frame rate is much more stable than is normal for my machine. If the FPS directly affects the speed of voices and animation, as above, it's possible that Okami internally caps the frame rate at 30 to preserve that, so I can't really fault them for that, but I know this is something a lot of gamers are upset about. I can assure you though, that unlike a lot of modern games, 30 FPS is smooth as silk for Okami and is really very appropriate. The entire game is very cinnematic, there are no fine detail animations that could be made smoother by higher frame rates, and it is not a shooter where 60 fps is necessary for good gameplay.
3) Graphics "quality" = No noticeable differences from medium to high. This could be positive or negative depending on your outlook. I turned my graphics quality down to medium to fix the FPS issues above. I noticed absolutely no loss in quality, in spite of using a lower resolution than my native option. The HD graphics are still crystal clear. I might try turning the graphics down to Low to see if that makes any difference either. The great thing about Okami's graphics is that they are so stylized that they stand the test of time, regardless of their "quality."
4) Graphics settings are a huge drain. This is kind of a continuation of point 3, and the real downside to it. I got a HUGE performance boost by dropping my settings from "high" to "medium" with absolutely no loss in visual quality. I don't know what Okami HD's graphics settings are changing, but whatever it is hogs performance. Do yourself a favor and stick to medium, you are not missing anything on High.
5) Some Keybinds are Fixed. The best way to experience this game might be with a controller, but I am trying this playthrough with my mouse and keyboard. Most of the in-game controls and keybinds can be changed as is standard for PC games, but there are a few that are fixed which are unfortunately the most annoying ones. In-menu controls for the Main Menu screen and the Settings Menu screen cannot be changed. They are Enter Key to select and Backspace Key to go back, which is just not standard. I would like to be able to change the keybinds so that E is enter and Esc is back to be in line with most modern games.
6) Menus are set up for console. If anyone ever figures out how to mod this game, I would like to see menu changes for PC that are mouse-responsive. At the moment, menus must be navigated with the WASD or cursor keys, and the enter and backspace keys. They are not mouse responsive at all. This goes for all menues in the game.
7) PS2 Camera movement defaults. If you want Okami's camera to react to your mouse like any other modern game, you need to go into the settings and change the camera to "invert X and Y axis." Just do it right away and thank me later.
Some other things that are not complaints but simply notes for people who played this game on console and are playing it again here:
- If you want that slow, smooth and deliberate celestial brush from the console, turn the speed setting for it all the way down.
- Turn your mouse sensitivity WAY down unless you want your camera flicking all over the place
- Most of the default keybinds for us in-game are actually very good and well thought out. If you don't like them you can change almost all of them
- If you alt-tab the game to do anything else on your computer, it will automatically put the game into Windowed mode.
Some exclusively positive notes:
- Because it is a digital download, the loading speeds are significantly improved from the original, both in the actual loading screens and in background loading. In my Ps2 version, I often encounter places were actors in the world haven't properly loaded, and what I see instead is the development marker for them as I am running up to them. This appears to be completely eliminated in this version even when running at top speed.
UPDATE 12/22: You can rotate the camera in Celestial Brush mode by using the WASD keys while holding down your brush key. Camera rotation is the inverse of most modern game cameras and that setting can't be changed, but it's not too bad to adjust to because the game stayed suspended while you're fiddling with the view.
I will update this review as I play if I encounter anything else I think everyone should know about.

If you've ever played mechcommander, mechwarrior, future cop or really any game with a mech on the cover you'll likely enjoy Brigador. If you liked classic westwood C&C games environments, attention to detail and music, Brigador will likely give you nostalgia. If you simply like quick and easy to play action games like nuclear throne or spelunky, Brigador is going to appeal to the same style of fun.
In a way the game is incredibly simple, you can just run in and shoot things until you get to the end, but it's so well made that the simplicity only really helps the game. You pick a vehicle, two guns and a special weapon (I recommend smoke grenades with the tauro mech) and need to complete one of three objectives per area, all of which involve blowing things up. Enemy AI allows for you to either stealth your way in or out, maneuver your way around at high speeds dodging shots, or simply bust your way through walls crushing anything in your way.
Despite all this, the game is tough: you cannot regain health at all except by killing enemies to regain your shields, so avoiding damage by killing fast or playing smart is essential if you want to get to the end and off of the planet. Ammo management is also an issue, as you need to either harvest it from your enemies without blowing it up first or regain it from depots that correspond to your ammo type, which are often surrounded by enemies. Keep in mind that if you don't need the ammo type, you can just use the depot as an explosive to still save you some shots. An added layer of difficulty comes from optionally playing as lighter, more agile mechs that definitely require finesse to control compared to other options such a pillar of scrap on treads. You can expect any vehicle to reward you if you use it right however.
As a game Brigador is definitely fun, as a mech game Brigador plain rules. The perspective, graphics, explosions, destructible environment and hordes of enemies you take down really make it feel like you're a piece of heavy weaponry and not just a reskinned human. If you like mechs, buy this game.

If you like Harvest Moon, Rune Factory, Animal Crossing, that one Nintendo game where you're a little prince and you're rebuilding a kingdom and a giant crystal tells you what to do, whatever, you'll love this.
Growing up my favorite DS game was Rune Factory : A Fantasy Harvest Moon. Cut to me in 2012 googling "games like Rune Factory for PC" after getting my first gaming computer. An article, that's far too old to look up now, covered the development of an "up and coming indie game" called Stardew Valley. I was HOOKED. I have email chains to Eric that date back to October of that year. I'd never cared **so much** about a game.
Delay after delay after delay, I was worried this was going to be the one that got away. When the actual release got closer and closer, I was worried that it wouldn't live up to my expectations. I mean, I had been waiting for 4 years, how could it?
Then February 2016 came. I.. I don't even know where to start. This game scratched an itch I didn't even know I had, an itch that had been there since my copy of Rune Factory got corrupted and I never got to play a game like this again, until now. I know I'm rambling, but this game.. will do that to you. You'll be telling your friends about a new crop/scarcrow/sprinkler arrangement you discovered that optimizes space, about the characters you're befriending and the heart events that follow, about the weird little dwarf dude you want to talk to but can't because you sold all your scrolls. This game will haunt your every waking moment if you let it. And I highly suggest you do. You can farm. Raise animals. Fish. Go mining. Fight monsters. Be the town ♥♥♥♥♥. Befriend the apple fairies. Destroy the sense of community and fall under corporate greed. Marry the depressed alcoholic. Do whatever the hell you want, this town is yours.
I love this game. I love Eric. I love this community. I love Willy (can he be the next bachelor?).

Where the game lacks there is a strong modding base to draw from, so between modding and randomly generated game elements, there always seems like more cause for replays. I have plenty more characters to recruit for Legend playthroughs...
People have different experiences with game stability. I have had very little instability other than through sloppy modding, so I can attest to game problems not being a certainty. The issues I've had with the game itself have at worst required me to go to the main menu and reload... like once every 100hrs. Other issues are not game-breaking and just sorta part of the environment you're immersed in.
The game is definitely different than XCOM 2012, improved in many ways- graphics, gameplay, pacing of the narrative development, challenge, creature models, customization- and lacking in only one: the horror-genre dread of engagement (because it's a lot more action-oriented now). XCOM 2 is a faster-paced version with less insanity dealing with the "global expansion" aspect, but both have a steep learning curve and carelessness is met with the usual mercilessness by the AI.
I'll recommend the game because the devs did a great job investing in the core aspects of their franchise, but it's obviously a bit of a niche genre that it fits into. Still it's worth giving a shot if you enjoy a more sophisticated process of liberating the world from alien occupation. 300+hrs so far have more than given me my money's worth...

A fantastic refinement and expansion of what Edelweiss started in their fun but flawed Ether Vapor. Astebreed is mechanically solid, easy to read and a joy to play for shmup fans. For newcomers to the genre Astebreed can work as a fantastic introduction. The game features a fantastic prologue chapter that functions as an in-game tutorial. There is also a gallery that demonstrates the various abilities and how to execute them with video and interactive tutorial segments. Finally the difficulty levels are well scaled, providing challenge and fun to all skill levels.
Once you learn the mechanics and beat the game it doesn't stop there. Astebreed features deep and rewarding scoring mechanics on top of all the other great features, so if you enjoy score chasing and leaderboards there is a lot of meat here.
Finally the presentation is about as flawless as you could ask for in this type of game. The anime stylings perfectly capture the feel of 80s and 90s mecha and space opera anime, much like Ether Vapor before it. The music, audio and visuals in game are top notch. This game is a tour de force for shmup fans and a triumph for Edelweiss' particular design concepts.

This game is a fast-paced, top down, mmo, bullet hell, rogue-like game in which you play as one of 14 classes and work to get better gear and max your stats. This game is extremely fun and rewarding, but also heart-breaking and causes many swear words to be spat out. At the time of writing this, I have a bit over 960 hours on this game. As you can see, it is extremely addicting and will keep you hooked for a long time, even if you quit after your character dies, you'll always come back. It's like a drug actually. As for the actual game it's self it's pretty simple, you run around, shoot at things, dodge bullets from enemies, kill things to obtain better gear and stat potions (which are used to max the 8 stats in the game Attack, Speed, Vitality, Defense, Dexterity, Wisdom, HP, and MP). As stated above, it's extremely fun and rewarding when your character is alive, expecially obatining better gear and loot. As for obtaining said loot, it can drop in a variety of 6 different bags. 1. Brown Bags-low tier gear that can be seen by everyone. 2. Pink Bags-low to mid tier gear that can still be seen by everyone. 3. Purple Bags-a bit higher tier gear than pink bags and can only be seen by you. 4. Blue Bags-Contain stat potions 5. Cyan Bags-Contain high tier gear and can only be seen by you 6. White Bags- Contain untiered items and can only be seen by you. (Untiered=better than any tiered items)
Anyway, there is a lot more to this game but I don't feel like explaining everything that in-depth so I'll just go over my few gripes with the game.
1. THE COMMUNITY - Oh boy, in a game about working together to beat dungeons and to help each other, you would think the community would be nice to each other but nope. There are people who drag enimies on to AFK players, leechers who just sit in the starting room and teleport once the people have made it to the boss, just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in general who get angry whenever they don't get the loot that they want and when you get it they rage at you, scammers, and sooo much more. I've found myself kind of playing solo at most times simply because I don't want to deal with the horrid community in this game.
2. KABAM (Sometimes) - Everyone always complains about Kabam because they made the game easier by adding pets and by making Tops (top tier gear) able to be bought in the Nexus. Although that was annoying, they've gotten better. Such as Wis-mod making 3 classes (Paladin, Preist, and Mystic) have their wisdom affect how much damage and how long their ability should last. Also, they added some dungeons (shatters, Shaitans, the Epic dungeons, Belladona's garden, etc.) they also brought back a couple old dungeons (LoD and BeachZone).
All in all, the game has a couple problems, but most games do. This game is very challenging and I love it very much.
Update: With the Deca Games takeover, it hasn't been very long but I can already tell this game is going to improve tenfold. The new owners seemingly actually care about the game, rather than the former owners just kinda sweeping it under the rug for months. Many people who quit the game because of Kabam are coming back and the community finally feels a little less toxic.

First of all Chucklefish posted almost daily on their website about the progress they have been making and will do so in the future.
All together they have been listening to the community a fair bit, which I for one appreciate a lot.
Moving on to the review of the actual game:
Starbound is a beautiful game with the most stunning looks in the genre (IMO).
You can choose between the seven current races, each with their own ship design and A.I.
The ship can be upgraded by solving quests for NPCs, which makes it bigger until you have a true dreadnaught
to explore the universe. Each ship type has a unique layout, all of them awesome!
The tech-progression has been reworked and at a point splits into three different crafting trees with different benefits and downsides.
There are a fair amount of different blocks and I spend at least half of my game time construction massive bases, temples, skyscrapers, caverns and so on.
Starbound offers a pretty big number of items to place in your constructions (or wherever you like for all that matters),
a paint tool to colour blocks, a wiring tool to create circuits. Circuits can be pretty complex and if you are creative you can even make switch puzzles and so on.
After the latest patch Starbound also features special missions you can obtain at the outpost. To those you have to beam via your ships A.I. and they are all pretty nicely done.
So if you like to create and build, to explore and to dig, if you like sience-fiction and space travel this is the game for you!

Brigador is a tactical isometric shooter where every thing in the environment is destructible. At the time of this review, the game is still incomplete but shows a lot of promise in it's well designed gameplay.
Brigador is a challenging game to say the least. A player's first inclination is to shoot everything in sight, but you'll quickly learn that strategy will get you killed pretty fast. Your ammo is limited, your HP don't regenerate, and the game features a perma-death system. With out careful planning and strategic thinking, you'll become scrap metal in an instant. The game has a high learning curve, and an equally high skill ceiling. The game makes no concession to casual players.
The goal of the game is to enter an enemy territory, shoot out 3 of their cannons, and then get the hell out of there. It sounds simpler than it actually is. In any given map, there will be tons of enemies swarming to blow you up if you're not careful, as well as environmental hazards. Gas pipes, oil stations, and other things can easily blow up in your face ending your run. Then there are mud, tracks, and sand that will slow you down. Though there are hazards, the environment is completely destructible, allowing you to make your own path to the goals, avoiding the dangerous main roads.
Before even starting your mission, you'll be able to pick your vehicle, weapons, and special abilities. there are 6 different vehicles that are variations of 3 different types, tank, mech, and hover. Tanks have good Armour and speed, while mechs can use a powerful stomp, and hovers can strife and are the quickest, but they're balanced with low armour and HP. They all have their own unique characteristics and stats, and the same can be said about the weapons and specials as well. The game offers a fair degree of customization and experimentation, allowing the player to tailor their ship to their play style.
Brigador also features detailed but visually clear sprites in an isometric environment. The aesthetics have a classic PC look to it, and it's one of my favorite elements of the game. The art is interesting, full of nuance, and does a good job at communicating it's overall theme and atmosphere of a dystopian future. The sound design is also quite pleasing, with an appropriately futuristic OST and sound effects that has impact. However, since the game is in early access, some sound effects aren't implemented and is distracting from what is an otherwise polished presentation.
There's a lot of stuff to like about the game, it's presentation, it's skill oriented gameplay, and the destructible environments, however in it's current state, the game does feel incomplete. Currently, there is only one mode to play, endless mode, nothing to unlock, no stat tracking, and no story mode. So basically, the game is bare bones feeling very very beta. Of course it's in early access and these things are to be expected, but it is something worth mentioning for any one expecting a complete game. Bragador does not feel complete. There is a lot of room to grow and I am excited to see where it goes. One feature I really would like to see added is some kind of multiplayer. But until the game is further updated / released, it doesn't give much incentive for the player to keep playing, other than it's core gameplay, and maybe experimenting with different combinations of weapons and ships.
Overall, Brigador is a very promising game, that in my opinion, has the potential to be a cult favorite. All the game need to do now is to fill itself out a little. Give the player a reason to come back regularly. We'll see how it'll turn out once it's a full release, but so far, so good.
Pros:
- Great classical looking visuals
- Challenging and rewarding gameplay
- Destructible environments
- customization
Cons:
- Missing sound assests
- limited game modes
- Feels incomplete

Explanation on whether this game is or is not Pay 2 Win
The game is free until 900 Power Rank (You will progress mainly through leveling up and equipment)
The game is grinding until 1200 Power Rank (Leveling up, equipment, and mastery no longer contribute meaningfully to Power Rank. You will be focusing on gems and forging)
The game is RNG until 2500 Power Rank (Normal gems are not enough to get the 1300 Power Rank needed for the next world. You will be relying on getting empowered gems)
The game is grinding until 3000-3500 Power Rank (I hope you like gem dust. You're going to need a few thousand to level up your 1-3 empowered gems to level 16. But wait, radiant empowered gems can go to level 23, right?)
The game is Pay 2 Win from now on (A level 15 empowered gem has a roughly 25-50% chance to level up, while a level 16 empowered gem has a 1% or less chance to level up. We already established that empowered gems are the only thing that can get you any meaningful Power Rank, and you're only allowed to equip 3 of them at once. So you are required to level them up to progress. Now, you COULD spend hundreds of hours grinding for gem dust, and MAYBE that will get one of them to level 17. But let's face it, that's not even grinding anymore, that's unreasonable, impractical, and just not going to happen. If you want to progress, you need ninth lives. There are two places to get them, the store, and contests. If you buy them from the store, that's Pay 2 Win. So let's talk about contests)
Contests give prizes for 1st, 25th, 250th, 2,500, 25,000, and sometimes for reaching a certain score. Ninth lives are high prizes, you need to place 250th or better, sometimes 2,500th in contests that free players have no hope of getting. Some contests are (mostly) fair to everyone, like blocks placed, dungeons beaten, enemies killed, etc. Ninth lives generally aren't given as prizes in these contests; and if they are, they're usually for 25th place, where you need to place/destroy millions of blocks, beat thousands of dungeons, of kill tens or hundreds of thousands on enemies, thanks to obsessive players doing literally nothing but the contest 12 hours a day for all 7 days of the contest. Those ninth lives aren't Pay 2 Win, they're just "You don't win".
In class contests, free players can easily get the 25,000th or better prize on their main class, even up to 10,000th place. Of course, without leveling up empowered gems with ninth lives, you're never going to win a ninth life in a class contest. So the class contest ninth lives are Pay 2 Win as well.
All that leaves is the mastery contest. And let's face it, unless you but the Essentials Pack, the Extra Life pack, the Arcanium Expedition pack, costumes, wings, mounts, etc. in the store, you're not even going to get the 25,000th prize. You can get some of those with flux, but not enough to get a ninth life in a contest, and getting that much flux is, as I said about gem dust, "unreasonable, impractical, and just not going to happen". Unless you buy stuff to sell for flux, but that means you're paying, and comes right back to Pay 2 Win.
Jade clovers, glittering horseshoes, and lapis luckbugs are MUCH easier to get (Actually possible to get without paying), however even the lapis luckbug is useless on a level 16 empowered gem.
So no matter what, you need to pay for ninth lives to level up your empowered gems to raise your PR to progress to new levels. When the game becomes P2W depends on how many empowered gems you find (I got 1 water and 3 fire, so my P2W Power Rank is about 3,000, because I don't have an air empowered gem). Without any empowered gems, progress will stop around 1600 Power Rank. With 1 empowered gem, progress will stop at about 2300 Power Rank. With 2 empowered gems, progress will stop around 3000 Power Rank. With 3 empowered gems, progress will stop around 3700 Power Rank.
You might be able to get to 4000 Power Rank without paying, but as I said before, mastery, equipment, leveling up, and normal gems contribute VERY little to Power Rank after 900-1200.
A mastery level only gives 2 Power Rank, and you will quickly run out of styles, craftables, and professions, requiring store items to get more mastery.
The highest level of easily available equipment is shadow 5, which only gives 150 Power Rank or so each. To get radiant equipment, you need massive amounts of flux to buy penta-forged shadow souls, you can make your own by spending roughly the same amount along with hundreds of eyes of q'bthulhu, or you can try to get lucky by getting them in a box (But to get enough boxes for 9 of them will definitely require paying). A free player is not going to be that serious about the game to get radiant equipment.
Leveling up a class gives 15 Power Rank (Previously 10), but it only counts the class you are playing as. Getting all 14 classes to level 10 won't give you 6090 Power Rank, it will only give you the 435 for your current class. Leveling up ALSO gives you 15 mastery, but at 2 Power Rank per mastery level, getting every single class to level 30 will only give you 122 Power Rank.
And normal gems? You can hold up to 6. At level 1, you'll get 20-50 Power Rank each. Max level might only be around 100 Power Rank, but you need to save your gem dust for empowered gems.
Trion seems to be attempting to make F2P progression possible, but don't hold your breath.

I bought it the day of the release. I was used to Terraria and I was excited to see the result in Sci-Fi (it was promoted as a spiritual successor of Terraria).
My Avian explorer was born few hours later (you can choose 7 different races each with its own backgrounds, styles, weapons, armors and space ships).

Farmed to cook new recipes or search for materials and upgrade our racial armor.
There were so much things to do i was already addicted!
I even fought an army of space penguins lead by a small one in a huge flying saucer !!!!
But after 25 hours, my character died. He was wiped with an update.
My little Avian came back; ready to venture further in this huge universe.
20 hours of fun. But spoiled with and other character wipe...
And you know what?
I didn't complain about it. Contrary to some people who forced Chuckle Fish to use a test version for its updates: something that many forgot to notice in their rants in comments about this year without an update on the released version.
This game was made with so much passion that I couldn't blame the team behind it.
The reason why we have been patient, why we are so many to support it...
It's because Starbound is why we still put one's heart and soul into its video game.
Starbound is the greatness of video games. Beautiful, vast, cute, clever and for all audiences that will surely catch your heart! So yes this game is about heart, even music are so beautiful that it might makes you feel as nostalgic as in Elder Scrolls franchise (still need more tracks on Starbound but it’s a really, REALLY good start).
And one year after its release they've dropped a HUGE update and now we can really enjoy the work they’ve done during all this time.
To sum up:
New quest system focused around an outpost you can access via galactic portals where you can find traders and npc to start new quests (first ones serves as tutorials). Tons of new characters, monsters and bosses.
Reworked worlds generation, every planets has a place of interest.
Crafting is deeper but tools ,more efficient, loose their durability quicker. Tons of new items, weapons, armors, clothes, materials and blocks.  Farming is easier, you can find more plants on planets !
Your ship can be repaired and upgraded to gain new rooms and tons of other cool options. Space travel has been reworked, easier to use but with harder requirements, in each system type has an upgrade necessary for your ship. In general you have to defeat a boss and find materials in the deepest levels of planets and  you now need a special fuel to travel in other solar systems (coal in FTL drive ? It's over !).
Combat has changed, ranged attacks uses stamina and close combat weapons can aim in a larger radius.
You can catch creatures and even tame them to help you in combat. And of course... VEHICLES ! They gave us tons of new vehicles ! Each race has its own but you can craft many others. From the sci-fi walker to the car or even boats.
But i will stop here my list beacause there is too much to write...
So if you read this review:
Don't go anywhere else on the store. Don't even hesitate.  Because this game is NOW a must buy!
