I am going to support JAX's review here. My reason for this is because I can tell you EXACTLY how I found out about Hitman Codename 47 and I was with my family and I remember asking my father to buy it for me and it's just a long story and a very sentimental moment for and this game only deserves respect. For a 2000 game it's an amazing work and an inteligent story line. I definitely had hard time adjusting to the controls and the graphics... Well you know it's not going to be outstanding but if you are in your early 20s or mid 20s you will definitely understand why I am attached to this game. It is amazing how much the Hitman franchise have evolved and I would never imagine there would be a movie when I got the game 15 years ago. I feel old being able to say 15 years ago and clearly remember everything but this memory is one of the things that made it very well worth it. It introduces you to the Hitman series in an amazing light and you gotta bear with it since nowadays game are a lot easier to control and technology have evolved to the point we have Virtual Reality. Even in Sci-Fi movies this idea was ridiculous 10-15 years ago. You don't HAVE to play this one in order to understand the story line but it definitely makes it easier to understand the idea behind Hitman and gives you a mental trophy; do not be fooled, this one is a tough one. In the more complicated levels you get a few chances to complete the level and pretty much restart a couple time after you died but don't expect convenient Save Games. You gotta really think here and beat the odd bugs here and there. I could keep on rambling for another 3000 words but point is this game is worth it, you don't judge a game just by how it looks and operates comparing to games noawadays. There are at least 10 major factors you have to take into account. This game did a great job portraying the life of a hitman and had an amazing story-line and really put you in the game and feels somewhat like a puzzle because it's not just aimless shooting and you die realistically after a couple hits or like 5-10 shots if you are hit in the kevlar vest. I enjoyed this game a lot and also enjoyed being frustrated with this game, it definitely brought back memories from when games took more than 5-15 hours to beat. I give this one 8.5/10 (could be less buggy and the saving system could be more intelligent and other very small factors made me rank it as 8.5/10) I tried ranking it without keeping in mind this became a successful Series and just ranked it as if this was the only Hitman game out there. Buy it, play and go back to the past :) Thank you kind developers and the publishing team.

Heat Signature is a classic example of a "programmer game" -- it's full of things that sound REALLY COOL in theory, and were probably incredibly fun to implement, but after the novelty wears off you realize they don't actually engage very much with the player's decision-making process. Missions quickly get repetitive, gimmick solutions you've done once or twice are generally not difficult enough to execute for them to stay interesting afterwards, and the grind gets even less tolerable when a character dies and you get to start from (mostly) scratch.
People have compared this game to Hotline Miami, but it screws up one of the most essential things Hotline Miami got right. In that game, when you die, you INSTANTLY get to try again. No loading screens, no fuss, nothing. In Heat Signature, if you screw up in a mission you get knocked unconscious (and thrown out an airlock if someone finds you in time) a process so slow that the developers gave you a fast-forward button to make up for it. Something very similar applies if you succeed in a mission -- you either have to fly the captured ship home (which can be done on autopilot, but still takes time) or manually pilot your pod home (which takes time and attention towards the end since you have to decelerate to dock.)
I suppose it's possible that when you get much deeper into the game than I am now there might be some purpose to this downtime -- maybe people come and attack you while you're in transit. As it stands now, though, it's just completely pointless delay between action sections I'm not completely happy with in the first place.

The battlescape is a slightly refined version of the battlescape in XCOM 1.  The geoscape is a bit different, and I think I prefer it.
The game feels pretty easy on standard difficulty.  The new conceilment system makes it very easy to defeat the first enemies you encounter.  The only thing you really need to know to win is that the hit-percentages are lies.  If it displays >70% you are guaranteed to hit.  Otherwise you are guaranteed to miss, so you shouldn't take the shot - use overwatch instead, or move to try to flank the enemy on your next turn.  Same thing applies when aliens shoot at you - if you are in full cover it's supposed to be a 40% modifier, but in fact they are guaranteed to miss, so always be in full cover.
The only possible criticism of XCOM 2 is that it is still very dumbed down compared to the original UFO.  But that's exactly the same as XCOM 1, so if you liked XCOM 1 you will like this.  Also load times are quite long, maybe 10 seconds.  Doesn't sound like much but it's ten times longer than most games take to load on SSD!

The flagship of the Valve company's cataloge of games. Half-Life was the game that push the boundaries of first person shooter games. It even helped Valve get to where it is today which paved away for other games Valve is known for. Half-Life takes at the Black Mesa Research Facility(a combination of Area 51 & the Los Alamos National Lab)  in the middle of the desert of New Mexico. As the  game begins there's no FMVs, cutscenes, or introduction sequence. You immidiately start the game in the role of Gordon Freeman, a Theoretical Physict who works for Black Mesa. When Gordon participates in an experiment with a group of other scientists, something went wrong and the entire research lab explodes. Upon waking up, Gordon realizes that the Black Mesa facility is in ruins where most of the staff is dead and the experiment gone wrong had some how created a gateway from another demonsion where various aliens and other horrific creatures straight out of every man's horror is running amok in the facility. Gordon must use his intellect, brawn, and the help of the last surviving scientists and security guards in order to escape from Black Mesa before he gets mutilated by the demonsional aliens. The great thing about this game is that there are multiple ways to kill the enemies with the wide selection of weapons you obtain around the lab facility. There are unlimited saves so in case you mess up you can either reload the last save or auto save of the game file. Those are just a few of the many pros of the game. Now for the cons which are minor: the ladders can be you worst enemy some times due to getting on or off is tricky, the scientists and guards who provide aid sometimes don't keep up or move at all, while you occasionally encounter a glitch that immobilze you from moving and you either have to reload you last save or quit the game and start it up again just to get out of the glitch. With those issues aside, this is an extremely good game to play. While todays gamers might find the graphics to be very dated, the complex plot and the length of the game play by passes its age. Half-Life would spawn various spin-offs and sequals as well is inspire later first person shooter games that used this game as a basis for the genre. Overrall this is a great piece of video game history here with a story that combines elements from Doom, Ridley Scott's Alien, John Carpenter's The Thing, & X-Files into one package will please any gamer or first person shooter fan.
Fun game, make sure you have a 360 controller or something like it before playing. Good story too.

Fabulous Food Truck is a click and drag time-management game based on preparing and serving food for customers on your food truck.
Throughout the gameplay, you will serve various types food: Hotdogs, Chinese Food, Pizza and Hamburgers, and some specials like Fries, Colas and Cupcakes.
There are customers who don't pay you, which you can click to make them pay the little money they have (even if you made a perfect serve), and there are thieves who steal all the coins on the table. You could arrest the thieves, but for that you'd need 1500 coins to buy the handcuffs, which you don't use, after you buy it, you just click on the thief to "arrest" him, you don't get any money back, and it's mostly worthless since you can always collect the money on the table before his arrival.
You don't get any reward for completing the game, or for getting a high amount of money or gold bars.
After the 6th level, you have to buy the bell to attract customers. The bell costs 100 gold bars and you get 1 gold for every 5 perfect customers you serve in a row. This is where mostly all players exit the game when it's possible to get through this level by buying the 1050 coins and 1 gold bar table decoration, which promises a higher amount of payment by the customers. The PC version of this game, instead of the mobile phone version, contains no microtransactions, but on the 5th level, the game forces the player, to try the bell mechanic, on the 6th level, the game removes all customers and make you fail the mission, the objective is for you to buy a new set of table color to get a higher amount of the payment by the customers.
There are only in-game achievements and no Steam Achievements.
On the first level of every section (and when a new ingredient or food supply is added), a tutorial is shown on how to progress in the game.
The game only supports Mouse Actions. (No Drawing Tablet; Controller or keyboard support)
If you wait too much time to get the food who is being cooked, it will burn, you will have to dispose of it, costing you coins and you will have to repeat the process in order to cook again.
The microtransactions were removed and were replaced by the second currency (gold bar) through chaining 5 perfect orders, leading to grinding the earlier levels when you need more gold. You have the option to, instead of clicking on the food and then on the customer, to drag the food to the customer, this method, even though it's the easiest and the faster one (and the most accurate), the player gets tired as moving the cursor around the screen giving orders, seeing as the game starts maximised, scales, and stretches all of its graphics to fit the screen,
The game has no settings/options menu.
The only option available is the Mute button.
There is no way to change the resolution of the game, and it's impossible to change from fullscreen to windowed mode.
The main menu of the game is ugly, only showing big and stretched buttons, and a food truck with the credits on the hood.
The graphics are very low quality, looking like they are from a "free games website".
There are only 4-5 original characters and keep appearing one after another, this is annoying.
In the loading screen, contains characters which don't exist in the gameplay.
Fabulous Food Truck contains only some sound effects, which don't change, and since your constantly in action, it's pretty hard on how to not get annoyed by the repetitive sound effect. (The same sound effect to the male and female)
Only exists 2 soundtracks, one which is the main menu music, and the other one which is the radio music.
All the soundtracks become anxious and repetitive after you get through half of the game.
The developers did a good job in reading the reviews and correcting a lot of the glitches, prices, and some of the problems reported by the reviewers.

Before-DLC Review
I’ve really enjoyed the challenge Darkest Dungeon has offered. There is a feeling of accomplishment when things work out well, but sometimes the game just likes to throw salt at you and laugh while you sit there, mad about having lost the best guy on the roster.
The Good
-Simple gameplay mechanics.
-The art style is beautiful.
-Narrator has an amazing voice.
-The music is pretty sweet.
-It offers a high amount of challenge.
-There is a vast amount of classes to obtain, each good for certain situations.
-Dungeon runs can be short, great for the busy player looking for a quick game session.
-Dungeon runs can be long, great for a longer game session.
-There is a Radiant Mode that has been implemented to make that game faster to play through.
-It has mods!
The Bad
-The story is good but not super memorable, but this is not a game to play for the story.
-Every action, even in town, must be thought out carefully.
-Inventory maintenance is rough, thus making...
-...the grind real to get the town upgraded to its fullest.
-The RNG is a bit insane, but this game was made to be hard.
The Ugly
-This game autosaves after every action. This is part of the challenge.
-Each location offers different enemies and obstacles.
-Learning the locations each class is good for takes some trial and error.
-The quirk system really changes how a character plays.
-A run can go sour at any moment, even if you thought you prepared well.
-The characters can become stressed and make bad decisions, or can become the hero.
This game may seem easy to play, but it is one hell of a ride. In some ways, this game has a very casual feel to it, but in others it seems to offer challenge to even the most well rounded gamers. If a good challenge sounds fun to you, I highly recommend picking this up. If not, I still say you should pick it up and try it vanilla, then go grab some mods to make the game play how you would prefer it, you filthy casual.

Okay. Being serious now. There's not much I can say about this game that hasn't already been said, so I'll keep it simple. The pixel art is absolutely gorgeous and the gameplay is a fun, relaxing experience.

This game is, in a word, art.
The graphics are timeless; while the HD quality enhances the visual appeal, the sumi-e inspire artwork is what truly makes it work, in much the same way that one does not need state-of-the-art cameras to appreciate images of famous paintings such as the Mona Lisa.
The music is a joy to hear, when it intends to be. When the gods are able to do their jobs and all is well, the soundtrack makes it obvious. On the other hand, when demons are running amok, the music is creepy, as if unseen evils lurk in every corner. All in proper measure, of course.
Though I have yet to finish, I know that the story has the perfect mixture of light-hearted and emotional points. The former revels in humor, while the latter can move people to tears.
The gameplay is certainly good, although I can't say that I have much experience with this particular style. The controls are certainly different, but I have, for the most part, learned these controls, which I find easier to use than the Wii version (which I also own).
I do, unfortunately, have some framerate issues (notably at the start of battles), but this only occasionally crops up, and my computer isn't exactly high-end, either.
All in all, I highly recommend this game.

One of the greatest games of all time has been done justice by this port - a PC port, no less.
Short and simple, Okami is a Zelda clone that fixes my two biggest problems with the series: one, that the games introduce many different tools and never expect you to use them for more than a dungeon or two, and two, that the games often have lackluster stories (from the 3 that I've played enough to beat, only Majora's Mask had me equally as invested).
Okami fixes these issues with so many small little quirks that its impossible to get the impact of them without playing. Characters feel much more alive and, while not realistic, are so much more memorable that I can easily list all the main characters in Okami from start to finish. In contrast, I've realized while writing this review I can't actually remember the name of really any main Zelda character except for Link, Zelda, and Tetra along with a few others. In addition, the use of powers instead of items to progress allows much more fluid and involved puzzle solving: you will be using the same powers you gained in the beginning of the game in new ways all the way until the end of it. This is in stark contrast to how most (older) Zelda games treat items: as throwaway puzzle solving or combat tools that do add depth to the game, but only for a certain segment or portion of the game, like one or two dungeons or boss fights.
As for the port, it allows the astounding artstyle to finally pop out at you like it never was able to before. Those of you who bought 4k monitors and GPUs to handle 4k, rejoice! From what I've read and seen, this port does support 4K, along with everything from the original PS2-era 480p to modern 1080p resolutions. Bugs are few to none, as in the original games and rereleases, and from what I've played controller support is perfect, and feels just like it did on the PS2 and PS3. For M&K users, movement and camera control feels kinda weird, but drawing is significantly improved from using a control stick (though I've heard that the 30 FPS cap does make mouse movement a little weird).
And, if you buy before the 15th, you get a ton of nice wallpapers that, as far as I know, are exclusive to this release. The second the game downloaded, I put one of them up and I have not regretted switching.
In summary, I cannot recommend this game enough. It is my favorite game of all time, and it is a nearly perfect experience with the exception of a lack of difficulty for most of the game. While the PS3 port is 8 dollars cheaper, I would honestly suggest this port because of the expanded capabilities and flexibility. Nonwithstanding my obvious bias towards the game (if you couldn't already tell from the profile picture and name), this game is a must play for anyone who likes adventure games. If you're worried this game treats itself like an anime, don't. Besides plenty of gags, the game takes itself seriously and, while I can't say that it doesn't indulge in some (alot) of fan service, it doesn't stay constant and tends to be more comic relief than something made to arouse (its ♥♥♥♥ing ink painting the ♥♥♥♥ are you gonna beat off to, you weirdo)
tl;dr game is good, im biased af towards it, its not anime

Assassin's Creed Unity is a very difficult game to review. It is a very large and very big game, both in game features and story elements, so the review will be related to that, and i will try to write, as briefly as possible, what is right and what is not with this game.
When I've played Ac Unity for the first time i've loved it, because it had clearly returned to it's roots (firsts AC games), but also evolved. That is, the parkour had returned, the big city and lots and lots of good parkour. It is fun, it is free, it's the core of an Assassin's creed game. Right there i knew what was missing in the last two previous games, the parkour, the free run. The Ac spirit is right there. Alex Amancio the creative director for this game and Revelations, is the only one (besides the original creator of Assassin's Creed: Patrice Desilets) that truly understands, what it is the true spirit of Assassin's Creed, and what an AC game, should be).
Climbing to a viewpoint it is a meaningfull experience, it lets you clear one whole section of the map (not just a tiny diffuse zone)
The music also, returns to a pretty good quality, et even has one special theme (the main theme of course) done by no other than jesper kid.
It is a shame then, that here comes one of the firsts catastrophic failures of this game...the accent for the characters of this game... nothing wrong with the acting, it is very good in fact, but, for some reason...alltough you are in france, in the middle of the french revolution, everyone speaks with an english accent.... why? you have to search for a whole cast of english accent people, why? at first it was somewhat strange, even funny, but then you start to get really angry at a french soldier saying "oyyy, get here! , i'll crash youu head!" Then you remember also, that in previous AC games, like Ac2, ezio had his italian accent, and it was perfect, so you really don't understand the logic behind this decision...then you learn many months later that the next AC game will be set in LONDON and you start to wonder if it has something to do with convenience to have english accent actors in this game....
But anyway, moving on, the story and the characters:
AC Unity is set in the french revolution, that was a very exciting time to place and AC Game, and it was in fact the next logical step to continue with, AC games (originally) spoke about freewill, fight for liberty of the assassins, and the chaos that comes with it, also the need to impose order and control of the templars.
French revolution was perfect, among other things was the beginning of the end of the monarchy  the declaration of human rights, the end of privileges for a few ones and the right of voice to the rest of the people, the so called third state, everyone else (well at least, a good number of everyone else) it was the beginning of a very important historical moment in the history of the world that would lead to many things, It was of course a very complex and difficult subject to translate into a video game. And sadly it wasn't very well done in this game.
The portraits of many of the characters of the french revolutions falls flat, most of the time, the depiction is very stereotypical to say the least.. to the point of being more of a satirical one.  The story itself, as presented, is a mess of different dates and important moments of what happened at the french revolution. The problem is not that it doesn't show many of the things that happened at the french revolution, because it does show a lot, but what it shows, sometimes it does at different times in different orders (sometimes it doesn't follow the chronological order of what happened) so it really is difficult to understand what is happening in the context of things (the french revolution as a context to the assassins vs templars story). The first time i played the game, i was happy to find many different moments of the french revoultion, that i knew it happened from reading books about it, here and there, all the time, (there was indeed and incredible amount of research for this game, and there is an historical moment happening on almost every main mission!!) but then i realized, that it was very difficult to make sense of everything that was hapenning , because of the way it is presented.
Of course, maybe you don't care about the french revolution, and maybe you don't pay attention to what is hapening. In that case you will be fine. What i like about this game really are the main characters. Arno and Elise are very good characters, very likeable. In fact, i think Elise de la Serre is the best female character of all the AC games. She is smart, very strong and feminine. She is very independent, and very strong willed.
I think the scenes with her and Arno on screen are the best part of the game.
As for the main story , not of the french revolution, but for Assasins vs templars....is practically non existent...like the present story (non existent) it is very clear that after the depart of Patrice Desilets, ubisoft doesn't know what to do with the story anymore.
But at least the love story between Arno (an Assassin) and Elise (a Templar), is a very good one.
So, as for the main missions they are fun, and this time, optional challenges are for the most part fun.
What really stands outs (gameplay wise) , is it's CO OP missions in multiplayer. Not to be confused with the multiplayer from previous games wich was a deathmatch arena. This time, multiplayer missions are just like regular missions, in Paris map, and is really fun (when it works).
Then you have the secondary missions: Paris stories and social club ones...there is simply just too much of them, one of the mistakes of this game, too much of everything, more than 50 secondary missions, it's gets boring very quick. Some are good, but they are lost among all the boring ones.
Nostradamus missions and murder misteries are a good idea, but badly implemented, and there's also too much of them.
But then you have the rifts missions, those are fun.
What is great about this game also, is the customization of your character. You can choose from more than 200 pieces of equipment plus different kinds of weapons. You can really make you character unique. The economy system and your cafe is allright i guess, like AC2, but it should have been developed more.
The collectibles are back as always, cockades and artifacts are fun to collect. Chests also, but there is too much of them (300!) and with a 3 level lock system that is unfair to the player until later in the game.

TL;DR Pick it up, it's only £11. It's certainly not perfectly playable, and key features are certainly missing, such as global voice chat muting (we had to leave a lobby while streaming from the "banter" in the background) but it's still a blast now, and will only improve in the future.
I'm a long time GMT player since the almighty Yogs first made their videos about it. I fell in love with lobby 1, had literally the sickest apartment (I still have my screenshots lying around somewhere) and made so many friends through it.
Then along came the opportunity as a donor to alpha/beta test lobby 2. The improvements that were made were astonishing, the outdoor explorable environments were such a huge change from what had become a slightly claustrophobic Lobby 1. Yet at Lobby 2's release, many planned features were still not available, and soon after came the news that Lobby 2 and the whole GMT mod was being transformed to a standalone game in Tower Unite.
I missed out on the crowdfunding by 2 days, somehow it flew under my radar. But here it is now.
Being Early Access the game is fairly buggy, as is to be expected. and the new Planet Panic is horrid for FPS lag.Then again, it's still the game I love, and I've already found people I remember from over 4 years ago! Minigolf and Ball Race outside of the few niggles I've had still feel like the game I know, but with a slight upgrade now. Unreal 4 is 50x better for this than the Source engine. Virus plays about 1000x better now for me. The Lobby looks even more beautiful in UE4, and at the launch of Lobby 2 I didn't think that would be possible.
Other problems at the moment include a memory leak, a lot of areas not particularly optimised, and a lack of key bindings. (that will be fixed soon) However with their fast ability to patch the game, 8 patches within 15 days of EA release, problems are quickly being ironed out and new content becoming available. Problems I've noted here before that are now fixed include, object interaction in 3rd person, inability to connect to plazas/game hosts and being unable to hit the ball in minigolf, causing in a penalty.
I'll be updating this as my opinion changes hopefully (if I remember)

strategic challenges have never been more present than in XCOM 2 - perhaps more so, with a constantly see-sawing balance of power and time restraints that often force you into desperate action. This isn’t a game where the heroes always win - it even assumes a canon; that you, XCOM’s Commander, failed to defend Earth in the last game.
XCOM 2 is set two decades after the aliens quashed mankind. With Earth now under alien rule, Your choices matter - from what research you tell your scientists to develop, to what facility you ask you engineers to build. It is this sense of agency that makes even micromanaging your base, or deciding where to send the Avenger next, truly exciting.
Most missions have a limited amount of turns in which to accomplish them, meaning a slow and careful advance is generally out of the question. It is a clever, cruel way of coaxing you into misjudgment, eking out risks when you should be patient. Sometimes you’ll be forced to send a soldier sprinting into the Fog of War just to get a grasp of the procedurally generated battlefields, but be that at your peril - they may end up toe-to-toe with an entire enemy squad and all out of moves.

All information about me that's relevant first: I got this game for 12 dollars from the Humble Monthly deal. I don't have basically no income that I don't beg for. I also have very...specific tastes. There are maybe 6 games a year that get released that I care to even look at, let alone play. I am also the most unlucky person you ever could expect to see, thus I hate basically everything that has a large basis in luck. Thus, it's quite easy to see that the original (unmodded) XCOM 2 was more than a little frustrating for me. I completed it on a friend's account (more like I forced myself to, to see what the big deal was), and felt no desire to support it personally. It felt...shallow. Strategy tends to be something I enjoy being able to play though, from Fire Emblem to Pokemon Conquest to the Civ series (and the various MOBA games out there). I even enjoyed the original XCOM. Its "hit chance" was still frustrating, but I looked over that.
So, anyway, I saw the massive coverage of the Long War mod. It added a couple of classes, infiltration, an ability at each promotion tier for the classes, and a few more things. It was pretty cool. I also found a Reliable Damage mod, which turned the "hit chance" in to "damage multiplier", which reduced the chances of having all your shots miss point blank (you can still roll a 0 for damage, if your "hit chance" were that low). It felt alot more complete. Not enough to put down 60 dollars, based on my last experience with it, but enough for the 12 dollars of Humble Monthly. My friend got deathly sick, and so he left the house to live with his mother until he ultimately died...which is why I'm not still using his account.
I have to say, I still found it more frustrating than fun for the first 10 hours, because you have to be absolutely perfect in every move, or you die, and without "save scumming" it's almost impossible to have the information for the perfect move, leaving it down to luck. (That's a fine niche on its own, but it is a niche that needs to be mentioned for the consumer's knowledge.) Even if you have a person devoted to scouting...there's no indication for what squares you need to move your revealed guys to, in order to pop the pod. I later Found a mod that adjusted some stuff, and then raised the difficulty because it made the game too easy (which basically just meant the enemies get more bullet spongey, but the mod's weapons dealt too much damge, so being a bigger bullet sponge was fine, and exactly what was needed).
So, why am I not recommending this game? Because...if you're just sighing every time a mission pops up, and you have to decide "is this really worth my time?" (rather than "is it worth my soldiers' time")....when that's the main part of the game... you are probably not enjoying yourself. Why is that? Probably because half the time in the missions is spent waiting for animations to finish. Like I get it! You're shotting him! Let me issue my other orders! I don't need to sit through a 20 minute cutscene every god damned time you're doing that! There's 50 other enemies! Even with mods like Overwatch/Evac All, and Stop Wasting My Time. Just so much god damned time is spent *waiting*, not *playing*.
Also, in the 30+ hours I've played, there's only been one mission where I've been on the bleeding edge - where the difficulty was perfectly on that line between "too hard" and "too easy." I must admit it was damned exhillarating...but getting to the region liberation is just so...it's such a slog. Not to mention the pay off was unsatisfying. At first I thought the exasperation at missions popping up was just "hey, you're spending an hour each mission, and maybe a minute or 2 in the overworld map, just ease up on taking the missions, progress the tech tree and build the macro economy and it'll be fine." No...it wasn't. I was pretty much entirely bored or frustrated for the entire (incomplete) play through, and I really have virtually no desire to go back and finish it. Oh, also, it's not exactly fun to be getting an income of 0 supplies every supply drop. That's a bit...silly. (Actually, I got an income of 1 supply before. That was rather exciting.)
But, of course, fan boys of the game are always extremely vocal about defending their precious gem of a game on the basis that this was a negative review rather than whether it was actually a helpful review..

Like Terraria? Love sandbox games? Love early access? Look no further than Starbound!
I won't write as long as I have, there is far too much to cover, I am writing this post-winter update.
Starbound is an epic 2D space sandbox game, with infinite randomly generated planets, and a basic hub world, (This is LAN and Singleplayerwise).  Crafting in this game is simple and easy to understand, as well as less expensive than it has been in the past.  There are a total of 5 different races to choose from, Avian, Hylotl, Floran, Human, Novakid, and Apex, each with unique crafted gear and abilities (ahem, sorry just gear, only Hylotl get something other than the basics). The story? Not measurable and insignificant, however since it is sandbox you can have your story be anything you can think of.  Online play is fun, it is great for RP, PVP, and Factions as well as other modded gamemodes too.  The weapons and enemies are randomly generated too, so all weapons, as well as the aliens you will face, will be different.
I give this game a 9/10 which is fair, however what bugs me is the lack of tech abilies you are given.

Bastion is visually stunning game with a clear and crisp art style that quickly makes you forget this was indie developed. The sound is equally impressive, with an array of well chosen musical tracks and one of the best narrator's I've ever encounter.
As you play through the game various actions and events are narrated by Ruck, one of the few survivors other than yourself in this colorful post-apocalyptic world. His smooth and soothing voice might be a gimmick but it sure as hell adds character to the game and lets you feel less alone when grinding through the hordes of enemies you encounter.
The gameplay itself is a fairly basic Diablo clone. You can carry two weapons at any time and got the option of using a special attack every once in a while and that's about it. Most of the more difficult challenges are about learning dodge and block timing rather than complicated attack moves.
It is a fun and cute little game and definitely one of the best indie games of the year.

The flagship of the Valve company's cataloge of games. Half-Life was the game that push the boundaries of first person shooter games. It even helped Valve get to where it is today which paved away for other games Valve is known for. Half-Life takes at the Black Mesa Research Facility(a combination of Area 51 & the Los Alamos National Lab)  in the middle of the desert of New Mexico. As the  game begins there's no FMVs, cutscenes, or introduction sequence. You immidiately start the game in the role of Gordon Freeman, a Theoretical Physict who works for Black Mesa. When Gordon participates in an experiment with a group of other scientists, something went wrong and the entire research lab explodes. Upon waking up, Gordon realizes that the Black Mesa facility is in ruins where most of the staff is dead and the experiment gone wrong had some how created a gateway from another demonsion where various aliens and other horrific creatures straight out of every man's horror is running amok in the facility. Gordon must use his intellect, brawn, and the help of the last surviving scientists and security guards in order to escape from Black Mesa before he gets mutilated by the demonsional aliens. The great thing about this game is that there are multiple ways to kill the enemies with the wide selection of weapons you obtain around the lab facility. There are unlimited saves so in case you mess up you can either reload the last save or auto save of the game file. Those are just a few of the many pros of the game. Now for the cons which are minor: the ladders can be you worst enemy some times due to getting on or off is tricky, the scientists and guards who provide aid sometimes don't keep up or move at all, while you occasionally encounter a glitch that immobilze you from moving and you either have to reload you last save or quit the game and start it up again just to get out of the glitch. With those issues aside, this is an extremely good game to play. While todays gamers might find the graphics to be very dated, the complex plot and the length of the game play by passes its age. Half-Life would spawn various spin-offs and sequals as well is inspire later first person shooter games that used this game as a basis for the genre. Overrall this is a great piece of video game history here with a story that combines elements from Doom, Ridley Scott's Alien, John Carpenter's The Thing, & X-Files into one package will please any gamer or first person shooter fan.

This was close to being a recommended title.
It's a solid idea that works well enough. You get a type of food (fries, pizza, noodles, burgers + fries) and you just have to serve that type of food to everyone. Cook the ingredients and make sure that everyone gets their food before they get mad. Reach the profit goal and off with you to the next level.
In between levels you get some upgrades to make sure that you can keep up with the orders. And here comes the first issue. The game is a mobile-port. So, the tap and drag method has been rigidly ported over to the keyboard and mouse and let me tell you... it ♥♥♥♥ing sucks. It's too slow and the hitboxes are so incredibly misplaced that upgrading your kitchen fully is not a good idea. It's a waste of money and gold and you'll just fall behind on your cooking.
Let's sidetrack quickly and talk about the graphics. They're♥♥♥♥♥♥ Everything looks pretty much hideous. Even the food looks like some irradiated cow♥♥♥♥♥♥
Anyways, you've been cooking and everything's going perfect and then.... where are the customers? What's going on? Instead of the full line-up, you suddenly have 1-3 customers. Turns out the mobile game had microtransactions and because of that, they started ♥♥♥♥ing over the PC community too. But they also removed their microtransactions, yet never balanced the game around that fact.
The game's previously premium currency, gold, is now no longer purchasable. But for some reason gold is still grindy to obtain. The basic updates require 1-3 gold each (which isn't even too bad), but the specials, which are needed to make the game more fair, are 50-150 gold. You'll reach the 100 gold mark by the end of the game. No joke. I managed to buy one upgrade, which was the radio, to make the customers not as unreasonably impatient.
So, overall, what value would I give this game? I got this from the Bundle Stars Mega Dollar Bundle, which had this and 27 other games for the measly price of $1. It's worth it for that. Strategy is simple at first and more complex as you crawl longer dungeons and as the dungeons increase in difficulty. Characters' skills that seemed like obvious poor choices suddenly become necessary and things you hated, like when your characters shuffle in their order, are now something you welcome.
The bosses are always exciting and nerve racking to go against and more so as the the levels get harder. Allowing a beloved character to die in a battle is allowable suddenly if it means the difficult boss can finally be slaughtered.

It's not often I find a game I like and dislike at the same time.
There is a lot to like about this game.  Graphics are nice and it runs smoothly.  Most matches are fun.  Ship selection isn't bad.  Crew banter is a nice touch and often funny.  There are also a lot of good people I've met playing this.
Now, there's a lot I don't like.  You can sit for 20 minutes without finding a PVP match.  The grinding to get something new can be annoying.  Some times it doesn't count your match, so be prepared to play 8 or 9 matches to get the 6 match daily gold drop.  Some ships have a ton of loadout changes, some ships have nothing at all.
What I like the least is that some ship types are very under represented or missing from the game completely.  Presently there is only has 1 carrier and nothing at all like a long range missile cruiser or an intelligence gathering ship.  There are ships with missiles and ships that can cloak, but nothing that fits into those 2 roles.  It would also be great to see some kind of boarding craft.  Something that shoots breaching pods or the like.
Regardless, still a fun game and free to play.  No one gets hurt if you give it a try at least once.

The below review is taken from my original post at
This game works on several levels and I can imagine it will make players of various genres very happy.
The world in which the game is set is one of light and dark, black and white, yin and yang. You play ‘The Messenger’ and your goal is to bring the two forces together once more. You complete this by roaming the stylised game world collecting black orbs, adventuring and solving various puzzles.
Whilst the game may initially seem esoteric, it’s very well realised and the design and controls couldn’t be tighter or more natural and flowing. A tutorial (seamlessly blended into the game) teaches you the basics. You have four main abilities, to create blocks, slice them, push them and destroy them. Whilst as the game progresses you unlock further abilities, these are the main categories. You can also jump, glide and pull yourself towards blocks that you have built, which speeds up your travel somewhat.
The sheer scale on offer is unlike anything I have seen in a game, aside from the fact that you can’t destroy the landscape itself, you can build and travel wherever you want. Out of curiosity, I built a tower heading straight up into the sky and had to stop when my finger was literally aching from pressing the trigger and piling blocks with no end in sight. Naturally, I then spotted a black orb in the distance and spent several peaceful minutes gently gliding to it, all the while being gently lulled by the tinkling, ambient music that accompanied my flight.
The music in the game is perfectly suited to what is taking place and travelling the map is a tranquil pleasure. The physics in the game are astonishing, the precision with which you can cut blocks and the way they behave with regards to their gravity and weight feel ‘right’. I found myself building sculptures and chipping them down much more often than I normally would in this type of game out of the sheer joy of it. Spotting a distant orb and gliding over, then slowly building your way towards it before spotting a door leading to a wonderfully designed physics puzzle after which you’d find yourself in an entirely different section of the game and then getting lost there for a while before realising you need to find your way back and once again getting distracted by the architecture and possibly another orb or puzzle completely worked for me as a player (that was a long sentence). It is both the kind of game you could dip in and out of for a few minutes or play for a few hours, either way, there is always a sense of progress and involvement.
The game world isn’t just a load of haphazard blocks, either. It’s a well-designed desolate landscape. On your journey through Bokida, you’ll see tumbling bridges, castles, plains, temples, plateaus and ruins, each with highlighted symbols that give you a brief insight into the history of the two worlds that you are destined to bind.
Summary:
I was very pleasantly surprised by Bokida, when I play a game I always mainly focus on the narrative thrust and the idea of random building/collecting/destroying without a story doesn’t interest me but Bokida blends all of these parts with a gently enthralling tale which always makes you feel like you are advancing even when you are seemingly exploring aimlessly.
It’s also not without its challenge, some sections took a few minutes to work through and when achieved, gave a sense of satisfaction, urging you on to the horizon to see what puzzles and breath-taking scenery await you.
Rice Cooker Republic are a young studio born out of the I.C.A.N. school of Game Design in Paris. If this is the result of their first foray into game design, I assure you there are many more marvellous things to come.

It was a frustrating moment when I found myself on an empty ship, cleared of enemies, and still could not finish my mission.
You see, the odd thingamabob my character had been contracted to steal (for a hefty sum) was behind a locked door. This locked door was unlocked by a keycard that, despite having searched the entire ship three times over, was nowhere to be found.
My character did not have a teleporter, neither with him or at home.
The situation seemed dire. I was about to give up.
Then... I had a crazy idea.
I left the ship I was in and tracked down another one. I slaughtered the crew and commandeered this second ship, painstakingly sailing it back to the place where the first was still spinning desperately, devoid of crew and life.
Piece by piece, I surgically cut the room containing the item I required off into space. Finally, it broke free, spinning into the void. I left the helm of my new ship, shot a window, and was flung into space. I recovered myself with my pod and chased down the single room containing the item.
I docked my pod to the room, went inside, and triumphantly recovered the item.
I might have gotten a good payout for that thing, whatever it was, but the real reward was the sheer pleasure of having ended up in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation and come up with a crazy way out of it.
That, truly, is the essence of Heat Signature - an emotional rollercoaster of failure-turned-fortune.
Get it.
While 30fps cap is a bit of a bugbear, this is the definitive best version of Okami, and well worth picking up. I can't recommend it enough.

This game was released on November 19, 2000. If you have been gaming since before 1990 and have patience, buy this game. I have followed the Hitman franchise but played the 2nd game first. You cannot hide bodies unless you just basically keep them out of site. If you are a Hitman fan, buy this game because it explains the beginning of the story and how Agent 47 came to be. If you decide not to play this game, Hitman: Contracts (3rd game) is a remake of Hitman: Codename 47.
Still, the game is a classic nonetheless, and is definitely worth the buy if you have patience. We all have those older games we grew up playing and would recommend them to others. Although this was not a game I grew up playing, I still give it 4 out of 5 stars. Without it, we wouldn't have the new and improved Hitman games.

This game has a lot of the things I like about roguelikes (procedural generation, emergent gameplay) and none of the things I don't (permadeath resulting in hours of progress lost).  Technically, it
have permadeath, but it's not the game-ender that it is in most roguelikes.
As you complete missions, your character generates fame which allows you to liberate new stations and thereby unlock new items in the shops.  When you inevitably die or get captured, sure you lose that particular character and all of the items on them, but your liberation progress and all of your unlocks remain.  Once I got used to that and stopped worrying so much about losing any one character, I started enjoying the game a lot more.
One piece of advice:
(click on an already-liberated station from the liberation screen).  These are the game's "puzzle mode"--you're given a specific loadout to accomplish a goal and unlimited, consequence-free retries.  By their very nature, these missions make you learn new ways of handling situations, or show you loadouts you never would have considered before (e.g., silenced automatic rifle + slipstream).
I can highly recommend this game to anyone who thinks the concept sounds even a little bit cool; I went into it thinking it would just be "ok-cool," and it exceeded all expectations.

I own every one of the traditional Assassins Creed games, from the first one right through Unity. I also tend to complete nearly every game I purchase. I'm not a 100% completionist, but I always finish at least the main story campaign (and usually all side missions unless I ultimately don't enjoy the game).
Nearly a year later and I still have yet to complete Unity. After each game bringing new and interesting features, Unity feels like a step backward in terms of setting and game mechanics. The improve free running system where you can influence whether Arno moves upwards or downwards during free run is a great addition. But after the addition of the Brotherhood, then hunting and crafting, and finally with the amazing sailing ship combat in 2-4, this feels like a stale return to the original AC2.
The time sink mobile app interdependency is also an anvil around the neck.
I have also been hoping for a change of scenery. Unity just feels like we've been there and one that before, 4 times now. I hate to say it, but between Unity, and the decision to set the next game in yet another European city setting has absolutely killed my interest in this series.
I truly hope a day comes where Assassin's Creed will provide innovation and imaginative settings once again. Until then, it's back to the AC2 trilogy, AC3, and AC4 for me.

Tower Unite released in a very early and broken state, even for an Early Access game. Maybe half of the features from GMod Tower are in the game day one, and the whole process is slow and unreliable.
So why have I recommended the game?
Frankly, I applaud the devs for getting the game this far. Tower Unite was being made with a shoestring budget of 73k, meant to support 8 people for however long the dev cycle lasted. In this time, they were meant to:
-Move their game running on the Source Engine using repurposed assets into Unreal Engine 4 with entirely new assets
-Remake and repolish several minigames
-Implement extensive home and player customization
-Have this all stably run on dedicated servers
It's a mammoth task, and I can totally appreciate releasing the game this early in development. The product itself, right now, is in a poor state, but the foundation's there, and purchasing at this stage in the game will only make its updates come sooner and be of better quality.
Loved GMod Tower, am ready to love Tower Unite. Good luck, Pixeltail.

strategic challenges have never been more present than in XCOM 2 - perhaps more so, with a constantly see-sawing balance of power and time restraints that often force you into desperate action. This isn’t a game where the heroes always win - it even assumes a canon; that you, XCOM’s Commander, failed to defend Earth in the last game.
XCOM 2 is set two decades after the aliens quashed mankind. With Earth now under alien rule, Your choices matter - from what research you tell your scientists to develop, to what facility you ask you engineers to build. It is this sense of agency that makes even micromanaging your base, or deciding where to send the Avenger next, truly exciting.
Most missions have a limited amount of turns in which to accomplish them, meaning a slow and careful advance is generally out of the question. It is a clever, cruel way of coaxing you into misjudgment, eking out risks when you should be patient. Sometimes you’ll be forced to send a soldier sprinting into the Fog of War just to get a grasp of the procedurally generated battlefields, but be that at your peril - they may end up toe-to-toe with an entire enemy squad and all out of moves.

Bastion is visually stunning game with a clear and crisp art style that quickly makes you forget this was indie developed. The sound is equally impressive, with an array of well chosen musical tracks and one of the best narrator's I've ever encounter.
As you play through the game various actions and events are narrated by Ruck, one of the few survivors other than yourself in this colorful post-apocalyptic world. His smooth and soothing voice might be a gimmick but it sure as hell adds character to the game and lets you feel less alone when grinding through the hordes of enemies you encounter.
The gameplay itself is a fairly basic Diablo clone. You can carry two weapons at any time and got the option of using a special attack every once in a while and that's about it. Most of the more difficult challenges are about learning dodge and block timing rather than complicated attack moves.
It is a fun and cute little game and definitely one of the best indie games of the year.
A Game to play when your feeling down, it puts a smile on my face every time I come back to play.

All information about me that's relevant first: I got this game for 12 dollars from the Humble Monthly deal. I don't have basically no income that I don't beg for. I also have very...specific tastes. There are maybe 6 games a year that get released that I care to even look at, let alone play. I am also the most unlucky person you ever could expect to see, thus I hate basically everything that has a large basis in luck. Thus, it's quite easy to see that the original (unmodded) XCOM 2 was more than a little frustrating for me. I completed it on a friend's account (more like I forced myself to, to see what the big deal was), and felt no desire to support it personally. It felt...shallow. Strategy tends to be something I enjoy being able to play though, from Fire Emblem to Pokemon Conquest to the Civ series (and the various MOBA games out there). I even enjoyed the original XCOM. Its "hit chance" was still frustrating, but I looked over that.
So, anyway, I saw the massive coverage of the Long War mod. It added a couple of classes, infiltration, an ability at each promotion tier for the classes, and a few more things. It was pretty cool. I also found a Reliable Damage mod, which turned the "hit chance" in to "damage multiplier", which reduced the chances of having all your shots miss point blank (you can still roll a 0 for damage, if your "hit chance" were that low). It felt alot more complete. Not enough to put down 60 dollars, based on my last experience with it, but enough for the 12 dollars of Humble Monthly. My friend got deathly sick, and so he left the house to live with his mother until he ultimately died...which is why I'm not still using his account.
I have to say, I still found it more frustrating than fun for the first 10 hours, because you have to be absolutely perfect in every move, or you die, and without "save scumming" it's almost impossible to have the information for the perfect move, leaving it down to luck. (That's a fine niche on its own, but it is a niche that needs to be mentioned for the consumer's knowledge.) Even if you have a person devoted to scouting...there's no indication for what squares you need to move your revealed guys to, in order to pop the pod. I later Found a mod that adjusted some stuff, and then raised the difficulty because it made the game too easy (which basically just meant the enemies get more bullet spongey, but the mod's weapons dealt too much damge, so being a bigger bullet sponge was fine, and exactly what was needed).
So, why am I not recommending this game? Because...if you're just sighing every time a mission pops up, and you have to decide "is this really worth my time?" (rather than "is it worth my soldiers' time")....when that's the main part of the game... you are probably not enjoying yourself. Why is that? Probably because half the time in the missions is spent waiting for animations to finish. Like I get it! You're shotting him! Let me issue my other orders! I don't need to sit through a 20 minute cutscene every god damned time you're doing that! There's 50 other enemies! Even with mods like Overwatch/Evac All, and Stop Wasting My Time. Just so much god damned time is spent *waiting*, not *playing*.
Also, in the 30+ hours I've played, there's only been one mission where I've been on the bleeding edge - where the difficulty was perfectly on that line between "too hard" and "too easy." I must admit it was damned exhillarating...but getting to the region liberation is just so...it's such a slog. Not to mention the pay off was unsatisfying. At first I thought the exasperation at missions popping up was just "hey, you're spending an hour each mission, and maybe a minute or 2 in the overworld map, just ease up on taking the missions, progress the tech tree and build the macro economy and it'll be fine." No...it wasn't. I was pretty much entirely bored or frustrated for the entire (incomplete) play through, and I really have virtually no desire to go back and finish it. Oh, also, it's not exactly fun to be getting an income of 0 supplies every supply drop. That's a bit...silly. (Actually, I got an income of 1 supply before. That was rather exciting.)
But, of course, fan boys of the game are always extremely vocal about defending their precious gem of a game on the basis that this was a negative review rather than whether it was actually a helpful review..

You're better off with Cook, Serve, Delicious. This game is just crap.
First, it's a horrible mobile port with amazing features such as:
- double currency system (coins and gold)
- the second currency is gained way too slowly and an item in particular is impossible to purchase because a playthrough makes you 200 gold and the item costs 1500
- no possibility to change the resolution
- no possibility to change between full-screen and windowed. I only got a windowed mode which didn't even fit my screen properly
- no settings whatsoever. There's only a button to enable/disable sound.
- telling me to tap on stuff when I'm using a mouse
- no keyboard support whatsoever. Since the game revolves around clicking things (which could be binded to keys), you'll perform much worse than on a touch screen
- huge♥♥♥♥♥buttons taking up ridiculous portions of my screen
- stretched background images looking terrible, this dev can't even get a wallpaper right
- achievements in-game, though no achievements in Steam
Then there's the usual set of bugs of who doesn't really care about their game:
- timer completely freezing, making it impossible to complete the level
- no customers coming at all for over a minute, making it impossible to make enough money to complete a level
- sometimes the soup ingredients won't show up on top of it
- soup cooks instantly. Not sure if intended, but stupid either way. Cola also gets cold instantly when placed in the fridge.
- "oops" sound sometimes occurring on random bursts
- you're supposed to get the money you're owed if you click on a customer who goes away without paying. Nothing happens and you don't get your money
- some customers coming with smoking visual effect as soon as they arrive (which are supposed to signal impatience I guess)
- achievements not unlocking (100 burger served achievement was locked while the 1000 burger served achivement showed 103 burgers served)
A level is 2 minutes of clicking on food, letting it cook and serving it to a customer. You get the opportunity of doing the same thing, with a few more ingredients (like ketchup or mustard on a hot dog) for 10 levels per area, in 4 different areas, for a total of 40 levels. Your goal is to make more than the amount of money present on screen.
There are people who don't pay you, and there are thieves who basically steal all the coins that you don't click on. You could arrest the thieves, but for that you'd need 1500 gold to buy the handcuffs, which is impossible to get.
The upgrade system is very barebones and consists of three things per area, which may be upgraded twice (at most). All of these upgrades are just increases in numbers (for instance, oven cooking 4 pizzas at once instead of 2).
The gameplay is extremely boring and exhausting due to the lack of keyboard support. Just imagine playing Cook, Serve, Delicious with a mouse, not taking into account all the bugs and technical crap this has. It would suck. Don't do it like I did.
Also, you feel like you really achieved something when you complete the game. You're just sent back to the main menu screen, no congratulations screen, no nothing. Yay.
TL;DR: Like all Digital Homicide games, this is card dropping shovelware. Get Cook, Serve, Delicious for a great take on the genre.

I find myself going to one planet, scouting the surface of the whole planet, picking up whatever ores and materials I can find, and then when I've gone a lap around I have enough coal to continue exploring another planet. I have no clue how it would be done, but I'd love it if there was more motivation to stay on one planet instead of just cruising all over.

I know that this is a crime, but I have only just for the first time completed Half-Life! I know right! But hey, I have never been one to really be on top of anything lol :-P
Anyway, the question is, is it any good? Now this is a bit of a redundant question as the whole of the world is fairly clear on this point. But I have just played it without nostalgia goggles, so maybe my opinion can be slightly less biased than some.
First off, the plot. Simply put, amazing. It is told - or rather not "told", but "revealed" - in a wonderfully immersive and instructive way, guiding you to self-discovery and your own interpretations of everything. There is a lot of wry humour and thoughts and considerable depth to the whole concept.
Second off, the characters. There is only one, and he is not even you. Gordon Freeman, the player character, is almost entirely devoid of depth - but that is not a bad thing. It is one of the game's strengths, as it allows a huge amount of player imagination to be used, and he is a perfect everyman in this sense. The one character I am talking about is a mysterious figure you see at various times...I leave anyone who has not played the game the mystery of this figure.
Third, the enemies. A diverse array of challenging enemies, with designs that may now be called standard, and even then were not the most original, but nonetheless they work and are used in one of the most effective ways I have seen even up to the present.
Fourth, the weapons. A variety of weapons, although not the most exciting array ever. Most of them feel plinky and weak, and the worst is the shotgun which seems to have b****r-all pellet spread, meaning the main use for a shotgun is rendered near-impossible to carry out. The exceptions are the ghostbuster gun (or Gluon as it is actually called), the Magnum Revolver, and the crossbow.
Fifth, the level design. Pretty good on the whole. There is a reasonable amount of variety overall, but a lot of it will be in dull corridors. That is the point, however, so it is not fair to criticise. There is a hideous over-reliance on single-routes to solve levels, and a dreadful over-utilisation on platforming elements which do not work comfortably within the dated engine and first-person perspect.
This leads on to the sixth aspect, gameplay. This is where the game is a mixed bag of fruit. It may have been wonderful for its day, but that is not the point. A game can be good at one point and become bad over time if the gameplay does not hold up - it is not something that is forgivable in the same way dated graphics are. Ladders are a joke, with your character either stuck inseperably to them or refusing to grab them when needed. Jumping and platforming, as mentioned before, is used far too much and is, honestly, hideous. A modern FPS with feet shown on your character, may be more tolerable. The shooting is functional, although as mentioned the weapons are not that satisfying or varied. The crosshair is also coloured and sized to be far too small and hard to decipher on the screen in the middle of the chaos. There is the suggestion of being able to be more stealthy, and this works well enough for a shooter of its generation, especially when stealth is unnecessary and who needs it lol?
Finally, atmosphere. This is where the game really comes in to its own. It is creepy when it needs to be, and it is dark, and deep, and rich. It can be scary, and sometimes you cannot help but jump. It is tense and action-packed, unrelenting, and surprisingly beautiful despite the dated graphics.
I will not even mention the graphics, as I maintain someone that judges a game on its graphics is not a real gamer at all, and such opinions deserve no time of day, as long as the graphics are functional (i.e., if they constantly crash or flicker so as to give a migraine that is obviously bad, but merely being blocky and pixellated or something is not important).
Overall, just buy this game. I give it a solid 8.5/10, even by today's standards.
Enjoy!

I'll make it short and sweet. FS is a F2P spaceship game, and all game-changing items can be bought without spending a penny. You will, however, require a grind to get some desired items, requiring about a week of daily playing to get the expensive stuff. Unless you want money wasted, be very cautious of buying DLC for this game, and if you are, buy something related to crew/implants, or ask others. Gameplay is typical of a MOBA: Capture bases, capture the enemy's home base, defend, etc, but with no minions. 5 ships on 2 teams "Jump" onto 2 lanes to capture bases that grant access to a home base. A third lane, known as gamma, has only one capture point. This point is activated every few minutes to grant buffs to whoever captures it. PVP, PVE, training, and a firing range for all ships is included. This game's combat/defense system is based on cooldown-based abilites. The game's vareity is in its ships and crew/implants.
The pros of this game are in style and potential. To me at least, the genre of capital-spaceship games are quite few, let alone a F2P one. Depending on some players, this game can be fun to play sometimes. But since I can't speak for all players, deciciding whenever or not the game is fun depends on you. The F2P model is acceptable and does not discriminate game-wise between a paying and an expierenced player. And that's all of the pros I can find.
The cons are rather blatant in this game. First off, matchmaking timing is a well known issue. Expect some occasional disconnects from lobbies, usually due to some players leaving before a game has begun. Second, there is only very basic game balance, with some ships being insanely overused and with others being insanely underused. If you hate metas, this game may not be for you. Third, the in-game community can be quite toxic. Forth, it is very easy to have "snowball" games - games of which are just lost from early on or are clearly doomed to be lost by an often meta setup of the enemy team. Fith, gamma is too short and too game-impacting in my opinion, as games can be won by an event lasting only a mere minute or two in a 20-30 minute game. Sixth, capping is extremely "encouraged" to win games. The saying is that if you can't cap, you suck. Even if you are ranking number 1 for damage ratios and around number 15 for K/D ratios, you're still crap if you can't cap - according to the communinty (See point "Third".) As a matter of fact, I hold those leaderboard positions.
I keep playing the game just for the leaderboards, and occasionally I have to focous on my goals rather than my dissolving team in order to have a reason to keep on playing. I play a rarely used ship, and I'm very good at it, but it tends to feel underpowered (*cough* USR destroyer is OP  *cough*.)
Overall, try and see if you would like it, but for now, I won't recommend it for the average gamer. Your milage may vary.

So after more than 172 hours into this game, and undoubtedly more to come, I think I can give a good Review on this game. I play on Superstar difficulty. You should bear that in mind when I review gameplay mechanics.
GRAHICS: 8/10 It's more centered towards consoles, of course. It's still good. My mom once passed me playing & asked "Are you watching March of Madness?" Should give you an idea.
GAMEPLAY: 9/10 The most important part of a basketball game is, of course, the basketball. & no one should be disappointed in this aspect. Even though this game is obviously more geared towards console users, the game is still miles better than previous titles in punishing the user for not having basketball simple IQ. You're going to hear a lot of people say that 2k15 was better. & I'll be honest it's easier to beast mode on Hall of Fame. But that's simply because you can cheese too much. Why I rate This game so high is because of its attempt to limit cheesing from previous titles & keep/improve upon the incorperation of real basketball concepts.
Shot Selection Importants:  Early after the games release you had players like Steph Curry missing 3 pointers taken early in transition, & unexplicably you still have players now with high 3 point accuracy missing open shots sometimes. The updates have fixed this a little, but I like where their heads where at. Because even though we have amazing 3 point shooters in the league, being a championship team is not about taking good shots, but passing up good shots for great ones. & more importantly the rhythm you're in when you take your shot is hugely important. The game will punish you if you aren't smart with the ball.
Knowing when a player is on a hot night & when he's cold is hugely important. & It mostly depends on his physical state & morale. If your player in MyCarrer has been on the practice court after back to back games & tomorrow he's got another match you can bet he's going to be tired as balls & miss a lot of his easy shots. If you're unfamiliar with 2k they still do a great job of programming the AI to play like the real team would. You can bet that the Clippers are going to punish you with a ally-oop if you leave a lane open. Golden State will punish you from 3 if you're not physical on Defense.
Speaking of Defense this is where I have to commend this game. In 2k15 the defense was too easy to press the boost trigger & run around defenders. You could just cut & boost around the Defense going to the hole way to easily. In this title you have to EARN ALL YOUR POINTS. You have to know how to break ancles, having the wallet to increase your stats aren't enough. You actually have to know how to play the game of basketball. When to create isolation shots for you & your teamates, how to do that on and off the ball, etc. This game has vastly improved the Defense. They won't let you get past them by just hitting the boost button.
MYCAREER 7/10: Let's address what's on everyones mind: Spike Lee Joint. Now I'm going to say it up front. This title has made me make a new rule about anything I play. "If at any point the story brings you to tears, you cannot rate it below 7/10. No matter how many hours the story is." I don't want to spoil anything folks, but there's a reason this game has the Story Rich tag. Spike Lee once again releases a controversal story which, in my opinion, tries to show you the life of what it's ACTUALLY like for most NBA players. It's not all shoe deals & fame but you still have a past. You still have friends from your past. The most important element of NBA life I think this story potrays is you will have friends & family leach off of your & it's how you respond to your situation that determines your success in the NBA. The positives of this story far outweigh the negatives, in my opinion. Then again I care more about basketball than the story.
Now we stll have to talk about the negatives. Your family is inevitably black. No matter how you swing it. This normally wouldn't be a problem for someone if you aren't racist, cause adoption, but the story makes reference about your sister being a biological twin. So it kind of ruins the immersion if your character isn't black. Which is why I think this title is different because it's not supposed to be you, but Freq. Why people are mad at this is because in times past you were able to be yourself & there would be relatively no story but you would sign shoe deals & be a megastar. I've tried to find a million different ways to say this but this game doesn't necessarily want your face on the story, but instead Freq's. It's the difference between role-playing a defined character or a silent protagonist in my opinion. A preference thing. But you can't doubt that the story is immersive once you get over yourself. I'd personally like to see more of this from 2k but extend towards other ethnic groups. Maybe even do a 2k story about the difficulties the first woman player might face in the NBA.

Why should you play it?
No other games out there like it. It's a MOBA structured similarly to other MOBA's like League of Legends but you command massive ships on your way to glory. It's currently in Open Development meaning the gameplay is changing constantly and the proposed update with Phase 3 is very exciting. There are around 50 playable ships and each one has a place on the team. Even better, the community is suprisingly docile and it takes a lot for players to be upset. If you love other MOBA's but feel like they may be too fast paced or you struggle to stay "competitive" then Fractured Space will give you a welcome break.
Why shouldn't you play it?
It is a Free to Play game, but in game purchases make your life a whole lot better. It takes a long while to gain enough credits to buy any ship that isn't 110,000. Additionally, gameplay can change dramatically with new updates. Lastly, the playerbase is pretty low, which constitutes fairly long wait times when loading a match.
Overall:
This is a phenomenal game plagued by issues that are common with new and underrecognized developers. Support them by getting this game and tell your friends about it too!

Gameplay is super fun, the pause mechanic gives you time to think about what your doing (and do it) without needing godlike reaction time, it makes the game nice and relaxed as long as you remember to pause, but it doesn't take away from the action and badassery.
It's also pretty fun how quickly things can go downhill, but how you can almost always recover as long as you think hard enough, sometimes the game plays more like a puzzle game than a top down shooter. Minute-to-minute gameplay is probably a 10/10 for me. There aren't a lot of ways it could be done better.
The game has some flaws too though, stealth can get kinda boring when you play it too safe, if you don't take some risks you're basically sitting around waiting for enemies to walk off from their group so you can clunk them and drag their body off, then rinse and repeat 'till the ship is empty. But you can always just ignore that playstyle.
The game can also get kinda repetitive since there's almost no story and you're basically doing the same thing (infiltrating ships) over and over again.
TL;DR gameplay is almost perfect but the game can get repetitive. 8.5/10

Had to come back and edit this review - this is quite a good game for the price.
Before I couldn't recommed this because after a few post-release patches, all of a sudden this game suffered from intolerable slowdown \ framerate issues. A google search and some tinkering resolved that, though. (If you are having slowdown problems that go away after restarting the game, this worked for me, set the SleepMargin value to 15:
)
My only complaint is that there really isn't much depth to this game - you see everything it has to offer in the first few hours (every enemy type, every item type, etc) and the procedurally created environments seem like a bit of a shortcut around the developers creating thoroughly thought out maps. I think at least for the defector missions they should have created static layouts that challenge the player. If you get a layout in a defector mission that is particulary difficult, you can just restart endlessly until you get an easier layout.
But anywho, this is quite a brilliant game. The developers dump you into this world of violent space piracy with only minimal training, kit and cash, and thats the brilliance of it. I'm almost 40 hours in (and nearing completion) and I'm still learning new and creative ways of dealing with the obstacles put before me with the equipment that I have on hand. As you go on you get much better at doing more with less, and coming out victorious from an enemy ship with a loadout that you couldn't imagine taking on this sort of a challenge with before is rewarding and fun. Its simplicity is what forces you to find increasingly creative solutions
Not the most complex or deep game ever created, not by a damn sight. There is no Triple-A story to follow or top-end graphics, but it isn't being sold for a Triple-A price either. Its simple, but still a whole lot of fun for the right gamer. If the developers come out with an expansion with new types of enemies and clauses I'd buy it without thinking twice.
