What an innovative and truly immersive game. I can't imagine any video game feeling more real, especially with certain parts of the storyline during the main game and the DLC. The plot itself is crazy good for both parts of the game. Also, the soundtrack is fantastic.

Landing in a mysterious forest, you're tasked with bringing the two stars back together. Lush, relaxing music pervades the opening scenes as you stumble upon what seem like long lost ruins. Immediately, you're thrown into a puzzle which does a terrific job of setting the mysterious scene. For this is not a normal world, things change and shift around. You can fall long distances and end up back from where you fell. Doors can perform acts of teleportation, leading from one side of the island to another. These are mechanics which expertly permeate the entire game but are never spelled out. For many of the puzzles, the solution is obvious but the path to the solution is a touch more trifling. This, in fact, is one of the game's biggest strengths, it's puzzles are a perfect balance of obscurity and difficulty.
A lack of hand-holding is a common theme throughout the game. Often frustrating, Rice Cooker Republic have perfected the concept. Outside of the brief tutorials, you're left to your own devices in a gorgeous monochromatic open world that encourages you to go anywhere. Whilst the world is filled with puzzles, there is no order to them. Stumble upon one, solve it, and the two stars are pulled closer to one another. The 'go anywhere' mantra is entirely achievable too. As the messenger, you're given the ability (amongst others) to build turquoise cubes upon most of the world's surfaces. Once you've got one block down, you can build off it further - the sky is literally your limit! At one point, I built a structure so tall that I hit an invisible ceiling and as far as I can tell, this is one of only two limiting factors to how much you can build. The developers have included an option to wipe your world clean of blocks in the unlikely event that you build so much that it brings your computer to a halt. At another point, I built a walkway around half of the world, reaching into the sky and providing a quick route anywhere I needed to go.
My walkway was almost entirely pointless, however. Something that filled me with joy as I transcended into the world of Bokida, was freedom of movement. Where many indie games get bogged down in clunky controls, Bokida excels. There's no falling to your death, there's no frustration in slightly mistiming a jump. You can glide around the world. Jumping off a tall building, for example, allows you to glide across all of the map with a bird's eye view, falling to anything interesting that might catch your eye. As you're gliding (or just running, for that matter), you can put down a block and use it to propel yourself forward. It's truly wonderful. Words fail to do it justice.
As alluded to earlier, the world is almost completely monochromatic, blue skies provide a colourful edge to the world but mostly you'll be dealing with white or black environments. But every so often Bokida breaks away from that and dashes the scene with vibrant colours which provide real 'wow moments', made all the more powerful by the lack of colour at other times.
Dotted throughout the world are 'echoes', black dots which you pick up as you approach them. You'll naturally come across them as you explore, picking up enough to complete the game. The rest are simple collectibles which provide no real reason to find. Having said that, there's plenty of fun to be had in exploring more and building that they might be a fun side-project for any completionists out there. There are also a number of stones which hint at a sub-story, each stone features symbols which translate into Lao Tzu quotes. I briefly looked for meaning in the stones but came up empty handed, beyond Steam achievements.
The story of reuniting the two stars is light on the ground, providing a simple narrative which gives you a reason to follow the game through to its end but, much like the rest of the game's mechanics and features, it remains subtle. Unusually for me, I never felt at any point that it needed to be anything more than it is. The world and it's smart puzzles were such a joy to explore that I felt plenty satisfied.
Never holding your hand, but never frustratingly difficult, Bokida perfects exploration, movement, and puzzles in a game which feels new and different. The monochromatic world is dashed with vibrant colour providing 'wow moments' and is, in general, just a fantastic space to explore and play in.

Bokida is a game about discovery and exploration more than anything else. It is one of the more abstract games you will ever play. It starts off by showing you a beautifully animated ying yang combination melding together and a Japanese voiceover telling you a story of a reunion that is supposed to happen and that you are the messenger who is supposed to bring together this reunion. That is more or less what get in the name of story from Bokida.
But it is not the story here that you should care about but the discovery and artstyle of Bokida which take the game to another level.
In simple terms, Bokida can be described as a more souped up and much prettier version of Minecraft. The gameplay essentially revolves around building and smashing cubes to reach the objectives in the game.
The most surprising thing about Bokida is how fast it opens up to the player. After a good and basic tutorial where you are explained most of the mechanics of the game, Bokida opens up the world for you to explore. Initially I was taken aback by the massive landscapes and the looming structures present in the first stage but slowly it dawned on me that the game has an excellent way of looping you back where you started.
Whether you fall of a cliff or go off in a zone far off from the main objective, it will loop you back seamlessly. The transition is so smooth without a single jumpcut or screen-fade that it will often leave you confused on whether it was the same room or there is something different this time around.
Even with all the looping, Bokida does provide you with a large playground in the form of every stage that is bereft of any sort of action and still is one of the most engaging and satisfying worlds to discover. Part of this is because of the incredible movement system present in the game. You can glide, jump and pull yourself across the landscapes while building massive structures of turquoise cubes to reach the objective. There is also no limit on how much you can explore or build in a single stage aside from how much RAM usage it takes.
This can essentially turn it into Minecraft for some crafty people out there. There are also some black dots called echoes present all around these said stages which stand in the form of collectibles in the game and might increase the gameplay length for some players and completionists. I said some because for someone like collectibles like these don’t mean much and do not enhance the value of the game.
Another complaint might be that there is some to no direction as to what you are supposed to do in the gargantuan world of Bokida. On the other hand, it also increases the satisfaction you get after solving each of its puzzles.
I am not the biggest fans of puzzle or abstract games in general, but Bokida is a rare case where I liked every minute of what I was experiencing.
That is what the game is, an experience more than a game. Sure it has the collectibles you might want from a game which can increase its replayabilty but the beauty of Bokida lies in its simplicity and the way it present itself. It is simple yet unique, large yet small and is one of those games which leaves a lasting impression on the player’s mind.
Bokida features one of the beautiful monochrome worlds I have ever seen. The art style is gorgeous and yet somewhat haunting. The colour of your cubes stand out in the stark white background of the stages. The architecture present in the game is outstanding and looks absolutely stunning while you are gliding across the landscapes.
It is so serene and so beautiful to look at that you might just want to glide and jump across the landscapes without making any progress. To sum up, Bokida is a marvel to look at.
Complimenting its visual style perfectly, Bokida features an excellent soundtrack. A smooth and soothing melody as the background score and subtle but unique sound effects like a distant murmuring of voices whenever you collect an echo takes the immersion to another level. There is voice acting in Japanese so that is redundant for the most part. But overall It has a sound design which goes with the flow of the game perfectly.
I have said it before and I will say it again, Bokida is a rare case in abstract games which actually works. Do not expect a thought provoking story or anything of that sort but look at it as an experience, a beautiful one at that. Bokida might be priced somewhat steeply for its length but for me it is completely worth the admission price. This is an adventure you won’t be forgetting soon.

3D open world adventure. It's a grand Easter egg hunt where every so often you discover secret entrances to areas containing physics-based puzzles.
The game first teaches you the movement and tools. Oh, and what glorius controls these are! You can use a controller but I found this to be one of those games where you need accuracy, and the right-stick just doesn't cut the mustard, you need the mouse for accurate targeting. WASD to move, spacebar to jump and tab (or 1234) to scroll through your four mouse-activated tools, which are: Build - set a 'seed' block and then extend more blocks from it in any direction - this is by far the most widely used; Cut - mouse wheel to rotate angle of cut and hold to increase length; Push - rarely used; Clean - remove blocks, hold to increase cleaning area.
The game makes you feel like Superman, as if anything is possible. There are huge mountain peaks which seem impossibly steep but as long as there's a slight angle you can bound up them like a mountain goat and when you reach the summit the world is laid out beneath you, all the better to spot the next black orb to collect. You then leap from the summit and glide through the air to home in on your 'prey' like a hawk. You instinctively seek out tall poles and land on the tip, giving you the best all-round vision of the scene below, just like a bird would.
I while ago I played Fumiko! which has a similar concept but I found the controls to be a bit vague and frustrating at times, not being able to accurately pinpoint landing spots or gauge distances properly. Bokida is the opposite. You can effortlessly land on the tiniest target, instinctively know whether or not you have enough height to make that ledge, and generally feel like you're in total control of your spatial awareness.
[ SECTION CHOPPED TO SQUEEZE REVIEW ONTO STEAM, SEE FULL REVIEW AT
]
The first aspect of the puzzles in this game is to actually find them and identify them as puzzles, this is not always obvious. Once you realise that you're supposed to do something, the next task is to work out which mechanics you're supposed to use on it and then, finally, solve the puzzle. It has an open, real-life feeling to it.
There are three types:
1. Monoliths - these are the 'main' puzzles which result in cutscenes and progress the gameplay. You can solve them one after another to complete the game quickly, but by doing so you will only experience a fraction of the overall game.
2. Easter Egg Hunt - there are 67 orbs hidden throughout the environment. I spent a lot of time hunting these before I ever went near a Monolith. You become more and more familiar with the world as you seek them out. Hot tip: make sure your screen is clean, otherwise you'll be chasing after that tiny speck of ketchup thinking it's an orb!
3. Hidden Areas - these are also optional, but are the best puzzles in my opinion. They force you to use your tools in ever more inventive ways, and sometimes reward you with new abilities. So far I can slow time and shoot/shatter blocks. These are non-essential abilities but they sure are a lot of fun!
A huge circle dominates the sky, a long cable hanging down from it with a rectangular object on the end of it (and later on, further cables to mark completed Monoliths). For a while I was wondering what this was for. I tried cutting it; I tried pushing it. In the end I realised that it's the marker of the centre of the world, so wherever you are you can get your bearings and always know where the centre is. It's good, but it could be better...
I would like to also see not necessarily N/S/E/W compass directions, but at least some kind of direction labels. You do get to know the world up to a point, but the monochrome aspect does not make it easy to remember landmarks. Ideally, press M for Map would be great!
Another slightly annoying feature is the way that the names of areas are displayed as you enter them - Observatory; Gully; Twin Peaks; Temple; Lagoon etc - but the name only lasts about 10 seconds before it fades out? Why is that? I constantly forget where I am, I want to see the title there all the time please.
It's a monochrome world of greys and whites but beautiful nevertheless. The light and shadows not only look great but also serve a practical purpose, to enhance your depth perception for judging your landings. Occasionally a puzzle solution will treat you to a brief splash of colour, for example bright, low-poly fish swimming around.
There has been talk of slowdowns when there are too many blocks used in the world. There is a 'clear all' function to solve this issue. However, I have 8Gb RAM and had no problems whatsoever in a world crammed to the rafters with my endless block structures. I even checked my RAM usage now and then to see if my mega-buildings were having any effect on my RAM. Nope. Nothing of the sort.
I have a 1920x1200 monitor and when I first played Bokida I was delighted to see that it filled my screen properly. Somewhere down the line it stopped giving me that as an option and now I'm down to the standard 1920x1080 - this may be my fault somehow, but thought I'd mention it.
In general, 90% of game music annoys me. Even some supposedly relaxing tunes. Bokida is in that 10% that I can listen to endlessly. It's pleasant when I focus on it, but it also easily fades into the background when I'm concentrating on a puzzle. I don't know what that elusive recipe is, but Bokida has it.
There are marked stones dotted around the world which display 2 or 3 mystical Chinese sayings. They don't seem to be clues or story progression although I could be wrong. For me they add a bit of passing interest but nothing more.
The general movement and climbing aspects are skills that improve with experience and it's a gentle, enjoyable learning curve. The puzzles have huge variety and are very engaging, with medium difficulty. The solutions can often be reached in many different ways, you can build them in a free-form manner any way you like. The solutions give a lot of satisfaction and you can stand back and admire your work afterwards, while smoking your imaginary pipe and leaning on your imaginary spade.
Achievements are mostly ones you have to chase after, which is good. Trading cards available if that matters to you. Steam Cloud, which will be especially useful for me when Linux support is launched, which is promised soon.
Some may argue that it's short, but those are people who make a bee-line for the end. There is more than enough content here to justify the price if you spend the time to look for it. Just messing around sandbox-style could fill many hours for me.
Even before I started with any of the challenges, I already found this to be a wonderful experience, climbing peaks, soaring through the sky, building/destroying structures and generally having a whale of a time. Once the novelty had (slightly) worn off, it was on to the thrilling task of finding orbs and solving puzzles.
I review many games, and usually I play enough to experience all the main aspects of the game, write my review and move on. I'm enjoying Bokida so much that I'm lingering with it and neglecting my other reviews. Naughty but nice.

Although my steam account says otherwise I have put hundreds of hours into this timeless Valve classic, I will not give spoilers about the game's Ending in my review so here is the bottom line
-Plot-
Half-Life is a first person shooter that puts the player into the perspective of the Black Mesa Scientist Gordon Freeman, whose objective is to exit the Black Mesa facility after it has been invaded by the Xen, A race of Extra Terrestrials from the Borderworld, as you progress through the game you will run into much stronger enemies from Enemies, to Scientists, to Security officers, to soldiers and even to a shady character known as the G-Man, Half-Life has quite an array of different characters to take note of.
-Gameplay-
In this affect Half-Life keeps me in a bind, the game plays fine, nearly all of the animations feel very fluent even to standards of today's games the mouse and Keyboard feels right for this experience, especially if you have experience playing PC first person shooters, controlling Gordon can be a little clunky at times especially scince Gordonn seems to walk at a very fast speed, and jumping seems to hold this odd momentum so when you have to deal with platforming a lot of faults feel more like it's at the fault of the character's physics rather than personal skill, but an upside to this is when you do land jumps or find secrets you feel very accomplished, shooting is almost spot on and unlike platforming, when you die from an enemy it feels like that is at the fault of personal skill and does feel very rewarding when you clear out a room of enemies
-Graphics and Audio-
this game really shows it's age through it's graphics, although this version does give you the option to use the "HD" textures, you still feel like you are playing a game from the late 90's, the visuals are still crisp espeially at higher resolutions and the HD pack does remake player models and some level Geometry, but still feels old, the game also plays very smooth, all of the animations are slick and all of the graphical effects feel right at it's time, as for the audio, the game has a pretty great soundtrack, although all of the characters voices may sound unclear at times the audio does sound pretty impressive.
-Overview-
Half-Life is a gem, and for me that's mostly because of nostalgia, it doesn't feel like a game that holds up Aesthetically but it does return the favor in every other aspect and I feel I must Recommend it just for that!

When they finally decided to update the game after almost a year, I was sort of excited. Considering that I had hyped over this project pre-release and felt like I couldnt be any more more dissappointed once I got a chance to play it, I figured that It couldn't get worse, only better.

was that there was much exploring to be done and nill explanation, it seemed incomplete how tier progression was lazily shoved in through similar craftable boss summoning items and that you could bypass certain features intentionally giving yourself a sense of instant control from the beginning. is that the new "balancing" features makes this game, simply put,

. To be able to progress to the next tier of gameplay, you have to play a one-way mission that is in essence Alien Isolation. (in its unforgiving difficulty and sh*tty AI) In the one solar system range you are given, you would think it would be enough to find decent gear to beat this mission, but it's not. Half-life is a story-rich shooter with some simple puzzle elements that struggles with the Goldsource engine and some other glitches here and there.
So I just finished Half-life and figured: "Why not make a review of it?". I can't say other than it's a classic. What a game indeed!
Dispise being an alltime masterpiece, it's not safe from glitches and mistakes. This game runs with the old but gold (no pun intended) Goldsource engine, which has its limitations (like crude-to-use ladders). Throughout the game you're sure to find some glitches here and there. You might get stuck on walls or levers. Also, sometimes the submachine gun MP5 won't reload or might reload but won't show to you (though it reloads, your HUD view won't update your bullets). Those are some of the glitches you may run into.
"GOTTA GO FAST". I think that's Freeman's motto. His speed is way too fast and, because of that, often you might fall off platforms.
This game is hard. Most people will agree. Enemies take bullets like if they are nothing and they lock onto you like some freaking aimbot! They never miss a shot! And if your HEV meter is gone, you're pretty much gone too because they can drain your life faster than you can say: "what the...!". It's trial and error at its best!
One other thing: this game requires English knowledge as intermediate or above. People who can't handle English properly might struggle. If you don't pay attention, often you might find yourself wondering what to do next. (Just a fair warning!)
Though there're all those issues, Half-life has that special charm that makes you want to keep going. You may have to try the same area a lot of times until you become a master on it, but you keep trying because you are in love with the story and wants to know what comes next. The plot is amazing.
The overall scenario presentation is alright. Some places are awesome and some are bland. Overall, it's OK.
I can't make enough justice about this game. It's a must play for everyone who likes shooters and simple puzzle-solving elements. Story-rich at its finest. Though, be warned: it's not an easy game.
Oh, by the way, Freeman is a crowbar master!

The first game in the Hitman-series is a great introduction to the series, but it is very clear that this game was made in 2000.
The story is really interesting and captivating, detailing the secret origin of Agent 47, our favorite Silent Assassin. The voice acting is also decent. While not as professional as the later games, they still fit, and David Bateson does a good job giving 47 the voice we all know and recognize. The graphics, if one accepts that it is an older game, are still pretty decent, and the game creates really great atmosphere in the levels, along with the fantastic music composed by Jesper Kyd.
The controls can be a tad difficult to get used to, although you do get used to it. Warning: The deafult controls aren't the usual WASD-controls, so I recommend changing them in the settings.
It's hard as crap, and while that definitely can be a good thing, it can also become quite annoying at times. There are times, where you lose the idea of what you're supposed to do and where you're supposed to go. It doesn't help that the maps are usually pretty large, and while you do have a map, it becomes easy to get lost if there is no clear goal on the map. The big maps can also be annoying when you die, and you restart at a much earlier point on the map, which means a lot of retracking to get back to the point required to continue the mission.
Also, while you can try to go Rambo in the missions, it's not a good idea, as you die very quickly, even when you use Bulletproof Vests.
Overall, while the game does have some annoyances that were common at its original release-date, Hitman: Codename 47 can still be enjoyed today, although it is required to overlook the shortcomings.
Last note: The mouse sensitivity goes crazy when I tried to change the resolution, so if that problem occurs, start the game again as an Adminstrator or change resolution to 800x600 in the Hitman.ini-file in the Hitman-folder.

The Story: You awaken in what appears to be a cell, which is in one of those lovely sanatorium's. There is a loudspeaker instructing you to do various tasks from putting your clothes on, scaling obstacles and using firearms to become an efficient assassin. Now after completing all the tasks you end up escaping from the sanatorium. Later on about you aka subject 47 end up as a professional hitman of the International Contract Agency (ICA), now known as Agent 47. He is briefed by his handler, Diana Burnwood, and sent around the globe to eliminate four criminal masterminds with large enterprises, companies and crews. You gradually go through the missions, learning as you go. To an interesting end for that part of this game series.
Game play: Hitman Codename 47 is played in a third-person perspective with a control setup is similar to a first person shooter. Each level is an open environment which is populated with NPC's such as civilians and armed guards. Now basically you as Agent 47. Carry out your assignments, which usually is to kill some one. But they can be other things your are told to do. Some may say the paths may appear linear in the game. But that is wrong there is many different ways you can accomplish your missions. But the game essentially emphasises stealth and silent kills without raising alerts, giving the player a higher financial reward for doing so. Penalties in the form of financial deductions are given, for example if the player kills civilians.
Disguise plays a large role in gameplay. Any NPC that Agent 47 (You) kills you can take their clothes which can help you in completing the mission. But you must also make sure no on finds that body or you disguise will be useless. So there is alot to the game play of this game which makes it a fun game to play in the Hitman Series.
The Graphics: Well if you compare them to the graphics we have they do not even stand a chance. But for the graphics back then when the game came out. They were certainly good. Even now I can still play it with how it looks.
Controls: Simple mouse and keyboard setup. You can customize your key to suit you.
The Music: What can I say the music with this is just works right in my view. It always had held a place in this gamers heart in the Hitman Series.
The Reply Value: Unless you wish to try possible different ways to do each mission. There is not much reply value.
Bugs/Glitches: Well back then I don't remember seeing any issues with the game. But now there is some. Due to the game not really made to work properly on higher OS's than when it came out. But don't let that stop you. There is fixes for start up issues on the Steam and GOG forums.
Overall: Story had me intrigued right up to the end. The game play is just right for this type of game, even for my psycho style I play some times. Graphics as I said good for when the game came out. But certainly couldn't hold a candle to today's. But that certainly didn't stop me from playing it. Controls simple easy to configure, what more could you ask for. Music just right for the game. Reply value it is there but not alot. Bugs/Glitches as I said for new OS/Systems yes, but there is fixes out there. So taking in the everything even when the game came out. I give this a 9 out of 10.

When the devs finish adding a lot of blocks to the game to balance the current companies, each one can be solely dependant on a single company, instead of crossing the military with the weaker for batteries. First things first: Last time I've played this game it was on a PS2. So be sure to mind the gap. Even then, I will cover aspects of the PS2 version, of the sequel on NDS, and of this re-release in HD. Good? Good. Here we GO!
When I heard about Okami back then it was very common for me to hear comparisons between this and Legend of Zelda, how many aspects crossed over, most notably the art style that for some reminded them of Legend of Zelda Wind Waker, an in my searches there were even that prototype trailer where the game was planned to feature realistic art instead of the sumi-e inspired from the final release. For me, art style wasn't what attracted me, but the simple fact that Okami was the closest PS2 would ever get to a Legend of Zelda.
And does not disappoint.
Okami's progression and Zelda's have many common points: you are required to earn the abilities to progress, the environment is designed in such way that every map feels unique and SHOWS unique aspects, the art and music are just perfect and something to be considered a masterpiece from PS2 era that stands strong to this age, even the way you grow your health is similar. The game spans HOURS, even if you do not count cutscenes, and there are many secrets to find even under rocks. If you die, chances are it won't count towards the end game results, due to how the game early on introduces you to a bit of a mercy function called "Astral Pouch", which acts like fairies did in Zelda except you gradually refill it by gathering food items.
But of course, for long the good memories of Okami have gone into thatfor me: a memory. We had to sell our PS2 as well as every game we had with it, just to get a Xbox 360. To this day, I regret that choice, should have kept the PS2, and nothing after that helped. PS2 emulation is awfully unreliable and unstable, there was no one I knew that had the system or the console. And with no sequel in sight... I felt a desire that could not be satiated. Not until Okamiden that is.
With Okamiden out, unfortunately all I could do was emulate, and it was very hard to get even 45 FPS on the PC I had by then, but I still forced myself to bear with it, I had to. Aside from the issues due to, of course, the dawn of NDS emulation, I still went on and enjoyed the game, getting a 100% on my second run and later runs of it. For a NDS game, it seemed to expand the boundaries of the system, just like a few games did too, and the style was still as pleasant as ever.
Now that I have a 2DS, all I seek is buying the game cart, however by now I'm waiting to see if it gets an updated re-release. If Okamiden gets an updated re-release, I will jump to it ASAP. How fast I'll buy it depends on where it will be released. If on 3DS, unfortunately means I have to wait availability in Brazil, which can take one or two months from USA release and half a month of shipping. But if on PC... I'll buy the moment the preorder pops up!
As a matter of fact, this is what I did: Bought Okami HD without a second thought as soon as I saw the news on Preorder. Didn't know of preorder bonuses or anything, I saw it and thought "OH MY GOD, I CAN RELIVE THE GOOD TIMES AT LAST!", and the fact it was to be released on my birthday made me squee in sheer joy. I didn't get anything aside of clothes on my bday, so when this game dropped into my account I could safely say Capcom gave me the best birthday gift anyone has ever given. Thank you so much, Capcom, for making my special day truly feel special for once.
Despite rising controversies in the Discussions and issues, I had minimal to no problem on my end: Okami HD runs smooth, the framerate is the exact same as it was in PS2, the keyboard and mouse support are really well implemented, loading times are really low and controller response is perfect. It really feels like I'm back to one of my favorite games ever, and without having to hog a TV.
So, in regards to a common controversy: The game IS 30 FPS, yes, but so was the original PS2 game, so is several other games all around. Even 3DS games are 30 FPS if you turn on the 3D mode, 30 FPS have been around for long, so why care now? I never felt it was 30 FPS, it always felt at a good pace for me. If anything this game could optionally have is a text speed slider, and... That's it, really. All else is perfect as is, there's no need to risk breaking the game for the sake of the "60 FPS is superior" meme.
As usual, Capcom delivers joy and hope when all seems lost. And as excited as I was for Okami HD to finally come out in a system I could play, I am too excited for the bright future they are giving to Mega Man and in believing that their games can succeed on PC.
One more, thank you Capcom, for much more than you can imagine.

Amber Gyasi is an old hand at infiltrating ships, but she's never faced a challenge quite like the Offworld ship she's about to jump onboard. The client is adamant that no-one see or be harmed and that Sojourn Monoceros be taken back into custody. Amber doesn't ask why, not when this much acid is offered.
Docking the breaching pod into the ship as quietly as possible, weaving through the detector arcs of the defensive guns, Amber slips through the airlock and immediately activates her slipstream device, her perception functioning at 10 times the normal speed as the rest of the world turns to slow moving putty. A couple of guards in a nearby huddle start to raise their heads to look at the blur of motion they can see but Amber will be long gone by the time they get over to the airlock to find nothing amiss.
Rounding a corner Amber has just enough time to see the automated turret before slamming on her trusty stealth shield, cloaking her in shadows rendering her all but invisible from the front. A second group of guards are standing by the turret, both equally oblivious as she hugs the walls, snatching a key card off one of their belts before slipping backwards through the door they were guarding.
Her onboard HUD flashes up a local map interfaced with the ship internals - there's some valuable loot in a crate guarded by more turrets and guards up ahead, with no-one inside. If only she could walk through this bulkhead she'd have it made - and so she activates her Visitor teleporter, appearing in the room and quickly opening up the cargo container to grab a key cloner - this could come in handy. She only has a second to appreciate the find before the Visitor abruptly yanks her back to her previous position.
Enough with the side objectives - the target is in a room up ahead with three innocent guards and a turret. Amber swallows and readies all her gadgets - this is going to be tricky. Activating the slipstream and stealth shield, Amber fires up her Visitor and appears behind the target, almost directly on top of him. She slams a prepared glitch trap set to outside the ship and backs up, trusting to the Visitor and Shield to keep herself safe as she directly interfaces with her breaching pod remotely, detaching it from the ship. A couple of seconds of intense piloting later and Sojourn is unconscious, secure inside the pod and restrained by the catching mechanism.
Right. Now how do I get out of here?
-------

This is not a tactical game. It is a rogue like game of RNG with an extra coating of artificial difficulty poured over the top of it masquerading as a tactical game. The difficulty is designed around an unrelenting tempo that forces the player into a status quo of high risk low reward situations.
The player is always behind the AI in both offensive and defensive capability which becomes increasingly exaggerated at higher difficulties. The element of surprise is never sufficient as you are not able to strike hard enough to take advantage of it. Similarly, conservative play does not produce any better results. As the RNG and the AI's high endurance means that you will not be able to attrite them sufficiently before they unleash mass destruction on your units.
Divide and conquer strategies struggle as well on the time sensitive missions as you are forced to rush against the timer. Resulting in triggering more AI than your units can actually deal with. These time sensitive missions make up more than the majority of the missions the player will be faced with.
Part of this arises from being constrained by the ridiculous action cost system which runs counter to tactical play. You cannot shoot twice, shooting before moving ends the units turn. This means that sustaining fire, or firing then retreating are not options. You may advance and fire, or you may retreat and more than likely not be able to fire from your new position. Your final option is to fire first and remain in your current location. This ham-fisted action system is then band-aided with abilities your units unlock. These abilities while better than nothing is still less advantageous then basic guerilla warfare tactics like fire and retreat drills. Additionally, these abilities usually have some arbitrary hindrance tacked on to further diminish what little advantage they provide. Overwatch is sloppy and of limited use compared to what should be covering fire. As unless you unlock a specific ability on a specific class it only fires on units moving rather than suppressing the enemy when they attempt to fire. Supressing fire exists as an ability in the game, however it also only has a chance to hit a target if they decide to move. Otherwise only a negative modifier is applied to their attempt to fire. This is really incorrect as firing would require a unit to atleast partially expose themselves to retun or supressing fire.
Other issues include the difficulty in predicting the line of sight both your units and the AI will have and how this will affect the probability of attacks hitting their targets. Tactical considerations you have to make like when to reload, expend grenades or how close to approach a target before being able to fire is completely ignored by the AI. I have watched the AI fire from far beyond the range that my units would normally be able to engage from.
Cover in the game provides a defensive bonus in one of four directions. This is less intuitive than one would expect though as the rules for flanking around cover are not apparent. At what angle relative to the cover, can a player expect that the cover bonus will be negated and what angle is required for a flanking bonus to appear? I have seen numerous times were flanking behind the AI with no cover between them and my unit’s line of sight provides no flanking benefit.  Also, how is it that floors are not considered cover when they completely obstruct line of sight and need to be fired through to hit the target?
One of the more comical features of the game is your units abhorrently low composure when under fire. In one instance, I watched as a unit in cover suffered some bad luck being struck with back to back critical damage. The unit entered a critical bleeding out state which provides some time to attempt a rescue. However immediately after this another unit began to panic left cover and ran towards the enemy position before turning around to throw a grenade into three of their comrades. Naturally this thoroughly scrubbed the mission. This would be hilarious if not for the games unrelenting tempo were any setback is almost certain to be game ending. In fact if the difficult in other parts of the game was dialed down, action system refined, and this comical difficulty element polished up a bit I would be quite pleased with the game.
The game also has some technical/performance bugs like poor framerates during cut scenes. I can look past that easily as the framerate and stability of the game in actually play was good to sufficient depending on the settings used. Occasionally the game will also lose track of what abilities are being used and they will not trigger correctly.
In short I, wouldn’t recommend this game for anyone looking for a perfectly thought out tactical turn based experience. However, the games story, history, advancement system/abilities, and uniquely punishing rogue like gameplay will give many players endless hours of enjoyment. I have enjoyed playing the game however it was gifted to me by a friend. Knowing what I know now about the game I would not have spent my personal money on it.

Compares well to games like Antichamber and Portal, of course, but to my liking also achieves the suspension of the real even further as with a game like Proteus. I’d even like to go ahead and introduce a term to describe this particular genre: Waking Simulators.
Simple mechanics, smooth physics and a sandbox of puzzles to direct your attention in a surreal dreamscape that challenges the possibilities of the real world. The sound and visual design is mature and professional and follows along the trend set by other impressive audio/visual design in games like Stanley Parable, The Talos Principle, Awkward Dimensions Redux and The Witness, begging the question of whether good developers choose first person adventure puzzlers or if the nature of contemplative exploration and problem solving gets to a deeper core of human experience than most gaming. Perhaps games are the most expressive form of art available, but at the same time perhaps the ones that are well executed simply manage to hide the boundaries of an exploration of art within our consciousness that is mutual to media and space.
This is still Minecraft gameplay without the inventory, vulnerability and monsters. Puzzles will still offer a relative challenge or frustration depending upon your experience with these controls and mechanics, and are sometimes predictable if you've played some of the stuff I've already mentioned, but it does strive for novelty and exhibits unique settings worth seeing should anyone read this review when cost isn't so much of a concern. (I'm getting that $100 Panoramical game after I'm done bankrupting myself on gardening another year, so don't ask me about value.) You build stacks of blocks that can be tipped over, sliced into segments with their own weight and momentum, or wiped away like an etch-a-sketch in a perfectly controlled explosion of negative light. It’s an open world, so you don’t need to go anywhere and can just stay where you are, but the variety of striking aesthetics will pull you along and you may even become compelled by the passing narrative. Which is first presented in a short film sequence that is actually quite superb in its visceral interpretation. The voice acting isn’t even annoying, which should count as excellent by a video game measure.
Honestly, if you’re bored by video games as I often am you won’t find a lasting attachment to this one, but what I’m trying to say is that perhaps a game like Bokida might embody that boredom in a mutually transcendent space. The search for meaning, thrills or bliss doesn’t particularly change from one mode of being to the next (redirecting one’s attention from the world to the game world), mostly because WASD is so mechanical, but this one manages to achieve the expected flow of a modern day FPS and provides mechanics that function well enough not to be a distraction from where the game really shines: its space.
I haven’t played in VR and don’t know how much better the experience would be anyway, but the game does excel best at audio and visual presentation so it’s to be expected that it might improve the game even further, especially if you could simply chop your hand rather than having to rotate the angle of your cut with a mouse and keyboard, note to dev should they read this,

Although my steam account says otherwise I have put hundreds of hours into this timeless Valve classic, I will not give spoilers about the game's Ending in my review so here is the bottom line
-Plot-
Half-Life is a first person shooter that puts the player into the perspective of the Black Mesa Scientist Gordon Freeman, whose objective is to exit the Black Mesa facility after it has been invaded by the Xen, A race of Extra Terrestrials from the Borderworld, as you progress through the game you will run into much stronger enemies from Enemies, to Scientists, to Security officers, to soldiers and even to a shady character known as the G-Man, Half-Life has quite an array of different characters to take note of.
-Gameplay-
In this affect Half-Life keeps me in a bind, the game plays fine, nearly all of the animations feel very fluent even to standards of today's games the mouse and Keyboard feels right for this experience, especially if you have experience playing PC first person shooters, controlling Gordon can be a little clunky at times especially scince Gordonn seems to walk at a very fast speed, and jumping seems to hold this odd momentum so when you have to deal with platforming a lot of faults feel more like it's at the fault of the character's physics rather than personal skill, but an upside to this is when you do land jumps or find secrets you feel very accomplished, shooting is almost spot on and unlike platforming, when you die from an enemy it feels like that is at the fault of personal skill and does feel very rewarding when you clear out a room of enemies
-Graphics and Audio-
this game really shows it's age through it's graphics, although this version does give you the option to use the "HD" textures, you still feel like you are playing a game from the late 90's, the visuals are still crisp espeially at higher resolutions and the HD pack does remake player models and some level Geometry, but still feels old, the game also plays very smooth, all of the animations are slick and all of the graphical effects feel right at it's time, as for the audio, the game has a pretty great soundtrack, although all of the characters voices may sound unclear at times the audio does sound pretty impressive.
-Overview-
Half-Life is a gem, and for me that's mostly because of nostalgia, it doesn't feel like a game that holds up Aesthetically but it does return the favor in every other aspect and I feel I must Recommend it just for that!

Hacknet is exactly the type of game I love to play, it has a great story that keeps you captivated the whole time. However, there was
moments throughout the storyline that I felt it had gotten a little repetitive, but it wouldn't be long until something popped up that peaked my interest once more and got my head back in the game.
You really get a feel for the different characters' personalties through the text provided which I love too, whether it be humorous emotions or empathetic. You truly get immersed within the world that has been created and you feel real satisfaction once getting the more lengthy jobs done. Although another point I want to make is I just wish the further you went on the tasks would become a
more challenging. Don't get me wrong, that last mission had my heart pumping like crazy, apart from that I would have loved to be tasked with something that really got my brain thinking. but that's just me nitpicking. Something which has come up in other reviews is the bugs and believe me I think it's just luck if you get the bugs or not. The bugs aren't huge or impossible to fix, there's plenty solutions online if you do happen to get one.
Another thing for me which stands out in games I play is it's a very relaxed playstyle, you aren't rushed to keep going on with the main storyline (when not in the middle of frantic mission of course). You can just stop and snoop around into people's lives, find easter eggs and little hidden gems within. It's safe to say there is some action, but it's not action packed so if you're into thrilling fast-paced games then hacknet isn't for you.
Overall I think Hacknet is a great game and everyone should buy it and play it if you're just that little bit enticed towards it, I doubt you'd regret it. It's one of those games when it comes to the end you want more and luckily when I played it, I could move onto Labyrinths which I did. :)

To put it very simply, it's like Terraria in space!
To put it more psecifically, it's not really... Shares certain similarities, but...
You get a LOT more Character customisation, and you're own personal home from home spaceship that now can actually grow over time. Generally Combat is more involved than Terraria, but less simple; Starbound has a decent Blocking system worked out for example. Every planet is like an entirely new world in Terraria, only with less regular dungeons, more variety, and scaling difficulty acording to your current equipment, and your need for challenge. While you can make your base on your ship, you can also make your base on a planet, setting it as your home. It just recently (this was written Feb 2015) had an update with introduced growing ships and the 7th race and major overhauls of many systems in game.
However, this is also very WIP. Nothing is fixed in the code at the moment, and most aspects of the game could still change, for example the Racial differences are not yet as well defined as they will be. (Most notably the Racial armour buffs I think)
I'd say if you haven't already bought it, but you're thinking about it, wait for a sale or a windfall and give it a try to get a feel for it. But do bear in mind that most aspects of the game are due to change at some point. Not Major mechanics (although possibly) but questlines and small details. I recommend it, but some would probably feel better holding off until it's further into development. (Still only stage one of three of the beta I believe) I wouldn't blame you at all if you did tbh.
To summarise: Similar-ish to Terraria.
Has much promise and potential.
Is an actual work in progress, so due to get better with time probably.

Half-life is a story-rich shooter with some simple puzzle elements that struggles with the Goldsource engine and some other glitches here and there.
So I just finished Half-life and figured: "Why not make a review of it?". I can't say other than it's a classic. What a game indeed!
Dispise being an alltime masterpiece, it's not safe from glitches and mistakes. This game runs with the old but gold (no pun intended) Goldsource engine, which has its limitations (like crude-to-use ladders). Throughout the game you're sure to find some glitches here and there. You might get stuck on walls or levers. Also, sometimes the submachine gun MP5 won't reload or might reload but won't show to you (though it reloads, your HUD view won't update your bullets). Those are some of the glitches you may run into.
"GOTTA GO FAST". I think that's Freeman's motto. His speed is way too fast and, because of that, often you might fall off platforms.
This game is hard. Most people will agree. Enemies take bullets like if they are nothing and they lock onto you like some freaking aimbot! They never miss a shot! And if your HEV meter is gone, you're pretty much gone too because they can drain your life faster than you can say: "what the...!". It's trial and error at its best!
One other thing: this game requires English knowledge as intermediate or above. People who can't handle English properly might struggle. If you don't pay attention, often you might find yourself wondering what to do next. (Just a fair warning!)
Though there're all those issues, Half-life has that special charm that makes you want to keep going. You may have to try the same area a lot of times until you become a master on it, but you keep trying because you are in love with the story and wants to know what comes next. The plot is amazing.
The overall scenario presentation is alright. Some places are awesome and some are bland. Overall, it's OK.
I can't make enough justice about this game. It's a must play for everyone who likes shooters and simple puzzle-solving elements. Story-rich at its finest. Though, be warned: it's not an easy game.
Oh, by the way, Freeman is a crowbar master!

Great game. Tons of blocks to choose from. The way you unlock blocks through either missions or by destroying other techs is great and has a nice pace. Not grindy. You don't unlock blocks slowly so as to be frustrated, but not so quickly that you see everything there is to see within a few hours. Love the little box that falls from the sky and spews out goodies when you complete a mission. Really kept me coming back. Creating techs is easy for beginners, but not so simplistic that you'll be bored once you get the hang of it. Lots of room for experimentation. Fun creating new techs:  ones that can go fast, ones that mine resources and make cash, ones that just destroy, wacky weird ones, and so on.
A few criticisms.  The game could use a little more instruction about how certain things work as I had to search the internet multiple times to figure things out. Combat is fun but a little simplistic. Often feels like you either just kite enemies until you can pick them apart or else rush in for a battle of attrition to see who falls apart first. Mission variety could be a little better.  Music enjoyable but can be a little repetative after a few hours. You do have the option to turn it off though.
Enjoyable to watch other techs explode all over the place. Nice variety of enemy techs ranging from little silly ones with funny names to behemoths (also sometimes with funny names). Reminds me of a cross between Space Engineers and Besiege, but is unique enough to carve out its own place in your library. Nice graphics. Great colors. Sound effects are decent.
Overall, really enjoyable. Enthusiastic thumbs up! Definitely worth $20. I've played 26 hours at time of review and expect to play a lot more. Good clean fun.

To put context into this: I'm a bit of a curmudgeon when it comes to games. I've sunk hundreds of hours into the flash version of Binding of Issac, and then I sank hundreds of hours into Binding of Issac: Rebirth as well. Once upon a time I had a 10% ascension rate on
which is not record breaking, but not too shabby either. I either really, really love games, or drop them after a couple of hours, and whereas I used to think how much I like a game was based on it being hard or action based one of the things I value above all else is how consistent the rules are and if I have the tools to bend them so I can succeed.
With that said, I can say (with my very particularly tastes and my very particular expectations of a game) Heat Signature is absolutely a hands down great game. The title looks at first like Hotline Miami, a top down twitch shooter, but the pause mechanic in Heat Sig allows you to do arbitrarily complex actions from the pause screen. Given the opportunity to deliberate, choose a course of action, and carefully execute it without the stress of live action makes the game play almost like a puzzler when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan- which happens on almost every mission.
It reminds me a
of Nethack where you're thinking between turns in the face of assured death- however Heat Sig seems as though the entire game was made to be built
moments of assured death and trying to escape them, rather than games like Nethack that just
plenty of moments of assured death where the lucky, brave, and exceptionally knowledgable can sometimes can eek their way through.
The creator has described this game in the genre of "Things Going Wrong", and I've also heard him describe the ideal situation in a game as a "Salvageable Catastrophe". Nothing plays with your emotions more than being completely screwed and seconds from capture or death, only to end up making it out alive by hook or by crook. And sometimes "crook" means accidentally blowing a spacecraft in half so you only have to deal with the smaller, more manageable half. Or hell, intentionally doing it, it worked out fine last time and your hands are sort of tied.
I also called out the original Binding of Issac because the original flash BoI had a very restrictive set of rules that governed it, but an expert in these rules could play them off each other and achieve almost any goal by manipulating them directly. My go-to example of an expert tearing that game apart is here:
, where the game world's opportunities are wide open and careful deliberation allows him to tear the game apart to his advantage. There's the
of shooting enemies and getting powerups, then there's the
of maximizing your ability to get power ups and items.
In Heat Sig the metagame isn't quite this intense (if the game relies on hidden rulesets for item pools, then I don't know it), but the game mechanics allow for
creative problem solving to circumvent enemies or problems on their face through a careful manipulation of the game world. The
is about shooting enemies and capturing bad guys, but the
is about warping the game world to make this easy. This includes a variety of things I've done on purpose (assassinating the pilot so the ship I'm on can't dock at an enemy base and capture me along with it) to and endless number of things I've stumbled on by accident (the aforementioned tearing a ship in half mid-fight, the remaining enemies flew off into the distance and I could pilot the smaller half back to a friendly base as there was no one left to fight on it). The game rewards creativity exceptionally well, and only a few times have I thought "maybe this will work" and been disappointed, and I was usually disappointed because the off the wall tactic worked too well and obliterated the guy I was trying to capture or send my rescue-ee off into deep space too fast for me to go and catch him.
In short, I am really taken with Heat Signature and advertise it to anyone who will listen. There are a bunch of other great mechanics that are worth investigating on their own for how they work just so well (the permadeath mechanic, timed levels, the limited inventory space vs the variety of enemy types, and the tradeoffs between teleporter mechanics), but suffice to say I just powered through my first galaxy and will be back to play a second galaxy. I seriously hope an expansion is a planned or in the works, because the game feels like it scratches the surface of what a well realized set of game mechanics can be used for.
Addendum:
I forgot to mention the cons to the game, which any good review would give. The first and biggest drawback is that some of the space ships you find yourself on have amazingly busy tilesets visually, and that makes it very hard to identify what is going on and where enemies are. My first sit down with the game I actually had to take a break because my eyes started hurting trying to parse the glitcher ship tilesets- I may be a wimp about this with my ageing eyes but this should probably be looked at.
Another notable issue is that there is a memory leak somewhere, and the game will slow to a crawl after hours of play. It's a testament to the game that despite individual levels being 10 minute spaceship hijacking vignettes, a memory leak that shows up after hours of play is kind of a big problem. Closing the game and re-opening clears it, but seriously. This isn't amateur hour, this detracts from an otherwise stellar game. The game stutters when you return back to an asteroid, so I'm guessing the interior never gets cleared from memory collectly but re-loaded on each return.
The last element is that the larger main story and the "Galaxy" itself feels like it needs a better narrative. The small procedurally generated storylines of missions don't hook into at the larger scope of the "Galaxy" much at all, and the disconnect is disappointing when you sink 30 hours over 2 weeks into the game (cough).
To add a final note to the matter of the main storyline,

Heat Signature is set in a region of space where four factions are at war with each other. Over the course of the game, the player controls several different mercenaries for hire, who are working for an independent client, trying to liberate space stations from the control of the factions, with the ultimate goal of ending the war. Each of your characters also has a personal mission, which could be getting revenge on someone who hurt a family member, or stealing a valuable item to pay off a debt.
After accepting a contract from the mission board of a friendly space station, you’ll pilot a small shuttle through space, and dock with a larger spaceship. You then control your character from an overhead perspective, as you wander around the spaceship interior towards your objective, fighting or evading enemy guards along the way. Each ship has a unique, procedurally generated layout. Action is real time, but you can pause to assess the situation and make a plan.
Contract objectives include killing or capturing a specific target, rescuing a prisoner, stealing a piece of technology, or hijacking the ship (which requires you to kill or knock out every guard on board). Some contracts are given a further twist with clauses, including bloodless (don’t kill anybody), silent (don’t set off an alarm) or enigma (don’t leave any living witnesses). Failing a clause doesn’t prevent you from completing the mission, but it reduces the amount of money you earn.
If guards see or hear you they will raise the alarm, which triggers the pilot to return to base. If you're still on board when they get there, you'll be captured, but you can kill or knock out the pilot to stop the journey, giving you time to complete the mission. Some ships have turrets that can kill you, but guards will just knock you out and throw you out the airlock. You’ll then have a few seconds whilst floating in space, to remote control your shuttle and catch yourself before you die of suffocation.
If your character is killed or captured, you start a new character with no progress lost in the overall campaign. Your new character’s personal mission might be to rescue your old character, and if successful, you can play as the old character again. You can have four characters active that you can switch between at a friendly space station.
The really enjoyable part of the game comes from the variety of gadgets available for use on missions. You can either buy them from a friendly space station, or find them in cargo holds aboard spaceships. This review would probably be a mile long if I tried to list all the cool stuff you can do, but here are a few of my favourites.
-	Use a crashbeam to deactivate a turret, or a subverter to make it shoot your enemies.
-	Some guards have energy shields protecting them from all types of damage. Deactivate it with the crashbeam, or use the subverter to cause their own bullets to bounce back at them.
-	The slipstream slows time, allowing you to attack multiple guards before they can react.
-	Use the sidewinder to teleport past a group of guards, or teleport directly behind one for an easy attack.
-	The swapper lets you switch places with a guard. Swap with one who just fired at you, to kill them with their own bullet.
-	Most spaceships have several internal doors that are locked, requiring you to collect keycards, held by guards. Or, you could just use the keycard cloner to make a copy from a safe range, even if there’s a wall between you and the guard.
-	Glitch traps are mines that let you set a teleport destination for any guard who steps on it. Set the destination outside the ship, so they suffocate to death.
Some guards also have special equipment, including strong armour that can only be penetrated by special weapons, and heat sensors which alert them to your presence even if you're behind them or in another room. Some can teleport to the location of suspicious sounds and some have bombs linked to their heartbeat which instantly detonate if you kill them. There’s a strong tactical, almost puzzle like, element to the game, figuring out the best way to use your gadgets to bypass each ship’s security.
Some of the funniest moments are when your plans go wrong, and you have to quickly adapt. One time I used a crashhammer (powerful non-lethal melee weapon) to knock out my target, who I had to capture alive. The problem is, this weapon hits with so much force, my target flew down a corridor and smashed through an exterior window, sucking us both out into space. I only just managed to catch us both with my shuttle, before we died. I had a similar experience with a glitch trap, which doesn’t teleport your character, but apparently it does teleport people that you’re trying to rescue.

Of course, no game is perfect. Enemy AI has a few flaws. Often the best tactic to use against groups of enemies, is to ambush them one by one on their patrol routes. However, it feels strange that the other guards don’t think “hmm, that guy has been gone for a while, maybe something is wrong?”. And whilst guards will react if they see corpses, they don’t seem to react to blood stains or weapons lying on the floor. Its also unbelievable that each ship seems to only have one pilot. Once you’ve dealt with him, you have infinite time to complete the mission. You can even leave the ship, head back to a space station, buy some new gear, go back to the ship, and no other guards will have taken over flying the ship while you were away.
And although it took me 18 hours to finish the campaign, I think I’d seen everything by the halfway point. Once you’re powerful enough to eliminate one of the factions, the rest of the game is basically just repeating the same mission types over and over again until you liberate enough space stations to take out the remaining factions. Whilst those missions are still fun, I was kind of hoping for a new type of mission or a new piece of late game tech to freshen things up again.
Overall, Heat Signature is one of the best games I’ve played this year, and I strongly recommend everyone to check it out. Its easily worth a full price purchase.

Brilliant game. I read all the comments below and almost didnt get the game but then decided might as well give a try. I definitely did not regret it. I have a GTX 770 2GB and I was running mostly on Ultra. No lag no issues didnt seem to cause any problems. Graphics are not splendid but they are good nonetheless. Experienced very few bugs in single mode. Coop mode was a bit more buggy but nothing too serious.
Now that aside, let's talk about the game itself. The story is interesting to say the least. A lot of characters, a lot of mixed emotions and struggles. Was never bored of following the main missions. The ending was a bit lackluster I must say. Some characters could be a bit deeper but wasnt really an issue. As for the side missions, in single mode you have missions which take a minute and give you a boost of cash, and others that are longer and more interesting. Coop missions are definitely fun as well but the qeues to find players often put me off.
The gameplay is in my opinion one of the best in the series. The new free run down option really improves your general mobility and its been a niche I felt needed covering for quite a while. Sometimes Arno refused to do things I asked him to but in general mobility was good.
They made fighting a bit more difficult since you cant kill a person using a counter anymore at all. If you fight a large mob a few will move back and start shooting at you, and it hurts. It does push you to actually be an assassin and not a crazed savage with guns blazing. Stealth is more difficult but you have a lot of tools to help you. Unfortunately you often end up killing everyone anyway but it feels gratifying to sneak in, take out the target and sneak out properly.
The city (Paris) is very nice to move around in. Crowd events always give you something to do. You can actually enter a lot of the buildings through doors or windows. Royalist give you trouble wherever you go. The crowd slowly starts to fight with you. I was never bored walking around. While some regions and buildings in Paris are phenomenal (and Im not even talking about Notre Dame), Ubisoft couldve made different regions more unique (Rome in Brotherhood and Constantinople in Revelations come to mind). One of the main things they added to Unity was massive crowds, that you can walk through while being blended in. I particularly enjoyed that part too, and it added to the feel of the revolution and all.
I definitely didnt cover everything in the game but I wanted this review to push people to get this game. Completely different experience from Black Flag as it goes back to the traditional AC feel back in the Ezio games, but its a brilliant game nonetheless. Buy it!

Soooo, Heat signature. Lots of fun, Kinda bland, Kinda fun.
Let's go over pros and cons.
Pros:
Gameplay -> This game feels great when you're good at it. Killing everyone who stands in your path, or stealing something on a huge ship without being seen by anyone. But that Is what can bore you. If you play to win, it becomes less and less fun (This applied to me with the last hour or two). If you play to lose however, the game becomes so much better. Doing the hardest mission with just a wrench may be difficult (almost impossible) but if you are insanely lucky you might complete the mission, just.

Music -> I'm not that much of a music lover. But the music doesn't make me want to kill myself, sooo, it will pass for me.
Graphics -> It can run on my♥♥♥♥♥♥PC and still looks fairly polished. So I guess this will pass as well.
Tension -> You know when you get to a hyped up final boss in an RPG or loads of people are counting on you for something? Well I felt that way several times (especially early game) during my time playing Heat signature so far. Few games do this for me, I guess that's a plus.
Achievements -> This is the first (and most likely only) game I have got all the achievements for (I spent 4 hours getting "one careful owner). The achievements gave me a bit of a drive to play more of the game and gave me a few ideas to have some extra fun. They are quite plentiful (46 in total) and they aren't stupidly difficult (apart from one careful owner)
Cons:
Glitches -> Many glitches; Many fixes. Not sure where to stand on this one but hey. I played through the game without losing my save, or getting trapped, so I don't particularly care.
No workshop -> Grrr. If there was workshop I could easily get another 30 hours out of this game. It will most likely come in the future, but it stays as a con for now. [This could get rid of the boredom after many hours]
Boredom -> I already spoke about this earlier. If you try too much, or you play the game carefully. You will get bored (eventually). Luckily everything is here for you to have the fun you really want.
Price -> Not so sure on this one. I definitely got my money's worth but a lot of people haven't. If you can see yourself playing this game for 10+ hours go for it. If not wait for a sale or something.
Well that shall do for now. Pretty good game. Just finished it. Might go start all over again.

Unplayable. I can play GTA V on its highest settings without a skip in the framerate, but this game thinks that every 10 seconds the screen needs to skip a few frames and point me in a completely different direction. If you don't think that won't get on your nerves after about 5 minutes, don't say I didn't warn you.
Likewise, the gameplay is equally bad. An example of the gameplay: I barely got past the introductory missions and accepted a mission to collect 3 severed heads from various points around a building. 2 heads were standard AC mission fare: collect a pair of keys, then sneak into the room where they're being kept, take out the guard and collect the heads. Other than the controls being practically garbage  the first part of the mission felt familiar.  (Silently taking out the guard from behind didn't work because the game failed to acknowledge the key had been pressed. I was forced to engage the guard in choppy, terrible framerate combat instead.)  The 3rd head, however, was carefully placed in a bag that looks exactly like several other bags in the area in direct sight of a dozen guards who could care less about the angry mob storming the building. Never mind the hundred plus people angrily shouting as they approach you, if that one guy steps slightly away from the mob and looks at an empty bag, shoot the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You can't look in the bag if a guard has been alerted, and the guards are alerted if you even think, "This game can't be that bad..." Sure, I could have tried distracting the guards with firecrackers like one might do in another AC game, but I didn't bother for the following reasons:
1: I assumed they'd immediately be alerted that I'm the culprit, and would instantly shoot me, because that appears to be this game's MO.
2: The game remapped its entire control scheme from previous AC titles and didn't bother to explain HOW to throw the firecrackers by this point.
3: If I tried to throw them, the screen would probably blink and point me in the wrong direction the instant before I threw them, and I'd probably end up throwing them directly at the wall behind me.
4: This distraction might have worked for 1 bag, but there were at least 5 bags to check.
5: At this point I was painfully reminded that the difficulty of the mission was shown as 1 out of 5 stars: Easy mode. Yes, Ubisoft thought putting a new player in the position of distracting a dozen guards while you searched half a dozen bags around a courtyard is practically a tutorial.
6: After going through every possible rationalization one can at this point to make excuses for this game, you just have to give up at some point. This game is unplayable.

I would have been ok with more timed missions than XCOM:EU, but it was excessive and I really just didn't enjoy it.
Now, the second time I tried playing was almost a year later. Many mods have been released, specifically the "Disable Timers" mod. BAM! Game was fun again. No longer was I rushing through every mission, I could take my time and do everything how I wanted. I finally played through and beat the entire game and loved it.
If you liked EU, there's no question that you'll love this, but be wary of the timers, it's your decision.

I know it's Early Access right now, but this game is coming along quite nicely. I've been playing it since the beta first opened. While it was plenty of fun earlier on, a lot of balance and polish was missing from a lot of mechanics to make it more than a pure sandbox. After the most recent, huge winter update, there's a lot more coherency to the progression of things. It's a sandbox, sure, but now it's a sandbox with much more purpose.
You can swing melee weapons in specific directions now. You can "mine" water/lava/any other liquid. There are legit outposts and stores now, and purposes for food beyond "don't starve to death." Mining feels a lot better, since your Matter Manipulator (ranged-use omnitool used to mine/place things) can actually be upgraded and used as your base tool most of the time. I mean, if you get really, really deep, and into some obsidian and blastrock, you probably want to go with a pick (no longer repairable, but pretty easy to make -- so, a limited resource for mining faster, but not chore-ishly hard to manage). You can now use 4 different techs at a time (abilities, such as double-jump/dash/etc.), instead of just the one from before. The first "boss" encounter/scenario is now a legit mission (and feels like one, even if it's kind of simple), instead of just being "build a beacon and fight a really annoying-because-it-always-flies-away-from-you UFO." In fact, the whole start of the game feels a lot better. The tutorial and all. Your ship starts out all damaged, and you have to get it fixed.
Anywho, it's got a little ways to go, but if you like sandboxy-type gameplay (very much like Terraria), then this is a pretty great game. I can imagine it's even more fun in multiplayer, but I don't usually get to play it near a very awesome internet connection, so I haven't really tried that out yet.

Still has room for improvement, very rare but harmless crashes to desktop when a PvP queue pops, so it's not like it's affected my play experience. Haven't had an in-game crash in a very long time. Run a mid-end computer and it can run on near-highest settings with no lag.

And also if you're just a bad player.
Loot boxes immediately makes me dislike the economy of this game. However, it IS a free to play game, so honestly I can't hate the game's economy model just because of this system. You directly purchase ships and do not get them from lootboxes, so that's nice, but literally everything else you can acquire is done so through lootboxes. As far as gameplay-pertinent items is concerned, that's crew ((each ship uses 5 unique officers; 1 captain and 4 other key members.)) and Crew Implants (additional stats to attach to your 5 crew members)). The pricing for all the above is doable when you're only trying to get one of the above, but put together the pricing (for both real money and in-game money) becomes a bit much. To note, you can directly purchase any crew member you wish that you don't own, but it costs as much as a new ship, which is a lot of credits! To my knowledge you cannot do this with implants.
There are a lot of missions and a daily login reward that help give you a continual sense of progression beyond the static reward from every win/loss, so that helps things out as well.
So a lot of people would wonder if a free to play game is pay to win. My 4/5 says, barely. None of the ships are outright better than each other at generic offensive, defensive or utilty roles. All of the crew are balanced to have similar stat distributions with how they affect your ship's statistics; one type of helmsman will give you 9%+ Maneuverign and 9%+ Turn Rate. Another will give you 12%+ Maneuvering and 6%+ Turn Rate. And vice versa, etc etc.
Each crew member has 3 implant slots, and each has a color denoting one of 3 implant types they can slot. Luckily, the game allows you to level up your crew members from level 0 to level 3. Each level turns the left-most implant color into a universal/legendary color, allowing you to slot any implant. You earn this EXP in every game and earn them from missions and you can apply it to any crew member you want.
Every implant is a generic stat and there are 25 types. 1% flat damage reduction, 2.5% armor-specific damage reduction, 2.5% broken-armor specific damage reduction, 0.8% damage bonus, 0.8% fire rate, etc. Every crew member can only slot one of each type of implant, but you can fit the same implant on a different crew member. What this means is you can slot 5 damage reduction bonuses throughout all of your 5 crew members, for a total of 5% bonus flat damage reduction.
If I remember correctly the game starts you out with 10 implants(?) maybe 5 crew members(?) I would have to look at a wiki or start a new account to find out.So honestly, being new the implants could possibly put you at a slight disadvantage, so for that reason I put this down to 4/5 rather than 5/5. However, the implants do open up potential new options to try playing a ship, such as something silly like 50% ramming damage, so I don't hate the implant system. Furthermore, the ability to choose what crew you wish to upgrade to hold more slots allows you to catch up relatively quickly in stacking implants. I just wish the implant system was not hidden behind loot boxes.
Guess that's all I have to say. Overall recommend it if you're looking for a free to play game to get into. I would suggest using money to purchase a starter pack or a few ships if you really like it, or just keep playing at your own pace, honestly.
