To put context into this: I'm a bit of a curmudgeon when it comes to games. I've sunk hundreds of hours into the flash version of Binding of Issac, and then I sank hundreds of hours into Binding of Issac: Rebirth as well. Once upon a time I had a 10% ascension rate on
which is not record breaking, but not too shabby either. I either really, really love games, or drop them after a couple of hours, and whereas I used to think how much I like a game was based on it being hard or action based one of the things I value above all else is how consistent the rules are and if I have the tools to bend them so I can succeed.
With that said, I can say (with my very particularly tastes and my very particular expectations of a game) Heat Signature is absolutely a hands down great game. The title looks at first like Hotline Miami, a top down twitch shooter, but the pause mechanic in Heat Sig allows you to do arbitrarily complex actions from the pause screen. Given the opportunity to deliberate, choose a course of action, and carefully execute it without the stress of live action makes the game play almost like a puzzler when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan- which happens on almost every mission.
It reminds me a
of Nethack where you're thinking between turns in the face of assured death- however Heat Sig seems as though the entire game was made to be built
moments of assured death and trying to escape them, rather than games like Nethack that just
plenty of moments of assured death where the lucky, brave, and exceptionally knowledgable can sometimes can eek their way through.
The creator has described this game in the genre of "Things Going Wrong", and I've also heard him describe the ideal situation in a game as a "Salvageable Catastrophe". Nothing plays with your emotions more than being completely screwed and seconds from capture or death, only to end up making it out alive by hook or by crook. And sometimes "crook" means accidentally blowing a spacecraft in half so you only have to deal with the smaller, more manageable half. Or hell, intentionally doing it, it worked out fine last time and your hands are sort of tied.
I also called out the original Binding of Issac because the original flash BoI had a very restrictive set of rules that governed it, but an expert in these rules could play them off each other and achieve almost any goal by manipulating them directly. My go-to example of an expert tearing that game apart is here:
, where the game world's opportunities are wide open and careful deliberation allows him to tear the game apart to his advantage. There's the
of shooting enemies and getting powerups, then there's the
of maximizing your ability to get power ups and items.
In Heat Sig the metagame isn't quite this intense (if the game relies on hidden rulesets for item pools, then I don't know it), but the game mechanics allow for
creative problem solving to circumvent enemies or problems on their face through a careful manipulation of the game world. The
is about shooting enemies and capturing bad guys, but the
is about warping the game world to make this easy. This includes a variety of things I've done on purpose (assassinating the pilot so the ship I'm on can't dock at an enemy base and capture me along with it) to and endless number of things I've stumbled on by accident (the aforementioned tearing a ship in half mid-fight, the remaining enemies flew off into the distance and I could pilot the smaller half back to a friendly base as there was no one left to fight on it). The game rewards creativity exceptionally well, and only a few times have I thought "maybe this will work" and been disappointed, and I was usually disappointed because the off the wall tactic worked too well and obliterated the guy I was trying to capture or send my rescue-ee off into deep space too fast for me to go and catch him.
In short, I am really taken with Heat Signature and advertise it to anyone who will listen. There are a bunch of other great mechanics that are worth investigating on their own for how they work just so well (the permadeath mechanic, timed levels, the limited inventory space vs the variety of enemy types, and the tradeoffs between teleporter mechanics), but suffice to say I just powered through my first galaxy and will be back to play a second galaxy. I seriously hope an expansion is a planned or in the works, because the game feels like it scratches the surface of what a well realized set of game mechanics can be used for.
Addendum:
I forgot to mention the cons to the game, which any good review would give. The first and biggest drawback is that some of the space ships you find yourself on have amazingly busy tilesets visually, and that makes it very hard to identify what is going on and where enemies are. My first sit down with the game I actually had to take a break because my eyes started hurting trying to parse the glitcher ship tilesets- I may be a wimp about this with my ageing eyes but this should probably be looked at.
Another notable issue is that there is a memory leak somewhere, and the game will slow to a crawl after hours of play. It's a testament to the game that despite individual levels being 10 minute spaceship hijacking vignettes, a memory leak that shows up after hours of play is kind of a big problem. Closing the game and re-opening clears it, but seriously. This isn't amateur hour, this detracts from an otherwise stellar game. The game stutters when you return back to an asteroid, so I'm guessing the interior never gets cleared from memory collectly but re-loaded on each return.
The last element is that the larger main story and the "Galaxy" itself feels like it needs a better narrative. The small procedurally generated storylines of missions don't hook into at the larger scope of the "Galaxy" much at all, and the disconnect is disappointing when you sink 30 hours over 2 weeks into the game (cough).

Heat Signature is set in a region of space where four factions are at war with each other. Over the course of the game, the player controls several different mercenaries for hire, who are working for an independent client, trying to liberate space stations from the control of the factions, with the ultimate goal of ending the war. Each of your characters also has a personal mission, which could be getting revenge on someone who hurt a family member, or stealing a valuable item to pay off a debt.
After accepting a contract from the mission board of a friendly space station, you’ll pilot a small shuttle through space, and dock with a larger spaceship. You then control your character from an overhead perspective, as you wander around the spaceship interior towards your objective, fighting or evading enemy guards along the way. Each ship has a unique, procedurally generated layout. Action is real time, but you can pause to assess the situation and make a plan.
Contract objectives include killing or capturing a specific target, rescuing a prisoner, stealing a piece of technology, or hijacking the ship (which requires you to kill or knock out every guard on board). Some contracts are given a further twist with clauses, including bloodless (don’t kill anybody), silent (don’t set off an alarm) or enigma (don’t leave any living witnesses). Failing a clause doesn’t prevent you from completing the mission, but it reduces the amount of money you earn.
If guards see or hear you they will raise the alarm, which triggers the pilot to return to base. If you're still on board when they get there, you'll be captured, but you can kill or knock out the pilot to stop the journey, giving you time to complete the mission. Some ships have turrets that can kill you, but guards will just knock you out and throw you out the airlock. You’ll then have a few seconds whilst floating in space, to remote control your shuttle and catch yourself before you die of suffocation.
If your character is killed or captured, you start a new character with no progress lost in the overall campaign. Your new character’s personal mission might be to rescue your old character, and if successful, you can play as the old character again. You can have four characters active that you can switch between at a friendly space station.
The really enjoyable part of the game comes from the variety of gadgets available for use on missions. You can either buy them from a friendly space station, or find them in cargo holds aboard spaceships. This review would probably be a mile long if I tried to list all the cool stuff you can do, but here are a few of my favourites.
-	Use a crashbeam to deactivate a turret, or a subverter to make it shoot your enemies.
-	Some guards have energy shields protecting them from all types of damage. Deactivate it with the crashbeam, or use the subverter to cause their own bullets to bounce back at them.
-	The slipstream slows time, allowing you to attack multiple guards before they can react.
-	Use the sidewinder to teleport past a group of guards, or teleport directly behind one for an easy attack.
-	The swapper lets you switch places with a guard. Swap with one who just fired at you, to kill them with their own bullet.
-	Most spaceships have several internal doors that are locked, requiring you to collect keycards, held by guards. Or, you could just use the keycard cloner to make a copy from a safe range, even if there’s a wall between you and the guard.
-	Glitch traps are mines that let you set a teleport destination for any guard who steps on it. Set the destination outside the ship, so they suffocate to death.
Some guards also have special equipment, including strong armour that can only be penetrated by special weapons, and heat sensors which alert them to your presence even if you're behind them or in another room. Some can teleport to the location of suspicious sounds and some have bombs linked to their heartbeat which instantly detonate if you kill them. There’s a strong tactical, almost puzzle like, element to the game, figuring out the best way to use your gadgets to bypass each ship’s security.
Some of the funniest moments are when your plans go wrong, and you have to quickly adapt. One time I used a crashhammer (powerful non-lethal melee weapon) to knock out my target, who I had to capture alive. The problem is, this weapon hits with so much force, my target flew down a corridor and smashed through an exterior window, sucking us both out into space. I only just managed to catch us both with my shuttle, before we died. I had a similar experience with a glitch trap, which doesn’t teleport your character, but apparently it does teleport people that you’re trying to rescue.

Of course, no game is perfect. Enemy AI has a few flaws. Often the best tactic to use against groups of enemies, is to ambush them one by one on their patrol routes. However, it feels strange that the other guards don’t think “hmm, that guy has been gone for a while, maybe something is wrong?”. And whilst guards will react if they see corpses, they don’t seem to react to blood stains or weapons lying on the floor. Its also unbelievable that each ship seems to only have one pilot. Once you’ve dealt with him, you have infinite time to complete the mission. You can even leave the ship, head back to a space station, buy some new gear, go back to the ship, and no other guards will have taken over flying the ship while you were away.
And although it took me 18 hours to finish the campaign, I think I’d seen everything by the halfway point. Once you’re powerful enough to eliminate one of the factions, the rest of the game is basically just repeating the same mission types over and over again until you liberate enough space stations to take out the remaining factions. Whilst those missions are still fun, I was kind of hoping for a new type of mission or a new piece of late game tech to freshen things up again.
Overall, Heat Signature is one of the best games I’ve played this year, and I strongly recommend everyone to check it out. Its easily worth a full price purchase.

Let's go over pros and cons.
Pros:
Gameplay -> This game feels great when you're good at it. Killing everyone who stands in your path, or stealing something on a huge ship without being seen by anyone. But that Is what can bore you. If you play to win, it becomes less and less fun (This applied to me with the last hour or two). If you play to lose however, the game becomes so much better. Doing the hardest mission with just a wrench may be difficult (almost impossible) but if you are insanely lucky you might complete the mission, just.

Music -> I'm not that much of a music lover. But the music doesn't make me want to kill myself, sooo, it will pass for me.
Graphics -> It can run on my♥♥♥♥♥♥PC and still looks fairly polished. So I guess this will pass as well.
Tension -> You know when you get to a hyped up final boss in an RPG or loads of people are counting on you for something? Well I felt that way several times (especially early game) during my time playing Heat signature so far. Few games do this for me, I guess that's a plus.
Achievements -> This is the first (and most likely only) game I have got all the achievements for (I spent 4 hours getting "one careful owner). The achievements gave me a bit of a drive to play more of the game and gave me a few ideas to have some extra fun. They are quite plentiful (46 in total) and they aren't stupidly difficult (apart from one careful owner)
Cons:
Glitches -> Many glitches; Many fixes. Not sure where to stand on this one but hey. I played through the game without losing my save, or getting trapped, so I don't particularly care.
No workshop -> Grrr. If there was workshop I could easily get another 30 hours out of this game. It will most likely come in the future, but it stays as a con for now. [This could get rid of the boredom after many hours]
Boredom -> I already spoke about this earlier. If you try too much, or you play the game carefully. You will get bored (eventually). Luckily everything is here for you to have the fun you really want.
Price -> Not so sure on this one. I definitely got my money's worth but a lot of people haven't. If you can see yourself playing this game for 10+ hours go for it. If not wait for a sale or something.

Final Fantasy III is a great retread that breathes new life into a classic NES title.  As a Steam port of a DS remake of a Japan-only title, this is by far the best way to play Final Fantasy III in 2017.  The remake was a complete overhaul of the graphics, characters, story, and content, which went a long way to spice up and modernize the 20-year-old RPG.  10 years later, the remake still holds up remarkably well.  Notably, the DS version's Friend Code/WiFi support feature has been scrapped, in favor of blending all of that system's bonuses into the game naturally.  Lots of new bosses and side quests extend playtime by a fair margin.  Extreme completionists also have a lot to love here, as each of the 23 Jobs has a bonus for complete mastery.
If you're looking for the gold standard of turn-based RPG combat, one of the best Final Fantasy Job systems, and a brutal final dungeon, you're in good company here.

Hacknet is pretty much what it says on the tin - a hacking-themed game in which you must meet escalating challenges throughout the course of its story, which opens with a posthumous message coming from a hacker who has disappeared.  Stop right there, though - the story isn't very strong on the conspiracy and ends up being a missed opportunity, so don't dive in just yet.
Those not familiar with command-lines need not fret as this isn't a full-blown OS simulator like other games in the genre.  While it does have its own level of CLI sophistication, the tutorial and pacing thereafter is carefully crafted as not to overwhelm the inexperienced.  Anyone looking to roleplay a super hacking machine can comfortably play this game without having a manual in front of them (though a notepad may help).  Rather than have you coding a bunch of exploits or what have you, your hacking terminal - which is beautifully-rendered, btw - is loaded with magical tools that do all the work for you.  You just need to handle the set up, if you will, and the software will do the rest.
What separates Hacknet from others in the genre is its combo of command-line terminal and graphical user interface (think X-Window).  The game is aesthetically pleasing to the eye with a mix of hi- and low-tech, giving the interface an authentic OS feel.  If you're not keen on typing every little thing (which you can absolutely elect to do), you can instead click on the GUI to navigate around most of the systems and poke around.  You'll still need to key in some commands, but there's a good balance here if you want to save some time with navigation and reading files.  Websites aren't functional, but they do appear in the game and give it that extra little flavor, with one exception being a Clicker game that you can waste time on should you so choose to.
So while the story doesn't really play out in the best of ways, the hacking is quite fun... at least for the first little bit.  It very soon becomes repetitive because ultimately the puzzles are limited.  You will be taking on contracts/jobs from message servers and they each boil down to a) get into the target system and b) grab some information or delete stuff.  Even though you are introduced to new tools (and thus, the difficulty of breaking into a system increases), the game rarely deviates from this formula, even when the story demands it.  It's not really until the latter quarter of the game when you're doing interesting stuff, not so much because the repetitiveness is gone, but more because the answers aren't quite as obvious.
I would have liked to have a more involved tale form throughout the game and as I said above, it's a missed opportunity.  It would make discovery so much more satisfying.  This isn't made much better by most servers being devoid of anything interesting other than some randomly-pulled bash quotes which, if you've been around on the Internet long enough, you've already read.  Still, this is a minor nitpick and beyond that, there was nary an issue with the game.  I encountered no bugs or crashes, except that I wasted a good 2 or 3 hours trying to go down a different path (which happens under very, very specific circumstances), which highlighted the inability to save-where-you-want; basically, failing to meet the conditions, even though I thought I knew what I had to do, meant that I had to restart from scratch repeatedly just to get there... however, this alternate path is completely optional and easily-missed.  I only put this here as a warning to achievement hunters.
At the end of the day, Hacknet is a fun game that captures the spirit of hacking without overwhelming the player.  I'm sure there are more hardcore games in the genre, but at that point - in my opinion - I feel it stops being a game and starts being a job.  Hacknet manages to find the right balance between authenticity and Hollywood fantasy so it's a very enjoyable experience.
Just be aware that the blue screens look incredibly authentic.  Don't panic.

I know it's Early Access right now, but this game is coming along quite nicely. I've been playing it since the beta first opened. While it was plenty of fun earlier on, a lot of balance and polish was missing from a lot of mechanics to make it more than a pure sandbox. After the most recent, huge winter update, there's a lot more coherency to the progression of things. It's a sandbox, sure, but now it's a sandbox with much more purpose.
You can swing melee weapons in specific directions now. You can "mine" water/lava/any other liquid. There are legit outposts and stores now, and purposes for food beyond "don't starve to death." Mining feels a lot better, since your Matter Manipulator (ranged-use omnitool used to mine/place things) can actually be upgraded and used as your base tool most of the time. I mean, if you get really, really deep, and into some obsidian and blastrock, you probably want to go with a pick (no longer repairable, but pretty easy to make -- so, a limited resource for mining faster, but not chore-ishly hard to manage). You can now use 4 different techs at a time (abilities, such as double-jump/dash/etc.), instead of just the one from before. The first "boss" encounter/scenario is now a legit mission (and feels like one, even if it's kind of simple), instead of just being "build a beacon and fight a really annoying-because-it-always-flies-away-from-you UFO." In fact, the whole start of the game feels a lot better. The tutorial and all. Your ship starts out all damaged, and you have to get it fixed.
Anywho, it's got a little ways to go, but if you like sandboxy-type gameplay (very much like Terraria), then this is a pretty great game. I can imagine it's even more fun in multiplayer, but I don't usually get to play it near a very awesome internet connection, so I haven't really tried that out yet.

One of the best fantasy adventure games ever made, and it's over 10 years old. While this port has two major flaws and some little ones, I just have to recommend it, that's how good it is. There is a reason why I sunk over 600 hours into this game on my PS2. So let's get to cons first and then pros (there's a lot of them)
Cons:
Major:
- No key remapping
- It's capped to 30 frames per second due to the physics engine breaking on higher framerates.
Minor:
- Annoying "voice acting", but since that can be turned off it's not that big of a deal
- Long cutscenes. You can skip them with F1 on keyboard but might miss some vital information
- Some road and path textures clip with the ground texture, causing them to blink. If you're sensitive to flickering lights be really cautious
Pros:
+ Absolutely epic storyline
+ Around 60 hours of gameplay, even more if you're a completionist
+ Beautiful artstyle
+ One of the greatest soundtracks I've ever heard
+ Solid combat
+ A good bunch of fun bossfights and minigames
+ Large semi-open world style world to explore with gorgeous landscapes
+ Impressive amount of secrets to find and collectibles to loot
+ It's not grindy
+ You are the sun god, hunting down demons in a wolf form. It's just badas*.
If you haven't played this game yet, I really recommend giving it a shot if nothing else.

Despite it's outstandingly fluid combat, overall enjoyable gameplay and great optimization(really, my potato GPU can handle it's graphics while keeping the game pretty), I can't recommend this game for multiple reasons.
To begin with, after over a year of it's development, it's stuck to only a few gamemodes, which are basically all the same, except on different map scales.
Aside from that, the grinding for each ship is horrifyingly boring due to the fact above. It takes about a week to get approx. 500k credits, and by the time that happens you'll already get bored of the game, because you already just did the whole thing over and over again so many times and none of it changed ever at all. And oh boy, I don't even want to imagine how long it would take me to set up a full crew of characters I wanted to have in it, since they drop randomly in "capsules" that are about as expensive as ships.
Also, multiplayer MM takes ages to get through due to the game being dead. But why is it dead? Oh, right, it's repetitive and not too replayable.
Look at Warframe, that game is grindy as hell, yet it keeps itself replayable because it offers you so many ways to approach each mission in every sense of saying it, while keeping the whole thing intense and never letting you easily predict every single thing that would happen the next... entire match? All you have to do here is see whether your ship can take on the other ship or not and the rest of it is just point & click action with some 1/2/3/4 hotkey presses here and there. Basically, just like in any MOBA game ever, except more intense and smoother.
So, all in all, the game will keep you playing it for some time, but it'll get boring way too soon, despite being epic and all that. If you really want space battles, find yourself something else instead, like EVE Online(subscription) or Battlestar Galactica(f2p), I guess.

I've never really written a full review for a game, but this one deserves the utmost praise.  I'm going to mainly talk about the port; the game itself is excellent and most everybody on the internet who has played it agrees.
Let's explain the elephant: 30fps.  Yeah, it's unfortunate.  But it's perfectly acceptable given the nature of the engine.  The PS2's CPU and GPU are notorious for being inexorably tied to one another in many ways, and games were developed with this in mind for performance reasons.  This is the only "con" I have for this port.
Resolution? 4k, no problem.  The art style flourishes at this resolution.  You'll notice some mildly blurry textures if you stop and stare at the scenery for a few moments, but don't do that, you're a fox-goddess and you leave trails of beautiful life energy (... okay, grass) in your wake.
Performance? Fantastic, though I'll admit my computer is likely a bit above spec for this game, especially capped at 30fps.
But HERE is the true reason I've left a review for this game.  It has complete 100% support for the Steam Controller API.  Games NEED TO BE DOING THIS.  Steam has created the best interface so far to let you use whatever controller you like in whatever game you like.  I'm sick of seeing XInput controller icons with my Dualshock 4.  This is why I was absolutely floored and delighted when I saw a square icon for the attack prompt.  (This is through the steam controller interface in Big Picture Mode, BPM auto from normal launch while controller is connected, as well as on Steam Link; NOT direct dualshock 4 driver access).
The devs deserve praise for this and other developers need to take note.  The Steam Controller API (Whether you use a steam controller or not) should be a MUST for all future games.  XInput is a fallback, period.
Now, time to make some brush strokes!

THINGS THAT TROVE IS AWESOME AT:
• Keeping You Entertained - You can easily lose track of time with this game.
• Involving the Community - Styles—basically skins for your gear—are almost entirely made by the players of Trove
• Stability - the mechanics in Trove are solid and they work as they should.
• Interactive Developers - Three of Trove's developers are also members of the largest club in the game, Voxel Busters, and they won't hesitate to participate in chat and such, making them easy to talk to.
• Sound Quality - Sounds are clear and distinctive, nothing wrong there.
• Graphics - The game LOOKS nice, which is always a plus.
• Consistency - This game isn't finished—things are always being moved around, so patches roll in every Tuesday morning. Only hotfixes occur on days other than Tuesday.
They do a lot right, huh? In constrast, there are a fair amount of things that Trove does wrong. If an item has (TRION) on it, that means the item isn't specific to Trove, but to all games that Trion manages (Defiance, Trove, ArcheAge, RIFT, Devilian, etc.).
THINGS THAT TROVE SUCKS AT:
• Optimization - Trove isn't easy on the FPS, especially when it comes to having a lot of players in a small area. I remember a few streamers with some godlike machines being astonished that they were getting only 5-15 FPS when throwing a pinata party.
• Configuration - Tying back into the first point, there is not much flexibility when it comes to video settings. You can't configure a lot of video settings.
• Latency - Let's face it; the servers running Trove are bad. I have never gotten a ping below 70 in Trove, and I have over 1.5k hours spent on the game (I switched to the Glyph launcher some time ago instead of running from Steam). The servers are laggy and I'm just used to it now. Actually, it might not even be the servers. It could be how players are connected. Whatever it is, getting a low ping is not possible.
• Server Issues - This one's not pertaining to lag, but to general server issues. Sometimes, when you go to enter another world, you get disconnected immediately. Maybe your actions are either delayed or completely dropped.
• RNG Dependence - Especially with this new Mantle of Power expansion, the game has become pretty dependent on RNG, or random number generator. The problem with such a high about of RNG is the lack of guaranteed progress. You can spend hours grinding and have it wasted simply because RNG wasn't in your favor. You could spend minutes grinding and have it boost your level significantly simply because RNG was in your favor. There's no correlation between effort and results when it comes to RNG.
• Misplaced Sights - The Trove developers seem to focus on adding new content a lot. That's great and all, but all of this new stuff bogs down the game and its performance. It feels like the need for optimization is growing while the occurrence of optimization is shrinking.
• Moneymoneymoney - I get that these games are not easy to maintain. They are complex games that need a lot of attention. Developers are the only ones who can give Trove the attention it needs. They also need to fund themselves, be it putting food on the table, paying bills, or whatever use they have for money. Even with all that, this game seems very eager and obnoxious when promoting its goods that cost money. For example, take a look at the new Gems system. You can use a Booster to increase the chances of a Gem being upgraded (RNG). The best non-premium booster gives you a 3x level up chance. The only premium booster gives you a 40x level up chance. That is a HUGE advantage.
Is this game worth your time? I'd say it is. It is very fun. It's got strengths and it's got weaknesses.

To put it very simply, it's like Terraria in space!
To put it more psecifically, it's not really... Shares certain similarities, but...
You get a LOT more Character customisation, and you're own personal home from home spaceship that now can actually grow over time. Generally Combat is more involved than Terraria, but less simple; Starbound has a decent Blocking system worked out for example. Every planet is like an entirely new world in Terraria, only with less regular dungeons, more variety, and scaling difficulty acording to your current equipment, and your need for challenge. While you can make your base on your ship, you can also make your base on a planet, setting it as your home. It just recently (this was written Feb 2015) had an update with introduced growing ships and the 7th race and major overhauls of many systems in game.
However, this is also very WIP. Nothing is fixed in the code at the moment, and most aspects of the game could still change, for example the Racial differences are not yet as well defined as they will be. (Most notably the Racial armour buffs I think)

Summary:
Good base, but lacks challenge, cohesion, and polish.
Certainly this game "scratches an itch," but it's essentially a series of loosely assembled mini-games without enough challenge or payoff.  I was a big fan of the developer's previous game "Gunpoint," and although there are some highlights in Heat Signature, it missed the mark for me even though this is essentially my favorite type of game (rogue-like space strategy).
Story:
The galaxy is at war, and your goal is to end the war by... killing a lot of people.  But don't worry, as you slowly take over the entire galaxy, no one does anything to stop you or get back at you for murdering all those people.  Or even lock the front doors on their space ships.
The personal missions of each character were a nice touch, especially if you've lost a character, since their parent/partner/etc can train up to get them back.  But ultimately, and for no apparent reason, every station is filled with cloned wrench-wielding super-spy assassins.
The ending was interesting, and added more than I expected, but frankly it only took away from the achievement of uniting the galaxy and did not leave a good final impression.
The dialogue was good, and I particularly enjoyed the conversation with Geneva Stonelock, but in general there wasn't much use of dialogue or character development.
Gameplay:
It was fun to figure out for the first couple of hours, since the game doesn't spoon feed you the mechanics, but ultimately once I figured it out, I could beat an "audacious" mission without trouble using a brand new character.  If a character ever dies, it's no big deal, because there's no "punishment" for losing a character, and every character is destined to be "retired" anyway, and they are only unique in the items they carry.  I ended up keeping one character in reserve for the final two faction liberations, but by the second one, the deadly, teleporting, armored guards looked more like stooges trying to keep up.
You spend a lot of your time flying around meaninglessly in a small ship going between your base and target ships.  It would have been much more fun if there were any weight to this time, but the only mildly engaging element, docking, could easily be avoided with a cheap ship that auto-docks.  If there had been more docking choices, such as a second dock that was advantageous but you had to fly through ship defenses, maybe that would have been fun.  Or fuel. Or ships hunting you.  But as the game stands, you can take your time and bounce off the side of a ship 15 times and no one cares.  No one fires at you, no one sounds an alarm, nothing.
There's no sense of urgency and you can probably finish the whole game by taking easy missions, and then doing the 4 samey hijackings to finally eliminate each faction.  I didn't go that route, because the game is actually pretty easy after the first couple hours, and then it's just a grind because you have to retire your well-equipped characters and then start all over from scratch 12-18 times I'm guessing.
The time spent in battle is quite trivial once you've unlocked the hammer.  Seriously, why are the two most powerful weapons a wrench and a hammer?  You can walk up to a group of 4 guards with guns (maybe more) and hammer all of them unconscious before they can even get a shot off.  Your hammer has an 8 meter range!
You can also knock out a few guards and then pick up all of their guns.  Since the cooldown time applies to each gun, you can just fire gun 1, switch to gun 2, fire that one, and just keep switching as you mow down a grouping of bad guys as though you have an auto-aiming machine gun.
There are several types of missions, but the gameplay is almost always the same, regardless. Kill the captain first to stop the alarm, then do whatever.  In fact, I basically killed the captain first then took over the ship 90% of the time, because the enemy ship can automatically set a course for your base, but your ship can't for some reason, and it allowed me to skip the "now fly home slowly" mini-game.
I liked the "damaged pod" minigame, but since you can pause to see what quicktime events you need to perform, it was also trivial.
Lack of Polish:
There are lots of little oversights, especially in the UI.  I'm playing in 4k so some of that usually pops up, but these seemed like general issues, such as labels covering up objectives, or buttons overlapping each other (so for example pressing "back" may take you into a mission because there was another button under the back button and the game didn't shut off collisions on the hidden button).
In the mission select screen, I would choose missions based on the gear I had, and the pause button is what's used to brings up your gear, but if you pause in the mission select screen it just overlays your gear on top of the missions and you get an ugly pile of unrelated text.
You can also teleport items to yourself while you're unconscious, sometimes ships collide and sometimes they don't, etc.
Conclusion:
Certainly, there are things to enjoy here, and I'm glad people seem to like it and the dev is (hopefully) making good money.  I look forward to their next game.  I just wish Heat Signature had come out 6 months later, with better combat balance, a more polished UI, a sense of urgency (like FTL's encroaching fleet), some character variation (maybe "quirks" like in Rogue Legacy or Darkest Dungeon), a better tie in for the liberation missions (where you play with an assigned set of limited gear), and a sense that anything matters.  Killing lots of people doesn't matter, skipping missions that seem to easy or hard doesn't matter, ramming your ship into another ship generally doesn't matter, getting "spaced" doesn't matter, getting captured doesn't matter, even dying doesn't really matter.  This could have been a great game, but I can't really think of a reason to recommend it other than that other people seem to really like it.
It's my hope that the developer sees this and uses it to improve Heat Signature or a future game, although I'm clearly in the minority so maybe I'm just wrong ; p

My honest thoughts about NBA2K16 and the NBA2K franchise:
NBA2K16's gameplay is great. The overall presentation is very smooth and the graphics have really stepped up its game since 2K15. I don't think the controls are as great as it was in 2K15, but I don't really have any complaint about it. No more ripped jersey shorts when players are dunking. No more of those alien-esque eye contacts when camera pans in on the players' faces. Also a lot less shot-clock cheese.
MyCareer this year has given me the most emotional turmoil, ever. I really disliked the story, as you probably have heard everywhere how Spike Lee tried to add in his 2 cents to 2K, which resulted in the your player's family being African American regardless of what color skin your player has. I do enjoy the many accolades your player is able to achieve and how quickly you are able to level your character up to at least an all-star level. One of the things I hated about the previous NBA2K MyCareers is how little of VC earnings you get after every game, but 2K has fixed that issue in this year's release.
MyTeam is a mode I enjoy very much. Every week 2K releases packs that you are able to buy and every week it has a different series of challenges that you are able to compete. 2K has really increased the amount of variety of player cards that you are able to receive. For example, for every NBA player there are multiple player cards such as the player's default card, dynamic ratings card, moments card, playoffs card, TBT player card, all star card, MVP card, and many more. Each card by the same player has different ratings depends on the type of cards, and it really adds in some flavor in collecting your cards and makes it exciting to open up packs because it always catch you off guard on what cards you may get. My personal favorite: a bronze Sim Bhullar rated at 69, but is an absolute beast in the post both offensive and defensively in the game.
MyPark in my opinion is... ehhh. The gameplay is really great and all, but a lot of the times the park is either empty or is just a bunch of people who have formed cliques, or squads, to play against each other. If you are just trying to play a game by yourself, good luck finding a match because "you can't sit wid us".
Now, onto the franchise. Ronnie Singh aka Ronnie2K, the NBA2K public relations and the main spokesperson, is probably the biggest joke in the gaming industry. The guy has very limited NBA knowledge and is terrible at trying to attract gamers to come back for more NBA2K. I remember sometime in April when @NBA2K on twitter reached 1 million followers, Ronnie2K promised every gamer will receive a gift as a thanks to such an achievement. So what did some gamers get? A simple T-shirt for MyCareer, a knee-pad upgrade, or bronze players for MyTeam. What did I get? A 71 Rating Kendrick Perkins. Yeah, what a joke. This really agitated the NBA2K gaming community and as such, the community started a #Unfollow2K movement which trended on twitter for a couple of days. The very next day after it reached 1M followers, the follower count was at 989K followers.
I honestly don't know if I would recommend this game, or any of the NBA2K releases going forward. Unfortunately 2K is dominating in the sports games with no other competitors in near sight (Yeah I said it, EA), so I might consider buying some future releases... keyword 'MIGHT'.
Thanks for reading this review. I hope you find this review helpful on making your decisions in purchasing this release or any of the new NBA2K releases.

The timeless classic action-adventure masterpiece Ōkami returns once more and it is absolutely glorious. I cannot recommend this game enough if you love adventure games and haven't played it yet for whatever reason.
The following will be a short review since I lack the time for a more complete one and keep in mind I have already completed the game on PS3 but rest assured this new PC version definitely sits as the definitive version of the game and here's why:
Fantastic and unique style that blends exploration, puzzles, light action elements with several weapon combinations and move sets, and all of this combined with the "Celestial Brush" which allows you to pause time and paint on your screen to use your godly powers to your advantage.
Absolutely beautiful soundtrack based on traditional Japanese music which perfectly conveys the uplifting emotion of the storyline. You could go as far as to say Ōkami boasts one of the best soundtracks ever composed for a game and it actually won "Best Score Award" at the 2007 BAFTA Video Game Awards.
It initially starts quite slow but in due time you will be launched on an unforgettable adventure throughout medieval Japan as the wolf reincarnation of the Shinto Sun Goddess: Amaterasu. You will meet plenty of characters based on both Buddhist and Shinto mythology, all of them with their own personality quirks and certainly quite memorable. By the end of the story, you will have lived through numerous exciting and surprising plot twists, incredible moments and the ending will most probably leave you crying in pure joy.
Based on ancient ukiyo-e paintings, Ōkami still looks absolutely fantastic to this day thanks to a timeless art-style and excellent designs. You will be transported to a magical world full of pure eye-candy.
Works perfectly on 2 of my computers, no controller problems at all and keyboard controls are great. New settings have been added to the game including a voice volume control and the previously missing loading screen mini-games which you might want to disable since the loading times are so low anyway.

The Final Fantasy series started in 1987 with the game "Final Fantasy" for the NES. This game was revolutionary for it's time and really made an impact on the gaming industry with it's take on the JRPG formula. Fast forward 3 years to the release of "Final Fantasy III" which was the last of the NES Final Fantasy titles. This game changed the core mechanics of the class system and made a lot of changes for the better when it comes to Final Fantasy as a whole. The question is, how does it hold up today, and more importantly, does the 3D remake hold up?
Just so there's no confusion, I'm going to be talking about this version of the game which is the 3D remake.
This game is a JRPG about 4 kids who are the "Warriors of the Light". You start off the game by taking control of out main protagonist named "Luneth". You later meet up with the 3 others who have been chosen by the light. These 3 characters are "Arc", "Refia", and "Ingus". Your job is to restore balance to the world by finding the crystals of Wind, Fire, Water, and Earth.
Well, as I stated earlier this game really changed the core mechanics of the class system. In the first one you chose 4 classes from the start and then you had to roll with it for the rest of the game. In this game you don't have that. In this game you start as a Freelancer which does absolutely nothing of value. However after you find the Crystal of Wind early on in the game you start getting access to jobs. You gain more and more jobs for every crystal you gather. These jobs work like classes did in the first game except that you can switch whenever you feel like it. There is a downside to this system though which I'll come to later. When you want to switch someone's job you just press "Job" in the menu and pick what character's job you want to change and what you want to change the job to. After you select a new job there is a Job Adjustment Phase. The length of this phase is decided by the job level of the job you're switching from and what kind of job you're switching to relative to the kind of job you're switching from. Another thing that this game introduced was the special abilities that the different jobs had.
Well, here is where it gets tricky to say how I feel about the game. The game is super well paced almost all the way through and it is actually one of the better games in the franchise when it comes to the pace throughout the game. You never really have to stop to grind for EXP. The only thing I decided to grind was Gil for a few rods for my mages. This amazing pace keeps up all the way through the game, until you get to this one point in the game...
and that's really a shame since it's the last place you traverse before fighting the final boss (which is not any better btw). And the problem is that once you enter the area you can't in any way leave it. And you may think you're a little underleveled when you get there and say to yourself "No, I'm fine, I'll just use some elixirs so I'm able to use my stronger magic spells for enemies. That kind of works until you get to the final boss and get 2-shot. Oh and btw, did I mention that you can only save on the world map? This leads to you losing 1-2.5 hours of progress just because of bad game design. I had to sit and grind for 20 levels before I was able to comfortably finish the game. Another problem is when it comes to the job system. There are some jobs that are FAR superior to others and when you realize you have a bad job it's probably already leveled to the point where you feel like you should just stick with it because it would take forever to get another job to be as high leveled as the one you currently have. At some points the game also kind of wants to force you to have certain jobs. There is one place for example where you absolutely want one of the jobs or it's a real pain to get through since the enemies multiply if you don't attack with a certain kind of weapons. Except for these issues the game is actually really enjoyable!
That depends. If you're new to the franchise I would rather point you to IV, VI, or VII. If you're however a fan of the franchise and you feel like you want another fresh Final Fantasy experience I would totally recommend this one. Just be prepared for the long hours of grinding at the end and you'll be fine!
As my final words I want to say that it can be a very enjoyable game! You just need to know what you're in for.

Fun, addicting, and at times a bit repetitive.
Pros: Creative combos and engaging 'consequential' physics engine lead to creative problem solving, not always bound by author's preconceptions. For example, if you have a 'leave no witnesses' mission, and you've left behind a few guards you can't kill, you can blink up to a capture target, activate a stealth shield and toggle vision to bait the nearby guards and your capture target to a room. Then you can throw a wrench at the window to suck all of you into space, and with your remote control pod you can scoop up yourself and the capture target. This kind of creative problem solving is very fun, and is the soul and spirit of the game. The generated worlds and missions leads to emergent story telling keeps the game fresh longer, but at times can seem grindy. The flavor text on weapons and items is humerous and refreshing.
Cons: AI seems a bit wonky at times. Guards on alert won't alert nearby guards, for example. The pause and swap items mechanic is intended, but leads to an 'infinite hands' syndrome, where the player can blink in, pause, subvert one guard's shields, pause, fire his gun at a target, pause, throw his gun at a target, pause, switch to longblade, pause, dash and kill with longblade, dash and kill with shortblade, pause, throw longblade, pause, and blink away all in about 0.2 seconds of game time. At first it seems rewarding, but later seems cheesy. The character dialog is uninspiring, but unimportant, so you're not forced to read through it.
Should I buy this game? At $15, I would support buying this game.

Starbound is a game about building, platforming and exploration very well comparable with games like Minecraft and Terraria. It has a rather strange setting, a mix of sci-fi and medieval. You start on a space ship that you will soon upgrade to be capable of faster than light travel yet most of the time you will fight with axes and shields and mine with pickaxes. A laser rifle can be just as strong as a sword in this world.
The whole world is procedurally generated, it's a whole universe with so many stars and planets filled with randomly generated plants, monsters, dungeons, villages, random gravity and day/night cycles and even randomly generated equipment that you'd never have enough time to visit them all.
You don't need to visit them all because as cool as this sounds in theory, planets of the same biome and difficulty tend to feel and play very similar and the randomly generated monsters feel way to generic, too. There is no need to visit planets of the same biome and difficulty level which effectively reduces the number of planets that will be of interest for you to about circa 15.
For a game that is about exploration Starbound feels surprisingly linear. You need to upgrade your suit to survive (unlock) new biomes and mine ores till you kill a boss and advance to slightly more dangerous planets. This repeats itself until you killed the last boss after about 15 to 25 hours.
Some Planets or rather biomes are really cool and it's fun to explore them for the first time yet usually you will not appreciate what makes them unique for a long time because the most valuable things about a planet - it's ores - are under it's surface. And theres little variation between planets/biomes below the surface. It's stone, sand, dirt and ores. Every so often you encounter a dungeon, and yes they are fun to explore. The dungeons are not entirely random but hand crafted pieces that are randomly distributed in the world and it seems that a planet only has pieces of one specific set because of which they feel way less generic than the rest of the game. But only every 20th dungeon - if not even significantly less - will offer something interesting to loot.
Most of the time chests and tombs will only offer money and non valuable items like bandages (they work like the least effective health potion in other games). You will likely loose the interest in looting them very soon. Getting to the end of a very difficult, long and well designed dungeon to find absolutely nothing in it for the x.th time is only fun until you realize that you're not just ridiculously unlucky but that this is how things currently are.
So neither the dungeons nor the surface are of interest, the only things truly unique to a planet. You spent most of the time mining underground. 90% of this game you will hold your mouse button pointing at stone and dirt. This is as much fun as it's sounds, that is not at all.
Now I know that fans of starbound will be intrigued to say "But you do the same in terraria, that's just part of this genre" but thats not entirely true. Yes Terraria and similar games require you to spend a lot of time mining too, but not 90% of the time. There are armor sets in Terraria that require you to kill bosses 2-3 three times, there were armor sets you could built from plants that you collected on the surface, there were armor sets that you crafted via drops from various monsters and many armor sets required you a mix of those which lead to very varied gameplay.
Mining was also generally more difficult in Terraria, it became harder but more rewarding the further you digged down. In Starbound the whole planet has one fixed difficulty level and you can easily mine for half an hour without getting attacked once. The surface of a planet, which rarely offers something valuable, is often times harder to survive than the core of the planet which offers valuable ores.
And you didn't had to craft every tier of armor in Terraria, you could easily jump two tiers or more if you were a good player. Similar you can do just fine in Minecraft with lower tiers of armor like the leather or iron armor. Starbounds progression system doesn't allow that, The devs force you to do things exactly in order. Equipment is more important than skills and experience. I do not believe that this is due to early access but a design philosophy of chuckle fish that they seem to be very unwilling to get rid of despite how often it is criticized by players.
Combat got significantly improved with the last patch, one aspect I still don't like is frequent use of health restoring items. They have almost no cooldown so you can easily pop 20 health restoring items in a boss fight. In other games they have a cooldown of a few minutes and are meant to be an aid. In Starbound you can just furnish 100 bandages in a main mission/boss fight and almost tank some bosses. Some can't be beaten without the usage of at least 20 of them. It seems that the devs intended the heavy usage of health restoring items.
I guess it's their way to "fix" a questionable design philosophy. Since progression is so linear you can't grind and farm better equipment to be better suited for a boss. You can only face a boss once you have the best currently available equipment (the game will literally not let you otherwise). In Terraria bad players could grind better equipment while good players could save time and face the boss with their current equipment. In Starbound a bad player will pop more bandages, a good player less.
But I still really enjoyed the main mission which require you to go through a dungeon and often times kill a boss in the end. They are fantastically designed and I enjoy them more than building arenas and spawning bosses in Terraria. They have a great, sinister atmosphere and are filled with many interesting traps. They are not properly balanced yet, the first mission was more difficult by far than every following mission afterwards and even harder than some highend bosses in Terraria, but that is something I can overlook in a game that is still in development.
If you like building beautiful castles, futuristic bases etc. that have no purpose other than looking good and enjoy it more than balanced and intriguing gameplay and don't mind grinding for it I highly recommend starbound. It offers much more furniture and block types/colors than any other building game I know of. But if you care more about balanced and variated gameplay than creating non-functional 2D pixel art I highly suggest to keep following the development of Starbound and wait for the next big updates before you buy it.

- you get a sense for a drama behind the scenes and the voice actors charactise well. There has been effort shown in the script and it is a little refreshing how much Lee gives reverence to the female characters in an otherwise apolitical basketball sim. That said - it isn't that great - all the drama falls away after the rookie season. High-school, college and rookie seasons are more like tutorials - which can either be seen as a plus or a minus depending on how new the player is and how much patience they have. Like many of Lee's movies, it's a half-success.
Some graphical and more frustatingly, animation bugs, are present. The player's shorts in cut-scenes tend to break-in-half and half-time shots of my player's legs clipping into his seat when it finishes with him on the bench are minor flaws. The animation can bug-out where you bounce around like a pin-ball meaning you can't contest that all-important shot - this tends to happen most on defence but it becomes increasingly rare once you learn proper defensive positioning. Letting the coach auto-call plays makes play move much faster and stay more varied. Couple this with a better camera view and defence becomes less of a headache. The players have weight to them and the bouncing around feels like a game-design choice to show this.
One things I noticed was that if I silenced commentary - this would silence the coach at half-time, the half-time interview and the end of game wrap-up but I'd still have them presented. The game lets you skip them but you will need to answer the halftime question, silently, if asked. The sound design of the game is really good otherwise (save for a few lame songs on the soundtrack)

Bastion is a wonderfully superb game.
The game play is solid and gets the job done. It's what you'd see in games like Boktai and Ys, You have  about 5 buttons in game, and for the most part everything works smoothly during combat, dodging, blocking and attacking all transition well and  the gameplay flows very smoothly.  The weapon variety is nice and lets you mix and match between 12 weapons, which you can upgrade, and 29 skills, which adds a nice variety  in game play and combat.  There's also some gauntlets and weapon challenges that add some more depth to the game's admittedly short main storyline.
The main draw of  Bastion is the atmosphere and storytelling. The story telling is paced very, very well with a narration that syncs with the game-play almost perfectly.  The story itself is very well done, and the beautiful soundtrack is the icing on the cake.
Bastion is my favorite PC game, and one of my favorite games ever, and I cannot  recommend this game enough.

The original story about the worlds best Hitman, is a difficult one, but worth it.
Outdated graphics, controls and gameplay are all bearable, but the reward is hours of fun. And frustration at the Scarface reference. The game gives you many options to complete your objective, some of which are not as obvious or easy to execute as others, so you start experimenting while carefully weighing risk versus gain, since there is no save function.
If you die, you restart the level.
To the end, missions get more complex and way more difficult, so difficult, that at one point I had to abuse the AI and wait with a drawn gun behind a door, waiting for the enemies to parse through it one by one.
Compared to newer games (Hitman: Absolution for example), this game is worse looking, has clunkier controls, but gameplay that is a thousand times better than Absolution.
That said though, if you want the best Hitman experience, get Hitman: Blood Money. You can skip Hitman: Silent Assassin and you should most definitely skip Hitman: Absolution.

Final Fantasy III was originally released in the year 1990 and was the last Final Fantasy title to be released on the Nintendo Entertainment System. It was among the three canon Final Fantasy titles to previously not get a domestic release in America. Not until 16 years later when a remake was made for the Nintendo DS. And this is what this game is, a PC port of the Nintendo DS remake. While it would of been cool to play the original version of the game, it unfornately was never given a release outside of Japan. So for the time being, this is the only version of Final Fantasy III, we may be able to play unless you buy the game directly from Japan, played the unofficial English port, or someone strikes a deal with Square-Enix. Like how Final Fantasy II was finally released domestically as part of the Final Fantasy Origins game for Playstation and the previously unreleased Final Fantasy V got a domestic release as well. With the conclusion of that history lecture, let me review Final Fantasy III. The game takes place on a floating continent that is seperated from the world below due to a flood that occured a millineum ago. Four young orphans named Luneth, Arc, Refia, & Ingus learn from a magical crystal that laid dormint in a newly opened cave that they are the Warriors of Lights are prophecied in legend. The four orphans are the floating continent and the old world's only hope in restoring balance of peace from the newly ressurected dark forces that threaten to consume the rest of the world and the population with enternal darkness. This was a fun game and offered the same appeal as found in Final Fantasys I & II. This was the first game in the series to have the main protagnogists as kids, as the original game the age for the protagnogists was ambigous while the cast of the second game are young adult. This was the first in the series to offer the "job" option where the four orphans can be assigned to a different role like a mage, monk, knight, summoner, etc. Each job gives a character different abilities or different items to use. Longer you fight against monsters with each assigned job, the more experienced the character is with that job title. This task is a nessecity in order to progress in the game. While the leveling system was reverted back to a simple experience point gain system as oppose to the more complex level system in Final Fantasy II, so leveling up your characters is easier this time around. The moogles and fat chobos make their debut in this game, as well as the first time the main characters can summon creatures, deities, and mosnters during the battle sequences. Any one who is a die hard Final Fantasy or RPG fan will enjoy what this game has to offer. It may not be the 1990 Final Fantasy III, but it is a great alternative to play and is currently the oldest numeric Final Fantasy title to play from Steam.

This game is really, really boring.  I remember thinking it was great when I was a little kid and I played it on Nintendo DS.  The combat is ridiculously simple and monotonous, though.  The many different interchangeable character classes do little to spice this up, because once you choose a characters class and enter combat, they have very few combat options to choose from.  As far as gameplay goes, there are several classes that are practically identical, so unlocking new classes is really little more than just unlocking new outfits.
One thing I do like about this game that I wish was in more fantsy RPGs is the presence of magic that player can (and sometimes must) use outside of combat to traverse different obstacles in the game world (and to heal).  I like for RPGs to offer gameplay beyond just combat.
All of the gameplay in this game is pretty shallow, though, both in and out of combat.  And there is *a lot* of combat, with the same few enemies, over and over again, and it gets old fast.
It is kind of a pretty-looking game, considering it's so low-poly... some scenes moreso than others.  That's one of the best things I can say about it.

Ok so first a little background.
Played Assassin's Creed since the first one and played all of the 'main' games but Roque at this point (so 1, all of 2, 3 and 4). And so far my favorite is still 2 (first one of the Ezio saga).
At this point I have finished Sequence 4 and I am doing a ton of side stuff since I will forget them otherwise :p
Now to this game. Mind that all of the following is my personal opinion.
The good.
- Feels like an Assassin's Creed game.
- Combat changed, meaning I have to relearn and readjust a bit.
- Changes to free running (free run normal, free run and attempt to rise, free run and attempt to descend).
- Co-op missions (been waiting for this for years).
- Murder solving and other side missions and events.
- 'forces' more stealthy behaviour.
The bad.
- Why am I suddenly on my desktop?
- My first co-op was laggy. Mission succeded but I ended up re-doing it solo after just to experience the actual mission.
- Lockpicking is boring.
- How did those guards NOT hear that gunshot? But wait, others did hear people screaming?
I can probably continue filling both lists for a whle if I really put my mind to it.
But the value to each point is more important. The negatives are annoying, but not game breaking and the positives are just that, positives. So far this game will be worth the money I spend on it, but only just. There is this feeling like something is missing or something isn't right. I cannot explain it really well since I do not know what I am looking for.
But there are also these mixed feeling moments. Groups tend to use their guns a lot more and you cannot evade them like in 3 and 4. It is annoying when you (accindetally) start a big fight. But on the other hand it means I have to approach things differently which is something I like.
So I will end this before it turns into me rambling on and on.

The Game concept is great, it's an extremely great idea, however after selecting your starter class, you shall find the controls incredibly unresponsive, to an extent where it is unplayable, they are so bugged, it's not even a joke, they expect You to tolerate insanely unsympathetic towards a pleasant user experience, the Dev haven't yet released any patch upon the matter so far, if this continues, the Game receive various complaints.

Finally a permadeath game with a satisfying sense of progression, as the stations you liberate provide lasting (albeit minor) bonuses for future characters.  Gameplay is tight and fun, whether going for a stealthy approach or a shoot 'em up style.  Dying is usually avoidable if you play smart, though plenty of edge-of-your-seat moments.  Example: I was playing a capture mission where I needed to grab an enemy character alive.  I made it all the way to my target and was just dispatching his two gaurds, when one of my shots hit the ship's generator, leaving me with about two seconds until the room detonated, creating a hole in the hull, killing myself and my target (who must be captured alive) in the process.
I paused, activated my "speed up" ability to slow time, jammed my target's shield, and threw my wrench at the target to knock him unconcious, then sprinted over and scopped up his limp body and dragged it just clear of the blast, just as it detonated.  The ensuing explosion sucked both of us out into space.  In the few seconds before we both passed out from lack of O2, I switched over to remote pilot my ship, blasted over, and managed to retrieve both of our precious bodies from the vacuum.
Moments like are thrilling, and not uncommon in this title.  It's not without its flaws, and the missions do get repetitive after a time, but I've loved my time playing Heat Signature and I definately recommend trying it for yourself.

While not necessarily a long game from start to "completion" (I've unlocked all but 2 achievements with 9.3 hours of play, and those last 2 are due to not having Steam friends who have purchased the game currently), I fully expect Heat Signature to be a game that I keep saved and pick up to play on occassion many times in the future, much like Binding of Isaac has been previously.
Heat Signature is a fairly simple game in structure (you use an escape pod-esque ship to invade larger ships and complete objectives, such as stealing items, rescuing hostages, or knocking out the entire crew and hijacking the ship itself), with many of the objectives being achievable in numerous ways. There are a handful of gadgets that can help you in doing this (such as stealth shields, grenades, and teleporters), and thanks to the game's ability to let you pause at any time (and use that time to switch gear, decide where to teleport, or who to throw your wrench at first), the ways in which you can handle each situation are expanded both by your experience and cleverness. For even more examples and practice at attempting these sort of challenges, each station you liberate opens up a preset mission, limiting you to specific gear or circumstances (Have you ever tried to catch up to a ship using shotgun blasts to propel you towards it? You can now!)
There are certainly ways in which I believe Heat Signature could be improved. As mentioned before, within 9 hours, I've completed most objectives (there are still challenge missions and nodes to be unlocked, but a lack of desire to do so). Once you've become used to the game, many of even the hardest missions become trivial (depending on what gear you choose to bring along). And even the largest of ships take little more than a couple minutes to complete.
Regardless of this, though, I still am very much a fan of this game and see it as one that I will continue to pick up and play every few weeks or months. I can hope to see more from it coming in the future, but even if there is not, I feel it's been worth it.

A wonderful little gem of a game that somehow takes the gameplay of its spiritual precursor, Gunpoint, and adds tons of depth and mechanics while also successfully transitioning it to an isometric, procedurally-generated title.
HeatSig is a game about bite-sized space heists.  You pick from one of four characters who happen to be sitting at a bar in space, and take them from humble beginnings with a wrench and one other unique item to being one of the most well-equipped thieves/assassins/hijackers in the galaxy.  The game serves you up a large array of missions of varying difficulties, some with special optional objectives that increase your pay, so there's almost always something for players of every stripe, be they stealthy or aggressive.
There are some small problems, though.  While liberating stations via the galaxy map adds an element of persistence to the game, it really only affects what you can buy from shops.  You have a stash you can send spare items to, but once your character dies, so does the stash.  This is further complicated by the fact that your character can only sustain so many injuries before your survival time drops to zero, and there is no way to heal yourself between missions.  One minor mistake takes 6 seconds off your character's initial 30-second survival clock, until you hit 0 seconds and the next hit kills you.
This implementation of permadeath is quite frustrating.  The game doesn't throw so much top-tier loot at you that it would be unbalanced to be able to stash some items for your next character - in fact, it would add a sense of choice between taking your best gear with you and risking its loss, or keeping it safe for someone else in case the next heist is your last.  The other option would be adding the ability to recover your survival clock for a hefty fee.  You couldn't do it every time you got hit, and you'd have to choose between health and buying new gear, but it would ease the sting of permadeath.  Having to start a new character and farm Easy and Medium missions (there is a notable gap between Medium and Hard) just to get some decent equipment is just busy work.
Perhaps most counter-intuitive of all is that the game drastically slows your progression towards your next liberation if you play one character too much.  It seems to think that people are more interested in playing as part of a cast of geared-up characters rather than just one - but this option would only really be attractive if you could somehow swap items between characters. I'd happily build one guy for stealth, one for offense, etc., but I'm not allowed, so I might as well just hoard all my stuff on one mercenary - or at least I would, if doing so didn't literally decrease my progression speed by a massive 95% with no way to remedy this.
HeatSig is best when you're rolling with a fully-geared character, using a mix of teleportation, stealth, and melee weapons to carve up your enemies.  There's a handy pause feature as well that allows you to stop time whenever you like to consider your next move, or group of moves.  There's nothing like planning a sequence in your head in the pause screen and then carrying it out exactly as you like it - and I don't think I'll ever get tired of sucking myself into space by shooting out a window as soon as I've completed my mission.
There's also the option to complete a personal mission for each of your procedurally-generated characters.  A nice touch, and definitely something to look forward to as you progress.
Liberating space stations also unlocks Defector missions, which are played with a character other than your own who always starts with the same weapon set.  It's a little slice of Hotline Miami tucked into HeatSig, though the layout of the ship you're invading changes every time you restart, so you can somewhat cheese the Defector missions into giving you a favorable spread, though the number of enemies and their gear remains mostly the same.  Still, it's a good, consequence-free way to take a break, and more effective practice than the built-in practice mode.
All told, there's a huge diversity of gameplay stuffed into what is actually a very tight, refined gameplay loop.  It's a game you can play for ten minutes or several hours at a time and have fun for the entirety of your time.  There's no penalty for simply failing missions either, so you're really encouraged to experiment and see what tactics work for you.  With a few changes to make the galaxy seem more alive and add some more persistent progress, this could be my game of 2017.

Seriously, I can't understand all those overwhelmingly positive reviews.
Everywhere I turn, people are saying HL1 is a must-play, a game than was a revolution for FPS at its time, but I just don't get it!
Actually, I get it. HL1 indeed is ahead of its time: the storytelling is immersive, the atmosphere is pretty good for a game that old, the whole world is nicely put together, the plot is very good.
Now, does it mean you should buy this game? Not at all.
You can try it if you really want to see the legend for yourself, but for modern standards, it's actually pretty bad.
Here's a (non-exhaustive) list of things that annoyed me:
-you're not walking through the game, you're skiing: Freeman moves likes he's got ice-skates one. The controls are awful.
- the crosshairs actually track the enemies, meaning you can't properly aim with your weapons. And of course you end up missing a shot every three.
-the sounds are pretty bad from a modern point of view, but I can't decently complain since it was released 18 years ago.
-the level design isn't that great: you often end up wondering what to do, because your objectives aren't clear
-the combat system is horrendous , both shooting - in part because of the crosshair system- and melee: even the smaller crabs will often claim 10 or 20 hp as you wildly swing your crowbar in a desperate attempt to kill them.
In conclusion, I don't want to b*tch about this game, but it's time someone reminded all those fanboys that this is NOT Half Life 2.

It's an okay product for $10. It's cool if you want to experience something different other than Train Simulator. Yeah some of the scenery is inaccurate and there's bugs galore, but what do you expect for a $10 game? The only severe issues I've encountered so far is that there is no tutorial mode for new players, none of the important buttons and levers (throttle, brake, etc) are mapped meaning first time users will have to manually map the buttons themselves, and the biggest problem is that the game crashes whenever you attempt to change the graphics settings. I don't mean crashing in game because you jacked the graphics to max settings, I mean you change the settings in the menu, hit "OK" to save it, the game crashes, and none of your changes are saved, meaning the game is perpetually stuck at the default graphics settings. I'll keep this game and play it as is because it was cheap and it's the only real simulation of the PATH line out there. However if the game cost any more than the current price, I'd be pretty unsatisfied. If you have experience with train sims and want a little something different, go ahead and get it. But if you're looking for something serious, pass this game up and get Train Simulator.

Ports are a tricky issue, no doubt about it, but I'm happy to say: Capcom did a pretty good job here! This is a great way to re-experience the game, and for those of you who have never played it due to not having a dedicated port, I recommend this one. If you're a big fan of Action-Adventure games, especially things like Zelda, then you will like this.
30FPS and lack of 16:10 or 21:9 support may be a turn off for some. Really, the game controls and looks fine at 30FPS. I had no problems adjusting to it, but if you run different resolution monitors I can understand the pass. Performance-wise, 30FPS was consistent through the whole experience, even during periods of heavy combat. The higher resolutions do the art style some serious justice. Nipon has never looked better.
Depending on how much you like side-questing, collecting and exploring, the game can take you anywhere from 20 to 45 hours to complete: on a first playthrough, no less! The game's use of drawing as a mechanic and the combat system go hand-in-hand flawlessly and mastering both keeps the game fresh throughout. You're not gonna get much better value for 20 dollars!

Apparently this game has a 30 fps cap, but that's not a problem. It's still Okami, one of the most beautiful and fascinating games ever made -- but for the "PC Master Race" instead of consoles.

... or you can emulate it in hardware mode instead of software mode and instead have broken mipmaps.

Your choice, really. This is the definitive version of Okami for sure, and it's a good enough game that it's definitely worth your 20$.

Before playing, open the configuration tool from the popup after you click the Play button.
Choose OpenGL as renderer and click OK.
Open Hitman.ini in the game's installation folder.
Add these lines:
Resolution 1920x1080
Window
StartUpperPos 0,0
Change 1920x1080 to your monitor's native resolution, ex: 1366x768, 1280x720, etc.
Save the file.
Don't bother with the built-in antialiasing option, it doesn't work (at least in my case).
Force AA through your graphics card's control panel.
Start the game.
You may need to change the controls a bit to make it less clunky.
Mine is configured like this:
Walk - W
Run - Shift
Walk left - A
Walk right - D
Walk backward - S
Turn left - Z
Turn right - C
Lean left - Q
Lean right - E
Perform action - Space
Toggle sneak - 4
