TL;DR:
Tower Unite, the spiritual successor to Garry's Mod gamemode GMod Tower, is a fun and entertaining multiplayer game which focuses on social interaction and various gamemodes.  While it is in an early stage of development, it is being regularly updated by the devs, who are visibly working hard to create an excellent product by the end of its early access phase.  I'd definitely recommend the title, as there's plenty of content to enjoy and even more content still to come.
Full Review:
Tower Unite is the spiritual successor to popular Garry's Mod gamemode GMod Tower, which unfortunately closed its doors on April 8, 2016.  The game was created as its own standalone product in order to break free from the limitations of the Source engine, which were very clearly hindering the developers.  Even though Tower is far from complete in its current state, it's clear that the devs are determined to create a fun and entertaining finished product able to be enjoyed by all, with the game being updated frequently.  I won't go too in-depth, but I'll give a quick overview.
Tower Unite is a virtual world game focused on social interaction.  The game's overworld features several shops, a theater, a nightclub, a casino, gamemode ports, a boardwalk, and of course the overlooming condo building.  Players are able to communicate through text/voice chat and customize their own personal condo.  Items for condo customization such as furniture and cosmetic items such as hats can be purchased via the shops by using currency acquired through playing various multiplayer games (accessed through the gamemode ports).  Each game is unique and features multiple maps to play on to keep things fresh.  Currency can also be acquired through gambling games in the casino such as poker and slots.
I've only just scratched the surface here, as there is an impressive amount of content to explore in the world of Tower Unite (keeping in mind its current state in development) and more is undoubtedly on its way, but this should provide a pretty good idea of what to expect while the game is in early access.  If this sounds like your type of thing, I'd definitely recommend the title, though unless you want to support the developers, I may suggest holding off on purchasing for a little while, at least until a bit more content has been added.  Even so, Tower is a game that can be enjoyed for hours on end, so grab a few drinks, grab a few friends, and get ready to say "good-bye" to your spare time.

I have really mixed feelings about this game. At first I thought about not recommending this game, but some elements such as co-op makes it worth while.
Lets just do the pros vs. cons:
Pros:
- Co-op. The first AC title with co-op and it's really fun. Co-op missions are implemented, and matchmaking is easy enough.
- Freerunning Up/Down. This feature allows the player to decide whether he wants to scale a building up or down, which works nicely once you get used to it. Less confusion on where you want to jump, which have been a trouble in previous AC titles.
- Difficulty. This game has an increased difficulty compared to previous titles, and difficulty is bound to districts. Also, the enemies don't attack one at a time, and can also shoot at you while other engage you. Snipers are also a nice addition, as they are very powerful, but more easily killed in close combat (and are most often located on roof-tops).
- Crowds. Paris is filled with people and the city feels alive and more realistically crowded.
Cons:
- Uplay.
- Story is rather dull, with uninteresting characters. Missions are rather monotomous.
- The game revolves around Paris (which is okay), but it's ONLY Paris, nothing else, just a huge city, little variation to enviroment.
- The game starts to lag at times, uncertain to why, may be only my problem.
- Uplay, did I say that?
- While the freerunning is good most of the times, some climbing issues occur, and obvious jumps to the right and left are not always permitted. And though the controls say "wall eject" or "climb jump", they do not always do so.
- No crafting, sailing, hunting or anything that made previous games fun.
- I don't really like Arno. He's very plain, and doesn't have anything remarkable with him.
Summarization:
Allthough I've listed plenty more cons than pros, the game is okay enough, but without co-op not really worth it. So if you have a bad internet connection, buy another game. Otherwise I would recommend it on a sale. Not really worth the full price, or the pre-order price I was stupid enough to get it for.

While not necessarily a long game from start to "completion" (I've unlocked all but 2 achievements with 9.3 hours of play, and those last 2 are due to not having Steam friends who have purchased the game currently), I fully expect Heat Signature to be a game that I keep saved and pick up to play on occassion many times in the future, much like Binding of Isaac has been previously.
Heat Signature is a fairly simple game in structure (you use an escape pod-esque ship to invade larger ships and complete objectives, such as stealing items, rescuing hostages, or knocking out the entire crew and hijacking the ship itself), with many of the objectives being achievable in numerous ways. There are a handful of gadgets that can help you in doing this (such as stealth shields, grenades, and teleporters), and thanks to the game's ability to let you pause at any time (and use that time to switch gear, decide where to teleport, or who to throw your wrench at first), the ways in which you can handle each situation are expanded both by your experience and cleverness. For even more examples and practice at attempting these sort of challenges, each station you liberate opens up a preset mission, limiting you to specific gear or circumstances (Have you ever tried to catch up to a ship using shotgun blasts to propel you towards it? You can now!)
There are certainly ways in which I believe Heat Signature could be improved. As mentioned before, within 9 hours, I've completed most objectives (there are still challenge missions and nodes to be unlocked, but a lack of desire to do so). Once you've become used to the game, many of even the hardest missions become trivial (depending on what gear you choose to bring along). And even the largest of ships take little more than a couple minutes to complete.
Regardless of this, though, I still am very much a fan of this game and see it as one that I will continue to pick up and play every few weeks or months. I can hope to see more from it coming in the future, but even if there is not, I feel it's been worth it.

A wonderful little gem of a game that somehow takes the gameplay of its spiritual precursor, Gunpoint, and adds tons of depth and mechanics while also successfully transitioning it to an isometric, procedurally-generated title.
HeatSig is a game about bite-sized space heists.  You pick from one of four characters who happen to be sitting at a bar in space, and take them from humble beginnings with a wrench and one other unique item to being one of the most well-equipped thieves/assassins/hijackers in the galaxy.  The game serves you up a large array of missions of varying difficulties, some with special optional objectives that increase your pay, so there's almost always something for players of every stripe, be they stealthy or aggressive.
There are some small problems, though.  While liberating stations via the galaxy map adds an element of persistence to the game, it really only affects what you can buy from shops.  You have a stash you can send spare items to, but once your character dies, so does the stash.  This is further complicated by the fact that your character can only sustain so many injuries before your survival time drops to zero, and there is no way to heal yourself between missions.  One minor mistake takes 6 seconds off your character's initial 30-second survival clock, until you hit 0 seconds and the next hit kills you.
This implementation of permadeath is quite frustrating.  The game doesn't throw so much top-tier loot at you that it would be unbalanced to be able to stash some items for your next character - in fact, it would add a sense of choice between taking your best gear with you and risking its loss, or keeping it safe for someone else in case the next heist is your last.  The other option would be adding the ability to recover your survival clock for a hefty fee.  You couldn't do it every time you got hit, and you'd have to choose between health and buying new gear, but it would ease the sting of permadeath.  Having to start a new character and farm Easy and Medium missions (there is a notable gap between Medium and Hard) just to get some decent equipment is just busy work.
Perhaps most counter-intuitive of all is that the game drastically slows your progression towards your next liberation if you play one character too much.  It seems to think that people are more interested in playing as part of a cast of geared-up characters rather than just one - but this option would only really be attractive if you could somehow swap items between characters. I'd happily build one guy for stealth, one for offense, etc., but I'm not allowed, so I might as well just hoard all my stuff on one mercenary - or at least I would, if doing so didn't literally decrease my progression speed by a massive 95% with no way to remedy this.
HeatSig is best when you're rolling with a fully-geared character, using a mix of teleportation, stealth, and melee weapons to carve up your enemies.  There's a handy pause feature as well that allows you to stop time whenever you like to consider your next move, or group of moves.  There's nothing like planning a sequence in your head in the pause screen and then carrying it out exactly as you like it - and I don't think I'll ever get tired of sucking myself into space by shooting out a window as soon as I've completed my mission.
There's also the option to complete a personal mission for each of your procedurally-generated characters.  A nice touch, and definitely something to look forward to as you progress.
Liberating space stations also unlocks Defector missions, which are played with a character other than your own who always starts with the same weapon set.  It's a little slice of Hotline Miami tucked into HeatSig, though the layout of the ship you're invading changes every time you restart, so you can somewhat cheese the Defector missions into giving you a favorable spread, though the number of enemies and their gear remains mostly the same.  Still, it's a good, consequence-free way to take a break, and more effective practice than the built-in practice mode.
All told, there's a huge diversity of gameplay stuffed into what is actually a very tight, refined gameplay loop.  It's a game you can play for ten minutes or several hours at a time and have fun for the entirety of your time.  There's no penalty for simply failing missions either, so you're really encouraged to experiment and see what tactics work for you.  With a few changes to make the galaxy seem more alive and add some more persistent progress, this could be my game of 2017.

So, I read some of those incredible tall tales of heroics (or infamous stories of remarkable heists?)  in this review section and thought: Okay, sounds interesting, but what is a Slipstream? And what is this game all about?
I've read some comparisons - FTL meets Hotline Miami, for instance, which admittedly feels wrong to me, but honestly, I liked both games and I love this one, so if you, too, like both the more tactical/strategic FTL and the more rythmic, frantic Hotline Miami, maybe you'll be happy with this, too. To me, it's more like Ronin or Gunpoint meets The Masterplan with FTLs aesthetics (and a suitable space scenario).
It's essentially a top-down shooter made for Mouse and Keyboard, with puzzle elements, random loot and heavy roguelite elements. I won't spoil the start of the story, but at some point you'll be playing as one of a number of more-or-less randomly generated characters, trying to fulfill missions to sow chaos and liberate space stations while also trying to earn money to get intel on a (also generated, character-related) personal story mission.
You do that by flying around in a pod (having a mission is optional, but makes sense) and dock that pod to the ship containing your mission objective (or other, random ships that appear around you) and then walking through the rooms of the ship, using melee weapons and guns to stun or kill members of the crew, hack or break sentry guns, unlock doors with keycards and applying a wide range of interesting gadgets, such as projectile-reflecting or stealth shields, time-manipulating devices and various kinds of teleporters to get to your objective.
You can always Pause the game and do a few things from there, such as change your equipment, check ranges and strategize, and even if unpaused the game will significantly slow down for critical moments (such as being spotted or while taking aim). Also, anything lying around (in opened crates or from downed enemies) can be instantly teleported to you for direct use. Convenient!
The controls are simple, intuitive and the pacing and feel is really great, enabling the kind of crazy antics that you read about in most reviews (and while not necessarily "easy" to pull off, they get astonishingly doable with some practice). While the game is very simple upfront, it is built relatively complex and allows for a lot of the things you'd expect (and some you probably don't!): Turning opponents shields on themselves, turning sentry guns, using airlocks or breakable windows to have people sucked into space - it's even possible to board another ship and control that and start shooting at the ship your mission target is in! And if you find yourself sucked into space - you can remote control your pod and catch yourself (and your target, if need be).
Equipment can be found on opponents and in cargo containers, as well as bought at a shop (which will gain additional stock as you liberate stations). You can only carry a set amount of equipment pieces (but you have a character-based, unlimited stash), but aren't restricted by type (so you could go all guns, or no weapons, or anything like that...). Equipment can come in various forms: Melee weapons are unlimited, normal guns use common ammo (which is tracked separately) and most other stuff has charges, either one-time charges (once spent, they're spent, and if the item reaches zero, it's gone for good), rechargeable (limited charges per mission, but refills automatically when you land on your station) or even auto-recharging (recharges during the mission). Items also have attributes such as concussive (non-lethal, required to capture people, if need be), armor-piercing, silent or some such, and modifiers such as long-range or high-capacity for some of the gadgets.
All of that, and money, is character-bound, meaning: Character dies, everything is gone - money, equipped stuff, anything in the stash. Only liberated stations remain. If you don't want to continue a character right now, you can switch between characters (but they will only have access to their own stash and inventory). You can switch back later.
Once your character has completed their personal mission and/or liberated some stations, they become too famous and less apt at liberating stations. You can then retire those characters, permanently removing them from your roster of playable characters. They get a nice plaque with their name and detailling everything this living legend accomplished (stations liberated, personal story fulfilled) and you get to pick one of their items, and a name for it, and that item (with that name, and a reference to your player name in the item text) can from there on out be found by any of your or your steam friends characters. A nice legacy.
In the end, it's a game about planning, and failing plans, and improvisation, and using all the tools at your disposal. It can be stressful, but incredibly awesome as well. It's a game of daring, audacious acts and epic wins, a game where I found myself gleefully hacking a sentry gun to kill some enemy guards, but one of them surviving and sounding the alarm (which starts a timer), then using a slipstream (time-manipulating device) and a sidewinder (teleporter that needs a clear route, however convoluted it may be) to get to the ships captain to knock him out (cancelling the alarm timer) - but alerting too many guards in the process, so now I was stuck in some corner of the ship, with some weapons and a visitor (a teleporter that can teleport through walls, but teleports you back after two seconds). So I did what any reasonable person would do: Used the visitor to teleport into a room with a window, fire one shot against a wall. Get returned to the original location, while guards swarm the room to investigate the noise. Use another charge of the visitor to teleport to just outside the room, in the hallway - I think one or two of the guards still saw me as I took aim to blow the window out. Boom. Half a dozen guards sucked into space. The mission suddenly got a whole lot easier.

I hoped this game would be a spiritual successor to Uplink maybe with a little bit more realism. Unfortunately the game falls short of that aspiration.
First of all, it's not any more realistic than Uplink. While you get to use real Unix commands, you don't use them in a very similar way to the real thing. Have no illusion, this game will not teach you anything useful in real life. There's nothing wrong with making your hacking sim game a little over the top with fancy animations and misused tech lingo, but it's not what I expected.
Where the game really fails to live up to Uplink, however, is depth. Remember how Uplink had news bulletins reporting on your mischief, other active hackers taking assignments and getting arrested when you rat on them, multiple banks with multiple accounts wiring funds to each other, and a stock market where you could watch your victim corporations suffer losses after you hack and destroy their mainframes? You will find nothing like this in Hacknet. All you get it a lot of random IRC logs pasted from
and some personal files and emails that are not written in a breathtaking way.
Is it fun? Yeah, especially if it's your first game of this kind. There's a thrill in accessing systems and files you shouldn't be looking at and there's even an overarching plot that's encouraging you to keep playing, but it all lacks depth, gameplay-wise, story-wise and writing-wise.
It's addicting.

This is me giving an honest "what I feel" review, I have had this game for a quite a while, I have put a lot of time into it as it is one of my favorite games I own. Coming primarily from EVE Online the game "slowness" doesn't bother me, I feel that is a small obstacle seeing how Edgecase designed the game to feel "big" that way but it still has an intense combat style that relies heavily on individual skill to know how to fly the ship provided and how to work with your team.
My main issue with the game however is probably core mechanics that Edge seems extremely reluctant to touch to any degree, almost refusing to see an issue with them, such issues as follows:
1. Healing factors for instance and how those factors play out in combat, the game is way to dependant on it. Ships for example who are given "immortality" in more than a few cases just because they have a healer sitting far away healing them, even if the said ship being healed has two capable assault oriented ships on them. It makes you feel completely helpless because you are left either waiting for the healers ability to heal to go on a cooldown or you go after the healer who just evades you and draws your DPS off the main target which then kills the other ship shooting it. This isn't a rare occurence, especially in bracket 4 matches where people generally know how to fly their ships and they quickly discover all the strengths of their ships varying from the abilities to the ships maneuverability. These things coupled with current crew setups with implants makes certain ships easily perform as something they were probably never intended to be.
2. Smart-guns are still somewhat of an issue, not with overall general attack power, but with their ability to be overly consistent while requiring minimal skill to use them especially when kiting people or curving your shots around corners. Aegis Smart-guns do way to much damage for a Smart-gun period, heavy or not, and its ability to spam shields with low cooldowns makes combating one extremely tedious.
3. Point Defense is garbage as it can be overwhelmed easily with drones/fighters/bombers, whatever you want to do it with. Making certain ships perform tremendously well as the PD has not just a hard time of shooting down drones consistently but also shooting down incoming missiles, ship bugs aside. Either missile health is way to high or PD attack power is too low, which also makes you question sometimes whether it is even worth it to turn it on in some instances when you can just save your energy for something else more useful, if you have it.
4. I would really like to see Edge go back and touch some of the ships they have applies massive nerfs to in the somewhat recent past, Enforcer and Brawler being two of them. Enforcer and Brawler are not COMPLETELY useless but they are definitely ships that depend on their teammates ability to stave off others so they can actually work. Enforcer has very high shot count which makes losing your overall damage to easy to do as missing 3 or 4 shots in your volley can drastically alter your damage in the end, making its consistency a problem, especially considering its optimal range. It needs to be able to apply its overall damage better with better consistency especially if it's going to be as squishy as it is. Brawler is alright if you have someone helping you, the pull speed is abysmal and can be evaded by some ships, they either run away from you or they pin themselves to a rock to avoid getting closer to you, the harpoon speed is too slow, especially considering its optimal range, it is easily avoided. The weapon's max "effective" or optimal range is 2,000m... 2,000 meters? The falloff is outlandish and it can be easily avoided. Plus the ship maneuvers like a borderline heavy ship, other medium ships minus MAYBE the Venturer can easily evade it
I am getting tired of typing this review so I will stop, I will still play the game as I do enjoy it, HOWEVER seeings these issues appear in matches does make me desire to play it less frequently, which I have done on occassions simply because I couldn't be bothered to sink anymore time into it on top of what I already have with current frusterations in game mechanics. I am familiar with the game, various tactics in the game, I have enough time to tell the difference, although I am not an elitist by any means.

I'm not the kind of person that usually puts out a review, but after playing this for a while, I feel like a few things can certainly be said.
First off, I want to congratulate Payload Studios on making fantastic strides since the game first came out. All the different techs and all the different parts they've added are so much fun to work with, and the different mechanics certainly work to keep even the biggest, baddest techs on their toes. I want readers to keep in mind that the things I'll be pointing out are certainly not marks against Payload, and are simply things that could stand to be improved. The game as a whole is very solid, and deserves a good look for those who like a survival/crafting sandbox game that brings something a little different to the table.
First of all, I don't think I can stress enough just how much a multiplayer mode would improve this game. I get lonely playing alone, and it would be super nice to be able to set up a game with a couple of friends to work together, building bases, hunting down techs, and overall just having a good time together. It would make the game so much more enjoyable, and I cannot stress that enough. And while I'm not the kind of player who particularly enjoys competitive play, but the way this game allows its players to build big, bad vehicles bristling with weapons and armor, it would make sense for a proper PVP mode to exist as well.
In the same vein as Multiplayer, I would certainly like to see Payload introduce its own tech-sharing services, instead of using Twitter as a proxy. If terratech had its own internal tech-sharing server, I would be much more apt to share the things I've built.
This also brings to light a bit of a balancing issue. Sure, it's wonderful to be able to build a monster of a vehicle and send it off to other players to wreak havoc, but I've seen some absolutely ridiculous techs pop up in my time playing. The difficulty curve is completely out of whack, especially when a titan shows up to wreck your base when all you have is a piddly little tech and piddly little guns that gets one-shotted by the storm of gunfire laid upon you. Perhaps limiting the number of blocks a player can put on their tech in relation to their GSO ranking would be a good choice, as would limiting the kinds of techs a player can encounter by that same merit, but I would also like to see an option to turn vehicle sharing off entirely, so players can choose to go up against only the creations of Payload Studios, as those seem to be a bit better balanced.
The spawning is an issue as well. I can't count the number of times I'd been wrecked only to spawn in a new tech and get my face mashed in by a gank squad that happened to be in aggro-range of my spawn point. A manual spawning system would be much desired, as it would allow a player to spawn in either back at their base, or pick a safe spot where they won't be immediately set upon by a raider with an unfair advantage.
The building and crafting systems are plenty solid enough, but they have a number of minor bugs that simply need some polish. (Resource chunks in silos sometimes get stuck in a transfer loop, chunks bypass refineries if several refineries are on the same conveyor chain or the refinery has a pass-through, advanced chunk builders sometimes eat resources without putting out the requested chunk, sorters skip every third chunk if fed a chain of chunks), It would certainly help if conveyors were a bit smarter, and the addition of conveyor systems for GeoCorp (Slower transfers, bulk chunk movement) and Hawkeye (Armored) would be much appreciated. The ability to use a furnace in the same way a fabricator is used would be nice as well, as it would allow a player to manually call for a fuel chunk or set the furnace to call one as needed instead of relying on inefficient sorters and conveyor chains.
Another addition that would add a whole new level to the way the game plays would be for Payload to introduce an aquatic biome and resources and blocks, perhaps even a corperation specific to it. We already have land and air covered, but why not sea, as well?
Phew, alright, I think that about covers it. All in all, I think the game is awesome despite my nitpicking, and for a game that's still in development, it has a lot to offer. It still needs some polish, some optimization, but don't let the things I've pointed out here prevent you from enjoying it as it is.

I'd like to start by mentioning that this actually a really good game. Yes, it has a few bugs here and there but at least it is still playable. For such a reasonable price, this is a good game. Remember, it came out in 2009 so we can't expect anything special. But for 2009, it actually has quite good graphics. The PATH route is quite a nice length, not too long and not too short. You can get a shift over, within about half an hour. The graphics inside the tunnels are excellent, especially the dynamic lighting that lights up the cab as you drive along. Above ground, the graphics aren't all that, but I really like the detail on the track and the signals are very bright which means you can see them from a long way off. When driving east above ground you can also see the Manhattan skyline, which I find a very nice touch to the game. In stations, you can enter free roam mode which allows you to explore. However, there is a very annoying platform bug which means that if you accidentally walk off the edge of a platform, it is impossible for you to get back up again. Therefore, you have no choice but to end the mission and start all over again. The people on the platform are static but for a 2009 game, we can't really complain. There are about three trains that you can choose from, but they all seem to be exactly the same inside the cab, so it doesn't really make any difference. Something that can be really annoying when driving is that you have to control the announcements manually by pressing keys. This can get quite boring. The station graphics could be a touch better but they are not too bad either. Another thing, is that you have to manually configure all the keys before you drive. There is no tutorial, so I guess you are just expected to learn yourself. The speed limits in the game are also very harsh. They can just change at any time. You could be just driving along at 40mph and then you notice that the limit has changed to 15mph, with a tight curve approaching. A major disappointment was that there is no speedometer inside the cab. You have to totally rely on the route monitor screen. Tight curves can also derail the train, if you are not paying attention to the speed restrictions. There are AI trains in the game, but you can only see them when you are above ground, and not in underground stations.
Overall, I rate this game 7.5/10. It has some very nice features and but also some really annoying bugs. But for such a cheap price, I'd say it is worth buying and it doesn't require a high spec pc to run either, although I strongly recommend you check the minimum requirements first, just in case.

Starbound is a game about building, platforming and exploration very well comparable with games like Minecraft and Terraria. It has a rather strange setting, a mix of sci-fi and medieval. You start on a space ship that you will soon upgrade to be capable of faster than light travel yet most of the time you will fight with axes and shields and mine with pickaxes. A laser rifle can be just as strong as a sword in this world.
The whole world is procedurally generated, it's a whole universe with so many stars and planets filled with randomly generated plants, monsters, dungeons, villages, random gravity and day/night cycles and even randomly generated equipment that you'd never have enough time to visit them all.
You don't need to visit them all because as cool as this sounds in theory, planets of the same biome and difficulty tend to feel and play very similar and the randomly generated monsters feel way to generic, too. There is no need to visit planets of the same biome and difficulty level which effectively reduces the number of planets that will be of interest for you to about circa 15.
For a game that is about exploration Starbound feels surprisingly linear. You need to upgrade your suit to survive (unlock) new biomes and mine ores till you kill a boss and advance to slightly more dangerous planets. This repeats itself until you killed the last boss after about 15 to 25 hours.
Some Planets or rather biomes are really cool and it's fun to explore them for the first time yet usually you will not appreciate what makes them unique for a long time because the most valuable things about a planet - it's ores - are under it's surface. And theres little variation between planets/biomes below the surface. It's stone, sand, dirt and ores. Every so often you encounter a dungeon, and yes they are fun to explore. The dungeons are not entirely random but hand crafted pieces that are randomly distributed in the world and it seems that a planet only has pieces of one specific set because of which they feel way less generic than the rest of the game. But only every 20th dungeon - if not even significantly less - will offer something interesting to loot.
Most of the time chests and tombs will only offer money and non valuable items like bandages (they work like the least effective health potion in other games). You will likely loose the interest in looting them very soon. Getting to the end of a very difficult, long and well designed dungeon to find absolutely nothing in it for the x.th time is only fun until you realize that you're not just ridiculously unlucky but that this is how things currently are.
So neither the dungeons nor the surface are of interest, the only things truly unique to a planet. You spent most of the time mining underground. 90% of this game you will hold your mouse button pointing at stone and dirt. This is as much fun as it's sounds, that is not at all.
Now I know that fans of starbound will be intrigued to say "But you do the same in terraria, that's just part of this genre" but thats not entirely true. Yes Terraria and similar games require you to spend a lot of time mining too, but not 90% of the time. There are armor sets in Terraria that require you to kill bosses 2-3 three times, there were armor sets you could built from plants that you collected on the surface, there were armor sets that you crafted via drops from various monsters and many armor sets required you a mix of those which lead to very varied gameplay.
Mining was also generally more difficult in Terraria, it became harder but more rewarding the further you digged down. In Starbound the whole planet has one fixed difficulty level and you can easily mine for half an hour without getting attacked once. The surface of a planet, which rarely offers something valuable, is often times harder to survive than the core of the planet which offers valuable ores.
And you didn't had to craft every tier of armor in Terraria, you could easily jump two tiers or more if you were a good player. Similar you can do just fine in Minecraft with lower tiers of armor like the leather or iron armor. Starbounds progression system doesn't allow that, The devs force you to do things exactly in order. Equipment is more important than skills and experience. I do not believe that this is due to early access but a design philosophy of chuckle fish that they seem to be very unwilling to get rid of despite how often it is criticized by players.
Combat got significantly improved with the last patch, one aspect I still don't like is frequent use of health restoring items. They have almost no cooldown so you can easily pop 20 health restoring items in a boss fight. In other games they have a cooldown of a few minutes and are meant to be an aid. In Starbound you can just furnish 100 bandages in a main mission/boss fight and almost tank some bosses. Some can't be beaten without the usage of at least 20 of them. It seems that the devs intended the heavy usage of health restoring items.
I guess it's their way to "fix" a questionable design philosophy. Since progression is so linear you can't grind and farm better equipment to be better suited for a boss. You can only face a boss once you have the best currently available equipment (the game will literally not let you otherwise). In Terraria bad players could grind better equipment while good players could save time and face the boss with their current equipment. In Starbound a bad player will pop more bandages, a good player less.
But I still really enjoyed the main mission which require you to go through a dungeon and often times kill a boss in the end. They are fantastically designed and I enjoy them more than building arenas and spawning bosses in Terraria. They have a great, sinister atmosphere and are filled with many interesting traps. They are not properly balanced yet, the first mission was more difficult by far than every following mission afterwards and even harder than some highend bosses in Terraria, but that is something I can overlook in a game that is still in development.
If you like building beautiful castles, futuristic bases etc. that have no purpose other than looking good and enjoy it more than balanced and intriguing gameplay and don't mind grinding for it I highly recommend starbound. It offers much more furniture and block types/colors than any other building game I know of. But if you care more about balanced and variated gameplay than creating non-functional 2D pixel art I highly suggest to keep following the development of Starbound and wait for the next big updates before you buy it.

It used to be fun, a nice little MMORPG with some unique ideas in it, cute character and enemy designs, maybe a bit grindy for my taste but the grind was the gameplay to an extent, like in most dungeon crawlers. But the thing is, the developers have gotten more and more greedy over time; I am not exaggerating, they *actually* looked over how their game stood and how well things were going, and decided to A. reduce the rate at which players gain in-game currency, B. make the things that were in the store for in-game currency more expensive, and C. not allow players to buy classes using in-game currency anymore. All for the
stated goal of encouraging more store purchases and less ability to get things without paying real money - they weren't even
to hide it or couch it in good PR terms, it's very blatantly "people weren't buying enough stuff, so we made things worse for non-payers". Don't believe it's that bad?
I get that with any free to play game, it's a fine balance. On the developer's end, they have to incentivize real-money transactions, while offering enough for free that people continue to join and play. Otherwise, they can't keep the game running or support their families. On the player's end, they have to be constantly aware that the developer
benefits from making playing for free a frustrating and difficult experience - just not
frustrating. In both directions, each side is in a delicate balance indeed, and the most important thing to cultivate is
. Developers should trust players to buy things if they're actually worth it, and players should trust developers to make things that
worth it, while offering enough reliable, quality free content to keep playing the rest of the time.
Trust is what enables this whole model to function, which is why one of the absolute
things a F2P developer can do is to take things
over time. Once offering something, especially for a long period of time, then taking it away is a betrayal of trust, and that's exactly what Trion has done with Trove. They lured people in with the promise of what the game
, and then took it away to make some quick cash. For the sake of the entire F2P gaming community, for the sake of better developers who respect their playerbases, don't reward this kind of cash-grubbing, short-sighted behavior.
Edit: Oh, and I'm not even going to get into things like the quality of recent updates, or the promised bounties for finding glitches that were never delivered. Those subjects are too nebulous for me to weigh in on - what I'm talking about here are factual matters that are well documented in public record.

I went into The Walking Dead with few expectations. I was only vaguely familiar with the comic's existence. I believe the show had at least started, but what little I'd seen of it bored me. I wasn't even particularly familiar with Telltale Games at the time, outside of knowing they handled newer takes on the Monkey Island and Sam & Max properties. That was it. And now, I can easily say The Walking Dead remains one of, if not, their best adventure game, even with more of the same world and visits to other worlds adopting the choices-with-consequence model The Walking Dead established.
Right off the bat, The Walking Dead manages to establish its setting at a breakneck pace without being confusing or unclear. You're in Georgia. You're in trouble. Then suddenly, you -and- Georgia, and the whole world for that matter, are in a whole lot more trouble than anyone bargained for. The core cast gets established fairly quickly, then the pace begins to ease up a bit to give you time to get comfortable with your new avatar and his associates. Lee, the one left to rot. Clementine, the one left behind. Kenny, the one left to act. And there are plenty of supporting characters, all distinct, many memorable, helping hold up these eventual pillars of the story as well.
One point of contrast between how conversations and action sequences is handled in The Walking Dead really struck me: it's the little things, like what you choose to say or whom you choose to say it to, that have the longest-running impact and the greatest effect on your overal experience of the game, and in most cases, there's no undo. Meanwhile, coming back from failure during a quick-time-event, which typically ends in fatality, is almost instant, and is the closest thing to "fixing" any of your actions you get a chance to do. This really helps emphasize the importance of the characters and their interaction over any sort of outside actors or circumstances that is the core of the game on the whole.
If you decide to play through The Walking Dead, you're going to cry. You're going to yell, too, and smile. You'll love some characters, you'll hate others. And the best thing is? It's unlikely the moments and people that fit those lists for you will match up exactly with anyone else. Even if you're not a fan of the other Walking Dead media properties, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

This is a bad game, and not because of the major glitches that have apparently gone years without being fixed.
To start, the story is mega boring. Your four characters have zero personality to speak of, and characters drive a story. Wait, what story? There isn't one. Your four heroes are given that role because reasons, and that's it. You travel from town to town where bad things inexplicably happen. FPS games have better stories.
The job system has some major flaws. First, the "transition" encounters when you switch jobs is just...pointless. It's not really an issue, but it's also unnecessary. More importantly, most of the jobs are worthless. Warriors are bad because Red Mages are just as strong and can also cast spells. Scholars are Red Mages without physical attacks. Evokers are bad because the effect you get is random. Monks and White Mages are fine, but are completely outclassed by later jobs, making you basically start over leveling just to get the same effects. The Thief sucks because stealing is garbage in this game; I have yet to steal something that isn't a potion. But you're gonna be grinding anyway, because you're gonna need so much gear, and you're not gonna get the money elsewhere.
The caster jobs don't have MP, they have spell numbers. Similar to spells per day in D&D, there are spell levels, and you get a certain amount of each level. Again, bad system. Think about a black mage. He'll have access to two Thundara spells, and that's it. In a boss fight, he then becomes useless, because his lower level spells do hardly anything. Same thing for healers. Oh, and don't even bother with "well, just use an ether" because those don't exist in this game. Once you're out of spells (those very limited spells), you're screwed until you rest.
Combat is straight up stupid. Early in the game, it forces you into combat while under the effects of Mini, twice, once against a boss. This means your physical attacks do nothing and you HAVE to have magic jobs leveled up and spells prepared. If you don't, you're screwed. Good luck. But in general, combat is really bad. Two main reasons. One, turn order. Is. Completely. Totally. Random. There is no speed stat to determine who goes first, there isn't even a class thing that says the quick jobs go first. Going into combat with the same monsters over and over with the same jobs, I saw every single combination of turn order. This makes it really hard to react to things, like healing. Makes boss fights unfair. Second, physical attacks in this game are just as random. You have a chance of hitting a certain amount of times. This, again, is completely random, and physical damage varies way too big.

I step outside. Autumn's crisp, cool, morning air kisses my face, leaving behind its numbing cold touch. Looking out over my farm, the morning mist begins to settle. Its beads of dew left behind on the crops, sparkling like diamonds in the morning sun. I take a deep breath of the fresh country air, its cool sting filling my lungs. “It’s time to harvest,” I say to my wife Penny as she steps outside. I give her a kiss before walking down the porch steps to start my morning chores. “Don't work too hard,” she yells after me, “and eat something good for lunch!” I wave back in acknowledgement and begin my daily chores, harvesting the first few rows of crops that are ready.
After a few hours pass, I make my way into town. In town, I make light passing conversation with townsfolk as I head over to the general store. After purchasing some more autumn seeds Pierre, the general store owner, tells me he worries for his daughter Abigail. Apparently she was out in yesterday’s storm trying to catch frogs and has come down with a fever. As I depart to make my way back to my farm, I make sure to check the town notice board outside the general store. Robin’s looking for someone to catch her salmon to make stew. I can do that after today’s chores.
Upon returning to my farm I finish harvesting the ready crops and honey from our bee hives, retrieve sap and syrup from our tree taps, and bottle our preserves, wine, and beer. I finish the day’s chores by planting a few more crops, using the seeds I bought today, and deposit the day’s harvest in our sell bin. I walk back inside, exhausted from a long day’s work. The warm air embraces me like a blanket as I cross through the door. As I shut the door behind me I begin to smell the delectable evening supper penny has begun to cook. The savory scents tickle my nose and cause my stomach to dance in anticipation.
Regretting my decision to assist with Robin’s request, I reluctantly grab my fishing rod from a chest in the living room. “I’ll be back later my dear,” I yell to Penny as I once again brave the cool autumn air. I make my way down to the local river. I reach my favorite spot, just past Marnie’s farm on a little island in the middle of the river, and I settle in. After a few casts of catching nothing but trash and seaweed, I finally real-in a nice big salmon. I pack up my rod and newly caught prize and begin my long trek to Robin’s house up on the mountain.
By the time I reach her house the sun has set. I quickly exchange my catch for a small reward and begin back down the mountain to return home. Fatigue setting in, my eyes struggling to stay open, I barely make it back to my farm home. Slowly I drag myself inside. The light are all off, Penny has already gone to bed. Exhausted, I fumble taking off my dirty work cloths and snuggle up next to Penny in bed. I close my eyes and the world fades to black, as a drift off to sleep to begin the next day.

Well another year and another NBA2K - This review assumes you are familiar with the series.
This year the team has given us something a little different and have included a story driven My Career mode, while some will hate it I thought it gave some fresh blood to the franchise and it can be mostly skipped anyway for those who aren't interested.
The game itself has been improved in several areas but to sum up it has become more realistic with the AI playing better and not so many easy dunks or silly looking alley oops in My Park for example.
Graphics and Audio are both top notch and the commentary is an absolute treat with a surprising amount of variation, gameplay has become in my view slightly harder which I luv and My Park has had a few tweaks for the better also, mainly toning  down the massive advantage that taller players had previously and dampened down the 3 point shot success rate in Sunset Park which was very annoying previously and turned the games into rubbish ball for 5 year olds rather than resembeling the real game.
Amazingly the game worked right out of the box - unlike the last 3 years releases which were full of bugs and issues that prevented many gamers from playing the game they bought for several days.
All in all NBA2K is still miles in front of any other BBall sim out there today and this year's release in my view has improved the franchise, given My Park a much needed face lift and brought back the highschool and university ranks to play through in My Career.

It wasn't easy to decide if I wanted to give this game a thumbs up or down, but in the end I decided to not recommend it.
The gameplay is fun, there is a decent selection of ships and customization, it's also decently balanced and the TTK of ships is medium to high so you spend more time playing and less time waiting to respawn.
One problem is that matches can run pretty long. That in itself isn't bad since playing is fun, but there is a certain grind involved unless you want to spend buckets of $$$ in the ingame shop. The reward for a 10min match or a 30 min. match are the same. So it is better to have lots of short matches than a few long ones.
Another problem is that there are just too few players for matchmaking. It takes 5-10 minutes for matchmaking to get 10 people together and there isn't much to do while waiting.
And last but not least: monetization. The soft currency prices are just insane (soft currency is currency you get from playing matches). As an example customizing weapons runs about 45k to unlock one choice, unlocking ships can go up to 925k. Without boosters I get about 8-10k per match, i.e. it takes forever to unlock stuff, even if you spend real money.

One thing that this game really nails is atmosphere, and that's saying something since there are zero fancy 3D polygons to be found anywhere. You really
like a hacker in this game, navigating systems you have no authorization to, extracting data from otherwise closed sources, and constantly being reminded that human behaviour is ultimately the downfall of any good security system.
The DLC is a separate experience that builds on the base game, introducing new mechanics, programs, and hacks. Minor spoiler, but when
it is an absolute amazing experience.
I cannot wait to dive into the user-created Workshop content, adding whole new chapters and stories that leverage the games mechanics, and I already have some ideas for my very own Extension.

Most of the difficulty of this game stems from horrible choices by the developers. Graphics are fantastic, and all the things that made the old XCom games great are present. But the end product is akin to hitting yourself in the head with a brick.
The best thing about tactical games is the choice and strategy therein. Being able to succeed in a variety of ways can be incredibly satisfying, and adds a lot of replayability to the product. But the difficulty and combat system in XCom 2 means there's really only one way to succeed. If you stray from the narrow path to victory, expect to lose swiftly. This is true for both the tactical missions, as well as the base-building of the campaign. Sure, there are tons of choices to be made, but the decisions usually boil down to "succeed and continue", or "fail and reload."
Learning how to win wouldn't be such a chore if the game interface was better. Nothing in this game is intuitive or explained well. I've played numerous XCom games in the past, but I found nearly every aspect of this game required an internet search to find out either what the feature did, or how to implement it. This is clearly not the same Firaxis that made Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, the game featuring arguably the best interface in gaming history.
There's a ton of great game in here, but what there is seems buried under heaps of poor design. Workshop mods seem essential to make this game even playable, but I've yet to find one that can turn it into a worthy successor to the XCom franchise.
This game is plagued with bugs and mechanical problems that render gameplay exceedingly frustrating or plain impossible.

The Walking Dead was one of the first games I was introduced to on Steam. I hadn’t ever played a game quite like this one. Before playing The Walking Dead, in my eyes games were limited to Pac-Man, platformers like Mario, multiplayer racing games, Zoo Tycoon, etc. I never really experienced a “choose your own adventure” game before, and prior to playing this game.. I wasn’t really all that interested in trying one either.
Although I went into this game kicking and screaming, an episode or two in, I was hooked. I was not a huge fan of the blood and gore, but that aside, the story was very inviting. I truly felt as if I was making all of the major decisions in the game, therefore influencing how my character, as well as all those around me would turn out in the end. I grew attached to some characters (Ben) that took me on an emotional journey at times, which was interesting to me, because I never knew that games could get you to feel such emotional ties to a fictional character.
Like I mentioned earlier, this game lets YOU decide how you want to play the game. You could play as the hero, or the villain. You can choose to leave people behind, and you can choose to save peoples lives. The most interesting part of the game is seeing how your choices you make earlier in the game can influence how your games pans out 2 or 3 episodes down the line.
You start out the game as a man named Lee. You do not know much about Lee, but you soon start to see his backstory unfold. He may have a criminal background, but you can choose whom, if anyone, you want to share this information with as you begin to make bonds and partnerships with people. You later run into a little girl named Clementine. You learn she is currently on her own when something terrible happened to her babysitter when her parents went out on a trip. You and Clementine team up and try to escape the monsters that seem to be taking over the area. She reminds you time and time again that the main goal is to find and reunite her with her family, until then, you are her guardian. The things you two will encounter and defeat together give you two an almost inseparable bond. You two start to learn things about each other not many people may know, which will help you in the end when you have to make some major life altering choices. You will meet a number of other survivors, victims, and criminals along your journey together. You will have to make decisions on who you trust and don’t trust, and hope that the people you do bring along for the ride will have your back when it counts.
Just remember that ALL of the choices you make, whether they are big or small will have some sort of repercussion. Some decisions you will have to make in a split second, and others you will have a little more time to think about.. but all your decisions are very important. Even though you may not always be able to save everyone from death and destruction, you have to remember your main goal is to keep Clementine safe. This is another layer to the game that makes all of your choices in the long run an emotional journey. Just when you think that you feel you’ve gotten away with something, remember you will have her watching you from the sidelines, learning to act just as you do.
I hope you do give this game a fair try. There is a reason it has been so successful, the writers do know what they are doing. The artwork is different which makes gameplay enjoyable. Even though you are placed in a time period that may be depressing and hopeless, the graphics somehow make you almost feel a glimpse of hope to reach for. Being an apocalyptic type game, there is a fair share of blood and guts, but most times it is safe to turn your head and look away for a slit second. Embrace this different form of gameplay and open your eyes to the new experiences and emotions that will rapidly unfold when you play this game.

Well, this series got off on a shaky start. If you are looking to get into the Hitman series and want to start at the beginning, you may or may not want to skip this one anyway.
To start off, the graphics look great for the time, even though the draw distance is fairly low. Also, on more modern systems, you need to mess with the graphics options a bit so static textures don't behave like animated .gif files. Before even touching control configuration or resolution settings, make sure to set the renderer to OpenGL, no matter what. Otherwise, on a presentation level, Hitman does it's job.
As for controls, they definitely take a bit of getting used to, and you'll definitely also have to mess with the controls for at least 20 minutes just to see what suits you. And some of the design choices for them, even for the time, don't make a whole lot of sense. Such as a dedicated sprint foreword key. Luckily, after at least five or so configuration changes, I managed.
Regarding sound, the music does a pretty good job most of the time at setting the mood. Whether things are tense and you are sneaking up on your main target to slice their throat without making a peep, or running through a Columbian jungle running-and-gunning, Jasper Kyd did a solid job composing it.
On a story level, the first Hitman is a bit basic, but still captivating enough to see through to the end. One thing that really spiced my interest is the references to movies such as Scarface or The Godfather.
And finally gameplay, well, it's a lot of trial-and-error. On many missions you will find frustration as the game expects you to sit though hours and hours of you dying from the same problem when the solution was literally in the last place you would look. I really can't blame anyone for looking up a guide or walkthrough for the game, as it really doesn't give you a clue sometimes. And in regards to the missions, there are not a lot of them, so this trial-and-error frustration doesn't last too long. Some can range heavily in length and aggravation, and most aren't very replayable or memorable. There is a difference between a proper lack of hand-holding (i.e. something akin to Metroid) and tedious bull$hit.
What also range between missions are the bugs. Yes, this 14 year old game that they are still selling on Steam still has bugs. None of them are necessarily game-breaking, but can ruin a would-be successful play through a mission. Some range from minor visual glitches, to enemies that spawn out of nowhere that somehow see through your disguise and murder you, to the game spontaneously crashing.

In the end, for IO Interactive's first game, and it being the year 2000 when it was released, I give it a bit of leeway. And as a whole it isn't a bad game. I have to agree with the Metacritic score of 73/100 it was given.
If you really want to start Hitman from the ground up and are willing to deal with a bit of annoying cr@p here and there, maybe wait for a sale unless you are really that eager.

To be perfectly honest, I was expecting more at launch, but that's how hype culture works.
There. I said it. Take the slight hint of bait or continue reading as any competent person would.
Anyways, moving on...
TU has some serious potential, and I can easily see this getting better quickly. Pixeltail knows what they're doing, and honestly I feel a bit bad for them right now with such a massive influx of bug reports and forum traffic. Have fun, guys :P

GIve this game a couple plays. The first game or two I did not know what to make of it, it was all sinking in... that said:
This game is brilliant.  I've been playing games since 1984 and I can count on one hand the amount of times I've been inspired this much by a single game.  1) Xcom UFO Defense (the old microprose version), 2) The first Metal Gear game 3) Final Fantasy for the NES 4) Faster Than Light (FTL) 5) Heat Signature.
You play a bandit/hero/terrorist/villian/assasin/person trying to get by/um... it's complicated... who boards ships, does horrible things to the crew under seemingly impossible conditions, and somehow makes it out alive.  It is all under the umbrella of you trying to "free" space stations but really who cares about that. The story takes a waaaaaaaaay back seat to the game play here.
The gameplay: (an example)
1) take the mission, you gotta kill some dude on some ship, with very little time to do it. Oh by the way he has a shield, and you don't have anything yet to penetrate a shield.
2) fly out to the ship as fast as you can, the clock is ticking on this mission (not all missions have timers)
3) you meet and board the ship undetected, lucky for you there is a skeleton crew, but time is running out because you fail at piloting your little pod.
4) You don't have time for keys, so you get past a keyed door by using your swapper which literally swaps you with your target.
5) You drop two guards with your wrench and pistol, the gunshot has alerted your target who comes running at you, shield lit up.
6) you turn with your pistol and blow out the window behind you as your target enters the room, sucking you both out into the vacuum of space.
7) you remote pilot your pod to pick you up before you die, your target is not so lucky.
See there are a million ways to complete a mission, you can be a door-kicker and come in like a typhoon, or you can be a sneaky little ninja who drags the bodies of his victims back to the pod leaving no trace he was ever there.
Loot in the game is fantastic, and say you want to jump aboard a random ship that happens to be bumbling past you on the way to your mission, just to check out its cargo??? Feel free, but you may get more than you bargained for.

Starbound is a game about building, platforming and exploration very well comparable with games like Minecraft and Terraria. It has a rather strange setting, a mix of sci-fi and medieval. You start on a space ship that you will soon upgrade to be capable of faster than light travel yet most of the time you will fight with axes and shields and mine with pickaxes. A laser rifle can be just as strong as a sword in this world.
The whole world is procedurally generated, it's a whole universe with so many stars and planets filled with randomly generated plants, monsters, dungeons, villages, random gravity and day/night cycles and even randomly generated equipment that you'd never have enough time to visit them all.
You don't need to visit them all because as cool as this sounds in theory, planets of the same biome and difficulty tend to feel and play very similar and the randomly generated monsters feel way to generic, too. There is no need to visit planets of the same biome and difficulty level which effectively reduces the number of planets that will be of interest for you to about circa 15.
For a game that is about exploration Starbound feels surprisingly linear. You need to upgrade your suit to survive (unlock) new biomes and mine ores till you kill a boss and advance to slightly more dangerous planets. This repeats itself until you killed the last boss after about 15 to 25 hours.
Some Planets or rather biomes are really cool and it's fun to explore them for the first time yet usually you will not appreciate what makes them unique for a long time because the most valuable things about a planet - it's ores - are under it's surface. And theres little variation between planets/biomes below the surface. It's stone, sand, dirt and ores. Every so often you encounter a dungeon, and yes they are fun to explore. The dungeons are not entirely random but hand crafted pieces that are randomly distributed in the world and it seems that a planet only has pieces of one specific set because of which they feel way less generic than the rest of the game. But only every 20th dungeon - if not even significantly less - will offer something interesting to loot.
Most of the time chests and tombs will only offer money and non valuable items like bandages (they work like the least effective health potion in other games). You will likely loose the interest in looting them very soon. Getting to the end of a very difficult, long and well designed dungeon to find absolutely nothing in it for the x.th time is only fun until you realize that you're not just ridiculously unlucky but that this is how things currently are.
So neither the dungeons nor the surface are of interest, the only things truly unique to a planet. You spent most of the time mining underground. 90% of this game you will hold your mouse button pointing at stone and dirt. This is as much fun as it's sounds, that is not at all.
Now I know that fans of starbound will be intrigued to say "But you do the same in terraria, that's just part of this genre" but thats not entirely true. Yes Terraria and similar games require you to spend a lot of time mining too, but not 90% of the time. There are armor sets in Terraria that require you to kill bosses 2-3 three times, there were armor sets you could built from plants that you collected on the surface, there were armor sets that you crafted via drops from various monsters and many armor sets required you a mix of those which lead to very varied gameplay.
Mining was also generally more difficult in Terraria, it became harder but more rewarding the further you digged down. In Starbound the whole planet has one fixed difficulty level and you can easily mine for half an hour without getting attacked once. The surface of a planet, which rarely offers something valuable, is often times harder to survive than the core of the planet which offers valuable ores.
And you didn't had to craft every tier of armor in Terraria, you could easily jump two tiers or more if you were a good player. Similar you can do just fine in Minecraft with lower tiers of armor like the leather or iron armor. Starbounds progression system doesn't allow that, The devs force you to do things exactly in order. Equipment is more important than skills and experience. I do not believe that this is due to early access but a design philosophy of chuckle fish that they seem to be very unwilling to get rid of despite how often it is criticized by players.
Combat got significantly improved with the last patch, one aspect I still don't like is frequent use of health restoring items. They have almost no cooldown so you can easily pop 20 health restoring items in a boss fight. In other games they have a cooldown of a few minutes and are meant to be an aid. In Starbound you can just furnish 100 bandages in a main mission/boss fight and almost tank some bosses. Some can't be beaten without the usage of at least 20 of them. It seems that the devs intended the heavy usage of health restoring items.
I guess it's their way to "fix" a questionable design philosophy. Since progression is so linear you can't grind and farm better equipment to be better suited for a boss. You can only face a boss once you have the best currently available equipment (the game will literally not let you otherwise). In Terraria bad players could grind better equipment while good players could save time and face the boss with their current equipment. In Starbound a bad player will pop more bandages, a good player less.
But I still really enjoyed the main mission which require you to go through a dungeon and often times kill a boss in the end. They are fantastically designed and I enjoy them more than building arenas and spawning bosses in Terraria. They have a great, sinister atmosphere and are filled with many interesting traps. They are not properly balanced yet, the first mission was more difficult by far than every following mission afterwards and even harder than some highend bosses in Terraria, but that is something I can overlook in a game that is still in development.
If you like building beautiful castles, futuristic bases etc. that have no purpose other than looking good and enjoy it more than balanced and intriguing gameplay and don't mind grinding for it I highly recommend starbound. It offers much more furniture and block types/colors than any other building game I know of. But if you care more about balanced and variated gameplay than creating non-functional 2D pixel art I highly suggest to keep following the development of Starbound and wait for the next big updates before you buy it.

Despite its age, I had a good time with this game. What Final Fantasy III does best is evoke the excitement of adventure. Fun character interactions, lively soundtrack and interesting setting manage to create a charming vibe and fit the theme seamlessly even with a weak main storyline. This will surely feel like a very classic experience as there's little depth not only story-wise, but in the gameplay department as well. The game won't hold your hand, the player will be forced to discover everything himself, even the simple gameplay mechanics.
Where the game starts to really show its age is the job (class) system. There is a relatively wide range of jobs, but after you unlock, choose and level up your first job, the game gives no reason to switch them other than the fact that "it looks different". You can experiment with different combinations, but in the end all of them are pretty much the same thing, and job level is the main determinant of character combat efficiency... Also, there is reoccuring enemy imbalance, which is the worst part of the game, because it forces you to grind.
Therefore, FF3 is not for everyone, but there is definitely value to be found in the game for those who are passionate about the genre or the series.

Okami is one of my favorite games, and it has been since the first day it released way back in 2006. A critical success but  commercial failure, it's been heralded as iconic through the years, warranting ports to multiple consoles despite its consistently low sales. It's been called a masterpiece, a work of art, and one of the best games to come out of the noteworthy PS2 era --  and I think that it deserves that title. Games like Okami are special, rare things. They don't come around too often.
The first thing you notice about Okami are the visuals. They're eye-catchingly unique, resplendant in a gorgeous visual style and different from not just games that came out in its era, but from most games in general, Okami looks like an ukiyo-e painting come to life right on your screen, and it's part of why the game has held up so well over the years -- even the old PS2 release is still a joy to look at because of the art style, and it's easily one of the more defining aspects of this title.
But Okami is more than just style, and it packs enough substance to rival any RPG of its era. Expect to sink 50+ hours into this game (at the least!) because it is PACKED with content! The main storyline is full of memorable characters and moments both poignant and thrilling, and the game world is gigantic, but never feels overly-inflated because of the well-designed and diverse areas you have available to explore. There's treasure to find in every corner and tons of secrets to uncover, with sidequests and minigames and all kinds of other adventures to have on top of the main event! Everything from digging underground for water to fishing up a whole ocean's worth of fish, playing something akin to whack-a-mole with actual moles and rolling various things up a hill to a big sleepy bear, all while restoring nature to a cursed land and unveiling its secrets -- Okami never runs out of things to do, and it's fun and frustrating in equal measure (and so very hard to put down once you sink back into the game!)
No review of Okami would be complete without mentioning it's most well-known mechanic -- the ability to directly interact with the game world via the Celestial Brush. The Celestial Brush is a powerful and fascinating tool gives you the power to change the world around you, and it really helps to set Okami's mechanics apart. You can turn day to night and blow the leaves off the trees, just as you can bring life back to a barren wasteland and call down lightning to zap your foes (and unsuspecting townspersons!)  You can make platforms appear -- or create them outright -- and call down vines to carry you somewhere you can't get to on your own, and you can fix broken bridges just as you can slice just about anything in half -- it adds a whole new layer of gameplay that makes you want to try everything and gives you the opportunity for exploration -- and even some customization here and there -- that really keeps you engaged in what's happening, at least to me. It's fun, too -- and sometimes something just being plain FUN is special in its own right!
There's a ton of interactivity in this game, where little things you do affect the world just as much as the big ones, from barking at stray dogs (they'll bark too!) to using your Celestial Brush to make the wind blow and confuse townsfolk, Okami seems to have an answer for every move you make. And on top of that, you can feed and befriend basically every animal you meet -- and you'll get rewarded for doing so! Dogs, horses, tigers... for people who like to collect things, there are multiple catalogs you can fill, from the treasure you've found to the animals you've fed -- I cannot overstate the delightful amount of content packed into this title. Okami features an amazing bestiary as well that catalogues all of the enemies you fight in the form of a gigantic scroll with painted images of each one. As the completed images reveal themseves across multiple related entries to be more than just a splash and a text blurb, it gives a real sense of accomplishment for completing it all and taking on even the most difficult enemies in the game.
You can probably finish Okami in 50 hours, but I've sunk over a hundred into it before just running around doing everything. It's nice to have a game with hours and hours of things to do that doesn't ask anything more of the player than a single purchase price.
Okami just feels well-crafted. Battling is fluid and fun and there are many ways to do it, with plenty of weapon combos to try and skills to unlock. Boss battles, too, are unique and exhilirating, and what worked for one might not work for another and can even backfire entirely -- and it's such a joy to experiment and to, basically, kick♥♥♥♥♥against your foes. It cannot be overstated how COOL it feels to just wail on a demon as a deity in the form of a wolf, whether it's with a mirror or a rosary or a sword -- and for anyone that cares, yes, you can evetualy learn a skill to lift your leg and pee on them for the added insult (and in fact, doing so, in addition to defeating enemies in a certain way, will even net you post-battle bonuses!) It's fun and it rewards inventive play -- but has a space for button mashers too in the form of the rosary weapon. You can tailor your own experience, and that means it's something many people can play -- and it helps that both keyboard and controller... controls... can be fully remapped to whatever you like.
As for this particular edition of the game, the port is solid. It supports 4k resolutions and so far, I haven't found any bugs. It picked up my controller from the get-go as well, and the game runs as smoothly as can be. It is capped at 30fps, but every release has been; Okami was originally coded that way, and due to its record of selling terribly, Capcom simply didn't have the budget to recode the game from the ground up -- as changing the framerate renders the game unbeatable and breaks jump mechanics outright. (It doesn't help that the studio who originally created this title folded years ago and is no longer working at Capcom to assist in the rebuilding efforts.) The loading-screen minigames have finally returned as well after their long hiatus -- but the ending theme, Reset, is still conspicuously missing from this release, to the disappointment of everyone (and me in particular.) But overall, it's a solid release within the constraints Capcom had to work with, and there are no problems I have found with the game itself or its gameplay on PC. (Though caveat emptor -- there seems to be some pricing shenanigans in other regions' markets, so keep an eye on that!)
In all, Okami is a real treat of a game with a huge world to explore full of fun characters, mysterious dungeons, and vicious enemies, all wrapped up in an eye-catching shell of gorgeous graphics and tied in a ribbon of storyline that holds your attention from start to finish. (The soundtrack is also impeccable, just for the record.) Objectively, it runs well and has a ton of content to experience -- and subjectively...
This game feels like coming home after all these years, it's so special and charming to me personally, and I'm honestly really happy that it's finally HERE, on PC, where I can gift it to my friends and they can finally experience it, too. I've wanted Okami on PC for years. That it's finally here, that I can write this review... it's a bit of a dream come true for me. This is such a special game -- I really hope that this review encourages someone else to explore how special it is for themselves.

World of Subway's 1 - The Path, is a game which is not for the hardcore train simulation fan's, some may like it, some may not, but in my opinion, it saves a spot in my book.
So when you get the game for the very first time, you can see that the menu is very basic and plain, but remember this is a game which came out in 2009, not 2015.
When you choose the timetable, the type of train you have selected and the location, the loading time takes about 10-15 seconds, so you dont have to complain about the time it takes to load.
Then you come to the one big downside of the the game which really ticked me off, when you get into the subway train for the first time, some of the controls are unbinded on the train itself which is annoying, so your going to have to go to the options menu and bind all the train controls that way.
The other thing that people may not like is the graphics, there very Mircosoft Train Simulator like, which doesn't bother me at all and the next downside to the game is the intercom voice when you arrive and depart every station, this can be also very annoying when your trying to drive.
The controls on the train are hard to master, but once you know and get used to the brake, reverser and everything else on the train, it can be easier once you do get used to the train controls.
So my final verdict is that this is not for hardcore train sim fan's, it's plain, simple, easy and fun, but If you are looking for a challenge, I should recommend World of Subways Vol. 3 - London Underground Circle Line, it has much more of a realistic like physics engine and you can get in and out in the train!  Which is a pretty sweet feature.
I recommend World of Subway's 1 - The Path for newcomers to train simulation, remember the controls are hard but you can bind them to whatever key you want on your keyboard, so it can be a bit easy for you.
