If you've ever played Train Simulator 2015, prepare to take a step down in terms of interface and controls and general functionality of the game.
I would say the price is a little high, perhaps $9.95 (US) would have been more appropriate than $19.95.
The camera controls are basic, there's no zoom, FOV or adjustment of exterior camera. You can't open the train doors unless the camera view is in the driver's cabin, so you can't see the doors opening and closing, or passengers boarding.
It's a very basic sim, there's no career mode or any of the usual things you find in  games. It has an indie "pet project" feel about it for sure!
It might appeal to someone who is familiar with this actual line in real life. If you've lived in NY, this sim might be interesting, but even then it's still niche.
Train Simulator 2015 has an excellent feature where you can move the camera from the front to the back outside the train, and zoom in and out and around, and still maintain control of the train. World of Subways has nothing like that. TS 2015 is a lot more expensive though, so the comparison isn't entirely fair. But now you know what you're in for.

Theres alot of other smaller things that just seem weird or broken like occasionally things get stuck floating that should have physics applied to. Most of the difficulty of this game stems from horrible choices by the developers. Graphics are fantastic, and all the things that made the old XCom games great are present. But the end product is akin to hitting yourself in the head with a brick.
The best thing about tactical games is the choice and strategy therein. Being able to succeed in a variety of ways can be incredibly satisfying, and adds a lot of replayability to the product. But the difficulty and combat system in XCom 2 means there's really only one way to succeed. If you stray from the narrow path to victory, expect to lose swiftly. This is true for both the tactical missions, as well as the base-building of the campaign. Sure, there are tons of choices to be made, but the decisions usually boil down to "succeed and continue", or "fail and reload."
Learning how to win wouldn't be such a chore if the game interface was better. Nothing in this game is intuitive or explained well. I've played numerous XCom games in the past, but I found nearly every aspect of this game required an internet search to find out either what the feature did, or how to implement it. This is clearly not the same Firaxis that made Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, the game featuring arguably the best interface in gaming history.
There's a ton of great game in here, but what there is seems buried under heaps of poor design. Workshop mods seem essential to make this game even playable, but I've yet to find one that can turn it into a worthy successor to the XCom franchise.

First of all, yeah X Com is great. I love the theme and I'm a great fan of the old games. The new concepts introduced in X-COM Enemy Unknown are mostly well done. they make for a more fluent overall experience. Though both new first and even more the second title just have some major flaws that just prevent me from enjoying the experience:
The battle system
I hate how you need to carefully manage movement in fights because you dont want to fight more than one enemy group at once. The second group of enemies could literally stand right behind the next wall and you could fight with grenades, missiles and what not... they won't care. But DON'T move your stupid close combatant to the wrong spot where he might see a glimpse of them they will charge and wreck you.
This relates to a bigger problem the combat system has, wich is balance and overall AI behaviour. Typically you dont want the enemy to take a single shot at you, crush them on first sight is the way to go in most strategies. If they start shooting, things typically go south, especially on Ironman Mode.
The AI is just non-existant, just try it out, they won't even focus fire or coordinate their actions at all.
They overly simplified mechanics and the battle field as well, poor maps design and and lack of true tactical options beside unrealistic, fancy "special abilities" make me go back to X-Com Apocalypse more often that I dare to admit. Where are solid vision control features, where are flying suits, skyscrapers with horizontal battle grounds, ....
Battles just feel grindy and cheesy on higher difficulty....
The tactical layer
There is basically one build order / tech order with slight alterations here and there, very little tactical decisions to take realy. I also dont like the base building aspect.... a 3x4 grid. realy? that's it?
The X-COM 2 mod Long War improves quite a bit on the tactical side, giving you the task to choose where to send your soldiers, how long to infiltrate etc. X-Com 2 vanilla? just bah......
Overall even though I played the game quite a bit and tried to like it, it just falls short to be .... a fun experience for me. Now I acknowledge there is a large group of people loving the game and they rightly do so. It is just not my piece of cake...
Too bad realy :(

TL;DR VERSION INCOMING!!!
----------------------------------
If you like socializing and playing games with internet friends, then this is a great experience.
Full Review Below
-----------------
It needs to be pointed out that this game is, at it's core, a standalone version of GMod Tower.  This means that if you tried GMT and appericated it, you will have a blast doing things you are familiar with in GMT.
Towers Unite is a social game that is driven by your interactions between you and other players. Hang out with friends, explore the plaza hub, play various minigames, and decorate your own personal condo using coins from the minigames.
The minigames are currently very basic but very engaging. There are only four currently, but many more are scheduled to be added soon. The minigames are the main way to acquire the currency(units).
Units are the ingame currency of Tower Unite, don't worry though. There are no microtransaction that let you acquire massive amounts of units to flaunt around. Units are earned quite easily, and most items are reasonably priced so that they are acquireable by everyone who really wants them,
The plaza itself is the main social hub of Tower Unite. There currently is a movie theater (which allows users to upload YT videos to display on a theater screen for other players to watch), a marketplace (allows the user to use their hard earned units to buy condo supplies), and a boardwalk area, which currently includes a ferris wheel and multiple vendors.
Finally, you have the condos. Your condo is your personal hideout in Tower. You can customize it to your heart's contempt. You can design a contemporary home, to a beach party paradice. You will be spending most of your Units on the condo if you plan on sprucing it up.
At the time of writing, the game has been out for about six hours, so if any of the following are added or fixed, I will update.
EARLY ACCESS WARNING
---------------------------
-Unfinished plaza features
You can walk all around the plaza for sightseeing, but a large amount of activites in the plaza are not yet implemented, such as the casino, the lazer tag arena, the arcade, and the bumper car arena
.
-Server Issues
I can't personally determine if this is true or not, but multiple admins have complained about servers crashing when users attempt to start a minigame.
-Optimization
Mid-Tier GPU Users have reported lower than average frame rates, despite their card being well over requirements. I had personally experienced these issues, but they dissapate after slight graphics changes.
-Unadded game modes.
This can be a make or break for some people. There are only four game modes currently. Ball Race (think monkey ball), Mini-Golf, Virus ( a zombie style infection game) and Planet Panic( a hovercar battle game).
Other famous gamemodes from GMT such as Ultimate Chimera Hunt( now known as Little Crusaders) are currently in development.
Overall, for it's first day out, I think its a blast meeting some of the people migrating from GMT. Most people and servers are welcoming and interactive. You do have the occasional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ers running around, but hey, thats the internet for you.
9/10 for First Day out.

I decided that I should change my review because of a few blaring issues that have come up after the initial hype of early access release.
The game completely destroys the spark that the Garry's Mod version had. There is a very distinct lack of social interaction purely due to the fact that condos aren't physically in lobbies, and that lobbies can be hosted by players. On top of that, gamemodes can be hosted and joined by players without going into a lobby, so the lobby serves even less of a purpose.
People went into their suites in the Garry's Mod version of the game because it was something people did while they were waiting to queue up for a gamemode. When you were all burnt out of playing gamemodes, you still went to your suite because it was right there, not a loading screen away. Other players would still go to your suite because it was right there. Without that, the game loses what social interaction it REALLY needs. It just doesn't feel the same.
I'll give them credit, though. They're nailing the rest of the game. If you have a group of buds that like playing gamemodes and will occasionally visit a condo to do random stuff, that's great, and it'll work. But otherwise, the game isn't the community-oriented one I remember.

After initially giving this game a bad review, I re-played it and gave it another chance. I would recommend it now, though overall my feelings are a bit mixed.
First of all, the gameplay is indeed improved from 2k15. Certain elements feel a bit more natural, though this is only the case in the single-player "campaign" mode. I still wish that blacktop games could be configured to act like the campaign mode (ie, focus stays on a single player rather than following the ball). The new play calling UX is nifty, but in practice, a bit complicated to access in the heat of gameplay.
The "pro stick" feature also somehow feels more refined and better done when compared to 2k15. And of course, the graphics get a nice bump. The game doesn't get interesting until after your rookie year, so I at least recommend playing it to your second season.
Also, the new "off day" feature is really well done. You can choose to split your time between various activities, each of which have certain benefits for your character/team. This gives a nice bit of relief from the 82+ game grind of playing through an entire season. However, after playing a season or two, it becomes less interesting as your player's abilities get capped out, and there's not much room to progress beyond that.
Much has been said already of the story and the whole Spike Lee thing. On the one hand, yes, it's extremely cheesy... aside from some typically flat writing, the racial elements of the story really turned me off. Every character is a complete stereotype of their race -- the strong black sister, the "keepin' it real" friend, the over-the-top Italian-American agent, to the whiter-than-snow GM -- who at one point even acknowledges his privilege by admitting that since his father was an accountant he went to boarding school.... is that really how you think white people live, Spike? Overall, Lee shows again that he's less interested in progressing the role that race plays in 2016 America rather than going down the road of the tired Chris Rock-era stereotypes.
Oh yeah, and unless you configure your character as being black, the game gets really awkward. Lots of people have pointed that out already, but it's worth mentioning again... your TWIN sister is black. Why?!?! If they had just dropped the "twin" part, then the story could make sense no matter what color your character is. Oh yeah, and sorry Jeremy Lin fans, you still can't make your character Asian.
That aside, there are some genuinely good moments in the story's writing. The character development, which is fairly predictable, does occur and you at least sympathize with some of the characters. There are also a handful of scenes that are really well done, with believable acting and compelling dialog. There is real potential for a good screenwriter (ie, someone other than Spike Lee) to take this concept and run with it.
How does Lee fail in this regard? Well, first of all, because it's Spike Lee, he just can't resist the opportunity to cut himself (and his beloved Knicks) into the plot. He breaks the 4th wall repeatedly, both by injecting actual film footage in the plot alongside the game-rendered storyline, and also interviews the characters in the story, which is just as cheesy and unwelcome in this game as it is in his films. And for every genuinely emotional scene, there is an equal and opposing scene which makes you cringe in shame.
Aside from that, Lee is too used to constructing films and is unfamiliar with creating a script and environment which is subject to subtle changes. For instance, if your character is white, then get ready for a lot of awkward moments in the gameplay (for the record, I went with the default black Freq since I don't really care what race/gender/etc the main character is). Beyond that, the events in the story don't really align to what happens in the game. No matter how terribly you play, the game's announcers heap constant praise upon your character. Also, you can't escape Freq, even after you complete the main storyline. The game lets you choose a nickname, but still calls you Freq, and even features fans in the crowd holding up signs bearing this. It's just not very thought through, and could be done so much better.
However, the story did not taint my overall enjoyment of the game, especially once I finished the main plot and started chasing rings. It's just that the story could be so much more... I hope that 2k17 doesn't abandon this concept entirely. They just need to revisit it with someone who is not Spike Lee.

It used to be fun, a nice little MMORPG with some unique ideas in it, cute character and enemy designs, maybe a bit grindy for my taste but the grind was the gameplay to an extent, like in most dungeon crawlers. But the thing is, the developers have gotten more and more greedy over time; I am not exaggerating, they *actually* looked over how their game stood and how well things were going, and decided to A. reduce the rate at which players gain in-game currency, B. make the things that were in the store for in-game currency more expensive, and C. not allow players to buy classes using in-game currency anymore. All for the
stated goal of encouraging more store purchases and less ability to get things without paying real money - they weren't even
to hide it or couch it in good PR terms, it's very blatantly "people weren't buying enough stuff, so we made things worse for non-payers". Don't believe it's that bad?
I get that with any free to play game, it's a fine balance. On the developer's end, they have to incentivize real-money transactions, while offering enough for free that people continue to join and play. Otherwise, they can't keep the game running or support their families. On the player's end, they have to be constantly aware that the developer
benefits from making playing for free a frustrating and difficult experience - just not
frustrating. In both directions, each side is in a delicate balance indeed, and the most important thing to cultivate is
. Developers should trust players to buy things if they're actually worth it, and players should trust developers to make things that
worth it, while offering enough reliable, quality free content to keep playing the rest of the time.
Trust is what enables this whole model to function, which is why one of the absolute
things a F2P developer can do is to take things
over time. Once offering something, especially for a long period of time, then taking it away is a betrayal of trust, and that's exactly what Trion has done with Trove. They lured people in with the promise of what the game
, and then took it away to make some quick cash. For the sake of the entire F2P gaming community, for the sake of better developers who respect their playerbases, don't reward this kind of cash-grubbing, short-sighted behavior.
Edit: Oh, and I'm not even going to get into things like the quality of recent updates, or the promised bounties for finding glitches that were never delivered. Those subjects are too nebulous for me to weigh in on - what I'm talking about here are factual matters that are well documented in public record.

A true classic, Final Fantasy III is a game that will scratch your nostalgia itches in all the right ways.  I completed the game in just over twenty seven hours and I felt entertained from start to finish.  The job system and related leveling up is a blast as is seeing all of the legacy monsters, spells, summons, and legendary weapons in the game.
On the other hand, much of the game does feel dated.  If that's an issue for you, you may want to seek a more modern JRPG.  Locations where you can save may be few and far between, especially in the later parts of the game, which could potentially result in frustrating deaths with a lot of ground to retread.  The story is generic, early Final Fantasy fodder - four warriors of light are here to save the world... crystals... blah blah blah.  The characters, although the game clearly is trying to get you connected to them, are bland and uninteresting, often not even saying anything for hours of gameplay on end.
For what I was expecting when I installed Final Fantasy III, the pros far outweigh the cons.  The game is certainly showing its age but it is still a very enjoyable game as long as you're in it for the old school feel and mechanics as opposed to a story that's going to blow you away.  I absolutely recommend it if you're in for that, however, I can't stress enough, if you're looking for a more modern game with a deeper story and more efficient mechanics, I would look elsewhere.

Aberoth is a MMORPG game. It's gameplay has a character progession system where you can level up different skills, complete quests, and kill newbies because you're not strong enough to beat that guy 5 levels higher than you.
The levelling system in this game is disgusting. As of writing this review, I have around 13 hours played and I'm only level 13. The tedious levelling system takes you HOURS to level up one level, if you're just starting up in a realm with many players. It takes far too long to level up once, and with the many players who are stronger than you and love to pick on the newbies, it's going to be hard to get yourself going.
The combat system is very hard for the new players and easily puts people off. There's a type of fighting called, "kiting", which allows you to hit enemies without taking damage, however,the enemies seem much faster than you and if the enemies get within 2 pixels of you, they hit you and if you're caught by 2-3 enemies you won't make it out of there alive. The items cost way too much to start off with and it's really hard to get gold to buy items and even if you manage to save up for some items, you lose all of your items when you die unless you use gold, to bind them, but even then, there's still a chance you'll lose that item you've worked on hours to get, which, in my opinion, is a terrible system. It doesn't seem to reward your hard work, as the enemies you try and farm desprately, whilst avoiding PKers (Player Killers), and overall doesn't seem worth the effort.
Now, Aberoth doesn't have a real story, instead it has small quests that give high risk for low reward. Each quests takes far too long, for example, one quest task you with collecting 50- yes that's right, 50 knives to collect and give to your questgiver. Now, this wouldn't be so hard, however you can only carry around 3 items at once unless you have an item to increase how much you can carry, and the location where you can get these knives is quite a distance away in another section of the map, and you walk EXTREMELY slow, and with the ton of enemies around, it feels extremely tedious. Not to mention the rewards are usually worthless as you'll most likely lose them in a few minutes because Bobkiller77 is a massive prat.
Now, there isn't much to say for the graphics. It's a 2D-pixel styled game, and in fairness, Aberoth has a great art style. Everywhere really captures the fantasy type setting and it fits really well, so I don't have much to say, it's great.
Aberoth has some great little pieces of audio. There isn't a massive soundtrack, just one track that is really annoying and sometimes never starts or doesn't restart once it's done. However the audio whilst doing actions are good. The walking sounds are good enough to not get annoying and the sounds whilst fighting are a personal favourite of mine. Again, not much to say. It's alright- not great, as there's no real music- but it's alright.
In conclusion, Aberoth is a frustrating mess that doesn't live up to the massive potential it has. Whilst it's just an indie game and doesn't have a heavy development, it's tedious, dull and blood-boiling and unless you have a massive amount of patience, I implore you to stay away until these issues are fixed.

Story
20 years have passed since the events in XCOM: Enemy Unknown and humanity has fallen under alien control. The once supportive council nations have sided with the new alien government during the height of their invasion. Using an administration known as Advent to become a disposable source of manpower, the aliens make an aggressive campaign to earn obedience and loyalty with earth's population. Harsh crowd control tactics and an abundance of Advent propaganda are utilized to invoke fear across the globe. With immense government funding they are a force to be reckoned with, in regards to both manpower and military equipment.
XCOM has become an almost forgotten remnant of the past, leaving many to wonder what the future holds for the human race. However, Resistance forces have burrowed themselves into small pockets of the world, working tirelessly to overthrow Advent and fight for what was once their's. With little resources and time, a small squad of resistance forces act on newly provided Intel. This lead suggests a possible location for a tremendously important figure that is being held in an Advent facility, the Commander.
Once rescued and revived from a medically induced cryo-sleep, the player (taking on the role of The Commander) is briefed on the current state of Earth. With a shell of what XCOM once was, you must gather resources and individuals loyal to the cause and restore XCOM to it's former glory. Technological advancements and utilizing your soldiers abilities to the fullest are the foundation for success, but strategic planning and careful military tactics are what it's built on. Expand the reach of the Resistance by aiding smaller Resistance forces, and set back Advent's development of a mysterious weapon known as the Avatar Project by completing important assignments and destroying key Advent facilities.
Gameplay
XCOM 2 is a turn-based tactical strategy game that is in a league of it's own. Never before have I played a game that has bestowed so much weight in every decision you make. On masterfully designed multi-level maps that are almost entirely destructible, soldiers are controlled like chess pieces with a limit to how many actions they may perform, or tiles they can move. With limited vision of your surroundings, every enemy encounter can be in the players favor through already established defenses, or brutally devastating by enemy flanking maneuvers and abilities. The presence of perma-death only adds to the tension of enemy engagements, and ending your turn pits your tactics against an intelligent and equally lucky AI.
Concealment is the latest and greatest feature, allowing you to enter missions undetected and grants you the ability to ambush your enemies. Solid defensive placement and foreknowledge can be the difference between a devastating blow to Advent forces or a fatal backfire. In addition, a multitude of weapons, armor, and utility items are at your disposal, assuming you researched the necessary criteria and had the required supplies. As well as new and useful abilities that give your soldiers a major advantage on the battlefield, granted you use them correctly.
What flaws are to be found in XCOM 2 however are incessantly apparent. (For Enemy Unknown veterans they may come at no surprise.) These include shots and abilities making contact through walls and objects, hanging animations in certain circumstances following Overwatch shots or soldier placement, numerous instances of clipping, and obscure lines of sight that are both infuriating and laughable. Now these are not game-breaking by any nature but they are certainly a nuisance. Furthermore, they work both ways so while you may be victim to some quite frankly BS shots, you too may find yourself with the same unfair advantage.
User interface and camera controls work well throughout the majority of the game, in small instances though they can be incredibly temperamental. One wrong click can mean the difference between short or high cover, spotted or concealed, dead or alive, so it's aggravating when action keys are click-through if a friendly soldier is nearby or when travel routes get finicky when rotating the map.
When not in combat, time is of the essence as Advent will make slow but steady progress to completing their Avatar Project. If they do, you have a short amount of time to attack a facility or complete specific objectives that stagger it's construction. A great deal of missions are time sensitive as well, requiring the player to make aggressive advancements and react accordingly to enemy reinforcements. Even without a turn/time limit, every action and choice comes with a reward or consequence and XCOM 2 does a great job at making you aware of the result. Tense combat situations, challenging AI and enemy variants, and an immense amount of player freedom and customization.
Sound
XCOM 2 offers as much depth in the sounds and music as it does in it's gameplay. Music is triumphant in success and shattering in defeat. Sound effects are appropriately fitting to each circumstance whether it's gunfire and explosions or destruction and animations. Aliens come to life with intimidating battle-cry's and soldiers express their panicked state or wounded cries in disconcerting fashion.
Dialogue and voice acting is dramatic but not over the top. A satisfying blend of military criticality  as well helpless emotions when things take a turn for the worse. Cinematic scenes are enjoyable both visually and aurally, however (and maybe this was a bug) facial animations noticeably lacked movement when soldiers communicated their understanding of each order.
Graphics
For a game that doesn't need to be graphically beautiful to attract strategy enthusiasts, XCOM 2 is stunning. The amount of detail in the environments, models, armor and weapons, visual effects and lighting are astounding. In what's simply an isometric plane comprised of tiles and levels, it is filled with so much character and tone that it comes to life the moment you touch down. Combat animations resemble movies in the re-positioning camera and the surroundings crumble and shatter from forceful explosions or enemy movement.
Unfortunately, detail like this comes at a price. My gameplay experience maintained solid framerates for the majority of the play-through. Key word majority, guess-timating that atleast 30% of my time was spent wtaching frames drop to as low as 24FPS and then right back up to 60. These occurrences were almost always during cinematic moments, whether it was in or out of combat didn't matter. Destructible environments make for a great gameplay mechanic but when it's framerate teeters back and forth regardless, more ground clutter and visual effects only hurt performance more. Luckily these instances don't take away much from the gameplay itself, but become immersion breaking with frequency. (Ultra on 2560x1080 - i7 6700k / GTX 980 ti)
Replay Value
Arguably infinite, nearly pattern-less. While most missions follow a similar formula for enemy locations and objective markers, the breadth of possibilities is so vast that you're never experiencing the same fight twice. On a global scale and even inside combat enemies behave intelligently and pose a threat to your entire Resistance. (And existence!) Procedural map generation and spurts of luck make for endless possibilities both good and bad. The options for squad loadouts and soldier variety can be the difference between a flawless victory or crushing defeat.
Wrapping Up
A must play. XCOM 2 delivers a challenging experience that leaves you tugging your hair when things go South and exhaling massive sighs of relief when they go right. Despite it's buggy nature and clunky performance, solid strategic gameplay kicks it into sixth gear to overshadow it's imperfections. In a genre polishing checkers, XCOM 2 is reinventing chess.

The following is my experience after a few hours of playing Long War 2 (the XCOM 2 Total Conversion), and the reason I remembered XCOM 1 as a better game than XCOM 2 felt at release. Long War 2 is simply the way the game must be played:
"It looks like the game I remember xcom1 being, and the reason why I didn't really play much xcom2, it felt too easy and less like a war and more like a series of little skirmishes. In war, people die, often.
So, I went into LW2 feeling pretty confident with my skills. Of course I lost 2 soldiers on gatecrasher and had to restart. After that I found out about the infiltration thingy, and looked it up. Pretty simple, and anyone who does not understand it, simply look for 100%+ infiltration, if it is not possible then simply avoid that mission.
Had 3 squads of about 8-10 soldiers with 2 casualties after about 12 missions, thought I was doing really good. Then, Mutons and Vipers (and their new variant) started appearing, as well as MECs. Had to abort a guerilla op which in turn gave the enemy a UFO looking for me.
Got hit around australia and the next scenario is a total nightmare. I sent my less leveled team, thinking I would get reinforcements if I lost people and thinking that I WOULD get hit really hard. But I was extremely underestimating the enemy.
Holding the line became something like an inverse D-day for a couple of turns, hitting the enemy and them dropping like flies. Then it started to go to hell, my soldiers dropping left and right, stun lancers and vipers picking off soldiers. mecs dropping misiles on my positions, and I couldn't even leave the ramp to look for the disruptor.
After about 10 turns of madness a gap appeared and I sent a shinobi to go kamikaze on the disruptor while what was left held the line. The battle was 36/42 for the aliens and I lost 6 soldiers KIA and 6 WIA (3 left behind)
With a squad crippled, Advent now attacked a Haven. Barely held the line with 3 more casualties and 2 wounded.
In just 2 missions, the game told me to sit down and cry as I only have 1 squad left (of badass soldiers from all 3 squads) and about 6 guys wounded and no replacements at all. Loving it."

Let me start off by saying that I agree with the vast majority that this is a very good game. So almost a year after it's been released, I think I can finally give an honest review that does the game justice.
Pros+:
+New combat system, which is harder and a lot more fun compared to previous titles.
+New stealth mode, which captures the moral of a TRUE assassin.
+New parkour buttons, for parkouring upwards and downwards, which make parkour so much smoother.
+An awesome story that occurs in the French revolution, which is personally one of my favorite historic events.
+A big variety of missions, collectibles and side missions that make the game more fun, so there's always what to do.
+An online co-op system, in which you could join other players in missions that are exclusive to the online gameplay.
+The atmosphere is captivating and very expressive. Makes you feel like you're really in a revolution.
+The graphics are heavenly stunning. They give the feeling of what you'd remember Paris to be like in that period of time instead of making you feel like it's happening now.
Cons-
-Glitches that make the game unplayable at time. i.e. glitching through buildings or falling underground.
-Low frame rates. Even on a powerful computer the game still struggles to find stability.
-Freezing and frame drops are annoying as hell, and most of the times it makes you put your controller down and quit.
-Graphics glitches, which to me were minimal to nonexistent.
This game is broken!
It could've been a great game, because the gameplay, atmosphere, story, mission variety, combat system, graphics and mechanics of it are almost flawless! Yet my PC (runs GTAV, Far Cry 4, etc.. at 30-50FPS) still struggles to find out how a game with such technical flaws works, which ,for that matter, it doesn't.
The frame drops, freezing, and low frame rates are disgustingly annoying, still after a year of the game being released and patched a bunch of times!
Moral of the story, you'd be better off playing this game on a console, since Ubisoft ♥♥♥♥ed up big time on this one.
Here's to the next title, and here's to hoping they get it together, technically, since they have a solid gameplay base.
Good luck!

First off, this game may not be everyone's cup of tea. If you are not a fan of Simulation Games like Harvest Moon and old school looks, it may turn you away. Don't let that throw you off though. This game oozes charm with its SNES style graphics and old school play style. If modding is your thing, there is a chunk of mods to take this further as well.
The game itself is Harvest Moon on steroids. A LOT of variety in crops and stuff you can do to make a living, upgrading your farm, relationships with the town, animals, foraging, and a bit of combat as well to mix things up.
PROS
Easy to use controls and Menus.
Charming presentation and old school graphics and feel.
Lots of stuff to keep you busy and playing around on your farm.
Mod Support is there, Nexus has stuff as do other places.
CONS
Expect a slow start and a chunk of grinding while you try and get what you need to upgrade your tools and farm.
Lots of repetition.
Combat isn't anything special and lacks much depth.
If you are a fan of Harvest Moon, you should be playing this game. End of Story.
If you are looking for a calm time killer simulation to spend your hours on, this will fill the bill nicely.
Overall, I HIGHLY recommend this to anyone. The old school charm, and throw back to the Classic Harvest Moon Games is a win in my book. Worth the price, and worth a look.

Also, for you completionists out there, you can spend hours trying to find all of the clovers and astral beads.
Each time you learn a new brush skill, or turn a barren patch of land vibrant again, or even feed animals you come across, there is a sense of accomplishment and you are rewarded with a visual treat.

I beat it on the wii, but still enjoyed it enough to justify purchasing it for PC. No regrets here.

The Original Gangster. The First Hitman game (Hitman: Codename 47) took the gaming world by storm when it came out in 2000 and remains a cult classic to this day.
One of the finest Stealth / Strategy RPG's of its generation, it puts you in the role of Agent 47, a shadowy assassin who is equally capable of slipping in and out of target locations un-noticed as he is of pulling out a pair of chrome-plated 'Ballers' and taking absolutely everyone out. With a broad range of missions from the 'Lee Hong Assassination' (Rooftop Sniper takedown) to the 'Massacre at the Cheung Chow Fish House' (No one comes out alive), the game provides a wealth of memorable situations you will talk about years down the road.
The game is not without its flaws - for a game nearly 14 years old, gameplay mechanics can be somewhat clunky. Probably the biggest gripe however is the in-game Save option, which does not exist. If you are spotted in the middle of a mission or die, you will need to start the mission over. While not a big issue in the earlier (shorter) missions, this can become extremely frustrating on the later missions where you need to navigate a huge mansion with tons of guards and after 20 minutes of perfection, one mis-step means you're killed and need to restart.
Do not let the gripes stop you from playing this classic which spawned 5 sequels and a movie to boot. This is the OG, the Original Hitman - where stealth, strategy and patience are virtues and the reward is the perfect hit.   Rated - (8/10)

Original review by 17 year-old Luke: "A narrator who compares with even Morgan Freeman, challenging gameplay and a deep story - with a unique storytelling style. If you have working hands: play this game."
While 19 year-old Luke agrees, I feel as though there's more to say, since looking back at Bastion: it still feels like one of my most significant gaming experiences of ever.
That viewpoint is perhaps somewhat nostalgic; this was one of the first real PC games I played back when I was still primarily a console gamer. So I will look back on it with that same sense of importance as Assassin's Creed 2 or Uncharted 2, the first two PlayStation 3 games I played.
Nevertheless, there are elements of this game that make it recommendable to anyone, despite its personal significance to myself and the close friends who played and discussed it with me back then.
Firstly, the narration is exquisite - and yes, past-luke, it does compare to Morgan Freeman. The narration really draws you into the world quite quickly, and although I don't have a vivid memory of the world that the game was set in, I do have a vivid memory of the (protagonist) kid's adventure through that world. The narration is your first contact with that world, right into the game's ending moments - which I won't spoil, but I will say that they are very well crafted from a storytelling perspective.
Secondly, I said the game had challenging gameplay. I'm not sure why I said that really. I did die a few times, but that was just because I wasn't used to playing with a keyboard and mouse more than anything. As James (M!dD3) points out in his comment, the gameplay is straightforward and simple, with a wide array of weapons to choose from and experiment with. And for those who want more out of a game's challenge - there are indeed way to buff your enemies in the name of bragging rights.
For me though, the gameplay wasn't a prominent factor. More important was the music, the soundtrack is amazing and undefinable by common genres. I've heard it described as "acoustic frontier trip-hop", so....yeah. Lovely. I still listen to that soundtrack today, and everyone I've encouraged to listen to it has loved the sounds: from friends my age, to adults, to grandparents.
However, a game's soundtrack isn't rated by the quality of the sounds alone; in-game that is an irrelevant quality. But the music fits the game perfectly. I can still recall the chilling hammer-on-stone clangs of "mine, windbag, mine' as I entered an eerie stage and began to learn more of the truth of the strange world. And don't even get me started on "build that wall" and "mother, I'm here" - or better yet, their lovechild: "setting sail, coming home", to this day one of my favourite songs.
The artstyle is equally captivating while in game, there's a certain childish element to the designs that mix with the seriousness of the plot - summing up the kid's overburdened mindset perfectly. There's a reason that kid looks so melancholy on the game's cover art.
And I suppose that brings me to the final element that I mentioned, the game's "deep plot". Yes, well, that's one way to put it. Let me just say the decisions I made in that game hold true to the way I intend to continue to view my failures and embrace the future for the rest of my life. That is by no means an overstatement, or some pretentious interpretation of the game's plot. This game is simple and important, that's all there is to it. So, as past-luke rightfully said: "if you have working hands: play this game."

There aren't many things I see wrong with it but I'll list what I didn't care for. I save a lot as I play rpgs, so being limited to 3 save slots was tough on me. The game at points isn't always the clearest about where to go next, but I expect that of rpgs. Lastly, be careful of switching jobs in an area you just arrived. I did that once or twice and was stuck struggling to raise my level so that I could survive the new area.
Overall I would really recommend it, and it's a great way to start the series since there's no big, complex story behind it. You can pick up/stop and not have too much difficulty in knowing what is going on. One last bit, it's controller friendly, but in my opinion setting the key inputs for awsd layout works great.

What didn't i like about this game?
Well for starters, the game does not help you along the way at all, no hints, no tips, no tutorial, nothing. Now before you point your pitchforks at me let me explain. i'm ok that a game dosen't hold your hand all the way, i'm just asking to learn the very basic of the game to be able to play. For example, the game does not autosave, you have to do that on your own. Fair enought, i'll just save manually, BUT WAIT, you can't save while your in a dungeon or town, you have to be in the world map to save. it's things like that i whould like to know before starting playing the game, becuse the first time i played this game, i went into a dungeon, died, and had to start a completely new savefile beacuse i haden't saved yet. I did realise later that there where NPC that told you about things like this but if you just happen to not talk to them, you missed out on that critical information and was kinda doomed to figure it out on your own.
Another thing i could not wrap my head around was the job system and the weapon support for every job. Job's are kinda like classes and as you raise yor job level you get stronger. Once again the game does not tell you what perks a job had, which weapon you can use while having a certain job, what spells you can use etc. You could learn this by talking to a specific NPC but once again, if you didn't you had to figure it out on your own. Also as you progressed you unlocked more jobs but changing to a new job makes your job level 1 again and you have to farm to be able to match the current level of the mobs and teammates.
That brings us to the weapon support, it was wierd. Now leveling up your job was just half the jouney, you had to have a good weapon to harvest that sweet level you grined for. Only thing is, the weapons your job requiered was only sold a specific stores at specific locations. You could pass two town with a certain job and almost don't get any support at all. This made it even harder to play certain jobs and which made me change back to other jobs just to be able to pass some areas. That resulted in me having to farm to get back the exp i lost while playing as another job. It was either that or playing as an almost usless charachter that made ruffly a third (or less) of the damage my teammates did.
Now get me right, i'm not agains farming. It's a great way to stay one step before the game, dedecating time to making your playthrough easier/funnier. But when the game requieres you to farm to progress, it's just get's boring.
This formula repeated itself several times and at this point i did not enjoy playing it anymore and just gave up on it.
I whould not recommend playing this game, i felt like it made it hard and boring to play certain parts of the game when i really should be fun and exciting. Not everything about this game is bad, heck, most thing are pretty good. But it wasn't enought for me to keep playing it.

Terribly disappointed by this game. Even the 3€ something during the most recent sale were too much, imho.
While the Game does use some Linux command line inputs to navigate on the computer (cd to change folders, ls to list contents, cat to read a file), those become useless once you completed the tutorial and gain access to the User Interface (mouse control), which is much faster.
"Hacking" works by starting skripts that automate the whole process. All you have to do is start the same 5 skripts by typing their name:
If there is a proxy active, use your own to overload it (click the overwhelm button).
If there is a firewall active, type analyze 5 times, then type solve and the password that was just revealed.
For any available port, type the name of the corresponding skript, wait for it to finish (about 10 seconds), then start the next one.
Sometimes, there is a time limit that never really got close to bothering me.
The story is either really weak or did not really start by the time I quit. You get a first E-Mail (I don't know you, please help me). Then, to build up your skills, you hack at least two dozen systems, always using the method described above, working your way up in some hacker organization you don't really know anything about. When you finally find that you are done with them, you start at bottom level of the next organization.
Conclusion:
Apart from my desire not to leave the game unfinished, there is absolutely nothing that would make me keep playing. Not recommended.

recommend this for those who have already played it as a kid, or for those who want to experience the classics.

• One of the most engaging and emotional stories I've ever played
• No other game has challenged your moral decision making like this one
• You end up getting attached to the characters and loosing them becomes heart breaking
• You are able to choose the fate of your character and the role you want to play

• Ending is heartbreaking and is a great way to wrap up the game

• Comes with awesome and short DLC that adds a little more to the game
• Graphics aren't too stellar even when maxed out

As someone who doesn't get very emotional, this game brought me to tears. The relationships you build feel realistic where you really feel like your decisions impact the plot. You are thrown into a world with a little girl and are forced to make decisions based on what you think is right. No other game has ever challenged you by telling a little girl the scary truth or lying so she is not afraid. For a "point and click" game it is very well done and the story will leave you breathless. The dialog is well done and the story has good structure as well. I wish more cinematic views with music were added to amplify the mood. Although a few things could be made more smooth, this has become easily one of my favorite games of all time and I highly recommend this game for anyone and everyone.

Greetings Everyone!
Let me start by saying that Final Fantasy is a game series that has been with me for as long as I can remember.  I learned to read though these games even learned new words, ideas and approached challenges through these games.  So, I am far from unbiased.
Remodeled and Ported:  If you can’t tell the game was remade for a more modern generation with maintaining a vast majority of the content (bugs and all) which is done very well for when it was made.  Understand that it was created for the Nintendo DS and not a computer however and it still retains the charm from when I first played it (on a poorly translated ROM) and the graphical overall is a nice touch as well.  With all the classic sounds and music it definitely takes me back while being fresh.
Frustrating but Simple:  One thing that I forgot about this game is how frustrating it can be from time to time; especially giving directions to the player.  There are times where you just don’t plainly know where to go and you spend a few hours flying, running or boating around hoping for something to happen.  Also, the magic system is based around old school magic which means you only get so many casts ‘a day’ (until you rest), no mana bar, no ethers and switching classes isn’t going to help either.  This initially created a lot of frustration for me (who knew almost two decades apart things would change the way I play games haha) but as I go used to it I found myself digging into my inventory for potions, coming up with other strategies (Bards are amazing) or just taking that final hit risk while my entire party is almost dead.  The system overall is very simple, trivially so to the point you forget the depth that is there until it smacks you across the face!
Some DLC?  Yay? Not sure:  There are some additions to the game, mainly a mini section (you have to cast mini on yourself) which I wish I was a bit more prepared for.  The game definitely doesn’t hold your hand and left spending an hour or so wondering what to do, especially if you have primarily physical based classes and the only magic you use is healing and defenses (aka me).  In hindsight I’m glad this was in the game, just wish it gave a bit more direction.  One criticism I will level is that the game was not really made for computers, it would have taken little to no time to update the standard keyboard commands, but they didn’t.  They did go as far as some basic ones and the game’s text does interpret it (which I appreciate).
Ultimately, if you like Final Fantasy you owe it to yourself to experience its history and if you are craving an old school RPG this might be for you as well.  However, if you are looking for some ground breaking system and immersive story I’d pass this up.  This was the groundwork of RPGs this is the history of where RPGs come from.  I’d still recommend a buy but just a warning.  Get out there and become the Warriors of Light!

This game was a disappointment since the first crowdfunding event started and failed. While GMod Tower was immensely hindered by GMod and every update that came out, it had established itself as a fun and silly distraction where you could just go kart racing as Solid Snake or Luigi or a Stormtrooper.
Tower Unite released buggy, laggy and server-congested with none of the issues seen in GMod Tower fixed and possibly even worsened by the engine transfer. That combined with the new pricetag and the lack of any features or gamemodes to speak of on launch put me off as well as all of my friends who I used to enjoy playing GMT with. To this day only three of my friends actually have Tower Unite and nobody else but us is willing to touch this game.
The added server browser and option to start game servers outside of a lobby spread the tiny fanbase to its absolute thinnest and it's impossible to get a game of anything going anymore besides minigolf if you're lucky. The game's performance is still abysmal and they still haven't added everything back from GMT, for some reason focusing on trite pointless garbage like bowling, fishing, trivia and laser tag rather than the actual major gamemodes they're still missing like Source Karts (or Accelerate now) or the top down zombie mode. Even now they fail to meet promises set in their projected dev timeline and every time I check back on this game expecting it to be vastly different I see virtually nothing of value new.
The sad part is that I knew all of this would happen. The first Kickstarter was a failure that I refused to contribute to because I knew that all of this mismanaging, hollow deadlines and playerbase thinning would happen and the only reason they eventually got funding was because they moved to a crowdfunding site that didn't require the goal to be met for them to get paid.
If this sounds biased or emotionally charged you're absolutely right, I miss GMT quite a lot and still don't see this ever meeting the height that the original did. Nobody has faith in this enough to pay for it and as disappointed as I've been every time I check back on this it's losing its point.
Don't buy it until it's out of early access, if they even manage to get it that far.

Playing this is a clear sign of how far the Hitman series has come in regards to improving its gameplay. This game is riddled with problems that honestly I'm surprised I kept playing it all the way until the end. In theory, this game gives you objectives and then lets you figure out how to handle them. In practice however, the levels only really allow for one specific strategy in order to complete them. It ends up becoming a game that, rather than being about finding creative ways to brutally kill people, is really just about figuring out what you exactly must do to finish the level and then executing it.
So there's basically no variation. Also the AI is beyond terrible. I've shot guards and, so long as nobody saw me shoot them, I could stand right next to the body as the guards run up to investigate without thinking that I was the one who did it. I suppose I should be grateful about this though, because you need to kill plenty of people to finish each level. And if you get caught, expect to end up in a massive gunfight that you can have serious trouble surviving. A single witness or one unsilenced gunshot can ruin everything. Sadly, while there are a few levels that truly allow you to be a sneaky hitman, there are more levels where you are just gunning people down. And the last level doesn't even try: it's a straight shootout without any chance for subtle tactics.
If you want to be a sneaky assassin, this is not the game for you. This game's only real value at this point is that it messed up enough that the game developers had to learn from the mistakes made here. And that led to them making the fantastic Hitman: Blood Money.
But there's no real reason to play this one. Save your money and your time.

Okay, I loved this game. I thought it was the best LEGO game I've ever played... At least until I unexpectedly hit the end of the game right at the end of The Desolation of Smaug. I thought it was the complete game, I didn't bother to read any reviews and so was very annoyed/angry when I hit the equivalent of a brick wall going at 70 mph because I thought I still had a whole third of the game to still get through.
Of course they did put enough sidequests and characters in that I'm still working on 100% completion but I still felt quite cheated and betrayed when I found out that there was no Battle of the Five Armies, and no plans for a DLC ever. =,(
That being said I have very few, if any, complaints about the game itself. It's just challenging enough that I can enjoy it, and when I play with smaller kids (Ages 3-4-7.) it's not too hard as long as you don't mind waiting\explaining\guiding in addition to being patient with them. At least the younger kids, if you've been around any kids for any good stretches of time, you already know that.
I had to tweak the options of course, Dynamic view tends to be a bit disorenting to me if there is too much back and forth during the levels. And the graphics made my computer overheat until I turned them down to Medium and Low, but even at those settings is still looked good, didn't get grainy or anything like that.
They use some of the same world that they do in LOTR LEGO, Rivendell for example. I just started that game but I think that's really nice. Of course it may have been easier to reuse parts of the world that they had already done previously, but like the kind of same world continuity that brings to the game.
Sometimes the quest locator/guide is...confused? It doesn't always get you where you want to go. And sometimes it will lead you somewhere and whatever you are looking for will be there because there's another quest you have to do first. But of course it won't tell you that. So that can be frustrating, but it's been long enough since the game came out that you can find multiple walkthroughs and tips online on just about any part of the game that might stump you.
Overall, a pretty solid game, so long as you know beforehand that it's incomplete. It's still hours of fun, especially if you get it on a good sale.

Okay, so i'm gonna make a 2nd more objective review of this game. I did not get into it very far. my 40 minutes in game was mostly spent reading text and clicking enter. this is going to go over the techniacl aspects of this game as a port NOT the gameplay or the story itself (there are tons of reviews for the original game, go look up those). The game initially gave me the few settings that i think are important for a pc port. Resolution, (it let ME go up to 1080p) refresh rate, (a little weird it let me go to 144 since the game is capped at 30FPS in game and 60FPS in menu) and windowed borderless (also weird since the main benefit to me for borderless is the freedom to mouse over to my 2nd monitor, more on that later)
The graphics look old, or "classic" if that's what you're looking for. Which is hit or miss for people. I presonally did not mind the older style graphics, but i was also under the impression that they would take the original Okami and give it some amazing eye candy. But after doing some research i found something interesting. THIS IS NOT A NEW HD REMAKE of the original Okami like i assumed it was. It is a port of  "Okami HD" that was realeased on ps3. The HD graphics are not what i would call current HD graphics. They are the same HD graphics from 2012.
The keyboard and mouse controls don't feel smooth or well thought out. Being locked at 30 fps gives the mouse a huge amount of input latency that i am not used to with my 144hz monitor, (but for people used to 30 fps on pc or maybe even 60 this might be fine for you). so it came at a big shock and was dissapointing. On top of that when i tried to use my xbox one controller (both wirelessly through a dongle and cabled with micro usb) the game did not register it. This seems to be an issue for some people and not others, so your milage may vary. So i was stuck with mouse and keyboard.
The UI does not feel natural and is one of the main reasons i can not say this is a good pc port. you have to navigate the settings with WASD and your mouse is never given the freedom to control it (which on a game released on PC seems terrible, and shows me that the devs didn't really give it any thought). Other various little things, like alt tabbing would change the game from fullscreen windowed to windowed at a lower resolution (1600x by something, i can't really remember) which then you need to go back to the main menu to re adjust those settings. (because it doesn't let you change it in game) And even after that i wasn't given the freedom to move my mouse over to pause my video on my 2nd monitor.
The game locks your mouse into the window at ALL times, meaning that i couldn't even do the simplest thing to close it (being clicked the X to close the window)  I had to back out of the game after saving, skip past the intro cinimatic (who knows why it plays everytime you go back to menu) and then click exit game.
For disclaimer for the next section, i have  I7-7700k and GTX 1070. the game ran at a rock solid 30 fps (lol) the entire time for me at high settings (but if it didn't i doubt it would run well for anyone) But what was concerning to me though was  that this game was using up 50% of my CPU BY ITSELF while at the same time only using 5% of my grpahics card. I don't know why it was hitting my CPU that hard and not even touching my graphics card. But that was just another sign to me that this game was not a good port.
Besides that there isn't much else to say. there were several other points that made me think this is a clunky and not well thought or worked out port. If all you want though is to replay the old Okami HD without having to dig out your old PS3, this game is perfect for you. But if you are like me and were looking for a remastered version of the game for PC that gives you all the benefits of your higher end hardware, this is not for you. i have already recieved a refeundsince there were to many imperfections in it for my taste. I will probably buy it some time later on a sale, but not for full price

One of the greatest games created by TellTale.
Based off of the comic series of the same name,
places you in the shoes of Lee Everett: a convicted criminal who must now survive in a zombie apocalypse. While trying to survive he runs into other survivors, most notably a little girl named Clementine. It's up to Lee to protect Clementine from both the undead and the living.
With the exception of a few minor characters who only appear in episode 1,
is not connected to the main plot of the comics, so even if you haven't read the comics or watched the show you can still fully understand this game.
The game is a point and click adventure that focuses more on the struggles of surviving/solving puzzles and less on mindlessly murdering hundreds of zombies (though there still are some action sequences). This will probably scare away most buyers, but the people who can get past this will find themselves enjoying one of the most emotional games available on Steam (to those that
want a mindless Walking Dead shooter, you can purchase the mediocre Walking Dead: Survival Instinct for double the price of this great game).
Along the course of the game you'll be able to make certain choices that may affect who lives/dies or how others treat you. Although these choices don't really lead to any major "alternate paths", they are enough to making yourself feel responsible for every choice you make. You may be tempted to redo your playthrough so you can redo one choice you made, but it's honestly better to just keep going since it'll make your current playthrough much more meaningful.
Every survivor in the game is fleshed out and has something that makes them unique. Whenever a main character dies you will almost always have a rush of emotions - whether it be anger or sadness. Unlike most zombie games you will actually care about the main characters and how things turn out for them. Overall, there are some really amazing moments in this game that may leave your eyes running.
I wish I could go into detail about how great each episode is, but I don't want to spoil them. Even if you aren't a fan of The Walking Dead comics - or zombie culture in general - you will absolutely love this game.

I enjoyed playing Heat Signature while I did, and may come back to it.  The gameplay is a lot of fun and I enjoy the concept behind the game.  Basically, you play one of several scoundrels who take on jobs to steal items, or assassinate targets, or hijack entire spaceships.  You start off with a weapon and an item to help you, and accumultate more along the way.  All of this is to earn money to complete a personal mission, which is generally much, much more difficult.  As you complete jobs, you also gain fame, which allows you to unlock more regions, which also unlocks helpful weapons or items.
The gameplay loop is pretty fun for a while, but you quickly reach a point where your character only has the option to take on difficult missions, and it's hard to get items necessary to complete the more difficult ones.  I did not complete any of the personal missions due to their difficulty.  I just got frustrated with always getting too difficult missions, so I reached a point where I would intentionally get characters killed off so I could create a new one, do easier missions and unlock more of the galaxy.
But sadly, it just got a little old for me.  It was the same thing over and over, and I lost interest.  I may come back to it later.  I do recommend it if you're a sci-fi nerd like me or just want to play something different, but I don't see myself ever completing the game.

So far I'm having a blast with it. It's almost like a cross between Hotline Miami and Deus Ex set in space. There's countless ways you can deal with objectives. Even if you don't have the proper tools for the job there's usually a way to deal with something so long as you use a bit of creativity. Have to capture an armored target but don't have concussion grenades? Lure him to a room with a window and shoot it out, then take remote control of your pod to catch him before he can suffocate. Did you screw up and you've got five seconds left before you're captured? Throw yourself out a window or breach the hull to space yourself and catch yourself with your pod.
I do have some gripes with it though, primarily with how repetitive it gets but more importantly the difficulty of some of the missions, especially the personal missions. Like regular missions, personal missions are randomized but are generated in a way that makes them more difficult than usual. The problem is that the way they're generated is more often than not done in a way that just isn't fun. For example, with the last personal mission I tried I was given an assassination target aboard a huge ship with 220 seconds to either kill my target or kill the pilot which would stop the count down. Pretty standard stuff right?
Oh by the way all the bosses have shields which reflect all forms of damage unless they're disabled. Still no problem right? I'll just save my subverters and crash beams for those guys. Haha no. Regular guards had shields too. They also had glitch teleporters meaning the second they heard anything suspicious they could simply teleport to my exact location. Now you're probably thinking I could have just picked them off one by one but it gets even better. The mission had the extra guards and extra sentry turrets parameters which meant tons of guards, usually grouped together in teams of five or six.
Still, personal missions aren't manditory so really I've just been able to ignore them completely. As far as I can tell the only rewards for them are a huge cash bonus and liberty boost which can easily be surpassed by doing a couple of hard-audacious missions which tend to be much more fun and balanced.
Despite my rant about the personal missions though, I'd still strongly recommend the game. I've only put 8 hours into it so far but I can still see myself playing it for a considerable amount of time to come.

I've been trying to work my way through this game, but it's been a slow road. I played it a few hours, got bored, tried FFV to see a better version of the Job System (and pretty much everything else), then came back to this game. I played a few more hours, got bored, then played FFIV because I wanted to play an FF game but was having a tough time playing this game. Then I played FFIV: The After Years, couldn't make it in very far at all because it's a tacky quasi-asset-flip of FFIV with a different story that rips off parts of FFIV's plot, and came back here to FFIII again...or at least I came back to my Steam games list and winced, just staring at this game on the list, not wanting to play it because I had so little motivation and enjoyment from playing it.
Anyway, I've made up my mind that I think I'm just going to stop playing FFIII. I played plenty of it to know that I don't like it and that forcing myself to play more of it won't make me like it, so I'll go into a few things I did and didn't like, and explain quite why it is that I have no interest in proceeding more into the game.
I didn't like FFIII, but I have to give credit where it's due. This game's soundtrack is great. I highly recommend listening to it on Youtube while you're reading articles online or a book, etc. I've gone back and listened to the soundtracks from I & II, and this series just has great music. Nobuo Uematsu is the man. You owe it to yourself to listen to the soundtracks of all the FF games he worked on, and some of more recent ones that even he didn't write. I do not support his "Crazy Chocobo" song, though, from FFXIII-2.
I don't have much to say here. It's got a sort of cutesy look that works well enough. The enemies look a bit meh, even compared to FFIV, which is done in the same style. This version of FFIII definitely looks better, graphically, than screenshots I've seen of the NES version, obviously. My only qualm about the graphics is the need to manually zoom in, which gives you a stupidly close view of everything, and you have to do it fairly often to look fo secrets. The graphics are pretty good.
This is a bit of a precursor to my gameplay section of the review. The job system lets you switch your characters from being warriors, to black mages or red mages, etc. You can do it any time, based on which crystal(s) you've reached in the game. I have issues with FFV, but its job system has reasons to use other jobs. In FFIII, on the other hand, if you are playing the game intelligently, you will almost never change jobs. When you get a better job, you drop the old one and never touch it again. You're rewarded for picking one class/job and sticking with it very far into the game. There are no benefits carried over between jobs/classes based on your progress in a different job/class, and it's just so pointless.
FFI and FFII allowed players to select the permanent jobs of their party members when starting the game. Since FFIII has an ideal set of jobs, based on the aforementioned info I covered, FFI and FFI handled jobs better by cutting out the silliness of switching jobs when switching jobs is almost useless. The only times it is worthwhile in FFIII is if you make the entire party something like blackbelts, which will make you able to wipe pretty much every enemy encounter in a turn or two, amounting to easy mode, and switching to your diverse party for the occasional boss, only. Oh, and it's supposedly worthwhile if you plan on power-gaming to character level 99 to use the onion knight class and steamroll the game.
What's really silly is that the most efficient way to level your characters' jobs is to have everyone block for a few rounds against the easiest enemy in the entire game, then win the battle. You can reliably level up a job one time per battle, and it takes very little time to do this, thus discouraging fighting as you travel, or even fighting in new areas with tougher monsters. Instead, it enourages you to stay in the easiest map in the game, grinding a job to max, then wiping the floor with everything that's not a boss.As a power-gamer myself, I can tell you that this is pretty broken, but I didn't find this aspect fun, even.
Long story short, this job system is pointless and they may as well have just done the FFI and FFII "pick your party member classes/jobs" permanently at the start of the game, and just stick to character levels, because my characters had the same basic function for my entire playtime.
If you ever played an FF game from the SNES era, or anything newer than that, and you thought "that story was a bit too simple," FFIII is going to amaze you at how much more simple and boring it can be. I did not complete the game, but from my journeys to the crystals I visited, I was never once interested or entertained by a single moment in the story, or by a single character. I'm not asking for much. I found FFIV's story to be meh, and its characters to be mostly quite shallow, but FFIII managed to suck every ounce of intrigue out of its setting. As far in as I got, the game was bankrupt of anything interesting going on, or any characters I actually liked.
In summary, it's one of those stupid "You're the heroes of light!" plots where you go see a crystal, visit a town, go to a dungeon, kill a boss, repeat ad nauseum. That happens in other FF games, but they tend to have more interesting stuff happening to keep players intrigued. Here, however, the phrase "I couldn't care less" would somehow manage to be an understatement.
This isn't bad, but it's also not all that good. I do enjoy how the game is turn-based, like FFX is later in the series. I like the active time combat system some of the other games have, but turn-based is nice for coming up with interesting combat strategies that the ATD system might cause players to overlook due to the time constraints of said system. The combat works nice enough, but the game lacks some of the spell variety of FFIV, and without the game mixing up your party like FFIV does, or having a job system with a reason to switch often, like FFV does, meaning FFIII is markedly simple. Simple can be good, but when everything else in the game was so lame to me, I really needed the gameplay to draw me in, and it did not succeed on that front.
With FFIII, you get quality music, okay graphics and gameplay, and a world that's Final Fantasy at its most regurgitated basic fantasy level, which characters who are arguably more disinteresting than the setting and what I saw of the story. I am not disparaging FFIV or FFV, because I think they did a pretty good job with the pre-FFVI fantasy settings the series leaned toward. The job system is one of FFIII's biggest features, but it's flawed to the point that its existence was not needed and choosing classes at the start would have been just fine, as in FFI and FFII. My recommendation is that you avoid this game, play something better instead, and check out the FF soundtracks, because there are some great songs out there.

Since release I checked in on the critical and user reviews across the webz about this game many times.
I could not help but notice its retail price had not dropped in like.. a year (how long has it been since launch?). Crappy games don't do that - the price goes down usually and fast.
So i picked it up. Man oh man I have not enjoyed XCOM this much in a long time.
It is not the same formula as the old XCOM so don't come in expecting that. Don't pick it up unless you have a gaming rig because it is demanding. As a point of reference, with some tweaks I am running comfortably on High and it looks and runs great. 3-year old MSI mid-range gaming laptop with a 970m gtx card - hardly groundbreaking there, and was only considered mid-high-end when it came out, awhile ago.
The quality of the port is top notch. All the settings you'd expect are there, the menus are execellent, everything is bindable, no mention of a controller, no changes require a restart or reload, no crashes or technical issues at all.
The atmosphere, music, sense of urgency and the gravity of each mission is awesome. I find myself actually caring about the outcome and having something actually at stake. The VIP rescue mission that you'd think I would hate actually resulted in an awesome emergent drama of sorts, a tough decision, and a major risk that paid off in full. Satisfaction, and it easily could have gone the other way. But it didn't, because I'm baf.
I am playing on normal, with ironman mode (constant save, no undoing anything) and for me the ironman mode is essential, I recommend that because the stakes are 'real' and things matter more.
There are more great things I could say about it such as solider progression and how that already feels so satisfying and I instantly got attached to one of them that I'm now trying to keep alive, but that covers the essentials for now..

Surprisingly good. In this game, the expectation of surviving with all your heroes alive is.. totally unreasonable.
Got this game recommended to me by a friend and after having watched him play it for a solid while, I was sold. Probably one of the most worthy purchases I have done on this steam account.
I've played this game for a while now and I don't expect that this is going to change anytime soon. You'll see a lot of complaints about this game being very RNG-heavy. While this is true, and you will get your♥♥♥♥♥slapped by continuous bad RNG (like entering the first battle with 80 stress due to traps and heroes inspecting curios with a negative outcome) you can absolutely do something about this. For example, the most successful explorations require the best preparation. Not risking killing an enemy and instead healing your hero, may save you from (negative) stress (resolves) on your party and/or a hero.
There's a lot of considerations to be made in playing this game. Paying a high amount of gold to get rid of a negative quirk is something I had never thought of when I was a newer player. But consider this; if a quirk lowers your dodge by 5 and you decide to get rid of this for a measly 1500-5000 gold, just think of the amount of times you won't be hit in the grand scheme of things. Gold is a limited resource and is used to upgrade your heroes, this also requires you to think about where you spend it.
Combat is fun in this game. There's two kinds of passive damage, crit% you can influence with equipment, as well as with abilities, there's stunning attacks, and a newly introduced stealth mechanic that disallows you from hitting the enemy with this ability for 2 turns. Then there's the different classes. There's nearly endless amount of party compositions you can build with (including DLC) 17 different hero classes available, allowing you to experiment with this. That said, religious characters do not want to venture out with the 'Abomination' class, effectively making a great composition I had in mind fall into shambles.
The art style attributes to the more sinister, shadowy feel of the game. Then last but certainly not least, the narrator is incredible. Along with the general narration of the game, it creates this extreme and inhumane environment, while the characters feel very humane.
