Pros:
+ Visually a beautiful game
+ Coming back to an expansive urban setting was welcome
+ Plentiful amount of weapons and armors
+ Arno & Elise are the best characters since Ezio Auditore
+ At its core there's a good story here
Cons:
- Even after Patch 5 the game doesn't run as well as it should
- Locking a quarter of the weapons and armor behind co-op missions
- Horrible attempt to integrate the Companion App and Initiates
- Combat is challenging but more frustrating and nonsensical than anything else
- Utter lack of a "modern" story-arc
- Lack of focus
The Bottom Line:
It honestly pains me to say that this is the first Assassin's Creed game that I cannot recommend. Obviously if you're a series fan you're going to play it anyway but for those with a more casual interest? Skip this chapter, you can find something else to sink 60 - 90 hours into.
I won't babble on about the horrid launch or how technical issues plagued the game for the first couple months - that's in the past and most serious issues have been ironed out. At this point, its current state is the best you're going to get and as long as you've got the hardware you should be ok.
I also won't go on about how much the Companion App/Initiates and the locking of gear behind Co-op missions was a questionable and down-right annoying choice. That's pretty clear as it is.
However what I will emphasize as being the biggest flaw of Unity is its complete lack of focus on what matters. Assassin's Creed 3 started a trend that has become more and more chaotic as the franchise has gone on. What am I referring to? Collectibles, side missions, and other distractions. While it's true that more-or-less every Assassin's Creed game has featured these elements, before AC 3 they were done in moderation. The focus was firmly on the story - its events and characters. Treasure chests, eagle feathers, and Templar Knights were there for those that wanted achievements/trophies, and side missions were few and far between and usually expanded upon or branched off from the main story-line or were simple and fun (like the "platforming" missions in Assassin's Creed 2).
Yet after Assassin's Creed 3 there was this significant push to fill the game-worlds with distracting extras. Suddenly we needed to collect hundreds of treasure chests and animus fragments, or carry out territory wars all over the place for a modest increase in our income. More and more the focus shifted from the stories these games wanted to tell and we found ourselves coming back to the next memory sequence with a hazy idea of what was happening and who these characters (both our own and the supporting cast) even were. This created a large disconnect between the player and the story/characters, suddenly Assassin's Creed was more about naval battles and treasure hunting and less about the timeless struggle between Templar and Assassin.
Unity takes this disconnect, this lack of focus, to all new heights. It wants us to pay attention, wants us to get invested in Arno and Elise's quest for revenge, the useless and static French Brotherhood, the Templar civil war, and how these play against the backdrop of Revolutionary France but then it throws distraction after distraction at you. "Play Co-op!", "Use the Companion App!", "Play through our 50+ Paris Stories and Murder Mysteries!", "Tackle theives and kill criminals hundreds of times for a reward!", "Find that random treasure chest that unlocks that weapon/armor!", and so on and so on.
Simply put: Unity lacks focus and it pays the price for that. Unity will fatigue you, it will annoy you, it will frustrate you.

First things first:
YES, it has keyboard and mouse support.
YES, you can use the Celestial Brush with the mouse.
YES, you can skip any cutscenes and text without needing to complete the game first.
YES, you can use a drawing tablet to play.
Now:
After the first few minutes (16 to be exact), I felt all the childhood memories resurface in my mind, the excited fan inside me screaming to continue in this beautiful game. Used to play the game on the Wii with 480p resolution on a small screen, now with 1440p on a computer monitor large enough to be fully immersed in this work of art, I can't begin to imagine what 4K will look like. Not only all the textures are sharp, but the added post processing effects from the original on PS2 makes the experience simply better.
This newest edition of Okami allows both controller and keyboard/mouse support, the game open to the Playstation or the "Wii" playstyles. I have not tested the controller part yet, however for the keyboard/mouse part, all the controls can be rebound to your heart's content. The camera is controlled by the mouse, in case you are wondering.
Using the Celestial Brush feels natural, comfortably giving you full control on your line work without horrid wavering drawing (Wii version with its Wiimote not being stable in your hand, for example). I miss the ability to change the thickness of the brush freely like on PS2, although at least there's the ability to paint a constant, thicker line instead.
You can also change the refresh rate of the game, as well as the resolution and if you want it fullscreen, windowed, or borderless windowed. Either you can't change to a 1920x1200 resolution if you don't have a 16:10 screen (even if your 16:9 screen is bigger than that), or it's locked at 4:3 and 16:9 only. You might get some black lines if you are using a 16:10 screen.
With all the positive above, I do have to point out the controls overall can take a little while to get used to. As for framerate, the Fan Menu can go at 60 fps, while the game itself seems to be capped at 30 fps. In any case, the framerate of the game was not wavering at all on either situations, which is a mega plus compared to, say, an emulator.
Overall, the game compared to its predecessing versions is simply stunning, completely worth the $20.00. This 30 hours game is a masterpiece, a classic, and simply a unique and fun experience. Now's your chance to play this amazing, way underrated work of art!
P.S.: For the artists out there, try out your drawing tablets with the game and see if it works. If you can move your mouse cursor with a pen, so should the camera and Celestial Brush. This can be a unique way to play~
EDIT: I forgot to point out by default, the right mouse button makes the alternate, thicker line. Now if you have some sort of plugin for a PS3 controller for detecting analog inputs, I wonder if the game will still recognize that data and allow you to draw variable lines, like on PS2...
UPDATE: I can confirm that Okami is playable with a drawing tablet like Intuos Comic and the likes. It actually makes for a very interesting playstyle! However, the camera is a little bit hard to control unless you have a very high sensitivity, since you can't just reposition your pen like you would with your mouse in this case. For the first time, I finally was able to really draw in Okami...

Full disclosure: I was a beta tester for both
and
, but my opinion isn't tempered or influenced by that fact.
-=The Good=-
Nice graphics
Two soundtracks to choose from
Score Attack mode
Three difficulty settings
Sharp controls and hit detection
Good diversity with the scoring system
Three different ship types to choose from

-=The Bad=-

-=The Details=-
In 2015, the Dreamcast got
; a fan-made vertical shmup that was created by a small team of developers. Upon release, it saw a pretty wide range of reviews. Some enjoyed it, but others found a number of problems with the game. Those problems ranged from gameplay issues such as it being too easy, to technical problems such as numerous frame rate stutters and unresolved bugs. But at its core, was a game that showed promise. It had nice graphics and music, but it needed more time in the proverbial oven. That's where
comes in.
Visually,
is a nice looking game. The CGI used to create the backgrounds and ships allow for plentiful details on all of the sprites in the game; from the biggest boss, to the smallest bit of shrapnel. The shading gives everything a nice 3-dimensional feel, while smooth levels of animation are featured throughout. You'll find some parallax scrolling as well, giving the pretty backgrounds a bit more visual depth. Explosions kick out debris, the bomb sets off a huge fiery explosion, the ships are colorful without going overboard, the sprite designs are nice... the game has the visuals taken care of.
With the sound, like the graphics, things are handled well. Explosions have a nice little thump to them, the rapid-fire shots use sound effects that don't get in the way or grow annoying, and the bonus item pick up sounds are also not grating. They all do their job and don't get on your nerves by being too loud or unpleasant. With the music, you've got not one, but two different sound tracks. The first OST is the same one that was in the original release on the Dreamcast, featuring generally quicker-tempoed electronica beats and nice-sounding synths to help get you in the mood to shoot and dodge. The second OST is a new one made for this release. The songs are the same in composition, but they've all been remixed to give them a whole new feel and atmosphere thanks to the new synths being used and some tempo changes. Heck, at times, the second OST sounds like something that would fit right in with the soundtracks of
or
(and that's a good thing). Either way, the tunes are good stuff, regardless of which OST you choose to listen to as you play.
The gameplay is a solid mix of scoring techniques and traditional shmup conventions. You have a primary and secondary weapon that can't be changed, but they can be powered up several times. These consist of bullets that fire from both your ship itself and the pods you get as you powerup, as well as missiles that add to your destructive capabilities. You can focus the shot into a narrower beam ala Cave mechanics, slowing your ship down (which helps to make more careful movements) and giving your shots more punch. The powerups are gained from destroying red carrier ships, and even if you end up dying, you still get to keep your powerup level as long as you collect your weapon icons (which is easy, since they get sucked to you upon respawning). There are airborne and ground-based medals to pick up for points by shooting enemies with the normal shot, but there are also bonus medals to be earned by getting in close to bigger ships and point-blanking them (killing them while you're right up against them). You have bombs to clear the screen of weak enemies along with the numerous bullets that are fired both randomly and in screen-filling patterns, and you earn these bombs by killing enemies while using your focused beam.
Yes, this game gives you a choice. You can either kill everything with the normal shot and get more points medals, or you can focus your shot and earn orbs that fill up the bomb meter and earn yourself extra bombs. This adds an interesting little twist to things that forces you to balance your playing between upping your score and getting that handy bomb for those moments when you're overwhelmed. And staying alive is important, as everything you collect is tallied up at the end of the level, along with how many bombs and lives you have left. So if you want to get a big score to put up on the Steam leaderboards (which this game supports), you'll need keep yourself in one piece and get your collection counters high. To survive all of this, you get three ships to choose from. Each one has a different style of weapon (wide shot, narrow shot and in-between), different movement speeds and different focused shot power levels. Add in the difficulty selections that change how hard the game gets by throwing more bullets at you on Normal and Hard, or by letting you have an auto-bomb feature when you're hit on Easy, and you've got a well-rounded game. You even get a Score Attack mode that consists of bits and pieces from all of the stages, combined into one longer, bullet-filled stage.
So... what does this game do wrong? Well, it doesn't have any major glaring problems, but it does have some smaller ones that still stand out. For one, it's not the longest shmup you'll ever play. Once you get the hang of things, it can be beaten in about 20 minutes. Not stupidly short, but it will go by pretty quickly. Another issue is that the enemies don't really have a wide range of attack patterns as they come on the screen. Most of them just appear at the top and drift down to the bottom. They're plentiful and fill the screen with aimed and patterned bullets, but it would have been nice to see more in the way of ships coming in and out of the play area from all sides. Next, there's some of the boss bullet patterns that feel a bit too randomized to be filling so much of the screen. As examples, the final boss' seemingly random puking of pink bullets (mixed with the green lasers and blue bullets) makes it feel more like you have to get a lucky spray, rather than figure out a pattern. Stage 4's boss shares this issue as well on Normal/Hard. Lastly, the endings. This is more of a pet peeve thing, but I like good endings. Ones you can sit and watch for a minute or two with some story text, some images or animations... stuff like that. Even shmups should have an ending like that, as it's part of the payoff at the journey's end. But
has what basically amounts to a “congratulations!” single screen and then BOOM!... credits. That's disappointing to me.
In the end, what can be said about
? It's a solid shmup, that's what. The visuals, the music, the gameplay, the controls, a solid framerate, a good challenge level, solid hit detection... the quality is there. It may not set the world on fire with originality or fresh gameplay mechanics, but what it does, it does well. There are also lots of options to play with; from setting the screen mode (TATE or portrait) and practicing levels, to changing the volume levels of the music/sound effects and making the backgrounds darker. Sure, there are a few little things here and there that could have been better, but none of them really break the game or make it unplayable at any point. So for those who played the original version on the Dreamcast, this game is a big step up on all fronts. It's what the original release should have been, and it's nice to see the game was finally given the time it really needed to come into its own.

From their name alone any keen arcade shoot'emup player should recognize Hucast Games dabbles in the Dreamcast-era of what we call retro. With a clear loyalty and passion for this golden age of shmups they've set out to keep the traditions of Japanese STGs alive with an explosive and intense modern polish in both visuals and gameplay.
takes this fierce and energetic take on the shoot'emup genre across 5 mesmerizing extraterrestrial stages, seeking to find its spot in history among the most classic of arcade shooters.
The visuals here set a standard in shmups of their own, and unlike its gameplay are not comparable to anything released in any arcade in the past. The settings range from sand-storm inflicted deserts to lush alien planets with autumn-red trees, and always pack a vibrant punch of color. With extra sharp, crispy high resolution textures and mind-boggling amounts of enemies and items on-screen at a time
also manages to capture the visuals of its roots through old school polygonal ship designs and giant-robo bosses that'll make any sci-fi anime geek's mouth water. This is a different kind of shootemup that is unparalleled in its visual chaos of bullets and celestial settings.
presents an arcade shmup soundtrack that is nostalgic on levels I cannot articulate properly through words. Somewhere between the surreal and otherworldly compositions of
and the heavy, chaotic and beats of
this soundtrack assaults the senses in secret and majestic retro ways that modern game creators and companies have been trying to tap into for a decade. It might not be something someone who didn't grow up with obscure Japanese shmups would get, but the sounds of the warm synth-y and space-y melodies couldn't make me any happier.
The action of
as with any shmup is focused on overwhelming blankets of bullets.  It's of a more twitch and reflex based nature, as opposed to the geometrical pattern memorization seen in Cave-styled bullet hells, with curtains of bright shrapnel flying in your direction at all times. Instead of sitting inside of small triangular safe-spots like in the aforementioned bullet-hells, you'll constantly be on the move as to avoid the fire. Luckily, many of these bullets can pre-emptively be cancelled with careful thinking and aiming by neutralizing their source, the baddie firing them. This gives Ghost Blade HD a classic and hyper kind of perspective like Toaplan shmups, and feels to me almost like a much snazzier, snappier, and crazier
.
Even on the easiest setting the later levels become increasingly insane and unpredictable leading to many deaths, which is great for a shmup. With such an accessible and exhilarating start but such a daunting and seemingly impossible end it means that
has a high skill ceiling, and a whole lot of replayability. It's easy to hop into for a few easier levels but will take you dedication and patience to fully complete without embarrassing errors and endless continues.
The game has a relatively simple scoring mechanic that should be familiar to arcade junkies. With each enemy or crate hit and destroyed your combo multiplier rises, and as they are destroyed shiny and attractive medals pour out. The amount that these medals give you is of course raised by the multiplier, so score chasers will be making a mad dash to kill and collect. It's simple but very effective, and incredibly rewarding watching streams of loot pour from your successful strikes as you rise through the Leaderboards.
When it comes to arcade shoot'emups
is the ultimate bliss-out. The Zen-ful state of mind needed to dance between the ballet of bullets, the mysteriously obscure and nostalgic soundtrack, and the gorgeously detailed modern visuals with a touch of retro sci-fi design come together for an unworldly and addictive score-chasing package.

One of the greatest games created by TellTale.
Based off of the comic series of the same name,
places you in the shoes of Lee Everett: a convicted criminal who must now survive in a zombie apocalypse. While trying to survive he runs into other survivors, most notably a little girl named Clementine. It's up to Lee to protect Clementine from both the undead and the living.
With the exception of a few minor characters who only appear in episode 1,
is not connected to the main plot of the comics, so even if you haven't read the comics or watched the show you can still fully understand this game.
The game is a point and click adventure that focuses more on the struggles of surviving/solving puzzles and less on mindlessly murdering hundreds of zombies (though there still are some action sequences). This will probably scare away most buyers, but the people who can get past this will find themselves enjoying one of the most emotional games available on Steam (to those that
want a mindless Walking Dead shooter, you can purchase the mediocre Walking Dead: Survival Instinct for double the price of this great game).
Along the course of the game you'll be able to make certain choices that may affect who lives/dies or how others treat you. Although these choices don't really lead to any major "alternate paths", they are enough to making yourself feel responsible for every choice you make. You may be tempted to redo your playthrough so you can redo one choice you made, but it's honestly better to just keep going since it'll make your current playthrough much more meaningful.
Every survivor in the game is fleshed out and has something that makes them unique. Whenever a main character dies you will almost always have a rush of emotions - whether it be anger or sadness. Unlike most zombie games you will actually care about the main characters and how things turn out for them. Overall, there are some really amazing moments in this game that may leave your eyes running.
I wish I could go into detail about how great each episode is, but I don't want to spoil them. Even if you aren't a fan of The Walking Dead comics - or zombie culture in general - you will absolutely love this game.

Great game overall, there's a lot of diversity as far as the different roles and abilities of the ships (of which there are many). Compared to other capital ship combat games like this that I have played, I can confidently say that this game has much more to keep my interest long term. Both game types have multiple (and timed) objectives and large maps or multiple smaller ones, which creates a lot pf tactical depth. Of course you may get stuck with people who simply rush into  every engagament and ignore any attempt at tactics, but that's going to happen to you in any multiplayer game. One downside is that certain times of the day have few people online and thus longer matchmaking times, but hopefully reviews like this and patience from the current players can help change this in time. Progression can be slow into some of the newer ships, but there are several low cost ships that really pack a punch, and while some ships are noticably less effective it is worth noting that some of the most "meh" ships actually fall into the mid to upper price range. All-in-all this is a very good game with some minor gripes, and easily the best f2p game I've personally ever played.

Premise is engaging and the game is cheap, but it certainly is a no-buy for me.
The game loop goes like this:
Hacking progress goes like this: remote computers have a different number of closed ports which you have to open with commands that you acquire as you progress. Each open port lowers the toughness of the target computer and, once it's low enough, you can use a magic command to hack it and gain access to its contents. There are a few extra things (proxies, firewalls, time limit and some per-mission modifications) but overall the process is tedious and revolves around repeating the same commands over and over.
Some other reviews mention that this game has some learning potential, which is wrong. The commands that you execute take no arguments and just show progress bars which go up at the same constant rate, forcing you to be glaring at your screen until they are done. Any resemblance to an actual UNIX command is just the fact that they are, indeed, executed on a terminal emulator.
The game got tedious after an hour. If you enjoy the loop, you might enjoy the game, but be advised that it is repetitive, almost non-interactive and a bit dull. The story is not engaging at all and just revolves around people asking you to hack things.

Basically, you play one of several scoundrels who take on jobs to steal items, or assassinate targets, or hijack entire spaceships.  You start off with a weapon and an item to help you, and accumultate more along the way.  All of this is to earn money to complete a personal mission, which is generally much, much more difficult.  As you complete jobs, you also gain fame, which allows you to unlock more regions, which also unlocks helpful weapons or items.
The gameplay loop is pretty fun for a while, but you quickly reach a point where your character only has the option to take on difficult missions, and it's hard to get items necessary to complete the more difficult ones.  I did not complete any of the personal missions due to their difficulty.  I just got frustrated with always getting too difficult missions, so I reached a point where I would intentionally get characters killed off so I could create a new one, do easier missions and unlock more of the galaxy.
But sadly, it just got a little old for me.  It was the same thing over and over, and I lost interest.  I may come back to it later.  I do recommend it if you're a sci-fi nerd like me or just want to play something different, but I don't see myself ever completing the game.

So far I'm having a blast with it. It's almost like a cross between Hotline Miami and Deus Ex set in space. There's countless ways you can deal with objectives. Even if you don't have the proper tools for the job there's usually a way to deal with something so long as you use a bit of creativity. Have to capture an armored target but don't have concussion grenades? Lure him to a room with a window and shoot it out, then take remote control of your pod to catch him before he can suffocate. Did you screw up and you've got five seconds left before you're captured? Throw yourself out a window or breach the hull to space yourself and catch yourself with your pod.
I do have some gripes with it though, primarily with how repetitive it gets but more importantly the difficulty of some of the missions, especially the personal missions. Like regular missions, personal missions are randomized but are generated in a way that makes them more difficult than usual. The problem is that the way they're generated is more often than not done in a way that just isn't fun. For example, with the last personal mission I tried I was given an assassination target aboard a huge ship with 220 seconds to either kill my target or kill the pilot which would stop the count down. Pretty standard stuff right?
Oh by the way all the bosses have shields which reflect all forms of damage unless they're disabled. Still no problem right? I'll just save my subverters and crash beams for those guys. Haha no. Regular guards had shields too. They also had glitch teleporters meaning the second they heard anything suspicious they could simply teleport to my exact location. Now you're probably thinking I could have just picked them off one by one but it gets even better. The mission had the extra guards and extra sentry turrets parameters which meant tons of guards, usually grouped together in teams of five or six.
Still, personal missions aren't manditory so really I've just been able to ignore them completely. As far as I can tell the only rewards for them are a huge cash bonus and liberty boost which can easily be surpassed by doing a couple of hard-audacious missions which tend to be much more fun and balanced.
Despite my rant about the personal missions though, I'd still strongly recommend the game. I've only put 8 hours into it so far but I can still see myself playing it for a considerable amount of time to come.

Morbo says,
"THIS GAME IS LOTS OF FUN, EXCEPT WHEN MORBO'S FRIENDS DIE!  I WILL DESTROY YOU!"
But seriously, this game is excellent.  I've always been an X-Com fanboy (so read everything I say with suspicion), but they've done the series a service with both this and the XCOM (1) games.  I can't wait for the next game.
What's great:
The combat system has been seriously upgraded in my eyes, even from the first XCOM game.  The addition of new classes and their own special skills has really changed how you play...in a good way.  The battles are more fluid and I think they're more difficult than they've ever been.  The difficulty is offset by capability, however.
There's no management of the mundane.  No, I don't have to reload ammo on my troops.  No, I don't have recruit hundreds of scientists and allocate them all to different labs.  No, I don't have to waste time.
The storyline is excellent.  I love the continuation of the original storyline and the way it plays into the story of this game.
What's not so great:
Little bugs here and there with my system and the graphics.  Nothing that's caused the game to crash yet, so this is really not a big deal.
All in all, this is an excellent continuation of the XCOM series and might be my favorite yet.

I previously wrote a negative review about a couple years ago, but coming back to this game after becoming more experienced with the Hitman games (and stealth games in general) has completely changed my perspective.
Hitman: Codename 47 is actually easier, believe it or not. The more recent installments in the Hitman franchise make disguises more tricky. You have nothing to fear from walking into restricted areas wearing the uniforms of your victims, there is no suspicion meter like in Hitman's sequel 'Hitman 2: Silent Assassin' which means you can pretty much go anywhere without worry, and you'll even receive warnings for the most part, but always tread lightly.
I'm playing The Lee Hong assassination BLIND and I figured out a good path all on my own. No Let's Plays to guide me or anything. Pure intuition.
Hitman: Codename 47 keeps it's complexity simple; Sporting almost a Simulation-esque / very "PC Game" style mechanics and interface, with the ease of execution you'd expect from adequate streamlining and playtesting.
AI paths and patrols are made obvious enough for you to quickly plot your attacks, jumping from uniform to uniform and progressing through the ranks, becoming a Sergeant to gain access to a room where the General awaits isolated, allowing you to then become the General. As you start wearing the uniform of a high-ranking individual, you attain the perks and benefits attributed with such status, including (but not limited to) access to restricted areas containing people or objects of interest [Check your objectives, bound to F2 by default] which you may need to fulfill a checklist allowing you to complete your mission.
The phrase "The Suit Makes The Man" describes this gameplay style perfectly.
No "dumbing down" here, just remember to play smart!

Ah, Starbound. Since the new stable update came out, I decided that I'd write up a review of what I like and don't like so far with this beta. So, to kick things off, we'll do the good ol' pros and cons list format:
Pros:
+Randomly generated things are always fun. And this game has those in spades. (planets, weapons, monsters, etc.)
+7 races with solid gear progression.
+Lots of character customization options.
+Lots of biomes to explore
+You can upgrade your ship now, and it gets pretty big when all is said and done. Gives you multiple rooms to put stuff in.
+Easy game to add mods to and make mods for.
+Good sense of humor.
+Multiplayer can be pretty fun.
+FPS and overall performance have improved greatly over the course of the beta.
+Dungeons are fun to explore.
+Lots of stuff to build with for creative individuals.
+Colorful visual style
+Great soundtrack
Cons:
-The outpost is cool, but it feels sorely underused. Maybe adding some more stores and things to do would help. Also the FPS gets really chuggy there, but that might just be my PC, idk. Still, the game should be more optimized in that area.
-Combat is certainly getting there, it feels more strategic after some of the newer mechanics were implemented. However, I feel like the weapons aren't varied enough. There needs to be something which makes them stand out from one another. The game dosen't give me the "itch" to get out and just kill stuff quite yet.
-The missions. Ugh. These are really bad so far, if you ask me. First of all, you can literally complete the first mission (the only one I've played so far, to be fair) with a flashlight and some bandages. You can just run past all the enemies and flip the switches on the boss fight. Second of all, if you die in the boss fight, you have to replay through the whole damn mission again just to fight it. We need checkpoints, based chucklefish. Checkpoints. At least for casual characters if nothing else.
-Quests are okay, but pretty lackluster so far.
-In game lore could be a lot better.
Okay, so next I'll adress some of the complaints which some of these Steam reviews often bring up.
Complaint: "Chucklefish doesn't update enough!"
Response:  Well, they haven't put out many stable updates. In that regard, no, they haven't been updating much. However, they've put out nightly builds which can be buggy or broken but often are fun. They at least give you a picture of how the game is progressing.
Complaint: "I don't want to play the nightly build, I want to play something that consistantly works!"
Response: Well then too bad. This is phase 1 of the beta. You know, the phase where the game is broken and you aren't going to get the complete Starbound "experience." (source:
The purpose of this phase is to test the game and to iron out the kinks in it's core mechanics. You are not buying a full  featured game, obviously, and you shouldn't go into Starbound with the mentality that you're getting one. Instead, go into it with a critical mentality, thinking "I'm going to test this and give the devs feedback so that the final product can be great!" That's the reason why this beta TEST exists, kids. So you can test the friggin game.
TL;DR/Verdict:
I'm going to recommend this game, at least for now. However, I'm only going to recommend it to the people who are seriously going to test it. While the game is enjoyable in it's current state (in my opinion), I can't recommend it to people who are buying it looking for a well-rounded experience.

Loving every last bit of it. By far very entertaining game with lots of possibilities.
The questing has been improved a lot, made even more important than it was before;
Crafting has been simplified to a point where it is easy to follow but still challenging to use, which is a big plus;
Planetary exploration feels more rewarding than it was before and spelunking finally feels just as rewarding.
Overall, I recommend this game. It is so well sought out, and with the new update you can clearly see that Chucklefish is going towards the right direction with this game.
But there are some minuses which need tweaking:
- Basically the whole monster AI is a bit too confusing. Sometimes they ignore you when you are close and sometimes they just escape.
- Some sounds that already became iconic have been taken off. I loved the monster screams and such, they gave monsters a more more threatening feel.
- Exploration might even be TOO rewarding. I found already high-tier weaponry within my first exploration in a Fierce Star system, and I find chests just about all the time.
- The tech system feels oversimplified. Basically, it felt more satisfying to craft a spacesuit or oxygen tank than just having an ocygen reserve all the time on because of the suit techs. Some challenge or changes on the techs would be nice.
But that's my experience with these two days of playing this game nonstop. I love the changes, now I can easily see this becoming the game which I start up the second I come home and just grind it nonstop.

Probably one of the best games I've ever played.
I played this to death on consoles years ago, and now I'm going back again. Rarely in gaming do the 'fruits of your loins' pay back in full as much as they do here. You are literally bringing colour and life back to the land of Nippon, and it's no hyperbole to say I've never wanted to see every single corner of a game world as much.
When an evil Orochi spirit is released upon the world once more, It's time for the gods to re-appear and throw back the dark tide. Enter Japanese Sun-Goddess Amateratsu, taking the guise of a legendary white wolf. Armed with her magic paint brush, she must utilize all her weapons and bring the world back to life with her magic brush strokes.
Sounds awful right? Well it isn't. It's superb. Never before or since have I seen combat mechanics quite like these. Instead of traditional attacks, you 'paint' your offensive attacks with your brush (Straight line for a slash attack. Draw a bomb for explosives etc;). So instead of generic cover shooter nonsense, you have to think about your attacks carefully. Each enemy has a certain weakness that must be exploited through the different brushstrokes you amass (13 in total).
Jumping from 3D to 2D seemlessly (See Nier), the world is so fabulously realized, that it's simply a joy to run around, get lost, search for items, and slowly turn it from a sickly green to all the sparkling colours of the rainbow. When a land gets rejuvenated and the hills and fields explode back to life, your jaw will hit the floor. Meld all of this with wonderful think pencil style graphics and one of the best scores I've ever heard, and it begs the question why this never took off.
Critically it was a darling. But commercially it died. So that's where we come in. PC users are a classier bunch. We don't buy a product. We buy games for us. Not because Sony or XBox tell us. We buy games for us. The fact that Okami never sold is lamentable indeed. The fact that it's available now for us, is to be cheered. If you want to be reminded why you love games, then look no further. Zelda? Mario? Uncharted? Okami beats them all (It's Platinum Games, what do you expect?).
So give this one try, guys and girls. Okami. HD. The greatest game you've never played.

This game is very recommended to anyone who enjoys MOBAs, sci-fi ship-based combat, or any type of tactical shooter or 3D RTS (i.e. Homeworld series(Also fantasic)).
As far as MOBA fans go, this is technically a MOBA, and plays like one if you force yourself to treat it as such.  Friends and I refer to it as an "Objective-Based Team Shooter" and I recommend you do the same.  Are there MOBA-ish objectives?  Yes.  Are they overbearing to the point that they will lose you the game the moment you try to do anything other than push them?  No.
There is an outstanding balance between the combat and objective portions of the matches.  The objectives "guide" you more than anything as you work with your team to push towards the enemy base.
Also, the game itself may not be completely perfect (few games really are) but at the very least the coolness factor is pretty much hard-set at 11.
Some issues that I find troublesome are the lack of options when it comes to loadouts for some ships.  This is probably just due to a balancing act for the different hulls and since I do not know how to make games, I'll leave it to the experts, but it is something I noticed.
The crew and crew implant system is well put together however they are incredibly difficult (read as:  Very Expensive) to acquire.  I feel as if the ships and upgrades for said ships are all very fairly priced (especially considering some of the DLC packs available) however the implant and crew packages are incredibly expensive with both in-game and premium currency.  Not to mention they are very rare to acquire from the random drops you get from daily missions.
There are a few other small things but I find those to be the biggest issues so far.
I imagine more modes and ships are coming down the line and for that I am incredibly excited.  The game mechanics allow for a large number of opportunities with game mode design such as a 3 on 3 "revive your teammates" mode where the respawn timers are excessively long so you must revive those that die on your squad (maybe with proximity).  A potential base assault mode where instead of capturing nodes to upgrade and then capture a station the station itself could basically be a "boss" that you must overcome.  Perhaps each "boss" could be constantly fighting in the center and the mining stations are scattered about and the player teams must tip the balance between the two juggernauts.  Or even perhaps a pure "deathmatch" style where you have two teams of 5 (or 10?) with a limited number of respawns?
As said, there are lots and lots of possibilities with this game and it's youth promises at least a couple of years worth of content to come.
Highly recommend this game from this solid developer and they deserve your support.

Want better support for settlement-building, like the ability to place props just about anywhere? DONE
Better textures? New monsters, weapons, armor, quests? DONE TO DEATH
The reason I'm giving this a negative review, however, is the Creation Club. They tried paid mods with Skyrim, and the community exploded with negativity and rallied around mods remaining free for use (donations accepted at the downloader's discretion, of course). Bethesda claims the Creation Club is not paid mods, but rather is "DLC," a fine distinction that apparently means the mods are subject to some regulation and internal testing... which, well, Bethesda games are never bug free, so take from that what you will. The worst part? Even if you have no intention of supporting this business model, a recent 2GB update was applied to everyone's game, containing the files for the pay-locked Creation Club content. Bethesda is, of course, free to pursue whatever business model they want, however reprehensible I may find it, but I am quite annoyed at them hijacking my hard drive space for content I never intend to use. Gods only know if that 2GB will skyrocket, should more paid mods become available.

Fantastic game. I've never seen anything like it. I like the developers and I like the gameplay. As for story, it writes itself as you'll see by many reviews with tragic and/or heroic stories made by players. The real fun of this game really shows up when you've mastered the mechanics and get yourself into/out of crazy situiations with nothing but wit and a few accidents. Some say it gets old after the start, but those who think so are missing out on the core of this game. The core isn't the wild stories or the head bashing breaking/entering action. The core is pulling off ludicrous missions (or situations) without the gear to do it. The game doesn't limit you by skill (as you'll see by the pause menu and actions) but it challenges your mind with out of the box puzzles and workarounds that the developers have the game organically generate. 9/10 game.

Basically what I'm trying to say is that if your going to play this game bring some friends or make some new friends fast. If you play solo this game is much harder, more grindy, and less fun.
Overall though, it is a pretty good game.

Firstly: Don't buy early accesss games, that is my stance on them. I bought this when early access was new. However I am sick of seeing negative review after review with half-truths and sometimes lies. So I write this. Some people claim it hasn't been updated for 2 years. False, it hasn't had a offical "stable" update for just under one year. In the interim it has had MANY nightly unstable updates that you can opt into. These are akin to old Minecraft "in-dev" "secret friday updates". Unlike those, these are optional, just in case you don't like your save file blowing up. Secondly, people claim they receive no news or updates. False, going to the offical website, they post updates extremely reguarlarly, the largest gap I can find is 3 months, WAY BACK when it was just beginning pre-orders and kickstarter.
Much of the fake or mis-quoted hate his from people who expected bang on the head deadlines from a early-access game.
As time and experience has taught me, this is a stupid thing to expect. Buy into a early-access game with caution that it might take longer than expected. This game is one of the better ones in knowing they are still working on it, as the reguarly infomation updates and the unstable builds show.
The most recent update has made the game rather fun, from what I have played, so many negative reviews points are a tad moot at present time, as the update is the stable build of the entire years worth of unstable builds been made...stable and released as a single patch.
In short: Anyone saying they never give updates or infomation are too lazy to check to check the offical site, and hence didn't even know about the existance of the nightly builds and are basing the judgement purely off "Steam didn't update".
I give the game a recommend for them been a early-access game that actually DOES GIVE UPDATES. But in my wisdom don't get early-access unless your very confident. Though with current content this game is easily worth the $15 I paid for ages ago.

What a huge disappointment this game is. As a fan of the previous game I felt sure I would enjoy the sequel despite reading quite a few negative reviews. Unfortunately the negative reviews got it right, this game is very much worse than the previous game.
Its obvious that most of the budget went towards the video sequences. In the first few hours of gameplay there are a lot of them. They are good quality and reasonably interesting, but I don't buy a turn based strategy game for the video sequences.
Pretty much everything else is poorly done. As others have mentioned, many of the missions are timed, which forces you to run forward as quickly as possible. Even the missions without timers aren't much better. For me, all missions resolved to save scumming - moving forward, revealing the enemy, reloading and trying numerous different options to get past the swarm of enemy troops. This would be fine except what ended up working was rarely something that made sense, it just happens to work because of some conbination of random factors.
Also, the manual is a joke and the tutorial mission is useless. Although I completed the previous XCOM its been years since I played it and I don't remember much. I shouldn't have to resort to guides in order so have some idea of what I am doing.
This game reminds me of why I avoid playing AAA titles. Lots of really high ratings from the "professional" reviewers who somehow manage to completely ignore the many faults of the game. Good thing I only paid $12 for the game from Humble Bundle.

Build your own combat vehicle, blow stuff up and loot what rains down, then make your vehicle even bigger, better and nastier with it. Build a (small) base to craft blocks you couldn't find or to defend a perimeter. Or build the most powerful tank you can imagine and send it after other players, that have enabled invasions. Rock-solid concept, fun and of high quality in every aspect.
It is definitely a fun game that makes you come back every now and then for yet another round of entertaining destruction, but with the lack of a long-term goal you usually loose interest after a few days. Just to come back a few month later to play the latest patch, have some fun, and drop it again a few days later. I can't tell how many times I restarted this game, and every time it was just as fun as the first time or even better. Sadly it lacks multiplayer. The devs say this might be coming in the future, but realistically at this state of the game I doubt it will actually happen.
The development is slow, but steady, and usually the patches are of far better quality than 99% of all other early access titles out there. I can't remember the last time I encountered a bug that kept me from playing, or any bug at all in fact. Every update makes solid changes, and adds new fun toys to play with. Also the support has been extraordinary friendly and helpful the one time I had an issue with my account, and fixed everything in no time. Original Hitman was one of the games of my childhood. This was the first assassin-theme game I ever played. The reason behind negative review is because we became spoiled. Times back then we didn't had that much variety of games and stuff we have now. Games like this was jewels. It all begins with a some bugs and glitches and end up in sometimes just terrible level design. Some events have no logic behind it, like say a mission in harbour, when a guy comes up from guarded doors, you can kill him and take his clothes, but guards still won't let you in for some reason. Beside all this, the game is relentless - you will die in a matter of seconds even on low difficulty. You of course have a restarts, but they have a little sense, since the guards already know that they need to kill you, and so you die, again. Also, why they would give you immense amount of money, when you can't even spent 1/4 of them, even if you buy everything on every mission.
This all leads to a complete frustration - the game you might admired so much back then doesn't seem so good anymore. To enjoy this game you need to get a time machine, otherwise it's just not worth it. Returning players may get some nostalgia out of it, but it will remain good if you won't push yourself. Tower Unite picks up where GMod Tower left off.
GMod Tower was a social gamemode within Garry's Mod (a Half-Life 2 Source Engine mod) that offered unique gameplay in a lobby where players can meet up, socialize, visit each other's condos (customizable spaces), play minigames within the lobby map, as well as other larger gamemodes on their own maps. GMod Tower dates back as early as 2009.
Then with the support of their fans and dedication of themselves, PixelTail Games takes it a step further evolving their once small project into a (soon-to-be) completed fascinating virtual world - Tower Unite.
Tower Unite is built on the Unreal 4 Engine allowing for a larger lobby map without the performance cost, as well as shiny, intricate, new graphics compared to GMod Tower with its limitations on the Source Engine.
More gamemodes, items, and customization options will be added. Some spaces in the lobby will be redesigned tastefully, and other empty spaces filled in accordingly.
You will be able to create your own servers to play with friends only, or join other's hosted games. Since previously you could only join the few official public servers.
Overall, this is the best party/social game on the market with a variety of gamemodes to play, and you get to choose whom you play them with.

Half-Life is a great FPS about surviving a secret government facility invaded by aliens after a scientific experiment gone wrong.
Half-Life is mostly linear (though it's a lot less obviously so than its sequel), yet the levels are still fairly well-designed, with the exception of some which are plain tedious (screw you, On A Rail.) The atmosphere is pretty good, though slightly lacking in environmental sounds, especially in Xen (an alien world you visit, which often lacks sound.) Most sounds come from nearby enemies, and those are great. They provide a feeling of tension, as you are frequentl in very tightareas and don't know where an alien (or more) is hiding. There's quite a variety of alien enemies, much more than HL2's 3 types of zombies: In total, 11 very different types of aliens, 2 bosses and 3 human enemies, all very different.
The gunplay is pretty satisfying, and there is quite a lot of variety: from standard weapons like pistol, revolver, shotgun and assault rifle wih a mini-grenade launcher, to crossbows, experimental cannons, alien hornet guns and living creatures that, when set loose, may attack you instead of your enemies! The AI also seems a lot smarter than most FPS, just due to the fact that it actually knows how to fall back when wounded to call more enemies.
The story is pretty basic (at the time it was fairly complex for an FPS, not so much today), and the ending is quite strange, but the locations you explore are fantastic, from laboratories to reactor cores to canyons to Xen, an alien world. The most irritating part of Half-Life has to be certain sections which have platforming. Platforming with the Quake Engine's momentum-heavy movement? Yeah, no.
It's still a great game, and well worth the purchase.

If you want a classic Final Fantasy adventure - look no further. The plot is simple but always moving, the job system is not as good as in later entries but still offers a fair share of variety for your team. And as the game constantly throws different challenges - experimenting with party combinations is key.
The music is beautiful and has some of my favourite tunes in all of the series (like Boss Battle and Crystal Tower's theme). Graphics are very simple, but all models are clear, and there is never any confusion on the screen, as to where to go and who to hit. So overall presentation is charming.
Overall - I like FFIII a lot, but the last dungeon and boss ruin it a bit for me. It's not that they are hard or anything, but there are no save points. It takes about an hour (depending on your party's power) if not more to go through Crystal Tower, Eureka and the Dark World. And all of that without a save point. Grinds my gears a lot, that.
All in all, I definitely recommend it, but be warned that a simple Final Fantasy does not mean an easy one. With the wrong jobs you will die and die a lot. So make sure to look for treasure, level up, try new jobs and explore.

One of the best stories I've played in a video game. I had played 40 hours of this game for PS2 back in the day. Always wanted to replay it and more than happy to spend the $20 for it. As a humble monthly subscriber was able to get a discount in the humble store, anyway.
It's my personal all-time favorite game. Wolves were - and continue to be one of my - favorite animals, and playing as a sun goddess in the form of a badass powerful wolf hit me in just the right places. The celestial brush is one of the most engaging mechanics in gaming and is done very well.
The story is amazing and I encourage new players to read through and suffer the cutscenes their first playthrough. Some information in the story is repetitive sure, and the final area
doesn't help that, either. For a game that lasts 40 hours and in spite of the issues of the final area manages to be engaging and fun the entire way is quite impressive.
The music and art direction are both impeccable. I can't imagine this game looking any different from the way it is. Some parts of the world are a 2D image that just grows bigger as you approach it and turns to face the camera, but rather than drawing away from the game graphically it draws you in with the art direction and has a function besides just being 'there.'
The world is open yet linear. You unlock new areas to explore as you progress through the story and can return to old areas with new abilities to discover new areas and receive more praise that was previously unattainable. Praise is your 'exp,' but you don't get it from killing monsters, you get it from doing things in the game world. Sometimes killing monsters nets you praise, but that depends on if it was part of specifically assisting someone in the world.
I'm not sure what else to say about this game. I just recommend it, since my own experience with it has been nothing but positive. I hope others will enjoy it as well.

Fun little hack-and-slash action game with a beautiful, pastel art style and unusually compelling naration.
The upsides:
* many weapons and skills to choose from, giving you near complete free reign on which weapons you bring with you and upgrade.
* some optional content, in the forms of arena battles and trials with the waepons
* the naration. Seriously, Rucks has one of the smoothest voices I've ever heard
* multiple endings, and a New Game+
The downsides:
* it's extremely short. My first playthrough took less than 6 hours, and I was dawdling a bit
* very linear, with no way to replay fun areas again short of starting a new game
* easy dificulty overall. You can optionally make it harder, but I was wary of doing so, under the fear I'd make it too hard and get stuck
Final Word:
15 bucks is too much for what you get here, unfortunately. It's good; it's not THAT good. But it's an easy pickup at a 50% or more sale if you want something memorable to play on a weekend.

You start out in a damaged ship orbiting an unexplored world. You'll have to find resources to repair your ship and after that you can go to more planets in that solar system and eventually be able to travel from there to other systems. You'll discover many creatures and other sentient races some hostile and some friendly. There are many different kinds of planets to explore and all unique with many biomes and dungeons to find.
Right now the game is in heavy development, but it is still very playable and fun.

Half-Life is a great FPS about surviving a secret government facility invaded by aliens after a scientific experiment gone wrong.
Half-Life is mostly linear (though it's a lot less obviously so than its sequel), yet the levels are still fairly well-designed, with the exception of some which are plain tedious (screw you, On A Rail.) The atmosphere is pretty good, though slightly lacking in environmental sounds, especially in Xen (an alien world you visit, which often lacks sound.) Most sounds come from nearby enemies, and those are great. They provide a feeling of tension, as you are frequentl in very tightareas and don't know where an alien (or more) is hiding. There's quite a variety of alien enemies, much more than HL2's 3 types of zombies: In total, 11 very different types of aliens, 2 bosses and 3 human enemies, all very different.
The gunplay is pretty satisfying, and there is quite a lot of variety: from standard weapons like pistol, revolver, shotgun and assault rifle wih a mini-grenade launcher, to crossbows, experimental cannons, alien hornet guns and living creatures that, when set loose, may attack you instead of your enemies! The AI also seems a lot smarter than most FPS, just due to the fact that it actually knows how to fall back when wounded to call more enemies.
The story is pretty basic (at the time it was fairly complex for an FPS, not so much today), and the ending is quite strange, but the locations you explore are fantastic, from laboratories to reactor cores to canyons to Xen, an alien world. The most irritating part of Half-Life has to be certain sections which have platforming. Platforming with the Quake Engine's momentum-heavy movement? Yeah, no.
It's still a great game, and well worth the purchase.

Terratech is fun to play and in general terms I reccomend it as a casual building experience. I have played Besiege in the past and I can say that I enjoyed the tech looks better in this one, and how much easier it is for something to work. The crafting aspect and factory building adds up well nicely. It's not Factorio, but it's still fun.
There are some negatives in the game that should be addressed however.
Performance:
Most importantly, I have had serious performance issues when a lot of resource chunks would be around. I'm running a good rig that can play Witcher 3 maxed out, so I guess that frame drops in what looks to be simpler 3d, is unacceptable. Factories need to be optimized as they lag too much when they get complex. Also they can get buggy in more complicated designs, which will not allow for massive building. These performance limitations are the main reasons I didn't enjoy the game 10x more. I enjoyed it casually but I know it could be better.
Gameplay:
There should be a better progression system. I unlocked Hawkeye, it took a while and it was a challenge. But the game still kept on throwing little puny "level 0" techs as opponents that could die one shotted. What's the point of building awesome techs then if I am to beat them so easy? Sure, there are some hard opponents but I really don't know what algorithms produces enemy techs, it should be fixed in order to scale up the difficulty as players progress. It feels random as is.
Environment:
The environment is good to explore and in campaign mode you get to go around it all, but it reaches a point that it just seems repetetive and boring in endgame, not adding to replayability.
Music:
Repetetive as hell, turned it off, maybe the worse aspect of the game.
So I think that the Devs should focus on optimizing performance and in gameplay terms they should be really focusing on adding aspects to improve replayability. Multiplayer feature would be really-really fun.

Firstly: Don't buy early accesss games, that is my stance on them. I bought this when early access was new. However I am sick of seeing negative review after review with half-truths and sometimes lies. So I write this. Some people claim it hasn't been updated for 2 years. False, it hasn't had a offical "stable" update for just under one year. In the interim it has had MANY nightly unstable updates that you can opt into. These are akin to old Minecraft "in-dev" "secret friday updates". Unlike those, these are optional, just in case you don't like your save file blowing up. Secondly, people claim they receive no news or updates. False, going to the offical website, they post updates extremely reguarlarly, the largest gap I can find is 3 months, WAY BACK when it was just beginning pre-orders and kickstarter.
Much of the fake or mis-quoted hate his from people who expected bang on the head deadlines from a early-access game.
As time and experience has taught me, this is a stupid thing to expect. Buy into a early-access game with caution that it might take longer than expected. This game is one of the better ones in knowing they are still working on it, as the reguarly infomation updates and the unstable builds show.
The most recent update has made the game rather fun, from what I have played, so many negative reviews points are a tad moot at present time, as the update is the stable build of the entire years worth of unstable builds been made...stable and released as a single patch.
In short: Anyone saying they never give updates or infomation are too lazy to check to check the offical site, and hence didn't even know about the existance of the nightly builds and are basing the judgement purely off "Steam didn't update".
I give the game a recommend for them been a early-access game that actually DOES GIVE UPDATES. But in my wisdom don't get early-access unless your very confident. Though with current content this game is easily worth the $15 I paid for ages ago.

I actually quite enjoy this game. It's a fun shooter (or brawler, because who doesn't want to smack a supermutant upside the skull with a rocket powered sledgehammer?!), the perk system is VASTLY improved from the previous games, and personally I enjoy the settlement system, whereby you can start rebuilding civilization and help all the serfs-I mean settlers thrive in the hostile environment of the wasteland. And of course there's Survival mode, where you need to eat, drink, sleep, deal with the hazards of disease, forego fast travel, and combat is more deadly for everyone: both yourself and NPCs. In my opinion, Survival Mode is the way the game is meant to be played. On other difficulties, enemies turn into bullet sponges very quickly.
A lot of folks claim it's a terrible Fallout game, and while I think it has a weaker story than previous games (Yes, yes, we all know New Vegas is everyone's favorite) I maintain it's a solid title. Like most Bethesda games, where it shines is in the mods. You can do just about anything you like with the correct mods:
Want the wasteland to be an overgrown forest? DONE.
Want better support for settlement-building, like the ability to place props just about anywhere? DONE
Better textures? New monsters, weapons, armor, quests? DONE TO DEATH
The reason I'm giving this a negative review, however, is the Creation Club. They tried paid mods with Skyrim, and the community exploded with negativity and rallied around mods remaining free for use (donations accepted at the downloader's discretion, of course). Bethesda claims the Creation Club is not paid mods, but rather is "DLC," a fine distinction that apparently means the mods are subject to some regulation and internal testing... which, well, Bethesda games are never bug free, so take from that what you will. The worst part? Even if you have no intention of supporting this business model, a recent 2GB update was applied to everyone's game, containing the files for the pay-locked Creation Club content. Bethesda is, of course, free to pursue whatever business model they want, however reprehensible I may find it, but I am quite annoyed at them hijacking my hard drive space for content I never intend to use. Gods only know if that 2GB will skyrocket, should more paid mods become available.

This game is brilliant.
The top down GTA-esque aesthetic really works with the strategic style, like a cleaner Hotline Miami.
The pausability lends a more measured approach to difficult missions, and enables feats that would otherwise be impossible, but are otherwise very slick. A little like VATS in fallout, without the miss chance.
There is a subtle layer of humour in the game, which are nice but don't detract from the overall experience.
The rogue-like elements of the game give a sense of over arching progression, but you also feel a harsh loss if a character dies in the vacuum of space, without fulfilling their destiny (and you lose their cool rare gadgets). Yet, there is a sense of closure, when your 30 mission veteran is bloodied and battle scarred to the point where you can retire them, and giving them legendary status.
The game swings between almost impossible, requiring split second (in game) precision, and no margin for error, proper planning and execution to quick smash and grabs, which in the late game give you an almost god-like sense of steamrolling an entire ship in 10 in game seconds. It depends on your mood which you choose to complete, whether it's to farm gear on a medium range ship, do some little ships for the money, or take on a large stacked ship for the challenge. There's a definite 'one more mission' addictive feel to this game.
I don't believe the game is ever unfair in its difficulty, the mission briefs outline the risk, and the rewards are commensurate to that. One exception being armour piercing weaponry is a nightmare to find, and many personal missions require it. (let alone armour piercing non-lethal weaponry!)
On the downside, I wish there was a little more enemy variation, and I don't know if there will be any kind of updates, DLC or expansions, so I can't say this is a complete negative. The game has not long been out, but I'd enjoy more mission objective variety, clause variety, maybe a new faction, new gadgets and guard gear. This is not really a negative, it's the sign of a great game that it leaves you wanting more.
Controller compatibility would be a huge plus, as I think it would lend itself to the strategic style in a couch gaming fashion, I find that mapping buttons with xpadder doesn't have the right feel to it, but maybe I just need to keep tweaking it.

This game is rad. Tom Francis is rad. Do you like sneaking around? You can do that. Do you like blasting into a room and smashing six guards unconscious with a wrench, and the last one flies out a window of the spaceship you're on, and you and that guard get sucked out into space, so you have to maneuver your own little ship to your drifting body to pick yourself up and re-dock with the big ship to get back to sneaking around and killing the hell out of guards and taking their stuff? You can do that, man. That's something you can do a lot of the time, actually. Plus, if you do it wrong and die, you've got a roster of plenty of other cool generated characters to choose from. If your character gets captured instead of dying, you might even get a chance to rescue your old character. If a Steam friend's character gets captured, you could even get the chance to rescue that character and rob them of the opportunity, like a true space pirate.
The galaxy is your oyster, so smash that thing open with a Concussion Hammer or use a gadget to ... well, the galaxy is already in space, but you could use a gadget to teleport it out into space if it were an enemy instead of the actual galaxy. Anyway, this game is very good. It has the "just one more mission" appeal that marks a quality quick-fire kind of game that you could pick up for just a mission, and take maybe a few minutes, or suddenly find your mouth dry, your stomach growling, your eyes red, your butt numb, and your family pleading for you to just stop playing the game already, man, it's a beautiful day outside, but you're like, "Nuh-uh, man, I want to break into more spaceships. That's my thing now."

If you pick up the special edition, you get all of the prototype builds too, along with developer commentary videos for each, featuring Mr. Tom Francis. Tom is also cool enough to offer advice on using GameMaker software to make your own rad games, even if you've never done any programming before, and he posted videos to that effect for free to his Youtube channel. Buying Heat Signature supports an independent developer who just wants so badly to make the game and game development communities more open, more accessible, and a more fun place to play and to enrich each other with new experiences.
Does this sound like hyperbole? Does it sound like a paid plug? What if I told you that everything I've said here is not only true, but that I actually paid to purchase this product myself so that I could write this review honestly? Not a paid plug. No exaggeration.
Buy Heat Signature, dude. It's good.

They should seriously just hand over The Elder Scrolls and Fallout to Obsidian Entertainment. They just have more competent writers in general, who actually take the time to make it lore friendly.
Let's look at comparisons.
Fallout 3 (Bethesda written):
-Involves son finding father
-Generic "I'm good/evil" dialogue. It's like KOTOR 1.
-Character automatically given a backstory that can't be changed.
Fallout 4 (Bethesda written)
-Involves father finding son (sounds familiar, right?)
-Has no care about original Fallout lore. You know, like how Jet got retconned into a pre war drug even though it's made from brahmin, which didn't exist until after the war.
-Dumbed down dialogue system. Most of the time the choices mean yes. Even no.
-Character given a COMPLETE backstory, as well as a voice actor. Seriously, that's one way to make RPGs bad. When I play RPGs, I like to make my own character with my own backstory. When I read dialogue options, I read them in MY VOICE, like I'm actually roleplaying in the game. None of that applies here anymore with that voice actor.
-Generic quests. *20 minutes into the game, when I got free power armor and a minigun with no effort* "Hey, a settlement needs your help"
Bethesda doesn't seem to know the difference between keeping players entertained, or keeping players occupied. They don't mean the same thing.
Fallout: New Vegas (Obsidian)
-Involves a 4-way power struggle between a town that was untouched by the war, where the dam is the key to its control since it powers the place. (I know, right? Something that isn't an overblown family problem)
-Actual, genuine feeling dialogue. The options actually feel like something I would say in real life. It also feels like more emotion was put into it.
-Your character is a blank slate, perfect for an RPG. The only backstory the game gives you is that you were a Courier, and stuff went down in the Divide. Everything else is free reign for what you wanted your character to be.
-Full of references and interesting characters. Especially companions. Raul, Lily, and Boone had some beautiful writing behind them.
Fallout 1+2:
This is the original stuff right here. I'll be honest, I never actually played them, but I heard that they were pretty amazing games. I agree to that, especially after seeing snippets of it on Youtube.
These were the Fallouts that defined and created the world you played in all future Fallout games. That means they're very rich with lore and writing.
I'll be playing these two along with Fallout BoS very soon.
As for the Creation Club, just no. A shiny piece of armor is more expensive than the other Fallouts on a steam sale. It's pretty obvious which one gives you more content for your money.

If you'd ask me about my favourite games of all time, Okami would be item number one on the shortlist. Really, if you are capable of liking things in general, I highly suggest giving this one a try. Just bring some patience as well; the game is most infamous for throwing about 15 minutes worth of unskippable lore into your face right at the beginning.

The Original Hitman, what can I say.
The Game plays extremely frustrating, but beating a level is a lot more rewarding than in most games nowadays.
Hitman wants to be hard enough to realize that killing people is indeed -not- a game but a hard job that can claim your own life easily. Something most shooters are lacking for instance. Hitman carries on the tradition of Thief, where intelligent stealth and planning of your equipment beats the loadout you are carrying.
And here starts the pain:
Stealth is nothing you just do, it is a hard earned skill of knowing what to do and when. Sometimes this means a Minute or two of simply doing -nothing- waiting, pacing and taking your time. Sometimes Stealth means being really quick and just not missing the right moment. Most of the Time Stealth means: Use one bullet max, the rest is knifework.
These lessons are hard taught in C47 and none of it´s successors retaliates so hard on missing out on any relevant detail. On the other hand you realy have a feeling of -beating- the game and not just dangling along.
This is why I enjoyed it just like Thief, back in the days, and am learning the hard way, that a lot of my patience and skills from back then have given way to a happy triggerfinger, which is needed a lot more in other games.
To Wrap things up:
C47 was clearly ahead of it´s time gameplay wise and it is still a challenge to beat.
The Risk and Reward system really works well and the frustration level for tiny misteps is enormous, as you wont be able to save a level.
It is just like going by Yoda: Do, or do not! There is no try!
