Before I start, SPOILER HEAVY REVIEW, although I feel I have good reasons for a negative review for a game I like.
I will say that I enjoy XCOM, I have since the first one, and this kind of sadistic gameplay intrigues me. I love it, and I will spend many more hours in it, but there is a reason why I am not going to recommend it, especially over XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
I am not going to focus on bugs/crashes/etc, since many of those can be system specific and not necessarily a general thing.
1) Tutorial
The tutorial is absolute garbage. It teaches you the base mechanics of the game BUT... Here comes a few points.
Point 1: It teaches you to not take cover while overwatching, also it teaches you to overwatch instead of engaging.
Point 2: It teaches you to go into positions where you have no cover.
Point 3: It only gives you a semblance of control, does not allow you to experiment with game mechanics, does not allow you to even try anything yourself, you are stuck on one specific path that will make any decent XCOM player grind their teeth from the decisions the game forces you to make. Probably one of the worst tutorials I have ever personally experienced (XCOM: Enemy Unknown had a tutorial that forced actions on you as well, but it did teach you about decent movement and didn't force you to do actions that were bad unless it got your trooper outright killed right away)
2) Progression
The progression of enemies in this game is completely crazy, ESPECIALLY if you played the tutorial.
If you played the tutorial you have very few decent troopers and you get dumped in to a mission where there will be a Sectoid. For new players being introduced to the game, they have barely finished a tutorial that didn't teach them anything, and they have to deal with a mechanic that can (without actually shooting a trooper) make a trooper inoperable for several rounds (panic), mind control them or make them near useless with a disorient buff... This is the ... "second" mission of the game, and if you did the tutorial you haven't even played one mission yet.
Also a few enemies you encounter early on (within the first 6 missions), each having their own frustrating mechanic, especially if you haven't played XCOM before (and many of these mechanics are new to XCOM).
ADVENT Stun Lancer: Can move incredibly long distances, which is in stark contrast to ANYTHING! you have encountered so far, rarely if ever shoots and deals an insane amount of damage early game which also has a chance to either stun your troopers (making them inoperable for X amount of actions) or outright knock them unconscious requiring you to carry them out of the mission if it is an evac mission. Despite them being this unique they don't stand out that heavily from ordinary ADVENT Troopers visually making them (especially for new players) harder to make out.
Viper: These guys can PULL! your guys to them, and grapple them, making them inoperable until you shoot the Viper. It can BEYOND this shoot an AOE poison that will early game be able to almost kill your troopers. This is guaranteed damage and if you didn't bring a medkit, you are screwed because that is the only way to get rid of it (or finishing the mission)
MEC: These guys are not as frustrating as the two others, but they severely limit your flanking abilities since they don't use cover as well as the fact they have 2 armor. The game has not taught you what armor is, or how armor works yet so some players may not have any idea how to deal with it (which will make these guys into bullet sponges early game) They also are the first AOE cover destroying enemies as well.
This is within the first 6 missions, and 2 of these are earlier than that. All of these appear earlier than most of their (less frustrating) counterparts in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, screwing the progression of the game heavily.
Just these things put together is one of the reasons I would probably never suggest XCOM 2 to a new player. Even more experienced players can get a lot of games ruined in the first couple of missions due to random frustrating control removing mechanics being introduced this early.
3) Frustrating Mechanics / Enemy Design
This ties a little into Progression but XCOM: Enemy Unknown in contrast to XCOM 2 did not introduce a lot of enemies that could outright take control away from you early game, while as I mentioned before this game introduces 2 of them within the first half hour to an hour of game experience. In a game already about RNG it speaks of the bad game design to have so many mechanics to take away the control of your characters (leaving you with less characters to deal with the threat) and some of these mechanics doesn't even have a real counter to them. Besides that I feel that they spent way to much time adding to many abilities on to their enemies due to them lore wise being an "upgrade" to the original troopers. Due to this addition of so many new mechanics to enemies, the enemies that were considered a threat (and didn't really receive an "update") in XCOM: Enemy Unknown are now incredible tame.
These include:
Mutons: They are introduced so late into the game that their pitiful 8 health and 1 armor is laughable. A lot of your troops have more than that, and half your characters will be able to oneshot it.
Berserkers: Rarely if ever a true threat, due to it's "frenzy" mechanic. You just shoot it while it is far away, and it kills anything close by, including its own allies.
Avatar: These guys are... super... insanely... underwhelming... They are supposed to be the cool♥♥♥♥♥psionic dude you have to fear, but it gets introduced in a ridicolous manner because it comes out of the left field with no time to react. Despite this, the trooper itself has rather weak damage, the most annoying feature is every time it takes damage it teleports to a different location. This is easily countered with half decent positioning. When I encountered it the biggest threat on the field was a Gatekeeper, making these "bosses" extremely underwhelming.
The pacing of the progression is very very bad due to these guys.
4) The Final "Boss"
The final battle in general is super super underwhelming. Surprisingly few enemies, and the enemies you do get to fight you can basically ignore if you have the chance to kill the Avatars.
Basically kill the first avatar, then you just kill the next two avatars as soon as they spawn. The fights prior to that, you ask? Well you get handed a new character "Commander Avatar" which has a massive AOE Void Rift that deals quite good damage, the ability to easily mind control any organic or dealing upwards of 14 damage in a line to enemies. This is beyond your first 6 troopers... So you have 6 really strong troopers and a 7th overpowered one... Yeah guys, totally tough final battle.
I don't think a lot needed to be changed in this game to make it okay. Introduce Mutons earlier, introduce Sectoids and Vipers later, and focus more on the simpler enemies early game, the ones that just throw grenades and shoot at you, instead of the ones that grapple/pull/mind control/panic your troopers.
Side Note: If anyone is going to tell me that the reason all of the above is okay because "This is XCOM"... Well, you may know how to play XCOM, you may know it can be frustrating and unfair at times, but that does not mean frustrating mechanics should be thrown at new players for the majority of the early game, which can easily feel uncounterable or straight up impossible to deal with. It is not an excuse for badly designed progression/game design.
TL;DR
If you are a new player, I can not recommend you to stay further away from this game. XCOM: Enemy Unknown has a much superior progression and a hell of a lot better environment to experiment and learn about the game before it starts throwing insane mechanics in your face.

I've been a big fan of Assassin's Creed since the first game. I loved 1, 2, brotherhood and revelations. 3 had some issues and was kind of disappointing (I wasn't a fan of how they handled the present day stuff). I held out on getting 4 because I felt burnt on 3. After reading a bunch of good reviews I caved and picked up 4. Two complete playthroughs of 4 later, it's one of my favorite games ever. Then came Unity. I waited until it was fairly cheap (30ish) because of all the bad reviews and bugs that it launched with. I loved 4 so much I just wanted this to bring back some of that feeling.
That feeling wasn't there though. This is probably my least favorite game in the series. Here's a few reason:
- Arno isn't a very interesting character. Even from early on his motivations for joining the Assassins don't make sense and they aren't really ever made convincing.
- The modern day stuff is basically non-existent. It's little more than a plot device to shoehorn in some non-period stuff for the locale. The story with Shawn, Rebecca, Juno, etc isn't touched upon or advanced at all.
- The combat is a huge step back. Granted, the counter-kill stuff from previous games made killing all who oppose you a little too easy, the changes they made just don't work. Instead of counter-kill you counter and then are able to get a few hit in. Early on it can take a dozen hits to kill an enemy and only a few to kill you, which is ridiculous. There's no counter-kill, no counter-shoot and no getting the enemy to kill one of their own by taking a human shield like you could do in 4.
- The controls are bad. They've always had issues but they seem particularly bad in this one. I got the double air assasination, something I've been doing with ease for several games now, and it only seems to work 15% of the time. I was almost convinced that they took out ledge hanging kills since the prompt for being able to do it was just never showing up. I was able to do it exactly one time in my whole playthrough so they didn't take it out, it's just broken. I joked with a friend that they must have added voice controls to the game since it seemed like I had to shout "climb the ♥♥♥♥ing wall" before Arno would do what I was trying to get him to do.
- Microtransactions. Sure, you could say "if you don't like them, don't buy anything". Of course I didn't buy anything. The microtransactions are still a terrible addition to the game because they fundamentally change the way the game works. Unlike previous games you have different pieces of equipment with various minor changes to various status and such. The only reason these exist is because the option exists to purchase them with real money. None of the previous assassins had worry about 10% faster cooldown of their eagle vision, it just worked as long as they needed it. Random♥♥♥♥♥♥like that.
- Almost every mission is a copy pasted "go here and kill the guy" sort of thing. I didn't like the tailing missions in the past few games but at least that provided a change of pace every now and then.
- I did enjoy some of the coop missions, but I hate that most of the good equipment only available these coop missions. You also have to spend points to unlock skills, which you only get in main missions and coop missions. There aren't enough of these in the single player to unlock all the skills. If you want to get everything you are required to play coop missions.
- You can't pet dogs or any other domestic animal. What. The. ♥♥♥♥.
Bottom line, I wouldn't recommend it, even if you're a big fan of the series. This might be my last AC game. I'll wait for reviews on Syndicate to see if maybe it's worth buying, but I've basically lost all hope that Ubisoft will go anywhere with this series anymore. They don't care about making a fun game, they just want to find new ways of monetizing the fanbase.

Without spoiling anything, there are also some parts of the game where you will be forced to change your party's jobs into a mage team, too. Finally, you -will- have to grind a lot in this game. Like, significantly more than later games in the series, which also disguise some of their grinding with side quests and other content rather than just a massive enemy difficulty spike when you set foot in a new area.
The story is a lot more sparse, but it's okay. Final Fantasy 1-3 didn't really have much in the way of stories. I wouldn't recommend it as a starting point for getting into the series (unless you just want to start with arguably the most difficult title and can get through the increased amount of battle difficulty and grinding in the game), but once you've played some of them, it's worth checking out.

The game has a unique concept and is very fun, but after 2-3 hours the game becomes VERY repetitive. You've basically seen everything at that point.
The AI is awful. The guards huddle up in 1 room, then if you wait a bit one of them will leave to go work in a different room. You kill that guy, wait, and then another guy will leave the huddle. Rinse and repeat.  Simply standing in a room next to the huddle and wait is ALL YOU HAVE TO DO, for almost EVERY mission. I have NEVER seen any instance where 2 guys go wander around at the same time.
The game itself is easy. As soon as you're spotted, time slows to a crawl. It gives you more time to plan your next attack, but it's a silly mechanic because you can pause the action at any time anyways.  There isn't an option to turn off time slowing down, so this makes the game laughably easy.  You have to kill the guard who sees you before he yells "INTRUDER" and alerts the ship, but when time is SLOW you can easily kill him before that happens. I wish him spotting you played out in real time - it would force me to use pause more and plan things out better.
The "hard" missions are only hard because they add in shielded or armored guards. All you need to do is grind to find an armor piercing weapon or a weapon to disable the shields and boom, then that mission becomes as easy as all the others.
I wish Steam had a "mixed" review, because this game is sooo close to being great... Fair price, fun concept, but seeing all the other Positive reviews with 10+ hours in the game seems misleading to me. I'm at 6 hours, which I'd say was 4 hours of mindless grinding and 2 hours of discovery and fun.  I'd rate it 4.5/10 as of now.

Sadly Fallout 4 isn't the next big game for Bethesda, nor is it a major revolution of the Fallout franchise. It's all very familiar (too familiar) and those who have played Skyrim (who hasn't?) will be right at home.
But that's the core of the problem: Fallout 4 simply feels like Skyrim with a massive texture mod. Some assets like plants have even been blatantly copied and pasted, revealing how little effort Bethesda has seemingly put into the game. The only difference is that Fallout 4 puts more emphasis on a tighter overworld while Skyrim's overworld was vast and open.
Technically the game is nowhere close to what could be possible. Textures often lack detail or load very slowly, animations are rigid and unorganic, certain areas cause massive framerate dips and the excessive use of Godrays and other visual effects is simply a poor attempt at trying to disguise the fact that Bethesda is still using the same engine they used with Oblivion and Fallout 3.
That out of the way, the game isn't actually bad. It's even decent and certainly worth playing. The skill system allows for many different playstyles, the faction system invites replays and the main character is more relatable than the voiceless Dragonborn from Skyrim.
Combat can be approached from many different angles and can be avoided completely if one desires to do so. Most of the time. Sadly enemy AI could be better. Either the enemies hunker down behind cover, occasionally pocking their heads out to fire a few shots and then return to cover. Or they blindly charge into your line of fire or into prepared mines. Never have I encountered flanking manouvers or anything that might suggest that the enemies, which usually appear in groups, are competent. Most deaths occur due to them lobbing explosives, firing from unexpected positions or simply because of overwhelming numbers. Companion AI is hardly any better, bordering on suicidal. Often your companion will charge into enemy groups, making stealthy gameplay difficult or impossible. Other times they will obscure your line of fire or pick up targets a mile away.
Overall Fallout 4 is a decent game, but nothing revolutionary. If you're out for good RPGs with better graphics, better story, better gameplay and little to no load times... play The Witcher 3. But if you liked Skyrim, can't resist checking out every nook and cranny of a game's world and simply love getting lost in a wonderfully dark, sarcastic and cynical postapocalyptic world, then Fallout 4 is worth a try.

It's a fun game both for casual play and for sitting down with for an hour or two at a time. Not without its flaws, but they hardly manage to compromise the fun you'll be having.
Visuals are good, controls are simple but solid and you'll rarely find yourself doing the wrong thing despite some degree of contextual controls(which is hard to accomplish! Props to the Heat Sig dev), and the music/sound design is simple but ideal(not cluttered with too many SFX, just a solid backing track and sound effects only when you need to know something's going on).
The good is that the game has a LOT of variety to toss at you, and a lot of fun challenges.
The only bad is that it takes a bit to start unlocking some of the variety, and it feels like adding a bit more variety to ship interiors and AI behavior would've helped make the game more interesting and a bit less predictable. Sometimes it's just a bit too easy to take advantage of the same AI behavior multiple times in a row, and until the variables start piling up, or unless you willingly challenge yourself, some of the missions are just a bit too formulaic.
Where the game really shines, honestly, is in the Defector missions, where you're given some of the game's more fun tools... but a selective variety of them, forcing you to employ some tools you normally never would(like Swappers, I mean, seriously, in most missions they barely have a point), more stealth and less violence.
The main game is mostly a stealth sim ala Dishonored or Thief, while the Defector missions are closer to puzzle missions, and they're REALLY strong.
If there's something the game lacks, it's a toolkit to develop your own pre-set defector missions and hostile ship layouts, and then to share these with others. Because there's a REALLY strong backbone for making cool missions(especially if you could alter NPC behavior while doing so), but the randomized nature of 90% of the game sabotages the potential a bit.
So, tl;dr it's a 4 out of 5 game, and I really hope the devs plan to patch in that last 1, because it feels like it's just so very close within reach. Definitely get this.

Though it was a bit challenging for me to decide, I came down on the side of recommending the game. There is an awesome game packed behind many things that annoyed me.
For reference, I'm really not a fan of roguelike games which some of my frustration just comes from that design. But that's not interesting here. I do think that even if you don't really like roguelike games, there is fun to be had here.
The first major annoyance is the game is pretty bad at teaching you things or actually explaining the rules. A few frustrations:
- The game doesn't actually tell you all of the buttons for everything. I found out about using 't' to throw a weapon and 'shift' on the pause screen to pan the camera from internet comments.
- Timers. The mission timers starting from when you accept the mission and not when you arrive is frustrating (since travel can take 20s) and doesn't particularly make sense. So just skip the missions
- Alarms can be stopped up to the instant they expire by killing the pilot. But leaving the ship (by your choice or getting thrown out) does not reset them. But you can re-enter the ship without any notification or visual difference that you might instantly lose your character
- You can use melee weapons to dash at enemies, but you cannot dash away. This sometimes leads to times when you pause and see a bullet coming but cannot do anything about it.
But these area all small in the end. The fun of teleporting around, swapping with others, and just putting your tools to the test is super fun. The game feels a lot like Metal Gear Solid 5 when taking over a base. There's a lot of approaches and none has to be best, but succeeding even when things start to go wrong feels great.
For me, the best part is actually the practice area (which clicking "restart mission actually generates a new one... which is annoying for practicing against a specific mechanic...). Here, you don't have to bother with the boring and pointless travel between areas. Failure doesn't matter, just try again. Experimentation and fun is encouraged everywhere. And there's still tons of stuff to play with.
So there's fun here, but for people like me, the end of the game isn't the goal. Just playing in the practice area is super fun. I just kinda wish the rest of the game was a bit more streamlined and there were fewer annoyances to make that feel worth while to me.

into a fountain. Honestly, if you didn't shed a single tear at the end, congratulations! You're a psychopath.

Before I start, SPOILER HEAVY REVIEW, although I feel I have good reasons for a negative review for a game I like.
I will say that I enjoy XCOM, I have since the first one, and this kind of sadistic gameplay intrigues me. I love it, and I will spend many more hours in it, but there is a reason why I am not going to recommend it, especially over XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
I am not going to focus on bugs/crashes/etc, since many of those can be system specific and not necessarily a general thing.
1) Tutorial
The tutorial is absolute garbage. It teaches you the base mechanics of the game BUT... Here comes a few points.
Point 1: It teaches you to not take cover while overwatching, also it teaches you to overwatch instead of engaging.
Point 2: It teaches you to go into positions where you have no cover.
Point 3: It only gives you a semblance of control, does not allow you to experiment with game mechanics, does not allow you to even try anything yourself, you are stuck on one specific path that will make any decent XCOM player grind their teeth from the decisions the game forces you to make. Probably one of the worst tutorials I have ever personally experienced (XCOM: Enemy Unknown had a tutorial that forced actions on you as well, but it did teach you about decent movement and didn't force you to do actions that were bad unless it got your trooper outright killed right away)
2) Progression
The progression of enemies in this game is completely crazy, ESPECIALLY if you played the tutorial.
If you played the tutorial you have very few decent troopers and you get dumped in to a mission where there will be a Sectoid. For new players being introduced to the game, they have barely finished a tutorial that didn't teach them anything, and they have to deal with a mechanic that can (without actually shooting a trooper) make a trooper inoperable for several rounds (panic), mind control them or make them near useless with a disorient buff... This is the ... "second" mission of the game, and if you did the tutorial you haven't even played one mission yet.
Also a few enemies you encounter early on (within the first 6 missions), each having their own frustrating mechanic, especially if you haven't played XCOM before (and many of these mechanics are new to XCOM).
ADVENT Stun Lancer: Can move incredibly long distances, which is in stark contrast to ANYTHING! you have encountered so far, rarely if ever shoots and deals an insane amount of damage early game which also has a chance to either stun your troopers (making them inoperable for X amount of actions) or outright knock them unconscious requiring you to carry them out of the mission if it is an evac mission. Despite them being this unique they don't stand out that heavily from ordinary ADVENT Troopers visually making them (especially for new players) harder to make out.
Viper: These guys can PULL! your guys to them, and grapple them, making them inoperable until you shoot the Viper. It can BEYOND this shoot an AOE poison that will early game be able to almost kill your troopers. This is guaranteed damage and if you didn't bring a medkit, you are screwed because that is the only way to get rid of it (or finishing the mission)
MEC: These guys are not as frustrating as the two others, but they severely limit your flanking abilities since they don't use cover as well as the fact they have 2 armor. The game has not taught you what armor is, or how armor works yet so some players may not have any idea how to deal with it (which will make these guys into bullet sponges early game) They also are the first AOE cover destroying enemies as well.
This is within the first 6 missions, and 2 of these are earlier than that. All of these appear earlier than most of their (less frustrating) counterparts in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, screwing the progression of the game heavily.
Just these things put together is one of the reasons I would probably never suggest XCOM 2 to a new player. Even more experienced players can get a lot of games ruined in the first couple of missions due to random frustrating control removing mechanics being introduced this early.
3) Frustrating Mechanics / Enemy Design
This ties a little into Progression but XCOM: Enemy Unknown in contrast to XCOM 2 did not introduce a lot of enemies that could outright take control away from you early game, while as I mentioned before this game introduces 2 of them within the first half hour to an hour of game experience. In a game already about RNG it speaks of the bad game design to have so many mechanics to take away the control of your characters (leaving you with less characters to deal with the threat) and some of these mechanics doesn't even have a real counter to them. Besides that I feel that they spent way to much time adding to many abilities on to their enemies due to them lore wise being an "upgrade" to the original troopers. Due to this addition of so many new mechanics to enemies, the enemies that were considered a threat (and didn't really receive an "update") in XCOM: Enemy Unknown are now incredible tame.
These include:
Mutons: They are introduced so late into the game that their pitiful 8 health and 1 armor is laughable. A lot of your troops have more than that, and half your characters will be able to oneshot it.
Berserkers: Rarely if ever a true threat, due to it's "frenzy" mechanic. You just shoot it while it is far away, and it kills anything close by, including its own allies.
Avatar: These guys are... super... insanely... underwhelming... They are supposed to be the cool♥♥♥♥♥psionic dude you have to fear, but it gets introduced in a ridicolous manner because it comes out of the left field with no time to react. Despite this, the trooper itself has rather weak damage, the most annoying feature is every time it takes damage it teleports to a different location. This is easily countered with half decent positioning. When I encountered it the biggest threat on the field was a Gatekeeper, making these "bosses" extremely underwhelming.
The pacing of the progression is very very bad due to these guys.
4) The Final "Boss"
The final battle in general is super super underwhelming. Surprisingly few enemies, and the enemies you do get to fight you can basically ignore if you have the chance to kill the Avatars.
Basically kill the first avatar, then you just kill the next two avatars as soon as they spawn. The fights prior to that, you ask? Well you get handed a new character "Commander Avatar" which has a massive AOE Void Rift that deals quite good damage, the ability to easily mind control any organic or dealing upwards of 14 damage in a line to enemies. This is beyond your first 6 troopers... So you have 6 really strong troopers and a 7th overpowered one... Yeah guys, totally tough final battle.
I don't think a lot needed to be changed in this game to make it okay. Introduce Mutons earlier, introduce Sectoids and Vipers later, and focus more on the simpler enemies early game, the ones that just throw grenades and shoot at you, instead of the ones that grapple/pull/mind control/panic your troopers.
Side Note: If anyone is going to tell me that the reason all of the above is okay because "This is XCOM"... Well, you may know how to play XCOM, you may know it can be frustrating and unfair at times, but that does not mean frustrating mechanics should be thrown at new players for the majority of the early game, which can easily feel uncounterable or straight up impossible to deal with. It is not an excuse for badly designed progression/game design.
TL;DR
If you are a new player, I can not recommend you to stay further away from this game. XCOM: Enemy Unknown has a much superior progression and a hell of a lot better environment to experiment and learn about the game before it starts throwing insane mechanics in your face.

Hitman; Codename 47 is a third-person stealth shooter and I/O Interactive's sleeper hit, which allows you to assassinate contract targets for cash and to unravel the past of the man known as Agent 47.
HItman Codename 47 plays smoothy allowing you to bind controls to stealthily drag enemies, holster weapons, talk to NPC's, drag away bodies from the sight of other enemies, assume their identity temporarily, use the environment to kill your foes, fire upon them with silenced (or unsilenced) firearms and amongst a huge list more. Hitman has unparalelled freedom in allowing you to take down your target as you want it, not how the game wants you to play.
Codename 640509-0401
is the designation given by the Prof. Dr. Otto Wolfgang Ort-Meyer a German scientist who worked on the genetics to create the world's best assassinator, with the recombinant DNA of 5 fathers all belonging to criminal overlords known as; Otto Wolfgang Ort-Meyer himself, Chinese restraunt owner Lee Hong, Columbian drug lord Pablo Belisario Ochoa, International terrorist Franz Fuchs and finally Arkadij Jegorov, a international gun launderer from Kazakhstan. Agent 47, his demeanour is cold, calculative and as sharp as a .338 Lapua Magnum round in your Cerebral Cortex, is set out to join the ICA, his base of operations that deliver him contracts to take up in assassinating his marks for money, however the marks set by his client may not be exactly say who he actually is killing. 47 goes on a conquest to find what gave birth to him and why he is the world's greatest assassin.
The gameplay in Hitman Codename 47 is that of a common third person shooter with stealth and action elements distilled to a flawed but fun pace. Patience is rewarded well in Hitman Codename 47. Mainly takes place in urban settings, 47 has the advantage of different places to execute killshots or strangulate your mark.
Just be careful of killing too many civilians will severely reduce your paygrade and the ability to purchase ammo and other equipment for the job will reduce your effectiveness significantly and committing mass murder of innocents/failing a parameter will inevitable cause you to fail the mission.
Codename 47 features detailed mipmapping, radiosity shadowing, high polygon counts and high resolution textures and use of physics ragdolls which were impressive for their time (2000). Though the repetition in the use of urban buildings is overused and the sprite/flat shaded sprites and textures for foilage are not very well done. The draw distance is terrible however antiquity of the engine and hardware available. The incredible scale of the levels can be hard to manuver and memorize.
The games audio has high use of fidelity (16 bit, 48Khz was considerably high) in its soundtracks and is focused mainly on its theme which has a Jungle and Classical genre feel to it, sound effects are done to great effect, representing a solid bullet shot out of a Sniper Rifle into the flesh of someones face.

I have heard many things about "Half-Life" in the years before I even bought it here on Steam. Having played the "Portal" games, it gave me a sense of what Valve Corp. does with it's games. But now I've played the game that started it all for Valve. It's over twenty years late for me, but does it still work to this day? Yes it does. It's an incredibly challenging experience that was way ahead of it's time. And it's still a fun game for me, even after I endured a first playthrough.
The game was very ahead of it's time in some context, and it was trying all sorts of things games of the 1990s weren't. For one, it balances what most FPSs had, action and puzzle solving. But at the same time, it was trying to avoid the gameplay mechanics that most games used heavily. Most games at the time used cutscenes and focused more on the action than it did on the experience, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but "Half-Life" took a chance and it paid off.
In this game, you play Gordon Freeman, a Theoretical Physicist at the Black Mesa Compound. This game made him a silent protagonist, which is a good way to get the player immersed in the role (even if you know nothing about Freeman's field.) But this game also makes sure you never once leave Gordon's point of view, even during the in-game sequences. This makes the story unfold before you, not watching what's going on in the background, so you literally have to draw your own conclusions based on what you see and hear. That makes the game very immersive and it still works in this modern age.
Also, rather than have levels, the game has chapters, and the areas of the game are interconnected, reducing the amount of loading screens and makes it feel more realistic. I like how they keep every game area connected to one another, making it feel like you're exploring this top-secret facility without letting the game show it for you, you're learning for yourself.
The gameplay is what you'd expect from an FPS, though it maintains an old-school feel, even as FPSs were beginning to aim for more realism. The weapons have a nice variety, my favorite is the Tau Cannon, cause it's the closest thing to a laser gun that you have. But of course, being an FPS of the 1990s, this game uses lots of platforming and puzzle solving, requiring you to spend a lot of time saving this game.
The enemy variety is okay, but at times, I felt that some enemies were unnecessarily tough, including the Marines. I found myself not liking to use the Assault Rifle that much, as it felt like I wasn't hitting the enemies hard enough. Also, some of the enemies were way too accurate, and their damage dealt to you was out of proportion to the amount you did (stupid Vortigaunts.)
This brings me to the complaints I have. There is an abundance of platforming in this game, and the controls are very stiff at times, you have little control when you're in freefall, and often, the drops are too high that you take damage regardless. Also, the game has a few poor level designs. Such as when you have to turn on a fan, you have to move fast or the fan will chop you up, and you can get stuck under it. Also, there's an area that's mined, and the lasers are so finely positioned that you have no room to mess up when you try to squeeze past them. It was hard to enjoy the game at times with this problem. But that's not all. It was hard to maintain power for the HEV Suit at times (given the abundance of enemies, it was lucky you even maintained it for long periods.) Also, ammo at times felt scarce.
But despite how much I despised certain points in the game, that just made me keep coming back and keep going. I still wanted to finish it. I was too immersed in the story. I wanted to see where I'd end up. And this game really was enjoyable, in the long run, it's another game I can come back to.
I can see why "Half-Life" has (and rightfully earned) become one of the best games ever made. It was a game that took a lot of chance for a first-time effort by a new game company, and it was a gamble that paid off. The story and it's immersiveness are what kept me involved, even if the game wasn't totally perfect. It's the kind of FPS I know and love, and it's one I'm willing to play through again.

However, if you are a player who doesn't know the story you will definitely find it odd that the game just ends without a true ending to the story mode. As with all Lego games released before 2017, there are bugs to be found with the engine and it can become a bit of a pain to switch between characters and weapons when many of them look the same. If that doesn't bother you then you will enjoy this title.

First of all, I absolutely LOVED Lego Star Wars as a kid, so I want to say right off the bat that i might be slightly nostalgia-driven when I say that I don't like having actual voices in lego games. It's not terrible, but a minor charm that the older games had was how all the characters would just grunt, and the rest would come from body language. This is also more friendly towards foreign children who don't speak English, just like I once was.
The game's story plays like a cheap very cut-off version of the hobbit movies. In fact I find this game to be way too connected to the movies, you aren't getting anything new, just a ♥♥♥♥♥ier version of the movies with some awkward humor thrown into it.
The game tries to implement some sort of trivial, bad crafting system, where you have to collect resources to create things to progress. Essentially this means that sometimes you'll have to look around in the level to find the right resources, but other times you might just have them already. Overall the system just feels extremely unnecessary and dumb. Why not just have like two items that you need to find and pick up to craft whatever you might need? Why add to the already annoying "smash everything to find coins" thing that exists in every lego game ever?
Also, the game is INCREDIBLY poorly made and glitchy. You'll constantly get half-stuck in places, leaving you having to mash buttons to get out, I once jumped off a dock into the water, but it turned out the one spot I jumped off left me standing at the bottom of the ocean instead of being flung back up, and as previously stated, I had to mash a few buttons to get back. It's not gamebreaking, but extremely annoying. I also got stuck with my boat between some white rock things, and you can't even get out of the boat without being at a dock. After mashing some buttons, the boat started spazzing about, before launching itself through the air and doing several flips, almost landing ON LAND, which I don't even want to know what would happen if that were to be.
One of the worse glitches I found, was in the first boss-fight against the white orc, the backstory one where Thorin gets his last name, Oakenshield. Me and my brother had fought through most of the level and were right at the end of the boss-fight. Somehow (I don't remember how, it was a while ago) I managed to get out of bounds of the map. There was no way for me to get back to the map, and if I remember right we ended up having to quit the level. We never bothered to progress any further than that.
The only credit I can give to this game is the fun we had exploring the main lobby area. This was also a glitchy experience, but it was way more fulfilling and honestly a much better adventure than anything the levels have to offer.
Lastly I also want to mention, some of the levels in the game are just ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. Why create a level out of the party at Bilbo's house? Why create a level out of feeding your ♥♥♥♥ing horses? The game is trying way too hard to stretch itself out, and it's just ♥♥♥♥ing dumb. Just make them ♥♥♥♥ing cutscenes, nobody cares about some dumb minigame about throwing plates around Bilbo's house.
TL;DR
Pros:
Very good in game lobby, had lots of fun exploring it and dicking about.
Cons:
Too connected to the movies, yet so much is cut out so it feels like a dumb, cheap version of the movies.
Extremely ♥♥♥♥ing glitchy. Made it super hard to enjoy.
The level themes are ♥♥♥♥ing stupid, for example the dwarf party at Bilbo's house.
♥♥♥♥♥♥, unnecessary, crafting system that just adds to the typical lego game grinding.
(I prefer the older lego games where characters were just grunting instead of actually ripping audio from the movies.)

The game looks cute, appealing,a bit childish though, many classes to choose from and the possibility to change the skin of the weapon, hat and face that you wear. The game is enjoyable when you are low mastery/level because you level up quite fast. Abit of killing, a bit of mining and you're fine.
A few dozens of hours later, you need to do much more to level up. Quite normal, since you need more xp to reach the next level. Except it's in way bigger proportions. At that point, it's called grinding. You have to spend hours and hours just to progress a little. Doing dungeons gets repetitive real quick.
A few updates later, you can't get new classes for free (you could unlock them through in-game money that you earned everyday) and you need to spend real money to get them. New features were introduced at the cost of making the game even more grindy. Don't worry, the devs also released some items that you can use to make progression faster, by buying those items (with real money again) to upgrade gems. Though, those upgrades may break the gem (unless you have the items preventing this). BUT, that still doesn't guarantee that the upgrade will succeed. So the tedious work and the time you invested to gather the materials simply go to waste and you need to do that again to MAYBE be able to upgrade a gem. You need to upgrade them several times and there are several gems to obtain, making you stronger. What happen when you get stronger? You are allowed to go in harder worlds, allowing you to grind better items that you need to upgrade too. And the cycle continues.
I don't like this game, and it doesn't like me either. I only (rarely) play it because a good friend plays it.

You need a fast computer. The game is really fun, it sometimes can get frustrating. If you buy this in early acess don't be sad that you lost your data when the next update comes out b/c it will happen a lot (it has happened to me multiple times).

It is hard to fully describe Starbound.
In this review I shall avoid using the word "Terraria" as although said game is good, I feel that comparing the two is an insult to Starbound's identity, innovation and frank superiority.
Starbound is a sidescrolling, planet exploring RPG of alarming and attention seizing depth. Whilst some elements and genre tropes may appear familiar, such as resource gathering exercises like mining and farming, the majority of the game is played out on a scope suitable of the name "Space Opera". Wherever your character is, be that underground digging for ores, on your personalised space ship or raiding on ancient alien tomb, the sheer scale of Starbound makes you feel profoundly small. Insignificant. As if you are only a grain of sand on a beach. Or rather a single point of light in a sea of stars.
However, it's a good insignificance. The worlds of Starbound are teeming with life and you feel as if you're an interloper trying to carve your path through and find your worth in a universe that has, and still can, exist without you.
Reading this, you may be getting the impression that Starbound is an unfriendly, confrontational game. It is in fact quite the opposite. With a distinct and well directed sense of humour, Starbound welcomes you into it's seemingly endless expanse with a smile and pats you on the back when you make successes small and significant. Coupling this warmth with the spacious and thoughtful soundtrack, the player feels at peace. Calm.
Of course, this Serenity can be broken at will with the games balanced combat or bold adventures into the unknown. But as with any great RPG, changes of pace are all of the player's own accord. And this truly is a great RPG.
Maybe I am pre-destined to like Starbound: I'm a huge sci-fi fan, I love lore with a sense of scope, I love a good complex character progression system, I love vanity items and things to collect. But what I truly love is when all of these things are addressed uniquely with a passion and an individual take that surprises and humbles. Starbound is in it's own sector of uncharted  space in this regard.
So of course I recommend Starbound. It is, in my opinion, one of the best RPGs to ever grace Steam. Buy it, explore it, become obsessed with it.
And remember: Never trust a penguin.

Starbound is a wonderful game, and well worth the money. If you follow their impressively active devblog you can see how dedicated the devs are and will understand that this is a work of love and dedication.
That said, this game is massively behind schedule and there are several reviews complaining about this. Frankly, the devs could have added a little more filler content to the original unstable, balanced the loot a bit and pushed it out. The original stable was a pretty fun experience in itself. But they weren't satisfied with that, they stuck to the project nearly to the point of insanity. They rewrote pretty much the whole game, and are still working on it. And it's great. I payed into the the original "kickstarter" and I don't regret it at all. The fact that the devs were clearly actively working on it, and regularly updating about it, made it okay for me. I think it was worth the wait.
The January 2015 stable build is a HUGE leap forward. It took some time, but this game is finally living up to it's potential. The devs still aren't satisfied by it, but I have to say it's a very rewarding experience, especially in contrast with  the original stable. They added a lot, but I think my favorite thing is mission areas that you can't build or dig in. No more bypassing the platforming sessions with ease, or cheesing bosses. Which would be really annoying, except that the reward for completing these has been worth it every time. There's still some grindy aspects to the mining. The combat can be pretty challenging at times too, but thankfully they've made it so the it feels a little more technical by rewarding perfectly timed blocks and adding shield health, so if you stay on your toes you can take on some pretty tough challenges. The combat finally feels balanced right.
Let me just sum it up here: The game, as it is now, is worth $15. This is a work of love and the devs aren't satisfied with it yet, I don't know if it will ever fully live up to their aspirations, but if they miss the moon they'll still end up among the stars.

First of all, calm down, it's Early Access.
Don't expect it to be exactly like Gmod tower because it's not. Not only because they can't use copyrighted assets, but because they're adding cool new content.
So the developers are still the same, they didn't sellout or anything like that.
It's the same Towers, but not on Gmod. This is how a good game does it by itself, but they need time, money and support.
The good stuff!
+ All old minigames are back (Virus, Ballrace and Minigolf, so far).
+ New minigames out and coming soon.
+ New items, new currency.
+ Very nice graphics. (though read the not-so-good section as well)
+ Developers are always there to answer any question.
The not-so-good stuff...
- If you have a low-mid end PC, you won't be able to run it very well, specially when you're in a server with many people.
- Virus doesn't feel the same (it feels much more fast paced, but maybe that's just me).
- Character customization is very limited. I hope this changes in the future, because all people have the same body types atm.
- Servers. This is what I don't like at all. 2 reasons:
1. People won't be joining your condo because it's going to be another server, and that's just a waste of time.
2. Too many servers that aren't official, even though they're dedicated. (so you'll see random people's dedicated servers filling up the list).
- If you play a minigame in any server, if the host leaves, the minigame is over.
- It doesn't feel like a community anymore, people just straight join into a minigame, or their condo. I don't know if there's any reason to join the plaza anymore. I miss the waiting queue for the minigames, but maybe this is more practical (I really wish everything would be in the same server though).
- Some annoying bugs to fix, but you know, it's Early access.
If this game never grew and stayed the same as it is now, I'd actually rate this bad, but since the developers are so hard-working and dedicated, I have no problem giving this a good review, because I know it will get better.
I was in the Private Alpha and content came out frequently and this doesn't seem to change. So give it a try, even if you don't play it now, you'll play it later for sure.
UPDATE:
Due to the hard work from the develpers adding new content from time to time, I'd recommend it to anyone, because it's getting really fun. I only wish there was more people around. Come play! :)

I'm not one for reviewing games but I had to for this with all the fun I've had with this product. It's a perfect roguelike game from my point of view with the numerous ways of dealing with a mission.
Do you go in guns ablazing with a shotgun in one hand and a rifle in the other? Do you run in with a hammer and hit people so hard they go through a window and get sucked into space? The vacum sucking everyone else in the room out with them, yourself included but you survive when you remote control your pod to grab you before your oxygen runs out! Or do you sneak yourself in and knock out only a few guards and leave with your mission completed without anyone the wiser about what you did?
There's so many ways you can do it, but one of my most fond memories from this game was I set up a Glitch Trap (which is like a landmine that can teleport its victim instead) outside a room I want to breach and stand right over it so when I swap teleport with one of the people inside they got thrown into the vacum of space while I quickly killed his friend with  slice from my longsword.
I love the little stories you come up with when all you know is the mission that someone needs to do for their personal reasons and if they retire you can name an item and you can maybe find it in the universe as you're exploring. While it doesn't have really any story it has the thing Rimworld had where you come up with your own stories for the charaters you find and come attached to.
The gameplay is fun, with an autolock of sorts with the melee so it allows you to snap to other targets if you have one that readies really fast for re-use. The guns can feel a bit odd at times, but that might just be my lack of extensive playtimes of topdown shooters-ish games since it might be from the lack of gun feedback such as recoil and the like.
Your little pod is nippy and moves very well and the 6x speed when you hold F makes it very fun to fly around and doesn't feel too sluggish if you don't hold down the button the whole time. And when you fly a massive ship which you can do, it feels slower and hevier with the amount of weight in it and you can use the heavy weapons on them to take out other ships or if you can't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with the aiming you can just crash into the other ships.
I like how as you become more powerful with weapons and gadets you get less reputation that goes towards liberating bases (which doesn't have a mission or anything, you just pick one you like the look of and you get it to allow you to go there to resupply and pick new missions and stuff.) You can capture ships and sell them off (although you don't get much for it when you do) and if you do an easy mission or one when you can take out everyone on it, its a good way to make a bit more dosh.
While there doesn't really seem to be an endgame from where I am at this point of time playing it still is addictive with playing I've done and I'm going to keep playing this for some time. If you're looking for a simple in princible but fun in exicution look no further than Heat Signiture for you needs!

If you look in any forums, reviews, or even talk to another person playing Heat Signature, you will probably hear a story. You’ll hear a wild, crazy story of a heist that they almost bungled up, but somehow managed to succeed. Or you’ll hear a story of a brilliant solution to a seemingly impossible problem. The game generates these stories by design. Suspicious Developments has created a dynamic toy box for players to jump into and play. They wanted players to come and make their own adventures, and to share them with each other. Which is why what I’m about to suggest might seem strange:
. Because making your own adventures is probably the best part of Heat Signature.
Heat Signature is a game that is very clear about its intent: it is a game about infiltrating spaceships. (For the record, I will not share any of my own anecdotal escapades in this review, as much as I desperately want to.) You’re hired to steal a top-secret device, or hijack a ship, or “off” someone, and so on. Further, the game is highly geared around playing smart.  As you clear out a level, you feel like an intergalactic Anton Chigurh, like a methodical, unstoppable force of power, focused on your task at hand. You have your standard array of melee and ranged weapons, but also unique equipment, like creatively designed teleporters (for example, one can swap your position with another person). There is a wonderful dynamism to all of the games interlocking mechanics, encouraging you to mull over the possibilities. Every time you take a bullet, you’ll be able to survive the vacuum of space a little less. And then, you’re dead. Forever. It’s a permadeath game, and when you die, you instead take up another character drinking in your honor at a nearby bar. The game is designed with smart and cautious play in mind, and all of these elements in concert make the player feel like a regular Sader Fiasco.
Sader Fiasco? That’s the master freelancer the game starts you out as– crashing through a window to your possible demise. (This may become a calling card for Suspicious Developments devs; it appeared in Gunpoint as well.) After a tutorial mission, Sader Fiasco retires. And… that’s about it for the story. There’s a little bit of world-building, and it’s actually stellar. All four of the in-game factions which you play against have their own unique politics, ships, origins, and moral codes, some of which determine AI behavior. What small amount of writing that is there, is witty and engaging. I genuinely wanted to see more of this story characteristics because they were so enjoyable. It’s a shame a lot of this information is locked behind late game missions because these factions are genuinely fascinating. Since Heat Signature emphasizes player-created stories, it deliberately drops any narrative. The game is procedurally generated, so a lot of the game is about seeing where these systems can take you as a player, but this also may be Heat Signature’s biggest downfall.
The problem is, while there are plenty of mechanical stories to tell, I can’t really think of many narrative stories I discovered myself. Characters will have personal missions to go for (revenge, debt, etc.), but that’s about as interesting as those narratives get. The non-mechanical stories are very limited and very empty in stark contrast to the mechanical ones. This doesn’t have to be a huge problem, but because the game lacks a broader narrative, it’s very easy to get lost in a directionless haze early on. You can focus on faction strongholds, sure, but this is a very vague and disconnected objective. The metagame feels slow and unproductive. You slowly liberate space stations, but they unlocked what felt like very little. You have this massive map screen which isn’t all that necessary. The only benefit is that you can encounter different ships than the ones you’re objective is on. I felt like all this empty space could have had way more things going on inside.
The problem of procedural generation seeps into the level design, as well. As the game gets into the later hours, I felt like I was dealing with the same missions over and over again. Ships start looking the same, AI has no variation, and the missions begin to blend together, with only a handful of objectives. They were fun, rewarding, and challenging missions that I had a blast playing and trying new solutions in, but they felt similar regardless. There are also a few mechanical flaws (the difference between lethal and non-lethal, for example, is totally trivial most of the time.) (Also, pro-tip: “T” lets you throw items or eject your pod; the game never tells you directly.) I seriously think Heat Signature could have benefited from the slightest story structure (especially with such an interesting world!), or a small set of predetermined missions, or a greater emphasis on roleplaying, or just something to keep me on track as a player as I figured out what I wanted to do.
Once you figure out what you want to do in Heat Signature, you can feel that click. What you want–or, at least what I wanted–was to take part in these wild space exploits. You have to take risks, you have to take missions you don’t know if you’ll be able to beat. You have to get wild. Because when you start to risk it, you can get the biscuit. You discover wild solutions. You discover wild failures. You begin to grin like an idiot as your plans spiral into failure, or even success, somehow. Unique client requirements like “don’t kill anyone” or “don’t get spotted” and limited equipment constantly encourage you to experiment. I actually think they could have gone even further with this; limit my inventory even more, expect extremely specific things from me, force me to really think and really get into these systems at play. Don’t let me game this system. Failure isn’t necessarily fun in Heat Signature, but it almost always feels like a purposeful failure. Your demise was clearly predictable, you just didn’t predict it. It’s a game about experimentation and discovery. That’s why you shouldn’t read any anecdotes or stories before playing, I think: it robs you of this joy. Learning to take risks and think outside the box is what makes Heat Signature so damn good. Discovery and revelations of how mechanics suddenly begin to interlock together into this disastrous concerto of missteps and mistakes or a miraculous delivery into success.
Heat Signature is a game about infiltration, but it’s also about experimentation and discovery. It presents you with a little sandbox of toys and lets you just have a go at it. It infected my mind at times, replaying moments of ingenuity over and over in my head. The game world is fascinating, but it’s too bad it lacks any story inside of it. The metagame is lacking, and there are lulls of excitement about, but that doesn’t negate the utter joy I experienced. There is a serious need for direction, one that almost had me stop playing, but I am so glad I didn’t. It’s a shame that Heat Signature doesn’t give its players more to go off of, because what is hiding in this game is shining and bright, and some people might miss it. It’s a game about little adventures. You need to figure out your direction because without you’ll miss out on the brilliant realm of challenging adversity Suspicious Developments has set up. By managing to discover that in Heat Signature, I stumbled onto an exciting and blossoming world of dynamic death-defying capers that is totally engrossing and full of stories.

[EARLY ACCESS REVIEW - CONTENT IS LIKELY TO CHANGE IN THE FUTURE]
Hey, guys.
I’ll start off by saying that I’ve been playing this game since it’s earliest private alpha release and I’ve seen the game change dramatically from the earliest stage to the point we’re at today, which is the early access release.
The very worst thing that I can say about this game is that sometimes it feels somewhat unresponsive or buggy. Now, I don’t mean the movement or the general interaction controls. What I mean is inventory, building, and some secondary functions. But as this game is just now coming out of it’s Alpha stages, all of this is expected, and in my opinion, isn’t very important (right now). However, I found it possible to navigate the world and it’s gamemode maps without issue as well as interact without having to jump over any obstacles.
The community is also one of my favorite aspects of this game. The people that have been apart of the GMod Tower community are some of the friendliest that I’ve ever met. Back in October, someone was giving game keys away for no reason. If free games aren’t a sign of a good community, I don’t know what is. With the players aside, the developer’s are also awesome. They often do Q&A’s on twitch and browse their forums a lot, responding to questions and helping out however they can.
Now, Graphically, I think this game is pretty good looking. The main world, known as the lobby, is definitely a piece of eye candy. All of the maps look pretty well done and I don’t have any complaints. Now, the characters on the other hand, are obviously in the early stages of development. There’s not a whole lot of customization for your character at the moment other than changing the color scheme of their skin, clothing, and hair. However, I expect this to change dramatically as customization was always one of the biggest features in GMod Tower.
The gameplay is pretty fun so far but I feel that it could be done better. The Golf gamemode, my favorite, is amazing and has improved from their mod. However, I feel that some of the maps/holes/rounds are too easy or just a waste of time. What I mean is that you hit the ball and regardless of the direction you hit it as well as how powerful you hit it, the result ends up being the same (give or take a few inches). Playing these holes once or twice is fine but when you repeat that menial process over and over again, expect it to be boring and frustrating.
I have a love-hate relationship with the ball race gamemode. I imagine it would be fun if it weren’t so difficult. At first I just thought I was generally awful at it but after playing with other people and seeing that only maybe one in every eight of us actually completed the course, I started to believe that the courses were just too difficult. Other than that, it’s a gamemode with a lot of potential and I’m looking forward to see if they’ll leave it as it is or make it easier for casuals like myself.
The other two game modes that are available I haven’t played much of. Virus is one that I loved in GMod Tower though. Right now, Virus seems like it could use some work and polish but the core gameplay is there.
The Condo design is a nice feature. You can completely customize your own condo from something as simple as the chair you’ll sit on to the material of the walls and floors. Nearly every feature about it is changeable and I believe that you’ll even be able to change the floor-plan in the future.
Overall, the game is turning out pretty well. It’s very obviously in it’s beta stages and needs a lot of work still but I can see a great game in the making with a lot of potential. I would definitely suggest it to anyone whether they’re looking to be overly competitive at mini-golf or they just want to watch youtube videos with some friends in the theatre or their condo.
TL;DR: It’s good, man.

I wanted to like this, guys.  It looked to me like a blend of Monaco and an easy-to-learn-hard-to-master puzzle game, which are both my jam.
But I didn't last a full hour before ragequitting for good, so, in the interest of helping anyone else with my druthers, here's why.
I like figuring out how things work, trying different ways to tackle a mission or solve a puzzle, understanding how things work, learning how the logic of the game world works, and trying again.  It looked like this game would work that way, but:
1) Getting TO each mission was a giant pain in the keister.  The missions themselves let you pause, let you control the behavior of your character precisely and elegantly with a few clicks, and the game carries out difficult tasks like a headshot or an 8-meter dash-and-bash all by itself -- but to GET to that part of the game, you have to control a ship careening through space at a billion miles an hour, on your own, with zero automation, with nothing but aiming your mouse, left button thrusts, right button brakes.  It is the opposite of the careful planning and meticulous execution that's waiting for you -- it's like playing bumper cars with a blindfold on.  I routinely spent longer trying to REACH my target than carry out my mission, and I hated every second of it.  It felt like a completely different game with the opposite design philosophy of the game I'd watched all this footage of.  If there were a mode that let me skip this part of the game, I probably wouldn't have returned it for a refund.
2) It is really, really hard to tell which of the tiny indistinct humans on the screen is your character.  The camera doesn't auto-center on you -- which is good, because camera control is good in games that need stealth -- but especially when you're still figuring out how to play, it means you spend way, way too much time trying to figure out which of the dudes in the little room is you ... and by the time you have, they've hurled you out into space.  Sure, you can pause at any second, but the little men are SO hard to tell apart that that doesn't help as much as you'd think.
3) You get hurled out into space.  That ... is ... well, I've played puzzle games and I've played roguelikes, and I've enjoyed both, but here's the thing.  It takes me more than literally one use of a mechanic to figure out how to physically, mechanically do it, and then I have to realize I need to.  The tutorial hurls you out into space once, so, okay, sure, the game has technically shown you how to do it.  But suddenly my character is running out of oxygen, and I need to figure out how to do something about it.  And then it turns out what I have to do about it is .... steer my pod again.  My pod.  That I just finished complaining that it was so hard to steer.  So basically your punishment for not even having started to master the precisely controlled, meticulously planned part of the game yet, is that you have to do more of the hard-to-control, chaotic, high-speed, can't-pause-to-control-this part of the game.  At this point I would just give up and let my character die because controlling my pod is very difficult.  I am not physically well-coordinated, and what drew me to this game watching LPs of it was how you could very very precisely control what happened without needing to have great reflexes.  Very frustrating.
4) THERE IS NO QUICKSAVE.  Cat just came in with a rat in his mouth?  Computer crashing?  Toddler screaming in the next room?  House on fire?  Any of the other million reasons you might need to quit this game right this very second?  Tough.  If you try to quit the game during a mission, instead of letting you restart where you left off, the game tells you helpfully, "Hey, if you quit right now, this character will die!  That okay?"  No, game, it is not.  Even when I'm playing a roguelike, and I expect I might lose all my progress at any time, a game will generally let me save and resume later in case, say, the stock pot is boiling over and I need to turn off this software for a while.  This is very basic modern game design, guys.  If I'm spending $$ on something, I need to be able to turn it off when Real Life happens and come back later without the game punishing me for it with a character death.

It wasn’t looking good. My capture target was surrounded by guards, all protected by shields. I had one charge left on my shield deactivator. I managed to make my target vulnerable, then knocked him out with my concussive gun. The other guards charged me but I retreated into my pod and detached. I then docked somewhere else, fired a gun to draw attention, and then as all the guards ran over to me I got back in my pod and flew back to the first area. My target was now abandoned, and I picked him up and flew away.
Heat Signature is all about boarding and raiding ships, with various goals ranging from "kill this guy" or "steal this item" to more complex things like "hijack the ship by neutralizing everyone on board" or special missions like "rescue a hostage without being seen." There are a lot of things to help you on the way, from standard weapons to things like crashbeams (which short out all electronics they hit) several different kinds of teleporter, and much more.
There are many ways to approach any situation. Say you need an item behind a locked door protected by three guards. You could a) use a shotgun to take them all out at once, b) use a stealth shield to get past them and pickpocket the keycard, c) play the role of the horror movie monster and pick off the guards one by one as they leave to do other things, d) teleport into the room, or e) destroy the room with a breach grenade, then dock your pod to the convenient hole in the ship.
Heat Signature revolves around an at-will "bullet time" effect. At any time, you can press spacebar to pause the game. This allows you to do things like view your inventory, teleport dropped items on the ship to you, swap equipped items, and time your attacks more effectively. The game also slows down when a guard spots you or when you aim a weapon. This setup allows you to do crazy things like clear a whole room without needing lightning reflexes or a time-slowing powerup. Even if you stumble into a guard’s line of sight, you have a few seconds before he identifies you and then a few more seconds before he raises the alarm, triggering a capture timer as the ship you’re on flees. This countdown can be stopped by killing the pilot, or otherwise removing them from their seat. And if you don't like any of your missions you can go out and raid some ships just because!
The characters you can choose from have different personal missions, and have different starting gear. Each time you retire or get a character killed or captured, you choose a new character with a fresh inventory. Items do NOT carry over. Think of each character as a different save file in the same world. However, you can find "heirloom" items --special items you name when you retire a character after completing their personal mission-- in ship crates or shops. You can even find your friends heirloom items! You can also rescue captured characters and rescue your friends’ characters. Combine that with randomized galaxies to get a true never-ending experience.
This game also loves to be funny. With item tooltips like "What if grenades, but faster?" (rapid grenade launcher), to "Few guards, not skeleton guards" (skeleton crew), to "this weapon causes people to die. usually forever" (lethal weapon) and other things that will make you laugh..
This game is surprisingly solid. The only bug I have found is when you try to "jump" from one opening to another, your character spazzes out and gets placed in the airlock.
A typical mission starts in the station, where you have 4 or 5 missions to choose from. You can see each missions’ main objective, pay, and any special conditions the mission might have. By selecting a mission, you can see the guards’ loadouts and get general info about the ship, such as alarm response time, guard quantity, and any special things the ship or guards might have. After choosing a mission, you go to your boarding pod and leave the station. You have an objective marker showing which direction the target ship is. After flying out to the ship, you then must maneuver to the airlock, avoiding the ships spotlights. Once docked, the camera zooms in and you can see the entire interior of the ship. Then you must make your way to the objective. This typically consists of killing guards and taking their keycards, then going to the next group and repeating the process, however you can also pickpocket the keycard or just use a subverter on the door. Afterwards you make your way back to the pod and head back to a station. You can also smash a window for a quicker exit, or hijack the ship and fly back in style.
In conclusion, Heat Signature is a good play and a great game for completionists. It is complex enough to be fun while simple enough to still be understandable. Everything is fair and I never felt that something was unfair unless it was my own doing.

I will first start off by saying that it has probably been over a year since I seriously played Aberoth, though I have plans on playing it at least casually again. I've loved this game enough to go online for one day specifically to buy another year of membership. The developer of this game absolutely deserves the support!!!
Some things to note when playing this game;
* Insure everything you can at the pub, because you WILL die a billion times! Insuring at least gives you a chance to keep some of your loot.
* Carry only what you are willing to lose, and store the rest in your vault.
* Be nice to EVERYONE, because it doesn't take much to get a bounty on your head and have entire realms after you. I've seen people literally evicted from realms simply because they were rude.
* If you're particularly wealthy, store your money in your vault rather than with the banker. Players can look how much money you have banked online, and can tag you as being a prospective person to blackmail or KOS for your epic loot.
* Team up with people who will have your back, and are willing to do loot drop rotations, etc.
* Money can accumulate quickly, even just by killing bandits and selling their weapons/boots.
Why do I say all this? Because a lot of negative reviews are about dying all the time and being PKed. To survive on this game, you need to make friends. It's a community based game with a large sense of justice. If you attempt to lone-wolf everything, the community is small enough that people will notice and take advantage of it.
If you can do the above, and you overlook the artstyle (characters kinda reminds me of Superbrothers: Sword and Sworcery tbh) and slow progression, you'll find that despite the appearance of a small game, it's actually incredibly feature rich. Unique features at that! For example; did you know you can create a staircase to heaven out of boots? Did you know you can get absolutely wasted? That's all one needs in a game!
Try the game, look up some tutorials, fall in love with the uh... unique graphics... And I promise you will adore this game once you give it a generous chance! (also expect to lose your stuff constantly. I was a somewhat well-known merchant, I know what it's like to make enemies and die lots lol)
P.S I do recall that a protection realm was released at some point during my absence, that stops your loot from being dropped. If it wasn't removed (tbh I hope it was because it kinda ruins the thrill), it's an option for anyone afraid to die by a players hand... You'll still die lots though. :D
Finally as a mod on Steam. No more stupid weird installations!.. Awesomness! :3

Hitman: Codename 47... Hitman 1...
This is an Interesting game from a Series that I have only just started getting into, I have always been interested in how far my favourite games have come from their source material; the first Hitman game I played was Hitman Blood Money and I loved it, and I was suprised on how many of the elements present in that game were not in this one.
The Beauty of Blood Money was the fact that the game could be played in pretty much any way you wanted; you could play stealthily, you could tactically pacify everyone one by one, or you could just shoot everyone. C47 however can't seem to decide on how it want's to be played, you can't really play stealthily because guards will shoot you for sneezing wrong, you can't pacify everyone because there is no non-lethal wasy of getting rid of guards, and you can't just shoot everyone because you die too quickly.
There is always one or two ways to beat a level as opposed to the large playground environments used in Blood Money, without a walkthrough you will be stuck on this game often leading to cases of unfair difficulty.
Am I saying that C47 is a bad game though? No. It is simply a game that has aged poorly in several ways; the control for example is bizzare: the walk forward and run forward functions are seperate buttons. Graphically the game looks really good for 2000's standards and there are some familiar elements in this game present in future installments such as the fibre wire and Sniper rifle suitcase. You are not punished for killing enemy mooks but you are for innocent civilians, a level of frustration is reached in certain levels however when you are forced into a shootout because there is no other way around the level.
It isn't really fair to judge C47 on superior sequels, but rather look at the game itself, it isn't a bad game, but certainly not a great one, I would only reccomend this to people who have played future installments of the Franchise who want to play this out of Morbid Curiosity
FINAL VERDICT: Average

It takes the tried-and-true one step further but ends up leaps and bounds ahead of the rest.
