There's quite a bit to say about Starbound, so I'm not entirely sure where to start. Bear with me here.
To begin, I suppose I'll get the meat out of the way: Is this the game for you?
This depends on your preferences. It's got quite a wide array of attractions-decent combat with various weapon styles and randomly generated loot for the warriors among you (Swordplay almost works like, say, Chivalry's, but less threatening), interesting areas to explore and new things to discover for those of you who like to explore an expansive game world, plenty of lore to find amongst the stars, farming for those who like a slow paced game, and of course lots and lots of junk for pack rats.
A large update just came through the pipe. This is a mixed blessing. On one hand, it's been about a year since the last one, and consequently it's packed with new content, gameplay, and tweaks. On the other hand, this is a balancing nightmare, and it might be a bit before it's all been tightened up.
Alright, now you know what you're getting into. Details...
COMBAT
There's Melee Weapons (Swords (one handed or two), Axes, Knives, Hammers, Shields), Guns (Rifles, Shotguns, Pistols, Revolvers, Launchers), and Staves (New and mysterious), and they all handle well in a 2-D environment. Earlier I said melee combat plays out a bit like Chivalry. That's pretty on the money. During combat, with a broadsword or a shield you can parry or block attacks (respectively). To parry, you need to time it correctly to block all incoming damage from that direction. With a shield, you can parry in the same way, or keep it up. Successive damage to the shield will break it (like Smash-it does regenerate) leaving you vulnerable. Gunplay is solid, but finding one you like can be tricky, and once you reach the next difficulty level you'll need to get a better one down the line (usually). Each shot takes a chunk out of your energy bar, which recharges quickly when not in use. You can keep firing while it recharges, but if you empty the bar, you have to wait for it to fill up completely to fire again. This keeps you or NPCs from firing a nonstop barrage, and tosses aside the idea of finding ammo. Staves are a new one on me-they draw from the same energy pool as guns but must be charged up. A grey area for me.
EXPLORATION
There is a LOT to find in this game. I've played since it was released and I don't think I've seen half of it. Very, very intriguing, and the lore you'll stumble across is good too. Each structure can tell it's own story, if you use your imagination. There is a LARGE caveat though, and it's this: before you can really get going and explore, you need to go past the tutorial and fight a boss. This boss is not properly balanced, and will take a few tries to get past. Basically, a few hours of your time and a meat gate block your way to exploration fun times. If you're in it to explore, you should only get this game right now if you don't mind investing your time and effort.
THE QUIET LIFE
Yes, there is a farming aspect. It's fairly lightly touched upon now, but later you'll be able to have essentially most of the game in a stationary lifestyle, if you choose.
ONE MORE THING
This game has an interesting music system, in that you can import ABC files (easily converted from midi) and play them once you've found an instrument. This keeps me entertained for hours. Once you cross a galaxy to the tune from Battlestar Galactia you can never go back.

[EARLY ACCESS REVIEW - CONTENT IS LIKELY TO CHANGE IN THE FUTURE]
Hey, guys.
I’ll start off by saying that I’ve been playing this game since it’s earliest private alpha release and I’ve seen the game change dramatically from the earliest stage to the point we’re at today, which is the early access release.
The very worst thing that I can say about this game is that sometimes it feels somewhat unresponsive or buggy. Now, I don’t mean the movement or the general interaction controls. What I mean is inventory, building, and some secondary functions. But as this game is just now coming out of it’s Alpha stages, all of this is expected, and in my opinion, isn’t very important (right now). However, I found it possible to navigate the world and it’s gamemode maps without issue as well as interact without having to jump over any obstacles.
The community is also one of my favorite aspects of this game. The people that have been apart of the GMod Tower community are some of the friendliest that I’ve ever met. Back in October, someone was giving game keys away for no reason. If free games aren’t a sign of a good community, I don’t know what is. With the players aside, the developer’s are also awesome. They often do Q&A’s on twitch and browse their forums a lot, responding to questions and helping out however they can.
Now, Graphically, I think this game is pretty good looking. The main world, known as the lobby, is definitely a piece of eye candy. All of the maps look pretty well done and I don’t have any complaints. Now, the characters on the other hand, are obviously in the early stages of development. There’s not a whole lot of customization for your character at the moment other than changing the color scheme of their skin, clothing, and hair. However, I expect this to change dramatically as customization was always one of the biggest features in GMod Tower.
The gameplay is pretty fun so far but I feel that it could be done better. The Golf gamemode, my favorite, is amazing and has improved from their mod. However, I feel that some of the maps/holes/rounds are too easy or just a waste of time. What I mean is that you hit the ball and regardless of the direction you hit it as well as how powerful you hit it, the result ends up being the same (give or take a few inches). Playing these holes once or twice is fine but when you repeat that menial process over and over again, expect it to be boring and frustrating.
I have a love-hate relationship with the ball race gamemode. I imagine it would be fun if it weren’t so difficult. At first I just thought I was generally awful at it but after playing with other people and seeing that only maybe one in every eight of us actually completed the course, I started to believe that the courses were just too difficult. Other than that, it’s a gamemode with a lot of potential and I’m looking forward to see if they’ll leave it as it is or make it easier for casuals like myself.
The other two game modes that are available I haven’t played much of. Virus is one that I loved in GMod Tower though. Right now, Virus seems like it could use some work and polish but the core gameplay is there.
The Condo design is a nice feature. You can completely customize your own condo from something as simple as the chair you’ll sit on to the material of the walls and floors. Nearly every feature about it is changeable and I believe that you’ll even be able to change the floor-plan in the future.
Overall, the game is turning out pretty well. It’s very obviously in it’s beta stages and needs a lot of work still but I can see a great game in the making with a lot of potential. I would definitely suggest it to anyone whether they’re looking to be overly competitive at mini-golf or they just want to watch youtube videos with some friends in the theatre or their condo.

TL;DR: If you liked GMOD Tower, you'll love this.
Well, where to start. It's the successor to the popular Mod for Garry's mod, Garry's Mod Tower, or GMT for short. Currently, when I'm reviewing this, there are four Game Worlds: Ball Race, Minigolf, Virus, and Planet Panic. I'll go ahead and break these down now.
Ball Race: Ever played Super Monkey Ball? Well, it's basically that, minus the world tilting.
Minigolf: Do I really need to explain this one?
Virus: Based on the TimeSplitter's gamemode, one player is infected and has to touch the other players to spread the infection. If the survivors last the time limit, then they win. If everyone gets infected, the infected win. The survivors have an arsenal of weapons to deal with the infected.
Planet Panic: An original Game World, where it's a sort of Capture the Flag, with a bunch of mini-flags that start off in the middle. You bring them back to your base. Sounds simple enough right? Well, the other team can steal your mini-flags for themselves, so make sure to protect them!
Edit 1: CASINO! One of the most requested features is here, and it's great. Currently as long as you pick the right machines, you're almost guranteed to make a profit.
Trivia! Using user-submitted questions, you'll never run out of new questions!
And right now, that's about it. I'll update this review as more features and Game Worlds are released. But I would definitely reccomend it, even in this early state.

If you look in any forums, reviews, or even talk to another person playing Heat Signature, you will probably hear a story. You’ll hear a wild, crazy story of a heist that they almost bungled up, but somehow managed to succeed. Or you’ll hear a story of a brilliant solution to a seemingly impossible problem. The game generates these stories by design. Suspicious Developments has created a dynamic toy box for players to jump into and play. They wanted players to come and make their own adventures, and to share them with each other. Which is why what I’m about to suggest might seem strange:
. Because making your own adventures is probably the best part of Heat Signature.
Heat Signature is a game that is very clear about its intent: it is a game about infiltrating spaceships. (For the record, I will not share any of my own anecdotal escapades in this review, as much as I desperately want to.) You’re hired to steal a top-secret device, or hijack a ship, or “off” someone, and so on. Further, the game is highly geared around playing smart.  As you clear out a level, you feel like an intergalactic Anton Chigurh, like a methodical, unstoppable force of power, focused on your task at hand. You have your standard array of melee and ranged weapons, but also unique equipment, like creatively designed teleporters (for example, one can swap your position with another person). There is a wonderful dynamism to all of the games interlocking mechanics, encouraging you to mull over the possibilities. Every time you take a bullet, you’ll be able to survive the vacuum of space a little less. And then, you’re dead. Forever. It’s a permadeath game, and when you die, you instead take up another character drinking in your honor at a nearby bar. The game is designed with smart and cautious play in mind, and all of these elements in concert make the player feel like a regular Sader Fiasco.
Sader Fiasco? That’s the master freelancer the game starts you out as– crashing through a window to your possible demise. (This may become a calling card for Suspicious Developments devs; it appeared in Gunpoint as well.) After a tutorial mission, Sader Fiasco retires. And… that’s about it for the story. There’s a little bit of world-building, and it’s actually stellar. All four of the in-game factions which you play against have their own unique politics, ships, origins, and moral codes, some of which determine AI behavior. What small amount of writing that is there, is witty and engaging. I genuinely wanted to see more of this story characteristics because they were so enjoyable. It’s a shame a lot of this information is locked behind late game missions because these factions are genuinely fascinating. Since Heat Signature emphasizes player-created stories, it deliberately drops any narrative. The game is procedurally generated, so a lot of the game is about seeing where these systems can take you as a player, but this also may be Heat Signature’s biggest downfall.
The problem is, while there are plenty of mechanical stories to tell, I can’t really think of many narrative stories I discovered myself. Characters will have personal missions to go for (revenge, debt, etc.), but that’s about as interesting as those narratives get. The non-mechanical stories are very limited and very empty in stark contrast to the mechanical ones. This doesn’t have to be a huge problem, but because the game lacks a broader narrative, it’s very easy to get lost in a directionless haze early on. You can focus on faction strongholds, sure, but this is a very vague and disconnected objective. The metagame feels slow and unproductive. You slowly liberate space stations, but they unlocked what felt like very little. You have this massive map screen which isn’t all that necessary. The only benefit is that you can encounter different ships than the ones you’re objective is on. I felt like all this empty space could have had way more things going on inside.
The problem of procedural generation seeps into the level design, as well. As the game gets into the later hours, I felt like I was dealing with the same missions over and over again. Ships start looking the same, AI has no variation, and the missions begin to blend together, with only a handful of objectives. They were fun, rewarding, and challenging missions that I had a blast playing and trying new solutions in, but they felt similar regardless. There are also a few mechanical flaws (the difference between lethal and non-lethal, for example, is totally trivial most of the time.) (Also, pro-tip: “T” lets you throw items or eject your pod; the game never tells you directly.) I seriously think Heat Signature could have benefited from the slightest story structure (especially with such an interesting world!), or a small set of predetermined missions, or a greater emphasis on roleplaying, or just something to keep me on track as a player as I figured out what I wanted to do.
Once you figure out what you want to do in Heat Signature, you can feel that click. What you want–or, at least what I wanted–was to take part in these wild space exploits. You have to take risks, you have to take missions you don’t know if you’ll be able to beat. You have to get wild. Because when you start to risk it, you can get the biscuit. You discover wild solutions. You discover wild failures. You begin to grin like an idiot as your plans spiral into failure, or even success, somehow. Unique client requirements like “don’t kill anyone” or “don’t get spotted” and limited equipment constantly encourage you to experiment. I actually think they could have gone even further with this; limit my inventory even more, expect extremely specific things from me, force me to really think and really get into these systems at play. Don’t let me game this system. Failure isn’t necessarily fun in Heat Signature, but it almost always feels like a purposeful failure. Your demise was clearly predictable, you just didn’t predict it. It’s a game about experimentation and discovery. That’s why you shouldn’t read any anecdotes or stories before playing, I think: it robs you of this joy. Learning to take risks and think outside the box is what makes Heat Signature so damn good. Discovery and revelations of how mechanics suddenly begin to interlock together into this disastrous concerto of missteps and mistakes or a miraculous delivery into success.
Heat Signature is a game about infiltration, but it’s also about experimentation and discovery. It presents you with a little sandbox of toys and lets you just have a go at it. It infected my mind at times, replaying moments of ingenuity over and over in my head. The game world is fascinating, but it’s too bad it lacks any story inside of it. The metagame is lacking, and there are lulls of excitement about, but that doesn’t negate the utter joy I experienced. There is a serious need for direction, one that almost had me stop playing, but I am so glad I didn’t. It’s a shame that Heat Signature doesn’t give its players more to go off of, because what is hiding in this game is shining and bright, and some people might miss it. It’s a game about little adventures. You need to figure out your direction because without you’ll miss out on the brilliant realm of challenging adversity Suspicious Developments has set up. By managing to discover that in Heat Signature, I stumbled onto an exciting and blossoming world of dynamic death-defying capers that is totally engrossing and full of stories.

But I didn't last a full hour before ragequitting for good, so, in the interest of helping anyone else with my druthers, here's why.
I like figuring out how things work, trying different ways to tackle a mission or solve a puzzle, understanding how things work, learning how the logic of the game world works, and trying again.  It looked like this game would work that way, but:
1) Getting TO each mission was a giant pain in the keister.  The missions themselves let you pause, let you control the behavior of your character precisely and elegantly with a few clicks, and the game carries out difficult tasks like a headshot or an 8-meter dash-and-bash all by itself -- but to GET to that part of the game, you have to control a ship careening through space at a billion miles an hour, on your own, with zero automation, with nothing but aiming your mouse, left button thrusts, right button brakes.  It is the opposite of the careful planning and meticulous execution that's waiting for you -- it's like playing bumper cars with a blindfold on.  I routinely spent longer trying to REACH my target than carry out my mission, and I hated every second of it.  It felt like a completely different game with the opposite design philosophy of the game I'd watched all this footage of.  If there were a mode that let me skip this part of the game, I probably wouldn't have returned it for a refund.
2) It is really, really hard to tell which of the tiny indistinct humans on the screen is your character.  The camera doesn't auto-center on you -- which is good, because camera control is good in games that need stealth -- but especially when you're still figuring out how to play, it means you spend way, way too much time trying to figure out which of the dudes in the little room is you ... and by the time you have, they've hurled you out into space.  Sure, you can pause at any second, but the little men are SO hard to tell apart that that doesn't help as much as you'd think.
3) You get hurled out into space.  That ... is ... well, I've played puzzle games and I've played roguelikes, and I've enjoyed both, but here's the thing.  It takes me more than literally one use of a mechanic to figure out how to physically, mechanically do it, and then I have to realize I need to.  The tutorial hurls you out into space once, so, okay, sure, the game has technically shown you how to do it.  But suddenly my character is running out of oxygen, and I need to figure out how to do something about it.  And then it turns out what I have to do about it is .... steer my pod again.  My pod.  That I just finished complaining that it was so hard to steer.  So basically your punishment for not even having started to master the precisely controlled, meticulously planned part of the game yet, is that you have to do more of the hard-to-control, chaotic, high-speed, can't-pause-to-control-this part of the game.  At this point I would just give up and let my character die because controlling my pod is very difficult.  I am not physically well-coordinated, and what drew me to this game watching LPs of it was how you could very very precisely control what happened without needing to have great reflexes.  Very frustrating.
4) THERE IS NO QUICKSAVE.  Cat just came in with a rat in his mouth?  Computer crashing?  Toddler screaming in the next room?  House on fire?  Any of the other million reasons you might need to quit this game right this very second?  Tough.  If you try to quit the game during a mission, instead of letting you restart where you left off, the game tells you helpfully, "Hey, if you quit right now, this character will die!  That okay?"  No, game, it is not.  Even when I'm playing a roguelike, and I expect I might lose all my progress at any time, a game will generally let me save and resume later in case, say, the stock pot is boiling over and I need to turn off this software for a while.  This is very basic modern game design, guys.  If I'm spending $$ on something, I need to be able to turn it off when Real Life happens and come back later without the game punishing me for it with a character death.

It wasn’t looking good. My capture target was surrounded by guards, all protected by shields. I had one charge left on my shield deactivator. I managed to make my target vulnerable, then knocked him out with my concussive gun. The other guards charged me but I retreated into my pod and detached. I then docked somewhere else, fired a gun to draw attention, and then as all the guards ran over to me I got back in my pod and flew back to the first area. My target was now abandoned, and I picked him up and flew away.
Heat Signature is all about boarding and raiding ships, with various goals ranging from "kill this guy" or "steal this item" to more complex things like "hijack the ship by neutralizing everyone on board" or special missions like "rescue a hostage without being seen." There are a lot of things to help you on the way, from standard weapons to things like crashbeams (which short out all electronics they hit) several different kinds of teleporter, and much more.
There are many ways to approach any situation. Say you need an item behind a locked door protected by three guards. You could a) use a shotgun to take them all out at once, b) use a stealth shield to get past them and pickpocket the keycard, c) play the role of the horror movie monster and pick off the guards one by one as they leave to do other things, d) teleport into the room, or e) destroy the room with a breach grenade, then dock your pod to the convenient hole in the ship.
Heat Signature revolves around an at-will "bullet time" effect. At any time, you can press spacebar to pause the game. This allows you to do things like view your inventory, teleport dropped items on the ship to you, swap equipped items, and time your attacks more effectively. The game also slows down when a guard spots you or when you aim a weapon. This setup allows you to do crazy things like clear a whole room without needing lightning reflexes or a time-slowing powerup. Even if you stumble into a guard’s line of sight, you have a few seconds before he identifies you and then a few more seconds before he raises the alarm, triggering a capture timer as the ship you’re on flees. This countdown can be stopped by killing the pilot, or otherwise removing them from their seat. And if you don't like any of your missions you can go out and raid some ships just because!
The characters you can choose from have different personal missions, and have different starting gear. Each time you retire or get a character killed or captured, you choose a new character with a fresh inventory. Items do NOT carry over. Think of each character as a different save file in the same world. However, you can find "heirloom" items --special items you name when you retire a character after completing their personal mission-- in ship crates or shops. You can even find your friends heirloom items! You can also rescue captured characters and rescue your friends’ characters. Combine that with randomized galaxies to get a true never-ending experience.
This game also loves to be funny. With item tooltips like "What if grenades, but faster?" (rapid grenade launcher), to "Few guards, not skeleton guards" (skeleton crew), to "this weapon causes people to die. usually forever" (lethal weapon) and other things that will make you laugh..
This game is surprisingly solid. The only bug I have found is when you try to "jump" from one opening to another, your character spazzes out and gets placed in the airlock.
A typical mission starts in the station, where you have 4 or 5 missions to choose from. You can see each missions’ main objective, pay, and any special conditions the mission might have. By selecting a mission, you can see the guards’ loadouts and get general info about the ship, such as alarm response time, guard quantity, and any special things the ship or guards might have. After choosing a mission, you go to your boarding pod and leave the station. You have an objective marker showing which direction the target ship is. After flying out to the ship, you then must maneuver to the airlock, avoiding the ships spotlights. Once docked, the camera zooms in and you can see the entire interior of the ship. Then you must make your way to the objective. This typically consists of killing guards and taking their keycards, then going to the next group and repeating the process, however you can also pickpocket the keycard or just use a subverter on the door. Afterwards you make your way back to the pod and head back to a station. You can also smash a window for a quicker exit, or hijack the ship and fly back in style.
In conclusion, Heat Signature is a good play and a great game for completionists. It is complex enough to be fun while simple enough to still be understandable. Everything is fair and I never felt that something was unfair unless it was my own doing.

Being both a Lego and Hobbit fan, I had to give this a go. I didn't set very high expectations for this game and good thing I didn't. Often for every 5 good things there was at least one bad thing. With that said, here we go!
Story: (8/10) *Spoiler Free*
The story is what you would expect from a Lego game, following suit with the movies story line, often utilizing the movies dialogue throughout the game, while adding some humour now and there. Often the story is explained through short 1 minute cut scenes after each level, and sometimes explaining through short exchanges of dialogue during game play. Having seen the Hobbit trilogy, the game does a surprisingly good job of staying close to the films storyline. You delve into the world of Middle-earth (before Lord of the Rings) through the protagonist Bilbo Baggins. Bilbo and Company must set out to the lonely mountain to reclaim their homeland & treasure, which is guarded by a fire breathing dragon. The plot itself didn’t “blow me away” or try to add/take away from the original films. But they were cute, funny, didn't overstay their welcome, and overall got a good kick out of it.
Gameplay: (9/10)
Being a Lego game, I knew that if one thing had to get done right it was the game play. And what do you know it was actually some of the best since Lego Star wars. I felt like they did an excellent job adding a level of variety while keeping that familiarity from past Lego games. If you are not familiar with other Lego games, the premise is more or less a linear platformer / collectathon where you get from one end to the other whilst experiencing the events that took place in the movies. Of course the game is sprinkled with the occasional puzzles and bosses. But where I was really began to fall in love with the game is the ability to collect another material other than currency, minikits, red bricks, and gold bricks, you often use these materials to build objects to progress further in the level. This of course is really smart of the developers because it gave me more incentive to explore and smash things. Of course being a Lego game you can expect to see a huge roster of characters, purchasing abilities and weapons which can be unlocked after completing levels, going back and replaying levels with any character you choose so you can maybe get those collectables, a massive “open world”, and so much more! I don’t want to drag on forever so I will just say that the game play was not a disappointment and was definitely the strong point of the game.
Graphics: (8/10)
I’m a big old-school gamer, so I don't know if these are acceptable graphics for today’s standards. It’s no Uncharted 4, but it has some really nice textures, really cool lighting at times, lots of color, and a very simplistic look which is pleasing to the eye. I don't think this is where the game shines, and it shouldn't, it's a Lego game. So if you’re expecting a highly detailed world full of texture or color then you may be in for a disappointment.
Difficulty: (4/10)
Its not my place to say if the game is hard or easy, because people have different standards of what "difficult" even means. In my play through of the game however I found it to be mind numbingly easy. Often I felt the game was holding my hand, constantly giving me hints of what to do (Which you can turn off btw). Oh, did I forget to mention that this game has bosses? Yah! And the ones that were in this game were terribly easy. There are only like 5, but just thought I would let you know they were a big letdown. I think we all know that where the difficultly lies is not in the combat or enemies, but rather the puzzles. And to my surprise there weren’t that many, and the ones that there were consisted nothing more than activating a switch, moving a block, or building something. Which is a big let down because I knew the older Lego games had great puzzles.
Verdict:
My biggest gripe with the game however (and alot of others would agree too) that not choosing to include the third movie in the final game was a massive let down, and takes away from the hobbit experience. It felt more or less like an incomplete puzzle because we only got to play 2/3 of a complete story. But you know what, with how much content is already in this game, 100% would have been a massive over hall and would have made it almost overwhelming. Overall I recommend this game to anyone who may be looking for a fun action packed plat former / collectathon, or anyone who just wants to kill 7-10-ish hours (30+ if you’re going for 100%). This game would be especially ideal for kids seeing as the difficulty is insultingly easy. Lastly I just want to note that playing with a controller and friend is recommended 

This game can be very difficult, and the things you need to pull off can be obscure and vague at best at times. However, its not exactly bad, just a bit poorly executed. Also the interface is fairly bad (I'm looking at YOU map!).
Unfortunately the game doesn't work on a quicksave/quickload system like a lot of FPS'/ later Hitman games, oh no. It works on limited checkpoint system that just respawns you at a certain point you got up to, without actually altering your progress made from up to that point. So lets say you bite the dust whilst having alerted every damn enemy in the map. They will STILL BE ALERTED. And a lot of the time, if you alert everyone and don't do something about it FAST, your main target will be alerted and he will haul it out of there faster than you can say game over.
I only beat about 3 levels before it got to the point where the game just got too hard and annoying for me. I just honestly gave up and just watched someone else play the rest of the game via the internets, and had no regrets in doing so. A lot of the things you have to do looks obscure and hard to pull off.
Later Hitman games are much more playable, so I suggest you ignore this one at first unless you have absurd amounts of patience, wit, and skill.

Lego The Hobbit offers a fun and entertaining look on the movies. Not only does the game follow the plot quite closely, the hub areas offer lots more content to explore, quests to do, people to bring fancy items that you find on your travels, minigames, and of course, the lego style slapstick humor.
It has the usual Lego game formula.
First do the storymode version of a level, then you are free to go back in FreePlay and discover secrets with characters and abilities that were previously unavailable. Like Lego The Lord of the Rings it adds the blacksmith. Find the design, craft the item if you have the required materials, and bring it to the appropriate Middle Earth resident, who will then reward you with either a Mithril Brick or a Red Brick, or perhaps a whole questline before you get to the grand prize.
I very much enjoyed this game, I'm still working on cleaning up all the various missions left and right, grabbing achievements as I go along. The voices are straight from the movie which adds to the fun, save that one female dwarf voice that makes me cringe, everytime I walk by. Apart form her, there's not much to dislike about it.
I guess the only thing that I would have liked to see different, is that they included the third movie in the plot. The story pretty much ends at the end of the second. They had plans to include the last movie in a DLC, but that never happened so the story feels slightly unfinished.
Nevertheless, there is loads of content, there is much to do, lots of puzzles to solve, even some timed events that make you run and jump against the clock across obstacle courses.
I absolutely recommend this game, it's fun for young and old.

Another Aldorlea game in the bag so time for a review!   This game is harder to quantify than those before it since for example Dreamscape has a better battle system in my opinion, but this game has a far better story.  Although again a simple one. On the other hand this game has the flaw of you really need the guide for it the secret rooms are sometimes a little too well hidden.  But this does not detract from how fufilling this game is.  And the pairings actually make sense.
However this game at normal and probably hard difficulty has a rather odd problem.  Virtually every character is a 'physical' character in which the MAT stat is virtually worthless. When I got the final party member I perma benched her, since you can do a pretty awesome combo if you do galvanize+enthuse friends for 33% crits on top of increased attack, and add in dropping enemies defenses? But still another gem of a game by Aldorlea.

The weapons look and sound great, ranging from the realistic combat shotguns and grenade launchers, to the science-fictional, high-powered particle accelerators. The level design is diverse (owing a nod of thanks to Jedi Knight), including the expansive research facility, some great outdoor areas, and foreign locales that are best left to be discovered on your own. Suffice to say, it never gets repetitive.
The only problems with Half-Life are the results of it being so ambitious. The fact that all of the humans in the game look like clones takes from the otherwise realistic atmosphere. The diversity of the levels and puzzles will undoubtedly leave you thinking some areas were better than others. But complaints that arise are simply a reaction to the fact that the game is so close to ideal. Half-Life is an exceptional single-player game and a solid multiplayer game (though the upcoming Team Fortress add-on may make it even better). It takes the tried-and-true one step further but ends up leaps and bounds ahead of the rest.

Recently played the game and finished it on normal mode.
I liked the following:
1) Interesting and fun conversations between each characters.
2) Character's thoughts are conveyed throughout the game, which makes the content and gameplay enjoyable.
3) Interesting system where you cannot just barge into civilian's houses and loot (like your average classic RPGs ;D)
4) The stroy was quite short in my perspective, but the storyline do just go straight to the point.
Suggestions for the game:
(a) The world map appears to be "locked-route" and it would be better-off if players are given the option to be able to re-visit without being barred from the main story.
(b) The side quest may be better if they are not time-event bound.
(c) The varieties of enemies can be improved, exepcially for bosses.
(d) There should be options for post-end game plays where you are able to attend to side quests or finding secret rooms in my opinion.
(e) If only other characters may also be optional to join the party while on the quest...
Overall it is quite a nice game with its own pros and cons. I would recommend it to friends who are interested in RPGMaker type of games.

I know this game was ground-breaking when it was released, but that was 1998. It's less than a year until people born the year Half-Life was released can legally drink in most of the world.
Half-Life hasn't aged well. The confusing level design combined with the unrewarding exploration makes it easy to get lost, and the frequent jump-scares make many of the unintuitive world elements seem unsafe.
You can't walk around a corner without a Headcrab jumping you from behind, but that veiny hole? No, it won't suddenly explode into gibs or trap you, it throws you into the air. Those disgusting alien pods that are totally going to pop and release a lot of monsters when you get too close? They're a new weapon. The slime in certain parts of Xen? Unlike earlier disgusting liquids which are radioactive, this specific one is totally harmless.
The physics will occasionally force you to jump on unstable crates and barrels, and if they tip, or if you destroy them, you're stuck. What's worse is the jumping in general. The game will sometimes force you to jump across small platform with no aerial control, or the strange mechanic of crouching in the air to fit certain smaller holes, usually air vents.
To summarize: Awful level design, unintuitive world objects, and bad jumping physics makes this game more frustrating than fun.

My primary compulsion as an RPG player is to loot everything, but we're playing as characters who generally don't do that.  Nice touch.  :D
Big complaint was controls.  Controller didn't work, F12 surprisingly restarts the game instead of taking a screenshot (so I had to play the final battle again to see the rest of the ending -- oops!), and keys were not remappable.  It wasn't crippling, but it was very inconvenient.

Stardew Valley is an incredible game that I would readily recommend to anyone whether you are into min/maxing or casual gameplay.
Immediately I fell in love with the charming NPC community, Pelican Town. The townfolk walk around the map on their daily tasks, making running into them much more natural than in other games. As you develop your routine, you begin to discover the routines of the NPCs and feel that you are a part of the town as well. It feels like these characters actually live in the town and enjoy spending time in the area. If you are looking for a game to interact with the NPC community, Stardew Valley is definitely for you.
I also supremely enjoyed the RPG leveling element of the different skills in this game. I never felt limited by being too low of a level, but when I gained levels I felt like new opportunities were available. Advancement through the game was smooth and clean. I never felt like I was grinding to get to the next thing. Instead I was working to further Pelican Town and make my farm beautiful.
I cannot recommend this game enough. If you are looking to see if this is the game for you, please PM me and I'll happily address your specific questions.

ACU has many problems, with few advantages. On the good side, we have decent combat mechanics, when the AI doesn't spam bullets, which is far better then the past few games. The new fighting style of perfect parring makes the combat fluid, and they mostly got rid of the Arkham combat style (slow and bulky, like you are Marvel's Juggernaut without the unstoppablity). Unfortunatly, the new parkour system frequently messes up, resulting in Arno jumping to the ground, jumping over or under your inteded target. Arno himself is more interesting than Conner of AC3, but still has minimal character development. As I am currently on the 11 segment of ACU, I feel justified saying that French Cardboard Man stays an arrogant little child for the duration of the game, which is the exact problem I always had with Native American Cardboard Man (Conner). The implementation of Co-op really helped this title have weight, as I spent several hours screwing around in missions with random players, however the constant breaking does get annoying. In the game, Abstergo finds you when you are in the Animus home entertainment thingy, forcing you to migrate servers. This gives you a chance to parkour through Paris to find an exit, without passerbys messing your flow up. That is, until they introduce the flashing red lines, which signify gliches (fake glitches). As someone who has never suffered from a flashing lights, my eyes would start burning during these segments, even if i had just started playing. If you are sezure prone, get a friend to play these parts. Over all the game is maybe worth a 4/10, with my bad experiances outnumbering my good. With a good combat system, you are able to bypass the crappy stealth parts, and combat is enjoyable again, like in the AC2 saga. Get this game heavily discounted. at $20, it can given decent funs. This game is still a massive disappointment after AC4BF, with the best parts of AC4BF being absent. Buy at your own risk.
PS: make sure your computer can run the game, as you will have a much better time if you can run the dang game

NOTE: This review was done with no purchased DLC. This review contains no spoilers.
*****Summary:
Darkest Dungeon is an experience that is best described as demoralizing, but for a good reason. There is an objective and a subjective way of looking at the game. Objectively, this is a great game and designed well. Subjectively, you might find the game lacking at first but rewarding in the right mindset. If you can take the bad in stride with the good, you will find a deep and rewarding experience. The gameplay is about risk mitigation. It's not about if you get terrible luck, it's about when you get terrible luck. The game accoplishes all of the goals that it sets out and even the outragious random luck has a purpose in the story and setting. I recommend this game to those that can let go and enjoy roleplaying. I want to leave you with this quote:
"It is possible to commit no mistakes and still lose. That is not a weakness. That is life"
++++ Good:
I loved the setting and the story. The art style is just so fitting with the Cathulu-esque like hopelessness that pervades the entire game. It wasn't unil, maybe, hour 60 that I really started to appriciate what the game was going for in overall theme and story. I should fault the game here for that as I feel it should force you into the Darkest Dungeon and beat the first area earlier in the game. Once I did that, I started to understand why my luck was always crappy.
The game casts you in a role of a decendent of the original owner that first deleved into the Darkest Dungeon. The game really takes your role in events very seriously. If you can let go of trying to cast yourself as one of the heroes, or even a group of heroes, you will find much more enjoyment in the role-playing aspect. The way the game screws with you on a mental level is part of the game, story, and theme. This is true even down to terrible randomness that you encounter.
The turned based gameplay is often satisfying on lower difficulties. The basic mechanics of the battle system are very good. These don't change on higher difficulties, but more things are left to chance on the higher difficulties. You are the one that has to deal with the changes in fortune. That's what the overarching gameplay is about. Each battle could be your last.
----- Bad
My god this game can be rage inducing. Sometimes, there's just nothing you can do about getting screwed over. The enemy will always have the upperhand and you will never become "powerful". You just become better equip to deal with terrible situations. It really took me a while (along with uninstalling and reinstalling this game out of rage about 4 times) to really understand that there's no reason to be angry. There's always fresh meat coming into the Hamlet. You have to be in the right mindset for the rage to subside.
The love of heroes. The game gives you the illusion that you should become close or attatched to your "heroes". It lets you name them, train them, and customize them ( in a limited sense). The heroes talk and seem to have personalities. I'm here to say that you must resist the urge to see your heroes as more than fodder. That's what they are. They do your dirty work for their own selfish purposes. The game could have done a better job of helping the player detatch from the heroes. This would help stop from people getting so angry or feeling so screwed over when the game's random aspects come into play. My suggestions to players is to just not name them from the beginning and realize that everyone is going to die. That's it. It's not a matter of if, but when.
The grind. Only towards the end of the game, when only the Darkest Dungeon remains as the only goal, you find out that a full team wipe means that you have to start at square one. Now, there are ways to mitigate that risk, but you will still be out 3 or so hours building a new team to enter the dungeon. The stage wagon will bring in up to Resolve level 3. I don't recommend going into the Darkest Dungeon lower than level 5 (level 6 is the resolve cap). That means that you'll be baby sitting new recruits until you send them into the meat grinder to, most likely, die in the Darkest Dungeon. This is the only time where the game gets SUPER tedious. Remember Ace of Spades, before it was turned into a turd that went against everything it was about?
Ace of Spades was a great little title for an unfinished Alpha. Weapons hit hard as they should, building a trench or wall was a MUST if you wanted to hold your position and survive, let alone deal with snipers in more open ended maps, maps where fairly large and could be mangled to fit whatever your needs were.. A shame the game is pretty much dead from last I saw (let alone a popular playground for cheaters), because it was a pretty damn good game that mixed building stuff and breaking stuff together and showed that both could be used to make for some fun matches.
And then came games like the current Ace of Spades, Guncraft, and even Blockade 3D here, who all share the same major problem: Building is a waste of time that gets you killed more than anything, and when you do build something, it just ends up hindering you more than helping, showing that all it is good for is pluging up entry points (which even then only lasts for a second before a rocket blows your blockade wide open).
But, see... While this game attempts to emulate the feel of playing classic Ace of Spades (going so far as to have a few assets that feel like they were illigaly taken right from the source), in reality it is probably the worst contender for Voxel-based builder and shooter, or should I say just shooter, since it fails in the building part.
See, while the classic and Current version of Ace of spades and Guncraft gives you what you pay for, this game is Free to play, but also it is free to play in the worst possible way in that every gun in the game besides the starter kit (and a select few unlockables that you gain though unlocking) require you to pay money for them, as well as all manner of gear such as helmets, TNT blocks, med kits and all sorts of other gear.
Now, this isn't totally bad... Most guns are modestly priced, with some of the cheapest guns and a fair number of gear under a buck.. However, rather than allowing you to buy any gun from the start, the game has a leveling system that locks certain guns out, limiting your selection and making it hard to find a good gun to buy early on. It could lead to some wasteful purchases, buying a gun only to discover it is worthless compared to higher grade guns, some of the biggest guns costing 4-5 bucks, said guns being a minigun, an AA-12, and even a heavy sniper rifle that can kill a fully armored target in a single shot, and can make helmets worthless.
By the way, some of the guns you can buy are also rip-offs, weapons that are hardly worth the investment compared to other far better guns that can be aquired at the same price (or even less), meaning that you run the risk of wasting money. With the leveling system limiting what you can buy, as well as the risk of wasting money on sub-par guns, this could be the dev's way of multi-dipping into your pockets and making you spend more than you want to spend on a F2P title. Did I mention that there is also a lot of gear that is limited and can only be refilled either by buying them or as a small level-up reward?
Fans will argue that yes, you can get a selection of free guns, and every level up gives you a small reward package of free nades, medkits, rockets and TNT blocks. While the latter is somewhat useful, the guns you do get are still nothing compared to what you could get if you put money in the game. Sure, some of them pack a nasty punch, but even then they don't have the benifits that some of the better paid guns have (such as large ammo clips, helmet-piercing, high rates of fires, and in one case a grenade launcher that used ammo that you buy that packs on hell of a punch).
And mind you, I was just babbling on about the guns. There is also other problems, like how insultingly small the 2 team VS maps are, how the 4 team Battle mode tends to get horribly unbalanced at times (which, by the way, no auto balance, so expect some really unbalanced odds often), with some of the teams focusing more on spawn camping than on completing the objective (and for good reason, since you get nothing for winning but all sorts of XP for killing people), and.. I hardly really played the other modes, but they were so forgettable that I guess that alone is enough to say about them. And of course, there is a cheating problem, but that is common in a lot of F2P titles, so it isn't worth noting.
I don't like screaming pay to win, but this game certainly does smell of it, what with how the only decent weapon a F2P even has is a battle rifle that can one-shot people in the head.. Unless they have a helmet, then it takes two shots, which further proves how the dev really wants to get you to spend money on either getting better protection for your skull so you don't die as fast or a gun that can bypass said protection and make it a wasted investment that only serves to screw with free players. Not only does it stink of P2W, it also is an insult to building block shooters, where the one thing that could make it easier for a F2P player (building cover), is made pointless with how it only serves to slow you down and get in the way instead of providing cover that can help save your life and allow you to shoot from a covered position. It's all just run in and try not to die, and thus a waste of the engine.

Heat Signature is a pretty addictive number with some flaws that mostly tie to grind repetition and pretty dumb enemy AI, and balance issues.
For the most part, this game is really fun. Hotline Miami-esque gameplay with a more indepth field of strategy thanks to how pausing works and how every decision you make has to be final. The game has you controlling one character at a time during missions, however over the course of the game you will be responsible for many characters rather than one, each of whom will obtain their own gear and currency, which is where the grind starts to kick in, and where problems arise with the loot and sense of progression.
Luckily enough once you get into the flow of the game this can be quickly overcome due to how quick and easy it is to start up a new character. But my main issue lies with the unfulfilling nature of each character's progression. Obtaining rare and really useful loot is a bittersweet affair, as that character will soon be retired, and then you start a fresh new character. You can't stash items in a pool for all characters to use, you can simply leave behind ONE item that then becomes available as a rare find throughout your playthrough. This is where the game kicks you in the balls regarding any sense of achievement and just makes each new character seem like a slog.
The actual gameplay is very fun and variable, with many ingenius ways to approach succeeding in a mission. There are, however, a few issues with balance. Enemy AI for the most part is pretty stupid. The game may throw some really difficult situations at you, but the penalty for failure is relatively low. Even if you get shot on the ship, you are merely thrown out, just to be rescued via your pod with very little difficulty, until you have reached the blood loss limit where after a half dozen or so times of being shot, you straight up die, which never happened to me during an entire playthrough.
Some items, especially melee ones, are massively overpowered given the dual wielding aspect. Guns for the most part are an underpowered last resort, that are only ever useful if you wish to waive Pacifist bonuses, and don't care about raising alarms. Not to mention ammo cannot be bought, making Armour Piercing guns kinda pointless up against the more readily available restockable nade launchers and Melee alternatives. After a while, it becomes pretty obvious which loadouts are superior, and which items you should unlock for your shop. There's no real reason to not bring alone a Key Cloner, a Sidewinder and Subverters. The game may have made more sense if they had created character skill trees limiting what you could use, making the game infinitely more interesting. As it stands, you have an entire arsenal of gear come the mid game just ready to be bought, making all missions far too easy.
All said, if you like the sound of the action in Heat Signature and aren't put off by the mistakes made with the rpg-lite progression of the campaign, there is a good 15 hours to be had here.

Final Fantasy III is an old school j-rpg with remade graphics. Recommending this game will depend on your ability to appreciate game design from the early 90s. To be more specific quest design, encounter design and story are all barebones.
Quests consist of going somewhere, kill someone, get an object, advance. There are very few sidequests, and exploration is limited due to the size of the world map and the convenience of transportation. That is not necessarily a flaw, as the game still has a good amount of content, and ends up more focused. Except at the end, you won't get lost or stumble in the wrong places, which comes at the price of fulfilling exploration.
Level design abuses the use of secret corridors. Basically some corridors are hidden behind fake walls, and completely dark, so you have to stumble across them. Also you often have to backtrack if you want to get every nook and cranny. Other than that it's basic but effective. The encounters are repetitive and lack the needs of strategy to solve them, you basically brute force through everything, as you seldom run out of ressources if you are well prepared. With that said, they still are satisfying because you can't save in dungeons, and as you advance the tension rises. That is, if you go into dungeons casually and unprepared, because otherwise the game becomes a cakewalk.
The story is minimal, but like it's graphics it has a cutesy kind of charm. Characters have no development, the story bends to accomodate for the gameplay, if you rely on a good story to carry your experience you will find it severely lacking here and I would advise you against this game.
Overall I found the game rewarding to finish, and I would recommend it on that ground. I like that you can choose whatever classes you like from a pool of 20+ jobs, I like the charming simplicity of this game, and I found it to be effective in what it sets to be. But I wouldn't recommend it for people who have modern standards, as the game clearly doesn't meet them.

Okami is an amazing game and deserves to be played. There is plenty of content here to have you playing for at least 45 hours or more. Fans of the series and newcomers should check this game out, especially if you love Zelda.
Also to note, its great for those with low spec rigs. Right now I'm not even playing on my gaming PC, I'm playing this on a surface pro 4. Sure I have to lower the resolution down sub 1080p, but the game is able to run really well on an integrated graphics card. I know that might sound like a strange positive to give, but I thought its worth noting that those with less than stellar rigs can still enjoy this game. EDIT - I can actually Run this at 1080p with mostly 30fps with the Surface Pro 4. So I can run this for certain at 900p.  So, to reiterate, this game will work well with low end hardware.
However, there are some issues with the port.
First of all, it doesn't support 16:10. I think its safe to assume ultrawide monitors will not be supported either.
30FPS lock, makes mouse movement seem a bit odd.
Limited Graphics settings. Only being able to choose between Low, Medium, and High
Now, even though the mouse movement seems odd due to the locked frame rate, the core mechanic of the celestial brush does improve due to the mouse.
All in all, I do recommend this game. But if any of the port issues really affect you too much, I can understand as to why you may want to pass.
Buy with caution.
EDIT - Just to add, yes this game is 30FPS lock. However, due to my experience, I can't say the port is terrible since it can run really well on less than ideal hardware. Not the best port in terms of features, but hey I'm just glad to see the game come out on PC.

I found Hacknet to be a refreshingly original experience. The first few missions of the game provide give you a chance to find your feet and familiarize yourself with the various tools at your disposal; a must considering the game is played largely through console commands. Once you've gotten the hang of things and mastered the basics you'll be feeling like a top-notch hacker, but by then the game will stop holding your hand and you'll have to rely on your own wits to overcome the challenges and objectives presented to you.
The game boasts an awesome soundtrack; fans of EDM and Retrowave will find themselves right at home here. The game is text-heavy which may be a turn off to some players, but those who aren't deterred will find a plethora of optional content that goes a long way to immerse you in the experience.
I have not finished the game yet, but other reviewers have indicated that the main story contains about ~10 hours of gameplay with the DLC Labyrinths adding another ~10 hours. Workshop support is available, and there are already a number of extensions released by the community that add longevity to the game.
All in all, this is one of my most satisfactory purchases on Steam. If hacking interests you even slightly, pick it up and give it a spin. You won't be disappointed.

Hitman Codename 47 puts you in the shoes of a born and bred assassin and sends you off after a variety of bad guy targets in a surprisingly open environment that lets you pick and choose how you will go about dispatching death this day.
You start off waking in a hospital gown, in a cramped room somewhere out in the world, the only hints to your identity a bar-code stamped at the back of your head and a computer chip in your brain. You are then quickly taken through a series of training exercises and then given your first assignment. You never ask why, nor question who it is that sends you on these missions. You simply are a hitman, devoid of any ethical dilemmas or personal identity. As you progress through the story you will eventually begin to discover clues as to your origin but for now, there are people alive that shouldn't be.
Each mission sets you into a open area with guards, civilians, cops and others roaming the place. Various events within the missions are timed, as your targets goes about their business and it's up to you to pick the time, place and method by which you dispatch them. Different missions provide different obstacles and while all the missions have a path of least resistance you will often find yourself experimenting with different plans.
Which weapons and items you bring with you is chosen at the start of the mission at a fee although you can also pick up and use what you find throughout the mission as well as take the clothes of any unfortunate henchmen or passerby you happen to kill or incapacitate and although it requires some effort to get past the suspension of disbelief it requires when a 7ft. blad psycho with a bar-code tattoo on the back of his head passes for an oriental chef with only a change of shirts the mechanic works wonderfully in the game and the many disguises and the various places they allow you to go opens up many more avenues leading towards your target.
In general the open-ended nature of the missions is what separates Hitman 47 from the pack. An early mission has you recreating the classic Sollozzo assassination from the Godfather movie. You can play along with the movie, stashing a gun in toilet, go to the meeting, excuse yourself and then come out shooting. You can also walk through the front door with your gun cocked taking out the targets henchmen first, or you can wait for the target to go to bathroom himself and shoot him through the window, or one of a myriad of other possibilities that the game gives you.
The game looks stunning for it's time, with high quality graphics and textures. The maps are big but never devoid of life. Sound quality is acceptable but nothing out of the ordinary.
It is not all roses however, the game hasn't aged well and what was great graphics back in the day is now all but unplayable to a modern audience. The lack of a proper save game function was not acceptable, even back then.
All in all Hitman Codename 47 is a great experience, the open maps and the many paths to chose from makes this one of the few true assassination games. A definite buy for any fans of stealth and subterfuge.

The best of all Hitman series. There was a remake called "Contracts", but this is better.
Itches a scratch no other game can. Especially after a long day at work.
The interface is shunned by some people, but I find it better than in the rest of the series. You can aim precisely with your "eyes" standing still - this is what hitmen and bodyguards do under those sunglasses I presume. basically you can "unhook" your reticle from the character and move his aimpoint around. This is important because, like in real life, you aim with your mind first and then take out a weapon to shoot that target, this brings another level of immersion, especially knowing that your character is a cunning assassin who is meant to be as inconspicuous as possible until the last moment.
There is also a more realistic representation of weapons in the game, for example you can pick up two different guns and use them akimbo-style, if you so wish, and have a beretta in one hand and a hardballer in the other.
It is not easy to create a game with same game mechanics, but also suited for different playstyles. The mission diversity is just right. From creeping in the shadows of a hotel, to starting a Rambo-style war in the jungle. Some see this as a drawback, but I prefer variety in games, especially inventive stealth ones like this title, where you can pick from a myriad of approaches to eliminate your target.

If you want to circumvent what makes this game challenging, simply browsing the Workshop for mods can solve that for you without too much effort.
What this game gets right is in its overall flavor. The setting, the story, the mood...everything congeals into a pretty amazing lovenote to H.P.Lovecraft fashioned as a roguelike dungeon crawl. The game mechanics are simple enough, but definitely rewards the player for effective customization and combination (and ultimately becomes necessary).
The mod community puts out pretty interesting content that can sometimes blend seamlessly into the game. Some will not. But rest assured that plenty of user-made content is available for whatever needs you happen to have.
I rather enjoy this game, and highly recommend it to anyone who digs roguelike, Cthulhu, dungeon crawling, gothic themes, or simply appreciates art. That said, if you find yourself the type of person who has rage-quit games in the past because of their difficulty or unfairness, then this game is not for you. Seriously, I'm doing you a favor here. Just walk right on past this one.

To start off, this game definitely has its fair share of bugs, population/matchmaking issues, and balance problems.
That being said, there isn't a community of people I enjoy playing with more than the people I have met playing this game. If you frequent the subreddit or the assorted forums, you might find the occasional player concerned about toxic players and problems with players quitting when things aren't going there way. This reveiw isn't mean to dispel those claims (I believe that within the middle-ground MMR you find some of the saltiest, hardest to work with players), but to tell people that if you look for those players who are genuine and enjoy communicating with their team, you will have a great time playing this game with them.
When I first picked up Fractured Space, the game wasn't a Free-to-play game, albeit it cost a mere 5$ to get into, and it most certainly didn't need to be. I understand that FtP has, thankfully, brought in a bit of a larger playerbase, but Fractured Space as a whole provides many hours of replayability, and an unlock tree that will definitely take some time to get used to.
Luckily, while there is a premium currency (platinum) in the game, no serious combat advantages can be gained through using this currency. At most, a few small upgrades to ship crews can be purchased, but the ships that take either more money or more time to unlock are arguably no better than the ships you first start off with. My favorite ship is actually a starter ship, even after all of the other ships I have unlocked and played.
My advice for anyone considering trying out the game, is to prepare for a bit of a steep learning curve at the beginning, and look to make friends early on to have people to play with as you go. That's how you're going to get the most out of Fractured Space.

There's a lot to like about Heat Signature: the gameplay is unique and entertaining, the aesthetics are top-notch, and the procedural generation means you'll really never play the same mission twice.
The unfortunate truth is that you'll experience everything you like about the game within the first hour. After that, you will  likely start to accumulate a wishlist of "Why aren't there..." ideas. Some examples:
... alien races with different traits or abilities?
... cloaked enemies?
... security cameras?
... doors with retinal/thumbprint access rather than physical keys?
... "Bloodbath" or "Massacre" contracts that require you to kill all enemies?
... "Protector" or "Guardian" contracts that require you to defend a friendly ship from invaders?
... robots?
... more distinct patrol/spawning patterns for enemy troops?
... decoy beacons?
... enemies with peripheral vision?
... mind control tools?
... stations to be liberated with perks that are actually interesting?
... theft missions with an objective that you might want to keep, giving you a real choice between completing the mission or hoarding some unique loot?
... obstacles to avoid when flying between locations?
Hopefully there will be an expansion or player-made mod in the near future that will breathe some much-needed life into this game. Until then, I'd recommend holding off for now.

I'm a long time player of the NBA 2K series.
For the record. Yes I like the game. Yes I think it's better in every way than it's predecessor. Yes there's loads of new content. Yes the graphics are better. Yes the game-physics are better. Yes the MyPlayer story is interesting, if a bit short. Yes all the game modes are better. Finally, the biggest pro of the game 2K actually seems to give a rats ### about us PC gamers for once! Big Ups 2k! However... The same problems persist across the board, in each and every game mode.
I'm a big fan of MyPlayer, but just in case your wondering, YES the problems I'll mention WILL persist in every game mode.
The famous GOLDEN BULLET principle is still in effect. Durant, Bryant, Curry amd other crunch-time shooters are still frustrating to guard; NOT because of their skill, though - that would be something I could live with - but the GOLDEN BULLET principle allows them to make three point shots through defenders hands, armpits and even their body.
Great Defensive Players have their own GOLDEN BULLET problem. Simply standing within 6 feet or so of a defensive "ace" will more or less remove whatever shooting skill you have, whether he's standing between you and the basket or not. Notorius Shot Blockers like Ibaka, Gibson and the like are able to block the shot without touching the ball. Tony Allen, CP3, LBJ and other Top-Thieves are able to steal the ball without reaching it, AND through other players. Same with Rebounds. - and YES I checked the replay.
Finally the "Make You Look Bad Effect" - Or in plain terms, "you" gotta be the one responsible for coughing the ball up: On offense, in key situations I'll push the pass button to make a pass - gee... - and in most other situations the pass will go off without a hitch. However in said situations the player in question won't make the pass at all, and I raise my eyebrow and think "Well whatever, let me just make another play." but then, in something like a few seconds I'm left thinking "Shaq'ting A Fool,"" when the player THEN makes the pass to the player I indicated seconds before, who, of course,  is no longer open at this point - Instant Turnover.
Also in a Defensive Rebound situation you quickly advance the ball to avoid turning it over to a CP3 or D-Wade or whoever who's crowding you and Hallelujah, you make the pass to an open teammate who takes it across the line as you sprint up the court, only to gawk in terror as your teammate passes the ball BACK to you before you've even crossed the line, AND YET SOMEHOW you still get the Turnover... Illegal screens, while they certainly do occur, is a little hard to swallow when the "screen" button is the only button you're pressing and yet the player STILL moves into the screen at random moments.... Same deal with a great entry pass into the low post, where the post player, for whatever reason loses the ball or gets it stolen; STILL YOUR TURNOVER. Funny, if you're the player in the post, and the same thing happens, it's ALSO your turnover. Finally there's the weird timing of passing system which I've yet to figure out how works. It's obviously very. VERY advanced, seing as directional passing is lot like playing russian roulette. One time in six the ball will be passed to a VERY covered player instead of the wide-open one you thought you were passing it to, and the reason? Well, I'm assuming there's a very strict timing as to when and where the directional passing indicates who exactly it is your passing to, and that it changes dynamically. That's fine, but it does have me swearing by Direct Pass more times than not, just to avoid brainfreezing directional passes which would land you on Shaqting A Fool in a heartbeat.
The AI controlling the rest of your teams, at times, is a little thick as well.... - I've never seen so many Defensive/Offensive 3-second Violations in real life Basketball, but defensively, you get the feeling you're either not being told you're supposed to be double-teaming someone, becasuse a big man is suddenly called for the 3 seconds. Several times in a row... (If it was a rookie from Europe, I might even think it was realistic. But lets be honest, when it's Noah, Dwight or even Tyson Chandler?!!! DPOY's? Oh hell no...) Offensively, it's usually a dude in the paint, having just passed outside and waiting for a wide open shot from a team mate that never happens...
(A singular piece of advice here. Unless you're an expert player or utterly desperate, forget the hold button down to Lead-To-The-Basket-Pass exists! I'm not saying this because of the fact that it's a dumb system, cause that should be obvious. The fact that you can't cancel the pass easily and the player will usually make the pass anyway even if the Cutter is standing neck deep in three defenders, IS, JUST, STUPID. No The problem is choosing the recipient. Leftstick should do that, except it doesn't. I mean it REALLY DOESN'T. I was being double teamed and i was right next to my teams primary penetrator so I thought, wtf go for it. So I pressed his direction on LS and held and held that Lead-To-Basket-Pass button down... The icon did NOT in fact appear and the guy didn't move. I then caught on as I saw a cutter coming the opposite wing, weaving through defenders, whom, of course caught whiff, and started defending the passing lanes. There's a reason this is the forgotten FF, and it's not just because lack of a translation for decades.
For those uninitiated to FF and JRPGs in general: Look elsewhere for your introduction, should you want one.
For those more inclined, I point you to FFV first.
For those who have played FFV, this is the same but less:  Little carries between jobs and switching is a nuisance, Boss AI is very limited (You pray they don't focus attacks on your healer and they can replace one of their attacks per turn with a spell, that's every boss for the entire game), there's no save points in dungeons, the plot is insultingly basic without even being enjoyably stupid, some jobs are direct upgrades others for no good reason, speed is very random in battles meaning healing is dangerously unreliable, the last dungeon is actually four dungeons and everything's so unmemorable that it's generally difficult to remember where you're going or why.
There are some good points, some cool uses of Mini and Toad, the job costumes are good and there's a large variety of jobs, there's some depth (speed is random, but thief is fast enough that it probably doesn't matter), the story is lighthearted, the visuals are pretty good in the reboot and the music is catchy.  There's also a guy unironically named Goldor who lives in a golden house filled with golden monsters and fights you by beating you with the gold gauntlets on his gold armour, so that's worth something.
Still, unless you've got to finish every FF, you can't get much more vanilla than this one.

For those not aware this is not the Final Fantasy III that came out for the Super Nintendo, that was actually part VI. This is the real Final Fantasy III that wasn't released in the USA till many years later.
This is a great old school turn based Final Fantasy game that continues the epic story about the Warriors of Light. There's a total of 9 playable characters with likeable stories and dialog. This the Final Fantasy that introduces the job system to the series. There's 23 different jobs and any character can use whatever job they like. There's over 200 different enemies/bosses to battle which you will be able to check with the help of the Bestiary, which is a menu that lets you see all the characters you've fought as well as show a record of achievements. There's also a nice variety of armor, items and weapons which include the awesome Legendary items(10 armor and 13 weapons). Like all old school RPGs it's a bit of a grind especially to get the Legendary items but if you played old school RPGs you know this already. Overall it's another great game in the series and I do recommend it.

Just before i wrote this review i started up the game and in the first level I played (in about a month) one of the characters decided not to show up to the party (gandalf (he is normally punctual!)). becasue gandalf was late i could not finish the level and so i stopped playing the game and finally wrote a review about it.
I guess iut would acceptable if the game autosaved every 10 seconds or something like that, so that you could gust reload the game and you would be of to the races, but no, lego games use a system where you have to wait for the end of the level before you can save (to be fare they they occasionally have some mid-level saving systems). So what ends up happening is you sit down to play your lego game and a while later you have a glitch that makes you restart the level and all the "accomplishments" that you had gotten are gone. The more this happens the more annoyed you get and then you buy a cat.
Just joking about buying a cat do not buy a cat becasue of me! Most people including me rather than buying a cat they stop playing the game and after a while they write a review so in total these games are Awesome i have so much fun playing them by myself and with friends but these glitches send me mad and i cannot overlook them. So in conclusion i would not recommend this game even though it has an amazing storyline and is really fun, I cannot justify reccomending this game becasue there are just too many glitches.
Oh and also did i mention that they could not even be bothered to finish it! they have not included the stuff from the third movie.
The one last thing that i would like to say about lego the hobbit is more of a statement. I will use a helpful metaphor to depict it. If you had a crossword puzzle that you wanted to give to all of your friends and you had one copy and a photo copier you would not copy the page and make a copy of the re-printed page and then make a copy of the re-printed re-printed page and so on, no you would make copies of the original to keep the integrity of the crossword. So what i am saying Lego should do is when making a game copy the first publication. For the hobbit copy the book and not the movie, this is becasue the movie is slightly different to the book and then the game is slightly different from the movie. The end result is that you have a game that is fairly different to the book instead of a game that is slightly different. Sorry that was a fairly laboured metaphor but i think you understand what i mean.
Anyway i do not reccomend this game. That does not mean that you should not buy it just that i cannot recommend it to you. If you are willing to look past the problems it is an amazing game.

Codename 47 attempts to execute on a complex and unusual premise. The game is focused heavily on stealth - primarily of the social variety, using disguises. While the game is marred by several design flaws, such as a lack of mid-mission saving, it remains an interesting game for those who won't be turned away by its extreme difficulty. Bastion is one of my all-time favourite games. You play as The Kid, a survivor of a terrible conflict, who has the sole responsibility of trying to piece his world back together, amongst the debris of those who are no longer with him.
It's difficult to know where to start, as so many aspects of this game blew me away. First of all, the narrator, Logan Cunningham, makes a groundbreaking debut as the voice of "the Narrator", perfectly capturing the ambience and style of the game, improving it ten fold.
Next, the soundtrack. It is actually amazing. It won both Best Original Score and Best Song in a Game (Build That Wall) at the Spike VGAs, which should highlight just how good it is.
The gameplay is fun and complex, and after I completed the story (roughly 15 hours I think), I found the extra levels huge fun, taking my full-played time with all 10-idol dreams completed to 26 hours.
Buy this game. If you own it, play it. You will not be disappointed. Highly, highly recommended.

Okay, I just finished XCOM 2 for the first time, and overall, I really enjoyed myself. Huge fan of all the previous XCOM material, so it's not surprising.
I think what I love the most is how the game follows the heroes journey. When you start out, your soldiers are weak and you just get pummeled by the aliens.
