It's a really entertaining arc, and the missions and advancements are paced perfectly. I got to a place where I was just about to restart and then everything started to click. It was a really rewarding experience.
For the most part, the missions are still very repetitive. I like the addition of all the timed missions, which stops me from overwatch turtling though everything, but it's essentially the same thing. Sneak though a map to find aliens and kill them 3 at a time.
I would have loved more diversity in the missions, like boss fights and missions that require different squad configurations and loadouts to be successful.

Having bought this game long after its catastrophic launch, complete with Ubisoft's official patch (and no doubt an apology), I can safely say that my time with Assassin's Creed Unity has been virtually bug-free... with the singular exception being, for about three days, constant crashes that seemed to defy explanation. After failing to rectify the problem as most Google search results told me I could (by turning Uplay offline), I ultimately discovered the problem: I'd been playing ACU with Steam switched to online mode. After turning Steam offline, I was finally able to play the game with only an occasional crash -- if even that. So, fellow Steam users: try doing what I did if you're having trouble running Assassin's Creed Unity. Might spare you a great deal of frustration.
The controls are satisfying and responsive. Granted there are a few times when the free-running interface prevents me from getting off a building when I want it to, but then again that could perhaps be applied to the rest of the AC games. The graphics and in-game physics are nothing short of astounding, although I have run into a few framerate issues during certain cutscenes (although this doesn't bother me all too much, though that's my personal outlook). The most impressive aspect of Unity, however, is its size and scope; no other game that I know of has ever managed to simulate the look, feel, and scale of a massive city as this one has, with its thick crowds of people and its enormous buildings. Seriously, in what other game can you climb all the way to the top of Notre Dame? That's just plain incredible to experience.
I can't quite comment on the story, as I've not run far enough into the main plot to look at it from a critical perspective, but as usual the modern-day interjections are a pain in the rear; frankly I'm far more interested in the historical backdrops and period pieces than I am in what all's going on in the present. Thankfully this isn't made to be the main focus of the game, and the modern-day segments are short and sweet enough not to detract too much from the overall quality of the product. I will say, though, that at one point there's an especially trippy mission early on where the Templars try to hack into the simulation program, leading to some very convincing glitch effects (something I'm sure Ubisoft must have down to an art form by now). This moment is very tense and gripping, however the glitch effects themselves might give an epileptic player a hard time, as they are very bright and flashy. SO BE WARNED!
Overall, I have to say I'm glad that I bought this game. If you're an Assassin's Creed fan, I say definitely give it a go. Now that it's been patched up and fixed, you'll most certainly have a great time with it.

When Heat Signature at it’s best, it’s phenomenal, but it takes too long to get there.
There’s nothing cooler in Heat Signature when you up against extreme odds and five seconds of in game time takes five minutes of pausing, planning, and executing in slowed time. You throw your wrench against the wall so the guy behind a locked door opens it. Then you pause. Switch to your sidewinder teleporter to get through the now open door. Pause. Teleport your wrench back to you. Shoot your silenced concussive gun at the one guard down the hall then run up and slice up your target before they even know what happened. Then shoot the window and jump into space.
Moments like that are the core to Heat Signature. They’re tense and exhilarating. And, unfortunately, not super common. Most missions either you breeze through or fail. Failure in this game can be pretty brutal. Often one mistake means you’ll have to abort the mission or can no longer play as that character. When you’re just starting out and don’t have access or know-how of certain equipment, this feels frustrating or too luck based. “Wait. Why’d that happen?” and “Oh… I don’t actually have anything that can deal with this right now.” Were phrases I muttered frequently until I better understood the game.
This is a game that some folks will undoubtedly love. It’s has solid computable mechanics that utilize AI randomness well, fantastic but unintrusive writing, interesting emergent storytelling, and an endless amount of procedural content. However, I found the learning curve to be too steep and the game didn’t really click with me until about 6+ hours with it. I wasn’t really expecting or have time for another 20+ experience to actually complete it.
My chief criticism with Heat Signature is its structure. There are persistent upgrades that you unlock, but with each character you’re constantly cycling through overly easy missions only to get to more difficult missions and probably die, or mess up and need to abort. You’re constantly getting set back to much less interesting content.
However when you can pull of those harder missions, it’s amazing. Some of the best gaming moments of 2017. The highs are SO high that I wish I was more excited for the game as a whole. If only it were a compacted 5 to 10 hour game with more of a focus on the emergent story mechanics. As of now, it just feels a bit too grindy and long.
The game does have missions called “defector missions” where you play a one-off character with specific gear. They are probably the best parts and are a great way to learn how the game wants you to play it. Example: I had one that started me outside of the target’s ship with no pod and too guns with limited ammo. I had to shoot backwards to push myself to the ship, get on board, slaughter everyone, and steal the ship. It was rad. But the best thing about those missions is that you can restart them at any time. Failure in them is not much of a set back, other than the ship’s layout being completely different.
As of writing this review I put about 9 hours into this game and liberated one of the four enemy strongholds. I don’t think I’ll be putting too much more time into this game. I like it, and it will likely have a fanatic community around it, but it’s just not quite what I was looking for.
If you’re looking for a good game to play with a podcast on, action-puzzle-like game, or something that you chip away at over months, then Heat Signature is a pretty solid choice. If you’re looking for something more focused, then maybe look somewhere else.

Except about 8 guards were now surrounding the loot crate room, all armed with guns. No problem. I waiting for the first of the guards to open the door, and stepped to the side as he unloaded a shot gun blast. Whew. About 10 steps behind him, was a buddy guard. I used a time slow down gadget to run past the first guard, used the switch places gadget to instantly teleport that few extra spaces with the late guard, and made it to about the midway of the massive entry floor before the remainder of the guards surged into line of site and all opened fire.
My screen was covered in spread shot, from one side of the massve cabin to the other. Even with the slow down time in place, there simply wasn't enough room to outmanuever the shots. One caught me. Okay, just avoid the rest. About 6 feet away from my escape pod, I failed to realize my time slow down was about to expire, and the shotgun projectiles suddenly resumed their full speed, and several of them slammed into me at once. Ouch.
Lesson learned. Do not attempt to explore random ships with only a dagger thinking you're Assassin's Creed skills will somehow subdue the superior defenses onboard.
Moving on, I quickly selected a new character and went back to dagger and longswording my way through several assassination type missions. Fun times.
Pros of this Game
-Characters experience perma death, but can be retired to preserce their life time stats and achievements
-Killing is fun, and is performed in a multitude of ways, ranging from weapon types to envirenmental assistance
-Mission types are bite sized, meaning you do not have to dedicate large amounts of time to have some fun
-Stats, I personally love stats, especially kill stats. Shallow think to like but too many games forgo this
-AI is well fleshed out. I feel like I can outsmart and outmanuever any of them, but never feel safe enough as to think I can't be caught in return if I mess up
Cons of this Game
-I can see where people may not like the finite mission generation system. A lot of it is cookie cutter and with a small pool of random factors. This can easily be fixed via future updates or mod support.
-With the limited amount of overall loot and special items, it can be very easy to feel like you've seen it all after liberating a few of the stations over the first few hours of gameplay. This is not a negative, but will apply heavily to people who get bored quickly outside the game's base mechanics
Some Suggestions
-Adding some form of player rivalry
I'd like to be able to take on a contract to beat another player to a mission of some sort that spawns in real time. First come, first serve. Or daily kill, knockout, loot, or mission complete charts that players attempt to stay at the top of to gain additional achievement listings for their characters prestige.
-Definatly more weapons and loot. This is something that takes work, and can not be expected to be released asap, but at the moment even I can feel the innate lack of discoverable items. Not bad for me, but many others will feel distaste.
-Add missions where living witnesses eventually come back and attack your station, or try to intercept you enroute to your next mission. Would let players intentionally draw more prey, or be punished by thinking that person they let live was a good idea.
-More stats! You know we can take the knocked out bodies of our enemies onto our pod or with us when we fly their ship back to our station? That isn't reflected anywhere. My stats need to reflect I was merciful to a few, and imprisoned some as well, instead of just letting them slip back into space to continue their pirate ways.
-Multi Part mission would be cool. Let me string together a succession of selecteable missions back to back before returning to station for reward. Better stats or reward for doing so, either or would be awesome.
A great game overall! For people like me it is perfect, as I adore farming for kill stats, and always enjoy the randomly generated mission objectives, with an overall objective to reach in game.

The Steam community seems to have a problem with over-rating rogue-likes. Don't get me wrong, this game is good, and really fun, but 95% positive is stretching it. When I buy a game like that, I expect an amazing experience, but there's so many small changes that could be made here, to make huge improvements. I feel like it could have used longer in development before being fully released.
Firstly, the big assertion with this game is 'you get yourself into terrible situations, then figure out how to get yourself out of them'. But if you're like me, and play cautiously, that's not really how the game works. There's never a need to go out of your way to do anything you're not equipped for, you can progress through the game just fine by taking small risks for less credits.
I don't really think you would have to think hard to find your way out of situations to begin with. It takes little more than a glance to see the details of a mission and if you're properly equipped for it or not. Guards patrol by themselves, down hallways and out of the sight of other guards. Even if you run into a room with two guards, two melee weapons makes you practically unstoppable against them. The quicker they strike, the more guards you can approach with ease. Even alert and time-limits, clearly added to give the game more difficulty, are completely negated for the rest of the mission by taking out the pilot of the ship
Then, even when you do get caught and attacked, they just throw you out of their ship instead of killing you outright. You pick yourself back up, and either resume the mission or abandon it, with no real penalty. The core difficulty for this game just doesn't really exist in the way the developers assert, nor how a lot of players would like you to believe. It's more reliant on you not caring about your choices until they get you into trouble, and playing careless, or even getting yourself into bad situations on purpose.
For those reasons alone I would not recommend this to people who 'try-hard' at the games they play. It's just a massive decrease in enjoyment for people like that.
And, realistically, there's not even a huge penalty for taking the easier missions, because there's no way of knowing what missions will hold the weapons and equipment that are actually worth picking up. The weapon and equipment system is completely RNG, but not really that varied. There's a couple of melee weapons, a few guns, and several gadgets, and most of the 'rogue-like' qualities for them is how quickly they fire, the range, and how loud they are. The good ones completely over-shadow the ones that are 'meh', and it leads to just doing several missions until you find weapons you can actually use on the tougher missions.
And the problem of variety doesn't just stop at equipment, characters themselves basically all play exactly the same. The tiny variations in starting equipment rarely makes a difference in the long run, which means each run is more-so dictated by what you manage to pick up while you play as the characters you've selected. Only the final mission offers any real static difference between them, and of course, you can't see what the mission will require of you until after you've been playing as them and gotten enough credits to get intel on that mission.
So let's talk about the changes I feel should be made to make this game deserving of that 95% rating.
First of all, increased equipment variety would make a huge change. Once there's a greater variation in equipment, they can stop handing out items that don't even feel like they were worth picking up in the first place. The goal should be, almost every find means you have a new way of approaching your situations, rather than 'I'll use this until I get a better one'.
Secondly, I do believe they should leave the universe as-is for a 'normal' mode. It's clear that people do have fun here, and a lot of casual players aren't going to be interested in the variety and difficulty that would be offered in my recommendations for a 'hard' and 'very hard' universe.
A hard universe needs to, first and foremost, stop pulling punches with the guards on a ship. There should be fewer single-patrol guards, and it would be ideal to replace them with multi-patrol guards. Each ship should have a number of back-up pilots that are detailed in the mission select screen, and each back-up pilot should go to the primary flight controls to take the helm once it's discovered that the pilot is missing. Perhaps adding some 'blood-hungry' guards that kill you on sight outright would also be a good idea, and this would also be listed in the mission briefing.
Next, the characters should be offer more variations in gameplay. Have characters that walk slower or faster, refuse to use melee weapons or guns or certain equipment, or get 'nautious' after they kill or die faster in the vaccume of space. Give all of them one or two negative traits, and perhaps ocassionally a positive one, so that every character feels unique, and must be played in a unique way.
Hard mode should also not mention details on enemy equipment, other than including if you need armor piercing weapons in the basic mission details. Increased enemy variations for all modes would also be great, and add a lot more flavor to the aspect of this change. After a number of failed missions a character would be forced to retire, meaning that doing well would actually be a requirement to progress, and you could no longer fall back on just abandoning your goal if you think it's too hard.
Very hard mode would offer MORE negative traits for characters, and NO mission details, other than the primary and side objectives for that mission. Credits offered would give you a general idea of the difficulty, but even the overall time limit would have to be discovered upon arriving at the ship. This would make every mission more tense, and really give a sense of accomplishment once you've done enough with your character to feel comfortable retiring them. Additionally, the back-up pilots would go to any available flight-control once there is an alert of an intruder on the ship.
I know that just having a thumbs down is doing to net me a lot of 'not helpful' replies, but honestly, I write this review because I want to see this game be better. I love the foundation, I just think there's so many improvements that could be made to move it from 'good' to 'great', or even higher.
If you find yourself interested in spite of what this review mentions, I would say buy it when it's on sale. Otherwise, wait to see what happens in post-launch.

Listen... all you need to know about this game is that you can flip through space as a color-changing being known as the Regal Giraffe. If that doesn't sell you on the premise here, nothing will.
Shu's Garden is a simple game about rolling around, eating plants, planting seeds, and jumping now and then, all conveyed by the ridiculously cute artwork and comfortable musical score. It's a good game if you want something to distract you that doesn't require much input -- it's kind of the digital equivalent of a fidget cube, something to do while you try and focus on, say, a lecture or something. And that's not bad at all! I can see younger children having some fun with this, there's not (that I've found) any really questionable content whatsoever.
It's just a simple, cute game about rolling around and interacting with things, and it does that well enough that I think it's a worthwhile buy if you think you (or someone you know) would get some entertainment out of it. If the artstyle or the mechanics don't seem that interesting to you, though, you probably aren't going to find much here -- and that alright! This is a wierd, niche little thing, and it isn't for everyone. But I got some amusement from it in the end, and so this ultimately gets a recommendation from me.

This is by far the worst Assassin's Creed game to date. AC3 is now 2nd worst in my book. It's clearly evident that the folks who worked on 3 were in charge of Unity as well. The same buggy gameplay and unbelivably poor enemy AI are prevalent.
And not to mention...glitchy, glitchy, GLITCHY!!! If you're wondering if it's still broken: well, its got some duct tape and primer on it. The cutscenes are fixed. It's never crashed or locked up on me....yet. Other repairs are evident, but its not totally "fixed" and I doubt it ever will be. The remaining issues seem to be embedded in the code itself, just like AC3; if you've played it. (And that game ate my 2 570HDs for lunch!)
I'm running a single 970 FTW with an AMD 6 core dedicated to PhysX at 1920x1080 @120hZ refresh. Textures take awhile to load. Game load times are too long. The draw distance is really short. But I was able to get aliasing under control to a playable degree. Temps are about 50-52 C no overclock, Kboost, or overvolt. I'm at "Very High" settings with HBAO+ on. I'm kinda thinkin its as good as its ever gonna get. I can run at Ultra, but its not playable.
There are still invisible walls, very VERY odd, immersion breaking NPC movements (most are really funny, I recommend recording them!) and frequent framerate skips. The way Arno moves through the crowd and how they react are the worst of the entire franchise. He's not part of the crowd; the NPCs just jut to the side all glitchy like. (Hard to explain) Also, trying to get Arno through an open window has just about caused me to break my damn controller! GET IN TEH F#^%ING WINDOW ALREADY!!!
Some things in this game are the best of the entire franchise: graphics taken as a whole (if you have the card to run it), Arno's parkour movement, lighting effects, and (finally) a sneaky mode! (which would be great if it worked 100%) The 3D map of Paris  is really cool too! I even found myself enjoying some of the later story missions. Early ones..not so much.
Absolutely everything else is horrible. There are side missions in this game where all you have to do is kill a rando enemy (who doesn't even have a name or story btw) and you get 1000+ monies. In some cases, like 3500. And he's located in the building right accross from you. And those little "missions" are everywhere! And Ubi has the balls to ask you to rate each one as a "memory". Lol 1 out of 5 stars...yeah! Oh and get lockpick skill EARLY. What a bunch of BS having locked doors and chests standing in the way of a good time! And they don't tell you what level the damn chest is until you're right next to it. I've wasted at least 3 hours total game time running to locked chests in the STARTING AREA that are too high a level of lockpicking. So dumb!
The guard AI is what makes this game borderline unplayable. It's terribly frustrating to try to control or evade the guards. You can't whistle them over anymore. Theres no "conscipts", theives, or mercs to hire anymore either. All you have is a firecracker to toss at the guards that "alerts" them, but they don't investigate. They just stand there dumbfounded half the time. The other half, they walk in circles or run at full speed in the opposite direction of where you threw it. If one sees you, they ALL see you. Smoke bombs and stun grenades are mandatory most of the time. But, I'd rather just be sneaky. You know, like an assassin! Not a grenade launcher toting idiot! Grenade launchers!! WTF!! Yeah thats real subtle!!! OMG why are there grenade launchers in this f@^%$game?????
I've had snipers shoot me dead through walls who can see you from the other side of a building, I've walked right past guards within inches and no alert, but then his buddy will see me clear as day from the other side of the f#$%ing room!!! And then the whole room is suddenly filled with guards from the entire floor! They run faster than the hero when they're chasing you (another feature present in AC3 that I hated). He's an assassin!!! He should be able to outrun guards! Thats why he's lighlty armored and they are not! Combat is a joke (new dodge and parry system is okay but it takes too freaking long to kill any of the guards!) and aerial double assassinations gltich all the time. Terrible!!
I love the Assassin's Creed series. I have 93 hours into Black Flag and I regard it as the best one to date. If the first one had 2's combat system, it would be up there in the top 10 best games of all time. But Unity....its so bad. Its boring! I don't give a rip about playing with rando people on the internet! Thats why I play solo, stealth RPGs! So I don't have to interact with the world!
Do I recommend it? No, not for the casual RPGer. If you're a die-hard AC fan, then you prolly bought it already.
Is it worth buying now? Only If you have an nvidia 900 OC series (or AMD 280x) or better graphics card and its on a Steam holiday sale. Otherwise, don't bother. This game is shredding my modern-day $350 graphics card and I can't play on max settings! I can with other titles though. As I mentioned, the graphics and lighting are what make this game worth playing. But thats about it. As a game, its not good.

The Steam community seems to have a problem with over-rating rogue-likes. Don't get me wrong, this game is good, and really fun, but 95% positive is stretching it. When I buy a game like that, I expect an amazing experience, but there's so many small changes that could be made here, to make huge improvements. I feel like it could have used longer in development before being fully released.
Firstly, the big assertion with this game is 'you get yourself into terrible situations, then figure out how to get yourself out of them'. But if you're like me, and play cautiously, that's not really how the game works. There's never a need to go out of your way to do anything you're not equipped for, you can progress through the game just fine by taking small risks for less credits.
I don't really think you would have to think hard to find your way out of situations to begin with. It takes little more than a glance to see the details of a mission and if you're properly equipped for it or not. Guards patrol by themselves, down hallways and out of the sight of other guards. Even if you run into a room with two guards, two melee weapons makes you practically unstoppable against them. The quicker they strike, the more guards you can approach with ease. Even alert and time-limits, clearly added to give the game more difficulty, are completely negated for the rest of the mission by taking out the pilot of the ship
Then, even when you do get caught and attacked, they just throw you out of their ship instead of killing you outright. You pick yourself back up, and either resume the mission or abandon it, with no real penalty. The core difficulty for this game just doesn't really exist in the way the developers assert, nor how a lot of players would like you to believe. It's more reliant on you not caring about your choices until they get you into trouble, and playing careless, or even getting yourself into bad situations on purpose.
For those reasons alone I would not recommend this to people who 'try-hard' at the games they play. It's just a massive decrease in enjoyment for people like that.
And, realistically, there's not even a huge penalty for taking the easier missions, because there's no way of knowing what missions will hold the weapons and equipment that are actually worth picking up. The weapon and equipment system is completely RNG, but not really that varied. There's a couple of melee weapons, a few guns, and several gadgets, and most of the 'rogue-like' qualities for them is how quickly they fire, the range, and how loud they are. The good ones completely over-shadow the ones that are 'meh', and it leads to just doing several missions until you find weapons you can actually use on the tougher missions.
And the problem of variety doesn't just stop at equipment, characters themselves basically all play exactly the same. The tiny variations in starting equipment rarely makes a difference in the long run, which means each run is more-so dictated by what you manage to pick up while you play as the characters you've selected. Only the final mission offers any real static difference between them, and of course, you can't see what the mission will require of you until after you've been playing as them and gotten enough credits to get intel on that mission.
So let's talk about the changes I feel should be made to make this game deserving of that 95% rating.
First of all, increased equipment variety would make a huge change. Once there's a greater variation in equipment, they can stop handing out items that don't even feel like they were worth picking up in the first place. The goal should be, almost every find means you have a new way of approaching your situations, rather than 'I'll use this until I get a better one'.
Secondly, I do believe they should leave the universe as-is for a 'normal' mode. It's clear that people do have fun here, and a lot of casual players aren't going to be interested in the variety and difficulty that would be offered in my recommendations for a 'hard' and 'very hard' universe.
A hard universe needs to, first and foremost, stop pulling punches with the guards on a ship. There should be fewer single-patrol guards, and it would be ideal to replace them with multi-patrol guards. Each ship should have a number of back-up pilots that are detailed in the mission select screen, and each back-up pilot should go to the primary flight controls to take the helm once it's discovered that the pilot is missing. Perhaps adding some 'blood-hungry' guards that kill you on sight outright would also be a good idea, and this would also be listed in the mission briefing.
Next, the characters should be offer more variations in gameplay. Have characters that walk slower or faster, refuse to use melee weapons or guns or certain equipment, or get 'nautious' after they kill or die faster in the vaccume of space. Give all of them one or two negative traits, and perhaps ocassionally a positive one, so that every character feels unique, and must be played in a unique way.
Hard mode should also not mention details on enemy equipment, other than including if you need armor piercing weapons in the basic mission details. Increased enemy variations for all modes would also be great, and add a lot more flavor to the aspect of this change. After a number of failed missions a character would be forced to retire, meaning that doing well would actually be a requirement to progress, and you could no longer fall back on just abandoning your goal if you think it's too hard.
Very hard mode would offer MORE negative traits for characters, and NO mission details, other than the primary and side objectives for that mission. Credits offered would give you a general idea of the difficulty, but even the overall time limit would have to be discovered upon arriving at the ship. This would make every mission more tense, and really give a sense of accomplishment once you've done enough with your character to feel comfortable retiring them. Additionally, the back-up pilots would go to any available flight-control once there is an alert of an intruder on the ship.
I know that just having a thumbs down is doing to net me a lot of 'not helpful' replies, but honestly, I write this review because I want to see this game be better. I love the foundation, I just think there's so many improvements that could be made to move it from 'good' to 'great', or even higher.
If you find yourself interested in spite of what this review mentions, I would say buy it when it's on sale. Otherwise, wait to see what happens in post-launch.

I don't usualy review games, but I felt the pnegative reviews on this game weren't well articulated and that the positive ones weren't very observant.
Aberoth is a game that completely forgets about the player. In some games this is a good thing; if you can create an immersive world which is indifferent to the difficulties of the player character, you can make a really good game, but Aberoth isn't immersive and it isn't really difficult either. You could call Aberoth time consuming and punishing at most. When I say that Aberoth forgets about the player, I don't mean that it doesn't give the player enough security or make it easy enough on them; I mean that it forgets that the game actually requires a human to interface with it.
First let's start off with the viewport borders. If you walk towards the right of your screen, your viewport won't travel with your character until you're almost at the end of it. So if I'm walking upward, I'll be only able to see about two foot in front of me yet I'll also be able to see about fourteen feet behind my head for no reason at all. To make matters worse, when an enemy is off screen, all you get is a little smash-bros style offscreen indicator with the enemy name listed. So if you see a little "(wolf)" at the top of your screen, they could be either two or twenty feet away. You'd have no idea.
Now let's look at the rogue fort near the starting castle. After killing enough bats and bumblebees or whatever, you're told to go into this fort to kill some boss. To get in, you kill the three guys standing in front of the door to the fort, then you walk on in and find the door that leads to his room.  As expected, just some guy with slightly more health and damage than the average rogue goon, and is easy enough to kill. The catch is going back out the front door. After beating the boss (who's likely drained some of your resources), those three guys you need to kill to unlock the front door can respawn out front as you leave the base. As soon as you go out the door, it locks behind you, and you've got three rouges sandwiching you against it. Were this preventable it would be fine, but there's absolutely no way to open the door without going through it and closing it afterwards, nor is there any way to look outside preemptively.
Even your own character can obscure your vision. I had a guy standing behind my character (with respect to the viewport of course; my character was looking staraight at him) hit me with a club twice before I realized I wasn't being attacked by a bat or something because my on character's body blocked my view if his attack. Tell me, would you really have to be bashed over the head with a club twice before you realized you were being struck? The game just expects you to see things from your character's perspective, but doesn't allow you to, and things like your items and your healthbar are just placed in the oddesd most inconvenient positions on the screen. It's as though this game was made as a simulator for bot players, but then had human controls implemented as an afterthought.
It's ultimately just uncomfortable and unenjoyable, and I haven't had to resort to complaining about the boring runescape style melee combat yet (which consists of hitting a foe, walking backwards while they swing, then doing a U-turn and attacking them durring their cooldown and hoping you don't get unlucky). It's bad in spite of the fact that there are plenty of mmorpgs that handle this sort of thing well. Take spiral knights for instance. It's a game I quit a while back due to issues with the newest upgrade system and droprates, but it keeps the camera pinned on the character, has melee which doesn't consist of just trading, has a variety of weapon types and enemies that interact with you in unique ways, and it exposes you to these mechanics from square one. In Aberoth you're just running around blind and trading damage with people so that you can get more gold to trade more damage, with virtually no descision making in combat whatsoever. This is what solidifies it as a "game for bots" rather than humans, and what makes it just extrortinairaly unentertaining.

Shu is pretty darn adorable, fuzzy-wuzzy and spreading seeds all about.  You get to play as a furry yo-yo bouncing between planets in a sort of 2D Super Mario Galaxy way - except no stars or mustaches.  While some say the game is a chill experience, I personally felt it leans toward something a very young child would enjoy with a parent.  There are no goals or levels to finish, instead you just explore, eat, plant seeds, and bounce about.  I happen to have a 7 year old daughter, so we gave it a nice long gameplay due to the all ages rating.
Firing up the game you have some options to jump from one character to the next.  A few other of Shu's cousins, a turtle, a giraffe with very stiff joints, and a bee.  Of those the easiest to move around is the bee, but it's not very interactive compared to the rest.  The turtle and giraffe controls were stiff in our opinion.  We generally enjoyed playing as the Shu family and would eat plants, jump from planet to planet, and sow seeds repeatedly.
My daughter was surprised there were no levels or goals. She was actually a bit confused when I explained it to her.  She bounced and ate trees for a half hour or so, but when I turned on my controller to play co-op with her the game took on a new dimension.  It was immediately clear to her that now we could play hide and seek!  That went on for an hour as I would jump to the farthest planet and she had to figure out where in the galaxy I went.  With the vegetation looking a bit similar, it's wasn't obvious where I would land.  A few times she got upset and I switched her to the bee so she could find me easier.  The best moments were when we collided into each other while bouncing around.  That was a little girl giggle-fest. :-)
With the brightly colored art direction, well done controller ( xbox ) handling, and charm I'd say this is a good title to get if you are either a parent looking for a fun game experience with your child, or someone who enjoys non-objective gaming.  If you don't like games without goals or levels, I'd steer clear away.  It's just not a game with goals in mind.  As for age range, I think somewhere around 6 or under is probably going to hold their interest the longest.  Have fun playing hide and seek if you can.
Disclosure:  a review key was provided by the developer

With all the negativity surrounding Destiny 2 and some other AAA titles, I figured there was no better time to try an indie game instead. I came across this one on the store for cheap and I was pleasantly surprised by how fun it was for me.
I had no particular issues with the gameplay except for one- the game froze during combat twice. Other than that, gameplay was OK. The menu system is coherent, movement around the map is fairly smooth, the map is not too large for your movement speed. You can tell the game is a little raw. The hit detection boxes around treasure chests don't always seem consistent. If you want to talk to an NPC a second time, you need to turn away from him, turn back to him and press the talk button... instead of just pressing the talk button again.
Dungeon maps are fairly simple- pretty linear, except for a fork here and there- one road leads to a chest, one road leads to the rest of the dungeon. Once in a while, I did notice some "gaps" where there was a slightly longer corridor than usual without any enemy, treasure or anything to interact with. This was rare, though. Besides, it seems like the goal of the developer was to make combat more spread out, but more eventful.
I thought the combat system was the strongest part of the game. It's a turn-based system similar to Final Fantasy X, but the encounter system is similar to Chrono Trigger, where you can see the enemies on the map and there is no separate battle instance.
The thing that keeps combat interesting in this game is that even though you see the same individual enemies throughout a particular dungeon, you never see the same combinations of them in one group (unless you choose to with the Battle option). On top of this, you will either be forced to use different characters due to story issues, or enticed to use them due to enemy weaknesses, and since each character has a large set of different abilities, you will find that battle will always be a fresh experience. There were several times where I thought I had come up with a perfect strategy to use for the rest of the game... until I leveled up two battles later gaining a new ability, changing the chemistry of my party.
Personally, I pretty much found every character to be likeable. Unfortunately, that might have been mostly because they were all pretty fun to play in combat. There's not a lot of story set aside for building the characters or establishing their motivation, except for a few lines of dialogue here and there. There are a few sidequests, but even those only contain a few bits of dialogue. Basically, we don't see much more than surface-level development from most of these characters- "This is their job/hobby and they feel angry/happy during when certain specific situations happen.)
The story is very simple; the MC finds out her goal near the beginning of the game and it doesn't really change for the rest of the game. Anything that happens in between is just a step to get to that goal. As I mentioned earlier, characters don't really have too many opportunities to grow all that much. However, there is enough there that I'd be interested in a sequel.
I thought the sprite and map graphics were solid- a tribute to the old 16-bit era, but better. The art style is nice. It's kind of like a hybrid between Japanese-style and American-style cartoons. I also liked the character designs for the most part, since most of the characters are pretty unique. I'll put it this way- if someone dressed up in an average-quality costume of Alyssa L'Salle, Chahn or several other characters, I'd know who they were supposed to be.
Like the gameplay, some of the cutscene artwork is a little raw. Sometimes perspective is off here and there or character proportions are off from one scene to the next. Animation during cutscenes is not exactly smooth (although that could be on purpose for effect). However, I think this all adds charm to the game and I don't consider the artwork a negative at all.
When I was debating whether to buy this game on the store, I saw that there was an option to buy the soundtrack. I figured that if someone was selling an OST, it probably didn't suck, but I wanted to make sure. I went on YouTube to preview the music, listened to 1 min of Track 1 and about :20 seconds of Track 2. I was sold immediately. You can hear influences from different space-noir fantasies, such as Blade Runner and Cowboy Bebop. Battle themes have a little Chrono Trigger in them with those burning bass lines. Throw in a dash of J-Pop and you have Cosmic Star Heroine. I don't know if that's what Hyperduck was going for, but that's what I picked up. Great job!
Despite what flaws this game has (which are to be expected from such a small studio), this game was a lot of fun. I would not complain if there was a Cosmic Star Heroine 2.

Pros:
+ Fantastic sprite art that is clearly a love letter to Chrono Trigger, only with better detail than CT had.  Also borrowed the delightfully expressive character portraits that go with dialogue from Phantasy Star IV, but much bigger and better drawn.
+ Cool sci-fi setting that blends nature and machinery.  Some environments are pretty dark and creepy, nice job with that.
+ Good musical score, fits the game well.  I was also fairly well shocked to find that the half-Japanese/half-English insert song actually had proper Japanese grammar and pronunciation.  That's gotta be a first for an indie game.
+ Legitimately fun battle system that doesn't just let you spam the same powerful attack over and over again.  You have to actually use your brain a little to set up the best move combos.
+ Likable, diverse cast of characters, several of whom are amusingly weird.  Plenty of personality to go around.
+ Lots of snappy character banter.  The whole game has the sort of snarky, self-aware, tongue-in-cheek sense of humor that I enjoy.
+ Pretty good story overall, had enough intrigue to keep me interested.
Cons:
- Basically no character backstory or broader worldbuilding.  Would've liked some of that, given the cool setting and diversity of locales you visit.
- Half the cast has sort of the same spunky, wise-cracking personality.  They're still likable, mind you, so this is a minor gripe.
- Pacing feels a bit rushed at times.  Characters make one decision in particular early on in the game with no hesitation that you'd think they'd haved agonized over at least a little.
- Some characters are way more useful in combat than others.  Same for some abilities.  Could've been a tad more balanced.
Verdict:
Well worth the $7.50 I paid for this game on sale.  Recommended for anyone who likes sci-fi and a fusion of old-school, 16-bit RPG style with a more creative battle system.

An old school jrpg made by Zeboyd Games, who previously did Cthulhu Saves The World, which I quite like. You’re Alyssa, a sassy top agent for a totally-not-evil government agency. You fight terrorists, giant killer robots, uncover a big bad conspiracy and save the day. All with delicious 90’s anime cheesiness. The game takes some clear inspiration from Chrono Trigger and Phantasy Star, among others, but does Cosmic Star Heroine have the giant feet needed to fill those big shoes? Let’s go over the pros and cons.
Cosmic Star Heroine succeeds as a nostalgic love letter to the jrpgs of yore. It unashamedly celebrates its inspirations and revels in its cheesiness. It’s an accessible and enjoyable game while it lasts and leaves a great first impression, but at the end of the day I feel it is a great combat system in an otherwise underdeveloped package. If, say, Chrono Trigger is a fancy five course dinner, then Cosmic Star Heroine is a banana chimichanga. It works as a bite-sized snack, but lacks the meat to join the seminal classics.
I rate Cosmic Star Heroine 3 out of 5 bananas.
1 bananas - Crap. Turn around & don’t look back.
2 bananas - Bad. Not really worth the time/money.
3 bananas - Average. Neither bad nor exceptional.
4 bananas - Good. Won't leave you feeling gimped.
5 bananas - Superb. A definite must-play.

So far the game has been fantastic! It feels like a modernized verson of Chrono Trigger, crossed with a sci-fi Deus Ex setting and given a classic anime flair and 80's-esque design sense. Final Fantasy III is a nice JRPG but definitely shows its age. This PC port is based on the Nintendo DS-Version from 2006 which itself is a port of the original NES game from 1990. The graphics are done in a reduced chibi-style that may not be everybody's cup of tea, but all models are surprisingly faithful to the original.
Pro:
- The barebone story is somewhat extended compared to the original
- The job system is pretty flexible and allows for some experimentation.
- Even without a real help box like in the FF6 remake you always know where to go next
- ~20+h of playtime without doing the superboss
Con:
- Formulaic "Go rescue the world" story
- Turn based combat with a large random element to the speed stat. This can lead to some bad luck in boss combats which otherwise would be pretty easy
- Weird difficulty progression: Some bosses in the mid game are much more difficult than the enemies in the surrounding area would suggest
- No save points in dungeons. The final dungeon takes over an hour to complete. If you die on the final boss you can repeat everything
- Itemization of some classes is strange. My black and white mage wore their starting head gear up to the last part of the final dungeon
- Changing job classes takes a looooot of grinding and some jobs become available really late. I ended up with just changing the job of 1 character to an advanced job class and still could finish the game without much problem.
Despite some of the shortcomings, FF III is enjoyable enough for an in its core 26 year old game. If you want to experience the evolution of the Final Fantasy games this is a good starting point that already has some of the elements and comfort found in later games, but is still charmingly unpolished.

I'll be honest; I didn't love Half-Life at first.
Maybe it was the fact that I played this game in 2016, 18 years after its initial release in 1998. Perhaps it was the serviceable but definitely outdated controls  I had to deal with, along with some annoying bugs and glitches. It didn't click for me. But after about an hour of getting used to everything, here's what I realized: Half-Life is real nice. Almost everything wrong with the game comes from technological limitations of the 90s. Graphics really start to show the wear-and-tear of 18 years; but they aren't bad enough to distract from the general gameplay.
I can't make any more complaints about Half-Life simply because the sum of its parts makes it such a good game. The story still entertains and is delivered well, throwing out lengthy cutscenes and text crawls in favor of gameplay-based storytelling. Enemy AI was amazing for its time and still functions well today; a variety of weapons and unique, challenging level designs keep things interesting through the course of this game. Most importantly, Half-Life retains a remarkable sense of immersion. You do things of your own volition - you never feel like the game is telling you to do something.
The best and most surprising aspect of this is its genuine difficulty. Make no mistake about it, scrubs: Half-Life is HARD. The game will throw you in tough situations that make you get off your silly high horse and think; try to play this game with the Doom mentality of run-and-gun and you'll get instantly wrecked by its puzzles and smart enemy placement. Playing through Half-Life in 2016 was a chore; it was a struggle. Most importantly, though? It was a genuinely fascinating, enjoyable little 10+ hour trip into the world of an FPS that revolutionized EVERYTHING in the world of video games upon its release. If it were remastered and retweaked today (read: Black Mesa), it would still be one of the best shooters of any generation of gaming.
A definite must-play if you want to stop being a filthy scrub.

XCOM 2 is a scifi turn-based strategy game and a sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
The premise is interesting enough. Instead of beating back the alien threat in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, the game actually assumes that the XCOM was defeated and the humanity was pacified under the alien overlords. All that's left of XCOM is a ragtag group of resistance fighters that continue the good fight using guerilla tactics.
Unfortunately the game doesn't really do a great job with this premise. Almost all the game mechanics have been copied from XCOM and just given a fresh coat of paint. Lots of them are rather immersion breaking too, like having to build up up the radio network or always having to pick from mutually exclusive dark event missions. I really wish Firaxis would have taken more cues from the original X-COM: UFO Defense and the Long War mod this time around.
On the other hand some parts of the strategic map are handled quite well. The game does make a good job of making you feel like you are really struggling with the lack of resources and personnel early on. You need to be careful with your spending and it's quite easy to make serious mistakes that will make your game much harder later on.
The tactical battles are more or less the same as in XCOM. Both the aliens and your squad have learned some new tricks, but overall the combat still has the same strengths and weaknesses. Unfortunately the extremely annoying enemy pod system is still here, although in a slightly improved form. On a positive note the new concealment mechanic is a nice touch, even if the game definitely could have done more with it.
Overall XCOM 2 could have been a pretty good (if flawed) sequel with enough changes to keep the gameplay interesting. Unfortunately, Firaxis did a terrible job with QA and the game is still a buggy mess almost a year after release. The bugs range from minor annoyances to major gamebreaking bugs and they certainly made the experience much less enjoyable than it would have otherwise been.
Considering how buggy the game still is, I wouldn't really recommend XCOM 2. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is generally a more polished experience and also has the excellent Long War mod. However, I might give XCOM 2 another chance once the recently announced Long War 2 mod comes out, hopefully by then Firaxis has done some further patching too.

Now, I review it having dropped another six hundred dollars into my PC, and am FINALLY able to play it as it was intended.**
Assassin's Creed: Unity.  If I put the past difficulties out of my mind, and review the product as it stands, on its own merits, this game is actually very, very good.  Don't get me wrong, if you didn't like other Assassin's Creed Games, you won't like this.  If you insist that the Naval Combat that first appeared in Creed 3 and was an integral part of Creed 4: Black Flag and Creed: Rogue is better than the Climby-stabby-sneaky, this is not the game for you.  However, if you wanted the series to return to the spirit of its origins, you will adore this.
Ever since Ezio climbed the ranks of the Brotherhood (In Creed: Brotherhood, I believe,) and gained Combo-kills and Parry-kills, every battle has been a crowd of 1000 men throwing themselves against the protagonist's weapons, as if whoever dies most gruesomely and quickly wins a night with... whoever was the hottest lady, at whatever time period we're talking about.  While that makes a modicum of sense for an older, more and more experienced Ezio... after two days of training, Connor can kill the British Army without breaking a sweat.  Moments after his ship exploding and being shipwrecked, Edward Kenway can declare Genocide on the Carribean and do it with a rusty sword he plucks from the sand.  Shay Patrick Cormac has broken ribs and a concussion, but what's this, a crowd hassling a nice Irish couple?  Not on his watch, and a flurry of violence begins that does not end until the earth itself is bleeding in a gutter.
Previous games kept raising the Hero's capabilities over the previous hero, and was stumped when it came to creating challenging enemies.  Here, Unity succeeds!  In making Arno WEAKER than his predecessors.  After all, he doesn't have the benefit of having played all the previous games.  You can parry and counter attack, much the same way as everyone else; but it's not an instant kill, it's just an opportunity to attack an unbalanced enemy.  Want to kill him faster?  Level up using Synch points to get new skills.  Buy better weapons with Money.  Use Creed Points to upgrare your weaponry or gear.  This is Character Progression.  This is a young new recruit progressing through the ranks, finding his place in an organization, and becoming stronger.  This is better.  I do not miss being a tornado of swords as much as I thought I would; indeed, I don't miss it AT ALL.
Being set in a more modern time, some enemies have guns.  Big deal, Connor, Edward, and Shay all dealt with enemies with guns, right?  Yeah, but in their games, the only guns that were deadly were the guns that the heroes owned.  Enemy guns were a nuissance.  They'd take out a pittance of health, and make you fall if you're climbing for a second.  If Arno gets shot by a farther away enemy while in a sword fight, you get staggered, allowing the melee guys to attack... and you also lose most of your health, or even just die, if the enemy's a high level guy.  You know, how Guns kill people really, really good.  That's why we have lots of them and not so many swords these days.
So how do you deal with these gunners who can shoot you to death?!  You... wait for it... ASSASSINATE them, preferably.  This is Assassin's Creed, not Idiot's Shrieking Attack on Everyone.  You want that guy over there dead?  He's got snipers on the rooftops?  Get up there, crouch into the new Sneaky Mode that makes you quieter and less visible, and assassinate those gunners dead.  If you can't get right up to them, don't worry, there's some silent mid-range kill options.
You'll be doing a lot more sneaking in this game than you did in previous games.  Well, I did all the sneaking I could in previous games.  Not because I had to; God knows it was faster and easier just to run into any place and murder everyone in an endless combo-kill (My record back in Brotherhood was 250-something in the training.  Ludicrous, no?  Should never have been that effective.  Maybe give it a three guy max, game?)  But here, you don't have the option to charge into 20 guys and kill them all.  In fact, when I DO sneak, and a group of four guys happens to find me, I'm genuinely afraid that I'm dead and will have to reload sooner.  No longer are all of my smoke bombs and stun bombs and extra tools a thing to use just for kicks; now I NEED those things to not get killed in an altercation with more than two enemies.
Earlier, I mentioned enemy levels.  That's a thing.  Every area, weapon, piece of clothing, and enemy has a level of 1 to 5.  Arno has a level too, but that's just an expression of what skills he's learned and what he's got equipped at the moment.  A level 1 guy can be wounded (dead for combat purposes, but still writhing in agony on the ground, incase you want to leave any innocent guards who jumped you "alive" for roleplay reasons,) in just one hit at level 3-ish.  You can hit him again for a Finisher that gives you Creed Points, but this isn't necessary.  A level 5 guy, with my current level 3 gear and weapons, will demand my full attention to parry and dodge, because one combo from him will have me near dead, and I'll have to hit him a LOT.  Generally, if I see a group at level 5, I make sure not to do anything to annoy them.
I'll boil things down here.  If you like the Sneaky parts, if you like the world and the story, and if you are SURE you have a pretty darn good gaming PC, this game is actually really good, and not deserving of the majority of the crap people give it.  Yes, the online mandatory bits were BS; they're gone now.  Yes, the requirements and bugs were BS; bugs are almost entirely gone and the requirements aren't as unreasonable now that you can get a good enough video card to run it at Ultra High settings for less than 400 bucks.
Give Creed: Unity a fair try, go into it without listening to either Hype nor Anti-Hype, and you should be pleasantly surprised.  I just got done with Rogue, and came here expecting (as all the reviews said) to be disappointed.  Honestly, I like this more than I liked Rogue so far.  And I really, really liked Rogue.  I guess the Creed was right; nothing IS true.  Especially from frothing angry critics ravenous for some groundbreaking new change.

This game is childish, but fun. The environments from the movie have been replicated very nicely; they are easily recognizable and look stunning, even in their LEGO look. You play with 2 - 10 characters at a time that each have their own unique capabilities. For example, one dwarf can shoot arrows, whereas the other one can move stuff around. In the beginning it took quite some time to get used to all these dwarves, remembering which one is needed to perform some kind of action. I am glad I didn't stop though, because you will not always be playing with so many characters simultaneously. However, this is both the strength and weakness of the game, in my opinion.
During the first playthrough, you complete a number of quests and the characters that are available during a quest have been predetermined. Many areas in a quest can only be reached or completed by a specific character. Thus, during the first playthrough, you can not collect all objects. Most likely not even half of them. To me, this is quite annoying because I do not have the time to be replaying a level multiple times to get the most out of the game (and you also need to remember where the spots are). I surely do not remember the special spots in the first levels that can only be reached by a character that was unlocked at a later time!
Also, the game is very easy, even when taking in mind it is also intended for children. Yet sometimes puzzles can be confusing because of the hint system which shows an icon when you need to switch to another character. But somehow the icon of your current character is shown at random moments as well, which makes you wonder whether there is something to do at that spot or not. Also, whilst some things are explained over and over again, some other major things are not explained. For example, I thought the coins had to be collected in order to complete some actions, but they are mostly used to buy characters (and maybe more, but the game doesn't tell you that!). So I spent a lot of time mindlessly collecting coins, which also respawn. Needing to smash objects all the time to gather coins, even in other people's houses, is quite childish, or even violent if you will ;) This just felt stupid and a waste of time, but it is up to you whether you do it.
All in all, the game is still a lot of fun. The quests are very recognizable from the book/movies, there are a lot of unlockable characters, the environments are absolutely beautiful (although the UI could use some polish) and there are many humorous moments. Just take it easy and enjoy the game :)

Underworld Dungeon was a pleasant surprise for me. It doesn't make any radical changes to the 8-bit dungeon, action-adventure formula nor does it claim to. It takes the best parts of the formula and enhances them while trying to minimise the negatives. The fact that the dungeons are randomly generated guarantees nearly unlimited replay-ability, sprites are original and creative, with each boss having a certain 'aura' or theme to them. A variety of items can be found in the game and the crafting system is easy to understand. Combat is fluid and engaging, very similar to Dark Souls. Difficulty is one of the areas where the game really shines, It strikes a perfect balance, without being too easy to the point of boredom while not making you want to rage quit. The game isn't without flaws though, there are a few bugs scattered around but none are game breaking, and while the game isn't ridiculously hard the learning curve is VERY steep, requiring a couple of plays to get the hang of. Overall though the game is well made, with every part of it shining with effort and potential and it's mind blowing to consider the entire game was made in two years by one person. Finally, with the game at its current state, I consider it to be a solid, engaging and original price of work that would be a great addition to any steam library. 8.5/10

If you're about to download this game, I recommend you pay attention to this review beforehand.
Unlike other reviews of this game, complaining more about the servers rather than the actual game and gameplay. This review, will cover the gameplay and the issues followng it. In order to act as both a warning, and a guide to those avoiding wasting money, and to those who still intend to waste said money.
First, I'd like to cover a major issue that others must know about before investing time into the game. The major issue is the fact that you mustn't play Age of Empires III: Complete Edition campaign. If you've only played the skirmish so far, you're safe. But your saves from the campaign will not carry over if you haven't already discovered this issue.
I were someone who wanted to play the game and unlock Japan as my home city, online suggestions said I had to complete all the acts. Luckily, I had only finished Act I so I'm not heavily bothered. But, it did take time. And it's time that's gone to waste. And after discovering that the Asian Dynasties was the proper version. I had my hopes, but they were quickly shut down.
So, I'd like to recommend that once you've installed the game if you haven't already. To start by searching for the file "Age3y.exe" which is the start up for Age of Empires 3: Asian Dynasties which, is the Complete Collection with the expansions on top of that. So play it safe, and heed my words before heading into the campaign where it'd be too late.
(I know, misleading title indeed.)
Now, for the game itself. If you liked Age of Empires 2 and are an opinionated person. Chances are, you aren't going to like this game because in comparison to Age of Empires 2. It won't meet your standards as it is quite different. But, if you're adaptable with an open mind. You will be able to accept this game and enjoy it's differences in comparison to the other games.
The changes are understandable, great graphics and high quality detail in comparison to the previous, means there'd be sacrifices. Sacrifices such as placing limitations on your population that are far smaller than what you're used to.
Limitations like decreasing the amount of resources you'd find scattered across the map, and instead replacing them with buildings that supply you with infinite amounts instead. Which, makes the game almost too easy.
Removing triggers, such as your villagers making their runs for supplies and back to each specific building.Replacing it with automatic transfers to your stockpile of resources. Which, also makes it too easy.
But, to make up for those easier adjustments. You gain a shorter game, which many people would prefer seeing as Age of Empires 2 games can stretch out for hours. Also, in place of all those changes. You have a new adjustment to the game which gives it more of a realistic touch and that is, communication between your mid-game units and your home city itself. Allowing you to call for occasional assistance with you and your conquest.
Which is something I can easily say I've come to enjoy.
Why did this recommendation start off negative as it should have, then point out the bad parts but agree with them in the process?
Because if you've tried to develop a game, then you'd know how difficult it can be. I haven't done it myself, but I have consideration for those who have. This game is good, despite its drastic differences. But, it is a nuisance that it lacks warning about there being two different games rather than the main with expansions on top. Hence the warning. And negative introduction.
I would give the game ratings in various areas to support it, but. It's a negative review, so I'll leave it at that.

This game isn't perfect, and can be frustrating at times (especially when you're new), but when you get the hang of using the ships it can be a lot of fun.
If you're new to the game, then keep in mind that it does take some time to get used to the ships and how to best use them. Even though this is an action game, there's as much strategy in it as there is combat. You'll do best once you know when to advance, what ships perform what functions (pure attack, healing, absorbing damage, etc), and what abilities the ships have (short-range blink/jump, cloaking device, missiles, fighters, bombers, shields, anti-armor, gauss cannon, nukes, etc).
Getting used to how to use each ship effectively can take some time, as can getting used to how to fight each ship when you're up against them. Once you start getting used to that, you might just find that you rather enjoy the game.

Tl;dr: this is my type of game: an open world rpg. It has a lot of planets to visit, and each planet has different features. There are fun and challenging boss fights and missions. There are also banana posters.
Definitely give this game a go if you are a big sandbox/rpg/action game fan.

A surprisingly polished indie RPG.
I feel like I should be lenient with my criticism because this game was made by such a small team. It really is quite an impressive game, with that perspective. That said, I've decided to share my honest thoughts. Or try to, at least.
Like many other reviews have said, the battle system is unique and interesting. It doesn't play like Magic: The Gathering, but it felt like it. To me, at least. I ended up spending many of my turns in battle managing, setting up and comboing skills. It was fun for a while, but eventually became troublesome. (I played on Heroine difficulty from start to finish. I can't speak for the other difficulty settings.)
CSH's story is paced like a summary. It seemed like Zeboyd Games was afraid of letting any single scene settle in. I would have liked to see some character drama. The story didn't draw me in. I couldn't bring myself to care about what was going on. And, the characters didn't seem to care either. The witty dialog was often funny, but that's all there was. Well, that and some brief heavy handed plot explanations. After clocking in 17 hours, I'm surprised at how empty the game's characters and story are. The setting was interesting, and all of the characters had a lot of potential. It's too bad more effort wasn't put into writing a more extensive script and adding some human themes to the game. CSH's story needed something to make it meaningful rather than just a placeholder. That said, I don't think they were going for anything serious or emotional. But, to me, melodrama is at the heart of JRPGs.
The pixel art looked fantastic and the character portaits (with all the different emotions) were great. I really liked the animated sequences. It's one of the best looking indie RPGs I've seen. Again, it's a shame there wasn't any emotional punch backing any of it up. HyperDuck SoundWorks did a great job on the music. It isn't really my style, but I can't deny it's really good stuff. It fit the game well. In fact, I'm listening to the OST as I'm writing this review. Laura Shigihara's contribution was a nice touch.
Overall, CSH showed me how hard it must be to make an indie RPG, and perhaps an indie JRPG in particular. I'm glad I played CSH, but I'm not sure I'll play it again. I wish Zeboyd Games a successful future in the indie games industry. It's clear they put in a lot of work into this game.
I almost didn't have any problems with bugs. There were a handful of graphical glitches that were no big deal. And, I did have to reset the game once toward the end, but because of the save anywhere feature it wasn't a problem at all.

I loved Zeboyd's previous short comedic retro RPGs
and
, so after reading CSH's description was convinced to buy it, to support the devs and their future projects. In the end though I was happy to have paid it half price, because, while nice, it wasn't nearly as good as I thought and hoped.
The first impressions are very good with the very nice graphics, BGMs, retro cutscenes and innovative battle system, three wholly different planets and several sidequests. However after a while the game loses steam and at about 3/4 of the story I felt I was going through the motions. The battle system feels needlessly complicated rather than strategic, poorly explained and the various ailments are mostly irrelevant; I largely stuck to my strategy of buffing everyone, healing and using the most powerful elemental attacks and had mostly no problems until the end of the game (played at Heroine difficulty).
Not to mention there still are bugs that sometimes freeze the game or make it so that battles never end.

Ah, FFIII. Originally released on the Famicom only in Japan, which caused quite a lot of confusion with the numbering, this is the last Final Fantasy (or at least the last numbered one) made for the third generation of gaming (NES/Sega Master System). After a 3D remake on the DS and a few ports later, it's finally on Steam.
Unfortunately, this remake is *too* faithful, and it doesn't quite hold up. There's no real sense of direction after the first dungeon, which you are dropped in straight away (literally). *SPOILERS* After you deal with a few random encounters and beat the boss, a crystal talks to you, and you appear on the overworld. You go to your town, watch a friend get bullied and then run off, talk to the village elders who basically say, "You have been chosen since birth by the crystals! It was no coincidence that it spoke to you now! Oh, and by the way, you're adopted!" (I kid you not, they flat out tell your character that he's adopted, and he has no reaction to that. It's not even because he's a silent protag, he just doesn't say anything back)*SPOILERS END*
Unlike the FFIV DS remake, there are no thought bubbles that appear when you use your menu on the world map, which would add some character to the otherwise stereotypical characters. You have your flat, adventurous main character, his best friend, a random girl you meet on an airship, and a castle guard. By the way, they're all 14 for whatever reason, even the castle guard, and they all look like they could be older. Don't expect the rest of the game to be any less cliche.
The OST is nice, I suppose. The standard town and battle music is good, but not great. The music for the Sealed Cave, the first dungeon, is...interesting. It's good, but it's not really what I would've expected for the first non-tutorial dungeon. I especially like "Into the Crystal Cave", as well as "Eternal Wind", and "Jinn's Curse", and that's all that I've liked from what I've heard so far.
The plot is slightly more complex than Final Fantasy I in that your characters actually speak and have...well...character! The plot is still plastic, and you still have to go on a cliche fetch quest for crystals after being declared the chosen ones, though. Also, *MINOR SPOILERS* you get an airship not even an hour into the game, which seems odd to me. I thought airships were things you got in the middle of the game, not right at the beginning with no effort. I'm not sure if I'm upset about it, because on one hand you get to experience the freedom of flight earlier, and on the other hand it cheapens the concept of getting an airship.*MINOR SPOILERS OVER*
The visuals are probably the best part about this game. The chibi style and colorful palette makes the world seem inviting and playful, which is probably the only reason I even played more after I got out of the tutorial dungeon. In this case, the graphics did make the game for me.
The gameplay, like the plot, is only slightly more complex than Final Fantasy I's. If you've played FFI, you know that if you make all your characters attack one enemy and the first hit or so kills it, the rest of your attacks will be "ineffective", because their target is already dead. This is the first game to fix that, and it does so by automatically selecting a new target for a given character's attack. Brilliant, right? Still, because this is FFIII and not FFIV, there is no ATB, which means that instead of a gauge filling up for a given character so they can attack, you just select new commands at the end of each "turn", like Pokemon. However, Pokemon has several type advantages and disadvantages, 4 moves per Pokemon, and loads of other things to make the combat more complex, while FFIII just has your choice of weapons, and I suppose a unique ability here and there when you meet more playable characters. Sure, the elemental black magic will be more effective against certain types, but it's still not the same complexity as in Pokemon, and even then, not everyone has black magic (although there is a way to give everyone black magic, but it's not worth it). For an apt analogy concerning FFIII's combat compared to FFIV's, think of coaching a football/soccer/other sport game vs. playing in one. FFIII is where you coach.
Oh, still on the topic of combat, sometimes enemies are faster than you, sometimes you're faster than them. It doesn't even seen to be a constant thing during the same battle, and so it can't possibly be due to different enemies being different levels even though they're the same type of enemy. This pretty much makes any strategy impossible to rely on 100%, which means straight up luck is now a factor. I suppose luck is also a factor in real life combat, but this isn't real life. When you get to the first actual dungeon, prepare to get destroyed if you didn't grind a lot beforehand. Yeah, it's one of those RPGs.
Should FFIII have stayed in Japan? Nah. While I bash on it quite a bit in this review, it's great to look at how far the franchise has come. Gotta have bad games to appreciate good ones, and all. Still, I can't in good faith recommend this to anyone, or at least this version, RPG lover or not. I hear the PSP version is the best, but I have not played much of it despite owning it. I'll update this review if/when I bring myself to play more of this version, but for now, I must give it the thumbs down.

XCOM2 is - to simply put it - a bloody brilliant game. Sure, it has it's own share of bugs and glitches, but overall it's a superb game,  that delivers a great experience.
Pros:
===
1) The modding community for XCOM2 is simply immense, and by itself takes this game to a whole new level.
2) Satiates my need for a good story. The story here quite interesting actually, and keeps you hooked to find out more about the alien's true motives.
3) Great alien and soldier animations.
4) Awesome graphics and colors.
5) Decent variety of solider classes and aliens in the vanilla game. The variety of soldiers and aliens can be increased further increased with some mods.
6) The new stealth mechanics are interesting and feel really cool if you pull it off.
7) Insane customization options thanks to some great mods. I've spent like 2-3 hours (at least) in my current game time just customizing my soldiers to look more badass! Hell, you can even customize the way Skyranger looks!
8) Randomized maps and units cater a unique experience in each playthrough
9) Very high replayability
Cons
===
1) Definitely has some bugs. One bug in particular that annoyed me (happened many times) was that i would hide a soldier behind a wall without any windows and providing full cover, only to find out it wasn't even there. Because, my soldier shot right through it at enemies while in overwatch. So, that was kinda confusing. Other common bugs include unbreakable windows/doors, doors won't open, certain tiles won't right-click from one angle - need to change angles to solve this.
2) Pretty hard. Frikkin hard actually.
3) Acute shortage of many resources mid-late game. Can't build so many of the cool stuff sadly, as aliens barely drop any loot, and even if they do, they vanish in 3 turns (loot reduces gradually per turn upto 3 turns after which it disappears completely). They chalked it up to the fact that alien things are rigged to self destruct. This honestly makes no sense becuse when a soldier picks up the loot, why would it stop self destructing? Also, don't even get me started on the fact that many times when you kill an alien, and it drops loot, it drops it where its surrounded by a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of other aliens. Don't worry, you aint getting to that loot in 3 turns. :)
Overall
=====
~~~~~
9/10

Xcom 2 is genius. The gameplay is fantastic, the new mod system is extremely welcome, and the overall feel is one of a gaming gem being refined in a new iteration. Unfortunately, it's not worth it.
The issue with this game is that it's incredibly unstable and glitchy. In most games, this would be annoying, but it's a kiss of death for Xcom 2. Imagine playing Ironman mode and facing a tough boss. You've beaten him down and somehow kept all of your ragged, wounded soldiers alive. One more attack will kill him, and your chance to hit is 98%. It's a melee attack. You've planned well. Your soldier strikes and the game crashes. You reload and do everything in the same order. Same result. You try and do things differently, and your party wipes. You keep thinking and eventually come up with a completely different strategy that will still work. Boss dies; game crashes. You reload, evac all of your troops to avoid the kill, and it crashes.
