Heat Signature is a game similar in aesthetics to Hotline Miami (excepting, y'know, the sci-fi aspects), but made by the creators of Gunpoint. Without several key features, Heat Signature could very well be quite similar to the aforementioned arcade shooter/beat-em-up/whatever. However, the game possesses several mechanics which drastically alter the feel of the game, when compared to Hotline Miami.
The first key feature is the permanence to actions taken in game. The game is perma-death, however progress is mostly saved, with the exception of losing the items you had on that character. This means that in every mission the option to bail is one which should be kept open at all times, because if you don't, you're likely to get captured and have to re-capture your guy again. This roguelike element means that every mission should be planned, extremely well. Which should be impossible if you know Hotline Miami, where the strange resurrection your character goes through is very much part of the game's tone and gameplay.
Allowing finishing missions to be possible in the first place with perma-death on (noting that when you get shot, you don't die straight away. Instead, the guard tosses you out an airlock, where you have to figure out how to not die of oxygen deprivation) is allowed by the ability to pause the game and plan out your moves. The trailer doesn't lie people. Watching that will give you a good idea of how the game plays. This makes this game extremely strategic, especially in some of the timed missions where you have a limited amount of real-time to either disable the pilot or get out.
The third is the items. What can I say? When the enemies are too tough, your guns are too♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you are too lazy, you can enter a level with a plethora of♥♥♥♥♥♥and not♥♥♥♥♥♥gadgets in the hope some of them will be useful. Instead of killing a man for the key, you might instead steal it right of his pants by slowing time and teleporting away. Or perhaps sprint to one of the terminals which allow you to manually unlock all doors of a certain security level. Much more likely is you'll use your key stealing gadgets, before realising it runs out of uses before you reach your goal, and have to teleport through a wall or use a reflector shield to get a man to kill themselves.
Anyway, alls said and done, Hotline Miami and Heat Signature is a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ comparison. Heat Signature lets you rocket into a ships window using only your shotgun and sheer willpower to get you there. Hotline Miami is completely different. Honestly a feel like a bit of an idiot now. But, Heat Signature is full of planning, ♥♥♥♥-ups, un-♥♥♥♥-ups, getting shot, having only 5 seconds to kill a man, hijacking another space trawler and using its missiles to assassinate a space-trawler, and wrenches. Wrenches.
TL;DR - The other reviews about wacky stories aren't rare incidents.

The guard rounds the corner and stres me straight in the face.
Quickly, I equip my shotgun and shoot him, but the noise attracts more guards. They enter the room and fire.
They have shotguns.
Shotguns are almost impossible to dodge.
I panic and flounder around. I am shot and unconscious. One of the guards picks me up and begins to (very slowly) carry me to an airlock.  The alarm has been set off. I have sixty seconds; less after I pick myself up out of deep space with my own remote-controlled pod.
The guard makes it to the airlock and sets me down. In one second, I'll be floating in space. That's fine. I've only gotten knocked out while bleeding 3 times before, so I'll still have six seconds to pick myself up.
I am shot into space at high velocity. I quickly remote control my ship to the general area, make the first pass at my body, and miss.
I begin to panic. I only have three seconds left. I quickly brake and zoom in towards my body, thrusting the ship's engines towards it at the same time.
I miss again.
The screen zooms out.
"Tonight, we drink to Margherita Cherry," it says. "Bled to death in space."
12/10.

As one reviewer put it, Heat Signature is a great "proof of concept." That said, it really is a fun proof of concept, and I don't regret spending $15 on it. I've gotten 25 hours out of it so far, and I will continue to play it until I beat it and unlock most of the achievements, but I've already done just about all there is to do.
More variety or a real storyline would be nice, as would having better incentive to play in different ways. I find myself reverting to the same familiar playstyle just about every time, simply because it's the most efficient way for me to deal with tougher enemies early on. There are undoubtedly other ways to handle these situations, but there's no *incentive* for me to find them. Some missions may require other approaches, but there are no rewards other than monetary, so there's no reason for me to do them.
If missions I'm not currently equipped to handle offered adequate incentive -- and stayed around long enough for me to equip myself to deal with them -- I would be eager to do them. Offer a nice high capacity rechargeable item, or better still, a self-charging item, and I would go out of my way to do them. Otherwise, I pick a mission that allows me to use my favored equiment, because why bother to do otherwise?
Nevertheless, I recommend this game. It's easily fun enough to warrant spending $15 in my book.

Most balanced free to play I've ever experienced. Frantic ship-to-ship battles of what I've always wanted in an online capital ship shooter make this game stand out.
Each ship has a personal style to it that is fun to play and can be difficult to master, but with a smooth difficulty curve. The ship guides posted for each ship are accurate and actually help quite a bit (take a look at them before you play that ship to get a better understanding of your role in battle). However, as these are team battles it can be frustrating if your team doesn't even try to participate in chat as the battles are very team focused, and communicating even a little to let your teammates know you need some help can determine if you can come back from near defeat. However, most games I've played involve getting matched with a team that will communicate.
I particularly like that every ship is "unlocked" as soon as you start up the game, as in, all it takes are in game credits (won through completing games) to unIock them, and there isn't  a distinct advantage other players have over you with the more expensive ships in games. You can use the premium currency to unlock ship skins, crew members, or ships if you so desire, but I have yet to purchase any of the premium currency and I've still had a blast playing this game.
I would and do recommend this to anyone, 10/10.

So, this might seem like an incredible statement to make, but IMO Cosmic Star Heroine is one of the best JRPGs I've ever played. And before the rush of "well you didn't play many" comments, I've played nearly every Final Fantasy title, old school titles like Breath of Fire I & II, Dragon Warrior, all the way to more modern stuff like Baiten Kaitos series. So I know what I'm talking about.
Cosmic Star Heroine does a lot of things right and very little wrong. It is true there were some issues right after release where there were some bugs (never encountered any personally) and some placeholder things were still there, but a majority of those issues have been cleared up. What is left is simply glorious.
The game pays tribute to Chrono Trigger in a lot of ways, from the way the overworld map is displayed and how the characters appear, to their character sprites and even the fact that all enemy encounters happen on screen rather then transitioning to a diffferent battle screen. Also the main character can obtain an accessory that allows for double technicques as CT offered. But from there, CSH strikes out to do its own thing.
The games battle system is perhaps the best part of it. All the battle music is simply awesome to jam to, and it gets to the point where you want the battles to stretch out so you can enjoy the mechanics, even though that's totally counter intuitive to the system. The way it works is that you have a set of abilities, and you can use them all once, before you need to use your defend command to restore them. Of course you could defend any time you want. You also get a selection of up to 4 items that can be used once per battle, and then 'programs' which are special one time per battle abilities specific to the shield that the character has equipped. Plus each character will occasionally enter a 'hyper' state which makes the next attack/heal they do move devastating.
None of these abilities are identical to each other, and they all do different things. The fun part is finding how they all work together, as finding the right combination of status effect, elemental weakness, and buffs can allow you to absolutely wreck everything. As an example, if an enemy is weak to water, you would use your main character to attack with a water ability. However if you have another party member buff them up, and have someone else cause the 'vulnerable' status on said enemy which makes the next attack do more damage, then you're looking at doubling or tripling what you would do normally. If the character is hyper it increases the damage more.
Of course how you lay out your characters is up to you, as they will learn far, far more then simply eight abilities as they progress. Do you give them mainly healing/buffing abilities? Do you focus on damage? Status ailments? A mix? Not to mention the various shields in the game offer certain abilities to use, despite not being the strongest shields available stat wise. There's a LOT to sink your teeth into, especailly with a total of 11 characters, plus the acquistion of a spaceship partway through the game which you can populate with crew members that all have various passive buffs they can offer.
The story is pretty solid as well. You're a galactic spy, working for one of the biggest agencies in the galaxy. After running a mission for your boss, you find out that he actually had asked you to steal a mind control device, and that he wants to use it to mind control humanity so that all is peaceful. From here you turn tratior, steal the item back, and fight back against his plans. Your journey takes you across three planets, plus two final areas, with a fair amount of side activity in the form of extra areas and super bosses.
The game also comes with four difficulties. My playthrough was on Agent difficulty, and I feel it was perhaps too easy at times. There is a difficulty below it, but don't bother with it because you'll most likely steamroll everything. In a similar fashion, don't play on the hardest difficulty outside of what is required for the achievement (the first battle) as its been said the difficulty is so ridiculously unbalanced it isn't fun.
I only have one small complaint, and its that the game itself isn't large enough. By the time you leave the first planet, you have 7 party members, with two more on the second planet and the last two on the final planet. From there you're about 80% of the way through the game, and it could've done with a slightly longer story, especially to flesh out a couple of the characters who don't get enough time to truly shine.
Bottom line, Cosmic Star Heroine has a lot to offer, Lots of replayability, wonderful presentation, and an awesome battle system. I 100% completely recommend it to everyone.

A throwback to old classics like Chrono Trigger, Cosmic Star Heroine utilizes a similar combat style, but with a very unique cast of characters and story that puts it into a league of its own:
The protagonist, Alyssa L'Salle, is a secret agent under the employ of a high-tech, well-equipped government agency seemingly content just to preserve order by subverting the odd terrorist cell. But when a top-secret mission gone wrong exposes her to information that casts her employer's motives into doubt, she and her allies decide their unquestioning loyalty may have been misplaced, and embark on a quest across the galaxy to save its unwitting inhabitants.
While the plot is straightforward enough, it isn't forced: There are clear transitions and good exposition for why direction changes at any one point. And while the cast, by conclusion, ends up fairly large, introduction of new characters doesn't feel contrived either. Plus, the variance in their backgrounds, motives, and species makes them relatable to a degree, not to mention the ability to configure your party setup at most points of the game (past the first few chapters) gives the player the power to play how they want, and effectively pick their favorites.
The environments and cutscenes are also dazzling, with appreciable attention to detail, giving a depth to the game uncommon to the genre. With fitting archtypes of enemies based on their setting, and different music for almost every one, dungeons don't blend together like in a lot of RPGs, and instead, it is always a joy to enter or discover a new one. Even the progression system doesn't feel like an arbitrary grind, with regular new skills and ways to approach battles constantly being introduced, and characters not in-party retaining the same xp levels, streamlining swapping members.
What I particularly enjoyed though, was the ease of gameplay. I'm not talking about the difficulty level, which is customizable to taste, but rather the simplicity of systems in place. The UI wasn't clunky or convoluted to no purpose. Status effects were kept to a minimum, so keeping track of them all, and how to inflict or avoid them, was never a problem. Equipment slots were few, but all had a clear function. Even losing a battle unexpectedly, rather than wasting potentially hours of unsaved gametime, prompted a simple retry/reload box, giving you a margin to redeem yourself.
Fresh mechanics, like extra active abilities based on equipment (which made preserving old equipment finally worthwhile, yay!), and swappable passives rewarded for thorough exploration and good memory, were also very nice to see. All-in-all, it's a beautifully-crafted title, and well worth the play for anyone looking for a fresh, sci-fi take on older classics.

XCOM 2 is one of the best turn based strategy games of all time, and makes an excellent sequel to XCOM Enemy: Unknown
Set 20 years after the previous game we learn that the aliens have officially taken over earth, and now XCOM is fighting as a resistance movement using a mobile base known as "The Avenger", an advanced alien ship to launch their operations from.
There are some new features to the game as well as improved features from the previous remake.
- Because the Avenger is a mobile air base, the player can move around the globe. Each country will have a certain amount of regions in it, you have to spend intell which is a new currency to make contact with these new regions. Each region will give you a different bonus, (similar to Enemy Unknown) as well as extra income at the end of each month.
- There are 4 new classes in the game. The ranger replaces the Assault class, and uses a shotgun for close range combat, they also carry a machette for melee combat.
- The engineer can be used to hack objectives from a distance, or heal their own companions, or perform a battle scan which is very useful in the field.
- The grenadier uses a light machinegun with a grenade launcher as a sidearm, while the snipers favour snipers (obviously) and a handgun.
- Retalliation missions have replaced terror missions, they are much more challenging and tough to comnplete.
- Occasionally a UFO will land that can be assaulted for supplies as a side mission.
- There will be 3 different guerilla operations, that the player can only choose one of to complete. This depends on what the player needs the most at the time in terms of rewards for completing these missions, for example one mission will reward them with intel and can counter a certain dark event.
- Dark events are 3 random events each month that work against the players favour.
- The customisation for the soldiers is greatly improved, we can name our guns, as well as change their patterns. We can give our soldiers a background story, and change their attitudes overall.
- The main aim is to prevent the Aliens Avatar project from being completed which can be slowed down overtime by destroying alien blacksite facilities or completing story mission objectives.
- The story has been greatly improved as well, answering more questions and delivering us with more cinematic cutscenes.

Well.. What should I say after having cleared the game? The story is well worth to be played and this game is a worth member of the Final Fantasy family. However, it should be contextualized in the years it was produced.
If you play this game with the eyes of a 80s-90s guy, you can only be amazed and positively surprised by the gameplay, the amazing storyline and the vastness of the world you will travel within, as well as the beasts you will encounter. The remake in 3D graphics maybe is not really nostalgic, but it makes the game experience far more enjoyable than in the past on NES and DS.
If you play this game with the eyes of a 2000s guy, you will be pretty disappointed: repetitive battle system, too broad job system (some jobs are completely useless, for example I'm really wondering whether anybody has ever used the job Ranger...), too many restrictions on weapons (for example, there is a job, I don't remember which, that can use basic bows and arrows at the beginning, but cannot use the advanced version of both.. Just why??), some almost impossible achievements (if you miss to open a chest or you miss to fight an enemy in some areas which you cannot get in later on, you have missed the achievements, unless you start the game from zero again and pay more attention...).
I am a mixture of both kind of players, nostalgic but not refraining some criticism.
My final comment and impression is more than positive anyway, because I'm a huge fun of FF Saga of all eras, and because overall is a very light game which doesn't requere too much effort and time to be played well.
Highly recommended to the historical fans of FF Saga, but good also to approach the JRPG world in a basic and friendly way.

First off I'll start with some pros and cons
Pros
- Unique art style
- Dark atmoshpere
- Challenging gameplay
- sexy narrator voice
- decent selection of characters and abilities
- diverse and changing enemies/locations
Cons
- Difficult RNG
- Learning curve that starts in the negative
- playing slow is the best way to win (almost always punished harder for risks than potential rewards)

If you are a die-hard Final Fantasy Fan who goes out of their way to play every game from 3-10 on Steam (1 &2 not yet released for PC) then Final Fantasy III is a must. First and foremost, this is a tough game to dedicate your time to beat. Currently I have held 52 hrs on record to play this game from start to finish. While the linear gameplay isn't necessarily that long, however it does take preparation to level up for the final challenge which is why it took me extra time plus completing much of the Steam achievement list.
As for the game itself, this version of Final Fantasy III is a remake of the original Nintendo DS handheld first released in the US in 2006. The original game came out in 1990 for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) in Japan only. The 3d remake retains much of the
difficulty and control schemes of the original version typical of any RPG genre type game. The story is pretty clichéd and bland compared to the later Final Fantasy titles, but it still doesn't fail to entertain as it is filled with many surprises, plot twists, and some humorous moments. Furthermore as a trivia fact, III was the first game that introduced many of the series highlights, including the job class system, summons including Ramuh, Ifrit, Shiva, and Odin to name a few, the hit point system that popped up when striking an enemy, riding chocobos throughout the world map, the first appearance of the moogles and the boss battle theme made its debut in this game as well.
The gameplay elements involve character job classes ranging from a knight to magic user, summoner, thief or job class with special abilities. Many more job classes are picked up along the way as the game progresses. Completing the game depends on the player constantly adjusting and upgrading on these job classes (it takes time & effort on this). Experience points that are used to level up on your characters and job classes are gained by defeating monsters randomly encountered on the World Map field or dungeon level, (encounters can get repetitive and annoying this way) as they are not seen.
This version does not include special features like a music track, or art gallery by Final Fantasy series artist Yoshitaka Amano, but does include a bestiary (viewable list of monsters defeated) which counts towards completing a Steam achievement. However, the bestiary is not viewed from the game's main menu, but rather much later in the game after achieving  a certain vehicle.
Overall, this has been one of the best classical Final Fantasy titles to play, but players be prepared for its classical difficulty and extended time to completing it.

I initially gave this game a negative review. After some thought and looking at forums and seeing how much the developers interact with players (even ones that leave negative reviews) I came to understand how much these folks love their game. So I will do a pros and cons review.
Let's just start with the negative, because at this stage there isn't really all that much to complain about.
CONS:
Performance lag. My set up is a little above average but nothing special. (Not going to give specs because I'm lazy) At some point in the game you will be fighting massive enemy AI and lots of them. The temperature of my GPU shoots up and my game lags to the point of nearly freezing. So there is surely a point where I can't play the game. Some of us reach that point more quickly than others and I am sure there are many out there who never notice a performance issue at all.
The CON behind this is that I feel I have to make the best 'garbage truck' to keep my world clean and therefore I always feel I am doing chores. It's like having a huge box of Legos, and always having to clean them up.
Camera. The camera can sometimes be a bit wonky. I wish you could toggle it to stay back and up of your 'tech' (what they call the bots in game)
that's about it for Cons....there are some minor nit picky things...options and features I wish were present....now on to the PROS
PROS
Parts and Progression
So many parts. There are just a crap ton of items. And the items are hidden and slowly revealed from behind a progression wall. It is done very nicely. It gives a great sense of having to explore the world, do the missions, increase in rank. I like the sense of progressing and unlocking/finding new items.
Incredible Concept. I do love the idea of the game. On one hand you have this amazing set of building blocks to build an awesome war machine, and on the other hand you have enemies to fight and destroy to cannibalize for even more parts to build with.
I just wish it didn't lag for me at certain points.
TerraTech is a game experience that is worth having tho!

I really love the X-Com series.  I remember spending hundreds of hours on the Enemy Unknown and Terror from the Deep as a kid and loving every second of it, even the long and tedious multipart ship terror missions and the alien base missions with tentaculats and Lobstermen behind every corner.  The 2012 remake was a welcome addition to the series despite it being simpler than the original.
And I definitely
X-Com2 for the
part.  Unfortunately, I just can't recommend it.
To begin with, there are the performance issues.  Random frame drops and stutters should NOT be happening with a GTX 1080, especially during in game cinematics.  Then there's the occasional hang ups on enemy turns.  The AI that usually takes no time to perform actions suddenly takes forever to decide what it wants to do for a turn, and then goes back to normal the next turn.  I still have no idea what causes this as it seems to happen at random times.  Also, there are weirdly long (relatively) load times when you're heading back to your main ship.  It really shouldn't take longer to load the base than it does to load a procedurally generated map but... it does.
The RNG is still, and will always be there.  Miss a million shots at 95% chance to hit, fail an 81% hack, get no engineers for the first two months but get 5 scientists, need an acid bomb/grenade but get everything but acid, get a useless (for your build) random skill from AWC, the list goes on and on.  You either deal with it by crying or savescumming.  But it's not part of why I don't recommend the game.
The main reason why I don't recommend the game?  The pacing.  I get it.  Timed missions make things more difficult since you have less opportunities, so you gotta make the best choice with what you got.  My problem with it isn't the difficulty as I've been able to consistently finish all the timed missions (without DLC bosses randomly showing up that is).  My problem with it is that it takes away most of your choices on how you want to play the game.  You have a myriad of options on how to bumrush to the objective (relatively) safely, such as smoke bombs, mimic beacons, etc but the fact remains is that you have no choice but to bumrush the objective.  In Enemy Unknown, there was some risk vs reward element there.  You can
to take the additional risk of rushing to get meld, the reward.  Here, you have no choice but to rush and the worst part is that
of the missions have some sort of timer (whether it's a real timer or one civilian dies every turn timer).  Majority of my missions consists of kill first enemy pod asap, destroy wall, and either put specialist behind cover with LoS to objective and hack objective or destroy relay.  Timed missions get a bit harder, as they introduce enemies with more health/armor/abilities, and then significantly easier as your specialist improves to reliably control mechanical units and when you can bring in Psi Ops who can dominate the tougher biological enemies, but
.
The next offensive part about pacing lies in the strategic part of the game.  Want to make contact with a new region?  No problem, just 5 days of scanning.  Except you scan half a day and ALERT, gotta fly off to save an ally VIP.  Spend half a day flying to the mission, do the mission, get that engineer drop that you desperately need, but it unfortunately requires 7 days of scanning. So you scan half a day of that before getting dragged into another mission that you
to do to prevent the dark event from adding more points to the avatar project, come back to scan for the engineer, scan a couple hours and ALERT!, your allies are being attacked, if you don't save them, you'll lose the relay tower you spent so many supplies on, so off to save them, and just when you think it's safe to try to scan for that engineer again, ALERT!  Resistance forces have disabled a train full of supplies so you gotta fly over and raid th- MOTHERF****R JUST LET ME F*****G SCAN IN MOTHERF*****G PEACE!!  It's offensive to the point where instead of getting your monthly pay immediately, you have to scan 3 days for it; 3 days that'll most likely turn into a week or more after all the interruptions.
And now you have a doomsday timer too, in the form of the avatar project.  Let the bar fill up and you have a set period of time to reduce the bar or it's game over.  So when you're trying to prioritize a path to reducing the avatar project and you get interruptions after interruptions, it gets assinine really quick.
And yes, I understand that there are mods that can change the pacing but from my point of view, mods shouldn't be necessary to make the game enjoyable.  Not to mention, updates can easily render mods obsolete, make your modded campaign unplayable, etc
Anyways, XCom2 isn't a bad game.  At its core, once you get past the mission timers, the tactical combat is great, the soldier customization has been significantly improved, weapon customization is nice, and certain things are less tedious (like having to manufacture new primary weapons and armor for each new rookie, you have a simpler upgrade system for the most standard stuff), and they actually made explosives super useful (makes the first couple missions on normal way too easy though).  The storyline also isn't bad (still ridiculous at points though) and leaves room to be interpreted whether it ties into the ending of X-Com Bureau or whether it's foreshadowing Terror from the Deep or Micronoids, etc.
tl:dr
I like this game but overall, I can't recommend the intended (unmodded) version to the majority of people as most of the game feels like there's only one way to play (rush objectives because 80% of the missions are timed and prioritize avatar project stuff) and that shouldn't be the case from a series that gave you so much freedom in your methods in prior games.

At it's core, I wanted to love this game. It has everything in an RPG turn based long term developmental strategy game that makes the experience fun.
It's the tactical nonsense that makes this game so frustrating and difficult to actually enjoy.
First and foremost, enemy units once alerted or brought onto the map are given both a free movement turn followed by a complete turn themelves. This may not sound like a big deal, but it essentially enables the enemy units to nearly completely outflank you or position themselves in such a way that you won't be able to complete your timed objectives with any surviving members.
Next, the timed objectives are ridiculous. You're given such a short time span to actually complete the mission (for instance, access the network in under 8 turns) that you literally have to beeline it for the objective with no regard for your units' safety. This wouldn't be an issue if you weren't being surrounded AND having to deal with eventual incoming reinforcements. There's no path you can take that doesn't require a conflict...so the only thing you can do is set up for as favorable an ambush as possible and then hope RNG works in your favor. If you don't get most/all the enemy killed right off the bat, you're not going to make it.
I'm all for difficult missions and challenges that require tactics, but once the enemy units get free moves, and constantly get missed on 80 and 90% hit chances while hitting your guys in full cover, and half your team panicks when a member falls unconcious from a single hit, yet is still nearly at full health....the game starts to get way more than frustrating.
It's not fun....and simply not worth proceeding. As much fun as the game looks, I'm already done with it. Thanks, but no thanks.

As one reviewer put it, Heat Signature is a great "proof of concept." That said, it really is a fun proof of concept, and I don't regret spending $15 on it. I've gotten 25 hours out of it so far, and I will continue to play it until I beat it and unlock most of the achievements, but I've already done just about all there is to do.
More variety or a real storyline would be nice, as would having better incentive to play in different ways. I find myself reverting to the same familiar playstyle just about every time, simply because it's the most efficient way for me to deal with tougher enemies early on. There are undoubtedly other ways to handle these situations, but there's no *incentive* for me to find them. Some missions may require other approaches, but there are no rewards other than monetary, so there's no reason for me to do them.
If missions I'm not currently equipped to handle offered adequate incentive -- and stayed around long enough for me to equip myself to deal with them -- I would be eager to do them. Offer a nice high capacity rechargeable item, or better still, a self-charging item, and I would go out of my way to do them. Otherwise, I pick a mission that allows me to use my favored equiment, because why bother to do otherwise?
Nevertheless, I recommend this game. It's easily fun enough to warrant spending $15 in my book.

I got a day off and decided to take a shot at this because I have been eyballing this game for a while now.
I just started and went from Level 1 to level 6 in a few hours. I liked the game play. It was fun and easy to start.
There are only 2 game modes but they have insane replayability because no 2 matches were ever the same. You can play Solo againt the AI and in Co-Op and PVP. I only got to do Solo. I had insane que times waiting for other players that I am going to assume were because I was playing during the day when people are living thier lives. You eventually get the ability to mod your ship/crew (I am working on it) and add implants. Graphics are good and it runs decently on my NVIDIA GT620.
As I progressed it got harder though. They give you a few ships to start with. You get to pick one at one point and you have to really look at you ship selections and decide what you want to do based on your playstyle. They only give you 3 choices of ships and they are good for starting players but then I realized that I was not going to be able to get any other ship anytime soon. The grind is beyond brutal but maybe worth it because by the time you earn enough to getthe ship you want you will really long since have mastered the basics of how to play the game. As I said before, leveling gets harder and takes longer and so does getting what you need. You can pay to get the ships and upgrades which will give you a huge advantage right out of the gate but if you are like me,  and on a financial budget that is not an option.
For Casual Gamers this is NOT the game for you. It is ok to check it out and see what it is all about but unless you are willing to spend a lot of time grinding until exhaustion or money on it you will get frustrated. For Hardcore Sci-Fi, Space Junkies who like Capital Ships then this is right dead center of our zone. I love it and will be playing a lot.

I bought this game on the first few days it came out on Steam, it looked good and I figured I would give it a try. I stopped playing after a week because of how much the game asks for you to get a good interent to prevent the lag from other players, but when I came back to playing recentlt, I became addicted again instantly.
I really do not get the negative reviews for Aberoth, it is a great game overall. Sure, the community can be a little bit awful at times, but the developer has made some very nice changes to that. There is an option in-game to become unfriendly, and if you are you can attack players and kill them. That can be a bit annoying at times, but if you kill a player, you will get infamy and eventually end up in jail, a clear punishment for being evil.
The game also requires for you to grind sometimes, but it also encourages exploration and making allies with others for more power. The gameplay varies quite a lot, forcing you to both run away, go and research on the interent (Even though that is not quite good in my opinion) and power through weak enemies.
I really enjoy the clear efforts the creator put into the game to make it avaliable to everyone without making this a Pay-To-Win. Sure, paying to get a membership for better stuff is easy and makes you better, but it doesn't completely create an annoyance for other players.
In conclusion, expect to put a lot of your efforts into the game to enjoy it, research a bit, ask around the community, see what they know, but expect to fail as well. The game will be fun if you think it is and not when you think it's not. So, try out the game, put a couple hours into it, as the game is certainly better and less crowded than it was when it first came out.

New and original turn-based rpgs are very rare these days and Cosmic Star Heroine manages to both have original combat mechanics and a very classical/retro feel. All the characters feel unique in battle and you can choose what fits your playstyle best. There are many choices to be made, as you can only have a certain number of abilities and items during a battle. Also, you will find weapons/shields that have different effects and sometimes you might choose a less powerfull weapon because it brings a unique boost to an ability that you like.
The game has very retro-esque visuals which may be a strengh or a weakness depening on your tastes. Fans of classical rpgs will probably like the style, while some other players might find this off-putting. Looking at the Steam screenshots and gameplay footage should be enough to decide whether this visual style is a problem to you or not. The music of the game is extremely well done and greatly contributes to the immersion in the game's universe. So even if you may think that the visuals look "bad", the music more than makes up for it.
The story of the game is not ground-breaking, but I thought it was quite decent. This is an indie game made by a very small team, so overall the game holds up pretty well. I greatly recommend it to fans of classical rpgs, as the game contains many references to this era. I cannot count how many Chrono Trigger references are in the game, which made the experience even more enjoyable to me !
The entire game can be finished (along with 100% achievements) in about 15 hours.

I really love the X-Com series.  I remember spending hundreds of hours on the Enemy Unknown and Terror from the Deep as a kid and loving every second of it, even the long and tedious multipart ship terror missions and the alien base missions with tentaculats and Lobstermen behind every corner.  The 2012 remake was a welcome addition to the series despite it being simpler than the original.
And I definitely
X-Com2 for the
part.  Unfortunately, I just can't recommend it.
To begin with, there are the performance issues.  Random frame drops and stutters should NOT be happening with a GTX 1080, especially during in game cinematics.  Then there's the occasional hang ups on enemy turns.  The AI that usually takes no time to perform actions suddenly takes forever to decide what it wants to do for a turn, and then goes back to normal the next turn.  I still have no idea what causes this as it seems to happen at random times.  Also, there are weirdly long (relatively) load times when you're heading back to your main ship.  It really shouldn't take longer to load the base than it does to load a procedurally generated map but... it does.
The RNG is still, and will always be there.  Miss a million shots at 95% chance to hit, fail an 81% hack, get no engineers for the first two months but get 5 scientists, need an acid bomb/grenade but get everything but acid, get a useless (for your build) random skill from AWC, the list goes on and on.  You either deal with it by crying or savescumming.  But it's not part of why I don't recommend the game.
The main reason why I don't recommend the game?  The pacing.  I get it.  Timed missions make things more difficult since you have less opportunities, so you gotta make the best choice with what you got.  My problem with it isn't the difficulty as I've been able to consistently finish all the timed missions (without DLC bosses randomly showing up that is).  My problem with it is that it takes away most of your choices on how you want to play the game.  You have a myriad of options on how to bumrush to the objective (relatively) safely, such as smoke bombs, mimic beacons, etc but the fact remains is that you have no choice but to bumrush the objective.  In Enemy Unknown, there was some risk vs reward element there.  You can
to take the additional risk of rushing to get meld, the reward.  Here, you have no choice but to rush and the worst part is that
of the missions have some sort of timer (whether it's a real timer or one civilian dies every turn timer).  Majority of my missions consists of kill first enemy pod asap, destroy wall, and either put specialist behind cover with LoS to objective and hack objective or destroy relay.  Timed missions get a bit harder, as they introduce enemies with more health/armor/abilities, and then significantly easier as your specialist improves to reliably control mechanical units and when you can bring in Psi Ops who can dominate the tougher biological enemies, but
.
The next offensive part about pacing lies in the strategic part of the game.  Want to make contact with a new region?  No problem, just 5 days of scanning.  Except you scan half a day and ALERT, gotta fly off to save an ally VIP.  Spend half a day flying to the mission, do the mission, get that engineer drop that you desperately need, but it unfortunately requires 7 days of scanning. So you scan half a day of that before getting dragged into another mission that you
to do to prevent the dark event from adding more points to the avatar project, come back to scan for the engineer, scan a couple hours and ALERT!, your allies are being attacked, if you don't save them, you'll lose the relay tower you spent so many supplies on, so off to save them, and just when you think it's safe to try to scan for that engineer again, ALERT!  Resistance forces have disabled a train full of supplies so you gotta fly over and raid th- MOTHERF****R JUST LET ME F*****G SCAN IN MOTHERF*****G PEACE!!  It's offensive to the point where instead of getting your monthly pay immediately, you have to scan 3 days for it; 3 days that'll most likely turn into a week or more after all the interruptions.
And now you have a doomsday timer too, in the form of the avatar project.  Let the bar fill up and you have a set period of time to reduce the bar or it's game over.  So when you're trying to prioritize a path to reducing the avatar project and you get interruptions after interruptions, it gets assinine really quick.
And yes, I understand that there are mods that can change the pacing but from my point of view, mods shouldn't be necessary to make the game enjoyable.  Not to mention, updates can easily render mods obsolete, make your modded campaign unplayable, etc
Anyways, XCom2 isn't a bad game.  At its core, once you get past the mission timers, the tactical combat is great, the soldier customization has been significantly improved, weapon customization is nice, and certain things are less tedious (like having to manufacture new primary weapons and armor for each new rookie, you have a simpler upgrade system for the most standard stuff), and they actually made explosives super useful (makes the first couple missions on normal way too easy though).  The storyline also isn't bad (still ridiculous at points though) and leaves room to be interpreted whether it ties into the ending of X-Com Bureau or whether it's foreshadowing Terror from the Deep or Micronoids, etc.
tl:dr
I like this game but overall, I can't recommend the intended (unmodded) version to the majority of people as most of the game feels like there's only one way to play (rush objectives because 80% of the missions are timed and prioritize avatar project stuff) and that shouldn't be the case from a series that gave you so much freedom in your methods in prior games.

At it's core, I wanted to love this game. It has everything in an RPG turn based long term developmental strategy game that makes the experience fun.
It's the tactical nonsense that makes this game so frustrating and difficult to actually enjoy.
First and foremost, enemy units once alerted or brought onto the map are given both a free movement turn followed by a complete turn themelves. This may not sound like a big deal, but it essentially enables the enemy units to nearly completely outflank you or position themselves in such a way that you won't be able to complete your timed objectives with any surviving members.
Next, the timed objectives are ridiculous. You're given such a short time span to actually complete the mission (for instance, access the network in under 8 turns) that you literally have to beeline it for the objective with no regard for your units' safety. This wouldn't be an issue if you weren't being surrounded AND having to deal with eventual incoming reinforcements. There's no path you can take that doesn't require a conflict...so the only thing you can do is set up for as favorable an ambush as possible and then hope RNG works in your favor. If you don't get most/all the enemy killed right off the bat, you're not going to make it.
I'm all for difficult missions and challenges that require tactics, but once the enemy units get free moves, and constantly get missed on 80 and 90% hit chances while hitting your guys in full cover, and half your team panicks when a member falls unconcious from a single hit, yet is still nearly at full health....the game starts to get way more than frustrating.
It's not fun....and simply not worth proceeding. As much fun as the game looks, I'm already done with it. Thanks, but no thanks.

Update: Unity lowered the bar to such a point that almost all the positive comments recommend the game because IT CAN RUN. The sympathy for the game is bordering Stockholm Syndrome. It is praised for doing what exactly every single game should be able to do: execute. It’s almost brilliant and a great business model, too: 1) Release a game with no content that cannot run. 2) Fix all the bugs. 3) Profit.
First of all Unity is actually a decent game but since this is supposed to be a part of the Assassin’s Creed storyline, it miserably fails to fit in, hence the vote down.
Secondly, of course, spoilers.
The overall feel of Unity is more like a fan fiction project with an enormous budget rather than a proper, canonical installment.
I think the most important thing that I would have liked to know before buying Unity is this: It has
. Apart from the occasional server change ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (which I think is a lazy excuse to include the Eiffel Tower in the game) there is nothing happening today.
Honestly I gave up on expecting any good story material after playing AC3, because the compelling and coherent story of the first civilization and their artifacts that will help prevent the 2012 apocalypse ended with Desmond. The story as it was revealed up to that point didn’t require the juno plot twist to be any better.
In Black Flag the sages were introduced, which were only conceptually replacing the artifacts. But I still had no problem with it, because the reason I play the games is the beautifully complex story that actually takes place today, which has layers and layers of narration embedded in each other. Like the way the game used to be about the modern day assassin Desmond, living Ezio’s life, who has visions of Altair and the way these characters are interconnected centuries apart (the last speech of Ezio in Masyaf).
But the good side is that you do not have to be annoyed about not being able to replay modern day missions, since there are none.
Maybe I’m mistaken but I remember an interview, explaining this initiate thing to be a way of supporting the immersion of the game play, that the player would indeed feel like the person who is actually in the animus. Well, it does not. and I do not. When there was this confused, interacting, afraid deep within and overall relatable Desmond, I cared about his story. His layer of narration was the buffer between the animus and the actual game. His presence was a mental bridge; he was there to suggest the mode of interaction and how to feel. Now that the game has no modern day content, no outer layer of narration that I can relate to and is based on a complete rehash of the finding artifacts plot with the one key difference that there is no cataclysmic end game like the DESTRUCTION OF THE EARTH, it is reduced to some kind of assassination simulation.
As it is stated by many other players, now the fighting is much, much better. It is more realistic that you can’t take 30 people at once.
Unless you use the smoke bomb generously.
I was one of the people who thought the fighting should be more challenging and I actually liked this improvement at first, but the fact that it is easily overcome by buying powerful enough gear and smoke bombs, does not make me believe that this is a genuine attempt to make it realistic, but rather a way to make players grind points, or much better, buy helix points to upgrade. The new fighting mechanism doesn’t require skill, it requires points. At some point, I ended up running into lifts like an idiot to collect extra creed points for a sword. There are nice improvements but all of them feel contrived.
Plus, since with enough smoke bombs, skill and gear the fighting is exactly the same, the only difference now is that you don’t see a damn thing through the shroud of the smoke while fighting. Or you can activate the eagle sense, of course, so now you’re fighting luminescent, solid colored bald figures.
Unity adds nothing to the main story arc and everything in the game is a rehash of an old concept, without proper justification (unless you count being cool as a legitimate reason). I could completely skip this installment and I wouldn’t miss anything story-wise:
Like Arno owning the Cafe Theatre is analogous of Ezio owning a town. But, well, Ezio is a ♥♥♥♥ing landlord! Why does the Assassin Brotherhood just give away the entire income of a huge cafe to this one seemingly insignificant new recruit?
What is the proper justification of the ancients devising a lightning sword, which is analogous of the apples and the shroud, that teleports to undefined distances? The apples and the shroud that was always there at every turning point of human history, as opposed to the sword which is there as a nice gimmick and an end game reward.
Why nobody is freaking over the existence of such sword and looking for it, instead of looking for the body of a man, who was explained to be an identical genetic copy of another man with the identical set of memories, who was already captured dead in the previous title?

Review: Aberoth is a hardcore online multiplayer open-PVP game that is NOT Pay to Win and updates every so often. With that being said, you will DIE several times, unless you've got the knowledge, skill, and endurance to continue playing this game. Everytime you die, you lose all your items held on you, but you have a chance to keep them using an "engrave" system. Items that are dropped will NEVER dissapear unless it is picked up by either another player or an enemy. NPCs are suprisingly interactable with text chat actions. Enemy NPCs can pickup and use items dropped by players or other NPCs. (You can even make some enemy NPCs drunk!) Expect ALOT of grinding in this game since leveling, quests, etc. can take time. (This can be repettitve at some point...) It is important to know the rules of community interaction ingame as well as using the wiki for help. The community is incredibly mixed consisting of several nice people or jerks. (I recommend playing with a friend) The graphics are a mix of ATARI and SNES which can be hard to get used to...
Verdict: 6/10 "A unique MMO that uses peculiar but fun/frustrating mechanics with a not so great community, but it's strangely addicting."

This game feels like an RPGMaker game done right. To be clear, it isn't one, but it is one of the few modern games that successfully captures some of the magic of 90's SNES JRPGs. The game plays very similarly to Chrono Trigger, with instanced encounters instead of random ones, a diverse and unorthodox list of party members, and a very similar style and quality of art. The gameplay here is turn based and very well balanced, with 4 active party members each with up to 12 different spells/abilites, 8 shared items that can be used once per battle, and a satisfying combo system. The game's story is pretty corny and pays homage to a lot of anime and jrpg tropes, but it is still fun. The art in this game is flat out amazing, there is such huge variety in the enemy, character, and level design that it baffles me that apparently only one person made all of this content.
Pros:
-Beautiful art style
-Satisfying turn based combat with a good underlying battle system
-15+ hours of content and very reasonable achievements
-Equipment and items scale well and are always useful in some ways, you aren't just always replacing old equipment
-No random encounters or grinding necessary
Cons:
-The hardest difficulty is poorly balanced, it feels like the devs didn't playtest it very much past the first level. Most people online also agree it is pretty unfair. The heroine difficulty is perfectly balanced though.
-Occasionally minor gui glitches and disappearing npcs in battles

Good and bad game at the same time. The reason for thumb down is quite simple - there are other LEGO games out there.
Let's start with PROS:
- it is a LEGO game. really, LEGO by Traveller's Tales is a thumbs up by a rule of ... thumb ;) those games are funny, based on our favourite stories (movies, books, comics), what not to love here ... well, you will know a bit later
- not a buggy LEGO game. I loved LEGO LotR until it occurred to me that I won't be able to complete the game because items, I have already collected, are missing in my "inventory". I played that one 3 times, but similar bugs happened during playthrough and had to stop. In The Hobbit nothing like that happened to me, only a few crashes ... but if I do alt-tabs or hard stop game by closing my laptop while in game ... everything can happen then, so I can tell that game is very stable.
- last positive - The Hobbit. I really like Tolkien's stories. Hobbit is really nice book ... for kids :) I don't know how it was possible to create 3 movies out of this quite short book. LotR movies should be about 3 times longer than they were. And here, you have it ... wanted to write ALL, but it's not the right word here and that takes us to ...
CONS:
- first - it's not a full The Hobbit story. The game is based on first two Hobbit movies. There was a rumour about a DLC with the story based on the last movie, but there won't be one and it's quite understandable if you know the book/movies and have played earlier games. On the Middle-Earth map you will have many missions placed next to each other, because nearly whole third movie takes place in a single area - around Erebor and "Lake-town". It's totally different from LotR, where you always moved forward on the map. Anyway, the game is missing some content and you know that.
- second - too many, boring side quests. Those are there only to give you more playtime if you want 100% completion.
- maybe not a big problem and really forced on the devs by the story, but main characters are all similarly looking (well ... those are the dwarves), yet they have very different abilities. It is a bit hard to distinguish between them at start.
- "female" voices, really, those do not sound female at all.
- DLC ... really, those should be a part of the game as those add nothing to the game. Just some items and characters to the free play mode. Ofc, those can help you a bit with fast start of the game, because e.g. you get Shadow Sword from DLC and you don't need a mithril one or the Sauron to break Morgul statues, but this is not a big help, really. Just get multipliers fast and you will get 10.000.000.000 studs achievement long before any 100% items/quests/bricks/characters one (strange, but achievement stats show something else ... ) and you can buy literally everything you will be offered by the game easily after getting 3 multipliers.
TL;DR
Again it IS a good game. Not a bad LEGO game. The missing content (1/3 of the story) and all those boring side quests I had to complete to get 100% completion made me give this negative note. Really there are other LEGO games, that gave me way more fun. Even the buggy and impossible (for me) to complete LotR.

I haven’t had this much sci-fi RPG fun since Mass Effect! Cosmic Star Heroine is a game with great Chrono Trigger-style combat, great characters and a beautiful 16-bit inspired art style.
The combat is the main draw of the game. There's a lot of freedom to arrange your party, the equipment and the abilities. Every battle feels like a fight to the end, as health, etc. regenerates. You will also want to try all your abilities and items in battle. This is not a simple, 'press A to win' game. You can avoid enemies, but you'll never want to. It's just fun to fight in this game.
Story-wise the game takes a bit of dip in the middle of the game. The start of the game is well-paced and interesting, but the storyline hits a bit of a wall. Luckily the game picks up again after, with the plot becoming more focused and some very cool characters/worlds getting introduced.
Technically there’s a few small glitches, but in general it runs great and I’ve encountered nothing game breaking.
Is this a perfect game? No, not all. The characters could have some more depth to them,the story at times tried too many things at the same time and its quite linear. Yet the game does draw you in like the classic JRPGs of the 90s. The devs are getting better and better with each game. I can't wait for what they have to offer next and I hope that they'll eventually make a sequel to this game one day.

This game is a tribute to the 16 bit jrpgs all us old people loved. and theres a lot to love here, but the problem is that its all very superficial and shallow.  Combat is lengthy and challenging, but once you figure out what works for you, you can spend as much time on boss fights as you do on regular battles. There are TONs of characters, and while the designs are excellent and cool, theres not much to them. they have no particular stories to them or any depth outside of their design and combat style.  take our heroine for example. The worlds and settings are visually appealing if underdeveloped.  same could be said about the enemies. in spite of it all the music is excellent and does more for the mood and character of the game than any of the other stuff.
but the most important part of any jrpg(im always told) is the story.  There are MOMENTS of intrigue and interesting stuff, but its as shallow and meaningless as the characters, the style, the game itself.  by the end you feel cheated by the lack of anything memorable.
Technically the game works. theres the occaisional graphical glitch, and npc dialogue barely updates, theres little point in backtracking or talking to people as they RARELY say anything new.  theres no option to reconfigure the keys and development seems to have stalled for the time being. so keep the date of this review in mind, they could have fixed it all at any point.

This game is an excellent old school Rpg, emphasis on the old school. Remember this game was orginally released April 1990 ( in Japan only), to put that in perspective it, Final Fantasy 1 came out for the NES in America that year! This version is a direct port of the DS version, which updated the graphics to a 3D engine.
There is very little hand holding, often you will find yourself on the world map trying to remember a single line of dialogue from an NPC that will direct you. While the flow of the game is pretty good, there is a few times that you will need to grind out levels (and Job levels). Again, part of the old school feeling of this game.
The Job system works for the most part and is designed to suit individual playstyles. Unfortunately there is many bosses that die easier to certain group make-ups. This can be a frustrating thing. Also a few of the jobs are direct upgrades from other jobs (white mage / devout or Monk / Black belt) rendering the previous job basically  obsolete.
Graphics
Well not the best looking game the graphics do a servicable job. This will not put your system to the test that is for sure!
Sound
The music and sound effects are pretty good and definitely have that "final fantasy" feel.
Story
As mentioned above the flow of the game is ok, but you do find yourself at certain points wondering where to go next (at least I did, anyway). Revisiting a couple of towns and talking to everyone may refresh the memory.
Gameplay
Old school! Grinding levels although arguably not required is recommended. The Job levels have a different leveling system, as in they don't level up using Experience points. There is a hidden job point system that sets your levels. To accumulate these job points you perform actions in battle (attack, guard, item, magic etc.)  When JP is accumulated to 99, Job level goes up by 1. Each action (except: Front, Back, Escape, and Flee) will contribute a fixed amount of job points to the character.
My only real complaint is when entering a battle the camera system often scrolls through the enemies. Really it comes down to like 3 seconds but when you're grinding levels it makes each battle longer than maybe it should be, this adds up over time. Again, just a very small gripe.
There is very large portion of the game at the end where you are unable to save. Although I was lucky and got through it all unscathed, I can imagine the frustration of dieing and losing everything after sinking a couple of hours into the dungeon. Save and save often! Even if you don't think you need to!
Overall I recommend this game especially if you're into Jrpg, and specifically ones from the past! :)

Darkest Dungeon is not quite what I had expected, to say it truthfully. And with that, I can say I was rather satisfied with it. With the dark, unforgiving world of Darkest Dungeon, every encounter could make the case of life or death, madness or revelation, and the end of your journey.  There's no such thing as 'being set up to fail.', there is no 'artificial difficulty', and there is no such thing as 'impossible'. There is only preparation, strategy, and risk.
Set into the dungeons in parties of one to four 'heroes', venturing into the many dungeons to claim what is yours and defeat the ever hardening foes of the dungeon. With all matter of enemies from beasts, to the undead, to our own fellow man, and the unknown Eldritch forces of the world, with cruel combinations of each as well. Their resolve tested and their skills strained, survival is questioned, and your supplies dwindled.
Turn based in combat, every action making a great difference in the outcome, either ending in misery with the inevitable death, mended wounds to prolong your journey, and bolster your forces to destroy the evils within, but no one lives forever, alas. Death is inevitable. It's simply a matter of how long until you can last until it finally takes it's grips onto you and pulls you under.
The task ahead is terrible, and weakness will not be tolerated if you wish to survive.
Even the taunts are worth the $$, go buy this!!

Heat Signature Review!
A game that combines some of the best parts of older gems, and creates something completely refreshing.
If you like FTL... Good!
If you like Hotline Miami... Good!
If you like Spaceships, Guns, Bullet time slow-mo kill everything in the room within a second with a few choice pauses so you can grab that gun with your right hand that the guard you just killed with your short sword in your left hand, and now you can aim to put a bullet in the other guard across the room watching the whole thing before he can alertm, and call for secruity.
Enjoy a open-galaxy sandbox where the main focus is taking on missions with one of your randomly shuffeled characters that can of course be found throughout the galaxy at Bars which act as your Home base for all things. Throughout the game you complete missions, which in turn give you the ability to expand your rebellion, and take over new Bars which unlock more characters to join the shuffle of character choices, and unique story quests with set mission where if you complete it you get more items within the marketplace back at your Bars.
The action of the game itself involves accepting a range of different missions from Stealth extraction of a certain individual on the ship without being detected to making sure their are no witnesses while you murder everyone you come across on the randomly generated ships. After the acceptance of a mission you will be piloting your little one man ship, and zooming across space to find your target. Once found you simply find a latch point (While ships generally only start with one point to begin with you are able to destory sections of the ship once you learn how to start getting creative with your missions) how you go about getting your way from Point A on the ship to Point B is totally up to you.
Overall it's a pretty solid game that feels unique, and I'm glad I can add it to my list of games I need to complete.
If that sounds interesting to you. Check it out!

Aberoth is a free online rpg in the style of games from the Commodore 64 and Atari 8 bit Computers. It's has text adventure characteristics, complicated mechanics and graphics that are very nostalgic of the early 80’s.
When I said aberoth is text based I meant it aberoth has no menus or status screens everything is displayed in text over the graphics. This can be annoying when you're trying to switch from different status for example: friendly & unfriendly. A mistake while typing this word could cost you, your gear/ gold.
Which reminds me of the drops system in aberoth. This makes pvp for the hell of it worth it; Because other players can drop their gear, they have about a 90% chance to keep it. Because pvp is so profitable other players are the most dangerous enemies in the game and you need to be constantly aware of them.
The hostile npc’s in aberoth are also very intelligent they are able to use items, manage their inventory and equip better gear making combat strategic. This also ties into PVP as many players will use the npc’s to their advantage.
In conclusion aberoth has one of the most dedicated and diverse communities of any game; it may be a good or bad community but the drama that comes with no moderation makes aberoth a social experiment that I intend to take part in.
A note on other reviews:
Because of the nature of aberoth many people die at the start of the game (killed by other players). A lot of people dismiss the game on the account of the “Comunity being worse then the game” -Some dumb♥♥♥♥♥who doesn't know how to write reviews.
Aberoth in its essence is a PVP game, cheap deaths and great loss are part of the difficulty. Also many of the other reviewers don't seem to have played the game for very long (at least the steam version). You may want to limit you Judgement of the game until you find a reviewer who has put at least an hour into the game.
I understand aberoth isn't for everyone, and many people will disagree with my review, but the one line reviews for aberoth are in fact written by upset newbs trying to vent their frustration for being killed 3 time at the start of the game.

I was a big fan of Zeboyd's previous titles before I'd even heard of this game, so when I finally picked it up, I was pretty excited. The first few hours of the game were really fun and you could tell that they had pulled out all the stops on this one to create something completely their own. The art has improved a lot since the BoD VII and CSTW days, which was the most obvious difference from the very start. The combat system is clearly influenced by Chrono Trigger, and it was nostalgic to come back to that system at first.
But it's not all good news. The most important aspect of any RPG, in my mind, is the story, the characters, and the setting. Well, the setting is certainly interesting. It's futuristic cyberpunk set on three different planets. You can't really go wrong there.
The characters, on the other hand, are pretty one-dimensional. You get a few interesting lines when you first meet them, and then there's not much else. The occasional quip pops up, but you never really feel like you get to know these people or that they develop meaningfully. They each have a sidequest, but it's not enough to flesh them out.
The story is pretty bland. It's the same sort of rebels vs. the empire retread we've seen a thousand times before, but it's particularly lacking in depth. I had a really hard time getting into it, and I was trying my best.
The combat feels strategic, but even on the normal difficulty, it's a bit of a slog.
You can fight the same battles again if you want to (for leveling purposes) but battles take a really long time to fight, so grinding isn't a very effective use of your time. The amount of power you gain when you level up is also pretty insignificant, and no matter what you do, you always feel like you're just about even with the monsters in terms of power.
What this means is that even though the system doesn't reward grinding, you really don't need to grind at all. Everything's pretty balanced. The exception to this is the hardest difficulty setting, which is so unbalanced that you get an achievement simply for beating the first fight in the game (which is harder than it sounds).
If you like retro RPGs, you'll probably enjoy Cosmic Star Heroine. I did, at least to a point. I still think it's a very flawed game, but it marks a significant improvement on the part of the developer, and I support that. Here's hoping their next game will be even better.

Cosmic Star Heroine is a throw back to the 16 bit SNES RPG era, if you enjoyed FF6 or Chrono Trigger, you'll like this. The classic ATB turn system forms the crux of battles. The game is quite short, (13 chapters) will roughly take you 15 hours. The graphics are charming and the soundtrack is mostly amazing. CSH allows to save anywhere and sprint all the time which is welcome. There are no random battles, enemies are always visible on the screen. Your characters level up, gain new abilities which you can swap in and out, see what combinations work for you. Your character's can equip shields & programs that grant them special abilities and powerful moves so you're encouraged to explore and search for powerful items. A little later in the game, the main character can sync major damage moves with other characters, like tri casting in Chrono Trigger. There's a good amount of variety in the locations also, from lush jungles to waterfall caverns to space stations and deserts. Recommended.

If you enjoy solid old-school JRPG gameplay then this one is a must-play. The battle system is a new spin on the classic formula and keeps combat exciting throughout. Easily kept me hooked for the 20-hour playthrough. You can tell there was a lot of care and attention that went to designing the combat in Cosmic Star Heroine, and that resulted in a system that goes toe-to-toe with classics like Chrono Trigger, and is arguably even more engaging and rewarding.
The ability to save anywhere and change the difficulty at any time is also a big plus, along with all characters gaining 100% EXP to encourage swapping, everyone being healed at the end of battle, rechargeable items that you can actually use without feeling like you need to hoard them, and a lot of quality-of-life improvements over other JRPGs.
However, if not having an amazing story is a dealbreaker for you, you might want to give Cosmic Star Heroine a pass. Like with other Zeboyd games, while the world and setting are interesting, there isn't very much dialog or exposition compared to other JRPGs so you likely won't get invested in the characters or the story.
Edit: Also worth mentioning that the highest difficulty "Super Spy" is much harder than the other difficulties and is designed to be played on your second playthrough if you're looking for a tough challenge. This gives Cosmic Star Heroine replay value as this difficulty will test even those who have mastery of the game mechanics.

Cosmic Star Heroine does several things right, starting with an original combat system that never feels like a grind and keeps the game feeling fresh throughout,  great artwork, character design, and music (from HyperDuck).  Story is solid, pulpy, save-the-world-sci-fi/fantasy that pays homage to its influences: 16-bit RPGs from the 90s like Chrono Trigger and Phantasy Star IV, as well as the gamut of popular sci-fi and video games from star Wars to Resident Evil.  The characters are memorable and the game doesn't take itself too seriously.
Some minor gripes: The inventory system is a little unwieldy.  It's often hard to know which item is going to be better for which character, especially when it comes to shields--there's a base stat, but then the shields sometime give awesome abilites to your characters.  You have to pay attention to more than just the stat to get the most out of equipment. I played the game on the Heroine difficulty and found it to be pretty rewarding--though I did feel like enemies were rolling over a bit by end-game.
Overall, I enjoyed this game more than anything I've played in quite some time.  Highly recommended.

If you are a collector of in game items, or achievements, this game is loaded with some time consuming ones or just plain hard ones --  Filling the bestiary with every monster in game.  Finding EVERY chest in game.  Leveling EVERY job to 99, on EVERY character. With a few thrown in for really rare boss monsters or weapons.  Plenty of easy, fun achievements as well, and nothing if skipped, that would ruin the full game experience.
I was very pleased with the game as a whole.  I didn't play anything else until I was done because it held my attention, and it was a wonderful throw back to a style in the RPG genre, that I for one, truly enjoy and love.  Well, WELL worth the time if this is your type of game.

It would be hard to rate this game negatively - it's really far from being bad.
But, sadly, unless you were present when it appeared, and experienced what news it brought into gaming, all you can see is an older game which plays *nicely*. Not fantastic, brilliant, just nice - it's new elements were used in the games coming after, becoming quite common. Half-life's value lies in it's gameplay and it's history, but mostly in it's history.
I remember playing HL in multiplayer during informatics class around '99-2000, but I couldn't experience the campaign. Though I remember that the lightning-gun, wasp-gun (both alien weapons), and the vast array of weapons, each with alternate fire mode left us all in awe - we played Quake 2 multiplayer before, and HL was a huge step forward.
Looking back to the game from 2016 (First game I played this year :) )  Half-life is a wild mixture of features that were great, features that could be improved upon and I couldn't really say a negative, besides the clunky bossfight.
The graphics aged quite well - as there are no cutscenes, you don't really need to check characters from up close to notice the bad lipsync. (Not to mention that Black Mesa apparently uses clone guards and a few cloned scientists, they are so alike :P ) - but for example the zombie of HL1 in my opinion is much, much creepier than HL2's if we compare their looks.
The sounds are great - footsteps can be heard and sound different on various materials. Also the 3D-sounds work incredibly well - with headphones you can pinpoint enemies by their sounds really accurately, and/or reacting fast for an incoming attack.
Weapon diversity is huge, and while I wanted to use the MP5 for the whole game, I was quite content to see that once there were no marines present who used the machine gun, I could find no more ammo for it - good point for story and world integrity.
Aaand speaking about the story - this is the point what I disliked about the game. I don't want to mention spoilers (Are there spoilers for a 18 year old game?) but the story basically consists of people telling you in A to go to B, and either you can directly go to B, or have to turn on/off some valves, doors, gates, enery to continue to B.  Many people says that this game is mysterious but that's only true because there is no world-building - you're Gordon Freeman, everyone's pawn and courier who runs forward, because he was told to do so, while the world is basically a corridor around you.  Not like it's a problem - afterall, game is from '98. While the story itself sounds really intresting if one's reading it, experience-wise basically I was shooting at everyone who wasn't wearing blue/labcoat and going forward... Maybe because of the constant first person gameplay (absolutely no cutscenes) I felt more like things there are just blocking me and are annoying than they were actually part of the story.
And to balance this, the story's parts I liked - mostly mechanics and ideas.
- The tentacle monster was a fantastic idea - disract with granades and sneak.
- I liked how the environment could change - like an airstrike near causes the window to shatter, opening a way to go instead of it being openable, or just straight-out open.
- Difficulty level changes more than damage and hp - enemy behaviour and attack patterns also change (to hell with Bethesda's harder -> bulletsponge difficulty scaling)
After finishing the game (LOTS of idling involved, both because chat and leaving computer) to be honest I don't feel like I played a legend. It was a good game that would have been absolutely fantastic if I play it ~15 years ago, but still holds up remarkably well, and posing more challenge on normal than Bioshock Infinite in 1999 mode (hardest) . Games definitely got easier. But it was good to see the game from start to it's end, and finally, it made me much more intrested in HL2 as I was :)

First of all this is more a review about the recent phase 2 update than the whole game.
I think the update changed so much into the negative that it deserved a seperate opinion.
The game as a whole is absolutley amazing, it is my first MOBA and i'm totally in love.
It's not like the other MOBA's you know and you might have played because ... F***ING SPACE BATTLES and what you see in the trailer up there is actually what you get in-game.
I played around 275 hours now and would give it a big thumbs up if there was not that recent update ...
With the recent Phase 2 update the dev's introduced a whole lot of new stuff, like more customization for your ships, revamped crewmembers and of course the implants.
Dont' get me wrong, i like new like stuff and adding more variety to the ships's loadout and how it play's is always great.
Now the stats on each crewmember have a much bigger impact and on top of that you can fit up to 3 implants to each crew (up to a total of 15 implants) to further change how the ship performs.
Now theres the problem: you just start of with 5 implants and if you don't have enough money, you're in a serious disadvantage to others.
Yeah you can buy them with credits but with the change to cut the credit-gain basiclly in half per match, there is long long grind to be even remotely competitive.
Before patch i made around 40k-60k a match on a win (with credit boosters) which is totally fine but now it's only around 25k.
So you can have to buy new ships which range from 110k to 924k each, crew pods which cost you 1,2mil for 10 pods and implants which puts you down another 1,2mil for 4 pods (each containing 5 implants).
And of course you can buy all of that with the premium currency ...
The amount of fun and enjoyment you get for playing does not compensate for the grind and the time you have to spent in actually making progress and i personally take a lot of that in advance and unlocking new stuff.
So for new players i would not recommend but you can always check back if something has changed and it is more enjoyable then now.
