Realm of the Made God is tough.  Especially if you aren't used to this kind of game.  It is an MMO with pixel graphics, a fairly active player base with quite a few servers, oh and perma death.  Did I mention that before?  No?  Well, that's a thing.  You start out with one class, the Wizard.  Play the game, and most likely die a lot, before eventually earning more classes.  The longer you live, the more...
"Fame makes a man take things over!  Fame, lets him loose, hard to swallow!  Fame, puts you there where things are hollow!  Fame!"
Sorry...the more fame you get.
Fame can be spent on a number of things, mostly related to pets and dungeons.  If you're just really bad, then head over to the EUWest2 server, and teleport to the fame train, where you will reach max level in only a few minutes if you are careful enough, and can stay to earn fame too.  As for combat, never stop moving.  Ever.  Bullet hell.  The only place it is safe to stand still and do nothing is Nexus, which if you're about to die is also a good place to teleport to to save yourself.
You have one attack skill, 4 equippable slots, a small inventory, possibly a spell or something, eventually you can find an egg and get a pet, and that's pretty much it.  No complex builds.  Just go out there, and get your butt kicked over and over.

Heat Signature Review!
A game that combines some of the best parts of older gems, and creates something completely refreshing.
If you like FTL... Good!
If you like Hotline Miami... Good!
If you like Spaceships, Guns, Bullet time slow-mo kill everything in the room within a second with a few choice pauses so you can grab that gun with your right hand that the guard you just killed with your short sword in your left hand, and now you can aim to put a bullet in the other guard across the room watching the whole thing before he can alertm, and call for secruity.
Enjoy a open-galaxy sandbox where the main focus is taking on missions with one of your randomly shuffeled characters that can of course be found throughout the galaxy at Bars which act as your Home base for all things. Throughout the game you complete missions, which in turn give you the ability to expand your rebellion, and take over new Bars which unlock more characters to join the shuffle of character choices, and unique story quests with set mission where if you complete it you get more items within the marketplace back at your Bars.
The action of the game itself involves accepting a range of different missions from Stealth extraction of a certain individual on the ship without being detected to making sure their are no witnesses while you murder everyone you come across on the randomly generated ships. After the acceptance of a mission you will be piloting your little one man ship, and zooming across space to find your target. Once found you simply find a latch point (While ships generally only start with one point to begin with you are able to destory sections of the ship once you learn how to start getting creative with your missions) how you go about getting your way from Point A on the ship to Point B is totally up to you.
Overall it's a pretty solid game that feels unique, and I'm glad I can add it to my list of games I need to complete.
If that sounds interesting to you. Check it out!

I waited to buy this game and so played Rogue first (I recommend playing in this order anyway as Unity begins where Rogue ended).  I think it was a good choice as I haven't experienced most of the game-breaking bugs that were apparent upon release.  I've played 30 hours so far and have only experienced one major bug: falling through the map during an air assassination attempt.  I'm running a Nvidia GTX970 with 8GB ram and 12GB VRAM, so that probably helps.  This game is without a doubt the most graphically beautiful of all the titles in this series.  I spent a good hour simply marveling at the graphical quality of the textures and environments.  I really like this game, as the story so far is good and there is TONS of stuff to do.  I think this is probably the best assassins creed since part 2.  That being said, there are still issues with the game:
The controls.  They are clunky, with the best comparison coming from the first Assassin's Creed game with Altair.  You want to do one thing, and Arno does another.  This gets frustrating quickly, especially when Arno randomly going in the opposite direction than you intended compromises your mission.  As many titles as there have been in the series, there's simply no excuse for how unresponsive Arno is.  I've played almost all titles in this series, and this one has the worst control responsiveness, by far.  This however doesn't render the game unplayable, just frustrating at times.  I've had a couple of nerdrage keyboard slamming moments as a result.
Lockpicking is unnecessarily hard.  I suppose this is a highly opinionated statement, but I really found that you can't master the timing, because the indicator activates somewhat randomly when you hit the space bar to trigger the pick.  This becomes less an issue with lockpick mastery upgrades, but I think they could have polished this system better.
Issues aside, I still recommend this game.  With the issues I read about from release, I don't think I could have recommended it then, but that's why I waited to play this game over six months after release.

I backed TerraTech on Kickstarter in early 2014 with the promises of multiplayer and have yet to see any follow through on those promises.  The kickstarter was funded in July of 2014, here I am 3 years later checking in with no updates. The most recent thing I could find online was the dev's Twitter post from August 2016 saying, "Yes! We will add multiplayer eventually, but for now we're focusing on the main campaign :)"
To quote their campaign: "Multiplayer is a big part of the TerraTech vision. Imagine building a giant flying mothership base with your friends, tracking an enemy to their base and planning an ambush. Or taking on your buddies in the challenge modes to see who can build the best vehicles for specific scenarios. Multiplayer action will appear in the game at full release."
The campaign had a stretch goal of £60k for ONLINE MULTIPLAYER that it did not reach but they were funded with £40k. The ONLINE MULTIPLAYER stretch goal stated "This is the #1 most requested feature, but it's a biggy. We're committed to doing it sooner or later, but if we hit this goal then we'll aim to get it in for our Early Access launch later this year, instead of waiting til the full release in 2015."
Never mind there not being a full release in 2015, or 2016, or 2017 (so far) but they haven't even added multiplayer yet. I was even gifted a free copy of the game in an email from the devs I think back in 2015 saying that multiplayer was coming soon and I should give the copy to a friend and get ready to play together. That copy is still sitting in my Steam inventory waiting for multiplayer to be added so I have a reason to hand it off to a friend.
At this point I am pretty certain the devs don't know how to implement multiplayer and figure if they just don't mention it for a very long time then everyone will forget, and we will. And then a few months later I'll be in my Steam inventory and I'll see that extra copy of the game reminding me of all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and I will come back again to see if anything has changed.
The game is fun but boring alone, I'll edit my review if any of the lie winds up being undone by multiplayer as mentioned in the kickstarter campaign being added to the game but I'm no longer hopeful now that we are 3 years down the road.

XCOM 2 is the action packed sequel to Firaxis's 2012 reboot of the X-com franchise started by Micropose in 1994.
In XCOM 2, you have lost, the Alien's have taken over earth and set up their own government known as the ADVENT coalition. Now XCOM is on the run as a resistance group now fighting to free Earth from the Aliens and ADVENT.
Pros
Cons
Overall XCOM 2 keeps the same tactical feel of its predecessor while upping the stakes. The lack of resources and soldiers makes every loss feel more real. combine that with the fact that every map will look different and play out differently makes for unique missions that require on the spot planning. The added modding capacity means that there are many mods to explore and have fun with. however, due to the nature of the game, XCOM 2 falls where many others would as well. the randomness of percentages and the limmitations of coding mean that the game is not flawless however it is still a game that you would enjoy many times over.

I've been a Final Fantasy buff for nearly 2 decades and 3 was one of those elusive games I never got to play due to the original never making its way to the West.  Thankfully this has been changed and the game got a nice faithful remake.  All I can say is WOW - I do not know how this game avoided a Western release the first time around, it was fantastic.
All the making of a traditional FF world (4 Crystals, Warriors of Light, etc. etc.) - and with enough flair and uniqueness to quite distinguish it from basically every other FF game even into modern iterations (I really liked the idea of '2 worlds' one being a floating continent).
The Job system is awesome and offers a huge variety of choices but does promote some serious grinding if you're into switching around.  If you don't like to grind then chances are you will finish the game with the default classes (Warrior et al.)
Probably the biggest downside to the game is that it features the archaic 'only 3 spells per level' mechanism that existed in FF1 and 2 - this is further aggitated by the fact that the game is no longer limited to simply White and Black Magic - you also have to find room to put your Summons in one of those 3 precious slots per level.  However I can understand that the game is technically just a faithful remake, and the system is what it was when 3 released in Japan.
Storywise this really feels like an early FF - and by that I mean the story is trivial at best (same as I and II).  You could text mash the whole game and you'd likely find you like it just the same as long as you like FF/JRPGs.  That being said - it's not an issue of the story being "bad" so much as the story just didn't latch for me.
Graphically it isn't too bad - it stands somewhere around where 7 does graphically.  7 makes use of parallax backgrounds and imaging layers to give the impression of better 'graphics' for their environments - but when you look at the character models you can see the difference - especially in meshing.   FF7 has better environments, but FF3's character models' meshes and overall 3D details are better - textures are bit poop, but still better than FF7s in most cases.
All in all it was a positive experience and one day I'll probably play again just for the fun of it.

I never played DS or mobile versions, so I can not compare, but I spent some time in port of original version for PSX. PC version of the Final Fantasy III is certainly fun, and updated visuals and interface brings a lot to the game. As with all the old FF games, there is not much story to speak of, the game is all about dungeon crawling and although you have some dialog here or there, most of them are simple and do not distract from action. I would actually sometimes appreciate more dialog in game, because it is easy to get lost in game sometimes due to lack of pointers about where to go next. You also have only four characters for whole game and all of them are active whole game if present (and alive), so you do not need to worry about managing and leveling up too many of them at the same time, which is common in some later games in the series.
Combat is turn based, but you are not restricted by time during turns, which makes it more strategic than more recent games. From modern FF games it is most similar to FF 10, although with less options when comes to spells, items or other actions. Final Fantasy III also uses job system. It means you can change character classes between fights, and there is more than 20 of them. Downside of it is that there is separate level system for character and jobs and no experience points and levels earned in one job transfers to another. Therefore you need to train every job separately and some dungeons require you to use specific jobs, which unfortunately makes some of them essential and other practically useless. And yes, the game does have random battles so depending on your preferences you will probably either love this style or hate it.
Bugs in PC port of the game is something which is spelled pretty often in other reviews here. As for my own experience, I knew about the biggest of them from the start and did not encounter any other mentioned here, my playthrough was pretty smooth. So I would recommend to save often to several files be sure (you have 3 maximum), never to return to your first town and use the restoration fountains after you break the rock which seals you in the first area, and you should be fine. Of course, the graphic is old for today's standard and locked in 15 fps in battles, true. But you are not exactly playing game from 2016 here and the the game looks nice as the chosen design fits its style.
In the whole, Final Fantasy III is certainly worth playing for all FF fans. LIke me, you may easily find that you will enjoy it more than some more recent installments in the series. Only given the price and age of the game, it may be better to wait for some steam sale.

While it is a port of the DS remake, it has enough of the simplicity and that grindy flavor to hit the spot for that early Final Fantasy JRPG nostalgia (note: I've experienced no issues with the port).
Much of this is owed to the fact that this game is almost a verbatim remake, which reflects the restrictions of the ancient technology of 1990, when the game was first released. The redsign of the game was primarily only a visual & audio makeover (updated music, '3D' environments & sprites, etc). The gameplay and construction are almost identical to the original.
This means that there really isn't much at all to the story, and the characters are pretty much completely flat. So if you're expecting the rich development you'd find in the story and characters of the later installments in the series (pretty much any of them after this one), look elsewhere.
Further, the maps used in the original games have been retained here - and that includes the limitations in design, as  So, similar to the limited story, dialogue, and characters, you'll find that they're disappointingly simple.
While all the above might seem like a pile of complaints, it's actually not. What has been redone, has been redone well. The visuals are limited to that of a DS, however im finding that the music is really enjoyable. All in all, it's been a fun experience - just don't expect this to compare to the modern (high-budget) maserpieces that the Series produces.
Bottom line: if you're looking for a nostalgic feel with a bit of modern flavor, this just might hit the spot.

Overall, I thought this game was very good. The thing that really stood out to me though was that this game is just a lot of fun to play. Sure, there are much better free to play games such as "Planetside 2", but Planetside 2 doesn't quite have the 'charm' that Realm of the Mad God has. Pros: I really liked the perma death part of the game some may disagree and find it annoying, but I think it is good so that that game has a good challenge to it. The game is very fluid and doesn't lag; I play on usually 4-5 bars of internet and have a fairly good PC (6 GB RAM and an I7 2.4 GHZ processor for those who care). I have never encountered any bugs personally although my friend got instanly killed randomly somehow in Oryx's castle.  Cons: This game is very pay to win oriented I have found. Generally in order to get anything good or get any money to buy things you have to pay. The money pays for unlocking different classes and buying good items. That brings me to my next point; the item/looting system in the game is not very good (unless you pay) because I tended to get the same items over and over again as well as getting very underpowered items. The devs need to add in a wider variety of items into the game that can be found in the item sacks dropped by enemies. Also, I feel that this game was meant to play with friends . . . the problem with that is there are really not many functions to play with your friends. Yes, you can make a guild, but you have to have played for a very long time to create one. It would greatly increase the multiplayer party potential if they made it so that any level/money/fame character can create a guild. Overall, this game is very fun to play as it may not have the graphics of other free games like Planetside 2, but that is by far made up in the overally fun I've had playing this game. Yes, I would recommend this game. Overal though, don't expect yourself putting in over 50 hours because the game wears out after awhile though, but the game is free, takes only around 30 seconds to download hence only takes up around 250 mb of space (give or take a little I don't remember the exact amount) so what do you have to lose? I would highly recommend at least trying this game . . . if you don't like it, it isn't hard to uninstall. I would rate this game a 7/10.

It looks like a pretty simple and crudely illustrated game ... and it is.  But it is also a good amount of fun.  Build your tower based upon cards "dealt" to you each turn, cast spells that can be either offensive or defensive, and protect your tower (or dungeon) whilst attempting to destroy your enemy's.  The random nature of the cards results in hilariously great, balanced, or woefully awful hands that influence your construction and strategy each game differently; the tutorial could, perhaps, be a bit more in-depth to assist your learning curve, but once you get a handle on it the game moves briskly and has some surprising depth.  Single player doesn't appear to have any campaign besides just playing the AI over and over, and it suffers as a result.  Multiplayer can be a bit hit-or-miss (mostly miss, unfortunately, but through no fault of the devs) as there aren't a tremendous amount of players online at any given time.  With better graphics and a "larger" publisher this game would be much more highly reviewed than it is; as it stands now it is a very good yield of fun for the investment.  Recommended.

I don’t have any excuse for what I did. It was reckless, I admit. If anything, I had other things playing on my mind. The kids at home waiting. Nothing overly dramatic; just wanting to hang out. And it had been a long job, perhaps the stuff of legends. One last job before ‘retirement’. Although I doubt anyone really did retire in the game. I’m sure we just take on new identities and continue as before.
Anyway, the job, as I said, had been long. Bodies were strewn across many rooms. In some rooms there was blood caked on the walls from the explosions. Guards scattered in bits and pieces down adjoining corridors. I know this is what I do but some jobs are bloodier than others. And as I’ve aged, I’ve preferred non-lethal weapons on missions where keeping people alive was important. They are harder but, well, sleep comes more easily.
At some point someone set off the alarm and the pilot set a course for the nearest station. That pretty much signed his death warrant. I found and dispatched him without too much trouble. The ship was then adrift. Space is big. The chances of crashing into someone else are pretty low. You’re expecting me to follow with - ‘not low enough’ but no, this isn’t that story. Not today.
My target, Alphecca Starspelt was further along in a room of guards. He was a guard. A grenade I picked up along the way was pretty much my only option. They have a two second fuse which isn’t long enough for the targets to get away when thrown accurately, which I managed. Then that was it. Mission over. Except it was a long walk back to the pod. Assassins' Creed: Unity has great gameplay.  It has been improved in almost every way from other Assassin's Creed games in combat, character customization, a true stealth mode, etc.
There are many graphical glitches, though.  While it is beautiful, there is so much pop-in and stuttering that it is obvious the game wasn't fully optimized.  These graphics issues can also easily cause ridiculous bugs.  Another downside are the microtransactions, which have their place, and it isn't here.
I, unlike most, will still recommend this game.  Look past the bad design choices and graphics problems (and bugs, if you can), put Uplay in offline mode, and play it like any other Assassins' Creed game.  The gameplay is great, but it needs some toleration of a terribly unoptimized and buggy engine to be enjoyed.  I used to hate this game; I learned to look pst its flaws, however, and now I actually enjoy it.

Thanks to the folks over at Id Soft, the shooting mechancis are rock solid. It feels like a proper FPS, and that's a wonderful thing. Less emphasis on VATS, more emphasis on doing your own damage. I dig that a lot. Level design is, for the most part, really great too. Bethesda's level designers have always been on point, and this is no exception. Great work there. Also has to be the least buggy game on Bethesda's custom GameByro I've played, so kudos there as well
The rest... well, there's a lot, so I'm only going to hit on a few points. This game is more of a sequel to Borderlands than it is to Fallout. It's a shooter with lite RPG mechanics, and it's all about loot. There's almost no depth to this game at all, be it quests, mechanics, or consequences. The writing is atrocious and craps all over the lore for absolutely no payoff, and there's no reason to retcon the things that have been retconned except sheer laziness on part of the writers. The game doesn't change much at all once you reach higher levels, thanks to the removal of 90% of the RPG mechanics. You're doing the exact same thing you're doing at lv50 that you are at lv1 with almost no change.
You might be asking yourself "if you dislike this game so much, why do you have over 200 hours in it?" Well, the simple explanation is that I spent a lot of time afk. My actual number is closer to 120 hours, and a large portion of that was forcing myself to play it so I could get my money's worth.
When it's all said and done, Fallout 4 is a painfully mediocre game. The things it gets right are far outweighed by what it gets wrong, and that's not even including the paid mods scandal. My review is entirely based on the merit of the game itself.

Stardew Valley is the perfect game for your Harvest Moon (or, in my opinion, closer to Rune Factory) itch, and it does things even better than the titles it plays homage to.
There's no pressure in the game to expand or grow. On the contrary, you don't have to pay any attention to your farm, and focus on other activities like monster hunting or fishing. It grants a great deal of freedom to expand as quickly or as slowly as you want to. The characters within the game are interesting, and some are far more complex than you might expect, dealing with things like PTSD and depression.
The game's art style is quite relaxing and beautiful, with a rich variety of colors. There's no performance hiccups that I've experienced either.
There's also a rich modding community that I haven't even started exploring yet.
In all, a fantastic game for a PC based Harvest Moon title.

need to try this. Play on the third difficulty (the equivalent of hard mode, I think) for the perfect balance of challenging yet satisfying combat.
- I'm a little over halfway through the game now, and I'd like to make two crucial updates. I lauded the combat system as balanced and difficult if you played on the 3rd difficulty, but I'd like to say now that characters are nearing the end-game, battles are far less threatening and they've turned more into endurance competitions. Enemies have outrageous amounts of health and their damage does not increase proportionally (well, maybe it does, but your HP pools are larger and you have far more healing options later in the game, so survivability is pretty easy, even on hard mode). I'm not saying this is particularly bad, but it DOES feel like the balance toward the end of the game sort of loses itself. I find myself getting bored in battles because they take so damn long (luckily, there aren't recurring battles unless you choose specifically to grind from the menu). Boss battles are still fun, but normal battles feel like a chore. Secondly, the last half of the game seems to just be making massive jumps in the plot, making it more and more about the individual scenes and predicaments than the overall story. The first part of the game is paced far better. Again, this doesn't ruin a lot, but it does detract a little. If my overall score would have been around a 9/10 before, I'd give this about a 7.5 or 8 now. It's still very good, but (as with a lot of RPGs [Dying Light, anyone?]) the end-game balance doesn't hold up as well as the beginning. Still enjoying it overall, but it feels less flawless than the first 5-7hrs did.
I missed purchasing this back on PS4 when it originally released, thinking it looked pretty slick but heard about some launch issues. Decided to finally go out on a limb with what limited spending pool I had for the summer sales. I have to say, I am 110% impressed and thrilled with my decision.
I'm a bit tired of the retro RPG style, but provided that the games have good/fun writing, interesting/fun characters, and deep/fun combat (if you'll notice, I really just want to enjoy my trip, even if it isn't a profound one), I will make an exception for just about anything. I was pleasantly surprised with this game. I purchased it on the pretense that it looked cyberpunk-esque and the art direction was pretty dope, despite being mostly pixels. I can say that the combat system blew me away with how deep the strategy was, and they don't bother wasting your time before you're neck deep in JRPG strategy goodness.
After I discovered the Shin Megami Tensei JRPG series (mostly on PS2 and 3DS, totally worth your time [go pick up all of them on the PS3 PSN right now!]), it's been hard for me to really enjoy turn-based RPGs anymore, as SMT has an incredibly deep, challenging, and rewarding combat system. It's made it very difficult for me to enjoy turn-based RPGs that don't provide me a good challenge balance. For those not familiar, SMT is almost like the Dark Souls of turn-based games, with one caveat: if you abuse the strategic mechanics you're given, you can go toe to toe with the strongest enemies. It's all about exploiting enemy weaknesses, planning multiple turns ahead to maximize damage, and rarely ever comes down to just mashing your button through turns. Cosmic Star Heroin emulates this style perfectly.
As soon as I started the game, I immediately began on hard mode (I think it's called Cosmic Star difficulty maybe? It's the third of 4 difficulties; the fourth was recommended for NG+), assuming that easy and normal would be too much of a cakewalk. I can say now, after having played a fair amount of the game, that this 3rd difficulty option is PERFECT for people who want a challenge, but not bone-crushing difficulty. It's balanced so nicely that you are punished for not using every tool at your disposal, but if you DO take advantage of your abilities and the battle mechanics, then you are rewarded with a tough (but not TOO tough) and rewarding adventure.
Speaking of the story and characters, they are good fun. Nothing particularly too deep, but after the first mission, you dive headlong into a conspiracy story that is very fun to be along for the ride. The game oozes with flair and style (one particular club band performance scene sticks out as incredible awesome and badass, not only for the music, but in how it furthers the action during the performance). There's lots of customization to be had here. Nothing incredibly deep, mostly involving what items each of your characters have equipped (which changes which sub-abilities they can use in battle).
For the price, you absolutely cannot go wrong if you're a fan of a.) cyberpunk/dystopian settings and/or b.) challenging turn-based RPGs with unique mechanics (I highly recommend you try playing on hard first, and lower the difficulty if you just don't like planning your turns too far ahead).
I play just about every new (J)RPG I can get my hands on; I'm a huge RPG junkie, especially turn-based ones with heavy Japanese influence. This one has quickly become of my favorites in recent years. I really, really hope they'd consider making a series out of this game, though I don't know if they will, since they haven't bothered serializing anything else they've done yet. Maybe we'll get lucky with this one; I'd LOVE to see more adventures from the lovable cast of Cosmic Star Heroine.

So, first ever Steam review so please be nice!
As a long time FF fan, I picked FF3 up as a historical curiosity more than anything, and frankly, that's the only reason to play it.  Time hasn't been kind to it, and it remains a fairly trite roll through JPRG cliches of the last 20 years.
That's not to say it's without merit.  It's perfectably serviceable, it functions and controls well, looks fairly decent for a DS port, has interesting challenges and generally does everything it needs to satisfactorily.  If you're not looking for anything mind-blowing or deep then it's a pretty fun way to kill 20 hours or so.
However, it is incredibly straightforward.  There's none of the emotional depth we've come to associate with the FF series, the characters are droll to the point of non-existence, the plot a simple series of macguffin fetch quests.  The job system is superficially interesting, but obtuse and grind-heavy.  The world is twee and standard, filled with cut-and-paste towns devoid of charm or character.
Overall, if you're simply looking for a simple fun romp through JRPG tropes you could do a lot worse, but don't expect any more than that.  For more mature, deep or involving games, you should probably look elsewhere.

Overall, I thought this game was very good. The thing that really stood out to me though was that this game is just a lot of fun to play. Sure, there are much better free to play games such as "Planetside 2", but Planetside 2 doesn't quite have the 'charm' that Realm of the Mad God has. Pros: I really liked the perma death part of the game some may disagree and find it annoying, but I think it is good so that that game has a good challenge to it. The game is very fluid and doesn't lag; I play on usually 4-5 bars of internet and have a fairly good PC (6 GB RAM and an I7 2.4 GHZ processor for those who care). I have never encountered any bugs personally although my friend got instanly killed randomly somehow in Oryx's castle.  Cons: This game is very pay to win oriented I have found. Generally in order to get anything good or get any money to buy things you have to pay. The money pays for unlocking different classes and buying good items. That brings me to my next point; the item/looting system in the game is not very good (unless you pay) because I tended to get the same items over and over again as well as getting very underpowered items. The devs need to add in a wider variety of items into the game that can be found in the item sacks dropped by enemies. Also, I feel that this game was meant to play with friends . . . the problem with that is there are really not many functions to play with your friends. Yes, you can make a guild, but you have to have played for a very long time to create one. It would greatly increase the multiplayer party potential if they made it so that any level/money/fame character can create a guild. Overall, this game is very fun to play as it may not have the graphics of other free games like Planetside 2, but that is by far made up in the overally fun I've had playing this game. Yes, I would recommend this game. Overal though, don't expect yourself putting in over 50 hours because the game wears out after awhile though, but the game is free, takes only around 30 seconds to download hence only takes up around 250 mb of space (give or take a little I don't remember the exact amount) so what do you have to lose? I would highly recommend at least trying this game . . . if you don't like it, it isn't hard to uninstall. I would rate this game a 7/10.

As a fellow who poured a fair bit of blood, sweat, £'s and d@mn near 400 hours into this game, I find myself asking a singular question that I'm pretty sure that a lot of other folks have asked and prolly know the answer to: "Where did this game go so wrong?"
I had heard of this game when it left the open beta and hit steam, and I was pretty eager to try this game, with users touting it as "What cube world should have been" amongst other things. I beared through the absurdly long queue times ('till those got fixed, props to Trion for that) and a fair bit of fun grinding for stuff and unlocking classes with cubits, trying out the numerous classes and seeing which ones I liked and cranking up my mastery (which is up at around the 200's) by collecting all the numerous stuff to collect.
Challenges, I did not mind, these were just another part to the grind that I was familiar with. The shadow tower update replacing shadow arenas I also did not mind, as those breathed new life into a part of the game that needed some tweaking. And while there were some things about the game that were kinda P2W, it never got to a point where it was considered unreasonable.
Then came the "Heart Attack" Patch, which among other things made classes no longer unlockable with the earnable non-premium currency. This meant that you could only unlock classes via class coins (of which you could get five w/o money) or by paying money for credits. This aptly named patch was the deathblow to my involvement with the game in any meaningful way, but I still checked on forums and the like to see if there would be new and upcoming stuff that would compensate for such nonsense. However from what I've heard with the new expansion, it's only gotten worse, what with the gem bulls#i7 that the other prominent reviews can tell you all about.
I should have known that Trion would turn this once promising game into just another P2W moneysink out of greed, being seemingly incapable of listening to their community and doing things regardless of their say (a select few elites withstanding) in the matter.
So now here we are, in a previous year I would have agreed with some of the people who reviewed this in the past in saying that this was Cube World only better. But now, I feel like I owe Wolfram and his wife Sarah an honest apology, because at least they don't let rampant incompetence and belligerent greed run roughshod over what could have been a lovely little game.
Abandon all money, ye who enter here.

Dwarf Tower is an interesting cross between Scorched Earth, Dungeon Keeper, Rock-Paper-Scissors, Battleship, and probably a few others, all squished down into a quick fight that feels a bit like a hand of poker.
Gameplay: You and your opponent each build a tower and try to destroy the enemy tower. There are several phases, each played simultaneously with your opponent. To start you get "cards" to place in and on your tower. Examples include new structures like tower pieces, new rooms like libraries, or new spells or abilities like Lightning. The cards you get are random and this is where most of the luck in the game comes into play; if you get unlucky and don't draw a "firefighter" card for example, you can be in trouble. The next phases are Utility, Combat, and Repair, during which you get to use the corresponding ability types. Combat spells damage enemy tower parts and the goal is to destroy the enemy Archmage Chamber.
You can't see inside the enemy tower. This is the Battleship part of the game. With targeted spells you mostly have to guess where an opponent's rooms are based on the tower shape. For example, crystals and libraries are more effective the higher they are, so attacking the top of the tower is likely to hit one.
Games are short, sometimes only a few minutes, so it's not particularly frustrating to lose due to BS circumstances like if the enemy started with 2 dynamites and they both hit your Archmage. When the match ends, another one immediately starts. There's no delay or setup time. It feels more like dying in a deathmatch FPS and respawning right away.
The game isn't particularly polished or balanced, and it doesn't really explain how things work, but it's simple enough that that's okay. This is a lot of fun multiplayer. Definitely pick it up if you have a friend to play with, or just challenge random people online. Against the AI the game is a little too easy.

Heat Signature is a game where you use crazy gadgets, to do crazy things in order to complete crazy missions. In one mission alone, I killed guard #1, swapped places with guard #2 who then died from a bullet from guy #1, then ran past a trap that teleported guy #3 into the vacuum of space. Teleported into the room with the item I needed to steal, then teleported back to my pod.
Not every mission ends so well though. I've been sucked into space, suffocated, blown up, stunned, shot, and captured. Fortunately, that's not game over, because characters are replaced and some can be rescued. You can retire the characters that are truly heroic as well, and pass on some really good gear for future characters. There are other incentives to retire like not gaining as much progress because your character is literally so awesome it stops inspiring people.
Overall, I recommend this game. The dark humor, clever gadgets, and ability to solve problems (that you probably created) can make every mission feel unique. I've taken to having each character specialize in a certain playstyle, so at any time I have 4 different gear sets to accomodate the mission accordingly.

This is how you properly tap in to nostalgia
The comparison between Stardew Valley and Harvest Moon is inescapable, but this harkens more to old harvest moon (and story of seasons, for that matter) games. The game play in early Harvest Moon games was always clear land, farm, sell, get more tools to farm better, repeat.
This is what Stardew Valley has at it's core, and what more recent Harvest Moon games forgot. The game doesn't shackle you to a 1 hour tutorial in which you're forced to meet all of the villagers, talk to some magic harvest spirits, or learn about the history of the town.  You just get some seeds and start at it, making your farm whatever you want. Recent updates have pushed that idea even further as you now have a choice of specialty farm (Ex: Fishing farm that is mainly ponds)
If you do decide to interact with the characters, they have some suprising storylines as you become more familiar with them. Some are pretty plain, whereas some other characters have really big personal issues that you're exposed to. It makes the interactions actually worth something if you care to learn more.

You enjoy old-school turn-based RPG's and like Zeboyd Games' previous works for their depth of combat more so than the humour
A valiant title with stellar combat, but not-so-hot everything in-between.
Zeboyd Games have found a wonderful niche with their absurd humour; whether it's Cthulu being a hero or playful RPG nudges like potion descriptions reading "Revives characters, unless they died in a cut scene". But in taking a step back from ribbing RPG's to create a semi-serious one of their own; there is little left to fill the void the humour has left.
The combat is easily the game's best point (and possibly the most sophisticated of all their titles) - so if that's your main draw, this one is a must-have! It's incredibly well thought out and designed to detract as far away as possible from the "mash 'Attack' command" of ye olde days. It's a curious combination: You gain damage modifiers (known as 'style') from using different attacks, many of which are one-use before you need to spend a turn recharging them all, and every few turns you hit 'hyper' mode which confers double-damage. Whilst these mechanics might strike you as bizarre (if inorganic), what it creates is an incredible strategic depth: Requiring a pleasantly surprising amount of forward planning and adapting-on-the-fly. You have to set the stage for killer combos whilst leaving enough room for triage and damage control, so as not to paint yourself into a corner with 0 moves and everyone on low HP... the worst time to be forced onto the defensive. Oh to loudly curse and praise a game at the same time. It's aggressive and fast-paced, yet gives you enough breathing room to think - a winning combo in any turn-based title.
Even early on it's very elaborate... And where you're fully healed between combats, this means that most fights can come down to the wire, not just bosses. And bear in mind each character can have up to 8 moves
down the line (not including extra abilities conferred by their equipment), with 11 or so unique characters overall. So very much an oversized blimp of content to be had.
My gripe, however, is everything else. Where it's no longer an affectionate, yet silly, parody; the absurdity is gone. But nothing else rises to take its place, effectively leaving it one pizza-loving character away from a Saturday morning kids TV show: Playful and inoffensive, but equally rather flat and bog-standard. Kim Possible, it grudgingly ain't. Not an issue by itself, but I found the combat to be rather sparse. Considering its strength, it was unusual to be sprinting around winding paths only to have 1-2 encounters per screen, if that, to the point that I found myself
random encounters to break things up a bit. Very unusual where combat is easily the wholesome champion of the game but, for me, a bit too underutilised to be able to carry the game on its own. With double the encounters, I'd be all over this game in a heartbeat.
So not a bad title by any means, but equally nothing outstanding either, and certainly not a rival to the previous titles; a shame considering the brilliantly-designed combat system. It's ultimately great fights padded out with way too much fluffy downtime.

Years in the making by established devs, Cosmic Star Heroine fulfills the promises of the "love letter to Chrono Trigger" indie JRPG. CSH provided 20+ hours of entertainment for a near-100% completion on Heroine (hard) difficulty without grinding. The battle system shines especially, introducing tactical elements which turn normal encounters into puzzles, doubly so for boss battles. The able writing overcomes a fairly standard plot, and the main storyline engages the player through its varied settings, well-formed characters, and a credible plot twist; its pacing leaves comfortable room for exploration and side quests. The graphics do right by the classic 16-bit style, evident most notably in the character sprites as well as the cutscenes reminiscent of the Sega-CD era, The soundtrack complements the spy-noir-in-space genre, combining with the graphics as a harmonious whole.
For downsides, a persistent menu bug, which forced a hard reset every time it arose, tempered my enjoyment palpably by the game's end.  Besides the bug, the menu itself has some flaws. For instance, the equipment menu does not display which non-party member is carrying the shield you want to equip, and the abilities menu does not have a simple way to re-order abilities. Eleven potential members of a 4-member party were too many for a 20-hour RPG. I found two characters completely unusable by the second half of play. Even as I enjoyed discovering some powerful ability-chaining parties, sorting through dozens of individual abilities became overwhelming at times.
I can recommend Cosmic Star Heroine as a fun, challenging JRPG that engages the eyes, the ears, and the mind, and I consider it excellent value for its price.  I plan to replay at the hardest difficulty level in the future.

"I feel that this game is as complete as it can be. Sure some things could be better, but I don't think this needs anything added. This is the reason I think that there's no point for waiting a next installement."
This is a quote from my short review of Xcom: Enemy Unknown+Enemy Within about 2 years ago. And after playing XCOM 2 it still seems very relevant. XCOM 2 in it's own right is an excellent game, but if you've played EU/EW there's the slight problem of the games being too similar to each other. I for one wanted to revisit EU/EW but instead bought this to satisfy my craving. It ended up being a perfect answer yet it made me wonder constantly that was the upgrade worth the money.
I have not played other XCOM games than EU/EW and XCOM2, and therefore my review only concentrates on those two. Played both on veteran difficulty(saving allowed). Played XCOM2 only once, 48 hours on the clock at the time of completion.
If you haven't played XCOM at all, the basic idea of the game is that you have two game modes. You build your base and control your resources, that allow you to get better equipment for your soldiers. With those soldiers you go on missions, and those missions gives you different kinds of resrouces. If you fail on either part of the game, it gets more difficult on the other part too. So it's basically very similar to Total War series, in a sense that you have to do Campaign properly to survive battles and do battles properly to survive in the campaign. Although in this game the campaign is real time and the battles are turn-based and you cannot autoplay or skip either. More about the actual gameplay can be found from youtube.
I so much want to review this as a recommended game. Yet I cannot recite the major differences of the two since I cannot really remember anymore some of the features in the first one. Most of the features I praised in EU/EW I could praise them here too. The graphics are stylized and fit very well, the atmosphere is still there, the music there to support it, the gameplay is stellar with only few hicups here and there. But essentially you're paying premium for a slightly better game. I could still go and play EU/EW and enjoy it without feeling that I'm playing a much more inferior game. I couldn't think of any downgrades from the previous game so XCOM 2 is a better game than it's predecessor but it also costs more and demands more from hardware.
For me the biggest upgrade was the level design and how the new features helped playing the game. The biggest new features are the stealth ability, evacing and the increased amount of timed missions. The first leaves more windows open for better tactics while the latter two forces player to make suboptimal moves. The player is now more in control how he faces his enemies yet having a timer means that there is a constant pressure to do suboptimal moves to avoid problems in the later part of the mission. Evacing forces player to think other than just clearing the map. The endless amount of enemy soldiers mean that one might get overwhelmed if one stays too long in the mission area.
Thought I think the game is outstanding I must say one word of criticism that is completely a problem in my personal taste. The game is quite difficult. There is a possibility for losing the campaign, unlike in any other tactical game I have played. You might lose a mission so bad that you cannot recover in campaign screen let a lone in the following missions. This is a feature XCOM is famous of, very similar to quite many roguelikes. The difference here is that the campaign can last really long, took me 48 hours when trying to do(or see) everything. So essentially if you lose, it might be after 20-30 hours of gameplay. I loved playing FTL:Faster Than Light and trying again and again to complete it, ending up 23 hours and maybe 50 runs. But I cannot think of myself actually playing this on harder difficulties so that I would end up playing multiple campaigns and losing most of them. I know the reward is just the greater when there's victory after multiple defeats, but the time consumed is just too much. I must emphasize, this is not something I think as a design flaw but as a feature that doesn't please my personal taste. The campaigns don't vary enough for me to make me want to replay again and again.
The game offers 4 difficulties, but since those difficulties affect all aspects of the game, it's usually quite a step to up the ante. The game could really use more options in difficulties, so that players that enjoy challenge in missions could only crank up it in those rather than making everything harder.
But essentially it boils to the already mentioned features. The game is an excellent game, with quite unique setting and gameplay. Yet it is very similar to it's predecessor XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within. If you have already played the first one and crave no more similar XCOM, don't buy this. If you want more XCOM, you have to think if the minor, yet great, upgrades are worth the money.

There have been jigsaw puzzles on computers for as long as gaming has existed. However, they’ve always been a bit of a hard sell genre for me. While I love my fair share of puzzle games I’ve never understood why someone would sit at a desk or a television to complete a jigsaw puzzle. I get those who are willing to go out and purchase a hard copy version. My American Mom used to have a puzzle on the go all the time. Ultimately, they would be framed upon completion and another wall in her beautiful Vermont country home would be adorned with her hard work, sweat, and tears.
But to play a jigsaw puzzle game on the computer. Where’s the fun in that? Yet, time and again I’ve been in a position where I’ve had to review them. For starters, EnsenaSoft released a few of them onto Steam last year. I reviewed each of them. There was never anything inherently wrong with the games. There was nothing that I could pinpoint and suggest that the developers went wrong there.
Consequently, it generally boils down to the one facet that is always personal preference. I know what I personally find fun. I know what I don’t. I get told by a fraction of my readers what they find enjoyable and what they do not. It comes down to the fun factor. I’ll let you in on a little secret. In the past, some of my readers have asked me why I’m wasting my time reviewing a jigsaw puzzle game when I could be doing something ‘better.’ Put simply, jigsaw puzzles aren’t normally the cool kids on the block.
To put it simply, the team over at Kingdom Games approached me to run a small giveaway for their new game. Now, we’d done the same thing for them last year when we operated under the Steamified banner. Kronus wrote a review for their solid religious-themed Five: Guardians of David. I believe we did this before FIVE: Champions of Canaan was released. It may have been a small part of their marketing campaign.
Now, it wasn’t exactly that simple. To be more professional we have a quality standards policy in mind. Further, I don’t want to run anything that wouldn’t appeal to a portion of our fledgling community. I checked out what this one was all about and I immediately felt as though the devs had put together a game that was different than the other games that I had played.
For starters, a multiplayer score attack jigsaw puzzle game? Who knew that completing jigsaw puzzles could become a competitive sport? That aspect of the game had me intrigued and I thought that it would open the game up to a larger crowd. A crowd who could enjoy the competitive aspect as well as the obvious relaxing side of putting together the puzzles.
Arguably, the most important part of a jigsaw puzzle game is the presentation. This obviously includes the artwork and therefore the actual puzzles themselves. The library that Kingdom Games have arranged for the game is rather deep. It’s certainly deeper than most of the jigsaw games that I have played before.
However, I believe that most of the images come from the public domain. They’re also relatively common images. If you’re a regular media watcher then it’s quite likely that you’ve seen most of these images before. For example, there are plenty of images of American cities, of the Aurora Borealis, famous Earth photos from space, etc.
I was more than a little impressed with the lengthy soundtrack. There are over 5 hours of music featured within the game. That means you won’t be alt-tabbing to get to your playlist anytime soon!
In all, aside from my disappointment at the copious amounts of pictures that I’ve already seen before I’m reasonably satisfied with the game’s presentation.
Gameplay Mechanics
Well, it’s a jigsaw game. It should be self-explanatory and for the most part, it is. Everything works as intended.
I had a quick few games of the local multiplayer. Again, it worked and it was fun trying to out quick my opponent. But they, sadly, got bored rather quickly. However, they’re not the type to put real jigsaw puzzles together. Therefore, I wouldn’t put too much weight into it. In multiplayer, points are awarded for accuracy, speed, and strategic placement. A nice feature to the multiplayer is that you can turn off scoring mode and build co-operatively.
The points scoring scheme is continued into the single-player version of the game. You can also play casually. Thankfully, when putting together the larger puzzles a save function comes in handy.
It must be mentioned that you can choose your puzzle board background. You can have the image already there, you can play with an outline or you can have none. I would argue that this can change the difficulty except for one thing.
Now, I never found a way to turn it off and I tried several times, so if you can then I apologize. The single worst thing about the entire game is that the board highlights your piece when you have found the right spot. This is somewhat infuriating. It’s almost like the game has an always on cheat mode built into it. Well, no, that’s what it is like. Now, if there was an option to use it sparingly then I could understand. But it makes the game trivial and almost pointless. One of the greatest joys of putting together a jigsaw puzzle is the challenge. When it’s too easy the game may as well complete the puzzle for you.
Which takes me to Showcase mode. Thankfully, it is there but I wish it unlocked as you completed the puzzles. Reward me for spending time with your game. Yes, I know you have achievements and trading cards (for Steam users) and that’s all well and good but showcase mode could have been the real reward for players completing the game.
As mentioned, you have Steam achievements and trading cards. The game takes advantage of those and multiplayer functionality. However, a couple of tips for the developers. Please incorporate cross-platform multiplayer (if possible). Further, incorporate Steam leaderboards so that we can see who has the highest score on individual boards. That’d give your title some longevity and add to its competitive nature.
Something sure to get the ire of the PC Master Race enthusiasts among you, the game’s Steam store page claims that the Steam version of the game is ‘the ultimate screen saver for your console.’
Jigsaw puzzle video games are always going to fill a specific niche. With relatively simple mechanics most developers can pull them off without too much fuss. However, I do like the potential of the competitive play as it strikes me as being different.  The presentation is reasonable but nothing spectacular. The game works as is intended and has quite a lot of available artwork to put together.
However, the downsides to the game must be considered in the final verdict. Although the library of artwork is impressive the fact that there isn’t much content that is actually fresh is a significant downside. Furthermore, the mechanic that highlights where each piece should go when you hover over the spot takes away much of the challenge. That Is the often frustrating but rewarding component of putting together jigsaw puzzles.
Ultimately, Puzzle Showdown 4K is an adept puzzle game that certainly fits a niche but has some drawbacks that frustrate and annoy.

I remember seeing the kickstarter for Cosmic Star Heroine back in 2013 during the great crowdfunding gold rush – after so long I assumed it had gone the way of many such kickstarters, stuck in development hell before being quietly dropped, so it came as something of a shock when it quietly snuck onto the front page of steam without fanfare.
Zeboyd have been in the business for a surprisingly long time, and managed to get in and make a name for themselves before steam dropped its trousers and spunted a torrent of poorly made RPG maker games right into the grimacing faces of users everywhere. I actually played both Breath of Death VII and Cthulu Saves the World back on the XBox Indie channel – at that time an irreverent pixel art RPG was actually a refreshing change, if you can believe it.
Cosmic Star Heroine is NOT an RPG maker game – everything here has obviously been lovingly drawn, animated and built from scratch, and to lump it in with such low effort fare is to do it a massive disservice. The hand drawn art is uniformly excellent and the 80s cyberpunk sci fi aesthetic is spot on. Graphically it’s somewhat reminiscent of chrono trigger (with enemies visible on screen before engaging), though the universe and story feel closer to Phantasy Star (particularly IV).
The plot and characters are also very true to that era, for better or worse – every character is drawn with a very broad brush and development is minimal, though they are appealingly designed and memorable in their simplicity. The plot itself is fun bubblegum sci fi pap, and while it has exactly zero surprises in store for anyone who has watched a film (or indeed played a videogame) in the last 30 years its brisk pace stops the player getting bored. Even though it does nothing new, there’s something to be said for doing something old as well as it does.
Where the game really shines is its combat. Enemies do not repawn and as HP and items are restored after every combat, the game has no problem with going all out with even normal enemies. Every fight is serious and engaging, and on the recommended Heroine difficulty trying to muddle your way through will result in a quick and embarrassing demise. Buffs and status effects are incredibly important, and will often be the difference between life and death. Fights in old 16 bit RPGs often felt like a way to lengthen playtime without actually offering meaningful content, and I would be quite happy to never fight a random encounter ever again.
My only real complaint is the dearth of side content. It’s pretty clear that the devs wanted the core game finished and released after so long in development, and I don’t blame them. However it’s a shame that we couldn’t have a side quest for each of your companions to flesh them out a bit and explore the universe, which we rush over at breakneck pace. There are a few short optional dungeons, as well as a couple of hurriedly truncated side quests that open up at the end game but it’s clear that there was content cut for time. I wonder if it’s time for Zeboyd to expand a little, as the enormous time in development suggests that this might have been more than two guys could handle.
In conclusion, if you’re after a lovingly crafted RPG that harkens back to that wonderful late 16 bit era, Cosmic Star Heroine will absolutely scratch that itch and I wholeheartedly recommend it – for 11 quid it’s a steal, and the devs totally deserve your support.

Not only do these updates waste time, they often come with errors (which might be why they update it so often) that prevent you from playing the game. This is happening to me right now and is not the first time.
Errors include:
-Changing your version of the game to the wrong version and preventing you from playing.
-Telling you that you need to 'verify' your game which results in Steam downloading an old version of the game so that Glyph will download the new version of the game. (This means you re-download the whole game twice)

Its not just poked motivation that prompted me to write this long overdue review, but a need to promote a solid different type of game that you’re probably accustomed to. DD isn’t a hero’s game. There isn’t central character that you bring from the small farm who happens to be destined to save the world from an impending and timely forthcoming apocalypse.
DD gameplay is a great new take on dungeon crawlers wherein you cannot invest time into a single character or elite group. DD is about attrition of war by various areas of physical death to mental incapacity of your standing group of adventurers.  You recruit, train, adventure, equip your troops only to watch them die from the horrors of adventuring. As stressed as your character get, you too get stress from watching them die! Which, you only begin again to throw bodies into the meat grinder. How fun!
Artistically it’s a wonderfully stylized game that fits well DD’s darkness and hopelessness. The music, voiceover only adds the atmosphere the task you must futility try to overcome. UI controls are simple as easy to use, clear in what you need and can do. The limited space of needed supplies in dungeon and treasure attained is a tough but fun management task.
Overall, DD is a different type of game that’s fun, refreshing, and highly enjoying (after flipping your table). I highly recommend it to Lovecraft, dungeon crawling, grinding looking for a challenge. Definitely not for players seeking heroes destined to win the battle because… prophecy? Density?

So, this is a short review from a Sci-Fi and future fantasy fan.
Rating: 9/10
Fractured space is a free to play, teambased capital ship MOBA. Where you get to fly gigantic ships in a team with other 4 captains. In this game they put the emphasis on the teambased.
There are three types and three sizes of ships.
Defensive
Offensive
Support
Light, Medium, Heavy.
So if you really want to be the Vanguard on the battlefield, holding the ground, or charge into the enemies, snipe them from afar. Or help your allies, by boosting their engines, repairing them or controlling your enemies. There is enough for everyone.
Gamemodes, there are two of them right now. Conquest and Frontline.
In Conquest players want to get the upper hand and strike at the enemies base in the form of capturing objectives and jumping between sectors. Capturing Gamma can really turn the tables around.
On the other hand Frontline is as many can guess a frontline of the battlefield, where you get non-stop action battling your enemies head on.
Opposition, the only other game similar to Fractured Space right now is Dreadnought. I've played both of them but Fractured Space is a winner for me here. In Dreadnought player is able to take on multiple enemies at once and survive. But as I said earlier. FS is more about teamwork. Where you really need to work as a team to prevail. And that's what I really enjoy. Multiple capital ships heading towards victory.
On the other hand Dreadnought has some features that I really like that are absent in Fractured Space. For instance energy redirection. Here you have abilities that technically do the same, but that depends on the ship you have.
In Dreadnought you can always "Put more power to the shields" And stuff. But I can't see that working in FS anymore.

Honorable mention about FS: I really like the diversity of ships in this game. Some of them do feel similar to others. But there's a lot to choose from. You start with three ships. and there's 33 of them right now (Patch Phase 2).
And if you want to spend more time in this game. It is worth it to purchase the Armada pack for 37€. Which gives you all release ships (31, excluding the new ones, like Aegis and Centurion.) The price is well worth the fun you get out of this game.
Final verdict: Do you like teambased games, is fighting capital ships in epic space battles on your "To-Do" list? Then I'd really recommend this game to you.
TL:DR - If you've tried Dreadnought but want something that feels a little bit more unique, and authentic with more emphasis on teamplay. Then Fractured Space is for you.
On the OTHER HAND! I do not recommend this game for those who just really want fast paced combat with quick gameplay. Fractured Space is about strategical positioning, and thinking things through. One mistake can cost you everything here.

Starbound, hailed as Terraria 2.0 or Terraria in Space.
Edit:
I have waited with reviewing this game until they posted more updates, but have owned it since it was released to the public - and had 200+ hours within the first 2-3 months of the game being released, a lot of those due to mods, but the game is coming around now on its own as well, adding a lot of the features mods used to.
If you loved Terraria, you will love this, no questions asked, just get Starbound and play it. If you never played Terraria, well ask yourself this:
Does exploring space in your own spaceship, in a 2D pixelated universe sound amazing? Does building cool space-bases throughout various random planets sound fun? Does exploring the universe and digging to the planets cores sound daring enough for ya'? If that is the case, then Starbound might just  be for you.
While I will recommend this game, I do have some minor (and I STRESS "minor", because I do love Starbound) issues that I am not fond of. The developer of the game promised large updates frequently, however, since it released 1 year and 2 months ago, there has been approximately 4 "decent" updates to the game - which have added a proper amount of content to the game. Starbound still has quite a ways to go before it should be considered a full game. And while I understand the quarrels of coding and programming, the actual design part of adding new blocks, biomes, monsters (although monsters are plenty as it is), items, weapons, etc. is not that hard in a 2D pixel game, and some of the updates focused heavily on adding only these (a lot of cosmetic stuff like hats), with minor additions to other parts of the game.
And just to make a note, if that previous paragraph bummed anyone out too much - I will repeat, I do recommend this game, and in the first 2-3 months of the game being out I played 200+ hours with plenty of fun and shenanigans. And I am eagerly awaiting the day Starbound is released as a full game. Starbound has a great future, and definitely has a lot of hours worth of content now (which is more than most Early Access games), and additionally there is a plethora of mods that will give you even more play-time.
So yes, I would recommend Starbound in a heartbeat.
Plus, the Winter Update just added Llamas in Space!

A great game that requires you to really understand the limits of your ship.  Even if the opposing team is really rocking, MOBA elements still help introduce absolutely intense clutch moments.  Do not go into this expecting a 1 v 1 brawl all about who shoots first.
The downside is that the game has a lot of complex elements that requires 2-3 hours of play to get a feel for.  It would certainly feel "hard" in the first hour, but use that credit boost to slide toward a ship after the first couple games.  Take heed the difficulty ratings, since easy to medium ships are generally "good starter" ships, whereas hard and very hard ships require in depth understanding of mechanics and high awareness in pilot positioning.
The community is great, if you're new, most players would actually tell you where to go and ask you to take a supportive role.  Kills / Takedowns are shared, so by all means don't ever feel the need to "blitz in" to finish somebody off.
It's a great game where player chemistry, ship chemistry, and piloting chemistry all mixes well.  I honestly can't find a way to praise it enough.  Ship details are drawn on with a purpose, and the maps look stunning plus being very scalable on the Unreal 4 engine.
In the end, it doesn't feel "Pay to Win" at all.  What I think would help is allowing players to "give credits" to newer players to help them tune and jumpstart.

Tom Francios long awaited follow-up to "Gun-Point" is finally here and he's making up for it by putting us right into the gameplay! Without a long exposition and you will quickly find youself in gut "wrenching" galatic corridor brawls very quickly! Be warned though! Brute force isn't always the solution as the harder missions may require going in with a strategy, rather than winging it (or you can wing it, the choice is still yours)!
Each character has it's own backstory, which helps fill out the much expansive and nebulous galaxy! Harking back to nights spent around the table with friends, some paper, and rolling the dice, player's will find an interesting balance between traditional topdown gameplay and strategy. Each mission has it's own requirements and you may need certain equipment before boarding a ship and going all slap and dash on the deck!
Each mission is short and can be played in a few minutes, which is convient with a work/life schedule like mine. Likewise, I find the game both relaxing and focusing with the well choosen balance of music and ambient soundeffects. Visually the art direction feels like it's taken Blade Runner and put it into a top down platiform set in space.
Dying can be harsh (I suppose death is harsh.) You might suddenly find yourself starting back at the bottom and having to grind back to where you were before, but you learn from your mistakes! All in all, I highly recommend this game!

This game is a remake of the Final Fantasy III (which appeared 1990 for the NES). The remake was created for the Nintendo DS, and has some enhancements. I never had an NES, maybe it was just luck, because that way the game was quite crisp for me. The game has a lot of upgrades, as far as I remembered the NES game had graphics which could be compared to older RPGMaker games. This has been changed, also there is a lot more of actual interaction between the characters. And the Jobs (or Classes) have to be leveled seperately to the Skill Level. The game also has a lot of grinding, which is kind of a drawback in some times, but in this game grinding actually makes a lot of sense.

Well, this was an interesting experience. In a nutshell, this is Minecraft and Counter Strike minus all the fun. It is a very unoriginal idea for a game.
The main gameplay revolves around two teams fighting each other. There are many gamemodes, with the classic Deathmatch, a tank mode and a few others. Along with shooting the other team, you are given a certain ammount of blocks each life and you may place it around the map at your will.
The main problem with this game is that there is no fun to be had. We all enjoy shooting bad guys but this game manages to strip away all the fun in that. One of the main reasons why it isn't fun is that it is very repetitive. You spawn in, run around the map and shoot the enemies, die, and respawn. Games like TF2 and CS do the same, but those games make you feel intense, scared, and at times tactical. None of those feelings are to be had while playing this game.
Another problem is that the game is highly P2W. Without spending a penny, all you get is a standard submachine gun, a shovel, a pistol and some blocks. Against people who bought their weapons (yes, those people do exist), you almost literally have a 0% chance of surviving a shootout with them, even if all your bullets land on their head. Speaking of heads, you can buy armor in this game that will give you even more of an advantage against those who don't buy armor (once again, people do buy stuff in this game. Crazy, right?). So in all, if you don't buy anything in this game, you're pretty much screwed most of the time.
The biggest problem for me is that the game is just highly unoriginal. You place blocks on the map and you shoot guns at people, there is not a single original idea in this game. One of the crucial points in making your game appeal to people is to have original ideas, or at least innovate on old ones. Blockade fails to do either, while giving us a bland and unappealing game. The maps are dull and seem to lack any knowledge on good level design, the guns are very basic and the sounds are straight from some stock sound website, and the overall gameplay is bland and boring.
The only thing good about this game is that it controls fairly well. I've seen games with really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls, but Blockade isn't bad.
Overall, I do not reccommend this game. If you want a first person shooter game, get TF2, Planetside 2 or Tribes Ascend. If you want one in a Minecraft type setting, I'm pretty sure there has to be some popular mods for Minecraft.

Ah, Fallout 4. I could go back and forth for hours on whether or not this is a good game, what makes it good, and why I would or would not recommend it.
It's a... difficult experience, to really get into, as a Fallout fan. You needn't look far to see people complaining that it's "not fallout" or "dumbed down the RP" or what have you. As for me, I like to think Fallout 4 took a more subtle approach to the whole skill choice and consequence part of these games.
Where previous fallouts would result in different dialogue, quest rewards, karma rewards, or whatever else might happen, Fallout 4 foregoes most of these things in favour of a more practical reward. There is no karma system, which I personally approve of because it no longer feels like I'm being judged arbitrarily for actions I might consider good, or rewarded for actions I consider evil.
A lot of that consequence-failure arises from the introduction of a voiced protagonist. New Vegas had its share of bad voice-acting (see the Khan that hides up in the mountain close to Bitter Springs), but Fallout 4's voice acting brought with it a very unique, new problem; budgetting. Due to the limited time and money allocated to the game, it would seem that the developers had to cut quite a few corners in developing branching quest paths that actually led to anything interesting. Instead, we end up with a bland mix of inconsequential options that all are all uttered with the same lack of emotion we've come to expect from the rest of the game. It's sad, but alas, so be it.
So yeah, the voice acting ruins many of the things people love and cherish about Fallout. The same goes for the forced backstory of the character and the terrible writing in the main story overall. But, if you look behind that, I think Fallout 4 could've been a gem, and that's why I'm still recommending it. Not for what it is, but for what I believe you can make it be (with a willful ignorance, modding, and survival mode).
I hate Fallout 4's main story for always assuming that I care at all about finding my potato-faced son. I hate that it makes me jump through hoops to find a guy when previous games would just let me walk there immediately if I knew where to go (see the process of finding Dad in Fallout 3, when trapped in Tranquility Lane). I hate that weapon durability was removed and I seriously hate that the big bad institute's motivations are so poorly written I could've done better when I was 12.
That said, I love fallout 4's world. I love exploring it, and I love that they revamped power armor and integrated it in such a way that it completely revises how one can play the game. I love that the gunplay is actually on an acceptable level now (it was never much of a selling point for me). I love the way survival mode makes me rethink my decisions on death, not just make me throw myself at that oh-so-familiar brick wall to see which breaks, as per usual. I love (some of) the companions, and I love settlement-building (in survival; where it serves a purpose).
She's not perfect, but she's still a Fallout game, and I love her for it.

Having played through and completed all previous AC games, it was a given that I was going to pick up and play this game. After the timber-shivering fun provided by AC4, this has proved to be something of a let-down despite (or perhaps because of) returning to a more classic Assassin's Creed template.
Revolutionary Paris is a great setting, and the streets are more crowded than ever before. But there are so many things to do - It is impossible to see Paris on the game map through all the objectives and collectibles. And for what exactly? The Detective side-quests were a nice new addition but beyond that, they crowd out the map and drown out the plot.
The plot is standard fare for AC; shadowy figures, betrayals, and reversals but has its moments with some exciting set-pieces (setting fire to a grain silo, time-travelling through France). A welcome return is the ability to direct the assassination missions yourself. Run in and stab someone? Bribe a servant to leave a window open? Create a distraction with a cart of fireworks? Your choice.
I would finish by saying that this game is probably better than Assassin's Creed III - but it is just so damn buggy. Glitching and crashing all over the place. So very frustrating. If you are someone who must play every AC game, then nothing I say is going to stop you. If you're a fan but can wait, I would wait to see if AC Syndicate is any better first.

I backed Cosmic Star Heroine for the basic game tier and I have to say that it is a fun RPG in the vein of Phantasy Star and Lunar with a little dash of Chrono Trigger. The combat system is fast paced and fun and the game is chock-full of quality of life improvements such as no random encounters (Unless you go into the menu to spawn one), being able to save anywhere, being able to change the difficulty on the fly, the game sending you right back before the battle that killed you so you don’t lose any progress, and the fact that you don’t have to struggle with item management because you’re fully healed after every battle and items are infinite use that are usually locked to one use per battle unless you have a special ability. The game is also paced super well in the sense that you’re always progressing, no dungeon outstays its welcome. The art and music are also super good, really selling that mid 90’s JRPG aesthetic. The only real flaw I feel the game has is that the writing is weak. It’s not bad, but the writing is just merely serviceable, the plot is pretty stock JRPG and the characters are all pretty one-note. Considering how many indie and AA RPGs have come out with good/great writing in recent years it’s rather disappointing. Regardless if you’re looking for a new JRPG style RPG to play Cosmic Star Heroine will definitely deliver.
