An excellent throwback to the 16-bit era of JRPGs, Cosmic Star Heroine is witty, imaginative, beautiful and has an excellent in-depth battle system.
The vast majority of the bugs - including all the game-breaking bugs - that plagued the game's release and which you have probably read about on other reviews have now been ironed out and the game is very much perfectly playable.
The story is very good and sucks you right into the game. Without giving too much of the plot away, you play a secret agent that finds out that the organisation she works for isn't exactly squeaky-clean, and endevours on a mission to uncover their plans and save the system. The story never gets boring and there are plenty of plot twists to keep you interested. The only critique I can give on the story is that the characters you play are somewhat lacking in depth.
Speaking of characters, you get to control a total of 11 of them - a significant number in any RPG - all of which play very differently - and it's interesting to find out which characters synergise with each other the most when building a party.
The battle system is very unique. A lot of turn-based combat systems fall in the trap of allowing the player to just spam "attack" to win most of the battles, but this is not the case in this game. For the majority of abilities, when you use them, you can't use it again until you use a defend ability. This trait, coupled with the "Hyper" system, which doubles the potency of your abilities once every certain number of turns, forces you to plan ahead on what ability to use.
Perhaps the most interesting feature of the game, is that whenever an enemy knocks one of your character's HP below zero (which would normally knock them out in any other game), if a certain condition is met, that character can survive with negative HP! That said they will be able to use one move (which again its potency is doubled) and if that character's HP doesn't go back into the black, it's curtains for them. That gives the character an interesting dillemma: Heal that character up, or go out with a bang?
Think you can best your enemies in a long drawn-out battle of attrition? Think again. The longer the battle goes, the stronger your enemies become. The developers clearly know that long battles are boring, and by adding this mechanic, it forces the player to go on the offensive, rather than turtling through them.
In fact the only thing I can criticise about the battle system is that the difficulty is very spiky. You do get to choose from four difficulty levels which you can change at any point in the game, so if you do hit one of those spikes, you can reduce the difficulty to get through it (and also increase it if you feel the game is getting too easy).
In a nutshell, I really recommend this game. It is 20 hours of pure nostalgia and fun and definitely worth the money.

I couldn't really get into the previous Zeboyd Games (Cthlhu Saves the World and Breath of Death VII), mostly due to the battle mechanics not appealing to me, but I have to say, Cosmic Star Heroine is a massive step up from those titles in many ways, both mechanically and presentation-wise.
It's a nice little JRPG made to look and play like those old-school games we all used to love. The story is very cheesy and light-hearted for the most part, but as I can tell, it was done that way on purpose. The setting itself is very interesting and done well. Throughout the game we mostly get to visit 3 different planets, all with their own cultures, landscapes, and natives. There are 11 playable party members in total. Although I did feel that some of them didn't get enough screen time and development, they all had something interesting going for them, whether it's in their background or mechanically-wise.
I found the battles to be pretty fun and well-balanced for the most part. Each character has a large choice of skills that they learn throughout the game, but there is a tactical edge to it. You can only equip 8 skills at a time to them, so you have to choose the ones most fitting to your playstyle and for the area you're in. The battles are turn-based as you'd expect in most old-school JRPGs, but it has a few interesting mechanics, such as Style points, which increase for each character throughout the battle and make them stronger for the duration of that fight, as well as a hyper bar which charges up and empties as the battle goes on, meaning that characters will be stronger during specific turns and weaker during others, which means you need to use strategy and use your most powerful attacks during those turns when the hyper bar is full in order to get maximum impact.
The combat and gameplay can feel a bit repetitive unfortunately, in a sense that most dungeon areas just feel like you're going from A to B, and fighting any enemies on your way, occasionally taking a side-path towards a treasure chest. Coupled with the fact that some enemies in late game can have a bit too much HP and take a while to go down, can draw things out a bit. So at times it's easy to feel exhausted when playing for more than an hour at a time, but it's not a massive drawback really because you can always look for ways to make your strategy more efficient.
The game also allows saving whenever you want, so it respects your time and doesn't expect you to play for hours without a chance to save (unlike many other games which try to mimic the old JRPG formula).
The art style is absolutely charming and very suitable for a game like this, and the music is also phenomenal and helps to immerse the player. Really, the presentation is superb on all levels.
Overall I would say, don't expect a super deep story. It is quite cliche and cheesy for the most part, and so is most of the dialogue. And don't expect anything revolutionary. But you can expect a fun little JRPG that is nicely put together with a lot of attention to detail that should provide at least 10-15 hours of entertainment and nostalgia.

A great game that requires you to really understand the limits of your ship.  Even if the opposing team is really rocking, MOBA elements still help introduce absolutely intense clutch moments.  Do not go into this expecting a 1 v 1 brawl all about who shoots first.
The downside is that the game has a lot of complex elements that requires 2-3 hours of play to get a feel for.  It would certainly feel "hard" in the first hour, but use that credit boost to slide toward a ship after the first couple games.  Take heed the difficulty ratings, since easy to medium ships are generally "good starter" ships, whereas hard and very hard ships require in depth understanding of mechanics and high awareness in pilot positioning.
The community is great, if you're new, most players would actually tell you where to go and ask you to take a supportive role.  Kills / Takedowns are shared, so by all means don't ever feel the need to "blitz in" to finish somebody off.
It's a great game where player chemistry, ship chemistry, and piloting chemistry all mixes well.  I honestly can't find a way to praise it enough.  Ship details are drawn on with a purpose, and the maps look stunning plus being very scalable on the Unreal 4 engine.
In the end, it doesn't feel "Pay to Win" at all.  What I think would help is allowing players to "give credits" to newer players to help them tune and jumpstart.

"Isn't this just like Hotline Miami in space?" I'm surely far from the only gamer who have thought this exact sentence after diving in the world of interstellar assassinations, spy action, dash-or-die situations and numerous failures that Heat Signature has plenty to offer. Yet, there's a bit more to it than the core of splatting your adversaries and botching miserably while doing so. If it's a good or a bad thing, I'm not sure yet.
Added to frantic action is a cool automatic bullet time that slows the world around you and gives even a slow-reflex sloth like me some time to react and possibly save my skin. Then there's a pause-anytime feature that is also vital to plan and execute your improvised strategies. With Gadgets. Now, these are the real dressing of the cake and the one that inspires you to experiment new wild solutions to your problems that usually manifest themselves when you once again were a bit too ambitous in your schemes.
There are also some reservations. Although Heat Signature is not as merciless as it could've been, giving you opportunities to succeed in mission even after botching it, it's still there to kill and maim you. That ain't always fun. Although its procedural nature leaves you aplenty to play even if one or ten or hundred missions go wrong, it's a bit pain to hang around the ship you were about to capture when the clock ticks seconds away and you just KNOW it's futile to try anymore. Same goes for the character who got dumped bleeding in the airlock, gets saved and has only about six seconds to recuperate next time the same happens. Oh, and one totally ugly part are the timed missions - the clock starts ticking that instant you accept the mission and every second you need to fly towards the ship and dock in it (which can also be some less fun pain at times) eats away from the fun itself - how to pull this incredible suicide mission in.
There's also a kind of a subgame where you liberate the other stations, opening up more gear and special missions, and there's yet a personal mission to defeat with even one of my characters. These things keep me inetrested so far. Time will tell how many hours the game will give and still feel fun and fresh. When writing this I've stumbled and bumbled about 15 hours in and love it much of the time. Should you buy the game? Heck yes! The price ain't half bad from  such a unique and compelling roguelite.

Age of Empires 3 tries some new ideas to break the monotony of RTS classics.  I have not played any multiplayer, but have beaten the single player campaign of the original and expansions.  The story of the original is a good time, but the expansions aren't as interesting.  Play styles vary considerably between chosen "faction", especially in Asian Dynasties.
Positives
+Playing different "factions" provides a unique experience, especially across expansions.  Your play style has to adapt to new mechanics introduced by expansions.  Adds replayability and keeps the campaign fresh.
+Despite being quite different from AOE 2, has the completeness you'd expect from this franchise.  Game looks and sounds great while feeling complete.
+Less micromanaging your villagers.  Farms/plantations (gold) and even some "wood farms" allow you to set and forget villagers instead of having to worry about running out of mines/reseeding farms.  There are trade-offs for these "lazy" sources of resoures, but It's nice late game to not have to worry about it.
+Ships look cool.  Zoom in on em', they look impressive.
+Enjoyable difficulty curve.  I played most of this game on hard (I switched somewhere early in the original game) and it was challenging, but doable.  The cards helped.  You could make it harder by not using certain cards.
On the fence....
-/+Card system...this is the main difference been AOE III and other RTS games.  You have a 20-card deck that provides "shipments", which can be anything from a couple of villagers to a trickle of wood resources to an upgrade or unit not available otherwise.  It adds another layer of strategy and I didn't mind it too much on singe player, but not sure how it goes on multiplayer.  You definitely have to use it, or at least I did when I played on Hard difficulty.
Negatives
-Story isn't super gripping.  Most RTS games I've played, story is pretty weak, so maybe I'm picky.  The original AOE III campaign is enjoyable, I will say that. The acts tie together well.  It's not that the missions aren't fun or varied, just that the presentation is poor.  Characters don't really grow on you, and historical significance is only learned from reading (for the most part).  I understand why the expansions don't tie together and I'm ok with that, but yeah...not memorable.
If you enjoy RTS games, you will enjoy this one.  Not much to gripe about here.

As I set out on my mission to rescue a captive aboard a ship in a warzone I didn’t think too much of it. The last time I had done this things went smoothly enough and I ended up stealing the besieged ship and returning it home with barely a scratch on the paintwork. This time however my plans were to be foiled by the horribly beweaponed battlecruiser that would show up approximately ten seconds after I docked. I took out the first dozen or so guards easily enough thanks to my arsenal of massive shotguns and hammers but it seemed like every time I cleared a room of guards it exploded seconds after I left thanks to the enemy missiles mercilessly barraging the ship.
So I sped up my efforts, ignored the rest of the guards and made a dash for the prisoner. No sooner had I retrieved him and turned around to flee the ship than I discovered that the port I had docked at had exploded and my pod was nowhere to be found. I ran for the bridge of the ship hoping that perhaps if I took over I might be able to return fire and escape… only to arrive at the door of the bridge a second before it too exploded. It seemed that escape was no longer an option yet I continued to carry my prisoner and made my way to an empty room in the middle of the ship hoping (naively) that maybe the enemy would get tired of firing missiles at me once they had finished killing off all the crew and blowing up all essential systems. They didn’t. Just as I decided that my best option would be to jump into space and abandon the rapidly exploding ship the enemy was kind enough to do it for me by firing on the room beside me and sucking me out in the void.
Adrift in space and separated from my prisoner friend I used my remaining shotgun ammo to haphazardly propel myself to the airlock of the enemy ship trailing behind the exploding wreck. Just about making it before I ran out of oxygen and ammunition. Only as I entered the ship and paused to survey the situation did I discover that my pod was still in fact alive… albeit several kilometres away and spinning wildly. I remote piloted it back towards me, shot past the prisoner I was meant to be rescuing just in time to watch him die in the vacuum and docked at the same airlock I had entered. Where I was promptly sucked back into space for neglecting to actually exit the airlock before docking with it. As I picked myself up and returned to the ship for some hammer based vengeance on the crew I couldn’t help but think that if only I had acted a little faster I could have saved that lonely man drifting out in the void.
10/10 Would jump out an airlock with a shotgun again.
----------
In short: It’s a bit like Faster Than Light (with more forgiving roguelike elements) combined with any number of bullet hell shooters (with a more forgiving amount of bullets flying at you) combined with various stealth games (with, again, more forgiving stealth aspects). In shorter still: It’s just excellent.
I say forgiving because the guards don’t actually kill you, they just knock you out and throw you out an airlock and provided this hasn’t happened to you too many times before there’s usually ample time to collect yourself with your shuttle and just return to try again. Killing the guards is usually more about strategy and a bit of planning than pure mindless chaos (though things can quickly descend into that) and since you can simply pause and take a second to plan things through at any time it never feels too panicky or hectic. The time limits before you get captured after being detected on all but the hardest missions usually do little more than add some urgency and desperation in your bid to capture the ship.
Where things get interesting is when everything inevitably goes wrong and you find yourself doing ridiculous things to try and make it home alive. Unlike Faster Than Light however barely scraping your way through one mission doesn’t completely destroy the rest of your playthrough and you can get injured quite a lot before your character becomes too weak to face another spacing. The liberation missions are also so entertaining and challenging that it keeps you striving to unlock the next… like the one which starts you with two teleporters and no weapons on a ship full of shielded guards.
You can take easier missions and avoid the suicidal ones for casual play or just roam around the vastness of the galaxy looting random ships. This is what I did with my first character in hope of getting better equipped to deal with his personal mission but after a handful of poor choices his next spacing would be fatal so I ended up just stealing a smaller ship and ‘assassinating’ my target by blowing up his entire ship and watching him suffocate in space… which was satisfying.
Wait, you guys expect me to buy mods on this already shallow shell of a game?

This game is an excellent mix of action and puzzles. You will need items to work the puzzles out, and the bullet time/pause mechanics let you do action movie stuff straight out of something like Guardians of the Galaxy. I could see some of the smarter players killing whole groups of enemies without even using a weapon themselves, just the gadgets. The game is easy to play, somewhat difficult to master, and rewards thinking out of the box as well as preparing yourself for each mission.
At the same time, it does have some problems. The environments are too detailed and colourful compared to how much you can actually interact with them. For the most part, you will feel like you are playing 2000s flash games from Newgrounds. Also, the random character creator is fun, but does not lend itself to great plot depth. In a sense, it is a more forgiving X-Com: you can make your characters quite deadly through your own skill and by building up a respectable inventory of weapons and gadgets, and you can grow attached to them when they have quirky names like "Dorado Comfort" or "Angel Voidborn". However, the characters are pretty much expendable and their personal narrative is just one mission, after which you can retire them. It is not something atrocious or game-breaking, but it does lend itself to accusations of shallowness.
Should you buy this game?
Well, do you want to play a Guardians of the Galaxy/Matrix/Max Payne-in-Space badass?

Okay I get that Unity tanked at it's release due to massive performance issues, but if you look past the issues and give the game a go after they were able to patch most of the issues in recent updates I think it is a really good entry to the series. I know the majority may not agree with me, and I certainly am not trying to say that Ubisoft and everything they put out is perfect but as a die hard fan of the franchise since the beginning I have to say I was satisfied with the game. And I think it is important to note that they recognized that they messed up with the release of Unity and responded with an apology AND made the first DLC free, which contained a whole new sequence, a new city to explore, and a variety of weapons to use in the game and I think that that's wonderful.
As for the series itself I know many people are saying it is the same game over and over again, and I think that the Far Cry series may begin to suffer from that as well, but I can look past that. While each Assassin's creed game at it's core is pretty much the same, I feel like there is always enough of whatever is new in the game to keep me entertained. For instance Unity changed the combat again, it is the same mechanics but it is much harder than any other AC game before, you cannot take on an entire army of soldiers, you can comfortably take on around 2-3, any more gets really hard. (Unless you have the special sword at the end). Bottom line is, Ubisoft has given us quite the Franchise, a Franchise that can go in so many ways and directions, there are so many time periods left unexplored that have so much potential, and i want to see those periods explored and I want to see where the series goes, provided Ubisoft avoids the problems that they have had in the past.
In my honest opinion, I think that Ubisofts biggest problem is that they are supposedly always working on two AC games at once, one at Montreal's studio and one somewhere else (I forgot they have a lot of offices i think). And I think that causes dissorginization within the company and that they should relax, take there time, and put games out there more slowely so that they themselves have time to reflect on the feedback from the previous game. Bottom line is I am really hoping that Syndicate puts them back on the rise, and addresses all the complaints the fans have had up to this point. I hope the series stays succesful.

I'm a huge fan of the saga, my opinion about it might be seen as "particularly favorable" to the game and its developer, but trust me on that; it's not. I will be absolutely honest about the opinion and the idea the game gave me whilst I was playing it. That said, that's still MY opinion of the game and someone might find himself disagree on that.
"The Walking Dead" was my first game played by Telltale games, I started it being kinda wary about it as I was a huge fan of the TV series. I didn't know what to expect from it, also starring all different characters to the series itself.
And it was for the best. The way Telltale characterize their personal characters was astonishing! It took me just a little to understand that I was going to love the game and every choice I was put in front of made me realize I was right from my first impression.
Certainly the game is far from perfect, some choices doesn't really give you the impression that your opinion, your choices, really matters. But when it finally comes down to reap what you sow, you realize that the game actually change and adapt to your choices.
It's amazing how the developers make you feel like you are weaving the game plot, trying to be calm in front of some hard choices but ending up messing it because of how you feel about a certain character.
The game ends up playing with you as much as you play it, making you feel real emotions about the game plot itself as it builds up in unexpected ways.
So, once you complete it, you feel that emptiness of missing something, some new discoveries, you start missing the characters they gave you as they were real.
That's what THIS kind of game should leave you with. Questions, emotions.. and that impatiently waiting to know what else there's next.
So yeah, I definitely would suggest the game to those who are ready to be surprised and that have the spirit to merge their consciences to those of the characters they are going to relate with. After all this is a game where your emotions will strictly be related to the choices you will have to do. Enjoy the game folks!

Dinner Date is a cynical rejection of the twenty-first century's emphasis and assurance that choices matter and free will exists. I believe it has been mislabled and is more akin to the horror genre, as it puts the player in the most horrofying position imaginable: the unconfrontable and ever abstract subconscious. This is the game's greatest strength, but was only made so with an update the developer released after gamers complained that the game took two mouse clicks to "beat." He responded to this apparent criticism by removing that requirement altogether, making the experience an automatic self-completion, regardless of actions taken by the player. This is the genius of Dinner Date. No matter how involved or uninvolved you are with Julian's actions, the story continues. You are no longer a necessity to the game, merely an allegorical component. This is a sophisticated choice. Wake up, sheeple.
Voyeurs might have a special interest in the game, or fans of the film Being John Malkovich (which I am willing to bet was an influence). Despair and disillusionment are ripe in Dinner Date, even beyond the story, which I am intentionally omitting mention of beyond it being perhaps the most realistic date simulation I have ever played.
On the technical front, the sounds are wonderful. Specifically, Julian's voice-actor has just the right level of whining to make the character believable and still likeable enough. The original soundtrack is charming, and the editing and mixing of the item sounds are minimal and acceptable. The controls are what they need to be, and the graphics are very much on-par with 2011 indie releases. There's nothing more or less than what is necessary.
One will take from Dinner Date what one is capable of taking from it.

This game is getting a lot of hate that I personally don't think it deserves. Most of the negative reviews invlove the pvp , permadeath, graphics, and grinding, but it doesn't really deserve this hate.
PvP in this game is a little brutal. At first it might seem impossible to get anywhere as you get killed and lose all your stuff. This doesn't always happen though. You have to work hard to have a fun time with it, and you won't go anywhere very fast alone. I made a lot of friends in this game, and that really helped but for the most part I've been playing solo. Ten minutes into the game I had already become a seperate class from the newbies thanks to some help from the community. Then I got killed.
Contrary to some peoples belief though, you don't lose everything when you die. There is a system known as engraving that gives you a high chance to keep items for a fraction of the items price. On the not-so-rare occasion that you do drop an engraved item there is a lost and found built into the game. I remember rage-quitting once because I lost my best weapon and some armor to an orc. A day later I decided to try to build back up, but once I checked the lost-and-found I found all of my items that I had lost. If some Idiot happens to steal your items you can kill him the get your items back, and most people will help you with this.
Graphics are pretty low-quality but it doesn't need to be any better. Everything is easilly identifiable and stands out vibrantly (unless your blind I guess).
Finally the grinding aspect. It's pretty rough. Some items like the blu bee shield, or a long sword take a long time to agquire. Like most problems in this game however this is solved with the help of a few friends (or an idiot trying to con you for a cheap price). Trading is also built into the game and is rather simple. With a rather large amount of gold or about two hours killing the same boss, most items are easy to get.
Honestly most of the problems mentioned in negative reviews would be solved if the played for another hour or if they checked the frickin' wiki. Literally everything is on there and it makes this game soo much more fun.
In a way I hope that this game doesn't get really popular because the community right now is full of dedicated, kind people. If it were to gain enough traction for the devs to get the money they deserve all of the lazy pieces of crap would ruin it for everyone else. I do recomend you play this game but only if your'e willing to spend some time on it, and not resort to being like the pkers this game used to be home to.

A robust top-down MMORPG, fun for all ages. Each class has separate perks and items within the virtual world of Realm of the Mad God. Huge community, many servers and options for playability. You can level each class up to 20, then grow fame to earn special shop items after maxed at level 20. Cross platform MMO experience is enjoyable across OSX, PC and Java.
Now, the pay-to-win scheme. This scheme was slowly built up over time throughout updates and patches. The bottom line of Realm of the Mad God is the business model, which keeps players playing and helps the developers to keep up servers. However, the scheme implemented has been highly controversial among players and ruins the gameplay for hardcore-styled players. Considering the only way to actually achieve highly-degreed items and pets in order to beat higher level entities is to pay money for these things, is something which considerably ruined the experience of Realm of the Mad God since it's initial release.
The community in this game is what really throws off most players. Spambots hopping on every server and spamming their websites where you can cash out gold, which are mostly fake and utilize data-mining. Basically any form of communication or friendliness in the game is rare since the chat gets spammed with automatic messages from the game and spammers all over the place. Who wants to talk in a realm either, where they're likely going to die? Did I mention gold is the only way to have a decent inventory in the game and costs real-life money to actually get? The entire business model is probably no different from any other bad F2P game I've seen yet.
The inventory in the game feels pretty satisifying with white-bag drops and specialized hotbar items. One thing about this game's inventory is that absolutely every time you die(usually from unwillingly getting teleported to Oryx for the first time) you lose
item you had in your inventory. You can get around this by storing items in your vault, but guess what? You have to buy gold in order to unlock extra vault space.Latency on the servers is a pretty big issue considering the influx of players scattered everywhere, not to mention the spammers I previously talked about. Even trying to hop onto nexus is sometimes literally impossible with the long delays and occasional game freezing.
The originality and theme of this game is probably one of the dullest, and storyline doesn't seem to exist. Every quest is "kill the monster," and the overall relevancy is unsolid. Maps seem pretty unorganized, and grinding in the game is near possible since the EUWEST server, the server with most loot, is always full with people spam clicking for hours to get inside. Normal realms seem pretty lame with hardly any good things to do except walk all the way across the infinite map to kill 5-6 monsters here and there. Then when you get into the good dungeons/castles, you can't even really play without dying unless you pay for really good items. Basically, the whole point of the game in a nutshell is to spend 20+ hours grinding, doing the same quests over and over again, buying loot, then dying so you can do it all over again so the developers can crunch on your wallet.
Movements are really limited, and any form of transportation across the map is physically impossible. Teleporting is an option, but you'll either end up in Godlands and die or end up closer to spawn then you were before. Pretty much 70% of your time playing the game will be walking endlessly through mostly empty areas. There's no special things like duck, roll, sprint or jump. I understand it is a top-down, but that doesn't mean they can't add features to actually dodge your opponents rather than using nothing except WASD, which is pretty slow.

This was a hard call on the thumbs up/down decision. What pushed me over the edge to a pro vote is that the game is clearly a labor of love.
Basically, the game tries to modernize some of the golden days of SNES RPG'ing and doesn't quite pull it off as well as I had hoped. I see alot of people talking about the combat as a good change, but while it was initially fun, its kind of like a puzzle you solve once and then repeat over and over again. You are forced to change up party members frequently, which helps some, but then it's still just, figure out how they combo, slightly adjust for elemental weaknesses, wait until turn 'x' to do your damage, and then repeat. I respect attempts at keeping the 'spam the attack button' style of play at bay, but ultimtately this approach didn't feel much better than more traditional JRPG turn based combat.
The story seems pretty fluffy and more of an excuse for the character to go out and be awesome than a plot that really makes a lot of sense or pull the readers in. It made for some fun moments, but there was very little in the way of character development or interesting dialogue.
Some of the equipment ability choices were interesting, but some were very frustrating. In particular, the player hits a point in the game where the main character pretty much gets her piece of defensive gear, which is what dictates a lot of special abilities and bonuses, and she is stuck with it. Sure, you can take it off, but then you lose access to the entire combo system. The balance on abilities seemed iffy, with certain attacks being exponentially more powerful than others. There is a lot of damage buffing that gets a little micro-managey and ridiculous near the end.
If you have an old school RPG itch and don't feel like weeding through all the RPG maker junk, then this is a good investment for your time, especially since its only $15. Definitely an easy pick when a sale hits. Don't expect Chrono Trigger or Suikoden out of this game, because you will be disapointed, but it stands well on its own right.
An entertaining and interesting little game, worth your time if games that are different draw you in, or like the very mundane.

A beautiful sci-fi RPG with some unique combat mechanics. The developers have a ton of experience with making turn-based RPGs, and just like their previous games, they've managed to evolve the combat system and add in some unique, new twists.
I played on the 2nd hardest difficulty, Heroine, which I thought was perfect. There are no "random encounters" in CSH, meaning every fight in the game you have to manually trigger by walking up to the enemies in the world. In many instances you can actually sneak around them and avoid the fight entirely. I played by fighting everything I saw, and felt like the balance, credits, and XP gain were all fair. I didn't actively notice any "repeated" battles in the game, meaning there was always a different combination of enemies for every fight. Many battles are unique in that they are designed to test a certain skillset of your party. There's a ton of variety and a lot of new-ness as you play. There was one part of the game that went on a little too long, though.
Every battle in CSH starts your characters off with a clean slate. All of your party members are alive, at full health, with all abilities available to use. In a lot of ways this system is "more casual", but really I quite like it as it makes playing a lot less tedious, and you're never thrown into a fight that you aren't ready for. Victory requires defeating all enemies in a battle, while keeping at least one of your party members alive at the time of the last hit. Extra party members are "picked up" randomly during story missions, which will lock you into using them for a bit to get a feel for them. Each character played vastly differently, and by the end all unlocked a ton of unique abilities. I found myself changing up characters quite a bit throughout. Side-missions also can force a premade party on you, and then not swap back to what you had before, which is annoying!
Each party member comes with their own abilities (up to 8 equipped), which you can customize and unlock as they level up. There is no "AP" or "PP" system here, an ability can be used immediately, and then it will typically get greyed out. Some abilities can be used over and over, but otherwise your character will need to "Defend (Rest)" to spend a turn to reset their abilities. Some super strong abilities can only be used once in a battle, and cannot be reset. In addition to this, each party member can equip a shield item which gives them "Program" abilities that can typically only be used once in a battle for great effect. Lastly, you also have "Items" which can be used by any character, and can only be used once in a battle. This system works really well and gives you a ton of ways to play out a fight, and allows you to cover weak spots in your character/ability choices.
Most importantly, the combat system revolves around "Hyper" and "Style" bonuses for characters. When your Hyper meter is filled, your next ability will hit harder and be more effective. Style is a percentage that increases your damage up to 100%. Anything above 100% is only used for "Burst" abilities, which also caps out at 300%. At the difficulty that I played on, there are many harder battles where you really have to manage your ability rotations around these bonuses... failing to do so will often lead to fights going on for too long and your party wiping. At the beginning it's not very important to pay attention to them, but you can really see the difference when you do play around them. You cannot beat the game by mindlessly selecting abilities, or "repeatedly hitting A" like a lot of RPGs.
The last key aspect of combat is that your characters can take damage and go into negative health if they have over 50% style. This is called "Desperation" and is important to play around. In most RPGs, you'd have to use heal pre-emptively to make sure that the enemy's next hit wouldn't kill your character, which could end up being a waste, but at the very least will drop your DPS output. With desperation, they have one turn while in negative health before they die. This allows you to use a heal, or any other important ability to help your teammates before dying. A handful of fights I delivered the killing blow with my final character's last turn, which is an amazing feeling.
The graphics are great and the world is extremely detailed at every corner. In a lot of ways it feels like maybe too much effort was spent on the graphics, but it's appreciated. There are also simple animated cutscenes which was nice, but at times it looks like they used overly simple 3D models instead of true pixel art which sometimes gave off a "cheap" or "budget" look.
The soundtrack is superb, with my only gripe being one of the battle songs is used way too frequently. I noticed some variations in boss battles and such, but it would have been nice to have different battle music in different zones.
My gripes with the game mostly revolve around bugs and the user-interface! Sometimes your party members are too slow and dumb to keep up with you, causing some bizarre visual glitches, especially on elevators. When battles start, often they take forever to "get into position", which causes the fight to take 5-10 seconds longer to start than it should have.
The UI and HUD, while pretty, are awful to navigate, and suffer from some useability issues. Sometimes the UI won't load elements when customizing abilities, causing you to exit and re-enter the menu. When you have a huge list of abilities or items, you can't scroll to see them until you select an ability to swap out. When you do swap something out, the UI doesn't immediately update to indicate the change. Equipping items, or even trying to compare stats between items (even your equipped item!) is tedious and error-prone.
During combat, you need to select an ability that targets an enemy to see their HP, Description, and Weakness; if you select an ability that targets all enemies, you can't see any of that information! Likewise, buffs and bonuses are not displayed on your HUD from what I could see... so you will really have to keep track of what you used during the previous turn. They could have incorporated this information in the HUD somewhere.
I appreciated the characters and story in the game, but they weren't anything particularly amazing, and didn't seem to vary all that much in writing. Previous games from this developer had much more complex, fleshed out, and interesting writing. Some of it is likely because they went with a much more serious tone, with a lot less humor and puns. They did manage to include a ton cameos and homages to their previous games, however, which I enjoyed.
If you're a completionist, some things are obscurely hidden and can be missed. Many "collectables" can be missed and won't trigger unless you have a certain character in your current party. Some achievements may be unreachable if you missed them the first time around. If you don't have a backup save (near the end of the game), you miss the ability to do a LOT of things, as those areas are no longer accessible. A lot of side content is actually locked out of doing early, but also locked out later on. There's this weird SMALL-ISH section of game where all these things can be done, but you have no idea and are never told... you just have to randomly explore everything over again to trigger them... during a part of the game where the main part of the story is too intense to not continue.
Overall, I enjoyed the hell out of the game and it was a blast playing it over about 18 hours. I Kickstarted it a bit over 3.5 years ago, and it's been a hell of a wait. It was pretty rough around the edges for the first month of release, and could still use some more polishing. I really wish more time was spent on the UI and writing, especially at the expense of the already insanely beautiful graphics. I highly recommend the game, even if it isn't perfect. The combat can easily carry the game on its own if it needs to.

At first glance, Cosmic Star Heroine might look like just another clone in an endless series of attempts to revive the 8/16bit era JRPGs. As someone who's old enough to have actually played many of the originals not long after they were released, I believe I can offer some valuable insights, regarding whether or not Cosmic Star Heroine is anything like the games its creators named as their sources of inspiration, namely Phantasy Star and Chrono Trigger. While I've never played Chrono Trigger before, I have played both Phantasy Star 1 and Phantasy Star 4 multiple times, and I'd dare say I know those games very well.
So, is Cosmic Star Heroine anything like those games? Well, my short version of the answer is "Yes, it is
like them". But what exactly do I mean by that?
I mean that Cosmic Star Heroine, like many other such games, takes the main formula behind the old JRPGs and tries to make it work. Except unlike other such games, Cosmic Star Heroine does most of the things right. Specifically, it engages the player with an interesting and dynamic story, and doesn't rely just on the "magic formula" to do the work. Also, unlike other games, the story will pull you into the interesting part right from the beginning, so you don't end up yawning between scenes. Then again, this might also be seen as a drawback, as you don't get the freedom to explore and interact with the world on your own, as you could, for example, on either of the Phantasy Star games. So while being interesting and fast paced, the main story branch is also linear and fixed.
The battle system seems solid. While I might not even be halfway through the game, I get the feeling like the battles are complex enough to be interesting on one hand, but familiar, intuitive and make me feel right at home on the other. Characters seem to come and go, similar to what happens in Phantasy Star 4. This adds some depth both to the story and to the tactical aspect of the battles, since you end up having to learn each character's strengths and weakneses, so you can use their abilities to your advantage.
You can choose one of four difficulty levels, and you can change it freely along the game. I've been playing mostly on "Heroine", the third on the list, which is supposed to be a bit challenging (although not the hardest). Most of the battles are pretty easy for me, but twice already I had to lower the difficulty to "Agent", which is considered easy (yet not the easiest) so I could get past a couple of fights I considered very difficult. I believe those spikes in difficulty are quite extreme, and it's possible they'll be addressed by the devs during future patches, but since changing the difficulty level is as easy as pressing a button, it's not a real problem, and might even be an advantage for players looking for the extra challenge.
The soundtrack is really nice, and so are the graphics (pixels). There's nothing really ground breaking about those aspects of the game, but they're more than enough to help make everything believable. I admit I was a bit disappointed, as I was expecting at least some better looking cut-scenes and maybe some voice acting (maybe like the stuff from Vay or Lunar), but the game does seem to work well enough without  any of those.
All in all, Cosmic Star Heroine seems like a really good game, and one of the few from the recent years, in my humble opinion, to actually do justice to the old JRPGs.

It`s a little hard to talk about Cosmic Star Heroine because, while I recognize it as a good game, it could have been so much more.
I`ll start with the PROS:
- The Spritework is amazing. Even NPC's seem diverse and well animated. While talking to some NPC's, i felt their sprite could easily be used to star their own games. Monster design is also interesting and varied, and there are a few monsters you won`t even see unless you venture into optional areas.
-The soundtrack is also well done. I love the battle theme, it really got me pumped during the whole game.
-The gameplay mechanics are WONDERFUL. Really: AAA developers should take notes. I love the fact that wou can go all out in every battle and that each item and equipment you find change the game in really different ways. Each character feels unique and their abilities provide a wide range of viable tactics. I was amazed at how, sometimes you would get an ability which appeared to have no reason for existing and then, a feel levels later, another ability would provide interesting synergies and completely change the way you play the game. Finding these synergies was the main reason that kept me going until the end of the game In my opinion, mechanically, this game has surpassed Chrono Trigger.
Now for the CONS:
- The story and characters are PAPER THIN. REALLY. Sometimes, I even forgot that some characters in my party EXISTED. There are a lot of characters that join you, but none of them seem like real people. Most of their backstories are inexistant or could be summed up in a single sentence. They have no meaningful  relationships prior to joining your party, and sometimes join you for no reason at all. The world and cultures of the races that inhabit it are interesting, but you only get a glimpse of them.  I know that zeboyd doesn`t take their plots too seriously and, while the humor was funny at some parts, i feel the tone and general lack of detail of dialogue and plot were really detrimental to the whole experience. It was what kept this game form being truly GREAT.
- There are bugs, and they are irritating. I ran into a few freezes and controller issues. I also had an experience that, after getting the ultimate ability for a character, it did absolutely nothing.
TL;DR : Cosmic Star Heroine is a game worth playing. I never thought an RPG could get by without a strong story and characters, but it's solid mechanics, great music and spritework and amazing battle system proved me wrong. I can only imagine how great this game would have been with a stronger plot and proper character develpoment.

Disclaimer: I almost exclusively play MyCareer and MyPark so that's what my review is about. After finishing incredibly boring and distasteful first season (Spike Lee shenanigans), it turns into a pretty good game. Rebounding is seriously improved over the past few editions, and park is better balanced (still not perfect, of course, but at least it's not full of 7'3 people). Stat caps are serious business this time around, and they really help that balance. However, it does mean that you hit the wall pretty early in terms of progression and then it gets really slow afterwards. Graphics are really nice and the game works fine for me in 4k on a single 980ti (60 FPS, no hiccups). Bit of a downside is that MyCareer still doesn't offer proper challenge and balance at higher difficulties. For example on Superstar, my team will simply lose more games than on All-Star, but I am still able to average around triple double (31-11-9) on my All-Around SF in 2nd season. As I set out on my mission to rescue a captive aboard a ship in a warzone I didn’t think too much of it. The last time I had done this things went smoothly enough and I ended up stealing the besieged ship and returning it home with barely a scratch on the paintwork. This time however my plans were to be foiled by the horribly beweaponed battlecruiser that would show up approximately ten seconds after I docked. I took out the first dozen or so guards easily enough thanks to my arsenal of massive shotguns and hammers but it seemed like every time I cleared a room of guards it exploded seconds after I left thanks to the enemy missiles mercilessly barraging the ship.
So I sped up my efforts, ignored the rest of the guards and made a dash for the prisoner. No sooner had I retrieved him and turned around to flee the ship than I discovered that the port I had docked at had exploded and my pod was nowhere to be found. I ran for the bridge of the ship hoping that perhaps if I took over I might be able to return fire and escape… only to arrive at the door of the bridge a second before it too exploded. It seemed that escape was no longer an option yet I continued to carry my prisoner and made my way to an empty room in the middle of the ship hoping (naively) that maybe the enemy would get tired of firing missiles at me once they had finished killing off all the crew and blowing up all essential systems. They didn’t. Just as I decided that my best option would be to jump into space and abandon the rapidly exploding ship the enemy was kind enough to do it for me by firing on the room beside me and sucking me out in the void.
Adrift in space and separated from my prisoner friend I used my remaining shotgun ammo to haphazardly propel myself to the airlock of the enemy ship trailing behind the exploding wreck. Just about making it before I ran out of oxygen and ammunition. Only as I entered the ship and paused to survey the situation did I discover that my pod was still in fact alive… albeit several kilometres away and spinning wildly. I remote piloted it back towards me, shot past the prisoner I was meant to be rescuing just in time to watch him die in the vacuum and docked at the same airlock I had entered. Where I was promptly sucked back into space for neglecting to actually exit the airlock before docking with it. As I picked myself up and returned to the ship for some hammer based vengeance on the crew I couldn’t help but think that if only I had acted a little faster I could have saved that lonely man drifting out in the void.
10/10 Would jump out an airlock with a shotgun again.
----------
In short: It’s a bit like Faster Than Light (with more forgiving roguelike elements) combined with any number of bullet hell shooters (with a more forgiving amount of bullets flying at you) combined with various stealth games (with, again, more forgiving stealth aspects). In shorter still: It’s just excellent.
I say forgiving because the guards don’t actually kill you, they just knock you out and throw you out an airlock and provided this hasn’t happened to you too many times before there’s usually ample time to collect yourself with your shuttle and just return to try again. Killing the guards is usually more about strategy and a bit of planning than pure mindless chaos (though things can quickly descend into that) and since you can simply pause and take a second to plan things through at any time it never feels too panicky or hectic. The time limits before you get captured after being detected on all but the hardest missions usually do little more than add some urgency and desperation in your bid to capture the ship.
Where things get interesting is when everything inevitably goes wrong and you find yourself doing ridiculous things to try and make it home alive. Unlike Faster Than Light however barely scraping your way through one mission doesn’t completely destroy the rest of your playthrough and you can get injured quite a lot before your character becomes too weak to face another spacing. The liberation missions are also so entertaining and challenging that it keeps you striving to unlock the next… like the one which starts you with two teleporters and no weapons on a ship full of shielded guards.
You can take easier missions and avoid the suicidal ones for casual play or just roam around the vastness of the galaxy looting random ships. This is what I did with my first character in hope of getting better equipped to deal with his personal mission but after a handful of poor choices his next spacing would be fatal so I ended up just stealing a smaller ship and ‘assassinating’ my target by blowing up his entire ship and watching him suffocate in space… which was satisfying.

This game is an excellent mix of action and puzzles. You will need items to work the puzzles out, and the bullet time/pause mechanics let you do action movie stuff straight out of something like Guardians of the Galaxy. I could see some of the smarter players killing whole groups of enemies without even using a weapon themselves, just the gadgets. The game is easy to play, somewhat difficult to master, and rewards thinking out of the box as well as preparing yourself for each mission.
At the same time, it does have some problems. The environments are too detailed and colourful compared to how much you can actually interact with them. For the most part, you will feel like you are playing 2000s flash games from Newgrounds. Also, the random character creator is fun, but does not lend itself to great plot depth. In a sense, it is a more forgiving X-Com: you can make your characters quite deadly through your own skill and by building up a respectable inventory of weapons and gadgets, and you can grow attached to them when they have quirky names like "Dorado Comfort" or "Angel Voidborn". However, the characters are pretty much expendable and their personal narrative is just one mission, after which you can retire them. It is not something atrocious or game-breaking, but it does lend itself to accusations of shallowness.
Should you buy this game?

Fantastic game. Great kinetic feel, varied ways to take out guards and complete missions. There's something especially satisfying about the sounds, especially when breaking glass or knocking out an armoured enemy.
All the different gadgets can come in useful in different ways, and the game lets you make your own shortcuts in whatever inventive way you can come up with. Want to leap-frog all the way to your target by teleport-swapping yourself with each of the guards? You can do that if you've got enough swappers. Want to stealth your way through, using a long-range key replicator to steal the codes for each door? You can do that too.
Getting to the final missions requires you to liberate stations, which unlocks purchases at each station (although all gadgets and weapons can be found in missions through RNG pick-ups). If I have one complaint it's that it takes too long to unlock your final missions. Some of the station liberations don't unlock anything, and just seem to be there to increase the length of the game.
Special one-off defector missions with limited load-outs also don't add to your liberation count, and the characters who do them retire immediately upon completion.
But this is overall a great experience, one that makes you feel extremely clever when you manage to sneak all the way across a huge space ship without being spotted, thanks to your excellent timing and use of stealth-and-slipstream combos, and then extremely stupid when you realise you left your wrench at home and you can't get out through the window.

Good and simple game with simple art. The easiest way to explain it is, think battleship. Each round you got cards, which might be extension to make your tower bigger, rooms to put in the extensions, or spells to put in your library. Then if you have enough mana you can attack your opponent's tower acording to your spells (some spell might attack the tallest part of opponent's tower, some spell let you pick a room in your opponent's ground level), and if you manage to destroy their archmage room, you win.
Mind you, don't expect some sort of immersing strategy game. This is a timewaster mini game, like Gun Done, where you play 5 minutes per session when you're bored and have nothing better to do, but as with that game, it's done well enough with proper price (slightly higher priced, but the gameplay is more complex).
My criticism is that I wish there's better feedback on the attacks. But for the price, the gameplay and style is solid enough.

I'll start this off by saying that I've not experienced any gamebreaking bugs or crashes while playing on this machine.  Performance is wierdly inconsistent but is playable.  I can't speak to the experience that others will have.
With that out of the way, this is not a good XCOM game, it's a great game, truly fantastic, but it's not a good XCOM game.  That's okay though, the original UFO defense is one of, if not my favorite games of all time.  I own it on multiple platforms and play Openxcom to this day.
Where UFO defense was heavily minimalistic mechanically, with most actions following the same set of rules, XCOM 2 has a great variety of additional features.  This gives this game many more areas in which it can fail or seem unpolished, the complexity and volume of unique mechanics being staggering. This isn't always a bad thing, although balancing certain things equally becomes difficult.  This gives you a greater degree of control and customization as regards units, equipment, and tactics.  Your XCOM is very much your XCOM.  In UFO defense your XCOM had very much a mind of its own, soldiers wouldn't advance how you would like, the missions were unfair as♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the main objectives seemed to consciously evade you.
XCOM2 does not have that personality, but as a game it is far more "playable" than UFO Defense.  You don't need a master's degree in patience and risk management to finish it, and some degree of randomness is removed.  XCOM2 is a handcrafted experience, like a fine Oak table, whereas the original is like a very nice tree that decides to grow through your living room.
It is an excellent tactics and management game, perhaps the best of this generation.  I feel that it is almost a disservice to both games, UFO defense being the other, to link them.  This game is unique, well crafted, challenging, and playable.  I very much recommend it.

For someone that grew up on JRPGs but has been bored by the vast majority of them for the past decade, Cosmic Star Heroine is a breath of fresh air. That's not to say JRPGs were better a decade ago. No no, the problem is that they're about the same. The modern JRPG just hasn't evolved much (or at least in the right direction) in the past 10-15 years. Cosmic Star Heroine is one of the few JRPG style games that breaks the mold to deliver an original yet comfortable experience.
- Instead of taking hours to get the plot rolling, CSH starts immediately
- Instead of a slow pacing that moves like molasses, CSH never stalls with dead time or filler content to pump up their "hours of gameplay"
- Instead of derivative and unchallenging combat, Super Spy and Heroine difficulties in CSH require tactical planning up to several moves ahead to maximize efficiency
- Instead of hoarding consumables, CSH encourages their use because they replenish after each battle
- Instead of cliche anime characters, CSH delivers amusing meme-friendly characters (not super original, but not as overdone either)
- Instead of tons of trivial enemies before a boss, CSH only requires 5-10 unique set battles before a boss and offers optional grinding for those who like/need it
Now, CSH isn't perfect. The plot and characters aren't the most memorable. It's a fun ride, but it's not going to blow you away. Super Spy (hardest difficulty) is fun and fair 85-90% of the time but the other 10-15% lacks balance and requires perfect play without grinding. Luckily, the difficulty can be switched from the menu.
Unlike so many titles in the genre, I feel like the game respected my time. I'd rather play 15 hours of excellent content than 5 hours of excellent content with 35 hours of mediocre content. CSH sits squarely in the first camp so you need to ask yourself if you do too.
If you're like me and have fallen out of love with JRPGs, you should buy Cosmic Star Heroine.

I really wanted to love this game, and to an extent, I do. But not as much as I thought I would.
I fell in love with Cthulhu Saves The World when I played it many years ago, and again when I played it again a few months ago. The neat characters, the awesome music, the vibrant graphics, and the punchy humor were all high points, and the combat offered a new spin on Turn-Based-RPGs that I really grooved into. Cosmic Star Heroine promised to expand on all of that and more, and while I was too late to back it on Kickstarter, I closely followed its development and looked forward to its release.
It could be a good game, but right now it kinda isn't.
Most of the negative reviews for the game mention bugs and other interface issues. Those are present, yes, but to me the problems in CSH go a lot deeper. Let me lay a few of my biggest ones out right now:
-Wonky collision detection. The movement is one of the fundamental problems here, and it really hurts the experience at times. Alyssa controls pretty well for the most part, but there's one main problem: you can pass right through NPCs without touching them. This makes talking to moving NPCs a game of chase, since you can't just stand in front of them and "block" their movement so you can talk to them. Other times there will be corners that you can clearly cut across, but trying to go diagonally will only result in you hitting an invisible wall. And good luck trying to figure out which angle you need to approach a chest from in order to open it.
-Lackluster sound design. I'm not talking music, the music is pretty good (though the battle theme is a little too mellow at the start), but in actual sound effects. There are the standard sounds - the beeps of computers, the whooshing of doors opening, the pew-pews of lasers - but they all lack the sort of punch that really immerses players into the world. A super ultimate high-damage strike from Chahn's purification torch sounds exactly the same as a strike from her basic attack, and while I'm not asking that all attacks have their own unique sounds, I'd appreciate a little more variety in the sound effects. And that's when there even ARE sound effects - some attacks (like Arete's drone abilities) don't have sound effects altogether, and although the pixel art cutscenes are GORGEOUS, the lack of sound effects makes it feel less like watching Star Wars on the big screen and more like looking at a picture of a Star Wars scene on the office wall.
-Limited Party interactions. For me, a big part of CStW was the cast of characters you gathered, and how they interacted with one another. Umi was a lovestruck, hopelessly optimistic sweet little angel, which contrasted nicely with Cthulhu's over-the-top villainy and machismo. These were contrasted by October's melodrama and purple prose, which also provided a nice foil to Paws' straightforward, matter-of-fact way of speaking. All the characters were two-dimensional at best, but their dialogue and conversations with each other were a lot of fun, especially when the whole party got involved. (Seriously, go back and use the chat option in CStW constantly. You won't regret it!) CSH has a rather large and varied party, with serious characters (Psybe, Arete), silly characters (Finn, Clarke), sometimes-both-characters (Dave, Chahn) and objectively best characters (pretty much any scene involving Lauren or Sue). But the problem is that they never interact outside of story dialogue - you just never get that kind of banter outside of a few instances, and while some of them are pretty good, others not so much. I'm not asking for thousands of lines of unique dialogue for each party member in each specific situation - just more than what we have.
The rest of the game is pretty solid. The game is vibrant and colorful, with distinctive character designs and detailed environments. The combat is fun and full of strategizing, as you use debuffs and buffs while you wait until you're in hyper mode to bust out the damage-dealing abilities. The music is alright, if somewhat forgettable (save for Lauren's concert. I could listen to that all day...), and the dialogue is, at times, pretty funny. And it's even set in the same universe as Cthulhu Saves the World, so that's pretty cool.
But after following it for two and a half years, and paying more than ten times what I paid for CStW, it's pretty disappointing to play the game and come away with an indifferent "meh." Maybe I expected too much. Maybe I'm just being petty. But it just doesn't have the spark that made me fall in love with CStW. The magic, as it were, just isn't there, and that's the most heartbreaking thing about it.
Ah well. Maybe next time?

Simply put, it is a very well put together game…end of.
You start by simply hacking into insecure computers and retrieving trivial information, but by the end of it, your hacking into the most secure computer in the game, while the computer you are hacking is trying to eliminate your computer.
Each puzzle can be repetitive which could be a problem for some people, but I found that I really enjoyed those sorts of puzzles, especially hunting for passwords and hacking security. The only other negative I could possibly say is that when a tracer gets your computer’s IP in game, it displays a blue screen, which I initially thought was my actual computer crashing, which was a bit scary.
The story line is really well told and I thoroughly enjoyed it. While the one mission where you COULD euthanise a person (you do not have to accept this mission) was a bit touchy for some people, the rest of the missions flowed nicely, and the final mission was hard but enjoyable to the fullest. The ending was very well executed overall and a good finish to the game.
The soundtracks really complement the game and give the game a full immersive feeling, and I can really appreciate the artistic talent of the people who created them. Likewise, the art to go with it is equally as impressive, and the UI represents a hacker-like environment.
The game itself is surprising accurate to real life hacking, with all of the port numbers corresponding to real port numbers in modern computing as well as their respective protocol.
Overall, it is an easily amazing and fun game, and am glad there is DLC to go with this, as I simply cannot get enough of this game!

Has some legitimate improvements over 2k15. Would recommend based on my initial reactions.
MyGM/Franchise has re-introduced 3-way trades and made some minor changes to add to the realism (promises to the GM now have consequences, trades destroy chemistry, staff contracts are negotiated, etc.).
Gameplay feels tighter than in the past. Shooting is far more difficult, but that seems fair. The timing of button presses and appropriate spacing is now an aquired skill rather than automatic. Players respond better to inputs and the sense of control seems more legit.
Ernie and Shaq are back, but now Kenny joins them on the desk. Add in Barkley next year, and it'll be worth it just for the pre-game/haltime/post-game shows.
MyCareer is actually a lot of fun. There's a lot more interaction than in 2k15 in terms of what to do on off-days and how to earn Virtual Currency (VC). The "Spike Lee Joint" is completely unnecessary, but starting in year 2 the game takes a huge leap foward and it becomes a real improvement over last year's encarnation of the mode. I'd recommend skipping every cutscene and just flying through year 1 ASAP. If you want to see the movie later, it's made available in your second year. It's not awful if you're a fan of Spike Lee, it's just way too much if you want to actually play a game. The entire cutscene film is nearly 2 full hours in length. That's ridiculous for a sports game.
All in all, a legitimate improvement over 2k15. I've heard online play is a mess, but I stick to single player. If you're like me in that respect, give this a try.

Fantastic game. Great kinetic feel, varied ways to take out guards and complete missions. There's something especially satisfying about the sounds, especially when breaking glass or knocking out an armoured enemy.
All the different gadgets can come in useful in different ways, and the game lets you make your own shortcuts in whatever inventive way you can come up with. Want to leap-frog all the way to your target by teleport-swapping yourself with each of the guards? You can do that if you've got enough swappers. Want to stealth your way through, using a long-range key replicator to steal the codes for each door? You can do that too.
Getting to the final missions requires you to liberate stations, which unlocks purchases at each station (although all gadgets and weapons can be found in missions through RNG pick-ups). If I have one complaint it's that it takes too long to unlock your final missions. Some of the station liberations don't unlock anything, and just seem to be there to increase the length of the game.
Special one-off defector missions with limited load-outs also don't add to your liberation count, and the characters who do them retire immediately upon completion.
But this is overall a great experience, one that makes you feel extremely clever when you manage to sneak all the way across a huge space ship without being spotted, thanks to your excellent timing and use of stealth-and-slipstream combos, and then extremely stupid when you realise you left your wrench at home and you can't get out through the window.

Post-Giraffe Review:
Major improvements have been made since I originally bought into the Early Access hype train. Though I will forever feel sore about being burned early on, after the latest update Starbound is now worth your hard earned cash.
You'll have an infinite number of people who will tell you that this is just "Terraria in Space", so I'll deal with that claim first. Essentially it is. If you loved Terraria, Starbound is a great game to get into if you've already played the predecessor to death, though in it's current form it still has less content.
Pros:
+ The latest update made progression in this game much smoother than previous versions, and at this point I would argue progression in Starbound is better than in Terraria. The newly implemented quest system makes "What the hell am I supposed to do???" moments much less frequent than in Terraria. I only found myself looking things up in the wiki once I got to the endgame, which for a game this open, is excellent.
+ Space ships. The last time I played Starbound seriously, ship upgrades didn't exist, and I was infinitely disappointed. Your ship was uncomfortably small, and in a game where you jump from star system to star system, setting up a proper home on a single planet was incredibly inconvenient. Now that each race gets it's own set of ship expansions, you'll have all the room you'll want to set up a proper ship with all your favorite bells and whistles.
+ Character progression: Anyone who played Starbound in it's earlier versions knows what a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥the Matter Manipulator was. Now that it's upgradeable, you'll find yourself enjoying being able to land on a moon to gather fuel, and ripping it apart with your 4x4 square of absolute destruction. The tech upgrades are also rare to find on planets, making unlocking new Techs a real treat. However, the main quest line rewards you with a full set of these cards early, so even if you have awful luck, you'll still be able to zip around planets with ease.
Cons:
- Native wildlife is still RNG pokemon, with some environment specific variations. I'm not against the randomly generated wildlife, but there are too few meaningful combinations or types and attacks - the two characteristics that really matter when you're fighting an enemy.
- Towns and civilizations have very small impacts on the world. You'll occasionally run into an npc run village or facility, and they're fun additions early game, but after seeing the same village on 12 different planets, it gets BORING. There needs to be more variance in their generation. Why not have a densely populated city planet? Unique variations of race specific hubworlds? Give me something fun to explore and stumble upon, Chuckle Fish.
- Your choice of race has practically no significance. Floran, Avian, Human, Glitch, etc. It doesn't matter. You jump just as high as each other. Everyone runs the same speed. Race specific tech is just armor and weapon variations. The fish race can't breath underwater, Glitch can become poisoned, etc.
My general rule of thumb for games is that I should be able to get at least an hour of fun out of every dollar I spend on a game. At this point, I'd say Starbound has reached this threshold. However it still has so much room for improvement, but with this developers track record, I would like to restate what I said in my first review:
Only buy this game if you're 100% satisfied with it in it's CURRENT STATE.
Pre-Giraffe Review:
Starbound is the go to example for why you shouldn't buy into an Early Access game without being 100% satisfied with the game as is, and not what it "will be".
I bought into the hype. I tried real hard to enjoy it, and for a while I did under the assumption that the game would improve. It didn't. Don't buy into the hype.
Buy Terraria instead. Better world, better progression, better combat, and loads more content.

Yes, Ubisoft made a mistake and released a very poorly functional game riddled with bugs and performance issues moreso than the average game.
But these days - that's almost expected.
So when everyone else acted like it was a 'huge deal' and started raging about it, I just sat back and waited for the patches to roll in.
About a week ago (from posting this comment) I played through for the first time so I can give an honest review about the game itself and not how "terrible" it is because there's bugs.
Looking back on the game, I only have one complaint:  GUNS.  Yea - I know, in this time peroid guns existed and in a real-world scenario it would be much worse.  But this is a game.
I've never been frustrated more out of any Assassin's Creed game than this one when it comes to guns.
In Assassin's Creed 3, Black Flag and Rogue -  you could easily counter bullets by using human-body shields which caused every bullet to be shot and blocked whereas in Unity you're forced to dodge them manually.
The dodge mechanic in Unity expects you to know exactly when the shooter is going to shoot - and if there's more than one shooter you're practically screwed since their shots will be on different timers and you can only dodge one.
That along with keeping up with melee combat is just too much.
What makes it worse?  The shots practically one-hit you, forcing you to chug medicine down everytime you get in combat - that and it seems like the NPCs automatically resort to shooting at you if you're more than 5 feet away from them.
I wanted to use stealth gear, but was forced to armor up like some sort of medieval knight just so I could live through the bullet storms.
All-n'-all, guns aside, the game itself was pretty decent.
It felt a lot like Assassin's Creed 2 minus a few features.
The focus on multiplayer would probably be the reasoning for that, if they hadn't focused so much on multiplayer then the game would have probably been a lot better as a whole.

I honestly liked this game a lot, however it did have its glaring flaws (as do most Assassin's Creed games that are the first to utilize new engines). A lot of buzz was going around about how buggy this game was, but for me, it was very rare for me to experience and issues, and when I did, they were pretty minor. The graphics were pretty damn good compared to every other AC game aside from the render distance being pretty wonky at times. It seems a lot of people complained about this game not running well on their PC, but honestly, just disable ambient occlusion and anti-aliasing and set everything else to either high or very high. My computer never dropped below 60 fps when I disabled these two options and I never noticed a difference in the visual quality from doing so. For those who may be interested, I'm using an i5 cpu with an nvidia geforce GTX 770, so my pc isn't exactly a super tank, but it's definitely not bad either.
With that aside, the main plot of the game was decent enough, the mechanics were smooth as hell and it felt great climbing and fighting, but I felt the stealth was quite unforgiving and it seemed like no matter what you did most of the time, you were eventually going to get caught because of there being a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of guards that you can't kill without being spotted. I attempted to 100% this game, but I eventually gave up for two main reasons: some of the coop missions were batshit hard if you attempted them solo, and to be able to see where all of the collectibles, missions, etc. in the game are, you have to buy it with Helix points. You eventually earn all the Helix points you will need for finding all the objectives if you play the game, but no more than that. Once you earn them, you can't earn any more, and if you spent any of them on anything else, then you'll have to start all over if you don't want to purchase any Helix points. It's a very interesting Lego game with a lot of side quests and well designed levels. There are a few major flaws though.

Fractured Space is a unique twist on the long-known MOBA genre. Instead of controlling the character, a player takes the command of a massive capital space-ship for a classical 5v5 competetive combat match. Unlike other games in the genre, Fractured Space is more slow-paced and places larger emphasis on tactical decisions and teamwork, rather than sharp reflexes or farming.
There are no individual leveling or item shops - all the customization is performed prior to the actual gameplay, while dominating the match provides shared, but manageable advantage for your team. There are 30+ ships to choose from, each with its own tactical role and combat features, and knowing the strong and weak spots of the ship is an important part of achieving success. They all feature different weapons and abilities, that require variable aiming techniques, value judgement and timing to produce best results.
Most of all, Fractured Space rewards teamwork, quick tactical decision-making and cooperation. Simply flying into melee against multiple opponents will get you nowhere. Picking the proper engagement range and attitude can help you take advantage of enemy weak spots and amplify your own strengths. Sometimes its not wise to engage at all and its better to wait for assistance or sneak past to take over objectives instead. In the end, this is a game where victory is paramount, and means are secondary.
Fractured Space features wonderful visuals and solid sound effects, decent tutorial and practice modules, good GUI and a dynamic, bug-free gameplay with no pay-to-win aspects. The only thing that this game lack severely is you - the player base is very limited and always can help newcomers. If you're in favor of MOBA-genre games, but has greater affection for Sci-Fi style, definitely give this game a try.
