It goes without saying that this game deserves all the praise it gets. I haven't played that much yet, but I know enough to give some info to help out those wishing to start the game.
Some beginner tips:
1. DON'T buy a coop when the game tells you to. Buy a silo first and then a coop. Hay is expensive as ♥♥♥♥ and can ♥♥♥♥ you over when you really need that money for seeds. When you have a silo, you can silth grass to make hay for free.
2. Save a little bit of each of your crops. I saved a lot of parsnips early on becomes they are one of Pam's "Love" items and it's super easy to get her to a 10.
3. Fishing is a great money maker early on. On days that you find you have nothing to do and lots of energy, default to farming. One Youtuber proved that you could make 100k+ gold in the FIRST MONTH if you have a fishing focus. I wouldn't recommend only doing that though.
4. I was intimidated by the community center in my first playthrough so I didn't touch it til the end of fall. Big mistake, start that ASAP. Most of the items are easily grown.
5. Get as much money possible before the 14th of the first spring to buy a bunch of strawberries. Great money. Blueberries for Summer, Cranberries for Fall. BE SURE to not just get them, get a good vareity for the community center and for easy "love" gifts for the people. (Haley loves Sunflowers, Penny loves melons, Pam loves Parsnips, Shane and Lewis love hot peppers, Linus loves yams, etc... All these are easily farmable and you can farm these on the side and still make a profit using strawberries, blueberries, and cranberries.
6. REMEMBER BIRTHDAYS. If you give some a give they love on their birthday that's a free 3 hearts! That's the same as giving them the same gift 6+ times! I found the wiki helpful in the respect. I didn't have time to guess everyone's favorite things.
That's all I can think of right now. Hope this helps guys, and I hope you have as much fun with this game that I do!

Overall I like it but I really want to know why the game was delayed so long. I can understand delaying a game to take the time to fix bugs and make the game feature complete before release but that clearly wasn't the reason for this game. Luckily you can save any time and the bugs seem to mostly be the easily repeatable kind rather than random so they should be eventually fixed (but again the the game evidently wasn't delayed for testing). One bug was actually helpful, a weapon that is only supposed to auto-revive the user once per battle revived many times per battle enabling me to defeat some optional bosses at a lower level.
Like past games by Zeboyd Games, it's a retro style RPG with the tedious stuff removed: no random battles, no need to grind (unless you play on higher difficulties or want to take on the optional bosses earlier in the story), no need to restock items, no need to heal after battles, no need to avoid using your best abilities to conserve MP, etc. The story isn't amazing but it's not bad and there is some humor and references to other games and media including some cameos from past Zeboyd Games.
There were a few playable characters I wasn't a fan of and basically just used when I had to but for most of the game I had a party I liked (and even the characters I wasn't a fan of have abilities that can sometimes be useful). I'm not a fan of the limit on equiped abilities at a time (it would have been nice to keep revive abilities equiped but with limited slots I had to give them up for abilities I need more often), but at least it lets you customize your characters a bit and you can remove the abilities that don't suit your play style. I tend to focus an elemental attack abilities (most enemies have a weakness which is displayed when you select the enemy with a single target attack) so regular battles were a bit repetitive: unload elemental attacks, unload other strong attacks, recharge abilities and repeat if necessary. It was still enjoyable and I think I varied my tactics more than in past Zeboyd games so there is a bit of depth to the battle system but it's still fairly basic. On higher difficulties you'll need to plan a bit more and pay attention to things like Style and Hyper Mode so if you want simple battles pick the lower two difficulties and if you want more depth to the battle system pcik the higher two difficulties.
Despite the disappointing issues I still recommend it though I probably won't be getting the next game from Zeboyd Games at launch. I like their games but if they don't want to fix the issues before launch I'll just wait for a bigger discount.

After what seemed like an agonising wait for release, Cosmic Star Heroine finally arrived and it was, is, fantastic!
What really sells this game, other than the nostalgia trip, is the combination of gorgeous pixel art and magnificent soundtrack - both are absolutely top notch. The visuals harken back to the Super Nintendo days with the likes of Chrono Trigger (which the game is only too happy to take inspiration from) with detailed well-animated sprites, gorgeous backdrops, and expansive maps for exploration, all backed by a magnificent soundtrack by the Hyperduck Soundworks team. The soundtrack oozes 80s style with lashings of sax and character, especially the character specific themes and battle scores ^_^ Another great aspect is the battle system, which tries a new spin on classic turn-based combat by shaking up the way you fight, no more relying on simply mashing "attack" but by introducing an indepth strategic skill system that makes you change up the way you fight during your encounters. The aesthetics and gameplay style take a lot from the aforementioned Chrono Trigger, indeed I'd go as far as to say this captured the magic of CT far better than other titles like I Am Setsuna --- it certainly had a better soundtrack and more tactical battle system, that's for sure. The piano-only soundtrack to Setsuna was lovely to listen to, but grew increasingly tiring as the game went on, whereas the soundtrack in CSH never stopped being incredible. Another lovely aspect are the animated cutscene snippets interspersed throughout the game, reminiscent of classic Sega CD animations, that also bring to mind games like Flashback and Another World.
Sadly the story isn't exactly going to blow anyone away because, while it was serviceable, it didn't really seem to have any gravitas or sense of importance. The Big Bad never feels menacing or especially dangerous, and the story moves along at a pace that could be kindly labeled as brisk at best and outright supersonic at worst, with some characters that unfortunately don't seem to get fleshed out as much as you'd like. You're shuffled from scene to scene at breakneck speeds, with events happening at a rapid pace, leaving you feeling - at the end of it all - like you could be missing half the plot. There are several sidequests in the game but there's no in-game logbook or way of keeping track, and many of the sidequests you don't even *know* are sidequests, not to mention the fact that they don't trigger until much later in the game, so it all has an unfortunate feeling of being a slightly incohesive experience.
There is one bugbear though and, depending on whether you bought the game at launch or several weeks later, could either be a serious deal breaker or a complete non-issue; bugs. It's a sad truth that the game launched in a very strange state with numerous bugs, glitches, and quality of life issues rife throughout. I had this preordered for years and played it to death immediately on launch, I encountered *very* few issues - other than a sequence breaking glitch at the start - but reading the forum shows a significant number of people encountering problems. Luckily the developers, of the two-man team at Zeboyd, have been fantastic at listening to feedback and busting their backs as they worked to fix it. All the major, and minor, issues you see reported on the forum have seemingly been dealt with - going by patch logs - and they're still going! Still working, still listening to feedback and implementing changes. Zeboyd are incredible at that, really engaging with their fans and working to fix issues while other AAA studios ignore and deflect, and often leave their titles unfixed for weeks or months on end.
So yeah, there are issues with the game, but those issue are - in my opinion - outweighed by the pros. The stellar soundtrack, the gorgeous pixel art and mapping, enjoyable tactical challenging combat, and the overall wonderful trip down nostalgia lane that takes inspiration from classics but never comes across as insulting or cheap. Made by a two man team, two more for the soundtrack, and has a full on budget price tag yet goes toe to toe with other, larger, RPGs of the same style. If you ever enjoyed classic 16bit jRPGs, you cannot go wrong with this, and while there is the feeling that it could have maybe done with slightly longer in the oven - and a larger budget - it really is a great game worth playing :)
...... and hey, if Zeboyd ever decide to go back and make a "Cosmic Star Heroine Redux", with a more fleshed out story, more areas, more fights, more more more, I'd be up for that! \o/

It suffers from what all free-to-play MMOs eventually contract: a terminal case of pay2win. It happens so often, yet it's still incurable. I started playing Trove about a week after it was officially released, and immediately fell in love with it. It was the greatest MMO I'd played in years; it was what Cubeworld was SUPPOSED to be. It was off to a rocky start, but only because the servers were being overloaded; everybody loved the game so much. The devs were kind, responded to player feedback, and worked hard on the game. It was this way for a good while. A bit simple and grindy at times, but it had so much potential, tapped and untapped, that I was willing to stick around. I always loved the microtransaction model it had; you could purchase cosmetics and a few things to speed up progress, but playing free was more than viable and enjoyable. Eventually, however, I began to notice more and more things appearing in the shop for credit (real money) purchase. I was a bit uneasy, but decided to ignore it, as the F2P gameplay remained unchanged. Then Mantle of Power happened. I even pre-purchased it, because it sounded amazing; finally, something was being done about the mile-long inch-deep combat system, and the game was getting some much needed love. What we got was an abomination. Suddenly classes are pay-only and can no longer be bought for in-game currency. The difficulty tiers got completely flipped upside down. Unfamiliar devs were taking over, the old ones no longer seen. The entire gem system was a mess, and a thinly veiled attempt at turning the game down the Pay2Win road. I tried to like the update, I really did, but I knew this would be the end of it.
TL;DR: Trove started out as a great game, but turned down the P2W path. Not worth even starting at this point if you haven't already.

Cosmic Star Heroine may be influenced by classics like Chrono Trigger, Phantasy Star IV, and Suikoden - which admittedly is a great pitch by itself - but don't fool yourself into thinking it's a cheap cash-in on nostalgia. The game has amazingly detailed pixel art, clearly showing the years put into it, the soundtrack is top notch - not chiptunes, either, and the writing is excellent. The game's overall plot is serious and more than intriguing enough to keep you playing, if a bit melodramatic, but it can also be very funny: expect deadpan snarking, absurdity, oblique references to Hitchhiker's Guide and Star Wars, among others, and just general goofiness.
Then there's the battle system. It's by far the most well thought out and unique battle system I've seen in a JRPG, at least in a long time. In some ways it resembles Chrono Trigger, with battles taking place on the same screen as exploration. Beyond that, though, it's vastly different. Everyone recharges health after battle, there's no MP, and items can only be used once per battle, but recharge after. Each ability can be used once, but the defend command also recharges your abilities. This encourages you to try out every ability and use different strategies, and combined with some other features, really makes you plan ahead. Especially on high difficulties, battles feel like puzzles, not just "mash A to win".
Of course, the game does still have bugs and is a little rough around the edges, as it is just after launch, and from a tiny team, but if you can forgive the (mostly minor) issues, you'll have a great time. It's around 15-20 hours, which might be a con for some, but as long as you don't expect a 60 hour game, you'll find its fast pacing welcome.

Zeboyd Games returns with their most ambitious rpg yet!  Cosmic Space Heroine is a delightful throwback to the 16-bit generation of JRPGs with great pixel art, fun music and an all around fun battle system and adventure.
This game is Zeboyd's largest work so far with an adventure spanning multiple planets with a good amount of optional sidequests that you can find/unlock as the game progresses.  From old rusty factories to lush alien jungles, their is a great variety in locations that you'll visit.  It's not overburdened with stuff to do in each place but just enough to make you curious about checking the corners of the maps!
The combat is where the game really shines!  You can have up to 4 party members, each with their own 8 user-set abilities.  Each ability unless specified is a one time use so if you want to refresh it you have to defend.  Along with abilities there is the HYPER system where you gain a charge every turn and once your HYPER bar is filled your next attack will do extra damage (or heal will be stronger)!  It flows in well where you constantly look at the enemy type and check if you have any buffs or basic damage abilities to use as you charge up the HYPER bar then you use your strongest moves or combinations to burn down your enemies.
I enjoyed how the various "Shields" you equip both increase your basic stats as well as give additional once-per-battle moves called "Programs".  Depending on how you set your team up, one could be a dedicated elemental magic user, another a healer, or just a straight damage/debuffer.
The character designs are fantastic: Alien Bounty Hunters, Cyborg bugs, Robot funk dancers, and more will assist our protagonist Alyssa L'Salle in saving the galaxy!  Plus you have the option of finding new "recruits" or supporting characters to give you an extra boost in battle.
For a single playthrough I'd say it's around 16-20 hours depending on if you really want to grind 100%.
While I did experience a few bugs here and there like other reviewers have mentioned, the developers have been working hard at fixing them and releasing patches quite frequently so the few soft locks/sprite errors I had were completely fixed by the time I finished the game.

If you're easily bored skip to the ending part of the review, if you're intrested in a more in derail description of the good/bad aspects of the game read.
Prepare yourself, it's going to be a pretty long story time here because this is part of the reason why i fell in love with this game and still playing it now and reached 200 hours on it.
I remember seeing not too much time ago, when DD was still in early access, a youtuber had a serie on it so I thought I could try it aswell (i was captured by the looks, the gameplay and the difficulty....yeah I am a SoulsBorne fan so jokes aside let's keep going).
My first approach to the game there was no difficulty choise, you only had the one that now it's called Darkest which is the standard (now you have Radiant, an "easier" one for beginners, and Stygian, that is good if you want a challenge even harder then the standard game, and still 200 hours I "don't have the guts for it") so I started and my experience was really bad at first.
Most of my heroes died i found myself with only 4 heroes left alive within few weeks, I felt lost and mostly hated the game mechanics and ufrair RNG(i needed to blame something the truth is I was just bad and unexperienced), and most importantly the perma death system, once a hero is dead he's gone forever, so don't get too attached to them.
I always was, and still am a little sentimental, so used to create team with heroes that i always used to rename with a lot of care and "love", so you can imagine how i felt to see all of them die one by one.
After this experience i stopped playing for a long time, then an uptade showed up for the game so I decided to come back to it, cuz I felt I wanted to improve myself, to win the challenge the game was for me, even under my behaviour towards "being sentimental" in this kind of games (which is a bad thing if you still wonder why I'm still talking about this).
That was a turning point, no more feelings in the way, the heroes are just the way you use to get money and upgrade the hamlet, so they can be prepared for what awaits them in the deepest darkness of the dungeon, and if some of them die, it doesn't matter, it's part of the game.
It was the first time for me being this way, but it worked! I started improving day by day, I understood the mechanics perfectly, learned every enemy in every level, how to counter them, how to kill them! So my heroes would die only when I would be reckless and challenge my luck (Overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer and the narrator always reminds you that).
Finally that sense of satistaction, the improvement, then other uptades came, new mechanics, heroes and places to go (See the Crimson Court), always getting better and better.
So what I'm trying to say here, if you're up for a challenging game with roguelike elements, dark setting gorgeous art and high learning curve, this is the game for you.
The cons, if you don't like grinding (in the sense that to level up early heroes you need to do tons of quests to get heirlooms and money, then later in the game you can level up the stagecoach and get experienced recruits, so i would say this is both a pro and a con, because it's the core part of the game itself), if you were like i was, impatient and mad at the game for not being forgiving and you don't want to take the right time to learn avoid it (plain and simple).
To round things up, it's damn good game that I'm willing to play more and more, it's simple as concenpt itself, but it's really well made, i felt a little disappointed by the shieldbreaker DLC and really hope it won't end like those triple A games with 1000 micro dlcs, but that we get more awesome stuff like the Crimson Court and the flagellant, that really improve and complete the game.

Hacknet is a puzzling mystery game where you take on the role of a hacker who must contribute to the computing world of hackers by breaking into systems with the use of special programs, navigate and modify files and data in such systems, and complete tasks for other people on the behalf of your faction. The game features the usage of actual terminal commands and coding in order to navigate the complex game, forcing the player to learn and adapt to the usage of this code quickly in order to press forward in game. The ultimate goal of the player is to discover the fate of a mysterious, experienced hacker that goes by the name of 'Bit', who helps out the player at the beginning on the game, allowing them to get up on their feet and stand a fighting chance against the brutal world of code.
The game is a decent length. For a slow gamer who wishes to experience and explore, this game usually takes ~15 hours to complete. Some quick cookies may find that they can complete the main story in as little as 5 hours, however.
Whether I recommend this to every player or not is quite trivial. An almost definite prerequisite for playing this game is the excellent ability to problem solve, and the capability to explore. This game isn't for every player out there, as there is certainly the possibility of frustration and boredom when the player cannot figure out what direction they should take or how to correctly solve one of the many challenging puzzles the game has to offer. For those that love to code and adore solving complex, challenging problems, this game is definitely a buy. If you see the game on sale grab it real quick!

Final Fantasy III is an unrewarding grind with a so-simple-it's-convoluted story reminiscent of Kingdom Hearts'.  The story is about the balance between light and darkness--and the game lectures and reminds the player about this balance a few hundred times throughout, as New Age-plagued JRPGs often do.
Its gameplay is where it fails on virtually every level: Most of the jobs are useless, half the abilities in the game are bugged and simply don't work, and players will lose hours upon hours of progress due to a complete absence of in-dungeon save points.  You can only save on the world map, and some dungeons are 5+ hours long.
Even players who only desire a peek at the advent of Final Fantasy's Job System will be disappointed, as the game's combat shoehorns players into a select few jobs, rendering the remainder not only unusable, but boring and uninspired as well.  For example, over half of the game's jobs are mere upgrades to existing jobs, offering nothing of substance on a gameplay level.
The music and graphics are sometimes surprisingly good.
I recommend this game to hardcore completionists and to Final Fantasy XIV fans who want to see the origins of the "Crystal Tower" raid.  To anyone else: don't waste your time.  Final Fantasy III is just not good enough to justify the time investment.

Most games with an entire front page of meme reviews telling epic meme stories of the actual gameplay tend to be wastes of your time or describing a better game than you will play.
Not here, in fact, the best way to review Heat Signature is to look at those stories. Every aspect of the game is built to generate those. It is a very awkward design space and will not be for everyone, but if it clicks for you, it is incredibly addictive.
The basic gameplay loop is you take a mission to break into a ship, you fly there, break in, and attempt to get from the entrance to your objective with as little fuss as possible. This might mean you slow-mo shoot as many guards as you can, or creep through beating them unconscious with a wrench, or teleporting through with a cloaking device to try to avoid getting seen, and so on and so forth. The options you have are limited to what the guards are resistant to crossed with what tools you have randomly found, with the bare minimum always being how full the ship is of exploding rooms and windows to space.
The randomness of your options is key to the game. Death doesn't mean much, nor does failure. You are only good for about five successful missions MAXIMUM with any character before it is time to retire, so the fun of the game is in working your way up from basic gear through luck. You eventually unlock top tier gear at your shop, but having a reliable loadout is the opposite of fun. Heat Signature is about using a wrench and five types of teleporters you randomly scrounged up to take down an elite ship and then throwing the wrench out the window to leap into space with your goods. It isn't about having infinite armor piercing ammo and an infinite shield disruptor to clean ships like you're a heavily armed Roger Wilco.
That's what Heat Signature asks: That you stop caring about making optimal plays, that you try to break into ships you know you can't handle because it's a lot more fun that way./

Heat Signature is a fantastic game.
From the creator of Gunpoint, it's an interesting mix of roguelike and hotline miami with a dash of persistent gameworld thrown in.
There are a lot of fun elements sprinkled in but the "meat" of the game is completing various jobs with a variety of objectives and conditions.
Each character is generated with a personal mission that they work towards - upon death or capture you can pick up as another character within the world.
There's an interesting approach to persistence - you slowly liberate stations and unlock new weapons and mission types as you play in a given galaxy, which provides a drip feed of new mechanics to keep you on track.
The space physics are neat, and like in Gunpoint, there are a variety of interesting gadgets and gizmos to play with here.
Shooting a hole into space might suck a room full of guards into the cold abyss, but it could also be a last ditch escape in a time of need.
There are some "friends list multiplayer" mechanics reminiscient of the ones in Shadow of Mordor through steam integration including naming a weapon to dump into the world. One complaint I have with this feature is that the game doesn't mix up the random weapons enough to make finding a friend's custom weapon interesting - this feature would be better with borderlands-esque weapon RNG but that's not really the point of Heat Signature.
Heat Signature is a strong entry and it does a great job of plucking mechanics from many genres to create its own ecosystem. Strong recommendation.

--Misson variety - slightly improved from older AC games. You still have the "go to the place and kill the person" quests making up 50% of them, but the other 50% have changed a bit.
--Abilities - Arno can disguise himself, among a few other new features. You can unlock these skills by doing missions, which seems appropriate.

--Specializaion - You can now chose to specialize in Melee, Ranged, Stealth, or Health. You can also split between two or more specializations, if you want. Adds an interesting mechanic to the game where you only get better at what you want to get better at.
--Progression - the development from newbie to master assassin is much more pronounced in this game. I feel it adds to the immersion and helps the game feel more realistic.
--New Climbing System - you now have options for climb up, go fast, and run down. It would make chases and freerunning a lot easier, if it worked consistently. I put it in good only because I feel like it will be fantastic once the bugs are worked out.
--Graphics - Wow. It's really shiny.
The Bad:
-- PIRATE SHIP REMOVED  D=
--Many abilities have been taken out of the game. Double assasssinations no longer come standard, same for falling double assassinations. There are a plethora more, but they're mostly minor. Things like pickpocketing are no longer possible outside of missions, although the code clearly exists because it happens in missions. You can no longer whistle while hiding to attract guard attention. Stalking zones have been removed entirely. Health no longer regenerates, you need medicine now. There's more, but I can't remember off the top of my head. It's basically like returning to Altaïr's weaponset.
--Game world is considerably smaller. There's a tutorial city, and there's Paris. That's all.
--Arno still has a tendency to get stuck to furnature mid-chase.
--Constantly nags you to play online with some mongoloid who doesn't understand subtlely. Seriously ubisoft, it's a slow-paced game with heavy planning, did you think adding 1-3 wind-up monkeys to the mission would really be helpful?

--Really, really, *really* glitchy. I've had to restart entire missions multiple times because I was stuck in combat or being attacked by invisible gaurds or some other BS. I encountered around 2-4 glitches per hour of play time, including game-breaking things like invincible gaurds and non-functional menus.

--Completely unfinished - the new climbing system is glitchy as hell and gets stuck all the time, the new combat system is glichy as hell and randomly kills you, and basically everything else is also glitchy as hell. This game needed another year of development, and Ubisoft's management made the greedy decision to release it sooner. They're morons.
--No clear difficulty warnings - you can wander into a 5-diamond zone as a 1-diamond newbie, and you'll just get crushed over and over again by the guards. The only thing that tells you that you're in the wrong neighborhood is a 3-4 second popup that has the name of the suburb.
--Runined Rogue - AC:R worked fine on my system with little to no glitching, until after I ran Unity for the first time. Now I get clipping issues, animation glitches, and floating scenery. It makes no sense to me, but it's the truth.
--Arno has no personality - the progragonist in Rouge is incredibly - almost painfully - bland. Our motivation to complete the missons is... to complete the missons. That's about it.
--Shoehorned anachronistic sequences - I won't spoil too much, but there are parts where the time would not match Arno's. Those levels are terrible and break the immersion nearly as bad as the glitches.
The Ugly
--Rendering issues - ofen when you're looking around on a viewpoint, you'll see 6-7 buildings out of the 20 or so that have extremely low-quality textures. That wouldn't normaly be a problem, but when the rest of the game is so high-defiinition, it looks extremely out of place and ugly.
-- The default assassin outfit - Arno's initial assassin outfit looks fine from th front, but you barely ever see it from the front, only the back. It looks really ugly from the back.
--That's about it - AC:U is beautiful, wether or not it's a good game. Those two are just about the only ugly things in the game.
Overall, it's a bug's nest and not worth the money.

Now, I'm just going to sit here for a bit until you move the mouse into the right position for me to finish writing the rest of the review. I know that feels fruitless because you aren't helping dictate the outcome of the review in any way, but your time has already been wasted, so you might as well see what happens...
Seriously though, a game that focuses on story and character is fine, but the story and character have to be interesting and compelling. Eating bread and thinking about how much you must suck to get stood up?... Doesn't cut it. We have no agency in the game or story which makes the requirement of "pick up bread" and "pour yourself some wine" little more than a "click to read the next paragraph" button.
Conflict is the essence of drama, but the only conflict here will be the struggle to decide if the effort required is worth it to get your $3 back.

CSH is a really cool sci-fi/SPACE ADVENTURES IN SPACE JRPG. Which in itself is already pretty rad, considering fantasy seems to be standard fare for most JRPGs.
Anyway, it takes a lot of influence from games like Chrono Trigger. It's got a turn-based combat system, but with its own unique spin on it. There's the Style and Hyper mechanics; Style goes up as you use abilities and increases your damage the more you have of it, and Hyper is a gauge that builds up and gives you a huge damage buff when it's full.
But perhaps more notably is the way abilities work. There's no MP or Mana or anything. Instead, you use an ability, and then it gets disabled (unless it's marked as Reusable). In order to reuse your abilities, you have to defend, which refreshes all disabled abilities. This is really cool, because it actually incentivizes defending. All in all, you're basically saving your biggest hit for your Hyper turn, and making sure you plan out the turns that lead up to that accordingly.
The characters are all pretty likable and well written (well, except for a few that were kinda meh). There's humorous, snappy dialogue. The story is pretty simple (Bad Guy's doing the Bad Thing! Go stop them!), but well executed nonetheless.
There's four difficulty options, I played through on Heroine (equates to "Hard", I suppose). It felt pretty challenging without being overly punishing, which is what I expected. Kept me on my toes. The game did start to get kinda easy towards the end, but maybe that was because of the the party/ability loadout I was using. Hard to say! There's also the Super Spy difficulty, which I guess you could equate to "Insane". I didn't touch this one, but if you're really seeking something REALLY hard, give it a shot. Also, you can change the difficulty settings at any time in the menu.
CSH lets you save the game anywhere, which is super nice. It's a game that really respects your time, in that sense. The pacing is also pretty good, there's never really a moment of downtime or anything, it just keeps moving forward. My final clock-in time was about 17 hours, but I'd estimate 15 hours on average.
Also the music is nothing short of fantastic. It's SOOO good.
ANYWAY, CSH is a nice lil' indie JRPG that is certainly worth your time and money. It's not the Second Coming of Chrono Jesus like some people would have you believe, but it's definitely a good game regardless. Buy it!

Having played this for quite a while now, I'd recommend it, but it has some problems.
You see, at the start, it's pretty fun. You start ou small, get better stuff, get bigger missions, all great. But as soon as you go above "hard" missions, they jump from "medium" (what hard really is) to "what in the living f*ck is this, f*ck this game".
I think the main issue is that you have nothing that really works against shields. Shields are equipments many thoughter enemies have that reflect any kind of attack. They come in two variants: One is active as soon as they spotted you, which is fine, it just means if you have been spotted, you better run because forget fighting back, hide until they go back to neutral. The other variant is always on.
Now, there ARE ways to kill shields. There are two types of tools against them, one just turns them off and one inverts them so their own shots get reflected inwards, which is pretty sweet. The problem lies in the numbers. Even "high capacity" variants of those tools come with just 5 uses, and the time when you actually encounter those enemies, they're on huge ships with many guards meaning those 5 uses are gone pretty quickly with still plenty of shielded enemies around. (there are a few other ways, like blowing out a window next to them, but they aren't really applicable most of the time and means you also lose everything the guard holds, like keys)
There are two types of enemies, common and boss. that just means the boss ones got slightly better equipment and are a fifth in number. mostly just those got shields, but for the highest level difficulty missions I've seen yet, there are many where every enemy type has shields (and proximity sensors and so on).
Combine that with a pretty short time limit, armor (which you can only ever defeat once you unlocked armor piercing weapons, which is btw way too late, before that you have to just not do any of those missions), huge ships and plenty of guards and it's becoming pretty much impossible.
Some tools are rechargeable, which means they get filled up when you visit a friendly station. The one time I finished off a ship full of shields, I had a high capacity rechargeable, and pretty much killed 5 enemies, went to the nearest station, came back, killed 5 more.. took tons of time and is not what I'd call fun)
Either the game should make it easier to get self-recharging tools (which you only see very rarely, I think I only saw them in special "deflector missions" which are sepparate from the rest), vastly increase the limit of uses (high capacity should be 20 uses minimum) or give us weapons that can bypass shields. You could go the way plenty of scifi went and only make lower speed weapons penetrate, like melee or even just slow types of melee.
Also, the time limit should be expanded or at least being spotted should not reduce it even more so you could rambo through to the captain, because in 9/10 missions with time limit, I was either caught or had to abandon the mission incomplete.
And before someone says to just not do such missions: you get 5 missions to chose from, maybe 6. if 3 of those have shields and/or time limits, you're stuck with some "medium" and "hard" ones that are actually a piece of cake and pretty easy.
Each time you get spaced, which means enemies killed you and throw you out the airlock, which is a nice idea in and on itself because it's a middle way between permadeath and just restarting at a checkpoint, the amount of time you can survive outside decreases. Would be fine if it was just for that mission, but it's permanent and I know of no way to increase it again, which means by the time you got all the equipment to tackle harder ships, being spaced once or twice, which will happen far easier, means you're dead.
Restarting at the start of the ship, maybe even through the menu, the way it is with deflector missions would be great. Some times you have really bad luck with the layout and, for example, a group of five enemies right in front of your entry point. Some times you manage to blow up part of a ship which makes it impossible for you to go further into it. Both cases mean you just have to abort the mission, which is no fun.
Give a faster way to travel through the huge ships. maybe teleporters unlocked when you reach them. it's really frustrating having to wander through the whole ship again just because you forgot a guy or something.
Last but not least, lower the difficulty of personal missions. with like 20 characters, I survived that maybe once.
to recap, ways to improve the game:
- weapons against shields or at least higher capacity or recharging for tools
- more self-recharging tools, period. One deflector mission had just glitch trap and a swapping teleporter (teleports you to where the enemy was and the enemy where you were) and I had a blast, setting the trap, standing on it and swapping with an enemy. But with the limited number of tools you can take with you this is not possible to really use without self-recharging tools.
- quicker way to get armor piercing
- longer time limit or less missions that have one
- a way to "heal" yourself to withstand space longer again
- add teleporters
- lower difficulty level for personal missions (if all of the above get implemented that may not be neccessary)
- a way to restart a ship, reroll it's layout
some additional points:
- fix the memory leak or whatever is responsible for the game getting sluggish after some time running. At several points it was nearly as slow as while targetting.
- Add a cheap ship type, like $5 or so, that would be a dinghy to your normal ship with which you could ram through windows if you go at them at full spead, sacrificing it but being able to start the ship where you rammed in it. could maybe alert the ship to make it not too easy. [note, maybe there is such a ship, I haven't unlocked all yet]
- add some more options for those wanting to ghost. like a hack tool that would hack access hatches to air ducts with shich you could bypass enemies. a way to lure enemies to your trap without causing alarm. light switches or fuses you could turn off so enemies would not see as far. always just cloaking or teleporting is boring and costs a ♥♥♥♥♥on.
- after the enemy spotted you, followed you and lost your trail, make them return to where they were. otherwise you some times get 8 enemies in a single spot you need to go through
- with how much emphasis there is on teleporting, teleporting grenade launchers should be included. Or at least some variety, like bouncing ones that you could (better) shoot around corners. as it is, grenade launchers are pretty useless, they alert everyone (shields go up) and often you're in line of sight of you shoot them

Aberoth is an old school RPG game that takes you back to the way games used to look on the 8 bit systems but with a twist, incorporating new features all the while keeping the old style feel alive and well. Your characters starts off in prison and must escape from orcs, throwing you into the deep end head first as this game is unforgiving to players at every step of the way, creating a challenging but highly enjoyable game play for those looking for more than easy mode. You will find that death is not the end but it will cost you dearly as you struggle and even fear going in to far too fast.
Pros:
-	The controls all be it are a bit on the manual side work very well for what they are intended for and allow the player to move quite freely.
-	An open world aspect to this RPG that allows you to explore how you see fit just be wary you don’t bit off more than you can chew.
-	A number of different creatures to keep things interesting and allow you to feel you are making progress.
-	A unique style of grouping system allowing as many players to join forces or to turn on each other at a drop of a hat.
-	Pvp is a real thing in this game but not overlay so, allowing players to decide whether to be friends or foes.
-	A great progression of quest that will ease you into the game but won’t be easy or too quick to accomplish, allowing you to earn your rank and items.
Cons:
-	A rather limited tutorial and help guide to set you on your way, making it a struggle to get started for new players.
In conclusion, Aberoth is an amazing old school RPG that will throw you back to when games were different but still very detailed and enjoyable in their own way. 4 out of 5.

Dwarf Tower is a simple game where you try to build your tower faster and better than your opponent while throwing spells at eachother. With simple gameplay and a small price, you will likely not be disappointed by it. While the gameplay is pretty good, and if you grab a friend you can have a good time together, it's not that big of a game that you can keep playing it over and over
The gameplay is simple and mostly intuitive. Build stuff, avoid getting wrecked, and sling spells at the opponent. The few issues are mostly ones that are a comfort issue. A lack of quick ways to select rooms and spells(The menu shows numbers, yet pressing number buttons on my keyboard does nothing, for some reason), and issues of being able to see just what is going on. Not the inteligence gathering way, that is, as you have spells and a room that help you identify rooms in your opponent's tower, but rather that as your tower is in front of your opponent's tower, your attacks will hit and the camera is trying to look at the action, but instead just zooms in on your own tower.
For some reason the screen goes completely black and shows only white text - quite a contrast with the normal bright sky behind your tower, and pretty annoying if you dont have mana or library/worker space. I'm not sure how that got through any sort of playtesting. At the same time, the options menu is severely lacking. They very clearly did not spend a lot of time on usability for the player.
With the rooms and spells that you get being randomised, you may experience a mild frustration as your tower burns down and there are no firefighters coming up at all for several turns. Luckily, with doors and clever building you can usually stop or slow the fire long enough to draw into what you need.
The graphics, as the screenshots show, are nothing to write home about. But they're functional and show you exactly what you need to know. The music is selected pretty well and overall it's a pretty good experience to play Dwarf Tower
That said, it is cheap, and it is small. Don't expect a huge game here, or a challenging AI to outsmart you. But if you grab a copy or two pack and share with a friend you can have a pretty good time for a few hours and get your money's worth

I somewhat support the Creation Club and here's why;
The fact that there is now a seperate facility for paid mods, which they are in all honesty, I think is great. The CC will encourage mod developers to innovate their mods and provide better mods. I admit, Bethesda hasn't given alot of stuff in the CC launch. But I don't think it is awfully bad. The fact is that Bethesda has kept the normal old fashioned Mod system. Which makes CC an extra. It would be a totally different conversation if Bethesda had solely relied on CC and taken down the old mod system. Futhermore, it allows Devs to be paid, although Bethesda takes their cut (No idea how much that is). Basically, True or False Universe is a game where animals judge you for your knowledge of trivia. Spanning funny, easy, obscure, absurd and tricky true or false questions, this game is a lighthearted pastime ideally suited for diversion in between.
With an overall clean look, bright colours and a bunch of cute animals, the game provides a laidback quiz environment devoid of time constraints, highscores or any gameplay relevant punishment for wrong answers. The sounds are clear with just enough spark to them to feel gratifying while remaining unobtrusive. The only thing that needs getting used to is that every session is limited to a certain number of questions; 2, 3 and 4, before returning to the title screen and continuing. This is an unnecessary minor annoyance at most, but can also be used to break out of an endless loop to avoid spending too much time on the quiz. As written above, it's best played in between.
Even with no real consequences, there's still the motivation to get at least one question of a session right to avoid the slightly unpleasant "SAD!" evaluation ... Aside from that, True or False Universe offers a neat platform for a relaxed trivia game.

Note: I'm one of the original Kickstarter backers for Cosmic Star Heroine so I've been waiting nearly four years for this game to come out. It's kind of crazy because I had just gotten out of College at the time. In the intervening years, I've moved from one end of the USA to the other, gotten a good job, made new friends and so much more had happened that I had honestly forgotten that I had backed CSH. I really don't want to write the review this way....but let's get to it.
The pluses to CSH: Worlds are decently fleshed out and they certainly created a unique setting. You get to meet a wide variety of races and characters that come with their own charm and unique visuals. They have done really well to craft this unique universe with some interesting ideas here.
The Battle system is probably the most enjoyable jRPG battle system I've run across as well. There's no grinding required though you can do random battles via the menu if you want. And there's a nice variety of abilities and strategies you can implement at the individual and team level. Stats aren't well introduced and aren't as intuitive as other RPGs though. But it makes for an enjoyable time as you exploit combos and elemental weaknesses in the enemies.
The minuses to CSH: The story is just....so boring. The characters are two dimensional at best and man does this game suffer for it. What Zeboyd humor and references are put in are a nice touch. But it's not nearly enough to outweigh the problems. The story mostly serves as a means to direct the player from one place to the next. While that does work early on, I was starting to crave some sort of change to the pace mid to late game. It's just "Hi, nice to meet you, do this thing, kill X enemies, kill the boss" rinse and repeat. There's not much for side quests or dungeons and they serve mostly as a distraction to give you nice items, most of the time.
It's a real shame that the story doesn't hold up because I think these would be very interesting characters to work with here. But they aren't ever allowed to develop into believable people. Even on quests that seem to be hand-crafted to build up backstory or maybe camaraderie, the characters are mostly silent during it with only the lightest amount of conversation going on. It's a completely missed opportunity. Made even more noticeable that 99% of the NPCs' dialogue in towns is completely forgettable/skippable. Or the cutscenes that were a nice bit of flair but ultimately pointless most of the time.
What ultimately stopped me was the various bugs and glitches I kept running into in the game. Most notable were the soft-locks where the game would randomly decide after casting a spell to "lock up" I couldn't cast spells, bring up the menu or anything else. There was also another graphic glitch that occurred when I swapped characters around. Or the game refusing to acknowledge that I hit the A button to read the dialogue. 11 hours in, I ran into another soft-lock and lost a significant amount of progress on the third planet you visit.
At that point, I was already losing interest and was just bored. The story didn't give me any reason to invest myself in the characters, the combat system was nice but it wasn't enough to finish the game over either. I'm also a little irritated that a game that was in development for so long that's approximately 10-20 hours had so many bugs present in the final product. Is it worth picking up? No.

I'll usually play a HO game when I'm eating. They are slow-paced, you mostly progress just by observation, and you can easily stop when you want to pick it up later. And better than most of the junk on TV, imo.
And then I found this. It's my new 'dinner game.'
You can play it in as small or large chunks as you want. I must admit that somewhere between 10 and 20 questions I usually find I've had enough and want to go do something else. But this is a Good Thing.
I'm loving the presentation and overall cheerful, cute style. The sounds and music are great and very suitable, and the overall concept is interesting, entertaining and sometimes even educational (/shudder).
I do have a few minor niggles. As a lot of people have said, returning to the main screen every 3 questions is a bit tedious and irritating. Maybe an option for sets of 3, 5 or 10 questions at a time would sort this out?
Also, I expect considerable work has been put into researching the questions. But for those of you who are also fans of the podcast 'No Such Thing as a Fish' (and if you like this game, you may want to check that out), a few of the 'facts' here have a 'Dan Schreiber' feel about them. i.e. was that
correct?!?! The only question that comes immediately to mind is the Stonehenge one. I used to drive past that nearly every day for about 6 months, so I'm naturally interested in anything about it. And I seriously doubt the answer presented by ToFU.
I see from the news that there have been updates to the questions, so maybe this second issue is resolved or on the way to being so.

Update July 31 2015:
With an updated driver and lowest setting my performance is fine.  It's still obvious there are a lot bugs not graphics related but most aren't game breaking, those that are come rarely.
Story:  The story is solid, nothing spectacular or new, but it's solid and the characters are just interesting enough to finish the story.
City: Huge and Deep.  This is the highlight, the city is huge and with the inclusion of interiors there is a lot more added depth to every aspect.
Gameplay:  Stealth and parkour have been tweaked for the better overall, still some trouble jumping through windows while free running but now that going down is just as easy as going up movemnet through the city is easier.
Co-Op:  Great, the only downside is that it may be difficult to find people for particular missions, but there is usually a mission available whenever.
Notes on older reviews:  The App and external programs aren't required anymore to get anything in game. So from the start there are a ton of chests and goodies available.
Overall:  If you are a fan of the series it's definately worth it if you think you can run it.  If you aren't it's not a bad place to start, but you might prefer to get it on sale if it's not your kind of game. 7/10 mostly negative due to poor design around apps and rushed buggy delivery, but those have been fixed (for the most part)
Original June 7 2015:
Short: Bugs, better have a great PC, if not play Rouge.
Long:  Over 6 months later it's still a buggy mess. A game should at least be able to run at 30 fps on the lowest settings with the min requirements.  If you aren't sure if your PC will run it, it probably won't, and if it does, not really well.  If you've invested in the latest and greatest or just happen to have a setup they optimized for than good for you, no sarcasm, please enjoy.  The rest of us are going to have to wait until they fix the remaining bugs.
I'm not bashing on the game itself, or even Ubisofts developers, if anyone is to blame it's the producers who try to push games out in annual cycles not understanding the hurdles of good programming.  I waited for a good sale before I finally bought the game, and only because it was with AC Rouge.  AC Rouge is the game you want if you aren't sure about specs, it's not anything revolutionary gameplaywise for the series but the story is great and the gameplay is solid.
AC Unity is beautiful though. even with medium and low graphic setting there is a lot of detail, I think there in lies the problem, too many resurces are spent on things not wholey necessary, and it drags down FPS even at the lowest settings.  I can play it with the same FPS at the highest setting, the only difference are the visuals.  I'm usually not even picky about FPS, I'm cool with a consistent 20, but this game isn't consistent enough to make me comfortable.
So yeah, I'm taking a break from this game, hopefully they continue to patch it and it improves within the next 3 months.  I don't mind waiting for a better PC or for them to patch it, but if they don't I likely won't buy any future games they release in this state.

The Walking Dead: Season 1 Review:
"I don't know much about you folks, but you keep goin' on like this, and that girl ain't gonna make it. You've got to think of her as a living person. That's it. You ain't little. You ain't a girl, you ain't a boy. You ain't strong... or smart. You're alive."- Chuck (Episode 3)
Wow. Just wow.
I had heard the hype for this game and had seen some lets plays of it but I was still eager to play it even though its been out for almost 3 years. So when it was on sale for $6 i decided to pick it up. These are my thoughts: I cant ♥♥♥♥ing believe i never played this game until now because to say the least, it is ♥♥♥♥ing masterpiece that every game with branching choices, point and click gameplay, or even just regular story telling should be held up to. I had played Back to the Future by TT, which had great characters, plot, and set pieces, but it was nothing AND I MEAN NOTHING like this game. This game made me cry, tense up, scream, and made me regret things like i never had before. It gave me experiences that i will never forget. You get so attatched to these characters that by the end you are sobbing in your chair and feeling helpless to the character's futures. Let me go over what i love about this game in seperate sections.
GRAPHICS/SOUND: The graphics in this game are astounding and run really well. The shell shading art style looks just like the comic its based on with bold outlines of characters and a mixture of smudges and fine lines making up the character's features. The Settings in the story also show the base with more varying colors and shades throughout.  The sound is also incredible with a great soundtrack ajusting to what choice, scene, or moment your in. It really hits you especially towards the end and is one of the reasons you will bawl your eyes out, its that influencing.
STORY: The story is the main pillar of the entire structure of the game because its not just a normal flat story but a changing round one which adapts to your playstyle or how much of a nice guy♥♥♥♥♥♥you want to be. This aspect of the game keeps the characters in new situations and always, I MEAN ALWAYS, has your choices biting you in the♥♥♥♥♥ The summary is this: Lee, a convict escapes from his crashed police car at the start of the apocolypse and meets a girl named Clemintine who lost her parents and needs to go to Savannah to find them, so you two look out for each other while surviving in a world that takes more than it gives. The story is always changing and really effects you as a person making you as Lee make opinions of people, make decisions people just shouldnt make, and having you as a pivitol role in who lives and who dies.
CHARACTERS: I already kind of covered the story behind the characters and i dont want to spoil the people that you meet so ill just go over our relationship between the two main characters: Lee and Clem. They feel like father and daughter throughout most of the story making Lee do unspeakable things for her and going to far lengths to keep her safe(*cough Episode 5 Cough*). This kind of relationship grows on you and will drive you to feel like Lee by the end of the story as you almost become him as a person trying to protect Clem. This is the strongest bond i have seen between characters in any sort of literature in a long time.
GAMEPLAY:  Lots of Point and click and lots of QTE's, yet it doesnt become annoying as all the QTE's and point and click elements are masked and complemented by suspense, fantastic narrative, and amazing tense moments mixed with character developments. Sometimes it can acually be frustrating with movement and clunky walking doesnt help at all (Thank God you don't control walking alot).
My Final Verdict:
Pros:
+ Characters
+ Changing stories/playstyles
+ Graphical design/sound design
+ THE ♥♥♥♥ING ENDING THO :(
Cons:
- Clunky movement (Im really scraping the bottom of the barrel though)
VERDICT:   10/10

I love JRPGs, but I find it difficult to sit down through RPGs with overly long exposition or rote, repetitive combat mechanics.  Enter Zeboyd, whose every game has been like a breath of fresh air.  So naturally, I preordered Cosmic Star Heroine and waited... and waited... and waited... and it's been worth the wait!
The game starts off with action and adventure, and never lets up.  The pace remains quick, the characters fun and light, the combat delightful and each character's mechanics encourage exploration of their abilities, and each new level/zone has simple little puzzles.
Most Zeboyd games have been "lite" snacks, a game you can finish in a few hours, but Cosmic Star Heroine has some real staying power.  I wouldn't quite call it a "full JRPG experience," but if Zeboyd keeps moving in this direction, we may well have a proper epic on our hands.
I have some quibbles: you quickly "level out of" the interesting items, which means that while you can swap in and out accessories and abilities, your weapon and shield tend to be dictated by what the "best" item is at the moment, which I find unfortunate.  The game has plenty of equipment, but given the good/better/best nature of weapons and shields, those choices quickly disappear into "just a handful useful currently."  The game also has some bugs, though the only one I've found is that sometimes the UI for editing abilities disappears and the only way to fix it is to quit out and restart.
Is it worth a buy, even at this price (which is far, far more than most Zeboyd games)? Yes, definitely.  This is the Zeboyd game you've been waiting for!

I've been playing this game since Open Beta, and my steam hours do not reflect my gameplay as I usually use the launcher provided direct from Trion. I've clocked about 2800 hours total on this game since it was made public to anyone. In that time, I've seen a delightful back and forth between the Artists that wanted to make a game, and the trials and struggles of keeping a game free to play. In Game, theres always someone to play with. Getting into a Shadow Tower (8 man raid) is as simple as posting to global 'looking for ST'. Finding a group to EXP with is as simple as jumping into a portal and following the first person you see. Clubs provide free build space that other games charge monthly subs for. The forums unfortunatly are full of people who dont understand how coding a game to play well takes time and that an MMO is a constant, ever changing product. Changes and improvements take time and testing.
However, I could NOT reccomend the game for a 'hardcore gamer', as much of the game's nature is casual. If your the type who wants to buy your way to the top, you might feel overly squeezed without doing some research on the DLC packs. (Such as the $30 package to get your first Radiant is nolonger wortwhile since its relitvly cheap to craft one now. It was awesome when the Radiant gear first launched and people were charing an arm and a leg. Now they drop from the higher level worlds.) Take it slow and enjoy yourself. Dont burn out playing 10+ hours a day.

Not since Cannon Fodder have I felt so miserable when one of my characters finally died. Admittedly, she was by this point so paranoid she refused all assistance from the rest of the party, but damn, I'd grown attached. And that is the essence of this game's appeal, the characters, while straight from central casting, still feel like individuals.
The game is tough, but polished and, while maddening at times, has never pushed me into a rage (despair yes, but rage no). So, you may ask, why do people play this? Are we all out for punishment? No! The game is just very addictive in that "Come on, just one more quick dungeon before I head to bed... whoops, it's 3 AM?!?!"
It is challenging, it will often feel unfair, but boy, winning battles and completing dungeons feels so very satisfying. You start to care about your chars (and there is an achievement about beating the final boss with the chars you get at the beginning of the game), especially if you name them yourself.
PROS
- Atmospheric
- Simple, but unique graphics and animations
- Great narrator voice
- Challenging
- You get to choose your ability-loadout
- Very satisfying when you beat a boss or dungeon...
CONS
- Very frustrating
- Expensive supplies
- Expensive treatment to get rid of debuffs and stuff
- Can get grindy
- Not recommended if you hate losing RNG rolls even when your characters are leveled and equipped with good gear
- Can feel a bit repetitive

Good remake of an old favorite.
Pros
- Job system is interesting with lots of options
- Decent amount of grind v. story.  Lots of opportunity to max everything though if that's your thing
- Bosses and new mobs can pose a threat
- Finishing a job gets you a legendary item for that class
Cons
- Some jobs are worthless
- Zero description of Job Points - had to read a guide
- Fastest way to level a job?  Just have all your guys Guard 7 times for an automatic job level at the end of the fight.  Should have been based on job special skills - Knights using Defend, Thief using Steal, mages using magic for the biggest boost, medium boost for normal actions like attacking, and very little for using items (unless Scholar) or Guarding.  I've maxed out a lot of the FF games and couldn't force myself to do it here.
- Low agility characters/jobs end up at a disadvantage if you don't use the Guard method of job leveling.  They don't get to take an action and thus level slower than everyone else.
- Legendary smith - difficult to access without looking at a guide, pops up in random places causing you to fly between two cities until she shows up at just to get your new job weapon, etc.  Poorly conceived.
- Nothing carries over when you switch jobs.  It would be nice to keep some residual stats - Knight to White Mage should keep a little defense or vitality.
- Save issue during the last boss.  Fight through a dungeon, fight boss, no save option except for quick save (does not allow you to resume there if you die).  Can't teleport or travel back to world map for a full save.  Enter final dungeon - if you happen to approach the final boss first like I did, you're screwed and you get one shotted meaning you lose about 20 minutes of progress and have to watch some really long cutsceens again.
All in all, glad I picked it up on sale and got to see what they did with the remake.

I would in full honesty reccomend LEGO® The Hobbit™ to anyone who wants about 40 to 50 hours of casual play, experiencing the story of the hobbit, but in a Lego Way. The only person I would not reccomend this game to are folk with no controller compatible with your computer. The Keyboard and mouse controls are horribly unresponsive and it feels like you are playing with rocks. Plug yourself in an Xbox or Playstation controller and you've got yourself a fine gaming experience.
lets go down on the Game itself. The music and soundtrack are directly borrowed from the movie(s) themselves and really put you in the event of where the game is taking place. For example the music in the dainty shire scenes is very tone down mellow folk music, while during epic battle we get music that fits well in with the battle thats going on.  As far as the atmosphere of the game goes, its very strong.
The graphics of the game are actually insanely well put together, and the textures look better than most triple A titles released today. However on low graphics the game looks solid and is much easier on your pc. On the subject, the game is not well optimized for PC. I say this because my computer is very strong (i7 and 980) and it has to work much harder than it should in order to run this game on high, so if your computer is a total dinosaur, reconsider before buying at full price.
When talking fully about the gameplay alone, its realitively simple and very similar to most lego games. Like other lego games they add more mechanics with each game. This game has a system of save and quit with a statue you can interact with in most levels, which is new for lego games as far as i can tell. This is definitly helpful because if you are buying this for a child you always have an answer for the "Just let me finish this level!!". More mechanics in this game
that got added such as the building mechanic where instead of just pressing one button and building it, theres a somewhat involved process  to choosing and placing bricks.
As far as the story goes I was somewhat dissapointed. This game does not include the 3rd movie and thus doesnt include the battle of the 5 armies. I wouldve thought they would add some kind of dlc but we got nothing. This is perhaps one of the only downsides to the only game and is actually pretty sad. However this lego game is part of the series of lego games that include voice acting, so you can actually feel for the characters and dont feel like you are on the outside of an inside joke like some other lego games. This game can actually tug at your heartstrings at certain moments and that suprised me.
Overall the game was very well put together and would very strongly reccomend it. Also if you get any bugs turn on Vsync and that should fix them. So if you are looking for some casual game to blow off from steam and experience a beautiful story, look no further.

This game is semi-good , semi-bad.
First of all , it has improved a lot from last years. From graphics , to better gameplay and structure of the mods this game has been the best nba 2k game so far. The models look more realistic than ever , gameplay feels a lot smoother but it has some flaws (more on that later). Defense has been improved a lot. There are a lot more animations and these make the game feel like a true NBA game. The atmosphere of the matches is good. Especially in moments where the score is in a critical condition and every move determines the final outcome of the game. You can feel the crowd . It breathes energy and "motivation " , so to say. One thing I really liked is the fact that If the home team loses by a lot , then you start seeing the fans leave the stadium and you end up with like 1k spectators or less. A small detail , yet a great one.
The commentators also do a great job both on the post-game and pre-game shows as well as in the game. Pre-game shows are very entairtaining to watch and they effectively fill the time you to wait for the game to load. In-game , commentators do a great job at transferring the atmosphere of the game to you , the player. Although some lines get repeated a lot and I would like to be monthly updates to them. Aside from these things , some things I also like is that every team has the right coach , a full-modeled character, and not a common one to all teams. In timeouts coaches talk to you and ask various things such as pressure more or shoot more , etc. . Also the soundtrack is good although it feels like it needs more tracks , a thing that may be asserted in the next game. It contains music from different genres , with Rap being the leading one.
Now to modes : I will only talk about MyCarrer and MyTeam because these are the ones that I have only played.
MyCareer:
MyCareer is pretty solid for another year , with the exception of the Spike Lee addition. And that's where the mode starts showing some problems. For example,  you feel like you dont have a lot of freedom . It's more restricted in comparison with the previous games. Your family and friends are black (no intention of racism) and that's awkward when you made your player a white person. Maybe Spike Lee oversaw that and didn't fix it. But aside from that you basically follow a premade story and you cant do anything to change it. I found the story interesting and I liked the fact that we had the chance to play college games. Even though they were small in duration , they were pretty fun. After finishing with the Spike Lee story , MyCareer gets a lot more interesting. Endorsements are a great addition to the game and a big reason to keep you in the game for a long time. Practise manages it as well. (although not in the same degree as endorsements)
MyTeam:
MyTeam is the game mode that's held me the most on this game. Almost all my game-hours are spent on this mode. It's fun , interesting and you have to think sometimes on how to make the most out of your auctions and so on. I really like opening packs whenever I have the money , even though pack odds are not very good, something that definitely needs to be considered heavily in the next NBA2k. Then you have the auction house. AH plays a huge role in the mode. It's  basically the one that determine if you're gonna be rich or not. You need to think sometimes on how to handle your auctions , like when to sell them , how much , etc. Modes are good too. Domination is definitely the mode you want to start with. After you complete it ,something that's not so difficult to do, you can hop in to Road To The Playoffs mode. There you play online with other players so make sure you have a good team. Gauntlet is another online mode too. Even though they are fun modes to play , the lack of stable servers makes them really nerve-racking and make you rage a lot. And that's a serious reason why some people quit the game. A lot of times I have found myself lagging for no reason and get thrown out of the game , thus losing it . This is a problem that needs to be immediately addressed in the next game.
Also 2k has to do something about people that buy mt from 3rd - party sites. It makes the AH go nuts and prices go way higher than they were supposed to be and that's causing the players to feel frustrated and quit trying to buy players.
Overall , I recommend NBA 2k16 to everyone that like sports games , and just wants to have fun. MyTeam is guaranteed to keep a lot of players busy with the game. Even though a lot of problems need to be addressed in NBA 2k17 ,  2k16 still remains a pretty solid choice for NBA lovers.

Ah, Fallout 4. I could go back and forth for hours on whether or not this is a good game, what makes it good, and why I would or would not recommend it.
It's a... difficult experience, to really get into, as a Fallout fan. You needn't look far to see people complaining that it's "not fallout" or "dumbed down the RP" or what have you. As for me, I like to think Fallout 4 took a more subtle approach to the whole skill choice and consequence part of these games.
Where previous fallouts would result in different dialogue, quest rewards, karma rewards, or whatever else might happen, Fallout 4 foregoes most of these things in favour of a more practical reward. There is no karma system, which I personally approve of because it no longer feels like I'm being judged arbitrarily for actions I might consider good, or rewarded for actions I consider evil.
A lot of that consequence-failure arises from the introduction of a voiced protagonist. New Vegas had its share of bad voice-acting (see the Khan that hides up in the mountain close to Bitter Springs), but Fallout 4's voice acting brought with it a very unique, new problem; budgetting. Due to the limited time and money allocated to the game, it would seem that the developers had to cut quite a few corners in developing branching quest paths that actually led to anything interesting. Instead, we end up with a bland mix of inconsequential options that all are all uttered with the same lack of emotion we've come to expect from the rest of the game. It's sad, but alas, so be it.
So yeah, the voice acting ruins many of the things people love and cherish about Fallout. The same goes for the forced backstory of the character and the terrible writing in the main story overall. But, if you look behind that, I think Fallout 4 could've been a gem, and that's why I'm still recommending it. Not for what it is, but for what I believe you can make it be (with a willful ignorance, modding, and survival mode).
I hate Fallout 4's main story for always assuming that I care at all about finding my potato-faced son. I hate that it makes me jump through hoops to find a guy when previous games would just let me walk there immediately if I knew where to go (see the process of finding Dad in Fallout 3, when trapped in Tranquility Lane). I hate that weapon durability was removed and I seriously hate that the big bad institute's motivations are so poorly written I could've done better when I was 12.
That said, I love fallout 4's world. I love exploring it, and I love that they revamped power armor and integrated it in such a way that it completely revises how one can play the game. I love that the gunplay is actually on an acceptable level now (it was never much of a selling point for me). I love the way survival mode makes me rethink my decisions on death, not just make me throw myself at that oh-so-familiar brick wall to see which breaks, as per usual. I love (some of) the companions, and I love settlement-building (in survival; where it serves a purpose).
She's not perfect, but she's still a Fallout game, and I love her for it.

I seldomly put up reviews but sometimes I feel it to be needed. Cosmic Star Heroine is one such case. I had no idea it was coming out so i was surprised when I looked in release lists and it had come out on the exact day I was looked. I instantly bought it because I liked Cthulu saves the world and was mostly curious. I have now finished the game and I can wholeheartedly say that I like every single aspect of this game, I would be hard pressed to mention something I truly disliked.
The characters are amazing and all of the feel pretty´much unique and quirky. They are designed incredibly well, I felt myself being amazed at the visuals at almost every turn, from the cook slightly animated scenes to the sheer coolness of the normal sprites, everything just felt great.
The combat is a pretty regular turn based system but with the hyper mechanic and loads of differenct characters and abilities to choose from, it never felt as if it stagnated, I was always changing stuff up and shifting characters.
It never felt as if the game dwelled too long in certain areas, I can admit I got confused as what to do in certain places, but that fixed itself by just talking to random people.
At first I was confused about the story, then it took off and while I kind of knew where it was all leading, I still felt encouraged to know more because everything else just pulled it so hard.
I did hear people have experienced a lot of bugs, I didn't experience one, but I felt like I had to point it out.
Zeboyd Games have shown me that they can create something really cool three times now and I am eagerly awaiting what else lies in store for the future.
Cosmic Star Heroine gets a huge recommendation for me, one of my favourites of 2017 so far, if not THE favourite. If you are even the least bit interested, try it.

A fresh take on the JRPG genre that takes classic gameplay elements and makes them far more convenient and interesting.
The game's combat takes its queues from Chrono Trigger (with a bit of Grandia). There is no mana or resource management; instead, skills have a set number of uses before requiring the player to "rest" or defend in order to regain their use. This makes combat interesting, alongside a system which buffs attacks every n turns (varying based on the character), allowing players to manage their skills wisely and think ahead to determine how best to deal damage or heal their party members. Also, you are fully healed after each fight which allows you to go all-out each time you encounter an enemy; this feature makes combat much less tedious than I have found it to be in other JRPGs, as much as I love the genre.
The setting is a mixture between Phantasy Star (less like the single player games and more like Online, IMO) and standard Cyberpunk, at least a few hours in. Perhaps this will change once I get closer to the end, and if so, I will update my review. The writing is very entertaining, characters are likeable and witty, and the setting itself is really interesting. One character that I am quite fond of is a "Gunmancer" who summons various guns to help her in combat. Another is a hacker who can literally hack into robotic enemies (of which there are many) to debuff them, deal damage, heal party members, etc. While roles are pretty clearly defined, the fresh take on them and a bit of skill/gear customization makes the game's characterization feel rather deep.
One complaint that I will mention is that, at least at the point I am at in the game, there has been no backtracking. While this sounds like a wonderful thing, I mean that I often cannot even leave the screen that I am on to explore an area I just left; sometimes I feel that I have missed things or wanted to talk to someone, but I am unable to as the game pushes me forward constantly. It is not a horrible thing, but it does make it feel as though I am not getting to explore as much as I would like at times. Take this with a grain of salt, as it may change and even if not, I am not that bothered by it- I just wanted to complain about something. :)
I am greatly enjoying Cosmic Star Heroine, and I hope that others will give it a shot. I admit that I have been following the game since it was first announced with bated breath, so I may be a bit biased, but I believe it to be worth far more than the $11.99 that it is currently going for.
