This is a fun game. You are basically trying to build your archmage tower while at the same time trying to destroy your rival's and keep them from destroying yours. Interesting dynamics involved in figuring out how you want to build your tower and also in managing your spells and mana to cast spells.
You are given a random selection of cards each round, which you must use or lose. The cards are the spells, rooms, and tools that you need to build up your tower and your attack (and defense) capabilities. The spells are put in your library inventory until you use them, which requires mana points, which accumulate from crystals you build. (One thing that I would like to be able to do is remove spells from libraries. It can happen that you put a spell in there and later lack the space for a better spell available.)
I had some confusion at first how to play, but I gradually realized how the play is broken into segments. While it is obvious when you enter Build or Combat phase that it is time to build or attack, some of the sub-segments weren't so obvious: for example, that "Pumping" was to assign some dwarves with this capability instead of actually pumping water out of a dungeon at that time. I think the game would be a lot more accessible to new players if there was a clearer demarcation between the segments of play, with perhaps a Help button to click on that describes what is happening in this segment of play.
All the basic information you need to play is in the game, even if it the information is presented in a manner that is a little rough around the edges. There is a tutorial that walks you through at least part of a game: my tutorial actually got stuck for some reason at some point, but I had seen enough to jump into a game. From what I did see, a little more direction from the tutorial on what is going on would be helpful.
The aesthetics of the game are simple but pleasing--I quite enjoyed the music and the simple artwork. I do kind of wish that you could see the little dwarves and archmages, especially when one of the archmages is defeated. But that is a very minor point and probably just a matter of taste on my part. (Actually it probably wouldn't work to show the archmage before the end because finding out where the archmage's quarters are is one of the points of strategy in the game.)
I would definitely buy the game again after having played four rounds (each takes about ten minutes to play, I think). I can see this game as one that I come back to from time to time for a quick archmage battle.

Dwarf tower is a little indie gem in the endless fields of AAA murder-everything-in-the-face games.
Set in a fantasy world, you are a mage with a ton of dwarf followers, dueling with an enemy mage.  You both build towers, use spells, and try to destroy eachother's archmage chambers.
Gameplay is an interesting turnbased strategy and physics gameplay.  No floating pieces of your tower unless they're connected to a levitronus.  Use doors and armor to keep out fire and flooding.  Fire spreads through your tower if it can, destroying anything and everything in it's path, so you need firefighters or doors.  Various other neat things.
The facebook integration that was there in the initial release DID kind of tick me off, but it has since been removed, letting me make this one of the *few* games where I would give a full 10/10.
The tutorial is pretty nice and decently explains the game, and the sandbox mode is nice for experimenting with building styles to see how they hold up to various attacks.  The music in use is some of Kevin MacLeod's awesome work, even if they couldn't get some custom music from him.
Overall, would give 10/10.
Also, just going to get this out of the way so I don't need to copy/paste a response everywhere: I was going mad on the reviews initially because the amount of people bashing the game for the same things, and not seeing that these things they were bashing it for were going to be removed the next update had me worried.  Given that the game got stupid amounts of negativity at launch, I was terrified it wouldn't make it to a stable point on Steam's stores.
And no, for those who are wondering, I am NOT related to the developers.  I'm just some guy who saw a little indie gem arrive on Steam, that I had been with for a bit of it's Steam Greenlight days, and I didn't want it to self-destruct because of a buggy launch.
That will be all...

Gotta beat this dead horse:
If you enjoy RPGs from the late 16-bit era, this is a no-brainer purchase.
You've got the story tone and humor of the Lunar games, the base-building of Suikoden, Chrono-trigger inspired combat (enhanced with the depth and lessons learned from Penny Arcade 3 & 4), a Phantasy Star-esque setting, and a Sega CD/PC Engine-style of presentation - anime-style cutscenes and all.
The soundtrack (again by Hyperduck Soundworks) is stellar and is chock full of catchy tunes that ooze 80s cyberpunk, with some atmospheric tracks and pulse-pumping battle themes for good measure.  The game's Indie Rock Band playable character even has a fully voiced track that would be right at home in an episode of Bubblegum Crisis.  It's all great stuff, at least in my opinion.
To get to the gameplay side of things: as the bullet point on the Steam Store Page says, the pacing is brisk - areas don't outstay their welcome but aren't 100% linear, either.  There's always a chest or three tucked in a hard-to-see nook or behind a switch-lowered barrier.  You can save literally any time you can open the menu.  There is no penalty for getting "wiped out" and losing a battle (other than the time it takes to restart/retry said battle).
You can also change the difficulty at any time you can open the menu, as well.   There are 4 difficutly settings, ranging from "I'm just here for the story" to "even the devs have trouble with this one".  This allows you to adjust things up or down on the fly if you find that battles are either too easy, or maybe that one fight (or Boss) keeps getting the better of you.
Combat is outstanding.  Each battle is a bit like a puzzle you have to solve using character abilities that synergize with each other or exploit enemy weaknesses.  But to be specific:
Turn based.  A bar on the far right shows you the exact order that each combatant  will act (both your own Party Members and your foes).  Each character has HP, a Style level (given as a %), and Hyper squares that fill one per round.
Each character has a set of up to 8 Skills.  A few of the weaker, basic attacks can be used over and over again, but most can only be used once before they are "greyed out" and become unusable.  There is no MP or anything like it.  The way to re-activate your disabled or used up abilities is to use your Defend command, which refreshes everything you've used.
Each character can have additional abilities gained from their equipped Shield (this game's version of Armor).  These Programs are once-per-battle and do not recharge if you Defend.  Items are much the same but are shared by the party as a whole - so anyone can use any item, but then it's used up and no one else can use it until the next battle.
Most abilities give you some % of Style.  Style increases the amount of damage you do and allows you survive otherwise fatal blows if it's above 50% (higher for tougher difficulties).
Each round, the character gains a Hyper Point and a blue box under their HP bar fills in.  When all the boxes are full, the character enters Hyper Mode for a single round; while in Hyper Mode, damage is doubled and the chance of inflicting any status ailment is greatly increased.  Each character has a different set of Hyper Boxes, meaning that Hyper turns very rarely overlap and are instead spaced out somewhat evenly as combat progresses.
I'm leaving out a few bits (Desperation mode) but the gist of it is this: in each combat, the key to winning is to "line up" your best attacks (or heals) with each character's Hyper round.  A character in Hyper mode who has been buffed by an ally and is exploiting an enemy weakness will deal SEVERAL TIMES as much damage as their basic attack would.
You need to "sneak in" buffs and heals and ability-recharging Defend commands during the rounds while Hyper Mode is still charging, then unleash the fury on the proper turn.  This is pretty much mandatory in the 2 tougher difficulties.  In any case, spamming the basic repeatable attacks won't get you much further than 6 feet under - you need to strategize and think a few turns ahead if you want to be successful, and the game rewards you if you line your abilities up properly.  It's a blast and ensures that each fight feels meaningful and they never become repetitive as you are always learning new abilities and (eventually) have 10 party members in combinations of 4 combatants at a time, meaning your options are always expanding and changing.
The story, as I said above, is very much like Lunar or Lunar: Eternal Blue in that there are high stakes and a serious undercurrent, but the snappy dialogue and irreverent banter give the moment-to-moment gameplay a lighthearted feel that balances the darker aspects of the main threat and villains.
There are some niggles, to be sure.  No option to change key bindings, issues with the game crashing when changing resolutions, issues with battles sometimes freezing (the poison status ailment is involved somehow), but honestly it shouldn't detract much from your enjoyment as long as you remember to save often (which you can, since you can save after virtually every battle).  I'm willing to bet most of this will be updated or patched out in the coming months in any case.
Kudos to Bill and Robert and the boys at Hyperduck - this is an amazing accomplishment and a hell of a lot of fun to anyone who pines for the days of Phantasy Star IV and Chrono Trigger.

tl;dr
Starbound, that one game made by that one company that is pretty good.
*FULL REVIEW*
Disclaimer:
This game is changing with every update, this review may change over time. And/or may be inaccurate at this point.
Edit: The review might be inaccurate at this point due to the huge update that came out on the 28th of January, 2015.
Starbound is a 2D voxel-based sci-fi scroller made by the UK-based company Chucklefish. Similar to Terraria you move around through the procedurally generated 2D world collecting resources and upgrading your equipment. So what is the difference you might ask?
Gameplay:
Gameplaywise I'l have to compare Terraria and Starbound, the basic gameplay mechanics like mining and fighting are pretty much the same, but in spaaaace. While it doesn't offer all that many items that change much in the gameplay (like the climbing claws) the basic model of Starbounds gameplay feels more refined.  Jumping is smoother, mining is easier(not too easy though), fighting works better.  And then you have the multitude of worlds to explore.
The World:
In Starbound you play as one of six races including Humans, Hylotl(the fish people) and Apex(super-apes), and are thrown into an immense world full of different and beautiful worlds ranging from low-gravity desert planets to high-gravity jungles. Every world has it's own enviroment and difficulty which makes every place you go to feel unique even if you know that there are probably other worlds similar to the one you just discovered. Infact, in the vast universe, feels, in a way, ancient. Not so little civilazation to make it feel empty, but enough to make it feel like there used to be something bigger. Mysterious and beautiful.
Graphics and Sound Design:
Despite some people saying different, I found that the music fit the game pretty perfectly, it got even better through time. It made the experience of discovery so much better for me. I felt like I was in an episode of Star Trek, just without Spock... Oh yeah, the game also looks pretty good for a 2D game. It sure feels "sci-fi-ish".
Multiplayer:
If you have not noticed yet, Starbounds strongest selling point is it's exploration. Just for your information, you can do it in multiplayer, too. It's pretty fun, you should try it. (Since I haven't played in a while, there might or not still be some connectivity issues)
Exploration:
As I mentioned above, strongest selling point, so there should be a section for that. Exploration is made fun through the worlds, the fresh combat and your Ship. Ah yes, you ship. This flying base is modular and can be taken anywhere. A savior, a home, your beacon of hope in this tough but beautiful cosmos.
Cons:
- Weapon variety. A lot of weapons but none that feel too different in my opinion.
- Some small problems with connectivity.(?)
Final Verdict:
A must have if you enjoy side scrollers, Sci-Fi and exploration. mysterious and fun to play. Best played in SP w/ breaks off to the multiplayer if you ask me.

I purchased this game shortly after its release, having been enthralled by Enemy Unknown. The sequel proved in every way as engaging, tough and absolutely addictive as the first chapter. I played it on average difficulty and it still took me over 80 hours to complete the campaign given the amount of loading and replaying I had to go through. And you know what? I enjoyed every minute of it. It is a very hard game (at times insanely hard), but it is also an extremely rewarding experience once one has mastered all the tactical options one needs to avoid getting his soldiers killed. And, just like in the first game, the fully customizable characters become somewhat similar to close friends as you follow their adventures mission after mission. Seeing any one of them die made me  load the latest save every time.
Gameplay has really reached perfection here, so the point that XCOM 2 plays like an extremely complex and multi-layered game of chess. And every move can mean victory or defeat for your team. But tactical combat has always been only one part of the XCOM franchise, and the whole strategy and management parts are still there, definitely more polished than in the first game.
I've experienced no serious bugs or crashes, not even as early as February 2016, There were (and still are) all those funny glitches with invisible aliens, soldiers shooting through walls and so on but they aren't a big issue and they never spoiled the fun of playing XCOM 2. I'm currently replaying the campaign after purchasing all DLC packages. I've heard a lot of criticism about the DLC scenarios, but I still have to play those extra missions, so I hope all the disappointed reviewers were wrong. :)
Overall a fantastic game, one of the best I've played in my life, so imnsho it's a 10/10.

Broader review
While lacking the polish of a typical AAA or even AA game, CSH does have its charms, especially when it comes to combat and the retro appeal of the games it found inspiration in. Being a huge fan of both Chrono Trigger and Phantasy Star 4 (god those online PS games were garbage) I had to pick this up right away.
The good -
Combat, character choice, and the fighting system take a little bit to get used to but they're fantastic. It's honestly some of the best combat in an RPG I've seen in a very long time.
The music is great and totally fits the genre and tone of the game. It's a good mix of Chrono Trigger and Phantasy Star.
The combat graphics, map graphics, and much of the animations are very Chrono Trigger. The menu comes a lot from Phantasy Star (as well as some of the options in combat). The main character is very remniscent of Alys Brangwin (though lacking an understudy like Chaz). The option of reminding yourself what you're doing if you're stuck or coming back from a break is great (better than Phantasy Star's which could occasionally be confusing) though I'm not sure the game is really long enough to warrent it in most situations.
The descriptions of monsters is usually pretty good when you curser over them.
The first mission is actually done very well, as is most of the layouts of "dungeons" and whathave you.
The average -
The humor is okay. It's not great. It's welcome and sometimes spot on but just as often misses the mark and is a little too predictable.
The weapon shops are pretty pointless as they are in most older JRPG type games. You literally walk to the store of the next town and always buy your upgrade. There might as well just be a guy standing there that upgrades your equipment for you for a fee, since there's nothing that new weapons bring to the game but bigger stats. The shield shops, many times, give more meaningful choices since they're your source of... "classes" so to say with their moves and effects.
Some of the ability effects are kind of random and not very pretty. Looking at a lot of teamwork abilities the protagonist uses.
Sound effects aren't anything to shake a stick at.
Game came out fairly buggy but it's charm made me stick it out for updates and I even helped with some bug catching.
The games this is based from never had any kind of map but I feel like at this point some kind of even rudimentary minimap would have been helpful in some form.
The price point seems about right on.
The bad -
Launch was a little bit of a mess.
While I know the game isn't designed to be as epic and long as CT or PS4 I do feel that the first six or so chapters go far too fast and it doesn't really give the player much time to absorb things. Which it makes sense, in a way, there isn't enough time for the player to appreciate or really process what's happening until they get through the sort of opening of the game.
Some of the reasons people join your "party" are fairly ambiguous at best. After the first four characters are in your party people just seem to fall into your party with little reason or commentary. Considering the game doesn't take itself too seriously that's probably not neccessarily a bad thing... but it did turn me off.
Controls are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for keyboard though I'm pretty sure they'll fix it in the future. Currently there's no remapping of controls. Play with a controller.

I'm already in love with this game after a mere 90 minutes.
I'm a huge fan of old-school 16 bit-era JRPG's, and i've played damn near every recent homage/throwback/retro version of 16-bit JRPG's that has come out over the past few years. Unfortunately, very few of them actually come close to capturing the same feeling that games like Chrono Trigger and FFIII gave (and continue to give) me.
Cosmic Star Heroine, in the little bit that i have played, has already managed to do so. The writing so far has been really good, the graphics and environments are nice, and the character designs have a great style reminiscent of Phantasy Star (which is a huge plus, in my book).
Most important of all, however, is the combat system. It is excellent, and has a deceptive amount of depth. There are no Magic Points or Skill Points. Rather, most skills can only be used once in each battle before they are locked off. In order to use them again, you must use your Defensive move, which refreshes all of your skills. This sounds cumbersome and slow, but it is anything but. Battles are actually pretty fast-paced for JRPG standards.
There are other interesting aspects as well, such as the Hyper meter; every few turns, your character gets a turn in Hyper Mode, causing any attack or healing that they do in that turn to be significantly amplified. As such, you must plan ahead and strategize when you will use each skill. It adds a great strategic layer to the combat, and you can't just simply spam the same skills over and over. There are also items that can do damage, cause ailments, or heal, that are shared between all party members. These items aren't spent with use, and refresh at the end of each battle, adding yet another layer. Once you get a few party members (which takes no time at all), the combat takes on a wonderful amount of depth . One character, for example, has a skill that causes her next ability to target all enemies (or allies, if it's a heal or buff). So if you know she's going to enter Hyper Mode in 2 turns, you can use that skill, then in the next turn hit the entire enemy party with her most powerful attack (which is usually single target). This may sound simple, but when you have numerous characters in your party and a wealth of skills, items, and abilities at your disposal, it becomes a strategic chess match. You must plan ahead, especially on higher difficulties (i'm playing on hard, and have already had some very tough battles).
Definitely check this out if you're a fan of 16-bit era RPG's, or just quality JRPG's in general. I can't wait to play more!

FYI: I'm not an expert on the Phantasy Star series, nor do I have much experience with the 90's RPG's
(except Final Fantasies, and some older Enix RPG's like Terranigma, etc.). Also I've only played this game for 5hrs, so far (and I'm hooked!)
I totally love the art-style of this game. It looks really nice. The cutscenes may look a little different, though but they still look nice and do a nice job adding to the athmosphere.
The next thing I really like is the soundtrack! It has some guitar influences and it also adds to the mood quite good. I hope that I'll be able to buy the soundtrack!
The game itself basically seems kinda straight forward. At least the first 5-6 hours are.
You're running/walking around and go through battle after battle and read lots of story related stuffs (mostly conversations). The map design so far isn't confusing, meaning you won't get lost that easily. Still you'll be able to find hidden Stuff. Also you sometimes get to do some small "quests" which offer a reward (either credits or equipment).
So far I haven't seen a "real" world map, only a city map which resembles to be a world map, therefore you won't be able to stray off too far. Given the fact that this games main feature is the story line, that's fine.
The battles are turn based and require you to use your skills in a sensible way. Especially at the beginning (Hard difficulty) you get into real trouble, if you mess around too much. After a while it gets easier, though (new party members, new skills, etc.) To successfully win the battles you have to think ahead, when you will use the different skills, because most of them can't be spammed. Most skills are "depleted" after one use but if you take a defensive stance for one turn, you'll get to use them, again.
One thing that wasn't clear for me at the beginning was the item-system. Usually in rpg's most items deplete if you use them but in this game, you can use once per battle. They won't be lost after using them. But to emphasize the tactical part of the game, you're forced to choose which items you'll be using in battle, meaning at the beginning of the game you may only equip 3 items. Between the battle, though, you may choose your loadout as you will.
Later on you'll be able to add more than 3 items to your loadout.
Also you'll be able to choose your party members, once you've progressed far enough through the story (haven't been able to do so, yet but there's a menu for that).
The characters are quite charming and offer a great variety of different skills (which btw. you can choose up to 6 for your current loadout per character)

Cosmic Star Heroine is a JRPG from the makers of Cthulhu Saves the World and Breath of Death 7. Designed to resemble a 16bit SNES RPG, Cosmic Star Heroine is clearly inspired by other classic JRPGs such as Chrono Trigger. Just looking at it causes the nostalgia to drag me back into my childhood.
With that being said, there are issues that bothered me as I played the game.
One of the first things that really bugged me was interacting with NPCs. You can walk through (most) NPCs and for whatever reason you have to be in a perfect spot to trigger dialog, which can be really frustrating, I often found myself walking around in circles around a NPC until I could actually get the chance to open dialog with them.
The combat, while it didn't really seem to be a big issue at first, ended up being one of the most frustrating factors of the game. I am sure the developers thought they were doing something "cool" or "unique", but all it really did was make fights longer and more annoying.
Characters have skills, abilities, items and "programs", all of these things have like a cooldown on them, so while in the midst of combat you can't just spam one thing. The issue is, not all characters have a basic attack to rely on while in combat, so eventually you are going to find some of your party members have nothing else to offer besides waiting a few turns to recharge their skills or abilities. It's stupid and poorly thought out.
Besides that, you can't really "grind" in this game, because from what I've seen, monsters are not recurring, they are scripted, so while you might encounter a monster in a area, you can't simply walk around to continue to fight it for more money or experience. And grinding is one of the biggest draws to RPGs, it's watching numbers go up.
The writing is yawn inducing. With RPGs of this nature there should be a balance that you strive to achive as far as it comes to dialog, unfortunately I often found myself just autoscrolling through mounds of text because I really couldn't find the energy to care about their poorly written story.
The map layouts are really forgettable, for the most part they take a fairly linear path, which may occasionally branch out for a few steps or walk back up upon itself, but it never really goes far enough to actually encourage exploration.
The game is mostly fine, even with it's tedious combat, terrible writing and uninspired maps. I just feel like it was really overhyped and as a direct result, the end product just doesn't feel as good.

Zeboyd has done it again! Cosmic Star Heroine is a 16 bit masterpiece! Amongst recent games such as Breath of the Wild, Persona 5, and Mass Effect: Andromeda, CSH is an indie game that draws upon one of the strongest forces in video gaming.
Nostalgia.
And boy does it work. From the very beginning, you're thrown into a detailed world full of highly stylized sprites, incredibly well-done backgrounds, and a fun and catchy soundtrack. It gets better from there. Different from previous games by Zeboyd, The gameplay is reminiscint of Chrono Trigger, with enemies visible on the main map and battles conducted on the screen, eliminating screen-switching entirely. This coupled with maps that are vibrant and alive, full of detail and color evoke memories of Lunar, Phantasy Star, and other 16 bit series.
There has been much detail poured into this game as well. So many little things make the worlds feel vibrant and alive, such as bugs running around on the ground, or birds that fly off when you approach too closely. Ambient sounds also make you feel immersed, as the hum of a generator getting louder and quiter as you approach and distance yourself.
The writing is interesting as well; interacting with NPC characters results in amusing references to previous Zeboyd games, anime, observations regarding the world you are playing in, and nods to the RPG genre in general.
The game is quite forgiving, as most battles can be won with a little bit of attention, even on 'Heroine' (Hard?) difficulty, and explains the unique mechanics utilized in battle via a short 3-stage tutorial. If you are a fan of classic RPG games, then this game will certainly trigger your memories and evoke the same excitement as you experienced with those. And if you're not a fan of the series, but want to try to get into it, CSH is an excellent choice.

I'm often a fan of experimental and artistic games, and this one certainly has its merits, but I do not think it is worth even the small price of £2.79.  The main issue, as many have mentioned, is the length.  It is a very short experience indeed, and unlike, say, The Stanley Parable, it has no replay value at all.  The player has no control over the narrative; there are some controls you can use to look around, idly fiddle with stuff and such, but the narrative will soldier on whatever you do, or indeed, even if you do nothing.  That's a shame; a veneer of 'immersion' with no substance.  It's very clear that the game is pretty much made by one person; I'm not sure whether it was a university project, but it does seem like one.  The graphics aren't amazing, even on the highest settings I felt like Julian was made of papier mâché, and the story all takes place in one small room, so most of the work clearly went into the script, and most of the budget to the voice acting.
The story itself is poignant and relatable, though the main character occasionally jars the relatability with a racist comment or a crude but oddly coy internal discussion about sex.  The voice acting is quite good, but occasionally clashes with the script creating an odd dissonance between the actor and the writer.  If only the actor had felt able to paraphrase and improvise a little, it might have come off more naturally.
Play it if it's free; buy it if you're interested and it's at least 50% off in a sale.  That isn't rare.  I feel depressed after playing it, but that's because it sometimes reminded me of myself and my own internal monologue, and it does this well.  If only the character were even more relatable, I could recommend this more heartily.

Turn-based RPG, before the days of the active time battle, there were the originals, this is a remake of Final Fantasy III originally released exclusively in Japan for the "Family Computer" ... That's how old the mechanics/storyline are. HOWEVER, there have been quite a few tweaks made to bring it up to date with what you would expect of a good RPG ... In the 90's. As far as storyline goes, it's pretty bland and generic. Collect the crystals, beat the bad guys, save the world. It does have some hidden humorous elements in it, but they're few and far between. This game is badly dated, but it's still a solid essential for a Final Fantasy fan, and it is enjoyable up to about level 40, when the grind from 40-60 begins, it will take you about three hours on a good day, and you pretty much need to be 60 to beat the game. DO NOT go into this game thinking you will 100% every aspect of it, and if you do, for the sake of sanity, make sure you kill every sea creature while you still have your sea boat, or you'll be SOL for getting that beastiary achievement. You will not want to replay this game. Sad but true, it's just not that immersing compared to later Final Fantasy games.
There are no voiceovers as seen in FFIV, there are summons, which are cool.
TL;DR
Grindfest, random-battle hell, old-school level up, good world maps, sometimes even surprising, bosses are not overly frustrating (There is no boss in this game that will one-shot your entire party* like later Final Fantasy games), bland storyline, decent graphics, decent amount of secrets. Overall a B- as far as RPGs are considered. There just isn't much to this game to compare with newer titles.

Lego the Hobbit is a great game with some flaws.
Firstly, the game is very fun to play - as with most lego games. It's enjoyable, well-paced, exciting and fun with a very diverse cast of lego characters and a nice range of levels and backdrops. the game LOOKS great - even the lego pieces have shadows and effects on them, and they really feel a part of the enviroment.
The sound design is also great, the voice acting is nice if a little repetative (excluding the narrator, who never gets boring) and the music is well-selected, and with one of the red bricks, you can even make the music more "retro".
The world is massive, suprisingly, and there's a ton of stuff to do from solving puzzles to find bricks or helping people out for the same reason. turning in one of the mithril items you have forged to someone gives you a red brick, a special extra item that gives you a bonus - while not consuming the item itself.
However the game does have flaws.
Because of the treasure system, allowing your character to equip [retty much everything in the game - characters have a problem with not feeling unique or needed. The only TRULY needed character is Saruman and Sauron, as they have specific functions exclusive to them that can only be unlocked through mithril treasure items.
Currency is also fairly worthless. The problem with studs is, because everything is so cheap, it's almost pointless to grind for money at all - even Sauron, the most unique and one of the most useful characters, costs just 75,000 studs - less than one full missions worth, in certain missions.
The game also has some notable performance issues. The game will sometimes lag massively, crash and bug out - and it's for some reason incompatible with windows Aero despite coming out in 2014.
Finally, the big characters like the trolls and the ork beserker are pointless. they're only used in the overworld, they can't be used in ANY level, and they only serve as yet ANOTHER mechanic to restrict the player and for no reason either! I do like the trolls design and the idea of using them but, because of the sheer lack of need for them (seriously there's like five things they can interact with) they serve almost no purpose. The game has so MANY mechanics that it dilutes the game severely as a result. Fewer mechanics with a smaller roster, even a mission or two less, would've felt a lot better.
I really enjoyed Lego: The Hobbit, but it;'s not a game i'd reccomend completing. Almost your entire game will be doing the quests, which wil start fun and end up an annoying mess. Buy it, have fun with it, but don't complete it unless you're fine with the above points.

It became evident, from the very first footage I saw of Heat Signature back in 2014, that this was going to be my kind of game. Now obviously I am fairly biased, having followed this game's developement for such a long time. If this game was released in its very early beta stages I would probably still have been all over it.
Now, with that out of the way:
Heat Signature is a top-down, Hotline Miami-style stealth game in which you use your small infiltrator ship to dock with bigger space ships full of guards and carry out different kinds of missions.
While I find Hotline Miami to be the closest comparison there are two major additions to the gameplay. First off: the game is set in a randomly generated galaxy that you can roam freely and gradually take over. Secondly, pausing the game not only let's you catch your breath and take in your surroundings, but also lets you line up shots and instantly swap items, making the challenge of sneaking through the various ships more based on figuring out a good tactic rather than twitchy, fast-paced action.
The game has a heavy focus on gameplay. "Well of course it does! It's a game innit?", well yes, but I'd actually go as far as to say this game has a bigger focus on player input than any other game I've ever played. While playing this game I feel like I'm making important decisions literally every second. Upon starting the game, you are not met by a loading screen, or a bunch of logos, or even a title screen. You are taken directly into the game.
"But this is a stealth game, right? Stealth games usually involve a lot of waiting."
Yes. Sometimes, like in most stealth games, you might want to wait for that one guard to take this particular patrol route before you continue making your way through the ship. This is where another one of my favourite features of this game comes to play; the fast forward-button. At any point in the game, you can press the F-key to speed up time. This will make even the longest travels through space last only a couple of seconds and also means that waiting for that guard becomes almost a non-factor.
This is what I love about this game. Everything is built from the ground up to make sure that the you are never bored and you never feel like you're just "along for the ride". It is what I feel every game should strive for. This is an interactive media and I would like if more games embraced that as much as Heat Sig.
Now I could go on, gushing about all the different features and mechanics of this game, but since you're reading this review you've probably already seen the lauch trailer so it feels a bit redundant. This game is super cool. It has teleporters and space ships and hacking and swords and really, really, really good writing.
Buy it. Play it. Then buy it again. Give this man your money so I can get more games like this.

WOW. The Steam Community completely failed this game. This is the reason these games don't exist - you try to make a game that does new things, and the gamers flood in, play for 10 minutes, then stamp a negative review on a game they shouldn't have been playing anyway. Why would you play a game you're conceptually opposed to, and not willing to learn? You were told from the start that this game has open PvP and stiff penalty for death. If you can't stomach that, why are you here? That's a freaking core game mechanic! Why kill progress for a niche group who desperately wants something like this to grow? At least 90% of the games out there are happy to cater to your childish mentality, where death means nothing more than a free teleport back to town and fully restored health.
This game was suggested to me years ago. One look at the game's Steam page and the horrible reviews, and I was convinced it was a shoddy game. Recently, I went back and actually read the reviews, and realized that the negative reviews painted a picture of a game that was exactly what I wanted to play.
Now since the gamer swarm fell on this developer, the same gamers who complain about the mainstream gaming industry's general lack of anything new whilst simultaneously lambasting this independent developer's free (FREE!!!) game for daring to try something new, because of that terrible failure of logic, this game's community and development stands weak and stunted.
I've never been killed by another player. I WAS attacked by one, though. What happened? A hero swooped in and pounded his♥♥♥♥♥into the dirt. Yes, I've been killed pretty frequently by NPCs, and yes, I raged, but you know what? I picked myself back up, went back to the NPC that killed me, and stole ALL of my gear BACK. And that feels AWESOME. That sort of epic♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't happen in other MMO's, and it's largely the fault of the community of gamers in general. I can't think of anything more shameful than such an example of holding back the progress of the hobbies you claim to love.
This game is a solid 10/10. You just have to know what you're getting into. I'm more than willing to consider legitimate criticism of this game. For instance, I hate the fact that the camera doesn't center on the player, arbitrarily limiting your field of vision severely. I hate that you have to click tiny, pixel-sized pieces of gold in order to pick them up. But the fact that the game has open PvP and stiff penalties for death are not legitimate criticisms, they're central freaking game mechanics. They are what make the game a unique and adventurous experience. If you can't take more than 30 minutes to learn what this game essentially is, you have no business rating it at all.

«Yesterday» («Вчера») выглядит как симпатичная трехмерная игра-головоломка, разработанная китайской командой инди-разработчиков.
Полагаю, что это очень короткая игра, потому что я закончил первый уровень менее чем за полчаса, а всего в игре 6 уровней.
Графика в игре хорошая, выполненная в минималистском стиле.
Игровой процесс напомнил мне своего рода Кубик Рубика (или Магический Кубик) с различными способами решения головоломок.
Уровни идут от простого к сложному. Думаю, что они понравятся любителям головоломок.
В «Yesterday» есть только одна музыкальная тема. Она довольно хороша, но может надоесть, если игра продлится больше часа.
В игре нет полноэкранного режима. В меню игры почти нет опций: вы можете изменить громкость музыки, прочитать имена разработчиков и выйти из игры.
Игра выглядит как мобильный порт, потому управление неудобное для компьютера.
«Yesterday» - это стандартная игра на движке Unity, сделанная скорее для планшетов, а не для компьютеров.
«Yesterday» претендует на то, чтобы быть философской игрой о свиданиях и любви, но терпит в этом неудачу из-за очень плохого перевода. Игра не способна показать чувства и проблемы в романтических отношениях из-за низкокачественного перевода. Эта проблема и была для меня основной причиной не рекомендовать «Yesterday».

I quite enjoyed playing XCOM 2 despite its shortcomings. The character customization options are great, the in-between the battles (i.e. when you plan your missions and try to form a resistance network) adds a lot of flavour to the game, and the different classes make it interesting as a strategy game. The story is a bit strange, but engaging enough.
I still have to say that XCOM 2 is not as great as a strategy game as I hoped, and frankly, my list of criticisms is long.
One of the central aspects is taking cover, and this system is very rudimentary - the game only distinguishes between "high" and "low" cover, meaning that cowering behind a low concrete pillar will give your soldier the same cover bonus as behind a railing (!).
The game is similarly counter-intuitive when determining the chances of making a successful shot and will brush off firing through a lot of obstructions such as destroyed walls, but don't you think you're going to hit a guy with shoulders as broad as a truck taking cover right before you on the other side of a tree.
This brings me to the whole system of calculating hit chances. As mentioned before, proximity in particular seems to be accounted for less than it reasonably should be, but fine. The problem is that there are a lot of attacks which do not require a hit check.
The worst example comes from the grenardier: he might miss the guy standing two metres away behind a tree stump while firing at him with a freaking GATLING GUN, but will never have any trouble bouncing off a grenade off a van to blow up the guy hiding behind it thirty meters away. In short, it is beyond me why grenades have a 100% hit chance.
The hit chance issue leads into what I'd like to call "Why PSI operatives are freaking ridiculous and shouldn't exist". You see, PSI operatives have a number of insanely powerful abilities, almost none of which require hit checks, and to top it off the offensive ones ignore armor as well.
Unlike regular soldiers, they are trained in a special facility and may acquire one of three randomly picked skills every five in-game days, and they may learn all of their available talents and basically become Charles Xavier minus the leg thing.
While most abilities have relatively high cooldowns, this is nowhere near enough to make them balanced. For example, the powerful PSI operative talent "Void Rift" is quite comparable to the Specialist's highest tier skill "Capacitor Discharge" - only that the damage output is slightly higher, and instead of being a once-a-mission talent it has a cooldown of 5 turns.
Perhaps the single most useful ability of the PSI operative is the simple "Stasis Shield" which allows you to stun any target (becomes invincible) for one turn. This works on any enemy - compare this to the Specialists' "Haywire Protocol" which has a CHANCE of stunning a MECHANICAL enemy. Granted, you may also seize control with Haywire, but the odds are bad, in particular for very strong enemies. On the other hand, Stasis reliably removes one foe, so you can just clean up everything else and jump them afterwards.
You think I am done already? Nope. Because Stasis Shield is one of the abilities that doesn't end your turn. Thus it is possible to first remove one enemy and then use "Domination" to take control of another (at least, this one is once-per-mission). This makes even large groups trivial.
In fact, I have recently finished an Iron Man game on the Commander difficulty level with zero deaths, and frankly, from the time I got my first PSI guy I just steamrolled everything. I then trained a second one for good measure, and at this point I did not even bother with advancing carefully any longer. During one mission, I obliterated all of the 12 end-game enemies on the map in a single combat because PSI Operatives are just so ridiculously powerful.
Perhaps the dumbest thing in this game is enemy sight, i.e. how enemies react to approaching squads.
You start the game in concealment, which basically means the sight radius of all enemies is heavily reduced; as soon as you attack an opponent, concealment is broken and ALL your squadmates will basically be visible for every enemy. There is no such thing as hiding behind a pillar and making an ambush, as the aliens are apparently all psychics.
On the other side, they are also all functionally blind and deaf, as a group of aliens might watch their brethren - who are standing mere meters away from them, i.e. clearly IN their sight radius - being shot and killed, but no way they're going to go in the direction of the obvious firefight. But should you enter their sight radius because you are pushing forward or playing a scout and trying to engage in close combat, their attack will be triggered and now you suddenly have another patrol on your hands (this massively decreases the usability of using swords).
Also, whenever combat is triggered (i.e. an enemy which was previously unaware of your squad sees them) all enemies will get a turn to hide behind covers.
This may feel a bit unfair at first (why do aliens get this interruption turn but I don't?) and is very counter-intuitive when breaking concealment (I'm making a surprise attack on the enemies, but they react faster than my squad?), but later it becomes obvious that it is a cover-up for an AI which can't handle reacting to player activity in the area (the aforementioned problem - enemy groups always mindlessly patrol the map until they spot a singular soldier somewhere).
The high number of missions with a time limit is probably another attempt at obscuring these issues, as it forces you to move faster and therefore increase the chance of running into enemies unprepared (otherwise, you could really just sit on a spot for ten to twenty turns, obliterate any patrol in this area, and then rinse and repeat twenty meters ahead).
Long story short - XCOM 2 has a lot of gameplay shortcomings.
But unlike for example "The Banner Saga", another one of the very few turn-based strategy games, it was easy to get accustomed to them and still enjoy XCOM 2 a lot.
Final conclusion: XCOM 2 is overall a good game, buy it if you enjoy turn-based strategy. If you're willing to try an oldie, Jagged Alliance 2 might be for you - it is rather simliar, but far superior strategy-wise (in my opinion). Just don't get Banner Saga.

TL/DR An excellent AC game that suffered from an abysmal launch, but which is fairly playable at this point.
The story of Unity is nothing special, but fully adequate.  One doesn't necessarily play AC for the story anyway, but it carries along nicely from the more recent games.
It's pretty easy to get around. My one complaint involves getting down from a roof. Arno simply doesn't like it, no matter how many times you push the buttons, causing me to constantly look for alternative, non-lethal jumps.
Of course, there's still that "My assassin is an idiot" feel when you are running down the street and suddenly jump onto an urn someone left behind, sitting there perched like an imbecile.  You jump off, but instead of landing on the ground, you make a magnificent leap onto a bench across the street.  Jumping from the bench, you now grab onto the beams over a doorway.  Arno, you idiot. I just want to be on the fricking ground!
Combat is fairly nice and responsive, but somewhat repetitive.  You mostly just swing, parry, etc.
Stealth is difficult, as the AI can see you in the most unlikely way.  Still, successfully going stealthy will usually make your life easier, although in most instances you can get caught and just slaughter everyone, regardless.
Co-op is a blast.  You can do free roam together and there are quite a lot of co-op quests. Some of these list as being for 4 players, but we've handled all of them with just 2.  You continue to get rewards for completing co-op quests even after you've done them a time or two.
It's highly unlikely that you will get 60fps on Ultra. I have a 980m with 16 gb of RAM and a 3.,5 ghz processor and get about 45. Medium graphics still look nice. Low graphics look...awful.
I haven't encountered any bugs.

This game has many lazy/cringeworthy parts to offset its potential, which I am listing below.
Good parts:
1) Battle system has style and disables some moves to bypass spamming the same techniques ad nauseum.
2) Nice overall cutscene quality and soundtrack to reminisce the Sega CD days.
3) Bosses can actually be affected by stun/poison, actually making room for strategy.
4) A type of adrenaline system so characters can continue fighting with 0 hp or gain an aura to do more damage motivates battles.
Here are the parts I couldn't stand.  First of all, it is very counter-intuitive; why can't alt+enter full screen this?  I don't even know about the manual they talk about.  To bypass this experience, go to system before starting a new game.  Otherwise you will be dumbfounded by tab being the menu key, escape quitting the game, and an inability to change that tiny window.
Now that is out of the way, here are parts I can't avoid:
1) Lazy/ripped off references.  I would rather play Phantasy Star IV with Alys/Chaz than these Alyssa/Chana ripoffs. Cosmic Star Heroine advocates inspiration, but it feels lazy.  At least the 3rd character is named Dave and not Chronos.
2) The Beast lacks cutscenes.  After Dave asks why won't the monster die, Alyssa kills it without a cutscene and the screen turns black.  What are we, little kids who trigger over death?  Also, I kid you not, he is generically called The Beast, and has none of the swag from X-Men's Beast.  The lazy part is the game makes a cutscene to show some chief type character with light reflecting off his sunglasses, but they fade to black and show the beast crushed by something rather than show the action to completely kill the mood and make me quit.
3) Chahn is completely derivative, unlike Alyssa who just has a similar name to Alys.  It just makes me lose complete immersion in the game.  Regarding Chahn's derivative nature, she has a red headband like PSIV's Chaz, and humatama equipped (hints at Phoenix Wright's magatama for a mystical origin). Chahn's movesets for her gunmancy (I kid you not) is that unique abilities for her would be to attack everyone by wasting a turn, or repeat her last gunmancy, which kinda undermines the point of style with this battle system to not repeat moves, though her fire attack is decent; better than using stupid healing guns, which I feel the other characters do much better. I will compare to the other 2 characters which are far better: Dave can stun/poison bosses, and Alyssa has many different attributes for weapons, so you can really fine-tune for weaknesses.
4) Weaknesses for enemies are automatically shown. As someone who doesn't play a lot of JRPG style games I was a little hesitant to pick this one up (I only have a handful in my library and most of them I have never played).  So far I have only completed the first 2 chapters I am very glad I bought this.
As some of the other reviews point out, the flow of the combat and the pacing of the story so far is a little on the quick side, which really appeals to "non-jrpg'ers" like me who don't want a long drawn out snail-paced story which requires endless backtracking and grinding.
The difficulty level can be adjusted mid-game so that also helps as well.  I left it on default (the 2nd easiest setting) and it feels right for me, it makes it just hard enough so I have to strategize a little in larger fights.
I am definitely looking forward to playing the rest of this.
*UPDATE* - After completing the story I can definitely say that this is my favorite game this year (so far).
The abiity to save anywhere was a really big plus for me, as I rarely had a big enough block of time to sit for a couple hours.  Also, as I previously mentioned above, the adjustable difficulty on the fly is nice as well.  I ended up increasing the difficulty to the 2nd hardest (Heroine) after I got the hang of things around Chapter 4 or 5 and it felt right. It wasn't overwhelmingly hard but I still died a few times against some of the bosses.
The story isn't award winning but I felt it was well written and structured in a way so that new characters joining your party didn't feel forced or unbelievable.  It also kept up the pace that is starts with, which can be good or bad depending how you look at it.  I myself loved it as it kept me interested and I didn't want some long dragged out story with multiple branches that don't move the plot forward at all.  The downside to the fast paced story is that there really wasn't enough time for character development, so it's hard to get attached to any of them.
I read a lot of other reviews pointing out a lot of bugs, but I didn't notice any through my whole playthrough (and I started playing the day after it was released, before some of the patches).  I am not saying that bugs weren't there, as obviously there were due to the need of those patches, but I must have gotten lucky.  Also, with one of the latest patches adding achievements I was a little disappointed that none of my previous accomplishments were counted, including defeating the "mystery boss" next to the mines.  Which took me quite a few tries even above level 40.
Overall... Awesome game!  If you were a fan back in the day of the old JRPG's and are looking for something that can be played in your spare time here and there this is definitely it.

First off - I'm a huge fan of the Final Fantasy series, so I might be a little biased because of that.
So what makes this game good? In my opinion it's the job system and a fantastic world is the main strengths of this game. The job system allows the party characters to switch between classes (like warrior, monk, black mage, etc.) giving them access to a variety of skills and equipment unique to each class and each job can be leveled up alongside the characters' "normal" level.
The world is vast and has a good variety of towns, caves and temples. Without spoiling too much it's also wonderful that the world is a lot bigger than you might initially think.
As for the gameplay it's a fairly traditional JRPG - especially if you've been playing the older FF games before. It's a turn-based battle system that allows the faster characters or enemies to strike first when commands are selected. You do have all the time you want to select commands, though, meaning there is time to be strategic.
While not overly difficult, you'll have to grind once in a while if you want to be strong enough to progress. I'm not going to put that down as a positive or negative thing as that is very much up to the individual. It's especially important in late game, though, and crucial if you're planning to take on some of the games optional bosses.
If you're looking to go for a Perfect Game (obtain all achievements) you should be prepared to grind relentlessly as some of the achievements here are incredibly time-consuming.
If I'm not mistaken this is a port of the iOS version (which is more or less identical to the DS version), which means updated graphics. It's not beautiful, but it has a certain charm to it - and it's definitely an upgrade from the original graphics.
The soundtrack also deserves a mention - it's good. As in really good. It contains revamped versions of Nobuo Uematsu's original compositions for the NES version of the game - I haven't heard the originals myself, so I can't compare, but the new versions are definitely solid.
My main gripe with this game is the characters, though. There's so memorable NPCs but the party characters are pretty boring and with only a little background story to each. Even though more is revealed later in the game it's still not particularly satisfying.
The story isn't anything out of the ordinary either, although it isn't downright bad. If you've played older Final Fantasy-games before it's pretty much a classic "save the world using crystals"-story.
But besides a boring cast of party characters and a somewhat bland story, the game is still worthwhile if you're into more old-school JRPGs and don't mind the updated graphics. The gameplay, job system and the world are magnificent and should entertain most RPG-fans enough to make this a worthwhile purchase. Don't expect it to be as story-rich and complex as later entries in the Final Fantasy series, though.

Just to start off, if you're looking at this game as a potential gateway to getting into traditional JRPG's, don't bother.  It will only serve to put you off the genre all together.  There are just too many things, like lack of save points and some cheap bosses, for someone that may want to play a more old-school game and is looking at FFIII, the earliest available FF game on Steam, as the game to start out with.
That said, if you've played a lot of old RPG's growing up, you may find something more to your liking here.  The story and characters are simple.  There's no voice acting, no FMV cutscenes, no minimap or compass to point you in the right direction.  I found all of the above a benefit to the game.  The story parts would be slowed down by voice acting and the generic story would be exposed further if you had to listen to it and instead of just reading text.  While the game is fairly linear, it does a great job at points of making you wonder where to go and there's a real sense of exploration.  There's like five or more villages you don't ever have to go to for any reason that are just there, and despite them being pretty small, it's a cool little thing that you'd never see in a more modern game.
The big thing with this game is that in was the introduction of the job-swapping system found in the earlier FF's.  There are twenty plus jobs and they're handed out at set points in the story.  The big problem is the last set of jobs are unlocked extremely late in the game and this makes using them to their fullest a pain.  You can switch jobs on the fly but there's a small penalty to stats for x amount of fights.  It's not a big deal and will only hamper you for a handful of random battles.
The big downside to the game is complete lack of effort when redesigning the boss encounters and the final dungeon in its entirety.  Every boss fight boils down to the same thing.  A single enemy will have a strong physical attack that hits one character and strong magic attacks that hits everyone.  Bosses will also always use these attacks back to back without interruption.  This means any character, even with full HP, is liable to get KO'd if they get RNG unlucky when it comes to boss turns versus your characters' turns.  It's such a cheap, low-effort way to add difficulty when designing bosses.  Every turn of every boss fight eventually winds up with you casting a group heal spell on an already fully healed group just to deal with the oncoming attacks.
The last dungeon and it's surroundings is one of the worst in RPG's and I'm sure you can find detailed reasons why elsewhere.
There's a lot of talk about grinding being necessary in this game and I find that completely overblown.  I never stopped my progress for the explicit grinding of levels/ job levels and beat the game with levels in the very low 50's.  Grinding some levels would have helped for the last boss to serve as an HP buffer but it's not necessary.  As long as you don't continuously change your jobs, you should be able to handle anything the game can throw at you as long you fight every random encounter you come across.  The secret boss though would require a ton, and I mean a ton, of grinding and I didn't bother with it.
As for the port, it's a super low effort one of the mobile version, not the DS version.  This means stuff like the UI is ugly and created to be touch based, but lacking in touch suport or mouse control in menus in this version and is just poor all around.  Even things like loading your game while in-game is obtuse.  There are only three save slots for who knows what reason.  I also ran into a problem where all dialogue box text had some type of artifacting or something that I couldn't find a work around for.  All that said, it's still supposedly better the FFIV PC port, which doesn't even have the memorize battle cursor function because it wasn't included in the mobile version and has 15 FPS in battles.  I used the memorize function in FFIII so I'll be missing it when I eventually get around to playing FFIV.  Square just doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥with any of their PC ports so none of this should be a surprise.
Okay, since this was really long, here's a short answer as to whether you should buy and play this game.  Don't if you have no experience with older RPG's.  If you do and are fine with not having things like save points and easily obtainable reviving items, cheap bosses and a terrible final dungeon, you'd probably get some enjoyment out of FFIII.  It's an enjoyable, but clearly flawed game.

Short review. This is a plotless, characterless, timewasting grind.
Long Review.
Lets start with the basics. I used to play the old final fantasy games on the SNES, which were great and even now worth playing on an emulator. I saw this on sale, saw the job class system and was reminded of one of my favourite FF games with the same idea. I thought i'd enjoy this game even more with the enhanced graphics and suchlike. Wrong.
The job classes
I'm about a quarter of the way through the game and i'm about level 25 out of level 99 on my first job for each character. It is only because of reading the wiki page I find out that there is no significant benefit at all to mastering a class.
In the prior version, sticking with a class and mastering it was a good idea. If one of your characters mastered being a white mage, then you could select white magic as a secondary ability when you started a new class. This allowed for interesting and varied job combinations. This new version makes you start from scratch every time you start a new job. There are even better versions of the starting jobs which you will have to grind through again to make them any good since they will draw no benefit from having ground from the basic class. Utter time wasting and demoralising.
The characters
Weak and shallow. A few lines of dialogue to establish the basic idea and then thats it. You might get one line here and there to create the illusion that the characters have any depth, but really? I've not met one person in the game which with a worthwhile personality. Even the villains which should be the driving force of a game are non-exisitant. Once you've ground through a dungeon you get to meet someone with two lines of dialogue before you kill them. Yawn. This is just endless grinding, over and over.
The plot
Wait? There's a plot? Really? A few lines from some crystal to tell you that you're the chosen one and then you're off. Um... is that it? You bet it is. Save the world? Uh... it looks fine to me. No maurading armies, no cataclysmic natural disasters, no iconic villians with master plans. Just a vague reference to darkness being imbalanced. It's like a stoned aromatherapist ate some alphabet soup and♥♥♥♥♥♥out a story.
Overall
If you like endless grinding and having to start characters over again and again, not having to worry about plots, characters or indeed anything being memorable about the game, then this is the one for you.

After playing the Famicom version of this game, I was hesitant to give this remake a try.  I have to say I was pleasantly surprised at how much of an improvement this game made over the original.  Rather than make an essay about the changes, I'll go point-by-point.
+ Better graphics, obviously.  Granted, the Famicom version looked marvelous in the 8-bit era, but since this is a PC-optimized port of the DS game, I'm glad to see some 3D graphics in there.
+ Better story.  The plot was a lot looser in the original, and the characters had no backstory at all.  By assigning default names to each character and expanding on their origins, the plot feels more cohesive and I connect with the characters better.
+ Better use of the job system.  It's still not as crisp as Final Fantasy V, but the major gripe I had playing the Famicom version is that many job types became obsolete very quickly.  Some were never useful from the start, and the Scholar job was only necessary for one boss fight.  This remake changed all of that.  More jobs are useful for longer periods of time, and even in the late-game stages you can downgrade to a lesser job and still function well.
+ Better difficulty curve.  The original game was HARD.  Frankly, without a strategy guide, beating that game would have been near impossible.  But the remake softens the blow a lot and makes the game much more enjoyable.  You never feel like you're bringing the game to a screeching halt so that you can grind job levels or character levels.  It flows much more smoothly.
Overall, this game was in dire need of a remake, and this one does the job quite well.  If you've never played Final Fantasy III, or if the Famicom version left a bad taste in your mouth, then I strongly recommend picking this up.  You'll be glad you did.

The gameplay itself is fair enough; it's an enjoyable puzzle platformer set to Tolkien's wonderful universe, and I believe you'll get your money's worth in terms of entertainment - however, there are two reasons that makes me give it a downvote.

Given that story mode is only part of the gameplay, with the greater world of puzzles still being good value, I'm almost willing to overlook this fact.
What I can't ignore, however, is that some of the world puzzles are buggy or outright broken. Some can be played around, others cannot - in particular the Mithril Megapult schematics puzzle. This one is completely unobtainable for me due to a bug with the cave door it hides behind; it is a well-known bug, and none of the workaround suggestions I've found have fixed the issue I'm having. That means I'll never be able to actually complete the game, and that makes me feel cheated even more than the 'only two of three movies' story mode bit does.
All in all, a decent game brought down by some really annoying flaws. Given the title's age, I don't think it likely they'll ever be fixed, which is a pity.

I must tell you the story of Angel and Lacerta Antares. After a few good and a few failed characters, I decided that this prospective young lady would take a stand against violence. I did not accept any mission that involved killing, and not once did I kill a person, preferring stealth or knock out tactics. Unfortunately, on her 4th or so mission, Lacerta was captured by shielded foundry guards whom she could not knock out or run from with her equipment.
Back at the bar and a little bleak, I noticed a familiar name by the counter, Angel Antares. Her personal mission: rescue her daughter. Her name and her mission went perfect, but unlike her daughter, I decided Angel wouldn't make the same mistake. Liam Neeson style, it was Taken time. With her two trusty pistols, Angel put down everyone and everything in order to prepare to rescue Lacerta, but her progress was slow and the ship she needed to raid held armoured and shielded guards. I decided a grenade launcher, pistol, a couple of sidewinders (clear path teleporters), and a swapper (switch teleporter) and stealth shield would get me through.
Angel eventually survived her way to a windowed room only two away from where Lacerta was being held. The only gear she had left was a rechargeable high capacity slipstream from a cargo crate (slows down time, makes you faster), and a pistol. Thirty seconds until capture. In the room with Lacerta were three armoured guards, and two with shields. The mission looked like a bust, there was no way I could sneak back the way I came, even without the alarm on. Angel would lose Lacerta and probably herself, unless... there was one other thing worth trying.
I had angel shoot the window and get sucked out into space, then ram the windowed room with her brick pod, quickly repair it, and make dock. The two had 16 seconds to escape now. Activating the slipstream, Angel sprinted in, grabbed Lacerta, and ran out dodging a hail of bullets, narrowly missing them. with 4 seconds to spare, Lacerta was secured in the pod and Angel ejected them both and flew to safety. Saving her daughter was her greatest achievement and marked the end of her career, she would retire leaving her daughter the heirloom of the slipstream, named Borrowed Time, that had saved their lives. Lacerta would re-enter fieldwork, maintaining her non violence policy, but this time she would be prepared and her retired mother would remain a living legend and a hero to the people.

This is an amazingly fun top-down shooter with a simple premise, select from a seemingly endless supply of randomly generated missions to hijack ships in space, rescue an ally, assassinate an enemy, or just plain steal something of value.  Each character you play has a personal mission they wish to complete, and there is also the overall goal of liberating all the space stations in the galaxy.
You can choose to go in guns blazing or take a more cautious approach to your ship assault, but in either case you have the option to pause at any time to plan ahead, switch your gear around, and forge ahead with your plan.  That plan will often go haywire and you'll have to adapt your approach, often relying on one of the many useful and clever pieces of gear that you've swiped from previous missions.
None of the missions take that long, indeed some harder missions have time limits of a minute and a half or less, so you can load the game up anytime you have a few moments.  It does get a bit repetitive and grindy if you play for too long in a single sitting, so long term game play may suffer if you don't like to grind.  Still, I expect to get many hours of entertainment from this relatively inexpensive game.

Let's be honest, this game is basically a slot machine.  10 plays in a row, you might die on one of the first two levels (especially on nightmare).  Then you'll randomly find one of the better low level items, and you'll cruise through a few levels murdering everything and gaining strength.  Beating the game on nightmare takes a LOT of luck.  The majority of my hours were spent on that task, because the odds are stacked against you, and you need amazing RNG.
Still, i obviously was interested enough to play it for over 30 hours, which is a pretty good endorsement.  If you want action, this is not the place to find it.  The enemies don't move, and there is literally no skill involved, besides the choice of whether you want to push your luck to get every item on the later floors.  However, if the idea of a casual little looty RPG where most games are over in just a few minutes, then it's totally worth the couple of dollars you'll pay for it...

Ok, so I Am Overburdened is a very simple roguelike.  Nothing moves except for you so you have to be very strategic about who you fight.  Of course you need to be able to escape to the next floor, but if you're low on health maybe you want to fight a monster blocking a health (red) potion first.  Black potions are kind of random, they could hurt you, they could heal you, they could give you a stat increase, etc.  Every three levels there is a shop where you can buy one of three items (unless you have an item that affects the shop to alter that).  Carrots, broccoli, etc increase your health, coffee affects your speed (helps you hit enemies first), meat affects your damage, pots/armor affects your defense, and shamrocks/lucky horse shoes affect your luck.  The name of this game is looking at the level and thinking who you want to take on and when you want to take them on to get items to buff your character.  All in all, it's a simple roguelike but I found it very enjoyable :)

A remake of an old NES classic that was only released in Japan for the 'Famicon' (their version of the NES). The story progression stays 100% the same with added vibrancy to the beginning to give the characters more depth than the original. The difficulty has been tweaked to attain somewhat of an easier feel. The original was very grindy, but they've removed a little bit of that in the first few levels of XP. They added in a few extra quests at end game to ascertain a level of difficulty of the original with a new boss that takes a lot of grinding to be able to stand a chance against, which is what every FF fan deserves at the end of a long haul of the game. They kept the buy in bulk discount which is great, especially at the beginning when gil is somewhat scarce unless you grind a bit for that. I'd recommend this game to any RPG fan who hasn't played the original or the DS remake for those that love a good solid story with improvements to an already awesome classic.

From my brother's review of the game:
My first impressions were quite good. I have been waiting for this game ever since I found out about it by it's upcoming physical release for PS4 and PSVita. Overall the trailer set my expectations reasonably high and I'm happy with what I have played so far. (the first 4 chapters of the game)
The characters (so far) have easy to understand motivations, and the dialog is just about the right length so that you can get back into the action of the game smoothly. I like how there is some thinking involved in collecting the extra stuff in each area, however the sudden and frequent "door locks behind you" stuff really bugged me, you need to save often, because if you explore and hit an "advance to the next room" toggle, you might not be able to go back...unless you load your game. (I know that there are clear story reasons for some of this, but from a gameplay point of view this bothers me, and disrupts the game-flow as I'm a very eager to collect everything. There are some unclear puzzles that do require you to move forward past a one way area, then after a plot point happens the game lets you return to solve it.)  So small nitpicks aside, the art and music work well with the setting and the action of what is going on.
The game runs best (imo) on a game-pad, but keyboard controls are also an option.
Yes, the game will exit if you change a setting, but that is a minor bug and will hopefully be patched out within a few days.
PROS:
+ Clearly a lovingly crafted retro RPG for all us fans.
+ Fun unique combat mechanics.
+ Very nice awesome pixel art.
+ Interesting Characters.
+ Not too much dialog in cut-scenes.
+ Respects your time, and allows you to save anywhere and anytime (outside battle)
+ Some battles can be replayed to grind for loot (it's in the menu for some reason)
CONS:
- Invisible one way triggers will force you onward and you can't go back. (unless you load)
- The ability select screen is a little odd to get used to, took me about 45 min to understand it and reordered my skills how I liked.

!FIX FOR GAME STRETCHING ACROSS MULTI SCREENS!
In the game folder "Steam\SteamApps\common\Final Fantasy III" right click on "FF3_Launcher" and  click on "Compatibility". Ignore "Compatibility Mode" I have it unticked. This game is in early access, so I don't know if this review will always apply, but at the moment it's quite disappointing. I acknowledge that this game is not finished, but the rate of updates has been abysmal with little to no improvements to performance. In my experience, this game stuggles even on decent computers, even more so in multiplayer with the framerate frequently plummetting below 10 and appearing consistently to be in slow motion. I tried to power through it despite the performance issues, but the objectives of advancing from one system to another by collecting resources and occasionally fighting a boss was boring to me, though I did often enjoy exploring some of the "dungeon" environments that spawn naturally on some worlds. You can build stuff, but there is no point as you can teleport to the safety of your ship at almost any time.
This game has the potential to be good, but right now is lacking. You've heard it over and over, but the fact of the matter is that this game is pretty disappointing so far. I'd like to see some better objectives, improved performance, and more frequent updates among many other things so that this game can ascend to something beyond mediocre.

tl;dr: This game is good. Get it, for f*ck sake.
longer version:
Look, I've tried plenty of moba type games like dota and lol and paragon and whatever, but none of them really managed to grab my attention. The only reason I even tried this at first is because it's space combat and the graphics looked good.
Those two things that drew me to the game are the things that shine most
The graphics, even on low setting for everything, are bloody amazing. Every ship has so much detail and is so unique in itself, it's incredible.
The combat is smoothe and satisfying. Even with the starter ships you can manage very well if you don't just rush in like an idiot. I prefer using the venturer as a starter, because it's got that neat little healing ability that keeps you alive for those few seconds extra, but the pioneer is also a very viable option.
Anyway, what I like so much about the combat is that it's simple, yet it's not repetitive. The 3d environment you can move in really makes every engagement interesting and unique. Especially when you're able to take on that larger or more powerful ship and you barely make it out alive, but you see the other ship explode in front of your face after a last volley of rockets. Beautiful.
The variety of ships you can pick is also simply very good. There's a ship for every desirable playstyle, from what I've seen, and all of them are very different.
Now, another important part is the question "but, it's a free to play game? Isn't it pay to win?"
and the answer is no! I was kinda surprised to see this too, but you don't really need to spend money on the game to do well. Sure, grinding takes a bit longer and you can't get all those fancy skins, but you can get all the ships if you just play long enough. So yeah! That's always good to see.
In summary, Fractured Space is a very solid game. Definitely worth a try if you're into space combat.

This is an amazingly fun top-down shooter with a simple premise, select from a seemingly endless supply of randomly generated missions to hijack ships in space, rescue an ally, assassinate an enemy, or just plain steal something of value.  Each character you play has a personal mission they wish to complete, and there is also the overall goal of liberating all the space stations in the galaxy.
You can choose to go in guns blazing or take a more cautious approach to your ship assault, but in either case you have the option to pause at any time to plan ahead, switch your gear around, and forge ahead with your plan.  That plan will often go haywire and you'll have to adapt your approach, often relying on one of the many useful and clever pieces of gear that you've swiped from previous missions.
None of the missions take that long, indeed some harder missions have time limits of a minute and a half or less, so you can load the game up anytime you have a few moments.  It does get a bit repetitive and grindy if you play for too long in a single sitting, so long term game play may suffer if you don't like to grind.  Still, I expect to get many hours of entertainment from this relatively inexpensive game.
