Promise:
If you are just searching for a Hack'n'Slash game using controller input and featuring all the mechanics you came to love about controller style hack'n'slash Smashing The Battle is the best bet on Steam right now (2017). Also if you until now only played classic PC hack'n'slash and wanted to try out something more console-like, this would be the game to get first. And don't fret it's mobile background, since nothing in this game can be bought via real currency.
Gameplay:
This game is not easy - you will fail missions if you don't focus while playing. There is a "comeback mechanic" where if you get too much damage in, your armor might break and most of the abilites are gone, but you gain a big damage boost which basically is a "second chance" at not failing the mission.
The only parts that you can really feel comming from mobile is the UI and the mission and super basic level structure including some clever obstacles, made for short bursts of playing and rewarding speed and skillful play with rather harsh ratings at the end of each mission, in the first playthough you might only get 1 or 2 out of 3 stars with 3 stars requiring you to use all the skills an dodge every attack in quick succession and with a sense for resource and impact to finish each mission as fast as you can.
Story:
The game features plot, i wouldn't call it a full story, but the plot is delivered consistently and keeps the attention of the player between missions, not interfering with the gameplay at all.
Graphics:
The character art is outstanding - at least for a fan of a slightly westernized Anime style - and is nicely animated in a flash-movie-like (or "Spriter" style if you are too young to know Flash animation) style of animation. The hand full of characters are not just slapped onto the product to gain attention, but received a lot of care from the artists. The 3D models are all in high quality with lots of movable parts. The technical aspect itself is rather low, since it was originally made for smartphones and tablets, so while the resolution can be as high as you want it, some textures are just slightly underneath HD standards.
Verdict: Recommended to everyone wanting to try modern, controller-focused hack'n'slash that's done just right and requires skill to play.

What a great game. I acquired this in a Humble Bundle recently with a few other titles. Without looking, I assumed it was just a game that was shoveled in to fluff out the bundle, and that I wouldn't enjoy it. I ended up loving it, and I'm definitely going to buy the DLC (and likely any more content that may come out for Hacknet in the future).
Hacknet, for lack of better words, is a Unix-based hacking simulator in which you use the combination of a point-and-click interface and a command prompt to explore the mysterious death of a hacker named "Bit." Bit has arranged to send automated messages to you posthumously, giving you leads that are just enough for you to find your way.
Being not much of a programmer, and unfamiliar with Linux and Unix-based command systems (idk man I just look stuff up and punch♥♥♥♥♥♥into the Windows 10 command prompt and sometimes it says words back to me), I felt learning to play Hacknet might be too daunting of a task. However, the feeling subsided in less than half an hour, when I was able to navigate through any device's file systems with ease, hopping from device to device, opening ports, cracking passwords, etc. Not long after that was I very immersed in the story (something I have a hard time being in MANY games).
While some aspects of the game can be done through clicking between devices, folders, and apps, other things are seemingly only possible by using the command-line, keeping the game immersive and making you feel, in a sense, accomplished. YOU cracked open all of Macrosoft's ports and got to snoop around in their sensitive files. YOU found a security loophole by exploiting a computer's connected smartphone. YOU made a clean getaway just in time before having your IP traced, clearing the system logs and running for the hills with some juicy new program you can use to hack *even more* devices. And you did it all with your analytical skills and an intuitive command system. In fact, there's even a point in the game where your OS/interface is essentially deleted from your system by another angry hacker, leaving you with a big black command terminal, having to plot through your own computer to restore the deleted files and get yourself back in the game. Just like in real life, each device you access seems like a sum of its parts, even your own.
The IP tracing mechanic is excellent, and pretty much exactly what you'd imagine seeing on some Hollywood hacker's monitor. It keeps the pressure on, even if it is slow at times. RAM management, learning what ports to use when, and being able to type quickly and remember which programs do what are important, and make hacking into each and every system rewarding in its own way, even if it doesn't have quite what you were looking for.
The visual effects are excellent, if a bit cheesy at times. The interface is simple enough that these "glitchy" or "tech-y" effects aren't too jarring unless they need to be, which keeps the game immersive but also fun to watch. I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature.
The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering.
Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them):
- The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure.
- I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome.
Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from
, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game.
If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

Gameplay: Average at best, simple button mashing with a bit of dodging. Hacknet is, by far, the most enthralling and immersive hacking experience I've played to date. Adding the Labirynths expansion, the game excels at managing your stress levels: there are times of low intensity, times of high intensity, and times of crisis-level intensity. There are also times of "dead"-intensity; that is to say, lest you remember some of the basic mechanics of the game, it's possible at a few points to feel like whatever situation you're experiencing is not salvagable. With the emotional rollercoast also comes incredible use of comedic relief, a little extra sanding to take the edge off.
Some of the best and brightest moments of Hacknet (and it's expansion) are when you'll find yourself laughing at an IRC log or stray text file's contents; some of them are when you'll find yourself scrambling to disconnect from a server before a trace locks in on your system; some of them are just... breathtaking, almost moving moments that could maybe bring you to tears, and yet further more are moments where your morality comes into play.
I've only played through the game (and it's expansion) once; I understand that, while limited, there are various other paths and routes that the player may choose to take instead. I'm definitely going to play through the game several more times to find some more secrets and goodies. I'm also interested in the upcoming Hacknet Extensions update, which will bring modding tools and workshop functionality to the table, adding even more content. I'm excited as I'll get out.
I will say, however, if you're not particularly technically inclined, it might be a bit difficult to get going, actually. Don't panic though: most of the game's mechanics have reference material readily available in game, so if you ever forget syntax or a naming convention, it's easy to find the solution.
If you're interested in science-fiction action/mystery thrillers, then this is a game for you.

Not much care put into its day one quality. Patches since then have made it bearable. Pre-ordered and got burned. DEMANDS A  HIGH PERFORMANCE PC. If framerate is important to you and you're on a medium range rig you might even have to turn down the resolution for better performance. Frame rate dropped down to near single digits on my rig (also medium range at the time of release).  [EDIT]: Optimization patches have gone out and it runs significantly better, but still demands a higher end setup)
Story was satisfying to me, rushed character development on the protagonist Arno might keep you from being invested in the story. Multiplayer matchmaking works wonderfully for me, however becomes repetitive as you need to repeat certain Co-Op missions to unlock different gear. You CAN however do Co-Op missions by yourself. "Club" system in place to consolidate players into defined groups (guild or clan basically) however i have yet to see this mechanic play out the way it is supposed to due to the absence of club participants.
New free running system works beautifully, and is satisfying. Yes you CAN get everywhere by holding RT, but finding the quickest/shortest path requires you to actively adjust your route and manually time your jumps.
Combat system IS more difficult (which is fantastic) and AI are more hardy which makes combat more risky, but WAY more satisfying. When fighting higher level enemies, you won't win the fight by just spamming [Attack] and countering every so often. The new stealth mode is a long awaited mechanic that works fairly well, though there is a bit of a learning curve when it comes to using the corner cover mechanic.
It is, however, a collectathon, requiring you to collect Artifacts, Chests, Cockades, Newspapers, and "Sync Points" to unlock certain customizing options for your gear and clothing. There are many well designed pieces of gear that give you certain stat buffs, and allow you to customize your Assassin.
All in all, a rushed addition to the Assassin's Creed franchise with many oversights at launch (and now). It remains a ghost of what was expected of it, but remains an Assassin's Creed game nonetheless. Leaves its past installments in the dust in cosmetic design and navigation. (Can't say much else). Hopefully some more care and time will be put into the next game. 7/10
EDIT: With all of the patches it has recieved, it is definitely worth a try if you have a decent rig. Much more satisfying (gameplay and story wise) than Syndicate. If it's on sale, I'd suggest picking it up. Optimally for $20.00 or less.

TLDR: this game is fun, a must buy if you're a Zeboyd fan (in which case it's 9/10), and a charming way to pass a weekend otherwise 7/10.
I originally put up my review about a week after the game came out and thumbed it down because quite frankly the initial release was basically little better than a polished beta. Despite the flaws I was able to finish the game and mostly enjoyed it so I promised to flip my thumb as long as the bugs were improved. The developer himself (comment below) assured me that they would do their best to rectify their game's issues and I'm pleased to say that now, about a month after release there have been enough updates to justify changing my review. Most importantly it really feels like a final product instead of a beta now, and to be honest I thought it would take longer than this before that was the case. Hopefully the game will continue to receive even more polish going forward.
As for uhh... an actual review of this game, if you come in expecting something epic like a 16-bit Mass Effect or a modern day Chrono Trigger you're going to be sorely disappointed. Pacing and style wise it really does feel a lot like CT, but it's more of a rousing romp than an unforgettable journey. Perhaps a more apt comparison from the same time period would be "Wild Arms with more playable characters and less puzzles" if anyone remembers that franchise.
The plot is something of a weak point and best not taken too seriously (a caveat to be applied to all Zeboyd games), but the battles are a lot more fun than any other turn based RPG that came out in 2017 (only halfway through the year but I'm calling it), the music is AWESOME and fits the game perfectly, and the graphics and overall atmosphere were just so pleasurable to me.
Again, 7/10 critically, 9/10 personally. Keep 'em coming Zeboyd! Hopefully not so many years apart this time! Now if you'll excuse me, the weekend is here so I'm off to replay the game for the achievements.

I have always enjoyed the first two Final Fantasy games, but their stories were sparse, relying more on conversations with random town folk to help fill in the blanks than to tell a proper tale. While Final Fantasy III still shows its age and might not have the sophistication found in later RPGs, it is still a worthy look back at a game that helped to continue to redefine the genre.
This version of the game on PC is based on the graphically updated version that made its way onto the Nintendo DS back in 2006. The visuals got an 3D overhaul, with a widened aspect ratio and some new features as well. If you are familiar with the DS or iPhone/iPad versions of the game this PC release will feel very familiar, but it still plays out nicely on a bigger screen.
Themes that persist and remain familiar in future Final Fantasy games such as the Warriors of Light and job class systems help populate this story. The job system is bare bones compared to what we are used to now in the series (and other games that use similar systems), and the game uses it more as a second experience system. On the one hand the characters have conventional experience systems that level up their physical attributes, and then there's the job levels which represent their skills. Managing both is easy, and the system does encourage players to jump their characters through multiple jobs, though there is some grinding involved as there is a warmup process where a character needs to fight a certain number of battles with a role before they're comfortable with it and can use its skills properly. You don't want to be fighting tough enemies in such a state, so you'll generally grind through easy battles each and every time you change classes.
This is a classic Final Fantasy title, which of course has both good and bad connotations. It means lots of menus and level grinding and of course chocobos and Cid and things. It is a welcome rush of nostalgia to come back to a game like this, which has aged well despite being nearly two and a half decades old. I'd be lying if I said that the graphical overhaul didn't make the game far more palatable (or the fact that the original game was never released in English), but the core mechanics should also appeal to old school JRPG fans. The game gets off to something of a slow start, with a lot of story and limited exploration during the first dozen hours or so, but once it opens up it is every bit the exploration-filled adventure Final Fantasy is known for, filled with little secrets to find and fun and diverse characters.
Having just played Bravely Default a few months ago and seeing familiar themes such as the four different adventurers brought together by circumstance and the presence of crystals as a focal point to the story, I could not help but be amused with how timeless the narrative themes are. That being said, Bravely Default showed just how much further game storytelling has gone in making something rich out of the basic thematic construct. That is not to say that Final Fantasy III has a poor story, but compared to the more modern Japanese role-playing game, it is fascinating to see how far the medium has come.
If you have already played the DS or iOS version of this game, there may not be enough of a reason to purchase it on Steam now. However, if you missed that opportunity before and want to experience an important part of Final Fantasy's early evolution, this is an excellent way to do so. The character depth and story detail might feel somewhat lacking compared to newer JRPG titles, but there is an expansive world here that begs for exploration as you grow your characters for future challenges. The overall package is an easy one to recommend.

This game is a classic, but in my eyes also one of the most difficult and challenging JRPG's i have ever played but i was quite curious to see how the additions would benefit the game as i finished the original NES game, here are my thoughts.
Pro's
-Run's well, many people have been having problems playing this game so i was very thankful that i did not encounter any bugs/glitches throughout my entire playthrough.
- Fleshed out characters. While i personally don't mind playing a bunch of create your own characters in a party, it was kinda of nice that each of the characters have a personality and backstory.
- The cinematics look amazing! Though they are not very common, their addition is very nice indeed.
- Like any other Final Fantasy game, there is a TON of extra quests/loot that is just waiting to be beaten/explored, at this point i am still grinding my way to the last few achievements (including beating the secret boss)

-The Job System! It's so cool that you could try all sorts of different strategies to fight enemies and defeat bosses. I just like that they have look a little different depending on which character is using the job
Con's
- Grind heavy! Thankfully having finished it before i was aware of this, i remember having to spend about 3-4 hours levellin my characters and jobs just to survive and beat some bosses so if you want to experience just the story without the extras, be prepared
So if you like JRP'S or Turn based RPG's, it should be right up your alley! I personally don't think it is worth full price, but definitely pick it up on sale and you'll get 50+ hours worth of goodness =)

Hacknet is, by far, the most enthralling and immersive hacking experience I've played to date. Adding the Labirynths expansion, the game excels at managing your stress levels: there are times of low intensity, times of high intensity, and times of crisis-level intensity. There are also times of "dead"-intensity; that is to say, lest you remember some of the basic mechanics of the game, it's possible at a few points to feel like whatever situation you're experiencing is not salvagable. With the emotional rollercoast also comes incredible use of comedic relief, a little extra sanding to take the edge off.
Some of the best and brightest moments of Hacknet (and it's expansion) are when you'll find yourself laughing at an IRC log or stray text file's contents; some of them are when you'll find yourself scrambling to disconnect from a server before a trace locks in on your system; some of them are just... breathtaking, almost moving moments that could maybe bring you to tears, and yet further more are moments where your morality comes into play.
I've only played through the game (and it's expansion) once; I understand that, while limited, there are various other paths and routes that the player may choose to take instead. I'm definitely going to play through the game several more times to find some more secrets and goodies. I'm also interested in the upcoming Hacknet Extensions update, which will bring modding tools and workshop functionality to the table, adding even more content. I'm excited as I'll get out.
I will say, however, if you're not particularly technically inclined, it might be a bit difficult to get going, actually. Don't panic though: most of the game's mechanics have reference material readily available in game, so if you ever forget syntax or a naming convention, it's easy to find the solution.
If you're interested in science-fiction action/mystery thrillers, then this is a game for you.

It’s really easy to look at Heat Signature and say “that looks like Hotline Miami in space,” and saying that is applicable to a point, but as you dig deeper in the game you find a much more challenging and puzzle-like system that rewards you for proper planning, use of a diverse set of tools, and great timing.
Heat Signature starts you out flying a tiny pod at super speeds across a portion of a galaxy to find a marked ship to latch yourself on to its hull in order to infiltrate and fulfill the objective of your mission. This could be something as simple as killing a certain person on board, but also could be something a bit different like having you steal an item or take over the entire ship.  Yet in the beginning, this is where it’s really like Hotline Miami.  You won’t have many weapons or items, and the enemies will be pretty easy to dispatch.  In all likelihood, you will be able to take them all out with your wrench and some swift blows to the head to fully take over the ship regardless of your objective.  Even if the crew has guns, holding a mouse button (or controller button) to ready your selected weapon will put you in a slow motion mode, which, with a little anticipation, will have you dodging their shots easily.  Then on top of that, getting knocked out or shot doesn’t immediately kill you.  You’re rendered unconscious and carried to an airlock to be jettisoned, but the only thing you’ll need to do then is remote control your space pod to come pick you up and either drive you back to the ship, or take you home to start a new mission.  However, all of this starts to change as you move in to missions that are more difficult.
Taking out a half-dozen guards wielding wrenches or pistols one or two at a time will seem like a joke as you get into the tougher missions of the game.  Every completed mission nets you some of the game’s currency, with it's mysterious droplet icon, and increases the amount of “liberation” that you have.  Once you reach a certain amount of liberation, you can unlock a new station, which will give you various small bonuses like additional items available in the station's stores.  The end goal of the game is liberating these stations and defeating each faction in the galaxy along the way.  In this process, you’ll also unlock increasingly more difficult missions that involve more rules and requirements on top of guards equipped with all sorts of life-ending tools.   Luckily, as you move along, you accumulate a nice collection of useful gadgets and weapons that make it possible to successfully complete these encounters.  Whether it’s armor piercing weapons, items that disable shields (or hilariously turn them against their wielder), or provide you with various types of teleportation, you’ll be much more capable as you progress.   But you are going to have only eight slots in your inventory, and most items will have limited ammo and charges, so what results is a scenario where you need to plan ahead, plan while you’re on the mission, and come up with a completely new plan when everything falls apart.
The most rewarding aspect of Heat Signature is when you’re going in to an extremely difficult mission where you’re dodging around patrolling guards, making use of an inventory full of crazy gadgets and weapons, trying to do it all under a time limit, and somehow pulling it all off even when half of what designed doesn't actually follow the plan.  The huge ships you’ll be running around later in the game and the complex scenarios you’re put in will give the game a great shelf life for a something that has such a relatively low base price of $15.  It’s fascinating how the game transitions from something so familiar to a game that requires ample pausing, planning, and essentially solving randomly generated puzzles.  Then on top of that, the game limits progression with a single character (assuming they don’t die or get captured) by giving diminishing returns on the “liberation” resource after you’ve done a certain number of missions.  This forces you to retire the character and start over fresh with minimal items, keeping the game interesting even after several hours of play.  It encourages the player to take risks and try more dangerous missions since no matter what the result, you'll have to retire that character to keep progressing.
Heat Signature is and indie game that delivers way over its price point and has an appeal that grows on you as you play, standing out from other indie games that tend to lose appeal as you dig in deeper due to a lack of depth.  As soon as you discover some cool gadget, weapon, or technique you can do, it adds another option in the already diverse gameplay.   I didn't know until hours in that you can pickpocket keys off of guards and that opened up an entirely new level of stealth options that I had never before considered.  If it had just one more layer of gameplay, maybe making the stations have more interactivity or something relating to the galaxy map, and a more refined artistic and graphical appearance, it could easily pass for a AAA game on par with something like XCOM with gameplay that keeps building on itself in an engaging way.  I fully recommend this title and I look forward to exploring it further to see what other fun bits it contains.

Hacknet is an enjoyable hacking/terminal simulator. I use the term hacking, loosely, but the player will be diving in and out of networks, taking admin access of machines, trying to remember and using a variety of tools to do so and looking for clues that lead them to a greater truth that someone is trying to keep hidden. That's where the real challenge comes in. I had to stop playing for some months because of a game breaking bug but revisited after a fix and recently completed it. It's better to do this all in one go so your commands and tools are fresh in your mind as you go deeper down the rabbit hole. The story will keep the player interested while the visuals and music do an excellent job of keeping the entire thing exciting. Hacknet is a tight package worth its ten dollar price.

However, there isn't much in terms of story, the levels have same "look" (with different layouts), and there are not many enemy variations. Difficulty is increased through increase in number of enemies, use of time limit / waves, and randomly spawning magnets/mines/turrets. This makes gameplay feel more and more tedious after a while. Having said that, at the price I paid I feel it's still worth it.

SMASHING THE BATTLE is a fun hack-and-slash game.
The story is quite simple but not every game must be a writing masterpiece. The controls are good and the music is quite decent. There are some mistakes here and there with the models of the heroines but you should be busy fighting enemies. It's a very repetitive so it might not be your coup of tea: if the story had 40 stages (instead of 60) in total it would've been much better. It has replay value with the challenges, missions (Steam achievements) and unlockable content.
Pros:
+Big anime tidies.
+You can choose an agressive or defensive approach despite the skills of both characters.
+Upgrades help you customize your playstyle.
+If you lose at a stage you still keep your progress in terms of coins and scrap.
+Lots of replay value if you like the game.
Cons:
-Very repetitive. All the levels at some point are repeated through the game.
-The music is good but more tracks would've been better.
-Perhaps the story levels are too many for the type of game.
-The ending is mere text. Some pictures would fit better.
Despite of the flaws it's a nice game to buy at a sale.

I'm not going to say that Bastion is perfect.  I'm not even going to say that it's an especially deep game, in that if you don't like it you clearly don't "get" it.
With that out of the way, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who wants a fun little beat-em-up with some stellar production values and a whole lot of heart.  Much of the game's soul comes from the narration in combination with the music, and there are a lot of little story tid-bits to be found in the game's weapon-challenge levels.  The world may have been torn asunder, but it still feels vibrant and alive.
I'd say the game is worth at least two playthroughs, one for each ending and to play around with weapon combinations that you never thought to try out the first time 'round.  Definitely worth a buy in my book.

This is a port of the DS version to PC and definitely one of the better Final Fantasy games out there. And it's all for one reason. CHALLENGE. Challenge. Yes, challenge. At various points in the game there are actually chances of being wiped. Phoenix Downs are in limited quantity. Dying means something. That factor alone makes the game far more enjoyable than  most of the other titles out there. The job system is really nice too. The game still manages to feel like an NES game with NES difficulty, but without terrible amounts of frustration. Saving is a lot more lenient than even the remake (alt+f4 will let you just go back to the last autosave; I don't think the DS version did that on reset). However, the end in particular can be extremely difficult. Be prepared!

I had, prior to this game, finished ff4,6,7,8,9,10,12 and  13 but never tried ff3- now I´ve not only played but also finished ff3 and yes, I do recommend this game.
final fantasy 3 is more of an old-school game (...what a shocker?!) than the newer games, in terms of jobs and dungeons. While there is a story within this game, and its a decent one, the playable characters are hardly the focus, but more about dungeon exploration and saving the world.
While that might sound bad, it was actually a pleasent experience somewhat, since there are so many classes to try and experiment with for the "right" combination to beat bosses and dungeons and advance in the storyline.
For example, if you feel a dungeon might have too many locked door, maybe you should bring a thief for that extra treasure. If you experience to have a dungeon filled with monsters weak to magic you want to bring a black mage, and if you feel the need for a good tank to absorb all that physical damage and dish some of that back you may need a viking or a knight.
Also, the game doesnt hold your hand, they want you to figure out stuff and explore on your own.
Anyway, it had a good strategical depth and for any rpg lover it would satisify but if you´re looking for a good story with great characters, and looking among the older rpg titles, Final Fantasy IV(4) will be a much better choice.
I will still grant this game 8.0/10

I love Fractured Space.  This is a team based spaceship MOBA game, so pick a ship to complement your teams composition and roll with it.  For the most part, I'd say the ships are pretty well balanced and I can do well with any of them in pvp once I trained the playstyle for each in the co-op vs AI mode.
I think the gameplay is really TOP NOTCH in my opinion, but I have some serious issues with the game's systems.
Here is a list of the non-gameplay issues I have with Fractured Space:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) No draft pick currently - only blind picks (however you can choose between a few weapons/abilities once ships are locked in)
2) Matchmaking is a little bit wonky sometimes putting a full group of solo players against a full pre-made which relates to point 3
3) The game population is slowly trickling away - which means longer wait times for matches
4) For the 'casual' mode your MMR (skill) values are visible which IMO leads to people dropping in ship selection when the team comp looks ugly. (which means you will have to wait again on matchmaking)
5) Skin prices and DLC are ridiculously priced - the commander pack is $60 WTF - it's not worth anywhere near that
6) Progression to new ships can be a bit slow at first until you figure out how to play.  They should have a free ship rotation on a weekly basis so people can try ships in combat before spending a weeks worth of saved credits on a ship.  If you can pick up the armada pack on sale - do it.
7) Crew seems worthless to bother with and takes >forever< to unlock all.
Thank you for reading - hope this helps.  I highly recommend trying the game because it is free.
-Shastamasta

Tank: Tanks are noramlly your slowest kinds of ships but will have the most health they also usally have weapons for midrange combat on there own they can take a good beating from multiple DPS but without Help from DPS or Support they will go down
Support: Supports can very from healing or Buffs or Drones supports on there own are easy targets so you want to stay close to other ships to help out more often have one support vs a team with non can make a very big difference in a  game

I'm not going to say that Bastion is perfect.  I'm not even going to say that it's an especially deep game, in that if you don't like it you clearly don't "get" it.
With that out of the way, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who wants a fun little beat-em-up with some stellar production values and a whole lot of heart.  Much of the game's soul comes from the narration in combination with the music, and there are a lot of little story tid-bits to be found in the game's weapon-challenge levels.  The world may have been torn asunder, but it still feels vibrant and alive.
I'd say the game is worth at least two playthroughs, one for each ending and to play around with weapon combinations that you never thought to try out the first time 'round.  Definitely worth a buy in my book.

Despite being a mobile game that was brought to Steam, the controls are very easy to figure out and all work really well, the frame rate is also incredibly smooth and satisfying. The tutorial character that guides you through out the game is really annoying and hard to sympathize with, but she doesn't detract from a solid hack and slash.

As a avid Square fan since FF7 and onwards, visiting this remastered old relic for the first time enlightened me on the foundations of the SquareSoft's (now SquareEnix) gaming mechanics. This game is certainly a remaster of history. Compared to the original Nintendo release, this game is colorful and more welcoming to the new generation of gamers who are interested in classical RPG.

Do keep in mind, as a classical RPG, the grind will be very real. The implemation of the Achievement system here on Steam is a good way to indicate your full completion of the game. So those that have played before  on a console may have something to go for completing the game again. If 100% is not your goal, you can blow through a regular playthrough at 25+ hours.

So, the only reason you could possibly be here is for a little mess around rpg. Well, that's great, that's excellent! I'm glad you want an RPG to just sit down and play!
Go get a WoW subscription, and don't waste you time here.
Now, before you fire back with 'but I don't want to waste money on something I'll never play.' Well, this is why I'm recommending WoW to you. You see, WoW is, what, 5-15 dollars a month? No, you probably just gagged, but here me out. In WoW, you can forge a good, strong character for free after you subscribe, and it's an engaging experience throughout your gameplay. You get some neat looking gear, you fight in story based dungeons, you can go said with a guild, it's a good example of a well done MMO.
Trove, and Trion Worlds in general, is an excellent example of a horrible MMO.
Now, those numbers I mentioned for price range,
5-15? Well, for Trove, it gets cranked up by way too much to, at least, 100 dollars. A week. Just to make the slightest bit of progress, that isn't even worth it, and to top it all off, after a few weeks, a guarantee you will never play Trove again.
As a learning game dev, I have learned so far that there are four major elements to games; Strategy, Luck, Gameplay, and Feedback. Sure, Trove does have some mediocre Luck in it, but that is the only element it does have. Strategy, Gameplay, and Feedback? You will find none of that here.
The 'Strategy' is so conveluted that it undoes itself because no player really knows about it, 'Gameplay' died back in Early Access, and 'Feedback' doesn't even show its face around here anymore.
You have to pay for progress, you have to pay for costumes to even attempt to look ok, you have to pay for the good gear, and you have to pay to get an entire teir of items that is entirely based upon luck. Not only that, but this whole game only appeals to older players. Don't believe me? Listen to this;
When I played Trove, ( which, as you could guess, was a lot of time ) classes were available for in-game currency. I was able to buy every class at the time and actually, somehow, find some fun in it. However, when I came back to see if there was anything left for me in the game, not only had they downgraded their game to make classes only available for real money, but I got a gift in my inventory which contained 10 class coins, which unlocks a class for no charge. I was stunned. They were slowly locking the doors to their game so they could slowly kill off the older players by sucking them dry like mosquitos.
To top it all off, TW promised their players, they promised, that the game would never become P2P.
Welp, they said that for ArchAge, too, and here we are now, with a game that is borderline unplayable because of the money-barriers. A big middle finger to you, too, TW.

I have played Harvest Moon: Back to Nature for roughly 2 years or so back when it launched, and immediately feel in love. Since then I haven't been able to find another game similar to it that could captivate me as much as HM did, that is until I found Stardew Valley.
Oh my god, its every thing HM was and more. Farming is the main income source for the game, but SV made so it's not the only viable way, if you don't wanna be a farmer, then don't, you culd be fisherman if you wish, or once something happen ( not gonna spoil it) be a miner! or be everything at once, the choice is yours :D
I would have to say what got me was the romance aspect of it, unlike most the old and even newer HM, they allow same sex relationships which for me is a huge plus, back when HM: Back to NAture released I have always wanted to engage some of the male characters, but the game wouldn't allow it, so this really got me hyped into SV.
Overall it's a pretty laid back game, do what you will whenever you want. The game's "story" ends on year three, something happens then (not spoiling) but the actuall game (farming, fishing, mining, relationships, festivals, acheivments and  etc) continue indefinitely. I personly detest grinding games, I don;t have the patience for it and I get easily bored of it, but Satardew Valley seems to always keep me entertained, even after I watched the same cutscenes, done every event, and whatnot a hundred times over, it is just that good.

Played this game for about two weeks.  I played the original XCom and XCOM Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within without any issues.  My main problem with this game is that someone at Firaxis said - "You know what?  Those XCom games aren't frustrating and arbitrary enough".  Hey there are
people with monk like abilities that love this game, and more power to them - but this game just started to feel like work.
The developers SAY that not every mission needs to be perfect but that is BS.  There is SO many things moving against you at the strategy layer that every mission needs to be near perfectly accomplished.  Two bad ones and your campaign is wrecked.
The game really started feeling like a chore after a certain enemy showed up.  Hey remember in the Matrix that cool scene where Trinity goes behind the agent and says "Dodge This!" and kills him because he has NO chance to avoid that shot.  Wasn't that cool?  Wouldn't it be cool if an enemy could do that to your forces and instakill one?  No?  Oh well - this game might not be for you then.
Anyway - mods really make this game fun - except some mods also make it unstable and there isn't really any way to tell how they will interact.  And if a mod starts acting up ... too bad.  Start over.  But now I have a reason to uninstall this game.  I have never been so happy to have a game stop working.  I assumed it was the mods, but from some of these comments who knows.
You know I have been really flippant about this game - and pretty frustrated.  It is frustrating because under the ridiculously overpowered enemies, the scripted missions which if you do too quickly will wreck your campaign.  There is a GORGEOUS, game that produces some real intense nail biting moments and satisfying victories.  But at the end of the day this game poduces way more negative emotions than positive ones and leisure should be about the latter.

I am awake.
I am drifting in the vacuum of space. I have nothing but a shotgun on me. Memory is fuzzy, but I must have been airlocked by security. The emptiness of space is unbroken, save for a ship at low thrust, leaving me.
I hesitate. But only for a second. I aim my gun opposite the fleeing ship and fire. BOOM. I hear the noise in my head, even though the sound of the firing weapon is lost and silenced in this void. BOOM. BOOM. BOOM. I fire and fire. The force of the gun pushes me in the opposite direction. Towards the ship. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. BOOM. BOOM. I am now making this noise in my helmet.
I am making headway. The ship is nearing. I can see my corvette docked at an aft port. I fire my gun opposite of that and soon find my hands clutching precious, familiar metal. I open the emergency canopy and crawl back into the safety of my cockpit.
I pull my helmet off this time. It obscured my vision when I needed full situational awareness. I grab a silenced pistol and a long blade. I step back into the ship and start down the hallway.
I was going to clean the lockers for the prize I was contracted to steal. Now. I just want to kill everyone onboard and scuttle the ship. I sneak up behind a guard that is gazing off into the distance. My long blade finds his heart and he falls. I turn a corner and see two men standing in front of a panoramic window that looks out into the void. I fire three shots and the window explodes outward - blasting the two hapless men into the vacuum.
They messed with the wrong pirate.

Side quests be like: Hey go here, *random location* kill God's abominations, put em out of their goddamn misery, and then report back to me.

Upfront TL;DR:
I recommend XCOM2 to anyone who is remotely interested in strategy/tactical rpg games and does not mind a few hiccups in optimization.
It is like a sci-fi Fire Emblem without anime cutscenes and support convos (all that waifu♥♥♥♥♥♥ and adds good graphics and destructible environments.
XCOM2's plot is the classic Good vs. Evil with some philosophical drops of "we are becoming what we set out to destroy".
The real story, however, is the success and failure of XCOM agents under your command.
BTW If you can't play a game without your precious waifus then download a voice pack for them and add them to your character pool. Pretty sure there are a bunch of neptunia heads and voice packs in the workshop. See, everyone's happy.
Introduction:
This review is tailored for those who have not played any iteration of XCOM, so that it better informs those interested in trying the game out.
Before continuing, I want to say that mods are a double edged sword in this game. They enhance play and decrease performance at the same time (subscribed to 300 atm). I cannot deny the fantastic additions graced to XCOM2 by the modding community, but I hope to review the ideas and concepts that the vanilla version succeeded/failed to accomplish on its own.
Specs:
i7-6700K @ 4.00GHz (4.36GHz)
16 GB RAM
GTX 1070
Pros:
+The ability to extensively customize your soliders contributes a sense of attachment to  soldiers you are ordering around, something most games cannot emulate.
+Map generation is very well designed/balanced so that the same tileset/area can offer many different avenues of play.
+Configurable settings via the xcom ini can further modify play, leading to more replayability. For example, you can change the base stats of every character/item in the game if you wanted.
+There is some base management, but it is not too extensive and does not feel tacked on just because "every other game has some form of it" (the original XCOM had this too).
+Combat is interesting and offers different approaches to problems through the soldier class system, plethora of researchable gear, and destructible environments.
+The emphasis on limited time (in combat and on a macro scale) to rebel against Earth's alien overlords provides a sense of urgency that many games strive for yet miss.
+Your soldiers and the aliens become stronger as the game goes on, which creates a sense of each side trying its hardest to defeat the other.
+Countless workshop mods offer something new and exciting to experience through multiple playthroughs.
+There is an ironman mode (Only one save state) for tryhards. Variable difficulty as well, which is good for new players.
+A game that discourages facerolling over every button on your keyboard.
Cons:
-You have to realize this game has its optimization issues.
-Loading screens can be long, depending on your settings and how many mods you decide to download. I think the base game does not have this problem as much as a heavily modified one.
-Frame rate drops slightly when discovering enemies, unloading from your transport, and initializing props to customize your soldiers with. These frame rate issues, however, can be easily ignored since they only occur at specific points in the game and do little to hinder the gameplay itself.
-Do not play at max settings, even the best rigs will have trouble stabilizing at that golden 60fps.
-Due to the nature of XCOM2, it being quite a long game, these problems seem to be more apparent later on when there are simply more characters in a given mission (larger squad size, more enemies, etc.).
-There are not many gameplay elements that I feel XCOM2 failed to deliver on, but indeed there are many annoyances within the vanilla version that have either been patched already or allieviated by the free mods inside the workshop.
Conclusion:
So if you do buy the game and see something that is offputting, check out the workshop to see if a solution has already been distributed.
More than likely if you see something as a problem, someone else has too.
This concludes my review of XCOM 2. If you made it this far, then congratulations on either scrolling fast or reading.

FFIII is as evil as it is captivating. While the story suffers from a few hiccups now and then, it never feels dull or grey. This remake takes you back to a time when games were challenging, testing the skill of the player, not just giving them consquence-less respawns. Example; Modern Game: "Last boss of the dungeon! *Dies* *Respawns at entrance to boss*"
FFIII: "Last boss of the dungeon! *Dies* ...wait...WAIT....WHAT!? I Haven't saved in hours!" This level of difficulty is shunned by most, but beloved by the rest. Games have not "Advanced". Have you noticed 95% of NEW games (2010+) are 89% cutscenes or QTE's? That's not gaming. That's proving that the gaming industry as a whole is dumbing their games down because of the apparent lack of motivation. FFIII is an example of how a game is meant to be, challenging yet rewarding. A game with a safe-fail system is in no regards challenging. It disappoints me to see the gaming companies flourish with so little effort put into their games (yes, you too Square). So please, if you want a REAL challenge, put your modern rpg away and pick this gem up.

Lego Hobbit is yet another Lego 3D Platformer by Travellers Tales. Seriously. This one came out in 2014. And it's based of only the first two movies of Hobbit series.
Yes, only from the first two movies. Warner Bros promised to whip Travellers Tales into making DLC based on the third movie, but then after a while they went all "eh eh eh not planning to make any videogames based on the third movie".
Yea, store page of a game masterfully avoids any mention that it's not complete.
It also came out on consoles that are Xbox 360, Xbox One, PS3, PS4, WiiU. And also had handheld version for 3DS and Vita which is your usual "same idea, different lesser execution" thing. Don't worry, from what I looked the PC version is among top.
Technically, it's about on same level as recent Lego offerings. Or maybe even worse. You know, bugs, crashes and getting stuck in geometry. I do remember crashing at the end of level 5 personally. And many people complain about some bugs in overworld.
Anyway, it's yet another Lego game. Casual, beat stuff, collect stuff. Watch funny cutscenes with voice overs. Do quests in open roam part. No revolution. Just same evolution of a snail.
Like, this time around a lot of destructable objects now drop additional loot: various materials. And there are some objects into which you must dispense a certain amount of materials that you gathered. Then once done, minigame will happen where the Lego object is being automatically built, then it stops at some point and shows which detail it's going to build next and you have to select it from 8-directional choice. Or else time will run out, which only means that you get less studs. Yea, it still wouldn't make you think.
Oh, and everybody can charge attack. Eh.
Look, this franchise is so painfully stale. I remember Travellers Tales for creating charming games like Galladan, Toy Story for 16-bit and Sonic R. Sad to see that they pretty much turned into yearly licensed Lego games factory. That now makes quite buggy games. And this one isn't even full experience. Not to say that it has much less than others though.
And there was so many games in Lego games that at this point you better approach it different from other sane game franchise: Instead of following Lego franchise, just pick the single game that fits your interest. And then don't care about others.
Really, I know that there are other franchises that don't change things up at all. But the thing is that Lego franchise is designed to not require much thinking. So kids will be able to beat it. Though at times it might be offending even for kids. And thus "almost reskin, more levels" doesn't work here, like, say, with 8-bit Megaman. Just changing little doesn't work. It really gets repetetive for real. No challenge, no new think for each level.
So eh. It still doesn't stop me from having to recommend it up, rather than down, as it's still a good game with some love and charm still being shown, Travellers Tales style.

Did you ever enjoy those old school type-in games on the Commodore 64, Vic-20, Apple, or Amiga computers?  If so, chances are very high that this old school retro remake will be well worth its asking price, if for no other reason than for nostalgia.  It's a pretty fun little game, but in this video, I score this game at a 6/10 and challenge the developer with 3 simple changes to pump up the score to an easy 8 out of 10...
Space Lagat is about as simple of a game as you can get.  You simply need to avoid a snake who moves just a tiny bit faster than you do.. and who since controlled by AI never has any problem making critical turns like you most certainly will as you try to time your [arrow keys] or your [WASD] keys precisely at the exact right second.
Your objective is to pass through the levels which is achieved by both staying alive and by collecting randomly placed diamonds which respawn one at a time once collected somewhere on the level.
Because the snake is faster and his turns are always perfect and because his pathfinding to get to you is really good, it would seem that you are doomed from the start.  But hold on brave space diamond collecting hero, you do have ONE weapon, and that is being able to spawn a web just behind you at the press of a button... as long as you don't currently have any other webs on the screen.  Placed at the perfect time right when the snake is just about to eat you alive, your web will snare the snake and force him to completely re-route his path to get you or be frozen and stunned for several seconds before continuing the same path in the chase.  This snare and learning how to use it at the perfect time is the highlight of the game for sure, and can definitely create some dramatic and tense moments.. even in a game with such old school and simple graphics.
Never judge a game by its graphics.  This game might cost under a buck, and might look like a type-in Commodore 64 game from 1983, but it's pretty darn fun.  Does it compare to Dragon Age Inquisition?  Of course not, but for under a dollar, I still have this game scoring a surpising 6 out of 10.. and the possibility of moving up to an 8 out of 10 even with the simple graphics and gameplay.  I believe that if the developer adds in controller support to help the player move easier, steam achievements to help reward the player for doing well, and global high scores to allow us to compete against other Steam users, that this game will be a great 99 cent classic old school game!
You can do MUCH worse here on steam in this price range which is flooded with no effort and lackluster asset flips and GameGuru trash, but this game could be a little more fun and offer more value if controller support, achievements, and/or global high scores are added!  Still not a bad score from me for under a buck grabbing a 6 out of 10 right now on launch day!

“Dinner Date” is a very interesting gaming experience, mostly because of the basic idea: You don’t play the character, you play his subconscious. You are not able to change anything, the story will always come to the same end. But in your position in the back of his mind, you are the only one, who can clearly see what is going on. You are the one who witnesses the metamorphosis from a lightly desperate, but kind man to a misogynist, slightly racist♥♥♥♥♥♥
The mechanics might be disappointing from a purely mechanical point of view, but they are much more than in most games not only the vehicle to get the story further, but part of the storytelling. The fact, that the game is able to play itself without you as your strange incapacity to change anything, but to play on, is not only a fancy mechanic, it IS the story that you witness.
“Dinner Date” messes a lot of expectations up, that you have in games and gives a whole new view on how game mechanics and narrations really work and what makes them up.

When it comes to thinking up dream jobs, I feel comfortable in saying that “space pirate” is one that will probably sit pretty highly on most people’s lists. Flying through the infinite void, sneaking on to massive spaceships, and performing daring robberies and dangerous assassinations – it’s all just so incredibly cool sounding. It’s this life that Heat Signature offers up to you, but can the reality really stand up to the exciting expectation?
Well, to begin with, things are much more confusing than exciting. Heat Signature’s gameplay style is very weird – you’ve got to strategically work your way through enemy ships, using a wide range of strange gadgets and weapons along with the ability to pause at any moment to help you obtain success. The best analogy would be that it’s a strange mix of Hotline Miami meets Faster Than Light, but it takes some getting used to no matter how you describe the thing. Chances are your first few missions will see alarms and failures a plenty, as you struggle to come to terms with what each item does, how the many different types of guard react, and how to even get to your objective in the first place.
Your first hour or so can be frustrating, then, but as things slowly click into place you realise this whole learning process is precisely what forms one of Heat Signature’s greatest strengths. This is a game that gives you the ability to constantly experiment, gaining more wisdom as you go, and using this newfound wisdom to come up with grander and more audacious plans. There’s a great joy to be had in pausing and taking your time to come up with a strategy that uses clever manipulation of the gadgets and features offered up to you, and an even greater joy in managing to actually pull it off when things get moving again.
If your plan fails, however, it’s not the end of the world. Indeed, like the developer’s previous title Gunpoint, even the act of failing can be fun. To see an unexpected flaw in your plan fling you into space or cause a massive explosion is more likely to incite laughter than anything else. As a result, you’ll often be willing to step outside your comfort zone just out of sheer curiosity of what could happen, even if the outcome proves not to be so favourable. Characters can die and their loot be lost forever, but when there’s an infinite amount of new characters waiting in the wings ready to forge out new stories of adventure, it’s not a penalty that will ever make you risk adverse.
It’s precisely these stories – those laugh out loud, surreal and amazing moments you instantly want to tell your friend about - that form the other pillar of strength that makes this game so great. Let me explain by sharing one of my own – I had only about 20 seconds left on a ship before my inevitable capture, the only escape being via killing the pilot, who unfortunately lay behind three levels of keycard security. The good news; I had a keycard duplicator. The bad news; the guy with the card I needed was too far away for me to pull off a successful duplication. My solution? Firing my gun and sending him and an army of other guards running to my location, duplicating the key moments before a hail of bullets headed my way, and then making a mad dash to the pilot to stab him to death with less than a second to spare. It made me feel like an incredible badass, and that’s many other tales I could tell. There’s many others I may never end up encountering - and perhaps it is only you who ever will.
It’s not just the individual moments that are important here, however. You see, Heat Signature has very little story that it tells itself, instead encouraging you to use your imagination to flesh out the world around you. Thankfully it’s designed so well it’s very easy to do this - growing fond of your characters, forging your own backstories and motivations for them based on what adversities they face. One of my own heroes was a deadly and deranged phantom, using flick knives and teleporters to kill all in his path. Another was a gadget master, using endless tools to basically never get into combat in the first place. Take a glance online, and there are hundreds of other people who have fleshed out their own characters in the same manner - it’s just nigh on impossible to resist doing.
However, this game by no means a flawless masterpiece. For one, it’s by no means an infinite sandbox – it doesn’t take a great deal of play to encounter everything on offer that’s truly unique, with only variations in ship designs or stuff like the range and capacity of your gadgets keeping things somewhat fresh. The scope for experimentation always remains, but I’ll admit it gets harder and harder to keep things fresh the longer you play. While the end game may be successfully liberating the entire galaxy, it takes so long to do this you'd have to be incredibly dedicated to actually pull it off.
I also had a few other minor issues. One is that some ship designs feels cluttered, making it hard to actually see guards and others important details within the fray of all the superfluous ship features dotted about. I also infrequently encountered an issue whereupon the camera would suddenly zoom out to the most extreme distance possible, which is something far from game breaking, but proved annoying nonetheless – especially when it tended to happen seemingly every time things started to get intense.
These issues aside, however, the fact remains that Heat Signature is worthy of your attention. It’s a game that manages to take your trials and tribulations, and make them feel like something far greater and grander than they have any right to be. It’s not perfect, but when in your mind’s eye you are controlling the greatest space pirate that ever lived... Well, I really doubt you’ll care.

My only other 'hacker' game I've played was Uplink so I will include comparisons with it.
Pros:
-There's a console where you use some linux commands like 'ls', 'mv', 'scp' and 'rm', so if this is the first time you use them, you get to feel the horror when you rm *
-The game really hits home the actual reality of gaining access to a system: maybe from brute force, maybe from exploits, but almost always from someone sending a password plain-text over an IRC channel or mobile device email.
-It's a bit more 'real' feeling than Uplink, due to the console, the irrelevance of geological locations, and the introduction of concepts such as 'ports', 'front ends', etc
Cons:
-The game is littered with a noticeable amount of spelling and grammar errors, enough that it doesn't feel like the developer planned to do it.
-It's still every bit as 'graphic' as Uplink; cracking a system consists entirely of executing programs that each crack their own type of port, and they all have their own little static animation they play.
-Most of the challenge comes when your 800ish MB of RAM isn't enough to execute them all when possible, and you have to wait for others to finish.
As for the story, I haven't finished it, so can't say.
If you really liked Uplink, or if you think you'd be really into a pretty simple Hollywood hacking simulator, it's an OK buy. I don't regret it.

It places players in the infuriating position of putting time into puzzles which cannot be solved.  This is the Kobayashi Maru in it's truest form, as it cannot be 100% beat without hacking the game files.
Additionally, the game will sometimes stop responding when trying to reach the menu, and the achievements for it are also broken. In place of getting one for beating 50 levels, you get the achievement for beating *all* levels, and then you get additional one for beating 100 levels. If the game hadn't been developed with so many bugs, it would have been alright, but I cannot recommend it.

Lately, I've been making a habit of trying out games with "Mixed" reviews--often, I find them to be the most interesting. Dinner Date is a game that isn't for everyone; some might not enjoy the concept, others might find it boring. This isn't a game in which the goal is clear,  and the end result isn't necessarily what you would call gratifying.  There are no bosses to defeat or world to save. To me, this game embodies "virtual reality" in a much more emotional sense.
You are the subconscious of the protagonist, Julian, as he experiences the agony of waiting on his "dinner date" to arrive. This means, you really have no control over what is happening. You can merely observe and react in the most subtle of ways. As the story unfolds before you, you are given a set of choices. Will Julian glance nervously at the clock, have a cigarette to calm his nerves or have another glass of wine as he bemoans his situation? The voiceover acting is very well done, and adds to realism of the game. If you've ever experienced the anxiety of anticipation. and the agony of disappointment, the game expresses both  perfectly.
In order to truly enjoy this game, you have to accept the fact that nothing you do will change its outcome. You are merely along for the ride, guiding Julian's thoughts and actions along the way via a growing number of options by pressing specific buttons on your keyboard, which lead to certain interactions. But it's not as if you're sitting there idle while a long cinematic cutscene plays either; it's an experience you can be a part of from start to finish. As Julian's subconscious, you are like the director with Julian as the actor. Considering the options are numerous, and you can choose them in any order you wish, everybody's experience in the game will be slightly different and unique to them, even if the ending is the same. It gives it a very personal feel which I enjoyed. Overall, this is an overlooked and misunderstood little gem of a game.

I wish there was another option besides "recommended" and "not recommended," because I'd give this game a "meh" if I could. I don't hate it, I just think it's the weakest of the first five Final Fantasy games--and the 3D remake doesn't really improve anything.
Aesthetically, I liked the chibi/Mii/MySims-looking character models more than I thought I would. Your main characters are all adorable, and the costumes for all the different classes are fairly detailed and interesting (though they look better in the menu thumbnails). But the character models are also really twitchy during battle sequences.
In general, I'm a big fan of the art style used for the Game Boy Advance remakes of these games. The smaller, more realistic sprites did a good job of capturing the dark, intricate, fantastical feel of the classical Final Fantasy universes. Look at the concept art from FFI-V. It's all weird, exotic, and unearthly, and I think the GBA remakes did a much better job capturing that feel with their overall designs. This game, however, goes for a more generic, cartoony atmosphere as part of an appeal to younger and more casual gamers.
The backgrounds to the battle sequences are the only truly appealing visual element in the game. Environments look empty and bland, both in the overworld and in towns and dungeons. Enemy models lack detail and also come across as bland. One of the advantages of the hand-drawn sprites from the GBA games is that they portray each enemy in a carefully designed, static pose, so each enemy gets to look pretty cool. In a 3D game, you see the whole enemy, and the enemy moves around even when it isn't attacking, so most enemy models come across as lackluster or unimpressive.
The transition to 3D also changes the way your character moves in the game. Instead of moving tile-by-tile, you have free range of movement--which means your character will get stuck on corners a lot. Furthermore, the near walls in every dungeon consist entirely of empty shadows, and it be difficult to see certain doors and entrances as a result (although hidden passages are usually grossly obvious).
I imagine I would enjoy this game more if I played it on the DS. The default keyboard controls are about as unintuitive as possible, and you can only change the controls on the start-up menu before you actually launch the game. A GBA remake would have been even better, I think, but I still think I would consider it my least favorite original Final Fantasy game.
For one thing, while the game has a fine story, the pacing and exposition are weird. You often have to extrapolate beyond what characters say if you want to have any clue what's actually going on. Usually, a FF game's story is easy to follow despite its many twists and turns, but this game has you holding on for dear life in terms of comprehension. One problem is that the game is a little too open-ended at points. You can often start down several storylines by visiting different towns, but you may have to wait for a few dungeons and crucial plot developments before these storylines ever feature into the central plot. The game allows for a lot of exploration, which is fun in its own right, but there aren't always worthwhile rewards to finding new areas before you're "supposed" to.
Also, the game has a frustrating tendency to almost require you to switch jobs in certain ways at certain places. For instance, the game features multiple (multiple!) dungeons that require you to traverse them under the effects of the spell Mini--which essentially makes all your physical fighters useless. Other sections of the game clearly push you toward   classes like the dragoon or the dark knight by giving you loads of specialized equipment in anticipation of a boss battle or an enemy type that will be hard to deal with otherwise. These gameplay designs would make for excellent teaching tools--if this my first time playing a game with an involved job system. It's not. These sections also hurts the game's replay value, since even experienced players don't always have total freedom to experiment with the different job classes and set up the party they want to use.
In fact, the job system in this game is kind of a letdown. One problem with being able to change characters' jobs at will is keeping track of all their equipment. While there is a fair amount of overlap in terms of which jobs can use what weapons and armors, carrying around or storing all that junk gets annoying after a while. And while most jobs progress pretty quickly, there isn't too much incentive to gain job levels with most classes. At most, a higher job level changes one or two minor calculations for class-specific actions you won't always use all that often. Job level is more important for mages, since I'm pretty sure it influences the MP they gain. Unlike the job system in, say, FFV, there are no major rewards for mastering a class either. You can't take abilities or even base stats (except HP) with you when you change classes.
But I think my biggest gripe about this game is its horrendously uneven gameplay. This game expects you to grind for several levels between just about every major dungeon. Try to go straight from one plot point to the next and you will probably lose. The boss battles are the worst offenders of all--they are all really, really hard. Regardless of how easily you managed to get through a dungeon's standard enemies, when you reach the boss, there is a good chance you will get a game over. And with no mid-dungeon save points, that means replaying an entire chunk of the game. Each boss is exactly the same too--they all attack twice with either hard physical attacks (that can inflict statuses) or magic spells that hit your entire party for heavy damage. The challenge doesn't come from figuring out an optimal strategy; it comes entirely from luck, as bosses have an unusual tendency to target your weakest characters and throw you back on your heels in survival mode.
The game gets better as it goes along, fortunately, and the vast job system does provide a lot of replay value. I'm just pretty sure I would rather replay Final Fantasy I on the GBA than fight through this game again--what with all its problems and its decided lack of polish.

It is truly a pleasure for the long-time fan of Final Fantasy titles on the Playstation to be able to play through classic games such as this in a reworked state. As much as it is a pleasant feeling of nostalgia to play them once again on a SNES, seeing some of the older games remade in such a way is really great--having them come to Steam is even better.
Don't be fooled by the slightly child-like visuals (they were, after all made for the DS and then subsequently mobile OSs). Final Fantasy III is an old-school RPG. The vast majority of the game remains what it was on the SNES to the core. It is unforgiving; there is very rarely a save-point before a boss. For those who remember these frustrating but extremely rewarding games with fondness, you will not be disappointed with Final Fantasy III. Some things about the old school, however, are not so great. Attacking a fire-elemental monster with fire and having it simply hurt them 'less' rather than outright healing them, appears to be a feature that Square-Enix probably should have tweaked before re-releasing this game, but I can forgive them--after all, as I said it *does* hurt them less...
The story is basic, as one would expect of an RPG of its age. Square Enix added a little bit of character development into the reworked version that at least helps to better differentiate the characters from one another. Nonetheless, if you wish to play for storyline rather than the excellent RPG combat mechanics that made Final Fantasy the definitive title in turn-based RPGs, then you may wish to look to the newer titles in the series now available on Steam, such as VII, VIII, and soon to be XIII.
I would certainly recommend this game to any Final Fantasy fan. Beyond that, however, I'm not sure I could recommend it. There are far better RPGs out there on the market and often at a similar price. The later titles in the Final Fantasy series, the Elder Scrolls, and Bioware's many titles are typically superior to this one if you plan on throwing 30+ hours into a game. As a fan of Final Fantasy, though, I enjoyed it. 8/10.

I've dipped into Fractured Space at various times during its lifecycle, but it's only been of recently that it has suddenly clicked with me.  Now I'm not going to beat about the bush here, but if you, like me, have never played a MOBA before, then there is a bit of a learning process.  However, I urge you strongly to stick with this one, because it's better than a Sunday roast and at free to play, significantly cheaper.
There's spaceships, and then there's Fractured Space spaceships.  It's like comparing a one man kayak to a supertanker, but take that supertanker and load it with a multitude of weaponry and cunning utility features such as "Chrono Blink", and you have a fearsome weapon of war.  Then take said behemoth of a spaceship and throw it into a multi-route arena with 9 other behemoth spaceships with the aim of the game being to smash the oppositions base.  If you happen to take down a Leviathan or two en route to victory, then all the better.
A balanced team can make a big difference in this game, you need to be aiming for meat, veg and roast potatoes, rather than beans, beans and more beans.  All out sniper teams will not win.  Period.  The next essential ingredient is teamwork, a team that communicates strongly will fare better than a team of skillful lone wolves.  And then you need to understand not only your ship, but every other ship type that you may encounter.  Fractured Space is very much of a rock, paper, scissors mechanic, and understanding which ships you are strong against vs. those that you should tuck your tail between your legs and run, is a key element.
Fractured Space initially seems a bit basic and daunting all at the same time, my early multiplayer games resulted in me demonstrating an unhealthy skill in respawning and failing to deal with ship classes that I should by all rights, be able to pummel into bean soup.  Was it due to the fact that they had paid hard cash to get better ships than me?  No.  Fractured Space offers premium ships and skins, but the upgrade is purely aesthetic.  It was simply a lack of understanding on my part of what goes into making a good roast dinner that was my downfall.  After several hours at learning a ship, I suddenly found that I was calling out tactics to my teammates, knowing when to push and when to warp back to base, heal up and defend.
The community on the large is very friendly and willing to help, if you don't know how to do something, someone, whether it be in game, or on the forums, will point you in the right direction.  My suggestion to new players is to run the tutorial missions, play a few games against the AI, and then when you do go into a multiplayer game, stick with your teammates and watch out for the call-outs, but beyond everything, have fun.
See you on the battlefield, you bring the meat, I'll dish the roasties.

This game is an absolute emotional rollercoaster.
This is the first game of Telltale's that I've played. And it got me so hooked I found myself compelled to buy both The Wolf Among Us and season two of Walking Dead. I have no regrets of doing either.
I have to admit that I was very sceptical when first entering the game. I knew it was a point and click, and that is why I didn't buy it way back when it was being released. But since it was on sale, and I've heard from friends it is worth a look, I decided to give it a try.
I found myself instantly hooked.
I don't like point and click games, in the sense you just observe, and do very little, or it is just not fun because you have to find things which are usually hidden on the screen and click them instead of actually doing something actively. This is not how The Walking Dead functions at all. Telltale has done an amazing job turning this point and click adventure into an experience like watching a really, really good movie or TV show, and actually having a say in what is going to happen.
I was baffled by how good it was. The more I played, the more I thought to myself, 'this game is gooood'.
And it's not just that I love the notion of surviving the zombie apocalypse on account of your wits, the characters are so incredible. You will get attached to them, and the events later will tear your heart out. That is a guarantee. A friend of mine who usually doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about anything, and is completely untouched by heartwarming stories, actually let out a single tear at the end.
There are no words to describe the amount of feels you will experience while playing this. No character is outright bad. You will feel bad even for the characters you disliked at first.
This is a tale of survival, second chances, but most importantly, family.
The greatest masochist experience you could ever wish for.
If you are the kind of person that loves getting their heart torn out, torn to pieces, glued clumsily back together and then made into eating it, you will love this game.
