I started playing final fantasy games about 10 years ago. I started with final fantasy X and was hooked shortly after. The series is amazing but I never went back to play anything below FFX. I heard the hype behind FFVII but I never like to buy into hype because it only serves to disappoint me usually. That being said, the very early final fantasys had sprites and I was not too interested in the low detail so I stayed on the other side of FFX.
Now, I saw this on sale at the Humble Store and I figured it would be a good time to try the older Final Fantasy games, given the polish this game had recieved.
It has a piece of gaming that I had missed with all the new games in the world now. It makes you want to play just because you want to discover new things. Not for the sake of driving the plot forward or saving X amount of people. It lets you do what you want and I get legitimately excited when I open a chest or find a new hidden area. It makes me feel like when I first started to play video games all so long ago and I haven't had this feeling since Valkyrie Profile:Leneth for the PSP. I actually want to grind and level my party up so I can kill monster and gain treasure. Almost a feeling akin to Skyrim but less open.
I guess it plays to the basic nature that players want to get treasure and go adventuring. Not for someone else but to see a new world, take a break from reality, of only for a moment. This game gives me a feeling I sought for a while and makes me like to play with the jobs and test out different party combinations.
Now, the game still has a linear story with areas opening up as you progress the role you are "destined" to fulfill but the game doesn't push that on you too hard. You know that you have to save the world or some such thing but it isn't the reason you are playing. Or at least why I am playing. It doesn't seem to be wanting to center itself around the plot. It seems to want to center itself around you doing what you wish the areas open to you leading up to the plot driven boss battle so you can continut the quest.
In conclusion, it gives you the illusion of freedom even though it blocks you off at some points. The exploring of new caves and little hidden sparkles is fun. 10/10 would review again :D

If you enjoy the older Final Fantasy games then I'd recommend Final Fantasy III. Now keep in mind that this is the real Final Fantasy III (not the Super Nintendo Final Fantasy III which was actually Final Fantasy VI, but renamed FFIII since it was the third FF game to hit the US). The graphic update looks good (keep in mind that this version of FFIII was originally a Nintendo DS game). The gameplay is typical turn-based Final Fantasy gameplay. It's hard to compare to the original FFIII since it never came to the US, so I've never played it. This FF game puts an emphasis on jobs. Which determine your skill sets and which weapons/armor you can equip, but don't worry you can change your job at anytime. You also level up your jobs just like you level up your character. So the higher the job level the better you'll be at that job, and you don't lose any job levels by switching back and forth. The story is nothing special, but being from 1990 it's pretty good. Bottom line is if you like the old Final Fantasy titles (you'll need to do some grinding), and you don't mind the graphics then you'll enjoy the game.

My lack of hours in this game is only due to my addiction to MMO's with more long term resolutions (EvE addict).
As far as internet space ship sims go this game for myself is a blast in 30-60 minute sessions (a couple of matches).
Like any other MOBA a certain degree of teamwork is required to have a shred of success.
This is not always a 1v1 balanced game, an expectation I also feel is unrealistic and ruins many game's pvp elements. Some ships simply destroy other ones, and the rest is up to the player to be strategic in order to achieve an advantage.
The maps provide plenty of obstacles to achieve this.
The cons IMO (other than my inherit bias towards longer-term commitment style games):
- Ship upgrades (in the tree) sometimes feel marginal, combined with an appropriate crew however can make a noticable difference.
- Early on match finding was harder, now more people have the game and finding a match seems to be quicker (so less of a con than it used to be!)
Other than that I have to say I do recommend this game. It is quite a lot of fun and it is not pay to win. Do give it a try!

Where's the middle thumb? Ah, whatever, I'll give it a thumbs-up, since it's mostly positive.
It's something I really enjoy. It's like real hacking, but easy. I mean, it's not every day that you can go online and crack into Microsoft's (Macrosoft, the "totally originally new company") servers so easily. Honestly, it's not completely Hollywood, but it's also not completely  realistic (of course). The idea of using a Unix-based terminal is actually really cool, and it allows me to brush up on my skills of using such. However, I find it a bit disappointing that there's such a limited RAM, which is now as limited as hard-drive space in--brace yourselves--
that there's so little, and for 7.6 hours (as of post) have I not seen any upgrades to it.
The gameplay in this game, however, is captivating. It's hacking: it's tense, it's sweaty, it's chilling: it's everything you'd expect hacking to be, especially once you start getting traced and the beeps start going faster. Now, do I think hacking in this game is OP? No. Do I think it's UP? No. I think hacking in this game is somehow in this uncanny valley of good enough but not enough good. It's, in a sense, "realistic". However, captivating realism isn't the same as slowing down reload speeds.
I find the game in it's fullest, a nice game. It's not the best, and it's not the worst, but for a hack sim, it comes very nicely aligned with--wait for it...
as a spiritual successor, but not extremely successful. There's limits to the game, of course, games always have that, but personally, it's more story-based with "hack" in the title.

It took me quite some time to finally buy this game, for the negative reviews made me believe that the RNG/game mechanism is terribly unfair.
But now that I have over 100 hours put in this game, I have finished the vanilla game, I can safely say that this really was not the case. I read on many occasions people saying that it is indeed too hard, for they have played video games their entire life and they still can't beat the game. That's like saying: I've walked my entire life, so I must be terrific at football.
Yes, the game is very difficult, and you will walk through the trial and error, like you would with any other challenging game, and if and when you fail, you will do better next time, knowing now what awaits you.
Of course, there are scenarios that will leave you with a feeling that the game just fcucked you big time. For example, I once lost a full health hero to a critter-level spider, just because they managed to land 3 critical strikes in a row, and left me poisoned. Unfair? Hell no, just unlucky, that's all. And guess what I do next time I run into those skittery fcuckers? I'll keep my torch bright, and stun the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them, while my DMG picks them out one by one.
I love that the game is made like this. Because this game is not about strong heroes who will march in and save the day. It's a bunch of humane "heroes" trying to push back the overwhelming evil that is lurking in the world, and because they are almost equally strong as you are, you need to improve your strategies and skills constantly.
The game looks beautiful, sounds great, and feels awesome, but maybe reconsider if you are looking forward to playing an easy game to relax, for I'm such a pus.sy, that I needed a friend to accompany me in teamspeak just to be my mental support as I fought my way through the intense last stages of the game.
The only actual complaint I have, is the Crimson Court DLC. But the review page of it already tells all that I feel towards it.

Ok, full disclosure from the start.  I'm a big fan of the Assassin’s Creed series of games.  I’ve played through all the core series so far and have loved each one (even AC3, which gets a terrible rap in my opinion).  I wrote a glowing review of Assassin’s Creed 4: Black Flag on Steam calling it one of my favourite games of all time!
The reviews for Unity pointed at a poorly optimised, buggy, PC version and some very questionable design choices (prominent micro transactions and annoying ‘companion app’ quests built into the game).  So I resisted a day one buy, partly because I wanted to buy specifically on Steam, rather than Uplay.  Partly because I figured these issues would be fixed in time.  But I caved in during the Steam Christmas sale and experienced first-hand the mess Ubisoft had shoved out the door.  At the time I was running a reasonably powerful system (an i7 3770K overclocked to 4.5GHz, 16 GB RAM and a Geforce 680 (with 2GB of VRAM).  My system is hamstrung slightly as my six year old Samsung monitor only supports a resolution of 1680x1050, though this does allow me to push for graphical detail at the expense of resolution.  Since the weak link in my PC was that my graphics card lacked VRAM I set the graphical options to HIGH and jumped in.
The game looked good, great in fact!  I was slightly surprised it was using the same AnvilNext engine as Black Flag.  Everything looked that much more realistic, especially the facial animations.  But then it started, micro stutter, every few seconds.  Just enough to make the game unplayable.  Feeling disappointed I quit after 5 minutes to patiently for a patch.  Though having been burned with similar Watch_Dogs problems I resigned myself to the issue never being addressed.
But it was!  After almost three months, and with the release of Patch 5, my micro stutter issue was fixed and I gave the game another run out.
And straight away I fell in love with it.  So much so that I picked up a 970 to see it in all its glory!
So what’s good?
As much as I loved Black Flag for the fresh new approach it bought to the series (and the stunning Caribbean vistas) I felt it lacked a lot of what I really liked about the first few Assassin’s Creed games.  I felt that the core mechanic in this series was parkouring through a well realised, historic city.  Unity brings this back and improves on it hugely.  The parkour just flows better than in previous games with extra animations for movement.  You actually feel like you’re moving quickly over, through and under the city.  “Through” being perhaps the most exciting enhancement.  There are now a large number of buildings in the game world that have been opened up.  Some of these interiors being fairly generic rooms with others being incredible recreations of real world locations.  Notre Dame is simply stunning in terms of detail.  The lighting illuminating the interior of this vast gothic cathedral is one of the most impressive things I’ve seen in any game to date.  It looks like something from a tech demo, and yet its fully interactive!  On the subject of lighting its equally impressive to see a cloud slowly move past the sun temporarily throwing shadows over parts of the city.  It doesn’t add anything to the gameplay but its little details like this that increase immersion.
But this is only a small part of a multitude of improvements that makes Ubisoft’s recreation of Paris in the late seventeen hundreds a real marvel.  Much has been made of technology that allows large crowds to populate the streets of the city and again, that is really impressive and immersive.  Wherever you travel in Paris there are people doing something.  Watching a beheading, clamouring to break into a church, protesting, singing, getting drunk, conversing idly.  The sheer number of crowd animations makes everywhere feel alive and while it makes a big difference and affords many more opportunities.  You can now effectively plan an assassination, remove your target and then disappear seamlessly into the crowd to escape.
This leads into perhaps the single best improvement to the series.  The overhaul of the missions.  Each of the core story sequences seems to revolve around finding a killing and key character in the story (I say “seems” as I’ve only played through the first 6-7 so  far).  But unlike in previous Assassin’s Creed titles you’re given a great deal of freedom in how you go about the assassination.  You can charge in, sword out, pistol at the ready.  But you’ll be in for a long, drawn out fight against tough opposition.  Alternatively you can use stealth and misdirection to avoid combat almost entirely.  There are often multiple routes through to a target, reminiscent of classics like Deus Ex.  And there are optional objectives to accomplish to help tip the odds in your favour.  Overall you feel in complete control of the assassination.  You make the plan, you execute it (and your target) and you adapt if something goes awry.  The enemy AI isn’t nearly as impressive as that in something like Metal Gear Solid 5: Ground Zeros (where there is real fear you will be hunted down if spotted) but still makes for an exciting challenge.
The co-op missions are surprisingly good too.  Initially I thought they were a bad idea.  Oftentimes this sort of thing feels crowbarred into the game.  But, as with Watch_Dogs, Ubisoft have integrated them into the game seamlessly.  You can either go to a predefined co-op mission location and the game will match-make for you, finding partners for your escapade.  Or alternatively you might be “interrupted” while around Paris by an assassin asking you to come and join their endeavour.  In which case you can accept or continue on with whatever you were doing.  The missions themselves feel well defined and are a lot of fun to play.  I haven’t figured out how to communicate with my fellow assassin’s yet (if you can at all) but everyone so far has “played the objective”.
So what’s bad?
I’m actually struggling with this question.  Obviously Ubisoft releasing an unfinished product then taking about four months to patch out some of the bigger problems is not good enough (and judging by some forum posts there are still lingering issues with those running SLI/Crossfire setups).  But if I were to judge Unity on its merits as a game (technical issues notwithstanding) there isn’t a great deal wrong with it at all.
Here are my nitpicks then.  The day/night cycle seems to have gone from previous games.  Missions take place at pre-set times during the day (or night) and that’s fine.  The scene shifts to accommodate these.  Other than that you have a slider in the options menu to adjust the time of day.  Given how incredible lighting is in this game it would have been neater had this been a gradual shift.
The parkour can be a little bit hit and miss.  Occasionally, while running, Arno will mount a table or chair, or wall and it will take some coaxing to get him down off it.  This can be frustrating when you’re trying to pull off a quick escape, after doing what an assassin does.
In conclusion…
I love this game, I really do.  I know it hasn’t gone down too well with other fans and has been unfavourably compared to Black Flag (the high water mark of the series) but for me it’s a return to the core of what made the Assassin’s Creed games great after a really fun detour.  Personally, I actually rate this slightly higher than superb Black Flag because of how incredibly realised (and beautiful) the open world sandbox is.  It’s the sort of game where you should just ditch the map (I really recommend turning the HUD widget off) and just explore historical Paris.  There really are opportunities and adventures to be had everywhere which (more or less) is why I love games in the first place.

I cannot support the idea of buying 2/3 of a game.
There IS a lot to like in this game.  They added an attempt at a crafting system (extremely rudementary and not very well executed), and they finally allowed us to see what the characters can do as we select them from the big list.  But that's mostly because a majority of the characters are virtually the same.  Which is more the problem with the story than the game.  It has the same type of overworld as Lego LOTR, with questing and such.  Elements of the overworld unlock as you play through the story.
All in all, on a technical level, the game's a fairly fun Lego game.
But the failures come in the adaptation.  First off, they chose to model the game after the movies.  Because of course they did, if they followed the book instead people would be confused and scared and not want to give them money again.  So we have crap like the stupid barrel scene, and the really, REALLY badly done Lake-Town bit (and a level in this game that just never seems to end - much like the movie).  And if they had based it on the book, they could have actually FINISHED THE BLOODY STORY!
No, instead, we get 2/3 of the game.  And that's all there will ever be.  There is no DLC for the third movie (which would be a terrible precedent anyway).  There is no second game (which would be about as sorry as Lego Indiana Jones 2).  What we are left with is an eternally incomplete product because they felt the need to rush this game out the door.
Do not buy it.  There are plenty of other Lego games to play instead.  And if you have already played all of those, there are plenty of other video games period that are far more worth your time than this incomplete mess.

As someone who loves building and world making, I had a blast starting this game and making a home world with my brothers and husband. I also liked the different classes and abilties, though fighting got pretty redundant and I spent most of my time making castles, underground railways and the like. The game is also shiny, which was a nice bonus.
Good things aside however, this game has some MAJOR flaws that killed all the fun and I haven't played in months.
1. Down Time. I dunno if it's still as big of an issue as it was when I started playing, but there were huge waits for upgrades that never seemed to fix the bugs that they were meant to that just lead to... yes, more down time. These were always scheduled on Tueday which was mining day, which was annoying.
2. Glitching. The worst issue was lag based and would put you back a couple seconds from where you just were, which meant what I would mine or try to build would not stay. My brothers and I also had issues with their created creations disappearing because the dev's would realize they screwed something up and had to go back in time... so goodbye anything you just made, it's not there anymore. Other people had issues with their home worlds being totally wrecked, luckily that didn't happen to us.
3. Repetition. There really wasn't much else to do in the game after you build what you wanted to. You can easily get to the top of all the crafting tiers except fighting and fishing...which are both pretty boring after a while.
4. Pricing and Whales. They treated their patrons poorly. I never actually did put any money into the game because the forums were full of complaints from those that spent hundreds of dollars into the game and were given content they couldn't use, like non-trade-able class coins for those that had all the classes...Maybe they've fixed it, I dunno.
But yeah, was fun for a little while, can't recommend though.

Disclaimer: I'm not finished with the challenge mode of the game.
My thoughts in a word: Decent.
Let's starts off with the basic stuff:
-The game has two characters, each with two unique special attacks and their own set of basic attacks and a different dodge animations. They share the ability to repair and an ability that pulls enemies to a sort of magnatism bomb.
-The game has 60 story missions and 80 challenge missions, each of which take a few minutes. Nothing very long, but the amount of content is decent.
-Enemy variety is good. There's a pretty interesting array of enemies ranging from weak melee fodder, to suicide bots, to laser bots, to arc fire bots, to homing bomb firing bots, and more. They're pretty varied and do a good job to keep you alert.
- A notable mechanic is that your SP regenrates pretty slowly, but you get +20 for dodging through attacks, so it encourages you to actually pay attention to the timing on your dodges so you can keep using special attacks (and repairs) for drawn-out encounters.
All of the above adds up to a genuinely fun game. That said, the place where the game falters is in boss design. Bosses are all just bigger versions of the normal enemies with a big radial AoE to keep you on your toes. They're not too hard to kill honestly, and they don't require you to change up your tactics much beyond watching out for the big purple circle AoE telegraph. The bosses are really pretty much as generic as the normal enemies, to the point that they're even reused (a lot). This means that between the mass of normal enemies and  lack of very interesting boss design, the game is pretty repetative.
I mean, imagine taking your favorite beat-em-up and then remove all of the bosses from it and replace them with tankier/harder hitting versions of the normal enemies. It's probably still a decent amount of fun, but it's missing something. That's pretty much this game (for me so far). I do think this is the kind of thing that could be compensated for by wide player character variety (think Musou/Warriors style games), but this game doesn't have that either.
Anyway, Smashing the Battle is worth a look, but it's not going to blow your mind.

This game is literally flawless, from the jaw-dropping graphics and responsive shooting to the smooth game mechanics and genius map design, it is a fine example of what a game should be.
The graphics in the game are outstanding, a truly impressive spectacle that only high end PC's will be able to utilise. The light shimmers realistically off of the pristine water, the environments are incredibly detailed, and the gore is so lifelike you feel like a part of the war.
The menu system is simple, effective and easy to navigate, allowing you enter a game in a split second. The options for your character upon entry are near infinite, with a huge arsenal of weapons and classes.
The gameplay is literal perfection. Shooting is reponsive, the controls are immersive and effortless, and the block mechanic is extremely innovative and creative, something I have never before experienced, and is well implemented into the gameplay.
If you consider yourself a fan of videogames, or even if you don't, you must play Blockade 3D. IT WILL NOT DISSAPOINT.
I give it a personal rating of 9.987/10 and give it an editors choice award.

This game is hard, very hard. But it is fair because it reminds you that it is every time that you start it. And it is fair, because you can win, as long as you are careful. And by 'careful' I don't mean just 'awake'.
Let me tell you a story that I think illustrates what this game is about:
*VAGUE SPOILER ALERT FOR 1 RANDOM ENCOUNTER"
So I played this game for a bit and managed to form a decent possee: one lvl 5, two lvl 4s and a lvl 3 character. And I took them on a short Veteran run, suitable for levels 4 and 5 and I figured that we can pull the lvl 3 out of it alive. Or find a new Position 4 character. It happens.
So, we rumbled our way through a few battles, not picking up too much Stress, even being able to afford drawing a few of them out an extra turn or two so that our tanks can heal a bit.
Then we found a curio an altar that said to do a certain thing if we crave abyss.
Acting based on the experience of ton of other RPG, I allowed myself to be optimisitic. Maybe I'll get a cool Cosmic Sword!!! or some strange perk!!!
And in Darkest Dungeon, optimism kills.
So, I did the thing and my precious party, which I have been building for the last few days got to meet some giant cosmic thing whith roughly the HPs of our whole part combined, protected up to chestickles and able to bleed us, blight us and summon minions on us.
Let me pause the story for a moment and invite you to consider how FAIR this outcome was: I was exploring a hounted ruins, already boxing above my weight and, upon finding and altar that promised to introduce me to Abyss I cheerfully press "Meet the Abyss" button. And I met Abyss. Not some stupid thing like "a hydra that you WILL beat but it MIGHT kill a character or two if you aren't carefull". Abyss.
I got lucky in the end and managed to escape. None of my characters died but they all got traumatized all to hell, gained negative quirks, afflictions and diseases. Now they are going to recuperate for a few weeks before being even remotely capable of going on another mission.
Decison - consequences. This is a great game. And fair.

So feelings I got from this game while giving it 25 hours of my live. From what I have played I must say I understand players that don't like this game as well players who do.
Let's take it pretty slowly.
You spawn in a prison with only task: Pick up the key behind the cell and escape. You find out there's a Inala who gives you quests, bank, you can hide/save your money in and  FOR FREE! There's also a Tavern where you can for a certain amount of money engrave your item, so next time you die you spawn with it. Community is pretty friendly, only thing that the screen is kinda small, map is kinda small and you cannot "go fullscreen" with it. No problem by me.
Okey, you start farming, you get better items, everything engraved, sometimes you die due to now knowing which monster is strong and which not, so as newbie you might just get lost in the world full of fantasy and get somewhere you should have never gone. There is 16% of losing your engraved stuff, plus you lose all your gold you have in your pocket. Ofc if you are brave enough, you go back to fight back for your items, you die again, lose more of your XPs and items.
You are slowly finding out, that this game is pretty repepetitive, because after some time you have to keep like 4 hours same boss to get some goodie out of him so you can move on, another boss you have to keep killing him at least 12 hours and I'm not counting in the time while you are getting killed by PVP players who takes your stuff and gold.
I spent 25 hours on this game, I did not get even through the first boss.
Conclusion?
Developers are trying to make this game community aimed, which is cool, but if you have no friends to play this game, it gets pretty old-fashioned and you start to realizing that any stronger player can kill you and you cannot do anything else then run to the town and try to hide in your vault before he kills you. It takes really A LOT of time to get somewhere where you could call yourself "player with better equipment" and you can still lose it pretty quicky, as well as your XPs and so your levels.
At all, you have to invest a lot of time, there's friendly community, but of course not everyone and some might just keep trying to kill you and take your stuff or if you cross their way, they will just kill you with 4-6 hits. Game is pretty interesting, even more when you get a guild and some friends together.
Why did I stop playing this game?
I would have to invest a lot of time into it to get to some interesting level, because this game is higher-level aimed, at PVP levels etc. and I have no friends to play it with, and since it's still the same, killing the boss over and over again, then losing some stuff due to PVP players or sometimes to my stupidity and not enough nerves to keep waiting, getting it back, while losing one level I was doing last 3 hours and then going for higher boss, who spawns even in a longer intervals - 20-35 minutes. That's all I can say, I stopped playing by "Ourik" who spawns as I said 20-35 minutes because it would take a long time to get some goodie from him and move on "to the next level". Chance he drops something good you need is like 8%? My guess and there are at least another 3 of 4 players trying to get that items as well. All I can say to this. I liked this game a lot, but after 25 hours I realized I'm missing friends I might play it with and I do not have so much time and nerves to be just dying over and over and still keep killing after 6 hours same boss to finally get some thingie I needed.
I recommend this game for players who have bunch of time, friends, nerves and like these styles of hardcore retro RPG (MMO) games aimed especially on community and later on as probably on every other game PVP.

A great game with an emphasis on teamwork and knowledge of game mechanics.
Fractured Space is a a beautiful game, with great visual and sound design. It has a very heavy focus on teamwork, so being polite, cooperating and reading your allies and your enemies behaviour is key. You WILL need to learn and fast. Each ship, similar to hero's in other MOBA and MOBA-esk games, has is strengths, weakness' and purpose. Understanding how to play each ship is key.
Most games follow a fairly similar pattern, cap mines, fight for Gamma, attack enemy base. Don't let that fool you though, just because the game has a mould, doesn't mean you have to follow it. Each match will have it's different fights, and in each fight you might have to play slighly differently. And if you emerge victorious from a fight, you do feel a sense of pirde.
However, it is not without it's flaws. The first and most important one is balance. With so many ships and so many factors to take into account, the game could be said to be unbalanced, and that wouldn't be wrong. It would however be a very narrow view. As a player with over 500 hours playing spread over around  2 years, I've seen unbalanced in FS, and it's done nothing but improve and the Devs have done nothing but learn (if slowly at times), but the game isn't perfect when it comes to balance, dare I say it will never be perfect, but which game is?
The single biggest issue however is the Match Maker, or MM. It uses a system called MMR, which is based on win victories and defeats, to "balance matches". Needless to say it's not the best system. It's been endlessly debated, moaned about, changed, tweaked and is a constant work in progress. If I were you, dont get angry about it, others will, but just try to play the game, help others and carry harder.
The second is to do with ECG themselves. Having talked to the Devs, I know they are a great bunch of guys and girls that only want to make the game be fun and enjoyable for everyone, they just have a funny way of showing it sometimes. From random experimental patches, suprise launches or lack of communication, ECG definitely have their own way of doing things.
Overall, Fractured Space is a great game with fun and varied gameplay, but not always balanced and with a WIP MM. ECG can seem to be a bit random at times, but they mean well.

Thefts, kidnappings, rescues, assassinations, hijackings - no job too big or too foolhardy. Armed, perhaps, with a teleporter that only transports you for two seconds and a wrench. Or a grenade launcher that hacks sentry turrets and a shotgun.
It's up to you to figure out how, and then, how the hell to escape with your life and target intact. It's a heap of fun.

Ok, so I've only been playing Assassin's Creed games for a relatively short time, and so far every one has impressed me in one way or another. Please don't listen to the haters who got salty at launch, because after waiting for the patches to come out (which I did before I bought it), I can honestly say that this is a good buy. I really love the story. It's kind of your run of the mill love and betrayal story, but I found it to be surprisingly emotionally involving, and it came with a few unexpected plot twists along the way. Also, staying true to the AC formula, there's a crap ton of side stuff to do.
The game is full of all kinds of eye candy, and is by far one of (if not the most) graphically gorgeous games I've ever played. Yes, the system requirements are ridiculous, but I can run it on "High" settings with my GTX 960 and i7 3770 with the FPS rarely dropping below 35, even in the most intensive scenes.
However, this game does have some cons. For example, I appreciate the devs trying out the whole new parkour mechanics thing, and to a degree it does work, but it still seems rather Beta-esque in terms of its reliability. Many times I found myself shouting "Why did you jump there?!" or "Ok, so I can leap over buildings but not a chair?!", especially when these bugs caused the death of poor Arno.
Overall, this game is fun, beautiful, and a good buy if you're looking for an exclusively next-gen game to keep you busy for a long time. So again, please don't listen to all the butthurt people. Yes, the launch went down the toilet, however, this game is now in a spot where it really is a great buy.

A classic RPG. Chances are that if you enjoy any RPG's at all, you'll most likely find something you like in this.
This is a port of the iOS version of Final Fantasy III, so it has an upscaled 720p version of the graphics. With that being said, things still look quite primitive and blocky, and the battle arenas more often than not look like you're stood inside a disc floating in space with a jpg wrapped around it. If that kind of thing is absolutely unbearable to you, than maybe avoid this title.
If you dont care too much about graphics, and you're all about the gameplay, FFIII works on a classic turn-based system, and has a classic Job system that Final Fantasy is renowned for. Character classes and archetypes are classic, recognisable and feel unique enough to make a difference in how you fight. If you've played Bravely Default, Final Fantasy 5, Final Fantasy 10-2 or even some of the Dragon Quest games, you'll feel right at home here with this classic rendition of the Job system.
FF3 provides you with quite a challenge at times, especially with the bosses, and even some monsters (Lookin' at you chimera mage) Can surprise you with an attack that can wipe out your party if you're rushing too much. I'm not saying be prepared to grind for years, but if you try to charge through, you're probably going to get frustrated when you reach the next crystal boss.
Some of the achievements are a serious pain, such as the 100% Beastiary and 100% Treasure achievement, due to some areas where certain monsters are missable completely, and the same is true for chests with no possibility to return to those areas. The last achievement that can be annoying is the "Jack of All Trades" achievement which requires you to reach Job Level 99 for every job, with every character. This is literally a matter of grinding, and even using optimal methods, it will take you several hours of mindless boredom and repetition to accomplish.
Overall, aside from some of the grinding, and the graphics leaving something to be desired, I'm proud to have this title in my library, and you should be too! Fingers crossed that Square finds it within themselves to bring more and more FF titles, and other RPG's to Steam.

So, before I go on and show my cards on why my personal experience with this game hasn't been exactly positive, I first would like to throw out there that I'm generally not a fan of randomly generated elements in games or roguelites as a whole.
If you do enjoy those aspects in a game, than by all means, ignore this review and go for it, because it just might be up your alley!
As for the parts that really drew this game down for me, here they are.
I make a strong comparison between hotline miami and heat signature when it comes to gameplay.
This was also one of the bigger reasons I actually bought the game!
I am a big fan of the topdown one-hit-and-you're-dead gameplay style which demands a fast response time and some clever thinking of the player on how to best approach a situation.
And in it's purest form, you get that in spades!
The main meat of the game is you running through a space ship with an objective in mind, taking out guards, disabling security systems and maybe grabbing some loot along the way.
So far so good!
However, to get to that main juicy meat part, which for me, was most of the fun, you have to travel to your destitation (the spaceship) in a pod after accepting the mission.
This consist of you holding the left mouse button for a while, as the ship flies towards the direction you're holding the mouse, and sometimes press the right mouse button ("the break") in order to allign your pod with the airlock of your target spaceship.
That's all.
And you will have to do this every single time after accepting a mission before you get to pull out your gun (or wrench of longsword or whatever) and enjoy that big juicy fat greasy main meat part of the game.
After a while, this just started to annoy me, like it was some annoying bump between me and my fun.
Also, aside from that, I'm not a big fan of the "time limit equals difficulty" equasion within games.
I am aware that Heat Signature is mostly randomly generated, from characters to the actual interiors of the spaceships, but stamping a time limit on what would otherwise be an easy or a medium difficulty mission and then call it a hard or very hard mission simply seems like lazy game design in my eyes.
Again, I'm just stating the problems I personally had with the game and am in no way saying that these are big gamebreaking faults which completely make the game unenjoyable.
If you can live with the flying mini-game between each mission and are okay with time limits in missions, then by all means, this game leaks quality on all other fronts and you should definitely pick it up if you can spare the cheddar.
But for me personally, the 2 stated problems I have experienced, did make me want to stop playing quite soon after buying, so for the like-me-minded individuals out there, I cannot recommend this game.

In this review, I will be going through the pros and cons of the game. It's quite a lengthy review, but at least it's more comprehensive than just one sentence saying "it's pretty good". So, without further ado:
The devs are really involved with the community. If you have a suggestion for the game, the developers are going to see it. If you find a bug, the devs (especially Adriano ;) ) are gonna hunt it down with a virtual machine gun for you. The community in this game is extremely strong. You even get to actively participate in the creation process of the game - there is a thread in the forums where people upload techs that the devs then showcase and put into the game as actual enemies.
The gameplay is unique and not boring. It is unique from other "build-your-own-robot" games in that there are much less limitations on what you can build, compared to other games similar to this. Some people say it's repetitive. Personally, I think that there is always something to do. For example, I might need to get a certain block, so I harvest the resources to craft the block, head back to my base, fight off an annoying little enemy trying to lay siege to my epic base, craft the block, go complete a mission, and then use the blocks I got from that mission to upgrade by base/tech. It's very fun. TerraTech also now has a creative mode, so if you really want to build whatever you want, you are able to do so!
The game is still in Early Access, so you can expect lots of weird bugs. But as I previously mentioned, the developers are literally working day and night to squish all these bugs. If you don't want a game with lots of unrefined details and random glitches, then maybe you should hold off until the game leaves Early Access. But personally, I haven't really found that many bugs in the game. It's not nearly as bad as some of the negative reviews say it is.
You DO need a relatively beefy computer. I have close to minimum specs (if not UNDER minimum, I'm not sure how the specs really work though) and my laptop only plays the game well while it's charging. Even though this is the case, I still love playing this game. It does have a lot of optimisation issues, but the devs are working hard to fix them.
Some reviewers have criticised the combat by saying that all it involves is slapping a bunch of guns on your tech. In reality, it's way more complicated than that. In order to make a successful combat tech, you need a big tech. A big tech means it will be slow and bulky, so you have to compromise by putting tons of shields and repair bubbles to protect your tech. But these need batteries, which are explosive and take up a lot of space, which means that..... you get the idea. Just jamming guns onto a tech is not always the answer. There are also at least 25 different types of weapons in the game, to suit every play style.
There is no multiplayer. But if you want multiplayer, then NEVER FEAR! Multiplayer has been worked on for months by the devs and is still a work in progress, so don't complain about the fact that there is no multiplayer currently! Be happy that the devs are constantly working on it. You can expect multiplayer for TerraTech by the end of the year.
In the end, TerraTech is a very unique game. It is very fun to play and has an extremely strong community, but it is in Early Access and so it still has lots of unrefined details and it has a long way to go until it is complete. But I don't think you will be disappointed by this game if you buy it. It's a great game to play, it really encourages creativity and it's just fun to mess around with. For it's current price, I reccomend you buy it, if your PC can handle it. Multiplayer is coming out soon, and TerraTech will constantly be improving over the next months or years to come.
In the end, my score for this game is: 7.5/10. However, I would give it 8.5/10 if I exclude all the bugs and optimisation issues.

This game is basically Lego Skyrim. Which is awesome. There's an open world map to explore, tons of side quests to do, and lots of weapons and armor pieces available to customize whatever character you play as. Plus the blocky Lego-ness of the game makes it really low-stress to play. There's no blood or tense gameplay here. Just hours of good fun.
One common complaint about the Lego video games is that after awhile, they all tend to feel the same. In this particular game however, the makers tried to make it feel a little more special than usual by adding a few new gameplay features...like mining, armor/weapon collecting, food/supplies collecting, and smithing (which was also present in the Lego Lord of the Rings game). These features really add to the gameplay, giving you an additional reward beyond money for every bush, tree, boulder, or piece of furniture you smash. The mining feature is not the easiest to use, however, since it relies on really precise timing and an instantly responsive controller. But it still isn't impossible to collect all the elements you need to complete the quests or smith the various items.
If you enjoy any of the Lego games, I would highly reccommend this one. Like I said, it's like Skyrim, but Lego. 10/10 for Lego Hobbit.

***This only takes the base game into account***
Ever wanted to crack down on some real terminal action to get a peek at what this hacking business is all about? Wonder no more, as Hacknet is here to "teach" you what "hacking" is.
Immersive, intelligent and just enough unix-commands at your disposal, Hacknet will convince anyone not computer savvy or not paying close enough attention that the things on your monitor sure looks like something you shouldn't be doing, almost like dark wizardry magic. For the most part, the game offers up this illusion at an convincing rate while being beginner-friendly. However, in the world of hacking, there is very little hand holding, so the faster you understand what the ropes are, the better.
To deliver a convincing hacking experience, music is paramount - as Uplink back in the day taught everyone. Here is really delivers, with everything from ambient barrens tunes fit for the breaks between each mission, to serious business from The Algorithm and wildly intense adrenaline pumping Carpenter Brut songs. Hats off, this album is even worth listening to way after you've finished the game.
As for the the main story, while not top shelf, is interesting enough to keep searching around for clues and getting a better grasp at what's going. As with any self respecting game that depicts hacking, it should have its sheer selectino of surprise elements, and Hacknet doesn't disappoint. However, this is usually found in side missions. The main story should've done more of that as well.
For each time you play, the game changes up names, IPs etc for the nodes to try to keep things sort of fresh, but the missions are mostly the same. All in all, Hacknet is a very solid, albeit simple at times, attempt at creating an immersive, "real enough" hacking simulator that most importantly is -FUN-. The list of unix commands are however at times frustratingly limited, especially if you know what you're doing. Since most of the game is very well laid out in terms of the interface, you start taking it for granted that you should be able to do more than you actually are allowed to.
For example, "rm file*" will not work since the terminal doesn't support wildcards. Pathing is also needlessly tedious, as it doesn't properly understand using root-nodes in paths. Props however for making it possible to furk up yourself, which is how it should be. Paying attention and going "outside the beaten path" is usually rewarded.

Hacknet requires reading and understanding of its core concepts to get the most out of the experience. For those persistent enough, the game also delivers some hilarious content as a nod to the efforts. Here's to hoping the developer makes more content to this game, as the main game is rather short. It'll take you only around 5-6 hours for the main campaign. A multiplayer mode would've been awesome in addition to random missions.
Rating: 8/10 - Play it!

This game is great. A lot of people seem to prefer AOE II HD but I don't. Here is why-
Better graphics:
This doesn't make or break the game and isn't the most important factor of game quality but it is worth mentioning. This game looks amazing.
Map Design:
A lot of people prefer the maps of Age of Empires II but personally I find that the trade posts and smaller maps make for more interesting games. Players have to compete for land far more and you can't hide away as well.
Era:
This is very individual but i prefer how most battles are fought with guns and cannons instead of swords and catapults.
Civilisations:
Again, this is often seen as a con for AOE3 but I way prefer how each civilisation is so unique. It makes the game feel deeper. When you get bored of one civilisation; playing as another one is completely different and a whole new experience. This is also great for team gameplay as certain civ combos work really well, like Ottomans and Japan.
Community:
This isn't a benefit of this game, but I felt like I should include it. The community is OK. It's mostly fine, but sometimes you get unbelievabley prententious and immature people who can ruin a game for you, especially if they are on your team and don't worry about supporting you at all.
You can still find some bugs but apart from that this game is brilliant. I don't really understand that low number of ppl playing it....

I feel like many of the reviews here are being somewhat unfair. People have been mentioning again and again how beautiful and thoughtful the art, story, narration and music are - so I see no point in saying more about the same stuff.
I do, however, would like to talk about the gameplay. I'm a casual gamer, and never pretended to be otherwise. I knew the game was too hard for me before I even started my first playthrough. Luckily, it has one of the coolest and most active modding communities around, and this basically gives you the option to balance things as you see fit, in addition to all the possible additional content. Want the hardcore stuff? you got it. Want a strategic hack and slash adventure that you can breeze through? you got it.
The pressure system can be frustrating, but that what it's all about - applying continues pressure on the characters. This is one of things that built my immersion the most. Along with the characters acting out of place, getting awful diseases and slowly developing weird personal quirks. Plus, your characters will die, a lot. And it's okay, because the willingly went into the darkest ♥♥♥♥ing dungeon.
I give this game a 8/10. Use the right mods for yourself, and you might get it up to 9/10. The only thing stopping this from getting a perfect score is that the animation can be somewhat underwhelming at times.
*Update
Just wanted to let you know I also nominated this to Steam awards under "Mom's Spaghetti", as it really does keep you on your toes all the way to the end. :)

Usually I really love artistic games and I really like the idea for this game. I also rarely wish I could refund a game I've bought from Steam, even if I dislike it. This is not one of those times. 2.99 is actually way too much for such a lack of game.
Positive things first:
- I actually did like the monologue and felt badly for the character, pathetic as he was. However, my dislike for the character rose as I realized that my actions did not have any effect on him.
- ...it's cheap?
Negative things:
- I don't know about anyone else, but my subconcious desires and fears do have some effect on my life, besides where I look. In fact, that is an incredibly random thing for a "sub-concious" to control. Looking back at the description of the game, I think it should be more evident that the point of the game is not to "play" but to listen. I wouldn't be interested in such a game, but I think they could have avoided a lot of alienation but spelling it out that this was a game like Dear Esther. There is obviously an aundience for this type of game, this really should be described better for this crowd.
- Again, looking back at the description, I see a lot of "unanswered question" type wonderings, but the game is rather straightforword. Julian does not like his coworkers. He does like Byron. There is no real reason to play after the first "act", because it is all spelled out there. I criticized its lousy gameplay strategy before but now I'm criticizing its storytelling.

Why should I care about Julian? Yes, it sucks that he got stood up, but so what? There is no mystery to him, which is fine in real life, but characters who spend 20 minutes or so talking about themselves should really have something interesting to say. Sure, he likes poetry, but so do a lot of people. And they are probably less insufferable and boring than Julian is. No new information is gathered in each subsequent act and there is no real reason to have the game continue with no new information or insight.
The game's story got ever-so-slightly more interesting near the end, when someone knocks at the door, and I did feel something at his emotions afterward, but that really doesn't excuse the 20 minutes of boredom proceeding that. Boredom can be used in video games and stories, but it should be rewarded or serve a point.
So, no, I would not recommend this game to anyone. It is not a game, it is not a compelling story, and it isn't even a good sleep aid, since no one could sleep over Julian's whining.

Edit 2017-11-23. The new Fair Points update helps, but there's still unexplained / inconsistent mechanics in the game. For example, for some weird reason I couldn't use my short sword to kill an unconscious assassination target. Or the defector missions: there's no explanation about what they're for and once you start one, you're locked into completing it when you can't return to your station. It's just confusing. The game's fun at times, but it still feels like I'm playing a beta of a game. This is a shame, since I love roguelikes and this game has a lot of fresh ideas and promise. I'll flip my review to positive when that isn't the case.
PRO: If you enjoy stealth games, you'll approve of this one, especially if you liked games such as Dishonored, which give you flexibility to go in guns-blazing or be silent and sneaky. The roguelike element is clever: you can even play characters who have a personal mission of rescuing a previous character you'd played who got caught (and then you can play as the rescued character again).
CON: It doesn't feel totally polished: items on the floor can be hard to distinguish from the background; ship interior design is a bit samey and repetitive; I've had some bugs, like where I warp out of the ship to my pod suddenly if the alarm sounds which is very disorienting; some of the mechanics could be explained better (it took me a second to notice the mission drop/chute thing in the homebase and it's not in the tutorial).
OVERALL: The flaws can be addressed in patches soon (I hope). The core gameplay loop is addicting, and the price is great.

An amazing space-themed rogue-like. You're a rogue / thief in space who steals, hijacks, murders and kidnaps his way to fame, glory and fortune, only to end up retiring in peace or burning out. And then you get another character, and do it all over again.
There's no skills or levels, only different kind of equipment  - and there's enough of those that you'll probably not play the same kind of character twice, since it's hard to get the exact same kit.
There's an overarching story about four different factions vying for control of a nebula (and the rebel group of operators trying to end this war), but it's not that important to the game - though the tidbits of lore you come across are cool and interesting takes on scifi tropes.
Overall, a great game, and an absolute steal at 13€ - if you're getting it on a sale, snatch it.

[Update] This is by far the most unstable, bug-riddled, glitched, crashy mess I've ever seen in a Lego game. It feels like they ran out of funding 3/4 of the way through production and shipped what they had.
Lego: The Hobbit is not a bad game by Lego game standards - it has continued to progress the formula, including the 'build minigame' from the Lego Movie game, adding team-up attacks between some characters and a resource mechanic (which perpetuates the grind, but is new nonetheless).
What this game -doesn't- have is an ending. It just stops after one mission with no conclusion to the plot, then the credits roll. That's it. Now go do the other 75% of the game that is open-world challenges and fetch-quests. You might think the character roster is up to par, but in reality 50% of the listed characters are just alternate costumes - they are no longer stacked per-character like the Harry Potter games - which also leads to having two of the same character in play at once.
Lego games are no stranger to bugs, but this is the first game that I've had multiple encounters with game-ending bugs. Be it being permamently stuck in an animation, the fast-travel eagle freezing in mid-air or the forging mini-game being incompleteable. These are not crashes, but event chains simply not working and requiring the game to be quit and restarted. There are also numerious examples of the game temporarily freezing or slowing down, but these don't end the game.
Many other people have said it, so I'll be breif. This game is unfinished. It has polish, the gameplay is as it has ever been, the world is expansive and there certainly isn't a shortage of things to do, but it feels as though the filler content vastly outweighs the structured content, as there are a number of abilities and character-types that simply do not appear in the main story, and only become accessable after you finish what story there is.
In short, there are better Lego games out there, and better ones will be coming, so you're better off getting one that feels like it's all there.

Okay first things first: Should you buy this game?
No. Just no. It's an okay game, but it's not a good fallout game. In addition to the somewhat traditional bugs and random laziness on Bethesda's part, there's a lot of stuff here that just screams "we knew the modders would fix this for us".
The Base Game:
This is a fallout game with better gun play, basically no dialogue options, and little to no role playing. A lot of the scavenging incentives have been taken away too in order to support the settlement system. Honestly it all just feels kind of dumbed down and lazy. It reminds me of the Fallout 3 ending (google at your own risk for spoilers, but you were either declared a dirt bag for doing the smart thing or killed yourself for literally no reason).
In general, the story of fallout 4 is okay. Truth be told the urgency of it doesn't really match the whole "spend 600 hours messing around in the open world" that we all love fallout games for, but I can't complain that much. The factions are pretty good, certainly better developed than in New Vegas or 3. As many people have said, the dialogue system has been neutered. I would argue it's basically been removed. You have 3 identical options and a fourth that says the same thing in a snarky voice. For every prompt and conversation.
The gameplay is better though. The guns handle WAY better. It almost feels like an FPS, especially compared to previous installments. Unfortunately, there aren't unique weapons for you to find/be rewarded with/kill people for.
TL;DR:
+Better gunplay
+Better graphics than the older games (duh), but it's nothing special
+The factions are nicely developed
-It's been dumbed down. A lot. I'd wager even new players will find some of these things off putting, like the infinite quest system.
-Let's be real, New Vegas was a better fallout game, and would be a no brainier if not for the gunplay
-There isn't any roleplaying in your role playing game
-The conversations system is like asking your kid if they want to take a bath before or after dinner, except you're not eating dinner
-Seriously, play New Vegas or 3 first.
On Mods:
Since Beth messed up the roleplay and story elements, basically the best way to play this is to mod this as much as you can. The problem is that with their new creation club program (and the steam workshop before it, if you remember that), Bethesda has made it abundantly clear they want people to have to pay for mods. I won't go into that right now, but just don't do that. Please. Go on the Nexus and donate to some mod makers if you want to spend money on that instead.
+The "updated" engine can handle better assets for mods
+It's pretty, and most of the modding community is working on this game right now.
-Bethesda is trying to kill the modding scene. Please, Please don't support this.
-Oh, and it's still THE SAME ♥♥♥♥ING ENGINE (yeah, the one they used in fallout 3, new vegas, skyrim, oblivion, morrowind, and some other stuff I'm forgetting. This engine is 15+ years old. )

How a developer would think to ask money for this travesty is unfathomable. The horrors begin with the main menu, where you discover that the mouse cursor and mouselook are simultaneously active, so that when you choose one of Air Control's modes, you also move the camera around. The background shot is of an underwater airplane, above which sits the game's title in a blurry font. That title doesn't sit in the interface, however. No--it simply sits above the aircraft as though the letters exist within the game's own world. Clearly, something's amiss, and if the main menu isn't enough to convince you, then the abominable zombie-human-dwarf cutscene that opens Casual Mode certainly should be.
The mess that follows is homely, unfinished, and inept. By default, an inexplicable array of buttons labeled "lock cursor" are strewn across the screen. You can remove them by clicking the "disable [lockcursor] UI" button at the top left, though that particular button needlessly remains in all its unsightliness. Remember: any cursor movement is accompanied by complementary mouselook, so interacting with the interface causes the camera to move wildly about. In this case, it's an airplane interior that dizzily rotates around you as you turn off the interface and guess at what your goal is. As it turns out, you're a flight attendant, and the big red sentient exclamation mark at the rear of the plane has a task for you: deliver some coffee to a passenger in the front.
Your next task is to pick pillows up from the floor, which means moving the mouse cursor over them and clicking them, a rather uncomfortable task if the mouse cursor has moved to the edge of the screen, as it just may have by this point. And so you point and click on the pillows, which simultaneously changes your point of view so that you're facing the passengers to the left. You might try to hit the escape key and try to restart the level, or abandon this rubbish altogether for a different mode, but doing so in any of the game's modes causes the mouselook and movement keys to stop functioning, and in some cases renders the level entirely inoperable.
Casual Mode plays out in a series of bizarre levels, most of them only a few seconds long, that have you moving from the back of the plane to the cockpit (yes, that's it), picking up a gun and shooting a terrorist, picking up trash bags, or performing some other mundane task. Every one of these activities is awful. Passengers sit in a catatonic state with their arms held stiffly in place. Terrorists don't move or animate in any way, and explode when they die. Sometimes there are weird colored cubes on the floor for no reason. In one ludicrous level, there's no gravity, and the game displays only a few frames per second. And every nonsensical task is accompanied by peculiar descriptions written in broken English. "You need to find reason while airplane fell down" says one dialogue window, right before you discover that ending the mission requires… opening a door. "You can open your inventory with a button situated in left" says another, even though there is no inventory button, on the left or anywhere, and the mission gives you no reason to have one.
You also get to be a mechanic, which means hovering over some buttons until one turns red and you click on it. More often, you get to be a pilot, both in Casual Mode and in Killjoy Mode, but piloting an aircraft in Air Control is a farce: the controls make no sense, the camera angles make no sense, and if you crash, you have to quit out of the game and restart it due to the aforementioned broken menu options. Crashing into the sea is particularly fascinating, as the water is actually a solid object; how the aircraft in the main menu managed to sink is a mystery.
You shouldn't forget Realistic Mode, in which you walk around in an airplane cabin filled with petrified character models while cursing the ridiculously low frame rate, and then do nothing because that's all you do in this mode. To be fair, though, doing nothing is preferable than wasting your time on this wreck, which advertises itself on Steam as "the best flight simulation in the history of computer games" and promises that it is "the first airplane game, where plane compartment is visible." Both of these claims are lies, of course, which only makes sense for a broken scam masquerading as a computer game.

An elf, a man and a dwarf walk into a bar. The hobbit laughs and walks under it.
Lego the Hobbit (LtH for short) is another prime example of Lego's continuing creativity. This game has variety, action, adventure, questing, humor--all the things I've come to expect in their recent games. LtH is a decent retelling of the movie, which is a not-so-decent retelling of the original fictional novel by J.R.R Tolkien. Though this game was a pleasurable experience for me, I have to admit that it has some large flaws.
First, the fact that this game only encompasses the first two out of three movies made by New Line Cinema. The Battle of FIve Armies was originally intended to be released as a DLC for this game, but Warner Bros. canceled this development. So now, we have a game that leaves off with a cliff-hanger, and no way to resolve that cliff-hanger besides watching the movies.
Second, the character customization. Every modern Lego game has one--a place where you can create your own Lego figure, and play with them in the game. In the past, this was an amazing feature in Lego games. However, in LtH, the character customization is somewhat lacking. This game does not let you equip a weapon or cloak to your custom character (no capes I guess?). This was extremely disappointing to me, as outfitting my character with cool cloaks and weapons had been my favorite part of Lego games in the past. While the customizer in itself has no lack of Lego parts to use on your figure, weapons and cloaks are not allowed >:(
Third, the difficulty of finding secrets. In the open world, secrets and mysteries abound. In previous Lego games, the variety of secrets was perhaps not as big (except in Lego LOTR), and they could all be obtained with relative ease. In LtH, secrets stay secret if you aren't extremely persistant. Just finding the blacksmith so I could craft mithril items took me the better part of two days. The instructions are rather vague, and certain puzzles and quests are extremely difficult to complete. This will be sure to annoy younger kids after a while.
Aside from these three flaws though, LtH is an extraordinary game for younger kids into the lore of Middle Earth. The story is pretty decent, and the combat is satisfying without being bloody or gory. This is perhaps Lego's strongest point--the ability to create massive-scale battles that young children will be able to partake in without worrying about gory imagery or blood. Overall, this is a good adventure game, but I would recommend waiting until a sale to grab it. The DLCs are ok, but I'd wait until a sale for those ones too.

I wouldn't recommend the game in its current state.
Combat is also *really* dull. It boils down to spamming as many guns as possible and stuffing as many batteries as you can into the vehicle so that your shields will be able to tank enough damage to win.
You can technically make some interesting builds and try to use clever tactics to win fights, but gun/battery spam is so effective that anything else isn't remotely worth the effort.
Bases and mining/crafting are basically pointless. The primary thing your base will get used for is to recharge your batteries for your shields. That's it.
There's a neat system where you can create conveyor belts and route materials to refineries or assemblers and stuff,
Building is also *way* too tedious right now to be of any use anyway.
___________________________________________
Edit: Potential ideas for improvement (since it's too long for steam to let me post it into the comments section):
I should preface these ideas by saying that I have no experience with game design or anything, so I don't know if they would work as well as I think they would, or if there's better ways to address the underlying issues or anything.
These might also be too much work to implement, depending on how the code is organized.
For building, there's two main things I can  think of:

The second would be having a mirror mode of some sort (which should, of course, be easy for the player to turn on and off while building), since most vehicles are symetrical, and it's pretty boring to have to build two copies of the same thing, just on opposite sides of the vehicle. Mirror mode should be able to be set either between two blocks, or in the middle of one block, so that both even and odd symetry is available.
For bases, the first thing would probably be if you could build small harvester drones (using a harvester version of the helper AI blocks, and player-built like everything else is) that would automatically seek out and harvest resources that grew within a certain distance of the base (range and speed shouldn't be especially high or anything, especially in the beginning, but could maybe be increased by using higher tier versions of the blocks required or something). The reosurce harvesting range from the base should probably also be displayed when building, so there's no guesswork of "will they be able to reach that patch of minerals over there?". This would make optimal base positioning require some thought, and actually give more reason to setup refining/building/storage stuff in the base.
This could be combined with the ability to tell the base to always keep a certain number of each part in inventory, so it would be able to keep replacement parts in stock for rebuilding your vehicle after combat. The player would, of course, have to properly setup the proper storage/refining/building system to route everything around correctly in order for the base to actually be able to build the requested parts.
There should probably also be a way to set a *maximum* for certain parts, so that the base can route any unwanted salvage along routes the player has setup to sell/scrap/etc the parts.
For all this to work, the black hole blocks might need to have input and output spaces added like other base blocks, or have mini black hole blocks that don't suck up parts in the world, but do allow the base to pull parts for scrapping from the inventory, or deposit constructed parts into.
For combat, the projectile speed probably needs some increasing, so that guns can hit moving targets a bit better (instead of having to either get right up in an enemy's face, or agro them and then just drive backwards in a straight line while firing). As it stands, building a fast vehicle doesn't seem very useful (except maybe if you're using missiles), since circling the enemies usually means you won't be hit, but also can't hit the enemies either.
Block health could maybe stand to be a bit higher too, since combat usually seems to be over a bit too quick to require much thought. Of course, balancing weapon damage and block health over so many different combinations of vehicles is always going to pretty tricky, and it's probably not possible to ever get it perfect, so this part probably isn't that big an issue at the moment.
As for the gunspam, I'm not really sure what to do about that. Having some more guns that are stronger but larger than the small ones would probably help (not strong enough to make small guns completely worthless by comparison though, mostly just so there's a bit more variety in size and power). Everything else I can think of offhand would just amount to putting arbitrary limits on designs though, which wouldn't be very fun or interesting for players.
With flying, I do like the idea of automatically transitioning between ground and flight controls, but it's fairly clunky at the moment, and often seems to requite ramping off a hill in order to take off, since on flat ground (like the salt flats) even vehicles where the front points slightly up tend to just lift their tail until the vehicle is only half flying, and then just keep the front wheels on the ground.
Granted, I haven't experimented with having some downwards facing thrusters for a vertical takeoff, but it would be nice if there was a button to swap between modes manually.
Of course, the AI for follower bots should also be improved so it doesn't get stuck so often, and can actually keep up with the player, but I imagine that's already planned.

Just another Unity engine builder game, poorly optimized which leads to stutter, especially at end game where Techs get much larger, they also don't seem to care about this as other peoples designed Techs and invasion Techs literally called "Lag Maker" or "Lag Machine" that abuses this poor optimization find their way into your games and do just as named -- cause you copious amounts of lag, which apparently Payload allows to happen.
Moving on to the "Sand Box" elements, or lack thereof -- painting itself as a Sandbox, but having maybe 15 different quests to do which simply cycle into the next re-painted version of the same quest becomes tedious after the first hour of gameplay, fine when you first start but later is pointless and annoying, especially since quests can bug and be stuck there, permanently unable to be completed. Recent patches now FORCE you to go to trading posts to get new quests ontop of which can only appear at random every day/night cycle at different trading posts, I guess this is "Incentive" to explore?
Moving on to the exploration aspect, or once again, lack thereof -- As mentioned above during this forced exploration surely you'll see some interesting things right? well no... all you'll see is re-hashed (procedurally generated?) terrain biomes containing 100% re-used rock, tree and landmark items, and if you travel on ground the game literally throws enemies in your path just for the fun of it, not true sandbox "enemies are roaming" but just crap them down from above right in your way.
Moving on to those rocks, trees and landmarks -- lazy collision meshes on ALL of them, every single one, mostly because they're the same as eachother, using mining equipment to stay busy while you "explore" is endlessly annoying when you literally see your drill or saws touch these items, and nothing happens, sometimes even 'ghost' rocks and trees after mining them they visually stay there.
Day/Night cycles.....do nothing but get in the way of the building aspect, you COULD use lights, but those are so poorly optimized it can cause lag even on extremely high end PC's, what's the point in having them then?
Camera controls...fight you the entire time you play, from forced camera movement to sometimes not even letting you adjust the angle for absolutely no reason, once again...you fight the camera every single minute you play this game,
Topping all of the above however is the fact that your camera is FORCED around the tech you pilot, even during building, even when your building on a different tech than you are currently piloting...
In this day and age not giving players 100% camera freedom is a very VERY bad mistake.
While it seems like all I do is gripe about it I still do recommend this game, like I said at the top it DOES have potential and all of the issues this game has can be fixed and I hope they do fix them instead of just sinking in with the rest of the permanent early access money grabs.

I am not going to give a stat lesson but I will just say that I think what people are blaming on a random set of numbers not going in thier favor is actually a designed algorythim that activates to give the worst possible outcome once a set number of factors is reached.  I played the same battle 3 times with 3 different groups and realized that there was nothing random about the outcomes at all.
There is almost no character customization beacuase the game makers want to be sure to control all of the outcomes...marginal gains countered by equal negatives.
I got my moneys worth out of the game but I found that this game like many others designed this way (rimworld) is intended to give you lots of frustration and leaves little to nothing to look forward too.  I do not recommend this game to people who like to game for the feeling of finding that +5 vorpral sword and getting to use it on your enemies.

In response to the many negative reviews this game has gotten recently (Click "Read more" for my own review):
This game needs compatibility mode when running on Windows 10 (I'm using WinXP SP3, but Win7 should work as well), and an ESO (Ensemble Studios Online) account can only be created from within the base game (no DLCs). ESO can be played fine on the DLCs, it's just that the account needs to be created from inside the base game.
Note that in the box that comes up when starting the game, selecting "Age of Empires III: The Complete Collection" will actually run the game WITHOUT DLCs. To play the DLCs, you need to select one of the other options. (The Asian Dynasties has all of the content of The Warchiefs in it)
My actual review:
+ Gameplay (Perhaps Age of Empires 2 was better in this regard, but this game still has great gameplay IMO)
+ Graphics (at least when fully zoomed out)
+ Destruction physics and ragdoll physics
+ Okay AI, with a wide range of skill level settings.
+/- graphics style (matter of opinion, look at the trailer and images to decide if you like it)
+/- somewhat long waiting time to start a match (usually 5-10 minutes for a 20-50 minutes long match), but not as bad as you'd expect for a game that was originally released in 2005 (retail version)
- AI cheats on higher difficulty levels.
- Online mode has a lot of unkind people, as there is no report system.
- Arrow keys bound to camera controls by default. This can be changed, but doing so takes a while.
- No way of rejoining left matches (if the game crashes, or if your internet goes out for more than one minute, then you're out of the match, and there's no way at all to rejoin it.)
- Ships are kind of weird (they're big and tend to clip into eachother)
- The AI handles ships very badly.
- Technical difficulties listed up above (Win10 issues, ESO account creation issues, and confusingly named options to run the game.)
