This game is very fun, but incredibly frustrating. RNG is a thing. I will be honest, I started a campaign and was doing well, and then the RNG set in. I had to abandon multiple dungeons and couldn't complete anything. Maybe I was doing something wrong,  but I decided to delete my game and start fresh on the easiest setting. It seems to be more forgiving. I would encourage all first timers to do so. This second game start has gone a lot smoother. Granted I have still lost some heroes, but overall I don't get as stressed out with the game.
This game has very pleasing visuals. So far I have enjoyed the story and challenge. There a 2 things I can suggest that could make your life a lot easier. Make sure to max out your wagon upgrades. This will allow for the cap on heroes slots as soon as possible. I would also up the recruits to 3 with the first dungeon. The second point I cannot stress enough is; this is not your standard RPG game. It can be very difficult between battling and managing your stress you will have plenty of problems as you learn the game. Do not be afraid to run away from battles nor abandon a quest from time to time. You will have plenty of opportunities to get loot and move forward.
*Update 11/29/2017.
I have now played the game for over 100 days in game. It hasn't been easy, but I have learned a lot. Not quite finished. Think I have to kill 1 more boss and start the Darkest Dungeon quests. I would like to offer some more advice. The first being mindset. Don't approach this game like other games. When it comes to grinding your characters, never expect to become godlike. I have been notorious for over-leveling my characters in pretty much all games I play. Because of this, the end game content is rather easy. Darkest Dungeon is not that game. Sure by grinding up the levels you will unlock harder more difficult content which will allow you to get better loot, but it comes with a price. Monsters in higher tier areas are more menacing then ever. Everything seems to hit way harder and your stress can skyrocket in the blink of an eye. Heroes will die. This is how Darkest Dungeon works. But don't let it bring you down, and do not be afraid to abandon a quest if it gets really dicey.
Next point. Slow and steady. Don't rush through the levels to unlock harder content too quickly. Take your time, enjoy the game and learn the enemies, because life doesn't get easier. Challenges arise. And this is a huge appeal to me. Also, do not be afraid to remove Heroes with terrible quirks from your roster. Keep that roster clean if need be. I have removed so many Heroes from my roster. This will allow you to farm resources and money to make your overall roster strong in the long run.
Final point. Based on my experiences, I would highly encourage maxing the following buildings in this order Wagon, Guild, Blacksmith. Also before completing these fully make sure to get 2 slots for your Sanitarium. I say this because locking in some good quirks as you level is a great idea if you plan on keeping the hero. Plus random events will happen that will make this cost free. When this occurs, you will be able to lock in 1 positive and remove 1 negative quirk at no cost per Hero. So doing that 2 times is great.

Edit 2017-11-23. The new Fair Points update helps, but there's still unexplained / inconsistent mechanics in the game. For example, for some weird reason I couldn't use my short sword to kill an unconscious assassination target. Or the defector missions: there's no explanation about what they're for and once you start one, you're locked into completing it when you can't return to your station. It's just confusing. The game's fun at times, but it still feels like I'm playing a beta of a game. This is a shame, since I love roguelikes and this game has a lot of fresh ideas and promise. I'll flip my review to positive when that isn't the case.
PRO: If you enjoy stealth games, you'll approve of this one, especially if you liked games such as Dishonored, which give you flexibility to go in guns-blazing or be silent and sneaky. The roguelike element is clever: you can even play characters who have a personal mission of rescuing a previous character you'd played who got caught (and then you can play as the rescued character again).
CON: It doesn't feel totally polished: items on the floor can be hard to distinguish from the background; ship interior design is a bit samey and repetitive; I've had some bugs, like where I warp out of the ship to my pod suddenly if the alarm sounds which is very disorienting; some of the mechanics could be explained better (it took me a second to notice the mission drop/chute thing in the homebase and it's not in the tutorial).
OVERALL: The flaws can be addressed in patches soon (I hope). The core gameplay loop is addicting, and the price is great.

After 70hours on this game. I can say it has been tons of fun for me. Fractured Space (FS) will definitely appease sci-fi loving gamers who enjoy space combat simulation. The controls are a bit wonky due to the lack of joystick support but the default WASD key shouldn't hinder you too much to enjoy navigating the asteroids dodging enemy fire, flanking, panic blinking to avoid a fusion beam. All those teeth grinding moments where you have only 10% HP left but still manage to jump home and live to fight another day.
I never had so much andrenaline and thrill in a long time from a PC game and FS is one of those rare gems. The game puts you in a position where you have tremendous control over the outcome of the game and you will find that it is uncommon to have a guy single handedly win the game because of smart planning and action.
This game is both strategy and tactic heavy. Knowing the weakness of the enemy ship, strength of your own and fundamental mechanics allows you to set up plays that makes you wanna pat yourself in the back and say "Damn man, I'm good!". FS is designed around a MOBA theme, where different ships will have counters on its own, it is imperative that the player sit back and follow the learning curve. New players will definitely benefit from playing different ships from varied roles. The ships are balanced and most importantly, YOU WILL NOT EXPERIENCE A GRINDFEST to get to another ship. THERE ARE ALSO NO PREMIUM ITEMS/AMMO that give will other players an advantage over normal F2P customers.
Although the gameplay is very rewarding, there some glaring bugs that needs to be ironed out but I don't see it as a problem through constant development. New players might be put off by the early losses due to bad team composition, I implore you to continue through the higher MMR brackets where the teamwork gameplay truly shines.
I highly suggest you buy the Armada pack once it goes on sale.

An amazing space-themed rogue-like. You're a rogue / thief in space who steals, hijacks, murders and kidnaps his way to fame, glory and fortune, only to end up retiring in peace or burning out. And then you get another character, and do it all over again.
There's no skills or levels, only different kind of equipment  - and there's enough of those that you'll probably not play the same kind of character twice, since it's hard to get the exact same kit.
There's an overarching story about four different factions vying for control of a nebula (and the rebel group of operators trying to end this war), but it's not that important to the game - though the tidbits of lore you come across are cool and interesting takes on scifi tropes.
Overall, a great game, and an absolute steal at 13€ - if you're getting it on a sale, snatch it

First off I haven't had a single gameplay or graphics glitch/issue (I got it after the patches). I run a single OC'ed HD7770 1GB (well below the minimum) it runs about 40 fps at 1920*1080 and will sometimes drop when loading large areas and stuff. The graphics settings are Environment: Med, Texture: High, Shadow: Low, Ambient Occulsion: SSAO, Bloom: On, AA: Off, VSync: On. You may think some of these settings sound bad, but in game play you really don't see it (and considering the crappiness of my GPU it looks very nice). In cutscenes the lower quality is visible, but it doesn't really matter (it doesn't effect the storytelling). The gameplay is highly replayable and very fun, the assassinations all feel different, even the multiple chasing parts of the game manage not to feel repetitive. Being 28.1 Hrs in I have completed the main quests, but not done much else. I feel the game will least 50 - 75 hours considering I have only been to about 1/3 of the map and haven't done the Dead King's DLC. My only problem with the gameplay is on some of the later harder assassinations if you die you go back to the start and need to do everything again. I was about 10 metres from escaping the area and a enemy shot me with a rifle :( and I had to redo about 20 - 30 minutes of gameplay again.
Even if you have to play at the lower/lowest (I have tried the lowest settings) quality graphics buy it for the fantastic gameplay.
Also the environmental/background audio for this game is awesome, it really helps give the world the feeling that it is alive.

edit: later impression:
beat the first of two story modes, started with the second of two characters
more of the same levels. Both characters have interesting abilities to try and make the most of, but the second character's moveset, if you can even call the amount of moves these characters can do a "set", is pretty uninspired.
These two have got less moves than a level 1 dynasty warriors character and never get more.
Granted, a lot of the game is about running around the square battlefields and kiting the crowds and dodging death, so it isn't fair to judge on the same criteria, since in this game evasive roll is the most important move.
The boss fights get sort of like a danmaku - bombs get randomly tossed about, each showing a ring of what their explosion radius is going to be, and you have to dodge and weave between all the rings, running from the mob and trying to take a swing at the boss - using abilities like, drop a stationary magnet that pulls the mob toward it, at key times. As I noted before, this games controls are pretty smooth, refined feeling.

The idea of commanding huge spaceships in space dogfights is what drew me to this game. The fact that is free just sealed the deal for me. Like the popular MOBAs out there, the game is free, and so all you lose by trying it out is time.
The game itself offers a very welcome twist to the usual "siege towers-kill base" of the aforementioned MOBAs, in that the game is centered around area domination. The way they split up the map (hence the "Fractured Space" name) also offers an interresting dynamic to the game. I consider it a good thing that the only resource in the game (Minerals) is shared with the team, and that there is no "farming" phase in the game. It feels like trimming the fat off a very delicious, laser-singed steak.This video explains more about how the game is played and what makes it different:
The ships are well designed and differentiated from one another. Every ship plays a bit differently, even if they belong in the same category.
Another important thing Fractured Space does right is how all roles feel satisfying. It does not matter whether you play a Support ship, an Assault ship or a Defense ship, the effects of your efforts are felt throughout the game.
Finally, all gameplay-specific unlockables are available with the in-game currency, so you're not really required to spend a dime on anything (even though the grind will take you a while).
Naturally, the game does have some problems, being fresh out of early acces now for a month. First of all, matchmaking. Since the player pool is still relatively small, I believe matchmaking should become more loose with chosing suitable players, so that games can be found more often. Matchmaking would be an extremely important factor in ranked games, which will presumably be added at a later date, but for casual play, there's really no need for matchmaking to take over 10 minutes of searching. Another minor issue is that of "daily quests". I appreciate the effort made by Edge Case Games to make the players' grind less grindy by offering bonuses for number of games played in a day, but I feel they could be more imaginative by adding game-specific quests such as "play with a Utility ship 2 times" or that kind of thing. The danger with that idea however is that it may change players' in-game behaviour.
Finally there is the issue of balance. The game seems pretty balanced to a rookie player like myself, but i'm sure there's a metagame being established somewhere in high-level play, and I do hope Edge Case are paying close attention to what's going on in all levels of play, so that they can balance the game properly at relatively close intervals.
Overall, the game is very good, and with the community slowly building itself up, I firmly believe that Fractured Space has a stellar future ahead of it.

It is not unlike a Rorschach test, you see what you want to see in this game. Unlike many indie darlings that deliver emotional stories, Dinner Date brings nothing to the table but some bread and wine.
That does not mean it is not an experience worth having, but do not expect the game to do the legwork for you. I could summarize the story, but it would detract from the experience. The premise however, is simple enough, a man waiting for a woman to arrive for a dinner date. As I am sure other reviews have pointed out, there is not much "game" here it more of an exercise in fiddling around. Your experience may be positive with the game, it may be negative; however, the experience itself is interesting and, like modern art, is really fleshed out in discussions after the fact.
You will complete the "scene" in approximately 15 minutes. My only real complaint is the price point of this “game”. I feel that $2.99 is excessively high for what it delivered. It was purchased on sale, and it is recommended others do the same. $1 is a safe price point.
Overall, recommended; but more of an academic experiment in exploring how gaming can tackle different methods of storytelling.

There's a scenario, in the philosophy of ethics, that asks you if it would be better to let a train stay its course and run over five people - or switch it and only run over one. Most people agree that they should - would - switch the tracks. But change the scenario a bit, where you instead have to push a person off the train yourself in order to save the five - and responses get more hesitant.
Make it five people dead in both choices, make the person you have to push off on death row - and you have the essence of The Walking Dead.
Strict utilitarianism would regard this game as a meaningless exercise in frustration. Despite what the game may claim, your choices aren't very significant. You can save a person - great, watch them die some chapters later. You can show compassion - great, you'll probably only have a pat on the back and some wasted supplies to show for it. You can pick all the fights you want - you'll get what you need done.
Most people aren't strict utilitarians. Therein lies the raison d'être of The Walking Dead.
Even if your actions have no long-term impact, perhaps the short-term impact is worthwhile. Maybe comforting that person is better than telling them to ♥♥♥♥ off, even if they'll die a scene later. Maybe giving your support to that person is better than telling them they're stupid, even if they'll do what they want to regardless. Maybe ending someone's misery is better than leaving them to the walkers, even if your hands get dirtied.
Maybe letting the train stay its course is better than pushing the person off, even if that person will die soon regardless.
But as the saying goes: one dead is a tragedy - one million dead is a statistic. When a person is tasked, over and over, with the train controls - do they constantly angst about it? Do they continuously murmur apologies and spend sleepless nights for the ones they shoved off and ran over? Or do they, at some point, wearily shrug their shoulders and punch the train switch based on the phase of the moon? Spare the other person on the train based on how attractive they look?
It can happen to the characters in-game, and it can happen to you.
Make your choice to play this game accordingly. The recommendation tells you my opinion.

You want to play "Final Fantasy III":
- To gain an appreciation for where the series, and many of its defining characteristics, come from.  This is where the Job Change system and many of the archetypes in "Final Fantasy" started.
You don't want to play "Final Fantasy III" because:

Before getting down to brass tacks, one needs to be reminded that this is an old game.  A 23+ year old game, actually.  So with that in mind, there can be times when FF3 feels archaic, grindy, and vague.  This is an NES game with a new coat of paint.  So, do not expect hand holding or a cake walk.
With that out of the way...
This is actually a port of a port, which usually instills fear into my heart, and while others have reported bugs, glitches, and downright unplayable circumstances, I have been lucky.  Nothing technical has disturbed my playthrough.  However, that doesn't mean the game is free from these issues.  It's kind of a, "buy at your own risk" sort of deal...
As for the game itself.  The new paint, while cartoonish, resonates very well with me.  While in battle, I get this odd deja vu feeling, because the art design and animations resemble FF9's quite a bit.  The world is just gorgeous compared to the NES version.  The music is the original, but redone with modern technology...you know...so it matches the non 8 bit paint job.
The writing, however, is atrocious.  I haven't played the original with the english fansubs, so I cannot compare the two, but this is easily B-team writing, if not C-team.  But, that's ok, because this game doesn't have a particularly good story anyway.  The story is...well...an NES story (it is basic and generic.  We don't see one of those classic Final Fantasy stories till the release of the SNES and FF4.)  If you want a good story, YOU WON"T FIND IT HERE!
But what you will find here is a fun and addictive leveling system.  Oh yes, the jobs system.
See, unlike some of the later games in the series where there are more party members than we know what to do with, this game has only our 4 innocent teens.  So, instead of leveling/grinding multiple people who may represent different classes, you focus on the same four heroes but have the option of switching their class/job.  There are 23 different jobs and every character can level each of those jobs (independantly of the other characters) to level 99.  This allows for diverse parties and the ability to adapt one's party for specific situations.
It's not as awesome as the ICONIC FF5 job system, but, this came out before that...on a weaker system...with a lower production budget...and a smaller dev team...
But, being simpler doesn't mean it's any less fun.
As for the battles themselves.  The ATB system hasn't been invented yet.  It's oldschool turn based.  The player inputs commands for all 4 characters at the same time, and they are executed in an order detrmined by the stats of both the characters and the enemies.  Then, repeat.  This can be a good or bad thing.  It can be frustrating if your mage strattles that line of sometimes healing before the enemy attacks and sometimes after it attacks...despite being the exact same enemy.  The system can be controlled to a degree if one knows the speed of their characters...and equips gear to make the characters faster or slower.
So, if one wants a TL;DR version...
-It's an OLD game (1990) with a new coat of paint
Pros:
-Seems remarkably stable despite being a port of a port.
-Job system is addictive and fun.
-Plenty of side quests/optional dungeons for treasure hunting.
-CHALLENGING!  Unlike many new games released today where one can get through without dying, there were many sections which took me a few tries to get through.  Strategy through trial and error creates a sense of accomplishment.
Cons:
-Horrible writing for a non existant story (indicative of late 80's/early 90's technology and gaming scene.)
-Kind of expensive for being a port...
If you are looking for a nostalgic, old-school JRPG game, here you go.  It's gritty.  It certainly won't appeal to many, "youngins," but if looked through the lens of the time it was released, it is a solid, and recommended experience.

Hotline Miami + FTL = Heat Signature.
At first, I was all like "ahh, kill everything", rushing like Rambo - and that's cool, you can do that, but then I started really taking advantage of the pause screen to use my different gadgets.  This leads to some really neat emergent gameplay scenarios.
For example:  I had to recover some technology.  Well too bad that tech was behind a locked door, and the key was somewhere in space, (because it was in the pocket of some guy my glitch trap jettisoned into space).  I used my swapper to swap places with a guard on the other side of the locked door, grabbed the objective and unlocked the doors.  Then I swapped that same guard into my glitch trap, sending him into the void too.
If you're a fan of the real-time combat and over-head play of Hotline Miami, but also appreciate the strategy/tactics of FTL and being able to stop/pause time to plan, then check this out.

My first character was Traveler Truth, and his mission in life was to rescue his kidnapped daughter. He was new at this stuff, but he muddled his way through, barely escaping terrible situations, building up a reserve of equipment, and finally saving enough to pay for the intel on where his daughter was.
He learned how truly nasty a ship full of shielded enemies is. He got captured one room away from his daughter.
When I went back to the character select I was in for a shock: one of them was Traveler Truth's father! Not only that, but he came with the perfect shield clearing weapon, a subverter grenade launcher. Pappy Truth was much more experienced, and by the time he had earned enough to pay for info on where his son was, he was ready to go. He found where the enemy's pilot was and took him out, leaving the ship dead in the water. Then he left, recharged his gear at a friendly station, and came back to methodically tear the ship apart to save his son.
Traveler Truth learned from his own mistakes and his father's triumphs, and less than an hour later, saved his daughter. The Truth family retired with two weapons named after them and six stations freed, leaving an indelible mark on the galaxy of Heat Signature that would not soon be forgotten.
Then, a couple hours later, I came across a character who wanted to rescue someone. Imagine my surprise when it turned out that he wanted to rescue a character from my friend's copy of the game! After a few good missions and lucky drops he managed to save Taiwan Whiteblood, and I chose to play as him next. All Taiwan wanted in the world was to kill the Offworld officer who had executed his son. He almost failed when he got knocked out and dragged out an airlock, the timer running out quickly. He went right back in, and at literally the last second he knocked out the pilot, took the controls, and accelerated past the station that the ship was about to dock with. He accomplished his bloody goal just a few minutes later.
That gave him enough liberation points to free another Offworld station, which was just enough to open up the stronghold liberation mission for the Offworld stronghold. Taiwan, left with no family and his revenge accomplished, knew what he had to do.
He rammed a ship into the stronghold while still at the pilot's seat. That night, everyone at the bar toasted to Taiwan Whiteblood, and they named the stronghold he freed Whiteblood Bastion.
Heat Signature isn't just a great emergent gameplay generator, it's an amazing gaming memory generator.

Before you get the pitchforks and torches to come after me for recommending this game, hear me out:
I recommend this game ONLY if you

understand that this game is

I love LEGO games. Each one does a great job combining the original story of the movie it was based on, as well as adding their own spin with LEGO humor. The Hobbit is no exception. I recently started playing The Lord of the Rings, and am able to compare their progression from one to the other. The Hobbit feels a little more refined in gameplay, and they added a few other fun aspects that I felt were done better than The Lord of the Rings. The Hobbit does a good job with what was from the first 2 movies, and adding humor to things along the way. They also have a bunch of extra content that will keep you busy for many hours. They even have a day/night cycle. So, when you think you've done all of the extra content, you in fact are only about halfway done with the extra content. There are also a TON of extra characters. 90% of them aren't needed, but they are fun to unlock and run around the world with.
As I mentioned before, this game is
complete.
From what I have read online they had every intention of including content from "Battle of the Five Armies". However somewhere down the road someone made the decision to not develop that content. Is that acceptable for a game company to abandon a project 2/3 of the way done and say "Here ya go, this is all you get"? Absolutely not. That's why I recommend only getting the game when it is CHEAP. Cheap development practices should mean they will charge the customer a cheap price. I would not recommend this game to someone new to the LEGO franchise. It may leave a bitter taste in their mouth and leave them questioning "Are all of the LEGO games unfinished like this?".
TL/DR; Get it if it is cheap, you are
new to the LEGO franchise, and you 110% understand that it's
finished. Don't get it if it isn't cheap, you are new to LEGO games, or not completely convinced the game is only 2/3 done.

Realm of the Mad God. ADDICTIVE. AS. ALL. HELL. Be warned, all ye who press the Play button!
Actually, with all seriousness, this game is really fun! I am an old skool gamer, so the pixelated style is right up my alley. The gameplay is also pretty good, with different characters and stats to level up by killing all sorts of beasts, gods, and conquering dungeons--including the one belonging to the Mad God Oryx himself.
There is lots of stuff to do, lots of people to play with and to help defeat your foes. Pets, rare items, dungeon crawling, beastie bashing... did I mention it is really addictive if you are into this sort of thing?
The big downside is the gold can only be purchased with real money, and the dollar to gold exchange rate really sucks (though I shouldn't expect complete fairness in a fantasy world, but still, $5 for 500 or 5,000 gold seems fair to me). There are some people who pay TONS to get the best gear, create the ultimate pet, and basically make themselves a pixelized Master of The Universe (He-Man not included).
With the constant, looming threat of permanent death (when you die, bye bye goes ALL your stuff... EVERYTHING), any money spent on your character will be tossed out the window the minute you fall in battle.
Overall, fun game, but the Pay-To-Win part is kinda lame. Gold exchange rate needs to be a bit fairer, but I doubt that will happen in all honesty.

Pretty great, actually. I was sort of expecting a button masher, but the combat mechanics are in fact well developed. You got your dodges, invincibility frames, special attacks and situational skills, different modes that increase your damage output for a decrease in defense. Good stuff here. The AI is a bit brain dead so far but it's not like I've played very far into it yet. The challenge modes seem pretty brutal though, and there are a lot of them, which I appreciate.
As a whole, Smashing The Battle reminds me a lot of Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae, a game which I really really like. And amongst many common traits, they also share the "virtue" of being well executed packages with fun gameplay.
The camera can be a bit wonky, it tends to end up turning bird-eye view, but it's easy to correct, even in the middle of battle. Nonetheless, it could definitely have used some better tracking. But as I understand it, this is supposed to be played in VR? I don't own or have any interest in one of those so I wouldn't be able to tell you how that works, but apparently it's there if that matters to you. It may either resolve or exacerbate the camera problems, I have no idea.
I wanted to leave this here as a "congratulations" to the developer, the game plays and runs great. He is also pretty on point with support, so that's definitely a plus. But also, I wanted to leave a word on the gameplay, since I bet a lot of people are going to see breasts and either immediately buy it or immediately dismiss it, which sometimes works but would be a shame here. This game deserves an honest shot.
A few mechanics are not as well explained as they should be. I have yet to figure out what is the purpose of "Scrap", even though I got a bunch of it.
,
Rescued workers have a really high chance of giving you another key when released. Always save them!
The rating system is a bit weird, and easily exploitable. Getting "Massive Kills" sometimes feels like it just fails, I have no idea what a "killstreak" is in the context of this game, but this is the only star that I always get, and the dodge counter, while cool, is not particularly well implemented. You can farm environmental hazards for those, or leave just a few enemies alive and farm them. So far, the numbers are always the same as well, and it feels like a missed opportunity. Have a stage where the requirement was to dodge a bunch of attacks would have been interesting, or clearing a stage without getting hit.
. The current system works fine enough as it is, but since the missions are already all pretty similar (as far as I can tell, which is not a lot) aside from the starting dialogue, not having more unique mission requirements feels odd.
There are different missions types. Most seem to be just arena type scenarios, you go in and get locked until everyone is dead, but some are waves, which I had already encountered but had forgot about, and I just stumbled upon a timed mission, which was nice. Even though the timer was actually really lenient I appreciate the change of pace. Good stuff.
I'm looking forward to unlocking the other character as well as the ability to get extra costumes.
Very nice difficulty curve. You start off with very easy and passive enemies but before long you are getting swarmed and fired upon from every possible direction. Situational awareness and good dodging become key, as well as efficient crowd control. Environmental hazards that are first introduced as simple obstacles along your path show up in later encounters and even boss battles, sometimes combined. Having to dodge spinning lightning rods, while the field is on fire, while a bunch of robots fire a ton of projectiles at me gave the game a very interesting vibe, almost bullet-hell -ish, but the punishment is never as severe. I have died when I got careless though, it certainly proved to not be the cakewalk that I thought it would be. Of course, you could always grind stages and upgrade the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your everything. Personally, I feel I've struck a nice balance.
I think I'll let this review be for a while and continue further into the game. I will probably update yet again once more stuff opens up and I have a better picture of the game as a whole. It's been very fun so far though. Definitely recommended.
So... I've now cleared both campaigns, played for a while. It starts pretty easy and stupid, the difficulty ramps up quite nicely and the last stages had me locked in the zone of situational awareness that few games can pull off right. I was surprised and pleased that upwards until level 25 of the second campaign (which would make it level 55 in general) the game was still introducing new attack patterns or expanding on older ones. It was really refreshing and made the last stretch of the game feel very tense as the bullet count on screen rose considerably. I also came to really like the camera going bird's-eye view because that IS the best view to deal with multiples incoming shots from every possible direction. Since attacks are telegraphed mostly by patterns on the floor, having a top-down view can seriously save you. So, yes. Camera. Actually pretty great.
The characters do play differently and required, at least in my experience and playstyle, different approaches to gameplay. With Sarah, I would usually gather enemies around with the magnets and try to clear them with the Great Spanner, her special attack, while evading anything I can for an SP boost, but her standard combo attack is pretty fast so I wasn't shy about getting in the face of enemies. I also never ever used her bombs. Mary's game for me was much more reliant on "hit 1" of her combo attack. Get in, hit, run. It was mostly an attrition game. I rarely used her "remote bot" with intents of exploding it, but as a means to get the surreal amount of fire off my back for a second so I could regroup.
About dodging: I really like how it works. Dodging consumes a bit of SP every time you use it. It's mostly negligible, but if you are low on SP and can't use your special attacks or Heal, dodging is probably what you want to do to get some SP back, since performing an Evade Bonus nets you 20 SP. The thing is that if you just mash the button, you are going to cannibalize your own earnings. I really like this system. It's not strict enough to be really punitive and screw you over, but it also hampers you back just enough that you will try to do it better until you can pull it off consistently.
"Massive Kills" still baffle me. Is it a number of enemies thing? Is it a cumulative damage dealt over HP total of enemies thing? I have no idea. I THINK it's damage related but I have no idea on how it actually works. I've farmed a few stages and consistently killed some mobs the exact same way every time, and I got the massive kill bonus about 50% of those times. It's pretty weird.
In retrospect, I think the additional suits have always been available for purchase, that's what "scrap" is for, but I never noticed as I never "confirmed" on the character selection screen before getting Mary. They are recolors, sadly, but they do come with special abilities. Running faster, increase in attack or defense. Etc. The bonuses are not the same from character to character, which I appreciate.
...I wish there was some sort of "point refund" system so I could try different builds or challenge runs.
All in all? Pretty good. Takes a while to warm up but it's worth it.

I play the NBA 2k games every year because basketball is my favorite sport and NBA 2k is, unfortunately, the only halfway decent sim on the market.  The problem with this is that they have no pressure to get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together.
I gave this game a positive review after playing maybe 10 hours because some basic issues with NBA 2k15 were fixed.  The movement feels more fluid than in that game.  NBA 2k15 is without a doubt the worst NBA 2k game ever made.  This is probably the 2nd worst game in the franchise though.  A new review is being written after playing many more hours.  I only play so many hours because I assume problems with the game are my own lack of skill for a bit, until you really get to notice specific problems.  I also just love basketball and keep getting fooled every year.  And it's such a shame because NBA 2k14 on next-gen console, not PC, had such great potential to be improved dramatically in the following years.  They removed all their progress for God knows what reason.
The big draw is that Spike Lee did the MyCareer mode, and frankly it's by far the worst career mode in any sports game I've ever played, or any game with any mode even remotely comparable.  They put you in a Spike Lee film basically, except Spike Lee was obviously not allowed to make something like he'd actually put in a film (most of his films are R rated and this game is E rated, so you can imagine all the things he'd have to censor himself about).
So they make your character's background be this incredibly stereotypical borderline offensive plotline, something which would be called racist if Spike didn't do it because it'd be called a parody of black life in New York.  You use 90s rap slang in a modern setting and have all kinds of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t happen which doesn't actually move the plot of you being a basketball player forward.  I'm shocked Big Daddy Kane didn't have a writing credit.  You play like 8 games, 4 high school 4 college, to determine your draft slot.  Not a terrible idea by itself.  But they paint your character the whole time as being this godsend of a player.  Think of the way Lebron was anticipated as a kid out of high school.  Yet, if you spend no VC on your character before the draft, he comes in as a 55 overall.  This makes your player the worst in the league, literally.
This is problematic for 2 major reasons: (other than the absurdity of being painted as Lebron and then coming in to be the worst in the league by far).

1) College and high school games are a complete waste of time.  Draft position couldn't matter less in any context, just your own role playing.  I normally care about draft position in these games, but they also usually care more about how I play during MyCareer in return.
2) You cannot skip this for new players.
After you're drafted, they only let you play 8 games of your first season.  It's abysmal.  Also, Spike's story actually has nothing to do with your real NBA career, i.e. the reason you're playing.  All it does is give you 2 hours of cutscenes interspersed between the pointless high school and college games.  There's hardly any actual story once you're a bonafide NBA player, which defeats the entire purpose of the mode.  The only thing you get are "meetings" with some select few famous players, and that's not actually anything more than clicking on menus and seeing some kind of a stat or VC boost at best.
The MyGM mode is plagued with the practice time issue.  It becomes a nuissance immediately.  The mode itself is pretty easy, it's nowhere near as complex as something like Out of the Park Baseball is, obviously, but it's probably as bad as its ever been.  The trade logic, despite promises to the contrary, is equal to how bad it always is.  There's always so many dumb trades you can pull off.  It boggles my mind that the game allows such game breaking trades to be made.
And the gameplay itself: again, the game feels better than it did last year, but not better than 2k14, and not better than almost any other year before that.  The shot meter is the one thing I like, and even that is bad half the time because you'll regularly miss perfectly aligned shot meter shots.  It defeats the purpose of the meter if you miss midrange jumpers with an 88 overall player on a perfectly in the green shot.
The game feels like one of those old hockey tabletop games where all the players are stuck to the floor and you can only rotate them to shoot in a puck.  The players feel stuck to the floor.  They are moved against gravitational logic into positions to contest shots in ways which, after watching replays, make you want to tear your hair out.  The AI still cheeses with the shots it takes and makes.
The teammate AI in the MyCareer mode is, honestly, worse than it was even last year.  It makes it so that on high difficulty you can average over 40 a game and a triple double and still lose by 20.  How am I supposed to win when I get double'd, pass it out to open guys who can't hit shots that I'd make in real life?  2k NEEDS to get their act straight because the game suffers immensely.
On PC the multiplayer modes have low populations.  The one mode which doesn't, where you take your MyCareer player to the park, has strange limitations.  If you don't choose to rep the park with the beach and the aquarium, you'll basically be left all by yourself in the ironworks park with no one to play with.  That mode has tons of hackers and cheaters in it, based on the complaints on the forums as well as what I've seen myself.  I haven't done much of that mode because the people who play that mode play almost exclusively that and you'll get killed repeatedly.  I'm really good at full team vs team basketball but the population is too low to rise in rank on that mode, all the people who play that regularly are already all at the top ranks.  You aren't allowed to play with higher ranked people for some reason in spite of population issues, it's a terrible design choice.
And the VC gouging.  Everything costs more.  More money.  Pat Riley talked about the disease of more, where people wanted more playing time and more money for themselves to break up a potentially winning basketball team.  Who knew that you could also apply it to a video game franchise about basketball?  This game feels like the biggest cash grab yet, and that's saying a lot given the antics of last year's game.  They kept the terrible ♥♥♥♥ing system of upgrading stats in blocks, and now you have even stricter limits on your player's ability to rise in rank.  I'm stuck at 88 overall, I can't figure out what I'm supposed to do to be allowed to go higher in rank.
And come on, 1000 VC for a ♥♥♥♥ing headband?  It's disgusting.  Absolutely disgusting.  I'm a fool for buying the game every year but I just love basketball so damn much.  If the Out of the Park guys made an NBA or even fictional basketball manager sim, I'd buy that in a heartbeat.  All the games that exist of that nature are awful, I've looked, so don't point me to that terrible basketball manager game that's on Steam. While I get the criticism this game receives, and the issues other players have really seem to be plentiful, the game has improved markedly for me with the last two patches. I mainly play MyCareer, and while the Spike Lee story really didn't add much to the game for me, it still is far and away the best basketball game out there.
The presentation is absolutely top notch, the graphics are outstanding and the game does a great job at emulating the NBA experience. The overhauled control scheme, while taking some time getting used to, is an improvement imo. And once you get out of the Spike Lee story, I found MyCareer in general to be much improved. Deciding between endorsments, spending time with teammates or fans and spending time in the gym adds a nice new form of progression to the game. However, I'd highly recommend getting the mobile app for the free daily VC, as earning it in-game can definately be a tedious process at first.
The gameplay itself is kind of intimidating to most people new to the game though, especially those not familiar with the game of basketball. I use the automatic offensive playcalling for example, and I consider myself a fan of basketball. Micromanaging all of the tactical aspects and playcalling during a game really adds a depth to the game that almost make it inaccesible. Thankfully, how much of the more in depth aspects of the game need to be controlled by the player is up to yourself. The game even offers numerous sliders to make the whole experience a lot more arcade like (or simulation like, if you're so inclined).
Even with all the valid criticism expressed in the other reviews here, this is the game for basketball fans. I own 2k15 as well and for me, this years version is an upgrade worth getting, especially as it's increasingly available at a reduced price during sales.

Half-Life 1 was probably the first game I ever played and strongly got me into PC gaming. Alongside Team Fortress Classic and Counter-Strike, I was so eager to swap from using a family PC to having my own PC just to simply play this game - that's how amazing it was, and still is! For its age, it has a really fantastic feel to it and an engine that has adapted for uses even today (such as Sven Co-op and other MODs).
The best thing about Half-Life of course is, as mentioned just now, the MODs that people create for this game. The GoldSrc engine is the only engine I see still being used very frequently nowadays and has such a great potential for newbie developers or even professional developers. Personally I have probably done everything possible with the engine, including map making, media (video/audio creation), modelling and more - it's a really great way to learn how to make your own MOD or possibly even your own game.
The actual game itself (Half-Life, its story and the multiplayer) is also incredible. The story is unique (and with the newer Half-Life games in the series, it's still unique!) and the multiplayer is addicting - especially on the MODs (TFC, CS, etc)!
I simply can't recommened this game enough - it's genuinely one of the best games out there!

This game is very fun, but incredibly frustrating. RNG is a thing. I will be honest, I started a campaign and was doing well, and then the RNG set in. I had to abandon multiple dungeons and couldn't complete anything. Maybe I was doing something wrong,  but I decided to delete my game and start fresh on the easiest setting. It seems to be more forgiving. I would encourage all first timers to do so. This second game start has gone a lot smoother. Granted I have still lost some heroes, but overall I don't get as stressed out with the game.
This game has very pleasing visuals. So far I have enjoyed the story and challenge. There a 2 things I can suggest that could make your life a lot easier. Make sure to max out your wagon upgrades. This will allow for the cap on heroes slots as soon as possible. I would also up the recruits to 3 with the first dungeon. The second point I cannot stress enough is; this is not your standard RPG game. It can be very difficult between battling and managing your stress you will have plenty of problems as you learn the game. Do not be afraid to run away from battles nor abandon a quest from time to time. You will have plenty of opportunities to get loot and move forward.
*Update 11/29/2017.
I have now played the game for over 100 days in game. It hasn't been easy, but I have learned a lot. Not quite finished. Think I have to kill 1 more boss and start the Darkest Dungeon quests. I would like to offer some more advice. The first being mindset. Don't approach this game like other games. When it comes to grinding your characters, never expect to become godlike. I have been notorious for over-leveling my characters in pretty much all games I play. Because of this, the end game content is rather easy. Darkest Dungeon is not that game. Sure by grinding up the levels you will unlock harder more difficult content which will allow you to get better loot, but it comes with a price. Monsters in higher tier areas are more menacing then ever. Everything seems to hit way harder and your stress can skyrocket in the blink of an eye. Heroes will die. This is how Darkest Dungeon works. But don't let it bring you down, and do not be afraid to abandon a quest if it gets really dicey.
Next point. Slow and steady. Don't rush through the levels to unlock harder content too quickly. Take your time, enjoy the game and learn the enemies, because life doesn't get easier. Challenges arise. And this is a huge appeal to me. Also, do not be afraid to remove Heroes with terrible quirks from your roster. Keep that roster clean if need be. I have removed so many Heroes from my roster. This will allow you to farm resources and money to make your overall roster strong in the long run.
Final point. Based on my experiences, I would highly encourage maxing the following buildings in this order Wagon, Guild, Blacksmith. Also before completing these fully make sure to get 2 slots for your Sanitarium. I say this because locking in some good quirks as you level is a great idea if you plan on keeping the hero. Plus random events will happen that will make this cost free. When this occurs, you will be able to lock in 1 positive and remove 1 negative quirk at no cost per Hero. So doing that 2 times is great.

This is the best casual Dota-inspired game that I've played. Heroes of the Storm missed the mark for me -- it was decidedly less competitive while not being quite easy enough to pick up without learning the meta. Fractured Space hits the sweet spot, with a wide variety of ships that manage to stay balanced while offering a lot of different ways to play. The lane-pushing gameplay has been stripped down to its essentials, which puts the focus on teamfighting and tactical skill -- where it should be IMO. Ships are locked behind a grind or pay wall, but the cheaper ships are very competitive and you get them at a very comfortable rate. The newer and more expensive ships will take longer to grind for.
My biggest complaints have to do with the UI. It's very difficult to spot the tiny text that tells you what disables are affecting you and what the status of your armor and the enemy's armor is, and though the AI crewmembers do a pretty good job of calling out relevant information to you, in big teamfights it becomes very difficult to tell what's going on, arguably more so than in Dota. A better HUD would make this game trully stellar.

1.	Game must contain real-time graphics – check
2.	Game must contain human interaction – check
3.	Game must contain at least 15 minutes of gameplay –check
Left off the list of requirements were fun, meaningful gameplay, script, and direction. This would have required some additional thought on the creator’s part and it’s just not something that could be bothered with.
There’s a warning right off that you are not playing … well, that’s as far as you need to read because there is no gameplay. Hitting keys on the keyboard will cause your character to look at different points of the screen as the events unfold. You’re greeted with a completely unintelligible and unscripted narration which meanders frequently and even manages to be a bit racist.  Apparently, you suffer from both Parkinson’s disease and attention deficit disorder since the camera is constantly faffing about. The entirety of the “game” doesn’t require your input and will automatically unfold even if you decide not to interact with it. Yes, this is a “game” that you don’t even have to play.
This is a product which can only be considered art by those who don’t know what art actually is. It’s like having a friend that extols the virtue of paintings of dogs playing poker.  If you’re one of these people that believes this is art or there’s some meaningful message hidden away to be examined with methodical thought then please just refrain from pretending to be a contributing member of society.
Stay as far away from this as you possibly can. Even the time you have taken to read through this regarding this work is time better spent generating dander or turning food into waste. Actually, that action produces something more valuable than this so I would encourage you to perform that.

Put simply, this game's sale price, one or two weapons and about 2 or 3 levels are its only saving grace. If you can get it to run at all, of course. I'm not the type of person that gives a thumbs down for nothing, so I'll delve a little deeper.
Before I go on, a word of warning: this game is wildly unstable and hard to get up-and-running properly. This is also one of the main reasons I gave it a thumbs down, it's just too damn unstable, even with all the patches, fixes and running it at 1366x768 if you have a 16:9 monitor, it's the only resolution that looks good and runs relatively well, anything above 1000px in height crashes every third quickload.
But let's say you got it to run, so what are you getting? As far as presentation goes, it's dated, but not entirely garbage. The weapon models are done alright, the character models not so much, but the enemies some of the environments are what stood out to me. The sound design is also pretty good, music is minimal but effective in helping the visuals set a really dark/gloomy atmosphere, the weapons sound really good too. The problem is, they only sound good.
The weapons in this game, while cool on paper, are the most puny, unimpactful pieces of trash I've ever seen in an FPS game, which is a shame, because in the original Blood, the enemies were tough, but the guns packed a punch hard enough to balance it out. Here, the vast majority of enemies take A LOT of ammo to kill. For example, there are these bug-like creatures that take 70 assault rifle rounds to kill. EACH. Granted, you can carry 500 rounds, but what the hell does that help if there's 3 of them along with some other (even tougher) enemy types, that maybe take 100 assault rifle rounds and 20 Tesla charges to kill? The Tesla cannon is the only weapon with some semblance of punch, but ammo for it is scarce. The Napalm launcher has been neutered to the point of insignificance. It simply kils nothing. Weak. I don't know if this is a problem with the actual weapon damage or the enemy hitboxes, but the bottom line is that the way the guns and enemies work together SUCKS. The only cool weapon is the Hook thing you get in the Nightmare levels, which spawns portals that shoot out chained hooks that pull the enemy towards said portal; if you spawn enough of them, the sorry sack of meat to end up in its grasp will literally by ripped apart slowly. Cool stuff. Why not more of that and less generic, bulletchomping crud?
I think the main problem with this game is simply that it's artificially difficult to the point of ridiculousness; unfair, cheap, and most importantly, not fun, 80% of the time. I'm not new to 90s FPS games (in fact, if you have a quick look at my library, you'll see that it's pretty much the bulk of what I play) and I completed the first Blood, but this game is just... frustrating. Most enemies are (as mentioned) bullet sponges, hit-scanning enemies have an accuracy so high that two of them will get you from 200HP to 34HP in a matter of seconds, hard-hitting projectile enemies are often spawned in small areas with no way to dodge the projectiles or even the splash damage, ammo is distributed poorly, health even more so, the boss battles suck (especially the Nightmare boss) etc. It doesn't click, most of the time is what I'm saying.
I could go on and on about this but let me just use the Behemoth enemy type as an example. It's the boss of chapter two. I had to empty 100 sniper bullets and the ENTIRETY of my Tesla cannon to defeat it. In chapter 3, it's a fairly common enemy type, and it's not even one bit weaker, not to mention the game often spawns two at a time. Sure, they infight with other enemies, but you're still wasting massive resources to defeat an enemy which ultimately doesn't even need defeating because you can just run past it. In general, the balance of resources vs. enemies that good FPS titles like DOOM, Quake, Shadow Warrior, Duke Nukem, the first Blood etc. got down to a tee is completely absent here. I literally speedran/skipped upwards of 2/3 of a level because I just couldn't be bothered to stand there and pump hundreds and hundreds of rounds into these tenacious wastes of disk space. Let me illustrate the situation: in the penultimate level, the game spawns three of these large, tough and powerful Lich-like enemies into a narrow-ish corridor. They fire napalm-like fireballs with huge splash damage and you have nowhere to dodge. Hm, should i just... run past and avoid them completely or use up all my hard-earned ammo so that I'm left ammo-less for the sure-to-follow boss encounter?
There is a forgettable and rushed story in there somewhere, but the voice acting is bad (even Caleb's voice actor, who is excellent, has some downright cringy moments), the villain is an annoying, pompous tw4t, the Chosen are about the least memorable crew I can think of. The expansion is less than two hours and has the most lazy writing I've seen in a while and the most annoying boss in the entire game (who the hell makes a boss that shoots undodgeable homing projectiles?). The only way I could beat it without cheats is to literally get it stuck in the world geometry and hold LMB until the thing dropped and I had the intense satisfaction of listening to Gideon's disgusting voice narrate the end of this nightmare.
That's not to say this game is ALL bad. It has a vibe that really hadn't been done before and honestly hasn't been done since. The controls are great and smooth, as they should be for a 90s FPS, the levels are non-linear and the architecture is, for the most part, well designed (even though some levels like the subway train or Cabalco offices are lazily re-used up to THREE times), and in terms of actual good gameplay; what about the other 20 or so percent that ARE fun? Well, the gore system and gibbing in this game is immensely satisfying, when everything clicks, it's pure 90s FPS mayhem as it should be, but this is sadly so rare that I can just barely state these moments exist.
All-in-all, unless you're a die-hard Monolith fan (which I can't blame you, they made much better things than this disappointment) or you find the prospect of bulletsponge enemies and frequent crashing fun, I'm having a hard time recommending this game, even if it does cost 1.5€ during sales. If it ran properly, I'd probably give it a "barely recommend" and just caution everyone to be aware of it's questionable design and cheapness, but since it's also a buggy mess, I just can't recommend it.

Actually, with all seriousness, this game is really fun! I am an old skool gamer, so the pixelated style is right up my alley. The gameplay is also pretty good, with different characters and stats to level up by killing all sorts of beasts, gods, and conquering dungeons--including the one belonging to the Mad God Oryx himself.
There is lots of stuff to do, lots of people to play with and to help defeat your foes. Pets, rare items, dungeon crawling, beastie bashing... did I mention it is really addictive if you are into this sort of thing?
The big downside is the gold can only be purchased with real money, and the dollar to gold exchange rate really sucks (though I shouldn't expect complete fairness in a fantasy world, but still, $5 for 500 or 5,000 gold seems fair to me). There are some people who pay TONS to get the best gear, create the ultimate pet, and basically make themselves a pixelized Master of The Universe (He-Man not included).
With the constant, looming threat of permanent death (when you die, bye bye goes ALL your stuff... EVERYTHING), any money spent on your character will be tossed out the window the minute you fall in battle.
Overall, fun game, but the Pay-To-Win part is kinda lame. Gold exchange rate needs to be a bit fairer, but I doubt that will happen in all honesty.

Well, lets get back to the game itself as of now at this point of day for my self review. Don't get me wrong here, despite all I said above I still love and like this game whatever everyone says about this.
+ Great visual and stunning graphics
+ Customizable Assassins
+ Good story or should I say a love story huh?
+ COOP System is remarkable
+ You can play singple player while searching for COOP is on going. It's not a two seperate modes. Sort of interlinked together which is great.
+ Do you know that when you're playing single player and someone is playing multiplayer that needs a buddy to play with then out of the blue a messenger will come running at on you or sometime it looks like an assassin is chasing you single player then tells you "A friend needs your help!" and you decide whether to accept to join him on a coop mission.
+ Replayability, you can keep on playing it even if you have completed the main story. You can still do the other missions that are not connected to the main story. I've completed mine in about 40hrs on the main campaign mission but I also did some few side missions and coop plays too. If you're gonna sync it 100% on everything might be 70-100hrs I guess assuming you'll enjoy coop and more exploration.
- Parkour and controls can be often frustrating than the previous ones (Others said it is fluid once you master it but I guess we need more time to learn it.)
- Demanding hardware requirements (This! Be ready for it and make sure you meet the system requirement.)
- Some small minor bugs I noticed on NPCs
- Sometimes it crashes after playing 3-4hrs not sure why. It's rare but it's there.
This game minimum system requirements is GTX 680 and min 2gb vram, this gpu have 1536 CUDA cores. This doesn't mean if you have a card higher than 680 in numbers you're good! Your GPU target must be in highend line not mid range or entry range. In short your card needs to be
GTX 760 / 770M and up, GTX 960 / 960M and up if you want to run it at least on med/high settings on FullHD resolution. Of course you can get some mid-range class cards and settle to run it on med/custom settings at lower resolution.
But I Still recommend this game despile all the negative reviews. If those negatives don't have the patience and virtue to wait for Patches then I feel sorry for them. I say buy it guys but only during SALE maybe on 50% or better on 75% off. It's a good game above all those negative reviews and hate of everyone who despised this game that much.
PS: Don't let the negative reviews fool your own opinion and judgement until you have tried it yourself. If you know you have good decent hardware the passed the system requirements then buy it and play with the video setting that you system can only afford to run. Do not be a dreamer on running on highest possible settings that your system cannot even afford. Don't make such comparison about optimization on other games. This is game is on a whole lot different level that everyone should understand, deal with it and accept the fact thats already how it is.

This game is very fun, but incredibly frustrating. RNG is a thing. I will be honest, I started a campaign and was doing well, and then the RNG set in. I had to abandon multiple dungeons and couldn't complete anything. Maybe I was doing something wrong,  but I decided to delete my game and start fresh on the easiest setting. It seems to be more forgiving. I would encourage all first timers to do so. This second game start has gone a lot smoother. Granted I have still lost some heroes, but overall I don't get as stressed out with the game.
This game has very pleasing visuals. So far I have enjoyed the story and challenge. There a 2 things I can suggest that could make your life a lot easier. Make sure to max out your wagon upgrades. This will allow for the cap on heroes slots as soon as possible. I would also up the recruits to 3 with the first dungeon. The second point I cannot stress enough is; this is not your standard RPG game. It can be very difficult between battling and managing your stress you will have plenty of problems as you learn the game. Do not be afraid to run away from battles nor abandon a quest from time to time. You will have plenty of opportunities to get loot and move forward.
*Update 11/29/2017.
I have now played the game for over 100 days in game. It hasn't been easy, but I have learned a lot. Not quite finished. Think I have to kill 1 more boss and start the Darkest Dungeon quests. I would like to offer some more advice. The first being mindset. Don't approach this game like other games. When it comes to grinding your characters, never expect to become godlike. I have been notorious for over-leveling my characters in pretty much all games I play. Because of this, the end game content is rather easy. Darkest Dungeon is not that game. Sure by grinding up the levels you will unlock harder more difficult content which will allow you to get better loot, but it comes with a price. Monsters in higher tier areas are more menacing then ever. Everything seems to hit way harder and your stress can skyrocket in the blink of an eye. Heroes will die. This is how Darkest Dungeon works. But don't let it bring you down, and do not be afraid to abandon a quest if it gets really dicey.
Next point. Slow and steady. Don't rush through the levels to unlock harder content too quickly. Take your time, enjoy the game and learn the enemies, because life doesn't get easier. Challenges arise. And this is a huge appeal to me. Also, do not be afraid to remove Heroes with terrible quirks from your roster. Keep that roster clean if need be. I have removed so many Heroes from my roster. This will allow you to farm resources and money to make your overall roster strong in the long run.
Final point. Based on my experiences, I would highly encourage maxing the following buildings in this order Wagon, Guild, Blacksmith. Also before completing these fully make sure to get 2 slots for your Sanitarium. I say this because locking in some good quirks as you level is a great idea if you plan on keeping the hero. Plus random events will happen that will make this cost free. When this occurs, you will be able to lock in 1 positive and remove 1 negative quirk at no cost per Hero. So doing that 2 times is great.

I'm a fan of the NBA 2K series for some time now, I have played every single game since 2K11 extensively and I have played NBA 2K16 for close to 150 hours at the time of this review.
NBA 2K16 is the best sports simulation game I have played to date. Unlike franchises like FIFA and Pro Evolution Soccer, 2K constantly reinvents it's game on a yearly basis rather than release the same product just with updated rosters every year.
This year's title is a big step forward from the last one and it manages to do a lot of things right, particularly now after a few patches.
If you're a basketball fan or even if you're just looking for a fun sports game to play casually, I would fully recommend you pick up this game even at full price.
The game's launch was not without it's issues, from gameplay tweaks that were made through patches and performance issues on PC... It was not a complete disaster but far from a perfect launch, from the inability for keyboard users to edit keybinds to graphic settings rendering the game unplayable it took some doing to get a great experience out of it at launch. As of the time of this review, most of these issues have been addressed though a little history never hurts anyone looking to make an informed purchase.
The game boasts fairly good visuals and don't even get me started on the gameplay... It is by far the best basketball simulation game I have ever played, actually make that the best sports simulation game!
Relatively low requirements on the hardware front make it accessible to a wide range of consumers which is always good though I'd recommend at least meeting the recommended requirements for a complete visual experience.
For comparison's sake, I run the game on a GTX 970 (non-OC) and an i5 4690k (OC to 4,2 Ghz) with every possible filter injected (8x Supersample + 8x MFAA + FXAA) via Nvidia control panel and it runs silky smooth at 60 FPS at a 1080p resolution without GPU usage ever going above around 80% so we're dealing with a decent port here.
When it comes to gameplay, most of the cheese tactics from previous years have been nullified in this year's game. Want to drive baseline and get a bucket everytime? Better boot up 2K15 then because it's not happening in 2K16.
Excellent AI defense makes it a challenge to score every trip down the floor, mindless attempts to get to the basket will most likely result in blocked shots than in points, attempting to thread the needle through defenders will probably end up in a turnover... These are but a few examples of how AI has been improved this year.
Most game modes are back and better than before, such as myGM and myTEAM. Up-to-date rosters, new and better animations and all other goodies that one might expect are also a part of the package.
The myCAREER mode was highly hyped as a Spike Lee directed story and I'm afraid it was arguably this game's greatest letdown. You follow your player's career since high school, into college and eventually into the NBA although in some key points along the ride you're faced with decisions which are presented to you but you really have no deciding power over what happens next. You're only able to play 8 games during your rookie year in the league (9 if your team makes the playoffs) the rest will be automatically simulated. This game mode opens up once you reach your sophomore year in the league however and from there the experience is excellent.
The typical flavor of the month builds for myPLAYERs still exist after every patch, if you're looking to play myPARK or other online modes extensively this information might be of value to you.
Also there are some latency issues for non-NA players, I personally can't make a jumper online because of this.
myTEAM mode gets content updates regularly, but not regularly enough and most of the content it gets is irrelevant. This mode along with myPARK are the modes I'd classify as the 2 main attractions of the game when it comes to online play so I definitely see this as a negative. Most new packs contain only 1 or 2 relevant new cards and the rest will literally never see the light of day and have no use aside from contributing towards collection rewards.
NBA 2K16 is a solid 9/10 if I was asked to resort to that rating system.
It's not a perfect game, but the issues it has have not dragged down the experience for me. The revamped gameplay and gorgeous visuals keep me coming back for more.
The game is well worth it's full price and a complete must-have for any basketball simulation fan.

First let me start by saying that my recommendation for this game comes with the understanding that it is incomplete, and that it likely won't be complete until Q3 or Q4 this year (2017) at best by my estimation. This judgement is based on the game as it is today, not for what the devs say they plan for it to eventually be. Furthermore, this is only a recommendation in the sense that there is no "situational yes" option, and this review will primarily focus on negative aspects of the game as it is now.
Missions are basically the equivalent of radiant quests in skyrim for those who are familiar with it - essentially it's just the game giving you the exact same mission over and over: [Kill X unit or group] [Gather X of Y resource] [Go to the supply crate], but in a different spot. You finish them and they'll just come back immediately after. Once you've unlocked all the important parts you won't even care to do the missions since you can build or buy them -money isn't an issue as time goes on.
Base building exists to a degree, but you'll come to realize that it gets tiresome being chained to one area so that you can always go back to your base. There's no map to speak of, only a radar, so you will eventually have trouble finding your main base if you build multiple to avoid that. In fact, the most efficent thing to do is plant a storage unit anywhere, and then carry a second on your tech for permanent access to your storage items without having to let your SCU set up, which defeats the purpose of building a base.
Block type viability is definitely an issue, as you'll be running into fights no matter where you go. The "construction" bricks are essentially the go-to thanks to durability and space for mounting more weapons, while 2 of the other 3 types are all but useless for anything save speed (which is useless unless you want a flying tech, which is also kind of useless). The third type of brick is supposed to be smaller in size than the construction, but meant to be heavy armor - but the fact of the matter is that they feel LESS durable than construction, and ultimately more of a liability than simply using construction bricks. This doesn't limit the creativity aspect of the game, but it does affect combat viability, and you're going to be in combat a lot. The alternative is to stack shields/repair bubbles, which requires a ton of batteries (explosion hazards), which will weigh you down until you move at a snails pace.
Lastly, the biggest issue with the game right now is optimization. Everything is fine and dandy for the first couple of hours, but when you start running into medium and large sized enemies, you'll find that the goal in their design was simply "stick as many guns on it as you can". This is a problem because enemies start showing up as full groups of 4-5 techs, and when they all open fire... Get ready for 5-10 fps. That's not even on high/beautiful, that's on "good" settings with a gtx 770 and an i5, well above recommended requirements.
All of that said, the game is still fun for those of us that like to create and destroy in equal measure. It's certainly a good way to spend some free time where you don't want to get invested in a story, or get caught up in a mission you can't leave part way through. You can drop in and out as you please, and you won't be too bored so long as you have an idea to try out, or want to blow things up.
TL;DR - Game needs some serious work in places, but is still functional, and is certainly worth a try. The biggest thing to worry about is optimization, so don't believe what is posted in the requirements section right now because you probably won't even want to play if you barely pass. Worst case scenario you ask for a refund, it won't take you 2 hours to figure out whether or not you like the game as is.
Edit: 11/7/17 Review still stands as is. Still has lots of giant enemies built entirley of batteries, bubbles, and long range guns. Still has performance issues and incomplete optimization, most notably huge FPS loss when near previoulsy mentioned giant bubble techs. Still has repetitve quests (though new types have been added to be fair). Also still worth trying.

This is the word that sums up my experience with this game.
I'm a huge fan of the Final Fantasy games and never judge them on graphics alone.
What really upset me about this game is its 'simplicity'.
I think they had some amazing ideas and concepts in this game but I felt they didnt elaborate more on them.
For example.
The magic system is broken down into different 'levels' 1-8 if I recall. For each level of magic requires its own 'MP'. The higher your Job level the more MP you gain. Not a bad system to that point, what really lets it down is you can only have 3 spells on each level. As far as I know and I could indeed be wrong but you cannot remove the spells once learned, again dont take my word on this point but I couldn't personally, remove them.
The only way to gain MP is through 'springs' and 'resting @ an Inn'. Sometimes there are just none of either. So yeah, fustratting.
The Jobs part of the game is far too shallow.

The ONE thing that drives me insane and I mean INSANE is the sheer amount of 'random battles', I mean dear mother of god  you cant go a few feet but you're in yet ANOTHER battle. It makes the game incredibly annoying and you combine that with a few of the points I made above, it makes for just a pain in the butt experience.
The storyline seems decent but the game mechanics are too simple.
In short if your a die hard fan such as myself, then play this, you'll enjoy it to some extent anyway.
Other than that, I dont recommend this one.

Pros

2) Simple graphics that can run on anything, anywhere.
3) Pseudo-penalty system with a simple system for mostly retaining items on death.
Cons

Spawns for even basic mobs are consistently limited -- absolutely no instancing short of paying for them. Consequently, experience is slow.
VERY few types of equipment and items.
There is not really too much to do once you've learned the ropes. Experience areas are limited.

Heat Signature captures very well the idea of emergent gameplay, of setting rules and boundaries and watching as I accidentally blow myself out into space trying to murder someone quietly.  The gameplay itself is fun and tense, with a surprisingly balanced progression system, mainly centered around items a little more consistently for a strong start.
What I like best, though, is the way the game frames your learning through experimenting and adapting.  I got a breach grenade launcher for the first time, finally giving me the ability to destroy chunks of the spacecraft I was in.  I saw a group and killed both them and the guards in the next room who were sucked out by the vacuum.  That's when I realized one of those guards had a keycard I needed to move forward in the ship.  And that's when I realized the full capabilities of the teleporter I had just picked up.  I'm forced to learn from my mistakes while running through ships and trying to pilot them away before another ship destroys them.  I'm forced to learn from watching my character die a slow death in space because I suck at piloting my pod.  This is a smart game, and I love the ways I'm stupid in it.

Although this game is mostly typing, the game is A LOT more fun than what meets the eye.
When you first look at the game, it looks like this boring typing thing and you would immediately scroll past it. But when you actually play the game. the first few hours are really fun ( depending if you can understand some of it). Sure, I may be just a couple hours in this game, but it's just so much fun that I couldn't wait to make a review.
The game is really interesting as, unlike other hacking games or movies, it has some realism to it with actual commands and it isn't your average Hollywood " BOOM. DONE" type of hacking as you have to take your time to be careful and not mess things up.
Sure, you may get frustrated at some points in the game but as soon as you find out how to get past it, it feel like you are a HACKING GOD.  Sometimes the reason I feel like the creators of this game made some of these levels hard was not just to have some challenge put into the game, but to also make sure that you are immersed into this game and to make sure that you are actually hacking something.
Overall, this game is AMAZING and I highly recommend to anyone who is reading this to, at the very least try the game.
I also forgot to mention that there is a pretty good soundtrack to it and that it's based upon the linux terminal and unix commands

Noir Syndrome isn't the best detective game, but it's one of the more interesting takes on the genre. I can't honestly say there are any other games I know of that can distill a whole organicly woven detective story into a few spare minutes, and that's something this game manages to achieve in a way that's also replayable. Noir Syndrome won't last you long in a single sitting, as repetition can set in after subsequent playthroughs in a row, but I've found it's a comforting and unique little gem to return to when I want to kill a few glorious minutes as a private eye.

Upon playing Noir Syndrome, I did question the meaning of “procedurally generated”. When I think of procedural generation, I think of something like Diablo, or Don’t Starve, not to mention all the rogue-like games out there. The point of procedural generation in games is to create a world which varies just enough to allow re-playability.
The way this works is very simple. You talk to people and collect a list of suspects. Once you have enough evidence, and through the process of elimination, you can arrest some one on your list. That is essentially the game. It reminds me somewhat of Where in the world is Carmen Sandiego, where you gather descriptors of your villain to finally arrest them.
Asides from the main mystery, you can try to complete challenges (for example, use a lockpick five times), collect costumes, hunt bounties, as well as ensuring you are well-fed (using money you gain from bounties or find in the world). You can also use your gun if need be. But these are all little things that have been added to the game in an attempt to create depth without actually doing so. When it comes down to it, all this extra is for naught.
When you solve the case, game over. If you want to replay, you start from scratch, with the killer being randomly generated, along with all the suspects and evidence. In reality, this game is not procedurally generated, rather it has a randomly generated outcome. In effect, the world, the mystery, and the story do not change from one game to the next, only the clues you use to solve them.
I think the effort put into making this game procedurally generated has, in turn, detracted from any of the noir-ish qualities it should have. Because it’s procedurally generated, characters don’t have personalities, or even distinguished faces (the pixel graphics are far from slick). While an intro sets the serial killer up to be some Egyptian cult fanatic, nothing more is ever mentioned or resolved around it.
Setting something in the mid-20th century, with Speakeasys, diners and the mob are not enough to make something “noir”. It’s the cynicism of the protagonist, the fatalism of the femme fatale, or the moral ambiguity of the resolution. Noir Syndrome does not have a story at all, let alone any of these things. The “noir” concept is a skin applied to a simple puzzle game.
But the soundtrack is at least jazzy.
Noir Syndrome is a little puzzle distraction in the same vein as Where in the world is Carmen Sandiego?. There is not a huge amount of depth to the puzzle, to the world, or to the re-playability, so I would hold off on buying the game for full-price, or perhaps buy the Android version instead.
